Eldinor the owner and bartender of the Seagull Inn is serving drinks here.
An elven lamplighter is resting here.

This is the most famous meeting-place in Harlond where people of all sorts exchange news, rumours, deals and friendships. Sailors from the entire coast of Middle-earth, as far as Dol Amroth and even Pelargir, are frequent guests here. For the sleepy, there is a reception and chambers upstairs.
1673: A vast variety of ropes are made here, from common tarred hemp-rope to soft elven ropes, which are far stronger than their size appears. Also, the heavy, coarse ropes used for ships' rigging are woven here.
1674:
An elven youth is busy attending to the animals.
A black and white cat is playing here.

This spacious barn has obviously been set up to function as a stable. Along two facing walls are arranged stalls and loose-boxes. At the end of each of the stalls pegs and stout racks have been fashioned, to accommodate tack and feed buckets; the uniformity of these suggests that perhaps these stalls are used by the mounts of the Elven garrison stationed here. The loose-boxes, by contrast, appear to be used less regularly, and are most likely for livery animals. But whether for steeds of citizens or visitors, the accommodations are universally clean and well-maintained, with thick beds of new straw on the floor, and clear water in long troughs for every animal.
1675:
A fine marble chessboard with ivory and ebony pieces is set here.
An Elven innkeeper stands ready to sign up his guests.

Happy to find a bed that does not heave and roll, sailors and travellers can get a good night's sleep here with their belongings safely stashed away. On the way to your room you see a bulletin board. It appears that you can easily find out about changes in Middle-earth. The Inn is downstairs.
1676:
A small sign rests on the counter.
Faldor the weaponsmith is here demonstrating his latest work.

Grey Havens is a peaceful town and not famous for its fine weapons, but the good old elven craftmanship guarantees that no junk is sold here. Few of these weapons ever find other places than as decorations in chic homes, but if need be, they are as sharp and deadly as any. The only exit from the small shop is to the west.
1677: This small street runs south between a few trees and north towards a large shipyard. There are no buildings around here, only trees with thick, brushy undergrowth. It looks like a park that is nurtured to grow wildly, maybe to remind the citizens of The Grey Havens of the wilderness outside their city walls.
1678: You stand on a small north south street. Many trees shade this road and the air is a bit cool. A large decorated square lies to the south and a large shipyard lies north. Off to the west barely visible through the trees is a small building.
1679:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

You stand in an ornately decorated square in the middle of the city. Many people relax here after a hard day's work and listen to the music of one of the many travelling bards who make a point to stop here. To the west and east you can see the two parts of a delightful garden.
1680: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The street continues north and south, running between buildings of all shapes and sizes. To the east, there is a small building, with the sounds of yelling, shouting, and clanging steel coming from within. To the west a narrower lane sneaks away out of sight.
1681: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
This is Central Street, which leads north and south. To the east, the clanging of metal suggests a blacksmith selling hard armour of high quality, and you can buy softer garments to the west.
1682:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An elven citizen is here enjoying the day.
A singing, happy drunk is staggering about here.
This is the beginning of Central Street. It continues north leading between many large and small buildings. To the west is a small park and to the east is a large white building.
1683: An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

You have entered a small out of the way park. The grass is well kept as are the bushes and trees that are scattered here and there. There are small benches placed under the shady trees in several spots and many elves come here for peace and quiet.
1684: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Although the lane is narrow, there is still room for trees planted at irregular intervals. They help to give shadow during sunny days. The people filling the streets have lived here far longer than mortals imagine and have had plenty of time to create a pleasant atmosphere. To the west you can catch a glimpse of Osse's well and the lane continues to the north.
1685: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The street turns south-east here, but an open space lies north through a small arch. The surrounding houses are old, some plain, some ornamented but all decorated with red and yellow flowers and an occasional climbing plant.
1686: This is a small yard that happened to be left open by the surrounding houses. Elven kids are playing here, and the local cats are hunting for mice in the corners. A low archway leads out to the street to the south.
1687: An elven tailor is standing here, tidying his selection.

This shop is very finely furnished. Exotic clothing and materials lie here and there, hung on pegs and neatly folded on tables. A wide selection of more mundane and utilitarian clothing is also available, for those who enjoy a more rugged lifestyle.
1688: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

A narrow, sneaky alley this is, but it is not at all unfriendly. Neighbours are talking loudly to each other from one window to another across the street and elven children are running around playing hide-and-seek in the backyards and obscure twists of the street. The alley goes east-west here.
1689:
A large bulletin board, entitled "Thieves' Guild Board", is mounted here.
A weapons rack stands against the wall.
An elven hunter is here, ready to teach.

Solid wooden beams criss-cross the angled ceiling of this airy comfortable house. A few narrow but equally strong wooden columns support the roof. During the day, light streams through the many round skylights. During the night, brass lanterns hanging from the ceiling beams come alight. Rows of spacious wooden shelves line the walls, filled with all manners of hooks, ropes, nets, strings, wooden and metal pieces, and a variety of hunting equipment.
1690: A clear spring generally used for relaxation is here.

This lovely area surrounded by a tall gate gives Cirdan a place to come and relax when he wants to be alone. In the centre of the room is a natural spring turned into a private bath large enough for several people to comfortably rest in. Since the water is constantly cycling through it is quite drinkable and very relaxing. Throughout the area are numerous trees of all types and some small bushes with pretty white and yellow flowers.
1691:
A sturdy bed made from solid oak lies here, covered in warm blankets.
A large stone fireplace with a roaring fire warms the room.

This beautiful house is richly decorated with paintings and colourful tapestries. A large fireplace is at the western end of the main room. Several smaller rooms are connected to this large one but they don't have the appeal that this main room does. A large oak table lies close to the centre of the room and it could easily seat 15 people. Through a gate on the eastern wall you can see a small wooded area surrounded by a tall fence.
1692:
A flagon has been left here.
There are two large yellow apples here.
A small oaken table has been set here.
On the table, there are a lembas wafer, two loaves of bread, a piece of cheese, a bowl of salad, and a mince-pie.
A large cabinet capable of storing goods is here.
In the cabinet, there are a chunk of salt, a cooking book, a cup, and a pan.
An elven cook is standing here, singing softly as she prepares a meal.

The large dining area feeds the town guards. Numerous long tables stretch out from east to west here. Several small adjoining rooms are obviously used for preparing the food served here. You can smell the wonderful aromas of fresh cooked food in the air. It appears that there is some left over food here. Maybe you can take some. There are exits north and west from here.
1693:
A small oaken table has been set here.
A large stone fireplace with a roaring fire warms the room.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

This large undecorated building houses many of Harlond's elven guards. It is sectioned off so each guard has a small private area. Most of the guards must be about in the city right now since only one is here. There is a large table in the centre of the room and a fireplace on the southern wall. The guard glances in your direction, wondering whether you need assistance. The building continues to the east.
1694: You stand in a dense grove of trees. It doesn't really surprise you to find a grove this dense in the city, since elves love trees and prefer to live among them. This is as close to the wilderness as the elves in the Grey Havens can get. A path heads north to the road and there is a gate to the west.
1695:
There are four piles of juicy grapes here.
Cirdan the Shipwright is standing here (glowing).
The elven lieutenant is here looking for any sign of trouble.

You have entered a large fenced in area. Some of the elves around here have started growing grapes. You can see many thick grape vines covered with plump and juicy purple grapes. The plants are well-pruned and you wouldn't be surprised if a great deal of wine is produced in Grey Havens simply because of this vineyard. There is wooden sign planted in the ground here.
1697:
A large bookshelf sits against the wall.
On the bookshelf, there are an ancient parchment, a map of Rivendell, and a Grey Havens map.
A huge clock is standing here.
An elven librarian is here taking care of all the books.
An elven lamplighter is resting here.

You now stand in the small Harlond library. This is only a smaller branch of the main library which lies across the Gulf in Forlond. Many of the books here are handmade copies while the originals lie in Forlond. Still there is a great deal of interesting reading here about the history of the elves and their interaction with the other races. The only exit is to the east.
1698:
On the ground, there are three carrots.
A woody evergreen plant grows here, with many stems reaching upward.
You see three potatoes on the ground.

Despite the benefits of living close to the sea, some of the elves living near here have joined together to grow a large vegetable garden. There are rows and rows of finely groomed plants. They are growing corn, carrots, potatoes and many other things here. Although the salt water from the Gulf probably makes it hard to grow plants, the elves are doing a fairly good job.
1699: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This village is filled with many pretty elven homes. Everyone in the streets seems quite friendly. Numerous trees and small bushes have been planted to make the area more beautiful. The village garden lies to the west and you see a statue to the south.
1701:
A large bulletin board, entitled "Tales", is mounted here.
There is a large sign attached to the wall near the entrance.
A retired fisherman works as bartender and cook here.

The smell of fish, fowl, tar and old tobacco greets you as you enter the old inn. Fishermen are sitting at wooden tables discussing the movements of the shoals, how to hunt sharks the best way, why the prices keep falling on the market, and telling some rather tall fish tales. The terrific atmosphere here is partly produced by the numerous fishing items hung on the walls including anchors, nets and stuffed fish, and partly by the great smelling dishes served here. You also see some duck-calling instruments attached to the wall. Many people here are eating from large plates of food. The exit is west, and there is another room to the south.
1702:
A large bulletin board, entitled "Free Peoples' Chronicles", is mounted here.
A large stone fireplace with a roaring fire warms the room.

This room is richly decorated by paintings and many old artefacts from the sea and it is enjoyed by sailors and townspeople alike. Many important decisions are informally made here while dining on one of the inn's specialities and a glass of wine. A number of people are sitting at tables here enjoying their meal. The only exit is north.
1703:
A weapons rack stands against the wall.
An arrow rack stands upright in the corner.
Standing in the rack are eight arrows.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

This tower rises about ten feet above the city wall and gives a commanding view of the surrounding area. You have a commanding view of the mountains of Ered Luin to the south. In times of war this tower would enable the elves to know well in advance if there was an approaching army from the south. The only exit is down.
1704: The ceiling of this room has been ingeniously constructed of glass panes, allowing an unobstructed view of the heavens, the sprawling city of Grey Havens, and the magnificent ocean to the west. A large tubular device is pointed out an opening in the windows towards the sky. Several comfortable chairs and large tables have been set out, and you can see a cluttered laboratory partially concealed by drapes against the north wall. One can see a large wine rack and beside it a finely crafted cupboard. In the centre of the room, a low marble fence surrounds an earthen platform, from which grows a sturdy young tree, no older than twenty years. Its broad green leaves rustle pleasantly in the sea breezes.
1705: The crystal orb shines here providing a bright beacon for approaching ships.

The impressive height of the lighthouse gives a splendid view over Harlond, with its mighty ships and crowded narrow streets, as well as Forlond on the other side of the gulf of Lhun. Far away, the blue hills of Ered Luin can be seen, but even the sharp eyes of the elves cannot see anything but the grey sea to the west anymore. Securely held by slender bronze arms, a crystal orb of rare beauty and luminance provides light that is seen from far out at sea. A spiral staircase descends downward.
1706:
There is a small sign on the bar.
The elven bartender is standing here, gossiping behind the bar.
A seagull is soaring above you.

This is the famous bar under the lighthouse, buried under the ancient construction. The place is dry (with the possible exception of its clientele), in spite of its location under sea level, and comfortably furnitured with wooden tables and an impressive marble bar.
1707: At the End of the Pier
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.

Here the pier stands clear of the land, jutting far out into the Gulf of Lhun, so that the mighty elven sailing ships might safely dock. Constructed from huge blocks of pale stone, the jetty barely shows any sign of the passing years and relentless punishment by the elements. Sturdy metal loops are mounted into the stone at regular intervals, for mooring ropes, but otherwise this construction is quite unadorned.
1708: A fair lady of the seas, Ciryariel, captains the white ship.

This is the midships and the lowest of the three exposed decks. The great mainmast of white timber dominates the centre of the vessel, secured to the sides of the ship by shrouds of silvery rope. Otherwise, this sailing vessel is surprisingly free of clutter - everything has its place, and its place is not to interfere with passage upon the decks. The deck is of a pale grey wood and has a slight camber to runoff the water that comes aboard. Pale golden rigging provides access to the square rigged mainsail of white canvas, which is hung from the main yard. Shining from the very heights of the mast is a lamp which casts a pale brilliance upon the deck. Before the mast, steps lead up to the foredeck and the magnificent prow, while steps abaft lead to the aft-deck and the wheel to steer the vessel by. On either side, silver brows provide access to the shore when docked.
1709: An elven guard is standing here at his post.

This small enclosed room has been built over the wall near the Harlond gate. Narrow slits in the wall allow the elven guards to see when someone or something is approaching the town. It is very crowded in here and the guard wishes you would leave so he can get back to his watch even though he does not expect to see anything dangerous in these peaceful times.
1710:
An arrow rack stands upright in the corner.
Standing in the rack are three arrows.

You are now on top of the city wall which stretches far in each direction. From here archers were able to help defend the city. At the eastern edge of the wall is a barricade which has holes the elves could aim through. Thus they were partially protected from arrows shot up from below. It is fairly dusty here now and there are some old arrows still lying here. It appears that it has not been used recently and that is certainly a good sign. Far to the east you are able to see the hills of the Far Downs where many other elves reside.
1711: Aboard the Ferry (at the quay in Forlond)
Daegil the elven ferry captain is here.

This small but robust vessel is actually a real sailing boat, since sailing across the Lhun might be treacherous at times. The elven boat is made out of pale timbers with some small ornaments. The sails are furled and secure, while the ferry is docked to the quay of Forlond.
1712: A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.

You have basically reached the end of the shoreline. The water from the Gulf of Lhun often runs into this area and it is quite wet. In most places you are standing in several feet of water. Many reeds and other tall grasses grow in here. Just a short distance off you can see the city wall. You can continue a bit further to the north if you wish, but since this area isn't patrolled very often you can't be sure its safe.
1713: A tall plant grows here, with grey-green leaves and grey flowers.

You have reached the end of the city. Here the swampy terrain runs directly up to the city wall. Fortunately the wall seems stable since large piles of dirt and sand help support it from the water rushing in and out. The area is filled with tall reeds and grasses and a number of small bushes growing in the water. You can also see some large piles of decaying wood. It seems likely that there used to be houses in this area until the Gulf took over.
1714:
A sign has been nailed to a post here.
A retired Captain stands here, selling boats.
An elven woman is here merrily walking along.

The shoreline takes a sharp bend here and you find yourself in a small cove. Towards the north the bank rises steeply and it appears that the elves divert some water into a pond. You can see several small boats floating about on the pond. The water there is calm unlike the water to the south in the Gulf. Many trees and small bushes grow here just a bit away from the shore where the sand has been overtaken by fertile ground. Off to the east the ground appears swampy.
1715:
A bass swims here.
A fat carp swims here.
A fat carp swims here.
A bass swims here.

Even though the shoreline bends north-east, the waters refused to be hemmed in and seem all the more free. The beautiful sky above, with the gleaming sun, paint a brilliant pattern upon the waves, and one can easily be entranced by gazing into its clear depths. The pond could tell stories beyond number, about countless ages and trials. An almost somber note can be seen far beneath the surface, resting at the sandy bottom. Even the most beautific settings and merry songs cannot fully erase the stain of the kinslayings ages before...and in the mind of the elves in this fair city, it is something that should never be forgotten.
1716:
A bass swims here.
A fat carp swims here.

The waves lap briefly against the sandy beach to the north, then return to the deep and clear water, further towards the centre of the pond. The surface shimmers and sparkles, sending prisms of light in all directions and dazzling the eye. If only the worries and problems of the world did not exist, and you could float here forever, without care... The thoughts of things to be done are quickly banished by your mind as these problems do cease to exist, at least for a short while.
1717: The waves of the lake lap up against your craft, inviting you to come play and dance with them and forget the cares of your mortal existence. 'Please,' they laugh, 'don't return to the solid and boring earth, stay with us and relive the best moments of your life and then experience even better ones.' The call of the sea to the elves is no mystery and now it is obvious what entrances them so. Occasionally an adventurous few drops leap up from the crests, and grace your cheek and skin with their cooling presence.
1718: A fisherman is sitting here in a boat in the middle of the water.

How lucky you are! Here, amongst the waves and ripples of this pond you are at peace. Bobbing slightly, feeling the warm ocean breeze and the sun warming your tired form, and listening to the soft water sounds, one cannot help but be serene and thankful for this refuge. As quiet and private as these waters are, they do not covet and hoard their kindness. They are more than willing to give of themselves to any who would accept.
1719: A king crab is crawling around in the sand here.

You have passed the end of the quay and are now on a sandy beach. The water quickly rushes in and out here and with each passing wave many small stones and shells are tossed about. The shore continues to the east and you can go back to the quay to the south.
1720:
A note here is attached to a post.
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.
A pigeon is strutting around here.

You have reached the end of the quay. The ferry which travels across the Gulf of Lhun to Harlond departs from here. You see a note here attached to a post which gives more details. The quay extends back to the west and there is a small beach to the north.
1721: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The dock here is filled with many small ships and boats. Most of them seem to be ships used for pleasure trips. One ship has just left the dock apparently heading off for a day of sailing. The quay continues to the east and west and there is a shop to the north.
1722:
A sign rests on the counter here.
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.
A noble Elf stands here, proudly displaying his valuable assets.

This is obviously the jewelry store. The shop is brightly lit and the light reflects off the many priceless gems displayed here. Although the gems and jewelry are stored under a glass cover, the owner will let you look more closely at a specific item if you wish. You can hardly imagine the value of all the items for sale here.
1723: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The smell in the air is enough to tell you that this is the fish quay. Many elven fishing boats are here while many others can be seen out in the Gulf of Lhun. Along the quay are many scraps of fish dropped by the fisherman who are not always the cleanest people.
1724: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This is part of the fish quay. A number of fishermen are here unloading the fish they have caught. In the large fishing nets you can see hundreds of mackerel and cod. It appears to have been a very good fishing day. The fish quay extends north and you can probably slip on board their fishing boat to the south.
1725:
A fishing net has been left here.
An elven boat-fisher is here hard at work on his boat.

You are standing on a large fishing boat. Many elves are running back and forth here almost seeming not to see you. Some are at work cleaning the boat while others are inspecting the mast and the rigging. The boat is quite large. There are four masts reaching up into the sky. The sails attached to them flutter rapidly in the wind here. You can also see many large fishing nets hanging here drying.
1726:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An elven citizen is here enjoying the day.

This quay is reserved for ships trading in textiles. At times there are ships here coming all the way from Pelargir. At least you are now away from the overwhelming fish smell. You can hardly imagine how the elves get used to it. The quay extends east and west.
1727: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This is where many of the large ships enter Forlond. Many ships are currently docked here. It is interesting to compare the elven ships with the ones here obviously made by man. The man-made ships look sturdier but somehow you doubt that they are. In any case it is very windy here and the sails flutter rapidly back and forth. Many sailors are hard at work on their ships either making simple repairs or helping to load or unload their goods. The shipyard lies to the south while the quay continues east.
1728:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An elven boat-fisher is here hard at work on his boat.

This is the part of Forlond's shipyard devoted to repairing damaged ships. The winds upon the Gulf of Lhun are quite strong and the waves they produce often wreak havoc on the great elven ships. Some of the ships need minor repairs like needing new sails, but others have more severe damage like destroyed masts or even actual hull damage. The elves working here are very good and in a short time these ships will be seaworthy again.
1729:
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.
The elven lamplighter is making his rounds through the streets.

This is half of the shipyard for Forlond. This area seems to be devoted to building new ships. There are several half-built ships here as well as some quite close to completion. One in particular is receiving its last touches of paint and will soon be ready to ride upon the sea. Despite all the hard work, the elves here are singing merry songs most likely written by shipbuilders millennia ago.
1730:
A coil of rope is lying here.
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.
An elven merchant is here doing his best to sell you something.

This open area has all the supplies any fisherman needs. You can see many fishing poles and nets. There are also many sails hanging here wavering in the wind. Having them outside like this is certainly the best way for the customers to see the sails' quality. There are also many piles of rope used for a ship's rigging and wood that can be used for a ship's hull or masts. The shipyard to the south probably gets many of their supplies here. Hung on an old coil of rope is a small sign.
1731: An elf is sitting here, fishing for a catch.

This is a short wooden pier reaching out into the Gulf of Lhun. At times many elven fisherman can be found sitting here casting away all morning and afternoon. A narrow jetty lies further to the south and several half-built ships can be seen to the east.
1732:
There is some snow on the ground.
An elven boy is sleeping here.
An elven boy is sleeping here.
An elven citizen is here enjoying the day.

This short jetty leads toward a tall lighthouse. About ten feet in width and forty feet long, the jetty has been constructed from the natural rocks of the harbour. As the waves of the Gulf of Lhun splash upon them, the rocks are wet and slippery underfoot, and this place seems to be permanently assailed by strong gusts of wind. Nevertheless it seems a pleasant place.
1733: This ancient lighthouse, and the one which stands in Harlond, across the Gulf of Lhun, were built to guide ships into the docks of the Grey Havens. Its stone walls seem untouched by the passage of time, as does the circular iron stair- case, which leads upward, its way lit by a row of torches fastened to the wall.
1734:
An elven guard is standing here at his post.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

This very large building houses most of the town's guards. It is sectioned off into many small areas so each guard has some private space. There is also a common dining area with an enormous oak table. Several guards are here at this time. They appear to be telling each other some amusing stories but you aren't sure what about. You can exit back east or there is a another door to the west.
1735: This relatively large room is where the garrison commander lives. He has a bed more than large enough for his tall frame. A window on the southern wall gives him a wonderful view of the Gulf and the lighthouse. It is obvious that he is a master of commanding forces. The walls are covered with weapons such as bows and longswords. There are also several intricately designed shields used as decorations. Small braziers high up on the walls light the room. Your only exit is back east.
1736:
A large bookshelf sits against the wall.
On the bookshelf, there are an ancient parchment, a map of Rivendell, and a Grey Havens map.
A grey haired elf is standing here, ready to share his knowledge.

The decor of this chamber tells you instantly that this is the mage guild. Shelves here are stocked with numerous potions and rare herbs. These items are mixed together in the many flasks and vials resting on the tables here in hopes of perfecting some new spell. Numerous sheets of paper are lying around possibly containing the secret ingredients necessary for some powerful magic. The room is lit by several small dim torches and there are also several small iron braziers probably used for heating liquids. You can go east back to Lhun Street or there is also a stairway leading up.
1737:
Resting on the counter is a small wooden sign.
An elven tailor is standing here, tidying his selection.
This shop is filled with many racks filled with fine clothes. There is an enormous selection here. You can almost certainly find something you would like to wear.
1739:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An elven boat-fisher is here hard at work on his boat.

During the night this is where many of the fishing nets are stored. They are hung here so they can be dry by morning. A number of piles of fish scraps are lying here indicating that this area is also used for cleaning and skinning the fish they have caught. A number of fishermen are here working.
1740:
A note is attached to the wall.
An elven grocer is standing here, quietly humming to herself.

This looks like a store where you can find almost anything. The shelves are stocked with all sorts of items. One side of the room has piles of torches and lanterns. Another side has freshly baked bread and some tarts. You also see some drinking containers.
1741:
A sign rests on a wooden counter in front of you.
A weapons rack stands against the wall.
In the rack is a backsword.
Gildor the blacksmith is here, busy forging a sword.

Although this shop is relatively small, it seems to have all your basic needs. You can see shelves piled with leather armour and simple weapons like swords and bows. This may be the only shop of its kind near here, since it is quite crowded in here. You can exit to the east or west. A sign rests on a wooden counter in front of you.
1744:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
A Fishmonger is standing here, loudly advertising today's catch.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

The smell of this place is enough to tell you that it is the fish market. All around are fishmongers doing their best to sell their fish. Elves crowd around trying to see who has the best product at the best price. Shops lie to the east and west, Salmon Run Road heads north, and the fish quay lies to the south.
1745: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This road is accurately named. It is directly downwind of the fish market and the fish quay and the smell of fish is quite strong. Although the smell might be a little annoying to many people, the many elves on the street do not seem to mind, and must be accustomed to it by now. The street continues north and a number of buildings stand to the east and west.
1746: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This road is accurately named. It is directly downwind of the fish market and the fish quay and the smell of fish is quite strong. It seems unlikely, but you almost think it smells worse here than at the market itself. Funny how the elves strolling around here don't seem to mind. The street continues to the north, a garden lies to the east, and a paved courtyard lies to the west.
1747: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

You have reached the end of Salmon Run Road. You only wish the fishy smell was gone as well. This is a very crowded area. There are large buildings to the east and north and many elves are running in and out. The road heads back to the south and in the distance you can see some large fishing boats.
1748:
A paper note with bold lettering is pinned to the north wall.
An elf sits here delving into some old tomes of elven lore.
An elven librarian is here taking care of all the books.

This huge building contains the history of the elves in Middle-earth and Valinor. If you wanted you could find an Elven account of almost every important event in their history. In particular, you could read about the dreadful kinslayings, the splendour of the secret city of Gondolin, the creation of the world by Eru, or of the building of these fair havens. It is all here and you are free to read whatever you like. Many of these texts are very old and you should be careful not to ruin them. Salmon Run Road lies to the south and the library's map room lies at the top of a spiral staircase.
1749: A sign is here attached to the wall.

This small room is filled with maps. To protect them from the passage of time, they are all encased in glass. You can look at whatever you like but none can be taken from this room. There are maps here from the old days before Beleriand was destroyed and newer ones like maps of this town. There is a sign here attached to the wall.
1750: On Top of the City Wall
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

After climbing the stairs you find yourself on a small stone platform on top of the city wall. The area is about ten feet square. From here and from other places around the city, archers could help defend the city. However in these peaceful times, this platform is generally empty. Elves often climb up here though since there is a fantastic unobstructed view of Ered Luin. The mountains stretch off to the north and spread far east and west as well. Their snow-capped peaks dominate the scene and in many places they rise above the clouds.
1751:
A mailbox stands here stuffed full of messages.
A heavy desk, made of solid oak, stands here.
A secretary is sitting at the desk.
A small rat runs about, oblivious to your presence.

This is obviously the post office for Forlond. Letters are piled everywhere and it is really quite a mess. Several elves are here working to sort all the mail. It may take a while but you can probably find your mail or leave mail for someone else if you wish. There is a sign resting on a table here. Just outside the building, a circular stairway leads to the top of the city wall.
1752:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
One of the strong town gatekeepers is standing here.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

In front of you lies the north gate of Forlond, the part of The Grey Havens which lies on the northern shore of the Gulf of Lhun. The gate is high and made of solid oak and banded with strips of iron. In several places intricate designs have been made in thin lines of silver and mithril. Beyond the beautiful gate you are able to see the high mountains of Ered Luin. To the south, Lhun Street leads into the town.
1756:
There is some snow on the ground.
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
A large fountain, made from grey stone, pours water from its centre.
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

This is one of the most crowded places in town. The road here is covered with white marble blocks arranged in a square. At the centre is a large fountain. Many elves are here chatting to each other and some of the elven children are playing in the fountain. From the north you can hear some rowdy elves so most likely it is a bar. To the east and west lie Salmon Run Road and Lhun Street.
1757:
A large bulletin board, entitled "Board of the Free Peoples", is mounted here.
A white-painted bench is here.
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.

This area appears to be a meeting place for all the elves of the town. Since the elves prefer the outdoors, they hold their town meetings outdoors as well. This is basically a circular area bounded on the north by the city wall and the imposing mountains of Ered Luin and on the south by Evergreen Park. Maple trees and elm trees grow in abundance here and there are also several rows of pretty flowers. Benches are arranged here in a circle for the townspeople so they can discuss important issues. A board nailed to a tree here most likely contains information relevant to everyone.
1758:
An elven boy is sleeping here.
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

The elves love all types of trees and here they have planted rows and rows of evergreens. You can see several varieties of pines and a number of spruce trees as well. There are also some evergreen bushes here. Even in winter this park is a beautiful green and the elves here often flock to it. The park continues to the west and there are also scenic areas to the north and south.
1759:
There is some snow on the ground.
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This small street is bordered by many trees which keep it quite shady. Several elves can be seen lounging around under the shade of a particularly large tree. Some elven homes lie along the southern border of this lane and a park lies to the north. Lhun Street lies back to the east.
1760:
An apple tree with bright green leaves grows here.
On the tree's branches is an apple.
An elven citizen is here enjoying the day.
The elven lieutenant is here looking for any sign of trouble.
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

This is really just an extension of the park further east. Many firs of all varieties grow here. Even in the winter many elves come here to relax in the shade. However there are also some fruit trees here. In particular, you see several apple and pear trees. You may be able to have a snack while you relax here.
1761: An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

The huge door to the north is made of white marble, a real piece of work. Incrusted in the door are diamonds depicting every arcane word a powerful mage needs. On the top of the door stand these words: ----- Aehnilaeo Toughadeuos Iristaetar ----- For those who don't know sindarin the correct sentence is Truth is elsewhere.
1762: This room is filled with a nice smell of flowers and essential essence. In this room Armazac prepares brew for his/her friends. With these potions they could get a higher strength, healing and so on. In the western corner of the room stand a strange artefact. This powerful artefact is built in a shiny material. And saying these magical words: By the Fluorescent Activated Cells Sorter Tell me what this item is made of.
1763: This magnificent hall has been paved with huge, flat slabs of marble. Against the west wall a towering standard hangs, resplendant in green and red. It is a breathtaking depiction of the shining home of Galadriel, Lorien. Large panes of glass allow ample sunlight into this room, and several young trees have been planted in the centre of the room. A smoky chamber can be seen to the north, whilst an open doorway leads off to the south.
1764: A small wooden bridge spans a stream that runs between the two sections of the building. The stream gurgles over a steep cliff, falling ever downward into the rolling ocean. Two small benches and a small table sit on this redwood bridge. The view is commanding, and ever tempting to elves longing to sail west for valinor, waiting to be greeted by their long departed brethren. To the east, the stream pours towards you out of a lush forest. The bridge leads to a large entrance hall to the north and to the more private rooms of the residence to the south.
1765: A huge clock is standing here.

Towering shelves of books line the walls of this large room. Some of the books look quite ancient, and some are quite new. A large, finely carved oak table is in the centre of the room. A plush chair sits on either side of the rectangular table. One end of the table is covered with many old scrolls, and prophetic texts, while the other is much more clear, save for some fine works of fiction. A large spiral stairway leads to the second floor. To the north, a set of wide double doors open onto a beautiful bridge.
1766: A doorkeep stands here ready to obey his master's wishes.

You have entered a quiet yard which is shaded from the sun by tall, broad-leafed trees. This area has been paved with broad, smooth slabs of granite and the tall brick walls which surround this enclosure stand almost fifteen feet tall. To the east, a tall vine-covered gate stands between you and Forlond. To the west, an impressive structure has been constructed amidst a forest of green trees.
1767:
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.
An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

Numerous elven homes lie in this area. It is one of the more densely packed areas of the town. Some of the homes are quite close together. It almost looks like a separate community. Young elven children are playing in the streets and they appear to be having quite a good time. A number of trees and bushes grow along the streets and the elves have done a good job of keeping the area around their homes beautiful.
1768:
A large bulletin board, entitled "Free Peoples' Chronicles", is mounted here.
An Elven innkeeper stands ready to sign up his guests.

Should you wish to find a soft bed for the night, this is the place. Many private rooms are here stretching off down the corridor. Each has its own version of seaside decor and it is probably easy to find one of your liking. Should you prefer a drink or some snacks before retiring for the night, the bar is downstairs.
1770: An elf is sitting here, fishing for a catch.

Tucked away in the far shore of the pond, this beach is an idyllic setting to relax in and dream. The white sand forms the dunes and ripples of the beach and it feels both cool from the breeze and hot from the sun. Forming an elegant skyline with the white sands is a sapphire sky, with clouds as white as snow and as soft as down. The wind, having blown over the waves, delights you as it plays through your hair and revitalizes even the most weary soul. Several homes lie in the area built by elves who prefer a bit of isolation in this fair city.
1773:
A venerable elven priest is here, willing to teach his art.
A helpful elven citizen is cleaning up the area here.

Softly the sounds of waves breaking upon the coast brush upon the ear, filling the soul with serenity. But beneath that the roar of the power and tumult of and angry sea rumbles through the peace, reminding one of the wildness of the sea. Both the unrestrained might and the graceful quiet of the sea are depicted in this temple. On the walls are frescoes of gentle ripples that the sailors pray for and love, while behind them, in a deeper blue, the stormy waves that sailors fear rise up. In the centre of the room lies a sculpture of Osse and Uinen, husband and wife, the two faces of the coastal waters.
1774:
An elven girl is sleeping here.
An elven citizen is here enjoying the day.

Tucked away from the main thoroughfares criss-crossing the city, this garden seems a quiet refuge from the otherwise hectic pace. No fishmongers disturb the peace with their yells, no stench of fish spoils the breeze, and no raucous clatter of wagons grate against your ear. Instead, the wind plays gently among the elms, filling your mind with a soothing rustle, accompanied by the pleasant murmur of the pond to your east. Its crystal waters seem a haven, beckoning your tired body to come and join it in a delightful swim.
1775: There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.

This lane is quite peaceful since it is far away from the crowded streets in the central part of town. The trees lining it make it quite shady and a number of young elves are playing hide and seek with you as they periodically glance out from behind the trees. The street continues east, a park lies north and a small village lies to the south.
1776: This broad hall has been finely furnished with comfortable couches and chairs. A wide hearth lies against the north wall, while against the west wall stands what appears to be a huge display case. Upon closer inspection you realise it contains a dazzling supply of pipes of all kinds as well as wide variety of pipeweeds and herbs. A beautiful but tiny fountain trickles softly near the eastern wall. The room is warm and comfortable and one could feel like resting here a while.
1777: The Housekeeper looks fed up with her job. She scowls at you unhappily.

As you enter this room, you feel comfortable and in peace. As you were in your own house. On the wall stands some paintings of fierce battles that Master Armazac did during his old age. Now when he wants to find peace on Arda he just stays here and studies the arcane of magic. There is a sign over the Housekeeper saying: Stay here if you wish, my house is your house.
1781: The crystal orb shines here providing a bright beacon for approaching ships.

Though this lighthouse is not as high as the one in Harlond, it still provides a wonderful view of the area. The city of Forlond stretches out before you and the background is dominated by the many peaks of Ered Luin. Across the Gulf of Lhun you can see the many lights of Harlond. In the centre of the room stands a solid marble pedestal, atop which rests the brilliant orb.
1782: Between the heights of the Pelori and the sea lie the drear marches of Araman. Separated from Valinor by the high fence of the mountains, this desolate realm is fit only for a few hardy grasses which grow.
1783: Though this is Aman, this stretch of coastline to the east of the mountains holds little joy, for no life thrives upon these shores. The wind is always strong and chilled and the waves break upon the stony shore, evoking the spirit of sea-longing.
1784: Beyond the bay of Eldamar, these lands grow little vegetation. The only sounds are the breaking of the waves and the mewing of gulls. Once upon a time, this land would have been shrouded, as the shadowy seas roiled against the shoreline, and it seems that the land has never known anything other than this emptiness.
1785: On the northernmost shores of Elvenhome, the coastal landscape changes from the enchanting home of the Eldar to the bleak plains of the land of Araman. Though less pleasant than the lands to the south, the coastline has a pleasant temperate clime, and the presence of elves is evident. Waves lap gently over pebbles of a multitude of colours, interspersed with highly-patterned shells and conchs discarded by denizens of the waters. Pale grasses grow above the shoreline, while isolated groves of scented lairelosse and scarlet-laden yavannamire give a dreamy aroma.
1786: This stretch of shore is where the Teleri decided to make their Haven, away from the radiance of the Two Trees, so that they could still espy the stars above. In these undying lands, many grains of golden wheat wave in the sea-breezes, while white lilies sway and the golden bells of silver flowers toll. Fragrant evergreen trees hold birds whose song never dies, while above come the melancholy cries of the gulls. A coastal path of white stones follows the coast southward from the gates of the city, its seaward side sheltered by a low stone wall.
1787: Woods of fragrant evergreens release their heady scent onto the winds of the shore. Tracks lead from the white path into plantations, where the fine timbers for the white ships of the Teleri are cut.
1788: Along the stretch of coast followed by the white path, shadowy inland meres provide a habitat for many waterfowl. Of these birds, most recognisable are the famous white swans who once pulled the Swan-ships of the Teleri. Pale green and silver Tasarion dip their laden branches into the waters, creating shade during the heights of the Sun. The calls of the fowl mingle with that of the breaking waves upon the shore and the lyrical sound of a voice.
1789: Northern Shores of the Bay of Eldamar

Within sight of the Lonely Isle, the northern shores of the bay are both temperate and pleasant. Flowering grasses grow above the reach of the tides, while the pebbles hold something of the magic of the land: long strands of verdant seaweed lie like hair upon the shore, while golden barnacles cling to the heavier rocks. The sounds of the sea fill the ears, while the salty tang tantalises the senses. The white path stretches along the coast, sheltered by a low stone wall and shaded in many places by groves of fruit trees.
1790: The Northern Shores of the Bay of Eldamar

The path along the wooded coast bends as it shadows the route of the shore which forms part of the bay of Eldamar. There is a strange atmosphere in the land, of a place that is half remembered in dreams of long ago. The call of a white gull is like an echo, reminding you of all the seabirds that whirl along the shores of all the lands of the world. The fine mist of sea spray whets the taste and the smell of other journeys in other times. The boat that bobs beyond the breakers, embodies all those boats that were ever set to sea. A waking dream, these shores are the true west, the shores of a world lost but to those like you who follow the road now hidden.
1791: The sea breaks in upon the land, the waters surging up a narrow inlet before receding. The pebbles that the sea covers are strewn with fair jewels of flawless pearl, rainbow opal and pale ruby. Beside, a sandy path lined with shells leads to a white house with a door upon silver steps. A banner reveals the home is that of the House of Kelwe, renowned singers amongst a race of renowned singers upon the shore. The song from the halls continues unabated, flowing from the open windows of the upper stories, though the identity of the singer remains a mystery. White birds wheel above the inlet as if an audience, adding their own accompaniment.
1792: Under construction are several ships, in a range of sizes. Covered yards hold neatly piled stocks of timber, along with several steel vats. Many houses of varying grandeur line the outer circle of the shipyards, but all are walled in white and fly pennants bearing the design of ships and swans.
1793: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Upon the strands of Eldamar, long ago did the Teleri make a home here, reluctantly forsaking the Lonely Isle. White walls surround the haven, extending around the heights of the cove to end abruptly to either side of the great sea-arch. No towers pierce the walls except at this point; twin turrets extend upwards, forming pillars which anchor a great pair of gates of pale shell and shining pearl. The eternal lights of the haven pour out of the open gates along the path that leads away.
1794: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The white walls of Alqualonde are here broken by a pair of towers which form the structures upon which gates of pearl and shell pivot. Stone doors on either side allow access into the towers, but stand closed. The main route up from the levels below, passes through the gateway.
1795: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The roadway forms the conduit between the lower levels of the hollowed cove and the walls above. Walkways slope off to either side to plazas and courts lined by halls and domed-mansions and lesser structures. Flanking the paved thoroughfare are cut steps and timber handrails, provided for those less sure-of-foot.
1796: A crystal pool, inscribed with the night sky, sits at the centre of the court.

Besides their love of ship-building, the Teleri revere the stars. So it was that when moving from Tol Eressea, they chose to build their home far from the light of the Two Trees, so that they might still gaze in wonder to the skies above. This circular court is dedicated to the first lights of the sky, made aeons ago by Varda. An inscribed pool stands at the centre of the court, while unadorned hedges mark the perimeter.
1797: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Upon the middle terrace of Alqualonde, an excellent view is afforded of both the houses of the town, and the ships moored in the harbour below. No wall protects the unwary as this is a working platform, with wooden cranes to haul and lower goods. Breezes bring the tang of the sea to the nostrils.
1798: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The most splendid of the houses of Swanhaven stands upon the middle terrace: that of Olwe, lord of the Teleri who passed into the West. With walls of pearl, its surfaces shimmer and shine a soft radiance, lighting up the northern wall of the cove.
1799: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The only walkable route to the harbour below is provided by these stairs cut into the southward wall of the cove. From the top can be seen the ships below, moored on the piers and landings of the harbour, the lights of the lamps casting a rainbow of colours on the beams which stow the white sails.
1802:
The ferry is docked here, ready to be boarded.
A graceful sign can be seen at the western end of the wharf.
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.

Within the shelter of the enclosed cliffs stands the stone harbour with its attendant ships. Diffuse lamps of pale colour are affixed to the dark walls of the cliff behind, lighting the crests of waves upon the sea. Dotted along the wharf are the white timber housings of goods and materials. Towards the eastern end, two silvery chains provide access for heavy loads to the platform at the top of the cliff. For others, the means of ascent is via a twisting marble stair at the harbour's western end.
1803: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

The only means onto the heights of the city, the stairs wind up the steep cliff via cuttings and switchbacks. Though slick with sea spray, the elves of the harbour negotiate the smooth marble steps with surefootedness, barely slowing in their route. For the less capable, silver chains provide a welcome handhold, while tall silver lamps show the way.
1804: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Set some way back from the edge of the cliff, the white platform nevertheless offers a view of the bay of Avallone. A single silver lamp illuminates the first steps on the way down to the harbour; others of its kin do likewise along the steep twisting marble route.
1805: Lined with white-faced stone, a large arch supports the earthen works above. Through the corridor whistles the wind, and its howl is mingled with the mewing of gulls. The wind brings with it the tang of the sea, and a fine spray of mist.
1806: Within the curving earthen work mound that circles the city is this open courtyard. Open and exposed, a strong breeze whirls about the alabaster sculptures that line the paths which meet at a fountain in the centre. The forms of birds above are cast as shadows upon the stones. Chimes of pearl-inlaid silver tinkle, but their strong tones bring a weariness to the spirit and the urge to tarry awhile and dream of latter days.
1807: A silver pool sits underneath the centre terrace of the Tower of Avallone.

Steps from the court below lead up to this terrace upon which the great tower of Avallone stands. Unique in construction, the tower is hollow, the halls of the levels being but the outer shell. The base of the tower is in fact raised upon four great stone columns, each some four score paces in circumference. Transparent crystalline stairs spiral up each column into halls of the first level. In the centre of the terrace, there is a silver pool, but it does not look like it contains water.
1808: Passing inside the western turfed heights, the path forms part of the route along the top of the cliff overlooking the harbour below. Along much of the precarious route, a white wall provides some protection from the worst of the salty wind, but in two places it is broken by elegant winching mechanisms which relay silvery chains down the face of the cliff.
1809: Three-storied and many-spired, the watchtower stands atop the earthen wall which surrounds the city on three sides. Narrow crystalline windows set in walls of gleaming mother-of-pearl look north, west, east and south. Yet, the path which climbs the turf from the east leads not to any portal, but merely circles the base.
1810: The path follows the south-facing cliff, its edge protected from a white wall. Interspersed along the route small golden trees bear spice-scented fruit resembling figs, while marigolds and violets grow in plots, watered by the sea dews.
1811: The white path passes through a short mosaic tunnel which cuts through the high earthen bank which surrounds Avallone. The mosaic projects the boughs of silver-leafed trees upon the arched ceiling, with nightingales passing under the eaves.
1812: The path continues east of the grass-covered bank, spawning another which leads north to other halls of the city. Trees heady with scarlet blossom line the route from the city to the eastern promontory of the island.
1813: Jutting out into the sea, this treeless high-cliffed promontory is the nesting place of uncounted numbers of gulls, petrels and pale cormorants. Many of these birds wheel above or cruise the near sea, diving for silvery fish, and their wails and calls fill the ears. Mixed with the sharp smells of the sea or the many subtle fragrances which waft from Avallone.
1814: A fair lady of the seas, Ciryariel, captains the white ship.

This is the midships and the lowest of the three exposed decks. The great mainmast of white timber dominates the centre of the vessel, secured to the sides of the ship by shrouds of silvery rope. Otherwise, this sailing vessel is surprisingly free of clutter - everything has its place, and its place is not to interfere with passage upon the decks. The deck is of a pale grey wood and has a slight camber to runoff the water that comes aboard. Pale golden rigging provides access to the square rigged mainsail of white canvas, which is hung from the main yard. Shining from the very heights of the mast is a lamp which casts a pale brilliance upon the deck. Before the mast, steps lead up to the foredeck and the magnificent prow, while steps abaft lead to the aft-deck and the wheel to steer the vessel by. On either side, silver brows provide access to the shore when docked.
1815: A graceful and slender tree grows here.

At the head of the bay, the river spills out in to the waters of the sea, forming the waters of Shadowmere, whose surface reflects the lights of the land. Amongst the turf which grows above the shoreline, a white path weaves along, its coastal side screened by a low stone wall. Beyond the wall, the pebbles of the stony beach lie strewn amongst rocky outcroppings, while shallow tidal pools team with green seaweed and pink shells.
1816: The banks of the river are luxuriant with a marvellous of fair trees, of pale yellow Tasarion and silvery Brethil and Neldoreth. Before the river spills into the sea, a low slender bridge of gleaming metal spans the watercourse, its rails garlanded with white flowers. A white path following the side of the river is met by another from the bridge, and at this juncture a low stone wall starts, following the path along the coast.
1817: The slender bridge of silvery metal arcs low over the rippling river below. Its rails are draped in garlands of white flower, whose sweet aroma is released onto the wind. At the summit of the span, the bridge swells to provides balconies on either side, replete with benches of beech. Thus a visitor might while away many an hour sitting above the watercourse and listening to its babbling flow.
1818: A graceful and slender tree grows here.

The river is marked by willow and low birch, which drink at the waters edge. The light casts the near shore of the river in shade, but within the dimness, the flash of red and gold and green and silver betray the presence of an abundance of freshwater fish. Upon the turf, a path emerges to pass onto the span which crosses the waterway.
1819: The Bay of Eldalie west of the Lonely Isle, the temperate waters of Shadowmere wash gently upon the jewel-laden strands of the Eldar. Lush evergreens grow in abundance above the shoreline, releasing the fragrant aroma of larch and fir. The grassy turf shows faint footprints which leave and enter the woods.
1820: The Southern Shores of the Bay of Eldamar
A graceful and slender tree grows here.

This coast of the bay is marked by inland meres surrounded by a multitude of reeded beds. Trees bearing lamps of varying hue cast a rainbow of colours upon the tops of the reeds, where flit great dragonflies and strange insects of blue and emerald and gold. The sighing and rustling of the grassy stalks mingles with the emergent buzz and hum of many delicate wings.
1821: The Southern Shores of the Bay of Eldamar

The coastline rises above the waves upon this coast, encircling the bay with sheer shores. Beneath the cliffs carven of translucent crystal, and the foam flowers upon the sea. White gulls wheel about the edge, their cries carried inland to the grassy coastal lands.
1822: Beyond the blessed lands of Eldamar lies the barrenness of Avathar. This realm of Aman was never brightened by the light of the Two Trees, and its drab terrain has not changed much with the coming of the Sun. Small hardy plants grow in clumps, threatened by the drear sea-mists that roil against the coast. This narrow strand before the mountains of Aman are rarely trodden.
1823: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Upon a paved terrace, raised by a wide dais of many steps, stands the largest structure of the city, the House of Finwe. A central dome of marble and silver tracery dominates the structure, while from each point of the compass four great halls spring, fully five stories in height. Many pale gems of crystal and adamant, topaz and citrine reflect the lights of the city. Pennants and flags fly from the balconies of the house, indicating that within the closed doors of the halls lives the Lord of the Noldor of the West, Finarfin.
1824: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Nestling on the lower reaches of Tuna, this walled garden provides shade to many flowering plants and shrubs. A path lined with chalcedony leads to the foot of a white tower which is topped by a silver bell. Adjacent to the tower lies a modest dwelling, its walls overgrown with vines.
1825: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Carven of crystal and lined by gleaming balusters of green beryl, the steps climb the upper heights of green Tuna. Though swept clear of diamond dust, the stairway still gleams in the myriad lights of the city. From either side, marble walkways lead to mansions of white stone, and gardens of repose where once the kinfolk of Noldor and Vanyar once mingled. Now, though it remains an enchanted place, many of the folk are gone, and the steps no longer throng to the footsteps of the Eldar.
1826: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

From either side of the steps, branch ways of Tirion, and white stairs. A myriad of things one can espy from the route: high white houses flying flags, tall towers topped by silver, terraces and courts where shrubs and flowers grow, and tree-lined lanes which allow access to monuments before sombre halls.
1827: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

From within the city can be seen Tuna rising, itself shadowed by the mighty mountain walls within which the city lies. Upon the hill from the gates are wide crystal steps, which climb to the summit. Within the circle of the city, a road paved with flagstones of alabaster provide access to other sectors, shining in shades of silver and gold, pale green and cream.
1828: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Tirion sits upon the green hill of Tuna, and the smooth walls encircle the city upon the lower skirts of the hill. Within stand the houses of the Noldor, the terraces and fragrant gardens, the golden fountains and the silver towers, built uncounted centuries ago when the world was whole. A great arch pierces the high white walls, its keystone as large as house. The silvery gates of the city hang open in welcome.
1829: A graceful and slender tree grows here.

Between the sheer glassy sides of the Pelori lie the enchanted lands of the Eldar. While the Two Trees still shone, the Pass of Light was filled with the radiance that streamed forth from the Blessed Realm. Even today, ages past, this land is still touched by enchantments. Fields of unfading rose release their scents into the air, by breezes that sing through the russet briars. Slender birches of silver limbs glow in the light of lamps which chime. It is in this land that the hill of Tuna rises, and atop the hill stands the city of Tirion. A path leads from the gates of the city down the northern side of the pass, towards the sea.
1830: A graceful and slender tree grows here.

In the cleft of the Pelori, lies the enchanted lands of Eldamar. Here the grass is greener than any tended garden. To either side of a white path, tall trees stand straight with branches bearing silver leaves, and bedecked by the soft golden light of jewelled lamps. A soft dew hangs upon the turf as if the spring sun had but newly risen. Carried by the strong breezes of the Great Ravine, voices raised in song drift through the woods. As the ground slopes upwards to the west, a spring emerges from the earth, its white waters froth and bubble as it tumbles by way of silver stairs down to the Sea. This fount of the Cilyaluine spills an ever-murmuring music into the air to accompany the song.
1831: The Calacirian is the head of the deep ravine delved in ages past to allow the light of the Two Trees to shine upon Eldamar. It also marks the closest any mortal of Middle-earth may come to the Valinor. The host of the Valar stands eternally before the pass, preventing entrance to all those unbidden. From beyond, you hear the toll of the unceasing bells of the city of Valimar, whose silver domes and jewelled spires you can but barely espy.
1832: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Cut into the side of hill, beside the mighty crystal steps, is the airy structure of the library of Tirion, where all the Eldar may come to reflect on the works of others. Built of glass and marble, the library is unusual in that many open spaces within and around the structure exist for the singing of songs. Much of the lore of the elves is maintained vocally, and rather than being a silent building of hushed voices, the library can echo to the lyrical voices of the bards.
1833: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Upon the flank of the hill, paved walkways form a terrace within which flowers bloom in fragrant splendour. The air is filled with the scents of jasmine and poppy, golden elanor and sweet-smelling lissuin, and many more besides. Small birches provide shade to carved benches of pale wood, where citizens can sit and dream amongst the breezes on the green hill.
1834:
A circular pool, adorned by silver lamps, blazes with a golden light.
There is a lit street-lamp on the border of the street, illuminating the area.

Upon the summit of Tuna is the court of the Eldar, the Great Square of Tirion, where all the most important discussions of the Noldor once took place. Dominating the expansive open space is the highest tower of Tirion, the Mindon Eldalieva, where Ingwe once held court. From its eastern side, a long beam of light emerges, passing down the ravine. At the base of the tower grows Galathilion, the white tree of the Eldar made in the image of Telperion by Yavanna. Beside this tree is a pool, brightly lit by golden light.
1835: Tallest and most high of the towers that stands upon Tuna, the inside of the base of the tower is a single vaulted hall. A circle of tall pillars uphold the roof and upper levels of the Mindon. Monoliths of unblemished marble, they rise to great capitals carved in many strange figures and symbols; and far above in shadow the wide vaulting gleams with dull gold, inset with flowing traceries of many colours. Deep windows in the girth of the tower provide shafts of bright illumination during the hours of daylight, but otherwise the only light comes from slender candles of scented beeswax which flicker in the breeze. A single narrow stair of silver and crystal tightly spirals upwards through the centre of the Mindon.
1836: There are many levels to the Tower of Ingwe, accessible by the crystalline stairs. The stairs lead to a chamber, decorated with the finest works of craftsmen. Jewelled chairs stand around tables which have been endued with detailed carvings. Many likewise well-crafted doors, studded with jewels, lead into arched corridors. Some of these portals of are firmly closed off by heavy doors of silver or gold. There seems to be an entire community contained within these white stone walls.
1837: The High Chamber of the Lamp

This is one of the many levels to the Tower of Ingwe that can be reached by way of the many crystalline stairs. Several ornate doors open up to halls with high-ceilings and great carved tables with high-backed jewelled chairs. Apartments branch off mosaic corridors with high arches. Impressive collections of Eldarin art and grandiose portals of silver and gold are abundant.
1838: Raised above the Great Square upon a dais, stands the lofty tower of the Eldalie. The colour of untrodden snow, this pinnacle contains the mighty lamp of Tirion, whose slender beam sends light down the ravine and out to sea. Large arched windows surround the lower level of the tower, while similarly styled windows dot the upper floors.
1840: The access to the decks below, the aftdeck provides sail by means of a lateen rig attached to the mizzenmast. Lanyards of silvery twine attach to the bottom of the loose-footed mizzen when unfurled. At the stern stands the elf at the helm, holding the elegantly carved wheel which turns the black rudder below. To port and starboard are lamps which constantly illuminate the aft.
1841: Centred upon the forward deck is the large foremast, overshadowed only by the mainmast. Square rigged, the yards hold the two curved foresails of the mast. Though impressive, the most striking feature of the foredeck is the prow, carved in the curving shape of a swan's neck of snowiest white. Its beak shines in the light like burnished gold, and its eyes are golden sapphires with pupils of jet. So it is, that the white ship looks as a vast swan when seen approaching from afar. Housed on the portside is the large adamantine chain which secures the anchor to the deck of the ship whilst silvery breast ropes from behind the prow provide secure moorings when berthed.
1842: Centred upon the forward deck is the large foremast, overshadowed only by the mainmast. Square rigged, the yards hold the two curved foresails of the mast. Though impressive, the most striking feature of the foredeck is the prow, carved in the curving shape of a swan's neck of snowiest white. Its beak shines in the light like burnished gold, and its eyes are golden sapphires with pupils of jet. So it is, that the white ship looks as a vast swan when seen approaching from afar. Housed on the portside is the large adamantine chain which secures the anchor to the deck of the ship whilst silvery breast ropes from behind the prow provide secure moorings when berthed.
1843: A fair lady of the seas, Ciryariel, captains the white ship.

The access to the decks below, the aftdeck provides sail by means of a lateen rig attached to the mizzenmast. Lanyards of silvery twine attach to the bottom of the loose-footed mizzen when unfurled. At the stern stands the elf at the helm, holding the elegantly carved wheel which turns the black rudder below. To port and starboard are lamps which constantly illuminate the aft.
1844: The Road to the Grey Havens

The road is perfectly straight here heading west or east. On both sides of the road, you can see a very dense group of tall, dark trees that prohibit you from passing through them. Looking at the trees gives you an uneasy feeling and you just want to get to a safe place somewhere. Oddly enough, you can feel something good somewhere close in the west.
1845: The road goes east and west without a care in the world for what exists on either side of it. As you walk, the trees far in the north appear to take on strange forms, which amuses you. Heading westwards will take you to the gates of Grey Havens near the sea. In the north, near the road, you can see a small hut which appears abandoned. Towards south, you see some quiet grassy fields.
1846: A young man in ranger's attire is here, travelling the roads.

The road bends here going south and west. In the east, you can see some fields of tall, green grass swaying slightly in the breeze. The passage north is too densely populated with tall, dark trees to allow you to pass through. The road is in a pretty good condition and it feels pleasant to travel on it.
1847: The road flows north and east from here, cutting through the quiet, grassy fields. Beyond the grass, far in the south, you can see a dark grove of trees that may be infested with wild animals. Far in the north, you see a similar growth of trees. The road, however, provides a strange sense of security and you feel glad for some strange reason.
1848: The road goes east and west here, leading to the Grey Havens in the west. You see fields of tall, lush green grass on either side of the road and gloomy looking groves of tall trees further beyond the grass. An oak tree stands on the north bank of the road providing shelter to weary travellers.
1849: The road seems endless and the lands around it just too quiet. You can see fields of green grass in either direction, all standing in complete silence. However, the road provides comfort and a feeling of safety. Remembering your destination, you again start moving fast towards it. Perhaps someday you will come back and find more about the land.
1850: The road flows like a river going east and west. Fields of tall and lush green grass are on either side of the road. Dark groves, possibly inhabited by wild animals, grow beyond the grass. The fields near the road are very quiet except for noises made by some insects. However, just being on the road makes you feel safe and secure.
1851: There is a lot of snow on the ground.

The road goes on and on, taking the adventuring soul to lands both strange and very seductive. On each side of the road, you see a vast stretch of grasslands swaying in the wind. Beyond the grass, in either direction you observe dark groves which might be inhabited with wild animals. To the west somewhere, lies the sea and the city of Cirdan, called Grey Havens.
1852: The Road to the Grey Havens

Here the road makes a turn from south to west, but a small and well-used trail leads to the north across some fairly bleak looking plains. To the Far Downs rise a few leagues and then cut off abruptly. A cut in the slope is easily noticed east of a small settlement not far away to the southeast.
1853: The Road to the Grey Havens
The road bends east-north here and enters the Far Downs. To the north and south the downs rise gently while the road climbs to the east towards a cut in the hills.
1854: The Road to the Grey Havens

The road here runs straight east-west through the Far Downs. A couple of miles to the east lies the small settlement of Greenholm where one may rest one's weary bones. The landscape all about looks fairly grim.
1855: An old signpost stands next to a junction in the road.

Just to the south of the road to the Grey Havens is a path which leads to the small village of Greenholm, where many a weary traveller has spent the night. There appear to be a few buildings to the east of the village and an inn to the west. You can see some thick smoke coming from the chimney of the inn. The village is surrounded by the far downs, which stretch as far as the eye can see.
1856: South of Greenholm the land is criss-crossed by dry-stone walls separating rough fields from even rougher downs. The land gently rises to the south and east it seems to cut off in a line from north to south - the edge of the scarp it would seem. To the north a small track leads through some fields in which the odd horse stands eating grass. The track runs down to Greenholm and the back of the courtyard to an Inn.
1857: The Road to the Grey Havens

Here the road slices through the chalk escarpment, to the north and south dull white walls rise up forcing you east or west. The road climbs up through the cut towards the hamlet of Greenholm, somewhere to rest your weary bones?
1858: The Road to the Grey Havens

The road runs east-west through the Far Downs. To the east the downs rise and fall gently but to the west the landscape is dominated by a sheer chalk wall rearing up out of the grasses. The road climbs through a notch in the scarp, angling upwards toward the hamlet of Greenholm.
1859: The Road to the Grey Havens
The road continues east-west through the Far Downs on its long journey from the Grey Havens to Imladris. The land around is fairly safe but somewhat bleak in nature.
1860: The Road to the Grey Havens
The road continues east to west through the Far Downs on its long journey from Imladris to the Grey Havens. The land around is fairly safe but somewhat bleak in nature.
1861: The Road to the Grey Havens
The road bends west-north here, winding its way through the Far Downs. A few leagues further to the west you can see a rather prominent chalk cliff through which the road runs.
1862: The Road to the Grey Havens

Here the road takes an east-south bend as it winds its way through the gently rolling hills of the Far Downs. To the west is what appears to be a pass of sorts and to the north a trail seems to climb up through the downs.
1863: The Road to the Grey Havens
The East Road runs east-west through the Far Downs. There is little in the way of habitation out here and little road traffic these days either.
1864: The Road to the Grey Havens

You trudge onwards along the ancient road, deeper into the silent, brooding slopes and vales of the Far Downs. All around the hills stand quiet but for the blowing of the wind over the grasses. The road continues ever on.
