The uneven floor of the valley is covered in bushes with broad leaves to make the most of the poor light levels the valley provides. These leaves seem to appeal to small deer which shift uneasily at ones presence. Droppings also suggest others mammals.
4974: West of the Emyn Sul, though the ground is not very fertile the area surrounding one is carpeted in green. Verdant bracken has taken a hold here, smothering the land in its choking grasp.
4975: Here you find yourself in a large room built at the base of the tower. Great beams of sturdy oak arch upwards from the stone walls to form a conical ceiling. Comfortable chairs lie around a carved table allowing guests to rest. An impressive door made of silvery metal stands facing north and is the only visible entrance to the tower. Built into the west wall are stairs which rise up to a door marked with runes. The stairs also spiral down into the floor from which a soft glow emerges. A large sign stands above a warm fireplace set into the north wall.
4976: This is little more than a low ridge facing north-south in the plains. Rising only a dozen yards in height, it is thrice this in width and thrice as long as it is wide. Small bushes grow on both sides of the ridge, but none on top. Centred on the flattened top, towards the southern end, stands the shell of a tower, made of a white stone.
4977: A large flat rock lies here, its surface etched with markings.

Within the monotony of the windswept plains, three trails come together at the site of a flat rock. There is no odour on the air carried by the wind, not even the rural smells of ordure. The centre of Eriador is a pretty bleak place.
4978: This is a narrow watery tunnel which descends to the east from where one can see the tunnel opening out. From the west, the waters froth and foam as they tumble along the tunnel, preventing one climbing up that way. Though this watery stream seems natural enough, the metal grating passing above is certainly made to dispose of things into the waters.
4979: This is the point at which the waters of the hill emerge from the rock, forming a pool in this gully on the side of Weathertop. A few stunted poplars grow on the rocky sides of the gully where the waters splash. The water then flows over the limestone, following an ages-old watercourse down the slope and out into the endless plains of the En Eredoriath. Disturbingly, the pool show signs that someone has polluted the source, as a crimson-coloured foam floats on the edge.
4980: Nestled at the foot of the northern flank of Weathertop, and southeast of the Weather hills, lies this valley. The slope is quite gentle, as the valley leaves the shelter of the hills. The vegetation supported is varied and substantial compared to the plains north and east. Perhaps the drainage provided by the valley is the clue to this.
4981: This is the eastward side of Weathertop, its conical flank supporting no more than hardy grasses to mar its countenance. The flinty soil is hard and porous and rainwater quickly disappears into the ground, only collecting in ravines. There hardy shrubs have a chance of surviving. Such a place is on the northeast face of the hill, from where one hears the babble of water.
4982: A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.

With the constant strong winds and the flinty soil, life here is harsh. On the exposed climbs of the hill, grass grows amongst the wide swathes of russet heather. Within the dips and runs cut by small streams, small flowering plants and short bushes also prosper, while there is evidence of rabbit burrows.
4983: From here on east, the Lone-lands proper start: the En Eredoriath. The soil and/or climate must change here in the vicinity of Amon Sul. Bracken which chokes the land for many miles in the west ends. At its ragged border, grasses and irregular stones form the landscape. Though flat, the surface is rugged enough to deter extended travel, particularly with the proximity of the East Road to the south and east.
4984: The river bends, changing from a southerly course to a more easterly one. Along the edge of the waters, stands of willows and small poplars derive sustenance from what is otherwise an inhospitable land. The high sides to the ravine make climbing out of the watercourse very hard.
4985: Unlike its course upstream, the waters of the Nen-i-Sul can now only be crossed using a craft or by swimming. The river has cut a gully in the limestone of the plains making it impossible to climb onto the plains east.
4986: The elongated shape of a stoat can be seen darting across the terrain.

The water runs down this gully cut into the eastern flank of Weathertop. Only at the edge of the watercourse is there any significant vegetation. Elsewhere on the slope only short, sturdy grasses grow in the harsh soil. The Nen-i-Sul at this point is only an average stream, easily fordable.
4987: The landscape is scarred by erosion and the plants struggle to grow as best they can. With no trees or large bushes, the wind blows without respite, blowing dust across the terrain. There are no pools or dips which harbour water-everywhere is dry. With this kind of terrain it is obvious why these plains have never been populated. The Lone-lands indeed!
4988: The Nen-i-Sul flows eastward, cutting this steep ravine in the limestone bedrock of the plains. The high bluffs on either side of the river prevent one climbing out to the plains some dozen yards above. Gullies along the side sometimes contain small streams which trickle down to the watercourse, swelling the river with every mile.
4989: In the course of its route to the sea, the Nen-i-Sul, known to men as the Weatherwater, turns this way and that. This bend takes the river again south.
4990: The empty lands lie all about, though the presence of the ravine a mile or so to the south means, one can only gaze beyond in that direction. This is a dull and inauspicious land, broken by very few major landmarks since the beginning of time. If the hill of Weathertop had been a part of a mountain chain like those in the far east, it would be a very minor summit. In this land, it is a dominating influence on the landscape, its conical shape renowned as a marker by which travellers may guide themselves.
4991: Apart from the course of the Nen-i-Sul to the west, little water lies on the land. Therefore the cracked surface is harsh on vegetation, only those plants adapted to an arid climate managing to flourish to any degree. From the cropping of the grass, animals must also live here but probably most are only small, such as like rodents or hares.
4992: A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The land about is certainly flat, and the thin soil suggests the name. Animal tracks are few but still evident on the ground. These marks range from small paw to large hoof. The odour of mammals drift on the wind to ones nostrils, yet though the brush hardly limits one's view, it is hard to catch a glimpse of the lands inhabitants.
4993: Northeast of Weathertop and into the vast reaches of the Oiolad, the plains are flat as far as the eye can see. Closer inspection reveals the eroded nature of the terrain. Short tufts of grass spring from the unlikeliest of places: cracks and crevices or a patch of remaining soil. Even weeds find it hard to grow as the ground dries quickly after the rain, the drops disappearing into the earth.
4994: This is the East Road, raised above the surrounding barren lands which form the western limits of the Lone-lands. No signs of life for miles around make the name quite apt, though the locale is not without features. Barring the way south-east is the thorny wall of hedge that marked the ancient border of Cardolan, one of the divided kingdoms of Arnor. Meanwhile further away, to the north-west is the conical shape of Weathertop, the last of the Weather Hills.
4995: The road through the Lone-lands continues on its east-west route. North lies the great expanse of plains, scrub and stunted shrub dotting the landscape.
4996: The road bends before continuing along its seemingly endless voyage across Eriador. The landscape is dominated by the terrain to the northwest, which consists of a range of hills rising to almost a thousand feet in height. The largest is also the nearest and it is the well-known Weathertop.
4997: The mighty road, pitted by pot holes and tumbled stones, stands raised on its bank above the surroundings. This point near the southern tip of the last of the hills marks the border between the lands west, and the Lone-lands east. Only the hedge of bushes spoils the nearby view, its thick thorns allowing one only a glimpse of the lands to the south.
4998: Near the border of the Lone-lands with the more hospitable South Downs, the hedge grows as far as the eye can see to the east and to the west. The trail which follows the hedge here splits, one route leading south into the plains.
4999: Long ago this trail within the northern border of Cardolan was probably busy with traffic, taking as it does a reasonably straight route beside the impenetrable briars of the Great Hedge. These days it is a barely traceable path among the short tufts of grass which grow in the thin and rocky soil.
5000: The trail bends, though whether this bend is to follow the changed course of the great hedge, or the hedge was cut to keep to the side of the track is only of academic interest. The reason for the deviation of the trail lies east a few miles away in the plains. A deep cleave in the barren land cuts across the route, its path going from north-west to south-east.
5001: Jhadur the Southron, wielding a sabre, is here, riding a trained horse.

The trail beside the impenetrable briars of the hedge stands at the top of a steep descent. Even here with the narrow gully, the cultivators of the hedge have ensured continuity, barring the way north.
5002: A red-breasted mallard swims about, periodically upending to look for food.

At this point in the ravine, the river has been artificially widened. Rocks have been laid across the deeper stretches so that it manages no more than a couple of feet in depth, shallow enough even for a brave or adventurous hobbit. Plants makes good use of this sheltered environment, sedges growing in the shallows while willows stand on the shores. Birds are also evident, particularly mallards which are unknown in any other part of the Lone-lands. The path that crosses the ford climbs back out of the valley on both sides.
5003: The course of the ravine cut by the river bends again, flowing east. At this turning, several small watercourses tumble down into the canyon from the parched land around. Though the change in course has widened the bend through erosion, there is no practical way to climb over the limestone bluffs.
5004: This is the Oiolad, the endless plain which forms the flat basin at the centre of Eriador. Circulating it are evidence of upheaval and subsequent weathering. For instance the South Downs to the west and the Weather Hills north-west show that great forces have been at work in Eriador in the past. North there are open, flat lands as far as the North Downs, while northeast is the shelf which cradled the old kingdom of Angmar. East, there are no such major summits until the Ettendales. Many miles of travel lay ahead for any traveller to those sites from this spot.
5005: A field vole has frozen to the spot, sensitive to your presence.

The soil is thin, and what there is is poor. The underlying limestone has meant that most of the water disappears straight underground through numerous cracks. Patches of grass try and bind the soil as best they can in this alkaline environment. Elsewhere, the ground is blown away by winds which have little to impede their progress. This situation seems similar in all directions, for at least several miles.
5006: Here amongst the empty lands, the scattered remains of a farm lie. Some measure of its boundaries can be estimated from the still orderly border of rock piles: the age-old remains of low stone walls. Very little evidence of a farm building remains, perhaps it was made of wood? However, though this is the Lone-lands, some visitors have stayed at the farm recently. Boot-prints mark the ground, but no more can be determined without closer examination. Further afield, beyond the farm, the rugged land of the En Eredoriath stretches for miles in any direction.
5007:
A sturdy trained horse is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Though the land is quite flat, on short scales it is broken and rough to travel upon. This trail, though no more than a cleared, well-trodden route, provides a simpler passage for those coming from the lands north or south. Some sunken depressions of land away from the trail hold the promise of water. However, all they contain is algae-ridden, stagnant pools, their edges host to sedge and nettle. The Lone-lands are not noted for their hospitality.
5008: The infertile land holds few edible treasures, so the traveller needs plentiful supplies to cross the deserted plains. This land was not always so empty, and the occasional outline of the foundations of a building show that once it must have been possible to survive here, even if a hardship. Even the mighty fortress of Arnor no longer stands upon Weathertop.
5009: Amongst the windswept flatlands of the Oiolad, this track passes. Birds live in the wastes, a few sizeable bushes housing a nest or the remains of one. The shorter plants that manage to grow have covered the ground, but the old ruts of the track can still guide the eye.
5010: In the open and eroded lands of the En Eredoriath, a ravine crosses. From its steep bluffs, a winding track is cut down to the river below. To the west, it heads towards the South Downs, where the grass is greener. A rusted hoop of iron and a tumbled pile of limestone blocks at the top of the cutting suggest some previous industry from long ago.
5011: In the flat lands the eroded soil reveals the underlying limestone landscape. Crumbs of soil and organic matter are bound together by clumps of grass which barely flourish. Lichens dot the surface of the bare rock, champions in the alkaline environment. Animals are obviously rare.
5012: The East Road crosses the Nen-i-Sul river. Since the river flows at the bottom of a sizeable ravine, an impressive bridge spans the sides in a single arch of twenty yards. The sides of the bridge are walled by the same limestone of the land, though with the centuries the walls have become badly eroded. The underside of the bridge acts as an amplifier for sounds from below, so the echoes of splashing reverberate, as the river passes below.
5013: The Lone-lands of Eriador. Few have never heard of them, as they cover most of the country. However, few dare to visit them, as they are an unforgiving for those used to the comforts of home. Small settlements such as Bree and the Shire exist like islands upon a sea of rolling plains and wastes. Many years ago men from the west might have been found here. Since the Kingdom in the North fell to Angmar, this area has died with it.
5014: From Bree to Rivendell, the plains of Eriador are infamous. Stretching across the land like a dull blanket, they dutifully stretch onwards. No water sources mean few plants and few animals, though the place is by no means a desert. Barren is the most apt description.
5015: This stretch of the Lone-lands is especially bleak. The landscape is flat as far as the eye can see for many miles, yet the terrain is not featureless. Narrow cracks and wide gullies cross the land where the rainwater has flowed into the ground. A large depression to the south perhaps has a similar origin.
5016: The plains of Eriador. Most have heard of them, as they cover most of the country, but few visit. Small settlements such as Bree exist like small islands on a barren sea. Many years ago the Dunedain could be found here, but since the defeat of Arthedain, the area has become desolate and in some places dangerous.
5017:
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

You have moved far into the plains. All around the green grass stretches towards the horizon. It would be easy to lose your bearings in these fields, but you do seem to recall the road being somewhere south of you.
5018: You are standing in the middle of the wide plains that reach far into the distance. You can barely see your feet as you make your way through. As the gentle wind bends the grass tracks of different animals can be seen, both smaller and larger.
5019:
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A grey hare stands alert, looking and listening for predators.

You are standing in a wide plain that stretches north to the horizon. The dry grass grows up to your waist and slight waves form on it in the gentle breeze. Here and there grows a single shrubbery and you can see tracks of several hoofed animals, as well as from lesser animals, such as rabbits.
5020: Though the lands about are flat, the travel is harsh. Cracks created by the lack of moisture cross the land, providing an inconvenience. Additionally, the strong winds which blow without remorse, buffet the terrain. The air they carry is dry and lacks any scent, as the only plants are occasional grasses.
5021: When the North Kingdom of the Men was destroyed, the people of Middle-earth no longer came to the centre of Eriador as they used to. Most of the areas became desolate and lifeless. So it was that the legend of the Lone-lands began.
5022: A shallow canyon has formed here, more than a mile across. It is fairly flat inside with just the hint of curvature to the depression. However, the sides are quite steep and pitted with clefts. The vegetation is especially barren, with not even grass growing. Some dark green weeds sprout in places, breaking from the hard dirt. The wind swirling around the bowl gives an eerie howl. Even more disturbing is that the ground seems to be perpetually trembling. It is ever so slight, but it is constant, like an earthquake about to spring to life. In every direction, the ways out of this canyon look equally poor, but a brief scramble should suffice.
5023: A grey hare stands alert, looking and listening for predators.
Pot-holes and sunken streambeds dot the flat land. The unforgiving soil supports little plant growth and even fewer animals. Water soaks quickly underground, but whence it goes is a mystery.
5024: Bend in the Old East Road

The great road bends, though why the builders shifted the course of the road in not known. The ever-attendant hedgewall to the south keeps its course so now the road diverges from the briars by a few miles. This allows some leeway to leave the road to the east but the barren land is not too encouraging.
5025: Bend in the Old East Road
A pony is standing here, ridden by you.

The road bends in its route. The road to Bree and the Shire now turns south temporarily before resuming its westward course. Beside the road stands a disused cistern, once used when the road was young. Beyond the road, the empty plains of the Lone-lands stretch, marred only by the ravine to the west.
5026: A pony is standing here, ridden by you.
Onwards and on the road lies, while all about the flat plains of the En Eredoriath offer little prospect. The stone-edged highway extends for many leagues in either direction, seemingly without end.
5027:
A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.
A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.
A pony is standing here, ridden by you.
You are standing on the Old East Road going east and west from here through the endless dry plains. A few bushes and a lonely tree grow by the way here but mainly there is desolation.
5028: The hedge and its attendant trail, descends west into a ravine cut by the flow of the Nen-i-Sul. Though the descent is not steep, the moisture of the area has made the ground slippery. Thankfully through lack of use, grass has grown over much of the path providing traction for the rare traveller.
5029: Keeping a respectful distance, this underused trail tracks the course of the hedge of Cardolan. For much of its great length, one knows the hedge follows the southern side of the East Road. However, to the east this partnership must end, as the hedge veers southeast towards Eregion.
5030: This is the overgrown remains of an old track running parallel with the great hedge to the north. The signs are that it is still in use, but it suffers from a lack of maintenance for many a year. Here, the trail wanders west and bends south, cutting a path through the miles of broken grassland. Following this trail south takes you towards a fortress standing out against the horizon.
5032: As you examine the grass closer you are able to discern what appears to be a trail running north and south. Looking south you realise that the trail leads from the road to a castle, a few miles away. To the east and west the plains stretch out in an endless sea of swaying grass.
5033: Within an endless expanse of overgrown grass, you journey. The geography seems pretty constant for miles around. To the north, not far away, you espy the reassuring sight of the old east road, making its way through the miles of desolation that is the lone-lands.
5034: On this side of the Weather Hills the ground is flat as far as the eye can see. The grass growing here is short and tough, and there is not a tree for miles around. The impressive thorny bushes of the hedgewall lie south of this ground, forming an impenetrable barrier to all travellers. To the north you can still see the Old East Road.
5035: Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.

Within sight of the East Road, lies the remains of the marker which denoted the meeting point of the three sister realms after the division of Arnor: Arthedain and its former stronghold at Amon Sul to the northwest; the downs of Cardolan to the south and west; and the endless plains of Rhudaur to the east. In the time of the Dunedain kingdoms, this marker was known as the Seroneldeon Tarma or Three-friends' Pillar. After the wars which broke the kingdoms, travellers passing along the road have referred to the ruins as the Folly of the North or more commonly: The Three-fools' Stone.
5036: A giant rat patters against you, squeaking maliciously.

The trail is old and poorly maintained. Vegetation from both sides of the trail have been allowed to grow freely, leaving only a small stretch of track still passable. Bordering the road to the south are vast green plains.
5037: After bending east, the Nen-i-Sul now turns south again, flowing along this limestone ravine towards the Hoarwell. There are no shore to the river and the sides of the ravine offer no purchase, except to small poplars whose roots have split the rock. Splashed by the water, the lower walls of the canyon are treacherously coated in mosses of a variety of hue: green, brown and yellow being common. Black water-lice move amongst this mossy world, while a lone snail crawls along the razor-sharp edge of a rock, oblivious to the danger.
5038: The river flows on to the south, carrying its waters collected from the Lone-lands. Hemmed in by the steep bluffs of flinty limestone, the river is channelled into a narrow and deep course. There are no banks to speak of so in the splashed band only mosses and small plants grow. Under the water, long fronds of green waterweed hang like hair in the breeze of the current. Within its clear depths, small black fish dart, while the occasional flash of silver suggests larger life.
5039: A black catfish is here, lurking in the mud.

Hemmed in by the ravine in which the river flows, one has little option but to let the waters carry oneself downstream or fight the current and make upstream. If it were not for this flow, one might be able to climb the steep sides. This is impossible however, as the walls of the ravine are mossy and slippery. Fish swim close to the surface, sometimes tantalisingly close. If one had a rod and line, this would make an excellent days fishing, but maybe this is not the day.
5040: The prominent fin of a silver-yellow fish breaks the surface of the water.

The Nen-i-Sul, or in the tongue of men, the Weatherwater bends. The ruins of a small port remain at this turning. On the outer bank of the bend, piles of ancient stones denote the stilts upon which a dock once stood. A poor choice perhaps, to build the berthing place on the point of the river where the current runs fastest. However, it was not built without thought as one can scramble ashore and follow a winding trail which climbs out of the ravine.
5041: A red-breasted mallard swims about, periodically upending to look for food.

The river bends again in its course, cutting through the lands within the confines of the limestone ravine. Its route takes its far, to become a tributary of the Hoarwell. The Hoarwell in turn merges with the Swanfleet at Tharbad, becoming in turn the river Greyflood which flows to the sea.
5042: This is the plains of the Lone-lands, where little grows and little feeds on that growth. Most people pass through this area quickly, not tarrying on their route as there are few distractions.
5043: The lines of grasses here suggest that these fields were once used for growing crops but have since been fallow. The boundaries of the crops can still be seen in the pattern of the vegetation that has taken over. The relative bounty of the land is a result of a slightly elevated land and the presence of a small stream which winds through the grass. There is no sign of a farm.
5044: Grass covers the once orderly lines of fields, suggesting that the area retains a better than average amount of water than much of the Lone-lands. The lines of the ancient fields are bounded by low hedgerows. A single hedge also marks the edge of the drop into the ravine to the west and south.
5045: From within this tower you can look out from the castle over the lone-lands and the south downs. To the north, you have a good view of the nearby trail which winds just south of the great hedge, which in old times marked the eastern border of the kingdom of Cardolan. Looking out of the east slit you see the hedge also, as it cuts its way across the great plains towards the Mitheithel river in south-western Rhudaur. Beyond the hedge, the plains carry on towards the Trollshaws, dotted here and there by small collections of wood and bush. Looking south, the grasslands stretch where sheep farmers still try and eke a living on the eastern ridges of the south downs. Finally, to the west lies the great Old East Road, its southern side lined by great thorny bushes for many miles. The Road passes the foot of mighty Weathertop and crosses the Nen-i-Sul river, making its way towards Bree-land.
5046: From here you can espy the surroundings to the north - the Lone-lands. You can see the nearby trail which follows the thorny hedge to the north. Crossing this trail is a rough track which heads out through the gates and through the hedgewall further north, the bushes being blacked there. You can only head up some steps into the remaining tower, or head back down to the castle yard.
5047: The castle walls loom above from all sides within these grounds, with some stairs leading up to the top of the walls. The stairs have many cracks and holes in them, some steps missing completely. There is a large stone building over towards the corner of the yard, with some letters etched in the stone above the doorway. Some grass grows in patches all around the yard with mud covering the rest of the land. Further south is the entrance to the castle itself.
5048: A large iron gate hangs here halfway open with its long sharp ends pointing towards the ground. The gate creaks loudly and shakes with even the slightest breeze. The slightest vibrations could bring the gate crashing down. There is a wooden rail freshly built just outside the gate, a place to tie the horses and walk through the gate. The surface of the walls around the gate has become discoloured from the rust that pours off the iron bars. A few bars from the gate are missing near the bottom from where the rust has eaten all the way through them.
5049: You are standing in front of the castle gate where the rusty old portcullis lies shattered on the ground in three pieces. The castle wall is full of holes but its structure is still pretty stable. Through the gate you can see a dusty castle yard.
5050: A lone hawk soars high above you.

The plains stretch on endlessly here, grass growing rampant through the untended years. This place deserves to be called the Lone-lands since hardly anybody lives in these parts. A castle stands here, although it has seen the best of its days. The walls are broken and impassable.
5051: The plains stretch on endlessly here, grass growing rampant through the years. It is no wonder that this place is called the Lone-lands, nary a soul lives here. However, here stands a ruined castle, its walls broken but still impassable to all but the foolhardy. It seems the only building within view.
5052: This trail half an age ago would have marked the eastern border of the former Dunedain kingdom of Cardolan. Directly to the north of the path stands the great hedge which served as a defence. To this day, it is still practically impassable. Beyond the thorns, to the north-west stands Weathertop, another part of the boundary, where all three of the Arnorian realms met. Given the many centuries, this trail surprisingly remains usable, though the stones which support it are in need of much repair. Looking east, the trail passes just to the north of an old castle. To the south and west the harsh landscape of the plains stretches for miles.
5053: You find yourself in grass up to your waist and it's quite hard to walk. Bending some of the grass aside you discern tracks of several small animals. The trail runs north and east of here.
5054: An Old Trail by a Fortress

The weather-beaten old trail makes its way through the endless plains of rocky grasses, following the southern edge of the thorny hedgewall of Cardolan. At this point, the hedge to the north has been burned and cleared and a wide path is now possible north. Beyond the hedge, the most prominant sight is the great hill of Amon Sul. To the south, a cleared road leads from the trail to the gates of a castle. Many tracks on the ground show that the fortress is still in use.
5055:
A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.
A giant rat patters against you, squeaking maliciously.

The cobbled trail makes its way through the great grassy plains of the lone-lands, making the journey that bit more easy. However, in several places the track is in danger of being lost as the years have taken their toll. A castle is visible south-west of here and that is one of the only features in this grassy landscape. The wind blows strong in your face and their is no tree or bush nearby to shelter from its fierceness bar the great line of thorns directly north of the path..
5056: A giant rat patters against you, squeaking maliciously.

You are following the remains of the Dunedain trail of former Cardolan. This inhospitable reach of the realm may still find use with the shepherds but it is unlikely. The grass grows across the stones of the trail, threatening to swallow it forever.
5057: The grass is quite low around here, lower than usual. It's strangely quiet here and the sky seems nearer than you've ever experienced it before. Looking westwards you notice a way through the great hedge. The grass also appears trampled in that direction.
5058: You are standing just south of some brushwood. The vegetation is truly prospering here and the grass is tall and green. Sounds of animals scurrying around reaches your ears.
5059: The grass is dry and brownish and cracks under your feet. It would be hard to move around without leaving obvious tracks here. Scanning your surroundings reveals nothing but endless plains, a small patch of brush to your east and of course the road just north of you.
5060: Here you have become entangled in a patch of thorny bushes which grow here. The bushes form a dense weave, and it is with effort that you struggle to move through. To the north, the plains clear to form the old east road, but in other directions there is just endless plains.
5061: Plains border the Old East Road which lie north of here, clearly visible beyond the swaying grass. South of you the vegetation is more sparse as the ground becomes increasingly rough and unfriendly. Tracks of small animals is visible in the dirt.
5062: You find yourself knee-deep in a sea of swaying grass. The plains border the road which runs north and east of here. More plains are visible west- wards and a craggy, rougher landscape to the south.
5063: The road bends again, offering to take you east and north from here. Looking south and west you see vast plains of tall green grass. Such vegetation is likely to harbour many small creatures for a hungry hunter.
5064: Sharp rocks and thorny bushes makes it harder to walk here. Not much grass grows between the rocks. To the west and north however, the vegetation is more dense. The rough grounds continue to the east and south.
5065: You carefully squeeze your way between two bushes and walk around some large rocks. The place is rather weird and it seems easy to get lost here among the many rocks but to your southeast you can see the remains of an old crumbling castle.
5066: The grass appears somewhat trampled here; studying the ground more carefully reveals some tracks leading to and from the road. Apparently some travellers before you stepped off the road here, perhaps to rest some before continuing their journey.
5067: You carefully squeeze your way between two bushes and walk around some large rocks. The place is rather weird and it would be easy to get lost among the many rocks. It's hard to move fast without cutting or hurting oneself on the sharp surfaces of the rocks.
5068: Squeezing your way through a couple of bushes you make your way forward. Small patches of grass grow between the unfriendly rocks that dominate this place. To the east some grassy plains are visible.
5069:
A small cluster of clover grows here.
A small cluster of clover grows here.

Making your way through the high grass is not as easy as you first thought. It is difficult to maintain a sense of direction when so much of what you see is the same. Westwards however, the vegetation becomes less dense.
5070: The trail following the southern side of the great wall of thorns is heading roughly from south-east to north-west. It looks to be still in use as the grasses are flattened along its length. Maybe merchants use this route or even the famed Rangers of the North, who knows?
5071: There is no way to cross the barrier of thorns standing to the north, that is for sure. What was once built and maintained by the marshals of Cardolan stands even though the realm fell to Angmar and plague. Another remnant is the stony trail that you stand upon as its cuts its way through the grassy terrain. The vista to the south-west is of a landscape of grass, dotted here and there by the odd bush. Further in that distance, the terrain rises and becomes greener as the fertile South Downs start.
5072: A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.

Walking around in these rough grounds requires great care not to trip and hurt oneself. It is tiresome and you long for some smoother ground to walk on. A few of the rocks have seemingly been toppled over quite recently, reminding you that you are not the first to visit this place.
5073: The ground here is strewn with bare rocks dotting the white plains. Slightly sloping upwards, passage to the west becomes more and more strenuous, as the grounds also get rougher and the rocks larger. To the north the grass grows dense and high, and takes on a greyish tone, while it grows more sparse east and south. A few faint high-pitched shrieks are heard from the sky, and you notice the shadow of a bird of prey hovering over the plains far southeast.
5074: The plains you are walking on are unusually quiet. The vegetation is sparse, except for the dry grass that grows up to your waist. To your west you can see a small fortress but otherwise the vista is desolate and dull.
5075: Endlessly the great hedge grows through the grasslands, the trail which you are upon doggedly shadowing it. The chalky soil in the surrounding prairie produces little else but hardy grasses. The wind blows across your face and the only real break from it is sheltering under the thorns.
5076: You seem to be on an old trail from the elder days of Arnor. Rocks and cobbles maintain the track still, but it is hopelessly overgrown as well. However, there is still signs that it is used, since the grass have been trodden down.
5077: Close to where the southbound hedge on your west side turns east, the ground is heavily cracked up by thorns and shallow roots here. The white, hard soil that dominate the slightly hilly plains to the east and north of here seems to provide too little nourishment even for the thorns, and they do not grow far in those directions. Grey and brown grass are the only species that care to grow there, and no signs of wildlife are obvious except a lone hawk high up in the northeastern sky.
5078: The old trail continues, offering to take the traveller northwest or southeast. The ground is hard and trampled and covered with small pebbles. Judging from the tracks and the trampled grass of the edges of the trail it is still very much in use.
5079: You stir up some dirt as you move and a small animal scurries away into the grass. Although obviously used, the trail is covered with rocks and branches from the roadside vegetation stretches over the trail in an attempt to cover it completely.
5080: The trail ends and begins here. Once it continued south over a bridge, but that bridge has been torn down for long. Not much remains of it except a few rotting planks on the bottom of a steep ravine that emerges from the bushes to the east and grinds its way southwest to the Nen-i-Sul. Thick and high thorns surround you on the south and east sides, hiding the trail from the morning sun. Only some sparse grey grass cares to live here, trying to fend off the thorns. Impromptu paths have been cleared to the north and east, doubtless since the collapse of the bridge.
5081: The thick Great Hedge that once protected the lands of Cardolan grows south of here, while white rolling plains stretch out in all other directions. Nothing much grows on them except for some short and coarse grey and brown grass, hiding in the shallow valleys between the low hills. Small dry brooks have dug their ways south for ages, and now look like wrinkles in an old man's face. Not much can be seen moving around, as the plains offer little protection for animals.
5082: The land before you slope slowly away south-westwards, with many small, dry southbound brooks between tiny rolling hills. The grass is scanty, coarse and grey, growing mostly in patches between large areas of white hard earth. The hard earth hurts the feet, but is easy to travel. In all directions these arid plains continue, with some higher grass only to the north.
5083: A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.

The grass grows high here, yet it seems dull and lifeless. The ground lacks any topsoil, and rain that falls here is quickly gathered in small brooks among the faint low hills, draining the plains. Stepping over one of these brooks you notice a very round and white rock on the bottom. North and west of here the grass retains its thickness and height, but east and south it grows shorter and more sparse for a few miles. A thick green-grey streak lines the horizon in these directions, indicating denser vegetation.
5084: Running in parallel with the road, these plains show many tracks of travellers having stepped off the road. The plains continue in what appears to be endless fields to the east and to the west. Examining the ground reveals tracks of both smaller creatures and of larger, hoofed animals.
5085: The road goes on east and west as far as you can see with plains on both sides. To the east, the grass starts to give way to a much thicker brush, the old east road cutting its way through.
5086:
A crumbling fountain is in the middle of the place.
A ruffian is sneaking around here, looking for some mischief to do.

An old fountain stands in front of the castle, many dead leaves fester in the still water that is left in the bottom of it. A brick pathway leads around the fountain from the gate, all the way up to the large entrance to the keep. Grass and weeds grow through the cracks that line this path. Ivy grows throughout the area, taking a stranglehold wherever it can.
5087: Large windows line the walls of this corridor, with huge red curtains hanging from above. The curtains are of dark red colour and extremely thick. A mural hangs from the other wall towards the inside of the castle, depicting a battle of glory for the castle. The corridor leads onward towards the south, with more large windows framed in thick wood. Many of them have been broken, glass left lying on the ground. Looking out through the broken windows you see an orchard in the yard.
5088: Along the western side is a large stone arch that leads all the way down the corridor. A frame made out of thick oak stands within the arches. There are a few large hooks in the wall on the other side. A broken handle from a large great sword hangs from one of those iron hooks, its blade long since broken off. There is a pile of a torn and scorched red cloth lying here.
5089: There are a few racks standing here, with some rusty hangers dangling from them. The racks line up in rows all across the room, with a few clothes hanging from them. There are some tattered clothes lying on the ground all torn or burnt. Some clothes hang from the racks closest to the door, their cloth newer and handled with more care. A small desk stands beside the door, its legs covered with cobwebs, and a small chair sits behind the desk. The chair itself has no cobwebs on it, and there are some tracks in the dust from where the chair has been moved.
5091: Some dried blood stains the walls of this hallway. There is a door here, and a large broken bar lying next to it. There are some tattered clothes with blood-stains on them scattered on the floor. The hallway bends southward where more objects lie on the ground undisturbed.
5092: There is a small broken door to the south with garbage piled in front of it making progress impossible in that direction. The walls are stained with blood and tattered clothes are scattered around the room. A wooden beam from the ceiling lies upon the ground, burnt beyond use.
5093: A large oak table stands in the middle of this room, with many garnished metal dinner plates scattered across its top. Remains of candles lie on the table in pieces while high above hangs a large chandelier with only a few crystal pieces missing from it. Along the walls are pictures of past rulers of the castle, their faces long lost from the many slashes taken out on the paintings. A large door stands just towards the south, with two large knights in armour standing before it. They have been rusted through, and their hands stand poised, yet the weapons that they once wielded have been removed from their grasp.
5094: It is dark within this old building, the stone ceiling has been kept intact throughout all the neglect in this castle. A few rotten cots lie in the corner of the building with rusted spears sitting beside them. An old desk lies broken on the floor on the other side of the room. A book rests barely on top of the slanted desk. There are some words written on top of the dark green book. There is also a small hole in the back of the building.
5095: This is the top of a small set of stairs that wind downward into the darkness below, with its walls made of a cold rough stone. There are sconces for torches to hang on the wall made out of a brass mould with carved statues on them, but no torches remain.
5096: A short burly man stands here, looking around for something.

The stairs from above widen out and reveal a large room containing rough tables and some instruments of torture. One skeletal body lies on the floor, with many pieces missing from it. Bite marks line the legs and arms of the former victim of this place. A cell, isolated by crude bars, is east of here.
5097:
A skeleton of some humanoid lies in the dust.
A prisoner is sitting here, looking at you with sad eyes.
A prisoner is sitting here, looking at you with sad eyes.

This is where the prisoners of the current occupants of the castle are kept. A small deep hole is over in one of the corners, with an pungent odour drifting up from it. A small cot lies on one of the walls with little left of it. The mattress is torn and scattered about the room. The only way out of this room is back west, through the iron bars, which though crude, are sturdy.
5098:
A pie has been left here.
A musty loaf of bread has been left here.
A loaf of bread has been left here.
A wooden box, made from rich wood, rests on the ground.
A small barrel made of aged oak and strong iron hoops stands here.

Here is a makeshift kitchen for the preparation and cooking of food. There is a crude oven, wood stacked beside it ready for burning. Several boxes and barrels are also here, possibly the loot from some raid on unsuspecting travellers who met their end against the current motley band who now control this fort.
5099: The corridor comes to an end here, with a large statue of an unknown soldier standing here, pointing his sword towards the east. A large mural hangs behind him depicting some long past battle and great victory. There is a large entrance to a darkened room here. There are a few broken and rusted swords lying on the ground here.
5100:
A sturdy bandit bodyguard stands here, eager to hack you to pieces.
A sturdy bandit bodyguard stands here, eager to hack you to pieces.
The mean bandit leader Barbaras grins at you and draws his sword.

There is a long path leading up to a huge golden coloured throne in this hall. The throne has many wild animals carved on it. The back is carved to look like a large bear and snakes curl down the sides. Some red curtains hang draping the room slightly on both sides of the throne, with two large statues watching over the throne with their swords in their hands drawn.
5101:
A rotten corpse is hanging here.
A half-rotten corpse is hanging here.
Bathmhurz the ancient troll lunges at you with iron-nails.
A powerful young troll stares at you.

This cave is hollowed out below the hole above. The trash in this room is piled quite high in the bottom, and the acrid smell is very strong. The bedding material consists of dried bushes and gnawed bones. The only visible exit is to clamber back up through the hole.
5102:
A powerful young troll stares at you.
Some ugly blow-flies are buzzing around here.

This is a low, wide natural cavern. The walls are quite rough and contain many crevices. The ceiling above contains a hole five feet across, where the process of erosion have removed the chalky rock. Someone has made an effort to cover this hole, as a large stone slab has been laid above. A timber post is wedged into the floor and under this slab, perhaps to lever it open? The floor contains a hole similar to the one above. The tell-tale signs of claw marks on the walls, and the strong odour reveal that trolls live here!
5103: This small tunnel must have been half-forgotten, it is such a tight passage. Maybe it was a sewer in the past, the strong odour certainly suggests this. The walls of the tunnel bear stone-cladding, but much of this has fallen into disrepair. Where stone-tiles have fallen into the crawl-space you have even more difficulty manoeuvring. Lets hope you don't have to retreat as you have no room to turn back now.
5104: Here the rocky passage bends sharply. The timber props here are few but the rough ceiling looks safe enough. An acrid smell pervades this area and it hangs in the windless air. The passage continues south into pitch darkness, or west when it bends north after a short distance. Another small tunnel can be seen heading east. It is very low and small, and you will have to crawl along it to pass.
5105: A black pond is here, filled with putrid water.

The tunnel that you are in bends rather sharply here. On first examination there seems no reason for this to happen. However, looking at the south way of the tunnel you see that part of a volcanic extrusion has been revealed. The ceiling here is lacking any support as the props lie rotting in some water. The only choices are to go east around this rock, or walk north into the dark.
5106: The great limestone rift, Orchabal's Fissure, starts and ends here. It course takes it westward, far far beyond ones sight. Though this underground feature exists in the middle of what was a land controlled by the Dunedain, only a rudimentary amount of building has taken place. The major feature is the roadway which is cut into the rock, making an underground path along the chasm, a place which would be too treacherous for normal travel otherwise. If dwarves had lived in numbers nearby, generations of dwarves would surely have made a great deal of fuss about this place, carving intricate designs into the walls, capping stones and creating stable arches through which to travel. Here there is merely a brass plaque next to another crack leading south.
5107: Judging from the columns which pierce the tunnel, this area once saw quite a lot of water flowing down from the rock above. However, at some stage the flow has stopped and the stone-structures have dried up, becoming weakened by the lack of humidity. Many of the ruddy-coloured stalactites have come crashing down, while a part of the wall has fallen away, forcing you to clamber over.
5108: In either direction, there is no sign of light or life. The years of waters trickling down the limestone have created a colourful spectacle: green and brown stains of minerals standing out against the lightly coloured stone. The direction of the fissure is comparatively well behaved in this section, giving the miners of the passage through the fissure little to do besides flattening the floor and removing dangerous overhangs.
5109:
An untrustworthy man is here, eyeing his equipment.
A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.

The fissure alternately grows and narrows, while the architects of the tunnel have made use of this natural route. At times one side of the trail falls away as a path is cut into one side of the great crack. At other times the ceiling drops dramatically making it only high enough for a short man to pass through without stooping.
5110: The corpse of Gahruuk the half-orc is lying here.

The great underground scar twists in its passage below the surface of the earth. Exaggerating this, the hewn passage within the fissure crosses from the northern side of the fissure to the south by means a slightly arched bridge. This bridge looks rather more unsettling than it really is, its construction having been further established by the accumulation of minerals which further cement the span. A large stalactite above the bridge narrows to a point some ten feet before reaching the span. A smaller stalagmite lies on one side of the bridge. Perhaps in a thousand years, these two will meet and fuse, providing another support to the man-made structure.
5111: Miles and miles one walks, not seeing any end. Within this great underground fissure, a man-made tunnel is roughly hewn. The uneven direction of the limestone crack means that the tunnellers have had to follow its route, minimising their own lot. At one point a rather large crack from floor to ceiling provides an obstacle to cross, a slow rain of drops creating a curtain of dripping water. At another point, several giant-sized boulders lie strewn across the floor, blocking much of the fissure and creating a strong breeze.
5112: This great fissure is long. It is very long. Stretching for miles in both directions, one has little choice but to carry on the quest to reach the end. The uneven nature of the tunnel makes the journey even more tiresome. The ground is slippery from the water that collects in small pools making an unusual source of drinking water. Beside the path that is cut into the fissure, mining equipment has been discarded. It must have been left here years ago, as the mineral-laden waters have coated them in a deposit of stone, making them strange additions to the underworld.
5113: This great scar definitely has an end, but it cannot be seen. The fissure is not without its features either. At one point the fissure might twist slightly, at others the roof comes perilously close before climbing again into the dark. Who would have thought that such a marvel existed below the wastes of the Lone-lands? Though the fissure seems for the main devoid of any side-exits beyond small hollows, here there is a sizeable opening in the southern wall.
5114:
A sturdy crate made of nailed wooden planks sits on the floor.
A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.
A stocky mountain mule is here, waiting to serve.
A large warhorse is standing here, clad in mail.

The cavern formed in the rock, seems to be the result of the collapse of some kind. From the subsequent deposits of minerals on the surfaces it must have been some time ago, but there is a slab of rock as tall as a tower which has broken away from one wall, only to rest its upper end on another.
5115: Mile upon mile of the fissure stretch away beyond your vision. Within this long flaw in the limestone shelf, the tunnel weaves its way. The miners have felt it necessary to support the ceiling in several places with stout wooden props. However, when you touch them, you notice that the wood has been calcified by the supply of mineral-laden water. Now the props are as much a part of the rocky interior as any other stalagmite or limestone drapery.
5116: This is a great fissure, yet it narrows to a crack just west of here. The limestone in which the crack appeared long ago shows all the signs of gradual mineral deposition due to the laden waters which have percolated from above: stalactites, stalagmites, flowstone etc. One important feature that has survived unscathed is a brass plaque attached to the northern wall next to a passage that is hewn into the rock.
5117:
The corpse of a bandit is lying here.
A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.

Roughly hewn is this passage, stretching many hundreds of yards from north to south. The majority of the rock through which the tunnel passes is limestone, a major component of both Weathertop and the central plains of Eriador. Water has over the centuries dripped into the passage, creating stubby stalagmites.
5118: An entrance to a passage is on the stair, the stairway briefly widening to provide a stopping-place where climbers can catch their breath. The stairs winding down are coated in dust and powered rock. However, the stairs leading up are in a far worse state, great chunks of flinty rock choking the route.
5119: The sounds of ones footsteps ring off the walls and cast echoes from the surrounding hallways. There is little dust on the ground to muffle this sound, unlike the dusty stairwell to the south. The passages north and east are cut from the rock of the hill itself: limestone, though it has been dutifully smoothed. The floor, although not level, is even enough for a conduit which these days sees virtually no traffic.
5120: Walking through this smoothly hewn tunnel is akin to stepping back in time to see the progress of the race of man. There are carvings along the wall and scenes of early man hunting and making camp, fire-making and celebrating. The frieze must surely predate the Dunedain and possibly even the time of the Numenoreans. Many hands must have once passed along the walls, feeling the works, their torches scorching and blackening the upper walls.
5121: A tiny spider is here, eating a tiny bug.

The dark tunnel from the west comes to an abrupt halt beside a wooden door, which is built into the north wall. The door has not coped well with the passing years, appearing old and mostly rotten. Markings and carvings once covered the door, but they have been ravaged just like the portal.
5122: Once perhaps this was some antechamber to a tomb, but vandals have sacked what goods were placed here. However, the paintings on the wall seem unmarked. A lord is shown in the various stages of entombment and his spirit's subsequent leaving of the body and taking gifts towards the sun in the sky. The floor is of hard rock, in the most part roughly hewn. The exception is the polished path of inlaid stone that curves from the doorway to the narrow chamber west.
5123: A rectangular plinth stands at the centre of this small room, creating a narrow space between the coffin on its top and the dark walls. The top of the coffin is broken in two, only the lower half remaining. The upper half lies on the floor disregarded. An engraving on the top has writing in a strange alphabet. The language seems akin to a distant form of Westron. All one can make out is the largest word, best translated to mean Ralgund. The coffin proper is empty. If this was where the remains of some lord or king were inured, they have since decayed or been looted.
5124: The passage has been cut through the rock of the hill in a roughly circular cross-section, no extra effort being undertaken to dress the stone. A few shallow depressions hold some milky subterranean water.
5125: The subterranean passage bends abruptly at this place. Diagonally across the passage from the inner corner to the outer, an archway has been chiselled. There is water on the floor, collected in shallow pools, but it is murky in appearance, and not fit for drinking.
5126: The roughly hewn path curves around the walls of the Deep. Though not as muddy as the ledge to the north, water creeps down the walls, across the ledge and trickles down into the depths.
5128: The architectural theme of the passage changes along its length. To the east, the passage is hewn from the rock and nothing more. In contrast, at this western end the stone has been meticulously worked. Limestone blocks dress the floor, walls and ceiling. While those of the floor are plain, the blocks of the walls depict an axe head motif: each block is the size and shape of a twin- bladed axe, set diagonally, details residing on each stone. The wall is broken to the north as great inscribed archway leads to a great chamber.
5129:
The corpse of a mindless slime is lying here.
The corpse of a mindless slime is lying here.

This is a marvellous cavern of great height, higher indeed than it is wide. The rock seems to be limestone, but the walls are imbedded with mica or quartz. A dim glow seems to light the interior of the crystals, casting the large cave in an eerie light. This light is refracted in the rain of drops that falls from many places in the vaulting of the cavern. The walls are slick with this water as it runs down to the muddy floor. The mud of this floor is a mix of fine grains of rock, suspended in a watery solution. This seems a marvellous place and it is no wonder that Athoin sought to protect it. However awe-inspiring this place might be, one gets the subtle feeling that one shouldn't tarry as the direction of north and south become blurred. Perhaps in some ways, the spirit of the dwarf lives on, or maybe there is some enchantment in the walls.
5130:
Some mud before you rears up to attack.
Some mud before you rears up to attack.
Some mud before you rears up to attack.

The constant drip-drip of water reverberates within the great chamber. Diffuse light illuminates the far walls as well as the great heights, encrusted with pale crystal. This wonder is in contrast to the mineral-laden mud around ones' legs that flows mysteriously, and a strange feeling of disorientation.
5131: Some mud before you rears up to attack.

Between Athoin's Vault and the deep cave of his father Theddin, stands this ledge. The mud from the Vault covers the rock, making the area treacherous. Directly east is the centre of the cavern: the Deep. The bottom is some way below, while its ceiling is lost in the darkness above. Since the cave is only illuminated by the radiance from the vault, its size can not be determined, though it is certainly large. Grey-green lichens grow on the limestone where the light falls.
5132:
The corpse of the Necromancer is lying here.
There are two skeletons here.
Ducaht (tooprettytodie), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Drazud (freshmeat), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Klaees (thedon), wielding the great black scimitar, is standing here.

Lying below the hill, remote from the outside world, lies this room dedicated to arcane research. The plaster walls are lined with shelves holding ageing scrolls, books, and manuscripts. In the centre of the room is a grand pine table, with numerous pieces of documentation resting on it. Dark stains mark the lightly coloured wood while next to some beakers stand irregular fragments of black crystal. Around the table, several strong wooden chairs provide a modicum of comfort, even though they are rather worn and threadbare.
5133:
A beautiful longbow, embellished with lines of silver and mithril, lies here.
A large steel keyring is lying here.
A quiver wrapped in gems and rubies lies here.
The corpse of *a Dwarf* is lying here.
The corpse of *a Half-Elf* is lying here.
A large stone chest with ebony bands stands here.
A sturdy crate made of nailed wooden planks sits on the floor.
A small oaken table has been set here.
A water barrel has been left here.
Ryokan the Cave Troll is here, fighting a shadow.
Kylhuk the Mountain Troll is here, fighting a shadow.
A shadow is here, fighting Zlo.
Zlo is here, fighting a shadow.

A kin of the other chamber, this one does not contain any books, but seems to be where most of the experiments take place. On the shelves sit trinkets as well as an assortment of household utensils. A small stove stands beside the eastern wall, currently unlit. Beside the stove, coals provide the necessary fuel. A deep recess in the southeast corner of the chamber contains a grating at the bottom, providing a means of disposal. Reams of paper line the desk which stands in the northeast corner, while the candle on the centre has burnt low. Notably, various flasks of strange liquids also stand. Beside the desk is a functional bed, the sheets turned down and looking rather in need of a wash.
5134:
The corpse of a living statue is lying here.
Ducaht (tooprettytodie), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Drazud (freshmeat), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Klaees (thedon), wielding the great black scimitar, is standing here.

The ledge around the great cave begins and ends here in the northeast corner of the Deep. A thick column of limestone is fused with the cavern wall to the south and the ledge does not continue around the obstruction. Rather, set into the column is a heavy door made from ancient oak, bound in iron and set with a lock. From beneath the door, a yellow light leaks out, illuminating the ledge.
5135: Maintaining a constant elevation, the ledge continues along the edge of the Deep. The sounds of drips roundabout ring in the confines of the chamber, while down below water gurgles. A shape occasionally moves out in the wide space of the cavern, but never close enough to be identified.
5136: The limestone shelf curves around the girth of the Deep, providing safe passage. Though slick with rivulets of water from above, the ledge is artificially roughened by notches, providing the much-needed traction. Low overhangs have been also pruned, but only to man height, so those taller must stoop as they edge their way along.
5137: The tunnel burrows crudely through the chalky rock. Sturdy timbers hold up the low ceiling which is crumbly to the touch. The passageway seems hundreds of paces in length though it is difficult to judge when you cannot see both ends simultaneously. The air is very dry and chalk-dust is brought up by your footsteps. No ventilating breeze dispels the cloud, which eventually settles. You have no choice but to travel north towards a bend which is just visible, or to head in the opposite direction.
5138: This is the end of the chalk-hewn tunnel, supported by stout wooden props. It ends abruptly at a dressed stone wall. A torch bracket is fixed to the wall, but the wood it contains is unlit. The tunnel heads north into the darkness.
5139: The walls of this chamber are close together, yet the walls are adorned with fine pictures. There is even one full length picture standing there depicting a battle between the forces of Cardolan and a group of Hill-men from the east. The only way out seems to be through a panel above your head.
5141: A pony is standing here, ridden by you.

The road runs eastwards and westwards as far as the eye can see. Bordering the road is what appears to be endless plains of swaying grass. Sounds of small animals moving around in the grass reaches your ears.
5142: A pony is standing here, ridden by you.

The ground which constitutes the road is trampled and shows many tracks of hoofed animals, probably horses. To the north and south vast plains of swaying grass invites you to step off the road and rest some before continuing your journey.
5143:
A bedraggled man stumbles as best he can across the terrain.
A pony is standing here, ridden by you.
To the south you can see some kind of fortification, though it lies many miles from here. The immediate surroundings are marked mainly by the road, which cuts through a vast, seemingly endless plain.
5144: You stir up some dust as you make your way forward. Small pebbles lie on the sides of the road. The sky is high above and you feel tired of your long journey. Perhaps you should take a rest before heading any further.
5145: A pony is standing here, ridden by you.
The road continues east and west from here, going through the endless plains which dry grass swaying in the wind makes you feel you are journeying through an ocean without a boat.
5146: A pony is standing here, ridden by you.
The road goes on east and west again seemingly forever surrounded by the endless green plains. Some low bushes are growing beside it.
5147: A pony is standing here, ridden by you.

The road bends here, continuing to the west and south. Plains border the road in all directions. The dirt is hard and trampled, and pebbles are scattered all over the road. On a surface like this, you are certain not to leave as many tracks as someone moving beside the road.
5148: The road stretches westwards and eastwards in what seems to be an endless effort to reach some unknown goal, always inviting travellers to use it to reach their destination. You are standing in an ocean a vast plains, the brown dirt of the road being the only solid surface in sight.
5149: The road winds away east and west before you like an ancient snake whose scales have begun to erode and rot from the passage of time. The stone tiles of the road are broken and scattered, with brown weeds and grass fighting for the patches of ground now uncovered. The land here is flat, but covered with many spiney shrubs and dark thorny brush. The wind constantly blows dust into the air, choking your throat and tearing at your eyes. An eerie silence hangs over this place.
5150: Making its miserable path through this blighted land, the road stretches east and west towards the horizon. Shadows flit across the road and hawklike cries pierce the air; you feel strange eyes upon you from above. To the north and south of the road extends a brown, trackless expanse of thorny brush. The bushes are taller than a tall man, and obscure all details of the landscape.
5151: The sounds of your boots padding upon the ancient broken tiles of the road rings in your ears as you wander along the road. Here it bends north and west around a dark cropping of brush and trees and becomes lost in the haze and distance of the plains. The wind silently blows into the thorny hedges which dot the road, making them wave as if they were either calling you or repelling you. You do not know which. The squawk of a swooping vulture alerts you that no place here is safe. You want to keep moving.
5152: The road winds east to south here through a seemingly endless sea of thorny brush. The bushes rise up on both sides of the road like walls, unnaturally tall, unnaturally deadly. The air is quiet and heavy; there is little sign of animal life. The squeaks of rats, and maybe of something else, can be heard in the thickets.
5153: These brushlands punish your sight with harsh views of desolation broken only by forbidding brush and the occasional tree. You wonder why you left the lush greens of your homeland for these hard browns and greys which now assail you. `How can anything live here?', you ask yourself, but you do not know. And you do not want to know.
5154: A huge warg is here, moving in for the kill.

Like a faithful guide, the road leads east and west through these brushlands that surround you. You cautiously do not stray even an inch off the well beaten path for, though you see and hear nothing, you are sure that out there, something is watching you. You feel safe upon this old pathway, where thousands have tread in time lost in memory but you wonder: Can it protect you from whatever lies hidden in the brush that is just out of sight? The thorny bushes are particularly tall on both sides of the road here.
5156: You continue to trudge within the comforting boundaries of the road which curves east and south here. Only the smell of death assaults your nose as you come across the skeletal remains of some animal, the like of which you have never seen in your journeys across Arda. You do not want to become a trophy to the victory of this brush over your will, you are determined to move on and keep moving until it is behind you. But there is nothing to be seen on any side save great brown thorny bushes and the tops of some of the taller trees which poke up out of the brush like the heads of drowning men.
5157: You follow the road which can take you either east or west from here though neither direction seems to be able to rid you of this infernal brushland with its thorny bushes, tall, rotting fields of brown weed, and dark, mottled earth. This place breathes rot and ruin upon you and you wish to be done with it. Though you walk heavily and your weapons and pack clatter together, you think you distinctly hear a crunching sound, like leaves being crushed under foot, coming from behind the brushline to the north.
5158: The old road straggles on to the east and the west, passing through a plain blotted and choked with dark, evil looking brush and brown weeds. The skyline is only occasionally broken by a solitary dark, gnarled tree, and the sounds of life so familiar to you seem stolen from this place. No living animal, save for circling scavengers above, can be seen anywhere.
5159: Looking like a beaten dog, the road whimpers west and south away from you. Again, strange noises reach your ears and you could swear you see shapes moving in the brush to the east and north along the road, where it grows in a great brown thorny sea. Yet it is hard to imagine what could move in so thick a tangle of thorny canes and creepers.
5161: The air is cool here as you walk upon the road, leading you east or west through the bushland. As you stop and survey your progress, you notice a dark shadow pass over the prairie and even the thorny shrubs scattered throughout seem to shiver at its passing, or is it just a trick of the eye and a play of the wind? Feeling cold that emanates not so much from the outside as within, you feel an urge to quicken your journey.
5162: You are standing on the Old East Road as it makes its way east-west through some gently rolling plains. In the distance to the southeast, the land becomes much rougher. Rising above the road to the east are some jagged hills. There doesn't seem to be much living here besides you and the grass covering the plains.
5163: The road continues making its way east-west through the rolling plains. You feel that you are all alone in this wide land. To the east, jagged, broken hills block the road's easy path, while, to the southeast, the plains become rougher.
5164: The road winds its way east and west here, skirting around the broken plains and hills of the Lone-lands to the east. The land to the north is more hospitable, but no less empty. You begin to wonder why there aren't any people living in these lands.
5165: The road winds its way west and east here, skirting around the sheer cliffs that form this side of the hills to the east and around the broken plains to the south. Coming closer to the hills, you feel a sense of foreboding. Perhaps in among the hills is the answer to the emptiness of these lands.

The road makes its way here east-west, skirting the broken hills of the Lone-lands to the south. To the north, the rolling plains continue, broken only by some trees in the distance. The jagged cliffs to the south seem to be impassable, except for the faint remains of a path leading up into them to the south.
5167: The road winds east and west here, making its way between the jagged, broken hills to the south and the rolling plains to the north. The plains to the north and west stretch as far as the eye can see, broken only by an occasional stand of trees. The hills to the south seem impassable.
5168: Here, the road runs east-west between the rolling plains to the north and the broken plains of the Lone-lands to the south. To the southwest lie an area of cliff-like broken hills. This land seems to be truly desolate.
5169: Running east-west, the road threads its way between the rolling plains to the north and the broken terrain of the Lone-lands to the south. To the southwest, the land rises up into an area of broken hills. Directly north of you, a thicket provides some welcome cover.
5170: A Bend in the Old East Road

The road runs north and west here, right under the shadow of the southern hills. The rolling plains to the north do little to warm your soul that has been chilled here under what seems to be the hateful watch of the hills.

Curving south and east, the road curves around the battered terrain of the Lone-lands to the south. Southwards rise some broken hills, while southeast, the terrain is slightly more manageable. To the north lie gently rolling plains.
5172: The road runs east-west here between the rolling plains to the north and the broken plains to the south. To the southwest, the Lone-lands rise up into a series of hills.
5173: Still travelling down this road, your surroundings make the Lone Lands seem seem an appropriate name. The only life you can discern in this desolate realm of Arda, are rabbits scuttling across the road and in the grass.
5174: You find yourself amid a stand of thorny bushes which tear your clothes and skin as you try to wade through it. It is at times so thick and dense that you wonder whether you will become stuck in it. But, fortunately, your constant pain pays off as your limbs move you, albeit slow and painfully, through this sea of thorns. `Where has the road gone?', you ask yourself as you scan the brush for any sign of the road, but unless your eyes decieve you, you find no sign of the road. It is as if the Old East Road never was.

This trail of barren plains turns northward as a stand of weeds and a line of brush block its path east or west.

The small patch of red flowers upon a small hill nearby must be close relatives to Seregon, the blood flower that grew on Amon Rudh. The hill will look drenched in blood in the mornings, shine like a red carpet during mid-day, and glow like a slow burning fire when the sun sets.

Not much can be seen from within the brush, but sounds of moving creatures reaches your ears. To the north the Old East Road is clearly visible. South of here, wide white plains begin. Far away beyond these, a green line is visible below the horizon - the Great Hedge.

The soil is mucky and brown, and fallen thorny branches reach up to tear your feet.

5212: A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.

Great stands of brown brush, its canes armed with sharp, tearing thorns, rise up all around, almost hiding from view some foundation stones and crumbled, overgrown walls. Perhaps this was a fortification once, but it is impossible really to tell. The grey stones have lost their corners, and resemble a scattered heap of frost-worn boulders more than the remains of any definite type of building. Muddy water trickles southward at the base of the stones.
5213: Thorny bushes all but block the light of day, growing unnaturally tall - as high as fifteen feet - and bearing broad, heavy branches covered with ripping thorns. The lay of the land can only be sensed, not seen. It rises sharply to the east, while sloping gently downward to the west where a muddy trickle wanders slowly among the bases of the huge bushes. Odd footprints can be seen in the mud, and the squeak of rats can be heard in the brush all around.
5214: Ducaht (tooprettytodie), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.

This valley is shallow, broad, and bounded by low embankments to the east and west. If it were not for the huge thornbushes which fill virtually every square foot of its floor, obscuring the small, muddy southward-tending stream from view, and which block and overhang every possible place where the embankments might be climbed, travel through here would not be difficult. In fact, it is very difficult to get out of the valley on either side. The thorns seem to positively resist, interlacing themselves to block passage.
5215: A large bush grows here, its great spiny branches waving in the wind.

This is the valley of a small southward-tending creek, muddy and nearly dry, which dribbles slowly through a succession of muddy pools. The valley is virtually choked with tall, brown-withed thorny bushes, whose tangled canes make travel almost impossible, particularly up the embankments to the east and west which are overhung by the huge and malevolent plants.
5216: This is a valley that trends northward and southward, at the lowest point of which a muddy stream, or trickle, flows at a snail's pace from one muddy puddle to another. The land is rocky and harsh, and it is hard to believe that this stream actually formed the valley; probably it is just the lowest point in these shallow hills. The valley is choked by the dense thorny bushes which surround you on all sides, and it is very difficult to get any sense of the lay of the land.
