The ground all around you is strewn with rocks, and the only vegetation which survives is comprised of several types of weed. Not far to the south a road snakes off into the distance, leading eventually to Rivendell, to the far east.
5574: Sharp rocks and stones litter the ground all about. At the edge of the road, just to the south of here, the rocks appear to be somewhat regular and rectangular, perhaps ancient cobblestones which once paved the way. Small stands of stunted trees can be seen here and there, but these are few and far between.
5575: To the south the Old East Road twists and turns between rocky grounds and steep ridges. The ground is rocky but strands of stunted trees can be seen nearby and weeds abound in the cracks on the surface of the road. The rocky terrain of this area appears to be ideal for snakes but prey for these creatures might be scarce since wildlife is sparse in this area.
5576: The soil here is dry and cracked even though a river flows close by to the east. At the southern edge of the plains lies the Old East Road, an ageing thoroughfare, which looks to be in dire need of repair. Heather and weeds fill innumerable cracks in the surface of the road, while rocks and stones lie scattered about.
5577: The old wagon tracks along the river, just east of here, lead from the south where the Old East Road can be found. The riverbank is steep and is likely to be difficult to ascend. In the north-west hills rise gently out from the surrounding plains and to the north-east the blunt shapes of a couple of towers can be seen against the horizon. The vegetation here is scarce, consisting mostly of weeds and a few patches of heather.
5578: Huge boulders lie scattered across the terrain making travel here difficult. Between the boulders, dense thickets have grown covering the treacherous ground. The Old East Road lies to the south, avoiding this inhospitable landscape. Towards the north and south the plains slowly transform into grey hills, that look barren from here.
5579:
A tall brown-skinned orc, with wide arms, examines you harshly.
A tall brown-skinned orc, with wide arms, examines you harshly.
A tall brown-skinned orc, with wide arms, examines you harshly.

This is the gatehouse of what used to be a mighty fortress. Small slits in the western wall allowed a small number of archers to control the entrance to the fortress. The gatehouse was built from large rectangular stone blocks and it has withstood years of erosion, though damage during the war weakened the far northern wall to an extent that it eventually collapsed under its own weight destroying the stairs that once led to the second floor. Of the enormous gates that once guarded the eastern entrance only the bronze hinges remain, but to the west a very rusty portcullis still stands. To the south is a structure that looks like it used to be the guardroom.
5580: Once this was a place where the gate guards spent time between watches. Someone has pushed the rubble, formed from rotten furniture, into a corner and placed bedrolls against the eastern wall. A crooked table made from several rough planks stands in the middle of the room and the remnants of a simple meal can be found upon it.
5581: Before you stands the last remaining guard tower of this stronghold. The stone walls of the tower are several feet thick and a bronze door, which still guards the entrance to the tower, has turned green. The last few floors of the tower are gone, the tower looking as if a huge sword had sliced off the top.
5582: This was once a large and mighty structure built to protect the old, and now nearly forgotten, Kingdom of Rhudaur. It lies well protected behind a river that the people of Rhudaur had named the Hoarwell. Before the structure fell into disrepair this was a powerful fortress that commanded the countryside for many miles. However, during some long forgotten war the whole northern section of the fortress was razed and only this courtyard, the gate house and a partly ruined guard tower remain.
5583: East of here, a large building containing stables, barracks and storage rooms once stood and was probably the last line of defence in the stronghold. However, the building became a death trap when the northeastern guard tower fell upon it reducing the building to rubble and the inhabitants to corpses. Not much remains of the guard towers: while part of the south western tower still stands the other three towers are nothing more than heaps of stone.
5584: The southern battlement still stands high above your head. Once long ago a high tower secured each end of the wall, but the eastern tower is now little more than a low ring of large stone blocks, while the western tower ends a few feet above the wall. The courtyard surface is made out of square stones fitted close together. Everywhere along the courtyard old twigs, pieces of wood and decomposing leaves litter the ground.
5585: To the south a tower once stood in southeastern corner of this stronghold. The tower was utterly destroyed during the assault that befell this fortress. As the tower came tumbling down it took parts of the wall with it into the river far below. To the east and north are large piles of stone that are the remains of a perimeter wall and a building.
5586: An extremely hot fire must have raged here during the assault because the stone blocks that once formed the towers wall are fused to the floor where they fell. This tower seems to have collapsed under its own weight and much of it has fallen south - into the river below. Weeds now grow here and there through the cracks and along the gaping hole in the floor.
5587: These stairs lead up towards the second level of the tower. They were built very narrow to enhance the defence of the tower. The slits in the wall were made to allow the archers on the inside of the fortress to rain death upon anyone who attacked the fortress. The ground is several yards below and a fall from here would have nasty consequences.
5588: Once this was one of the four towers built to guard the fortress, but now only this tower still stands. Halfway up the northern side of the tower there are three large holes causing the tower to look as if something similar to a huge sledgehammer had repeatedly struck it. To the east a stone staircase begins to spiral towards the second level.
5589: Much of the northern section of the fortress is in ruins. While the northern wall of the fortress, which was once over 15 feet tall, still stands, nowadays it is little more than ten feet high. The two northern guard towers have fallen inwards onto the courtyard and to the west there is a huge pile of grey rubble obstructing movement in that direction.
5590: A huge stone giant is sleeping here.

North of here, the northeastern guard tower used to stand. However, the piles of rubble you see before you, blocking passage to the north are all that remains of the tower. The northern wall, which once joined the now ruined tower, has several holes in it that were created by a large catapult.
5591: This room was probably used to store emergency supplies for the guards in the tower. Remains of swords, almost rusted beyond recognition, lie against one of the walls. To the east a seemingly long tunnel leads into the darkness.
5592: The Rhudaurian king that ordered the building of this fortress realised that its position behind the rivers made it possible for his enemies to trap the garrison inside. So a long tunnel, going east under the river, was dug to ensure that counterstrikes as well as escape could occur from the stronghold. The tunnel is rather damp and the walls are covered with moss. To the west it ends in what seems to be a rectangular room while the eastern end of the tunnel is shrouded in darkness.
5593: The tunnel is rather narrow here and water trickles in through narrow fissures in the roof above your head. The rusted remains of old torch-holders line the walls. The smooth floor slopes upward from here in both directions, creating a low point, where almost a foot of chilly water has accumulated. The footing is extremely treacherous, for the combination of water and thick, green moss make it quite slippery.
5594: The walls and the floor of the passage are black granite, crossed by a few purple mineral veins. The stonework is reminiscent of dwarven stonework, but the shapes are lighter and the lines are not so deeply cut. At the eastern end of the passage a few stone steps lead up into the darkness. The only flaw in the perfection of this finely-wrought tunnel is a rough-sided hole at the base of the stairway.
5595: A rusty mechanical contraption hangs from the ceiling.

The ceiling here is very low, and the black granite walls curve inwards slightly below it, just short of forming an arched roof or a dome. A few steps lead downward at the western end of the chamber, and another set of stairs leads up the northern wall to a strange rusty contraption that hangs from the roof.
5596: This fairly straight tunnel seems to have been dug without regard to the kinds of rock it passed through, but then the softer grey stone must have crumbled under the pressure of the many tons of rock and collapsed, revealing the base of black granite underneath. Broken slabs and chunks of rock lie all around you, almost completely blocking the eastern part of the passage.
5597: The tunnel is almost perfectly round in shape as if it had been dug by a burrowing creature that made no distinction between up, down, left, and right. The floor merges smoothly with the walls, and the walls arch to form the roof. Only deep scratches in the rock that look like marks of sharp claws suggest that maybe the creature preferred to walk or crawl on its paws and did know the difference between the floor and the ceiling. The tunnel is fairly level, but to the west it slopes up, entering a wider passage.
5598: Built to enable troops to move safely between guard towers, this tunnel appears to have been carved through dense bedrock. In the eastern end of the tunnel there is a pool of old rainwater that has leaked from a rectangular hole in the roof above. A massive stone stair leads up through the hole. In the western end of the tunnel there is a massive metal door.
5599: This is a perfectly circular chamber. The walls are fitted with fine-cut, interlocking flagstones. A short passageway leads north to a rectangular room and a stone stairway leads through the ceiling high above you. To the east there is a metal door.
5600: Rough rocks and boulders stand tumbled all about you, and the floor is thick with smaller rubble and debris. The unfinished walls, floor and ceiling of the tunnel suggest that this place might not have been wrought by the hand of dwarf or man, but here and there the tell-tale signs of tooling seem to offer the support an opposing view. What does seem clear is that the massive rock- fall which closes off the tunnel to the west of here was brought about quite deliberately.
5606:
A stone guardian is here, fighting YOU.
A stone guardian is here, fighting YOU.
Vehement the Man (VV), wielding a steel claymore, is here, fighting a stone guardian.
A horse of the Rohirrim (ulo) is standing here.
Nirwen the Silvan is here, fighting a stone guardian.
A sturdy trained horse is standing here.
Tasen the Hobbit (TT), wielding a nimble blade, is here, fighting a stone guardian.
A stocky mountain mule is here, waiting to serve.
Rurar the Dwarf (RR), wielding a mighty dwarven axe, is here, fighting a stone guardian.

The first thing that strikes anyone stepping into this chamber is the feeling that a power older than the power of these hills and also much more violent is present here. This presence seems to weigh heavily on the senses - the air seems hard to breathe, and even in the direct light of a lamp or a torch everything around seems darkened as if seen through dark glass. The ceiling of the chamber is very high, and in the western wall there is an arched door, which looks as if it had been made for a giant. A sloping passage leads down from the opening in the eastern wall.
5607: The passage slopes up slightly as it runs from the east to the west, where it seems to end in a level chamber. To the east of you an ornamented door in the rock marks the entrance into the underground crypt. Far overhead the stone walls bend slightly, forming an arched ceiling. The passage is about ten feet in width and even more in height, and one can only wonder what the stone-masons did to all the rock they had to cut out.
5608: 'dispel magic' door to open exit w

No outside light penetrates into this corner of the cavern, yet the darkness is not as complete as one would expect so deep underground. Luminous veins and specks of minerals in the stone shine with a weak bluish radiance, unnoticeable in the bright light of a torch or a lantern, yet enough to guide the eyes used to the dark. The western wall of the cavern seems to have been smoothed out and polished by the stone-cutters, but no markings of any kind can be seen on its surface.
5609: The cavernous expanse continues to the north, west, and east, its dome-like ceiling lost in the dark. Even though the panels in the floor conceal graves, there is nothing morbid about place; instead, there is a feeling of timelessness and serenity. The dead were brought here and put in the stone to rest, and the hills have accepted them and forgotten them as only a thing older than any living being can forget.
5610: This is the northern part of an enormous cavernous chamber in the very heart of the hills. Obviously, it used to be a natural hollow in the rock which was made into a crypt where the priests of the temple have buried the dead. The stone-masons did little to adorn the place; the walls and the ceiling seem to have kept their original shape. Ornamented panels in the floor mark the places where slabs of stone were cut out to make place for coffins, but no name, date, or inscription marks the panels. The cavern continues to the south and to the east; an arch in the northern wall leads into a smaller chamber.
5611: The stairwell ends here with a wide arch that opens into a cavern-like chamber. Judging by the room's present shape, the stone-cutters who carved it were either unable to cut too deep into the stone, or afraid to disturb the weight of many tons of rock above, and so contented themselves with chipping off sharp edges and corners and smoothing the floor rather than trying to give the room a finished form. An arch in the southern wall of the room leads into a larger chamber.
5612: A shadowy haunt floats here, oblivious to your presence.

It is very dark and quiet here, as if the darkness was muffling all sounds. This part of the cavern has not been touched by the stone-cutters; the walls, the floor, and the ceiling have kept their natural shape. Ancient beyond all human memory yet untouched by decay, the place looks unreal, half-familiar, and somewhat sad like a picture from a long forgotten dream.
5613: This part of the cavern is darker than the rest, but there is an unmistakable draught of fresh air coming from the shaft that is cut in the ceiling of the cavern. A narrow cast-iron stair winds around an iron pole and disappears in the darkness of the shaft. The iron steps were crafted to look like lace, yet they can obviously support great weight.
5614: The wide stairs of the spiral stairwell lead down into the dark. Carved from the bone of the hills, the grey stone walls are plain, not decorated by anything except an occasional coloured vein. In some places the strength of the stone defeated the instruments of the stone-cutters, and they were forced to give up, leaving the walls or the steps slightly uneven.
5615: A winding staircase leads up and down from the landing. About ten steps below you the walls and the stairs merge with the darkness, as if the stairwell was ending with a drop into a bottomless pit. Some light and a draught of air comes from the above.
5616: The hidden passage runs from the east to the west. The walls are covered with pictures of burial ceremonies and of other less peaceful rituals, carved in stone with merciless precision. At the eastern end of the passage you can see a heavy dark curtain, covering the entrance to some room. To the west the passage seems to end in a landing of a stairwell.
5617:
A grey leather-bound book has been left here.
A large bookshelf sits against the wall.
A long stone fireplace with a dim red glow warms the room.
An evil priest is here chanting and praying to some foul entity (glowing).

The high ceiling of the small dark study is lost in the gloom. A heavy marble desk in the centre of the room is littered with books and scrolls, some of them quite old and fragile-looking. One wall of the study is lined by bookshelves, the other is covered by a dark curtain. The third wall is occupied by a fireplace in which the embers of fire glow with a dim red light. No lamp or candle lights the room, the owner of which is obviously used to working with no more light than the glow of the coals on the fireplace.
5619: A shadow suddenly leaves its place on the wall, trying to reach your neck.

There is a heavy trapdoor in the ceiling of the narrow shaft in the rock. From the trapdoor a winding cast-iron stair descends the shaft into the darkness. Just next to you there is an iron door set in the rock wall; a faint draught of air comes from behind it.
5620: The ceiling and the walls of the chamber are plain grey stone except for two bands of some unfamiliar bluish alloy which are fixed to the walls where the walls join the floor and the ceiling. The floor is covered with square panels, each of them engraved with the same ornament of a square with chipped corners cut into four parts. In the western wall of the chamber there is an arch that opens into a dark hall.
5621: Gloom seems to fill the air of this dark hallway which stretches north-south ending with a low arch. A finely crafted lamp hangs over the arch, shining with a cold white-blue radiance, but its light is not bright enough to dispel the gloom in the hall or to penetrate the darkness beyond the arch.
5622: It is very dark here, and there is a draught of cold air coming from the south where the hallway is choked by debris. Obviously, a wall and a part of the ceiling had once collapsed here, blocking passage in that direction. Some of the chunks of stone look like pieces of ornamented panels; a few are curved as if they had once been parts of an arched structure.
5625: The four windows look out in the four directions on the gloomy landscape. Overhead you can see two crossed beams on which the heavy bell once hung, rung in praise, mourning or just out of boredom. Somebody cut the thick rope, and the bell now lies uselessly on the ground. The sides of the bell are grey, but inside it is still shiny and seemingly untouched by weather and time, as if it were only resting and waiting for the day when it would ring again.
5630: Slits, several feet apart, for archers have been cut along the wall. These slits and a rectangular hole in the ceiling are the only ways for sunlight to enter this room. The stone stairwell continues up towards the next level, but some steps are missing along with a large portion of the northern wall.
5631: Just below, some of the stair's steps are missing along with a large portion of the wall. The stairs spirals upwards towards the third level of the tower and slits for the archers are cut into the wall at regular intervals. Bits of useless rubble, upon many of the stairs, remains where it fell many years ago.
5632: While this tower was once several stories high, now this floor, the third, is the highest floor remaining. All that remains of the floors above this one is the huge pile of stone just beyond the southern wall. During clear days, a keen eye can see for many miles from here. The partial roof above is what used to be the fourth floor and is made out of planks supported by huge wooden beams some of which are missing and those remaining extremely rotten. To the north and to the east very narrow doorways lead to old and crumbling battlements.
5633: Built to guard the southwestern corner of the Rhudaur's Kingdom, this strong- hold was a pivotal spot, for any enemy army approaching from the west across the last bridge was easily repulsed as long as this fort stood. From here a small bastion of soldiers could watch and harass any enemy approaching from the Last Bridge. However, when the Kingdom of Rhudaur fell, the fortress became a refuge, but eventually it was overrun and left in ruins. This battlement, the western section, has a few holes but is mostly intact. However, the eastern wing of the battlement, which took substantially more damage, lays in ruins and that which remains is unsafe.
5634: This corner of the battlement has suffered heavy damage from the elements over the years. With the abandonment of the fortress, there was no one was left to oversee its maintenance. After every heavy rain, water would collect on and between the boards of the wooden floor as the rain water ran from the tower to the west into this corner. Slowly the floor began to rot, leaving it in a state in which it could barely support the weight of a small child much less the heavier mass of a grown adult.
5635: This battlement leads from the southwestern tower to the roof of a massive gatehouse. Once, a crenellated parapet lined the top of the wall granting archers excellent cover, but now it has crumbled along with portions of the gangway's railing leaving many small sticks and stones upon the boards which form the floor resulting in unstable footing.
5636:
An orc sentry is here on patrol.
An orc sentry is here on patrol.

Here, high above a ford in the river Mitheithel, an effective defence could be made of the fortress gates. From here, archers could fire upon anything approaching the gates with the only dead-ground being an area just below the walls. To the north of here, many years ago, the battlements were reduced to ruins during an assault upon the fortress.
5637: The size of the gatehouse below you, with its thick walls, must have caused it to be a daunting prospect for conquering. During sieges this section of the roof, a few yards back from the wall, was used to store spare arrows and other supplies needed for defence. A narrow hatch in the roof leads to the floors below.
5638: Scattered across the floor are the remaining parts of the mechanism that was once used to raise and lower the portcullis below. The eastern wall, which faces the courtyard, has a few narrow vertical slits that enabled archers to defend the gatehouse after a breach of the main gates. Against the northern wall a set of stairs leads upwards towards the roof.
5639: The gatehouse was considered to be the defence's linchpin in the event of an attack upon the fortress. Thus, the gatehouse was designed to accommodate numerous archers protected behind thick stone walls. To enhance the fortress's defence and to make an assault upon it even more costly, three large holes were cut into the floor to allow the defenders to pour hot oil upon those assaulting the portcullis. Other than a huge hole in the northern wall, which was made during a successful conquest of the fortress, the only other openings are the archers slits in the western wall. Being one of the few remaining rooms that is still able to provide shelter in the fortress, this room has often been used by wanderers as a refuge since the fall of the fortress.
5640: Just to the west of here, in a narrow canyon, the river Mitheithel flows rapidly towards the south. On the other side of the river a large but ruined fortress can be seen. It appears difficult to get to the fortress from here because a wide river with steep banks blocks direct access to the fortress.
5641:
A snake slithers towards you.
A grey hare stands alert, looking and listening for predators.

A vast rocky plain spreads towards the north, broken only by the narrow valley with the Mitheithel to the north-west and a dark and brooding forest to the north-east. The grass that grows here is coarse and grey and the few trees that cling to life are bent and misshapen. The ground is covered with small sharp rocks and slopes toward the river. On the far side of the river, atop a high rocky mound, a ruined tower can be found. It appears that the tower was once well fortified and long ago might have been nearly impossible to take by force of arms.
5642: The floor of this dense forest slants downwards towards the north-west where the river Mitheithel flows while due north the forest becomes more sparse. The land here is wild and pathless making travel difficult even though the forest thins to the north. To the south lies the edge of a deep ravine. The sides of the ravine are steep and while it would be easy to slip into the ravine, it will be much more difficult to climb out.
5643: The trees stand densely packed all the way to the southern bank of the river Mitheithel. The ground is covered with a soft mat of brown needles that were underwater not so long ago. On the other side of the river a ruined tower can be seen against the horizon. It is in ruins and a huge heap of stone blocks at the base of the remaining tower suggests that it was once a lot higher.
5644: Bounded on two sides by the river, a grove of trees fills this region making it a safe haven during floods. To the north the river Mitheithel joins with one of the tributaries that flowed from the highlands, and together they create a large fork in the water. In the middle of that fork, at the northern edge of the joining rivers, a ruined tower, upon a cliff, can be seen against the backdrop of the horizon.
5645: These fields, squeezed between the river Mitheithel to the west and the dark forests to the north and east, form a narrow valley. The rough ground is composed of rocks of many different sizes and shapes. Close to the edge of the river, bushes grow in dense patches with large barren spaces between them. To the south the ground gradually becomes more level and an old road leads towards a large stone bridge in the south-west. On the other side of the road the ruins of a number of small decaying buildings can be seen, standing as a clump in a copse of large trees.
5646: The land among the hills is pathless and travel is encumbered by fallen trees and tumbled rocks. The tops of the high trees are swaying slightly in the wind and the ground is covered with patches of heather underlain by a soft mat of brown needles. Further northward the forest looks denser and darker as the signs of wildlife in that direction become sparse.
5647:
A huge grizzly bear is here, roaming the wild.
A snake slithers towards you.

The ravine winds its way though a sombre country of dark trees. The sides of the ravine are steep and the footing uncertain. To the south an old and obviously decaying road can be seen at the foot of the sullen hills. The smell is heavy and musty, probably because of rotting vegetation.
5648:
There are two wooden clubs here.
You see two sturdy pairs of rigid leather trousers on the ground.
A grey hare stands alert, looking and listening for predators.

The shallow ravine slowly leaves the Old East Road behind as it starts to twist its way northward towards the Ettendales far north of Rivendell. The western slope of the ravine is rather steep and it is littered with rocks of all sizes and shapes. Further north the hills around the ravine rise higher and higher and the forest that covers those hills looks dense and dark.
5649: Bend in the Old East Road

At this location the Old East Road sweeps northward to avoid a cluster of large and decaying buildings that lies in the grove of trees to the west. Not much remains of the buildings - one is partly burnt down and another looks more like a pile of rocks then the building it once was. On the southern side of the road vast plains that were once farmland spread across the land towards the river Mitheithel in the south-west.
5650: To the north of The Old East Road there is a narrow ravine that leads north- wards through the steep lands on the north side of the road. From here the road is several miles east of a narrow valley in which the Mitheithel flows. On the south side of the road the land is more level and in the distance a dark and sombre forest can be seen.
5651: The road runs east-west through a dark green forest. To the northwest the forest is cut by a narrow ravine, which leads northwards through the steep hilly land. It is quiet here, and the silence is at times so complete, that one can hear miles away the sound of waters of Mitheithel swirling against the three great arches of the Last Bridge.
5652: The road leads steadily east-west through the unfriendly country of dark trees winding among the feet of sullen hills. Here and there upon heights and ridges you can catch glimpses of ancient walls of stone and the ruins of towers; they have an ominous look.
5653: The road runs west-south here. Some tracks lead away from the road to the north, cutting in two the uneven grassy plain and eventually disappearing in the forest which runs up a hill-slope. Looking in that direction, you can see a tall building on top of the slope, the lower part of the building almost completely concealed by the trees.
5654: The pines here are not very old, yet something in their appearance gives them a tired look, as if they have been standing here for many centuries. A shallow ravine cuts through the forest to the west. To the south you can see the Old East Road make its way through the terrain. To the north the forest seems to become lighter; looking in that direction, one can see spots of bright colours in the gaps between the trees.
5655: Not yet hardened by the cold wind and the harsh winters of the Lone-lands, young green pines grow here on the very edge of the Old East Road. The boles and the branches of the trees seem to be disproportionately thin, and the fresh green colour of their needles seems to be too bright for this cheerless landscape.
5656: Neither grassland, nor heath, nor swamp, this odd patch of land looks as if somebody put it together by mixing pieces of all the three types of landscape. The two tracks, that cross it from the north from the south, seem to have been made by one passage of a very heavy carriage with very big wheels. Except for that, there seems to have been little or no other traffic, yet strangely enough no vegetation grows on these tracks, and the ground around them seems to be whitened as if with early frost.
5657: The road bends north-east here passing a hill to the north and a dark forest to the south. A small stream trickles out of the forest onto the side of the road and disappears in a ditch. The stream carries a few tree-leaves of an odd shape: they resemble a clawed paw of an animal.
5658: The Road turns west-south here, following the bends of the feet of the hills. Some pines grow on the crown of the hill to the north, their tops and branches sharply outlined against the sky. The hill to the east of you is very high, and its slope seems impossible to climb.
5659: Here the road bends from the north to the east and continues straight east, leaving the hill ridge to the north. To the south of the road you can see three stones, obviously set there as marking signs. The stones are so weathered that you can no longer read what was written on them once, but even if you could read it, you would probably find it no longer true anyway.
5660: The highest point of the hill ridge is just above you, but the slope leading to it is an almost vertical rock wall which there seems to be no way to climb. To the south of the road at some distance you can see a stone arch rising in the middle of a grassy plain.
5661: Following the bends of the feet of the hills, the Old East Road runs east-west on its way from the Last Bridge to the River Bruinen. South of the road the grassland stretches to the very horizon, patches of grey and patches of green blending at a distance into one carpet of a grey-green colour.
5662: The Old East Road is running east-west here. A hill with a wide flat crown rises to the north of the road. On the other side of the road everything is overgrown by weeds, but just to the south of you the thicket is cut in two by a wide ribbon of land covered with a carpet of a heather-like plant.
5663: The road runs east-west here. A ridge of hills rises above you to the north. Wide stone shelves lead up the side of the ridge allowing one to climb all the way up to the top. Wormwood grows to the south of the road, swaying in the wind and filling the air with a bitter smell.
5664: Leaving to the north the last hill of the ridge, the Old East Road bends from the west to the south, continuing its way through the grassy plains. On the southern side of the road everything is overgrown with weeds; a heathery plain stretches out to the east.
5665: The Old East Road turns north-east here, winding along the foot of the hills. Ages ago the road already ran through this land, and ages from now it will probably still run through it, even when all the old walls and towers crumble down, and no other trace of Men is left in the Lone-lands. Buildings wear down from use, but a road gets stronger from use. Buildings suffer from their owners, but a road cares not who uses it or for what purpose, for rain soon washes away any traces and any defile. Buildings can be burned down or knocked down, but a road can only be destroyed by a flood or an earthquake, and if destroyed, it will probably be restored, while somewhere there are people who need to pass through this land.
5666: There is some snow on the ground.

The slopes of the hill are covered with trees, which climb all the way up from the forest to the north. The hills to the west are less forested, and the crown of one of them is completely bare, except for a lonely rock rising in its middle. The eastern and the southern sides of the hill are almost vertical, and far below to the south you can see the Old East Road.
5667: A finch flies low above the ground.

A small mound rises here on the border of a pine forest. The sides and the top of the mound are covered with heather, and there is an even circle of stones set on its top like a crown. The heather plants inside the stone circle have white flowers and a serene look as if, like the flowers of evermind, they were dedicated to mourning the dead.
5668: On the Crest of the Ridge

This is the highest point of the hill ridge and probably the best place to get a view of the Lone-lands. Far below you can see the Old East Road sweeping round the feet of the hills, and far to the north you can see another hill ridge rising dark across the sky. A building rises on the westmost point of the northern ridge, but at this distance it is hard to make out any details.
5669: From this rocky hill to the north you can see most of the hilly plain overgrown with trees, grass, moss, and heather. Whoever placed the hills on this plain must have been following some clear plan at first, but then grew bored and scattered the rest of his store at random.
5670: A lone grey rock rises in the middle of the wide flat crown of the hill. The top of the rock is carved in the shape of a deep bowl. The inside of the rock-hewn bowl is blackened as if by fire, but the water in the bowl is as clear as a crystal, not a blemish marring its transparent depths.
5671: The hill ridge runs from the west to the east. Far below to the south the Old East Road holds on its way from the Last Bridge to the River Bruinen. Pine trees and fallen rocks cover the northern slopes of the ridge, which drop into a narrow dark vale. The southern slopes are almost bare and descend to the road in a series of stony shelves.
5672: Some decades, maybe some centuries ago, somebody laid a few wooden beams in the forest soil here to prevent it from sliding down into the narrow valley to the west. Whoever took care of the forest then is now probably long dead, but the wooden beams still seem quite solid, even though they are now old and overgrown with moss. Dark pines and firs rise all around you; if any paths ever passed through the forest here, they are now concealed by a thick carpet of pine-needles.
5673: A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

The valley turns north-west here, growing wider to the north. The floor and the sides of the valley have a rounded shape, as if somebody had scooped out the sandy soil of the forest with a giant scoop. Conifers grow on both sides of the valley, and its floor is covered with dry branches and pine-needles.
5674: The long valley is narrow, deeply cloven, dark and silent. Trees with old and twisted roots hang over cliffs and pile up behind into mounting slopes of pine-wood. The slopes to the north and the south are pathless, encumbered by fallen trees and tumbled rocks.
5675: A woody evergreen plant grows here, with many stems reaching upward.

Two slopes meet here. A rocky slope to the south climbs to the top of a hill with a wide flat crown, whereas the sandy northern slope rises only about ten feet upward and then disappears in the forest. To the east the sides of the depression become steeper and closer to each other, forming a narrow valley.
5676: A hill ridge rises just to the south. The level ground continues the steep side of the ridge. The pattern of rocks, moss, and trees on the ground repeats the pattern of the slope so accurately, as if one sheet of turf with rocks, trees, and moss on it was drawn both across the sheer hillside and this level slope.
5677: The hills have now begun to shut you in. The Road behind holds on its way to the River Bruinen, but both are now hidden from view. A path leads up the slope of the hill to the south, picking its way among the boulders. Pines follow the path, marking its turns, but stop just short of the top, as if unwilling to settle on the highest point of the land.
5678: A few pines grow on the rocky crown of the hill, looking down at the Old East Road. The slopes of the hill are a mess of rocks, moss and fallen branches. In the middle of the circle of pines rain water has collected in a slight depression in the rock. The water is clear and cool, and pine-needles float on its surface.
5679: Rocks have been torn out of the ground here and strewn around, as if this place had been a playground of the stone giants. The rocks and the ground are powdered with a white substance which looks like rime or salt. A few rocks are broken in pieces, as if the inner pressure had made them burst apart; their insides glitter with small colourless crystals.
5680: Thick green moss covers the ground here, in places completely concealing pits, ditches, stones, rocks and small mounds. The moss seems unnaturally thick and soft, as if somebody put or planted it here on purpose, wishing to hide something beneath it. To the south a hill ridge rises at some distance; to the east and to the north you can see a sombre forest.
5681: The air is very dry here, and there is an unpleasant smell you cannot recognise. Some rocks lie scattered on the mossy ground between the trees. Judging by the shape of the rocks, they had once been partly melted and then allowed to cool in whatever shapes they assumed. The moss on the ground around the rocks is black, as if some substance in the soil made it change its colour.
5682:
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

The trees here are mostly oaks, but their foliage and bark are somewhat darker than normal, and the leaves seem to be of a slightly wrong shape, although when you look at them closely, you see nothing unnatural. The soil is very dry, and there is almost no undergrowth. The forest ends just to the south of you, where the ground slopes down into a rocky depression.
5683:
Some pine nuts lie scattered upon the ground.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

Pines and oaks grow together in this part of the forest, but if you moved in any direction, you would find that the trees soon separate. The oaks will follow you to the west or to the north, whereas the pines run down the slopes to the deep valley in the southeast. The leaves of the oaks seem to be darker than the pine-needles, but this could be a trick of the uneven lighting of the forest.
5684: Here a river once cut its way through the thick soil of the forest, washing away clay, sand and any vegetation that got in its way. Now the riverbed is dry and covered with pine-needles, and only the gnarled tree roots that hang from the cliffs remind of the valley's origin.
5685:
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

The forest ground slopes into a deep ravine to the west. To the north of you the way is blocked by a hedge of young fir-trees, their branches hanging so low and intertwined so closely that no animal larger than a fox could possibly find there a gap large enough to squeeze through. Spider-webs hang on the tips of the branches of the trees, a few drops of water on them shimmering like tiny crystals.
5686:
Some pine nuts lie scattered upon the ground.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

In this part of the forest for every live pine there are two tree-stumps or uprooted pines, as if somebody had once set out to destroy the forest completely, but then gave up the task, being either bored, content, or just no more in need of pine-wood. To the south the way is blocked by a hedge of young firs; to the west you can see a small clearing behind the trees.
5687:
A small mushroom grows nearby.
A bright red mushroom is growing here.

A faint trail, little more than a small path, winds its way through the forest. In places it is choked with fallen stones and trees, but at one time it seems to have been much used. To the west the trail bends slightly and disappears from sight among the pine-trees. To the east the ground slopes down, and the trail follows the curves of the slope.
5688: In the middle of the forest clearing stands a huge ant-hill. You see no live ants around, but the ground is littered with dried ant corpses, which is just as well, because the ants appear to have been disproportionately large with savage-looking jaws. Pines stand in circle around the clearing, and the bark of some of them looks as if it had been chewed on.
5689: The forest around you is black, but not as if it had been burned out by a fire. Rather, it looks as if somebody had converted all colours into black and white. Gone are not only the bright colours of the flowers and berries, gone is also the green of the leaves and the brown colours of the ground and of the bark. The trees around you are black and cast black shadows on the parched grey ground.
5690: This clearing in the forest is nothing but a circle of completely burned ground. Whoever burned it out, had done it more than once and quite thoroughly. No grass grows here anymore. The trees that once stood here are now nothing but black stumps, and even the stones on the ground are completely black with soot and cracked from the heat of fires that raged in this circle.
5691: The forest is very dark here, but not because it is very thick. It consists mostly of broadleaf trees, but the leaves of the trees are very dark, almost completely black. The undergrowth is scarce here, and also very dark in colour. The few forest flowers also seem to have lost their bright colours and become grey, with the faintest tinge of their natural colours.
5692: *a noble Elf*, wielding an ornate, steel-shafted warhammer, is here, riding a pack horse.

The forest continues to the north and to the east of you, getting thicker and darker. A mound of rocks is piled on the ground here. The rocks seem to have been once heated to such a great temperature that they started to melt, but then were cooled and became solid again. On the top of the mound there is a flat black stone with a slight depression in the middle; unlike the rest of the rocks, it seems to have been unaffected by the heat.
5693: A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

The ground here is covered by a carpet of green moss. A few small mounds rise from the moss, dotted with red berries; some insects hop around them. Some patches of the moss are whitened as if they were sprayed with a white paint, and the berries on these patches are white as if they were unripe. The ground becomes more rocky to the south. A forest stretches out in all the other directions.
5694: *a noble Elf*, wielding an ornate, steel-shafted warhammer, is standing here.

This is the edge of a sombre pine forest which begins to the west of you. The vegetation here consists mostly of young pines and fir-trees climbing up the slightly rising slope to the stone ruins which dominate the top of the hill to the north. Looking at the ground, you see what seems to be tracks of enormous wheels, much deeper than any cart-tracks you've ever seen before. No undergrowth or moss grows on these tracks, and the ground around them seems to be slightly whitened.
5695: The trees are denser here. Their boles are thicker and branches are strangely misshapen. To the south there lies a slab of weathered stone, dotted with patches of dark green moss. Its surface still bears some ancient markings of unknown significance. There is some stale water in a pair of deeply cut depressions below the markings.
5696: A bright spot among the somber pines, a small grassy hill rises here in the middle of the forest, covered with many small flowers like an elaborate embroidery. The flowers grow here in patches, some of them white, some yellow, some blue and some lilac. A few have black borders or black centres as if they were in mourning. To the east and north the ground slopes up, but to the west the forest drops into a deep ravine.
5697: Pines and firs are the only growing things here. There is no undergrowth or young trees, because nothing can survive on the barren soil which consists mostly of rocks, sand and clay. The only sounds in this forest are made by the chilly wind, which comes here to play from the plains to the north.
5698: A thick carpet of heather covers the ground here. In some spots the heather is completely withered or discoloured for no visible reason. Obviously, even this plant, which often grows where other plants would not, does not like the rocky soil and the harsh weather of this land.
5699: The barren plain stretches to the north, its dull grey broken to the northwest by the glittering grey ribbon of Mitheithel. A few patches of heather grow on the edge of the plain, but farther to the north even the heather gives up, leaving the rocky ground completely bare. The realm of Angmar once lay in that direction, and even though it is now long gone, it is said that its shadow still lies on the land.
5700: The ground slopes up steeply to the east, climbing a rocky plateau. At some distance to the south a forest of dark pines and firs rises on the slope at the base of an ancient building. In contrast to the trees of that forest, the few trees that grow here are crippled birches that seem to be a mockery of their namesakes from green sunny lands. The tallest birches are about five feet tall and bent to the ground as if the weight of their branches did not let them stand straight.
5702: The steep tree-covered hillside rises from the forest to the top of the hill in the east. Looking up, you can see the ruins of the wall and an old building, which looks as if it had once been a temple or a castle. To the south the forest recedes, allowing you a glimpse of the Old East Road.
5703: Leafless and barren, the trees stand here as a picture of desolation created by the northern winds or the winter cold. The dry branches bend to the ground under their own weight and break with a loud cracking sound. To the south an almost vertical side of a hill rises before you, its rock surface grey-green with moss and lichen, seemingly the only living things in this place.
5704: The Entrance Hall of the Temple

The large domed hall had obviously once been the entrance hall of the temple, leading to the altar room and to the inner chambers. The walls and the roof of the hall still stand intact even though the heavy granite columns that supported the roof have been broken to pieces which lie on the ground in piles of rubble. The back part of the hall is completely choked by the debris and does not allow you even a glimpse of what once lay beyond.
5705: A stone building, which had probably once been a castle or a temple, rises to the north of you. This place seems to have been the courtyard of the building. In places you can still distinguish the base of the encircling wall, and among the rubble you can see the remainders of the regular pattern of the stone pavement. The rest looks as if somebody once lifted this courtyard like a giant bowl and shook it well till there was no stone left standing and no piece of a wall left unbroken.
5706: Pines grow here in a corner formed by two hill-slopes. The rocky slope to the north leads to a saddle between two higher points of the ridge. The slope to the west is much steeper and covered with green moss and climbing pines. It leads to the top of a hill, on which you can see some ancient ruins. Between the pines on the western slope there is a somewhat discoloured patch of moss of an irregular shape.
5707: A mixed forest of conifers and broadleaf trees grows on the mossy ground. The foliage and the needles of the trees are as dark as if the sheer cliff that rises to the north was shutting out not only the northern wind, but also the sunlight. There is a rock shelf on the side of the cliff about halfway to the top, and there seems to be a dark opening in the rock wall just above the shelf.
5708: There is no undergrowth here, and trees stand somewhat apart from each other. The ground is very dry, as if parched by great heat, and the leaves and bark of the trees are black or grey, as if the same heat that dried the ground has burnt them so strongly that they have never been able to recover their natural colour. Instead of the ordinary smells of the forest, there is a smell here that you cannot identify - neither the smell of rot, nor the smell of fire, but something in between. A high ridge rises to the north of you; on all the other sides you can see nothing but the forest.
5709: A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.

A small stream flows through the forest here, its water clear, cool, and smelling of pine-needles, even though no pines grow in this part of the forest. Farther from the stream the trees and the undergrowth are black, but trees and plants on the stream-banks are green, as if the water had healed them or made immune from whatever drained colour from the rest of the forest. A few patches of flowers clutter by the stream, their bright colours a sharp contrast to the blackness of the forest around.
5710: A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.

The forest stream trickles down into a hollow under the roots of trees, feeding a small pond. The sides and the bottom of the hollow are brown forest soil, but the water of the pond is so clear that it seems to be shining. You can see every stone on the bottom of the pond and the few insects and small fishes that hide in the shadows. The water of the pond smells of earth and pine-needles.
5711: A wolf spider is here, among the trees.

Trees stand very close to each other in this part of the forest. The air smells of pine-needles and moist earth. Spider-webs hang among the trees, some of them as big as four feet in diameter. You notice that for some reason somebody had cut down a few pines here and let them lie. Following with your eyes the line formed by the tree-stumps, you see the beginnings of a path.
5712: The air here is stiflingly damp, and any noise or sound seems to fall heavily onto the ground, as if it was instantly drenched by the moisture. Many trees have been uprooted here and arranged into neat piles, obviously prepared for use as building materials or firewood. Whoever did this must have had inhuman strength despite quite human reflexes and quite a human desire for a wooden dwelling or a hot fire.
5713:
A tiny, harmless centipede is here.
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.
A brutish forest troll is hunting here, looking for some tasty flesh.

The forest soil is soggy and in some places gives under your weight, as if the forest was in the process of turning into a swamp. A few rotten trees lie on the ground here blocking the passage to the north. Lichens and moss grow on their bark, and inside the hollow trunks some insects scurry among the moss.
5714:
A low shrub with bright green, oblong leaves is growing here.
Scattered in and on the shrub, there are a handful of blueberries.
A woodpecker is here, tapping on a tree.
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

Pines grow so densely here, that it is hard to pick the way between their roots and trunks. The forest soil is brown and moist, and despite the lack of sunlight every inch of the ground between the boles of the trees is covered with thick undergrowth, which seems to be fighting for a spot in the rich soil. You can hear a faint sound of flowing water, but it is not clear from which direction it is coming. To the north the ground slopes down, and the forest seems to recede.
5715: A sheer cliff rises out of the forest to the west of you. About six feet from its base a clear spring flows out from a crevice in the rock face, trickles down into a bowl carved in the rock and drops from the bowl onto the ground by the base of the cliff as its journey through the forest begins. There is an air of majesty and timelessness about the spring as if the power of Ulmo still flowed in its water.
5716: Up on the height the air is cold, and the wind almost blows you off your feet. A gnarled old pine grows here, bent but undefeated by the wind and the cold. The roots of the pine hang over a shallow pit, which looks as if stone had once been quarried there. Lower down you can hear the tree-tops moaning and sighing as the wind passes through them.
5717: The forest is now far below, and the side of the hill is an almost vertical rock-wall in which there is a stony shelf and a shallow cave, a mere scoop in the cliff. The wind blows furiously on the height, as if trying to break the ledge off the wall and send the chunks tumbling into the forest.
5718: Lhurank (brenny), wielding a narrow runed awlpike, is standing here.

The rocky slope rises from the forested plateau to the north and drops away sharply just a short distance to the south, forming a narrow saddle between two higher points of the ridge. To the west a building with a tower rises on the height. To the east a rocky ledge leads along the southern face of the ridge.
5719: The ground here is mostly bare rock with an occasional earth-filled crevice. In some of these crevices and holes a few hardy pines and firs have managed to secure their roots. Whether because of lack of nourishment, or because of the wind and the weather, the trees stand bent in all kinds of weird shapes, as if undecided in which direction to bend.
5720: A few patches of lichen grow on the rocky ground. To the north of you the plateau ends with a twenty feet drop to the barren rocky plain below. The way to the south is blocked by a sheer cliff; in some places the rock of the cliff is as smooth as if it had been cut by a knife.
5721: A high ridge of land rises above you, its dark edge against the sky broken into many bare points like teeth of a blunted saw. The forest has reached its base and there stopped, as if wondering whether the ascent would be worth the trouble. Carefully selecting the path among the boulders, one might be able to climb to the very top of the ridge and enjoy the view of the forest.
5722: The ground rises to the west step by step as if the soil had once slid down here layer by layer. The slope looks stable now, and the steps are covered with moss and pines which climb all the way up to the top. To the east the ground becomes more level and eventually flattens out turning into a rocky plain.
5723: The rocky plain stretches out to the north and east of you. As far as your eyes can see, the land to the north is coloured in various shades of grey without a single green spot. To the west and south the ground slopes up slightly; a forest of dark pines rises on the slope.
5724: A large eagle soars above you.

The only changing thing in this grey landscape is the sky, to which every traveller after a while willingly or unwillingly turns his eyes. A rocky plain might have some kind of personality given to it by the look of its rocks, moss and lichen, but no watcher would want to look for long at anything with no life or movement of its own.
5725: To the north, a barren rocky plain seems to stretch out to the very horizon, but if you strain your eyes, you can distinguish at the very edge of sight an uneven dark line, probably the beginnings of a mountain ridge. The unfriendly North lies before you, the land with plenty of rock and no inhabitants or vegetation, the land where all the evil kings have built their citadels until Sauron decided he preferred warmer lands and company of Men.
5726: Heather grows on the side of the road, its faint fragrance unusually distinct and sweet in the fresh air. A few heather plants have white flowers and look slightly larger than the ordinary heather; these plants also seem to smell stronger.
5727: The road makes its way through the lands that are now called Lone-lands. They have not always been called so; Men once dwelt here, ages ago. Legends tell that they became an evil people, because they fell under the shadow of Angmar. But all were destroyed in the war that brought the North Kingdom to its end. It is said that the hills have forgotten them, but a shadow still lies on the land.
5728: A strange kind of weeds dominates on this patch of grassland. Most of the plants are from two to three feet high with very thick and tough stems and meaty leaves, grey-green on the outside and silvery-grey on the inside. The flowers are white five-petalled stars, disproportionately small for such tall stems and thick leaves; something in their appearance gives them a mournful look.
5729: Judging by the ditches that cut the ground at regular intervals, this must have once been a field, cultivated to grow crops. Weeds have now taken this spot of land for their own, claiming the place that once belonged to more civilised plants. Some of these weeds are probably descendants of the plants that were grown here by people: there is one that looks distinctly like corn but has thorns on its stem and is of an unpleasant brownish hue.
5730: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

This village had probably been destroyed in a war and abandoned ever since. No building has survived the centuries of desolation, and you can only see where the houses and streets had been by noticing where the ground rises or falls slightly, or where the vegetation changes in type or in colour. One can only wonder whether a great city fallen and abandoned would leave more traces in the landscape, and whether its ruins would take much longer to overgrow than the ruins of a small village.
5731: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

This had been a village once, but it was so long ago that all one can see is where the buildings had been. This uneven square, slightly rising over the ground and completely covered with weeds, must have been one building; that rectangle must have been the other, and this uneven shape might have been a cross-like base of a temple. This patch might have once been a main road or a square because it continues the overgrown road that entered the village to the north, and this one might have been a major street because it is covered by a carpet of the same heather-like plant as the main road.
5732: Weeds of all sizes, shapes and colours grow here. To the west of you an ancient cemetery lies behind a low wall. The wall is not more than two feet high and seems to be purely decorative, yet it seems to have done its part in keeping the weeds out of the cemetery and not letting it overgrow completely.
5733: Hundreds and hundreds of tombstones rise from the ground at this abandoned cemetery, protected only by a low wall and open to the sky and to the wind. All the tombstones here are blank, marked by no inscription or symbol. Whatever has left these graves unnamed - necessity, accident or design - there is nothing here to tell you what had happened, when or why.
5734: The weeds are not so thick here, and in places there are even patches of ordinary green grass. To the east you can see a cemetery behind a low wall. The wall is about one and a half feet high, obviously built to mark the borders of the cemetery, but not to keep anyone out of it. The stones of the wall are covered with moss and climbing flowers, little white and lilac bells with black edges like black ribbons worn in mourning.
5735: The grassland rises slightly to the west, ascending the slope of a low hill. Something seems to have stopped the ubiquitous weeds half-way through the ascent, and only the plain green grass and a couple of field flowers made their way to the top, where a few white birches proudly rise, crowning the level slope.
5736: Tall white birches rise all around, an unexpected bright patch in the sombre landscape where all hills and forests are dark or black, most grasses are grey, and the sky seems to be bleak even on the sunny days. Somebody might have planted these birches here for some reason, or else they might be one of the few things still remaining from those long forgotten days when these lands had a brighter appearance.
5737: A patch of white attracts the gaze to the east, where a clump of birches rises on the top of a low hill. By contrast, the forest to your north seems as dark as if somebody had painted its trees black. Nature seems to have been reluctant to allow such a sharp change of colour from black to white, and so it painted this patch of land between the two patches of forest grey with a few occasional spots of green.
5738: To the east and south the forest gradually thins and finally succumbs to grass-covered plains. In the other directions the forest is still dark, dense and brooding. Tracks of small animals can be seen here and there on the ground, but it is hard to discern what type of animals made them.
5739: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

Baleful primal trees of unholy size, age, and grotesqueness leer above you like pillars of a temple. This is the edge of the forest and the trees have thinned. Grey fields take over to the west and to the far north a large river flows down from the Ettendales.
5740: Bleak and grey plains stretch all the way to the southern horizon. The land here looks rocky and vegetation is sparse. A dark forest with large twisted trees grows to the east; at the border it looks thin, but further in it becomes almost impenetrable. To the north-west lies the remains of old wheat fields, but no one seems to have cultivated them for many years and now most of the top soil has blown away.
5741:
A large marmot is here, scurrying in between the rocks.
A badger is here, exploring for food.

A low pile of rocks hinders easy movement towards the north. These piles, made by some farmer long ago, once served as a fence forming the boundary of the wheat fields. This area, never cleared is covered with grey rocks and the soil between them looks dry and unfertile. Some lonely strands of wheat seems to have spread here from the old wheat field in the north.
5742: Once, long ago, the border of the ancient kingdom of Rhudaur was just south of here and on the ground the remains of long forgotten skirmishes can still be found. Despite the presence of the river Mitheithel, some seven miles to the west, the soil here is very dry. And while mostly only weeds manage to grow here, bits of wild wheat can also be found. North of here, the land was once cultivated many years ago, but is now untended.
5743: A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.

Between the sharp stones which litter the ground here, some small bushes and a few stunted trees have taken root. The only other vegetation that inhabit this area is the tall and bleak grasses. There are not many wild animals around, though there might be some fishes in the fast flowing river to the west. On the other side of the river, nine miles north, a tall ridge hinders travel.
5744: At the bottom of the short steep slope to the west the river Mitheithel flows towards the south where it will eventually join with other rivers to become the Greyflood. The ground nearest the river is muddy and very slippery, but elsewhere the ground is dry and cracked. While some bushes grow close to the river, the few trees that managed to sprout here died long ago.
5745: A field vole has frozen to the spot, sensitive to your presence.

The ground dips down towards the river north and west of here. There are some faint traces of irrigation channels, that in former times were used to lead water towards the wheat fields east of here. At the edge of the river there are piles of debris that have washed up over the years.
5746: To the west the Mitheithel can be seen as it flows from its sources in the Ettenmoors. The soil is more rocky here than it is in the old wheat fields east of here. Between the rocks bleak bushes and high grass manage to grow. On the western side of the river vast plains spread out as far as can be seen.
5747: A grey hare stands alert, looking and listening for predators.

The ground here slopes gently westward, towards the far off river. This spot seems to be the southern edge of an old wheat field. To the south, beyond a low pile of stones, a cast plain takes over and the ground there becomes rocky and barren.
5748: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

This is the border of what seems to be an old wheat field. Men once cultivated this land but it must have been ages ago. The soil seems to be unfertile but some scattered straws of wheat still manage to grows here and there. Long ago, someone took all the stones that were ploughed from the field and used them to build a low stone wall at the southern border of the field. The wall has slowly collapsed over the years and nowadays it has begun to look more like a heap of stones.
5749: This is the southeastern corner of what once was a large cultivated area. To the east of here lies a large and dense forest, while to the south a rocky and bleak landscape takes over. However, to the far northwest distant mountains can be seen on a clear day. A low pile of rocks, which was once a fence marking the edge of a wheat field, hinders movement to the south.
5750: The huge trees that inhabit this dark and brooding forest stand all about you, though they become more densely packed towards the east. While it is possible to locate a grey field beyond the forest to the west, the branches make it hard to distinguish many details. Several roots near the surface of the soft soil makes walking across the forest somewhat hazardous.
5751: This is the centre of a dark and brooding forest that bears an aspect more than unusually sinister. Ancient lightning-scarred trees seem unnaturally large and twisted, while the other vegetation is unnaturally thick and feverish. Of wild creatures there are none.
5752: A huge, black wolf is here, ready to devour.

Lightning seems to have struck the black trees of the forest here and there, falling this tree, scarring that one, burning a spot on the ground here, splitting a tree-stump there. The trees here are older than those to the north, and some of them seem to be dry, but as their black leaves do not change colour and do not fall off when they dry, one can barely tell the dead trees from the living ones.
5753: The forest ends sharply to the east, the few remaining trees scattered as if retreating in haste. Just a few steps to the south of the last black tree some white birches stand with such a proud look, as if they were an army that was set there to beat back the unfriendly black forest and proved victorious in the task.
5754: A waist-high evergreen shrub grows here, with thick, reaching branches.

The burial mound on the forest border is covered with green grass. Upon its western side the grass is white as with a drifted snow: small flowers spring here like countless stars amid the turf. Whoever rests in this green mound must rest in peace now, for time treats the dead better than the living, and the houses of the dead better than the houses of the living. Time erases towers, temples, cities and villages, yet keeps intact a mound, a grave, a crypt, a cemetery.
5755: Rocks have been set in the ground at regular intervals, indicating that this completely overgrown patch of land had once been of use to people. Centuries ago the last people abandoned this land, letting it rest, and centuries might pass till they return here and till somebody again turns this patch of grassland into a field or a pasture.
5756: A tall arch, made of plain grey stone, rises here, marking the entrance to the cemetery that lies behind a low mossy wall. No inscription marks the arch, but a strange sign is engraved on the top: a square with chipped corners, divided into four parts. A few climbing plants have set root by the base of the arch and made their way up the arch; their bell-like flowers are white or lilac with a black border.
5757: The ground is very even here, as if this was once a cultivated field. The soil is moist, dark in colour and probably quite fertile, but nothing except weeds grows here now. The weeds grow very thickly, making it hard to move. At some distance to the north you can see the Old East Road running at the foot of a ridge of hills, their dark heads sharply outlined across the sky.
5758: Once this must have been a fairly wide and well-used road. But the only way to notice that it was here before at all is by looking at the vegetation on the ground. Around the road the land is completely overgrown by thick and thorny weeds, whereas the road itself is covered by a carpet of some plants, which would seem to be heather if most of their flowers were not white.
5759: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

A silvery-grey, bitter-smelling sea of wormwood sways around you, a new wave passing through it with every gust of the wind. To the northeast the Old East Road passes through the terrain. To the west and the south the grassland changes colour, as the wormwood blends with the other weeds.
5760: A huge, black wolf is here, ready to devour.

As the trees to the north grow thinner, the stream becomes quicker and noisier, as if it was eager to get out of the cheerless forest. For a while the stream follows the curves of the forest ground, then rushes down from a steep bank, slows down to a trickle on a level slope and so reaches the border of the forest and the Old East Road.
5761: A Stream in the Dark Forest
A wolf cub happily plays here.

Stumbling at the roots of the trees, fallen branches and rocks in the forest soil, a small stream makes its way through the dark forest. The trees around the stream are so still as if they were listening to the sound of flowing water.
5762: A wolf cub happily plays here.

No oaks, beeches, or other cheerful green trees of sunlit lands grow in this forest. Unfamiliar dark trees reach to the sky, their bark almost black, and their black branches and foliage covering the sky in such an intricate pattern, as if somebody cut it out of black paper or wrought out of black metal and then glued to the sky or nailed to the tree-tops.
5763:
A large toadstool grows nearby.
A huge, black wolf is here, ready to devour.

While the dark forest has begun to thin it is still very dense, dark and difficult to traverse. A small clearing has been created here when a tall lonely tree was destroyed by lightning. The bones and chewed corpses of several small mammals lie partly buried in the weedy, fulgurite-pitted earth, so apparently some kind of predator roams these woods.
5764: A grey hare stands alert, looking and listening for predators.

These are the outskirts of ancient farmlands. These lands were most likely abandoned when war resulted in the removal of the North Kingdom. The soil here was once very fertile but now most of it has blown away leaving a thin layer that contains a grey and unhealthy look. The old farmlands spread out for many miles towards the south-west and finally ends at the edge of a narrow valley that is bounded by the flow of the river Mitheithel.
5765: This is the centre of what was once a farm's huge field capable of growing enough grain to feed a large population. That population disappeared when the kingdom of Rhudaur was first absorbed by its larger neighbours and later destroyed by them. Some strands of wheat still grow around here, but mostly the vegetation consists of various types of weeds.
5766: Wheat and tall green weeds have managed to grow in the shallow, dry topsoil found here. Once this area was cultivated farmland, but the farmers are long gone and the only traces that they were once here are some low stone walls used to divide the fields and the faint traces of irrigation channels.
5767: A large boulder lies in the middle of the field but the other rocks, which are scattered across the dry soil, are much smaller. A wide river, towards the west, forms a boundary between these fields and a vast plain which continues for many miles. A distant road cuts through the terrain, as it traverses east and west, with the western section obscured by a high ridge line.
5768: This region, bounded by the river Mitheithel to the north and west, has flooded many times in the past and faint traces of irrigation channels can still be found upon the ground. The riverbank down to the water is steep and rocky, but grass and bushes, which are more abundant close to the river than further inland, provides some footing on the otherwise slippery bank.
5769: The river curves around this steep bank to the north and west. On the bank lies some old trees that were uprooted upstream by some long forgotten storm and swept along by the river until they struck this bank. To the south-east the old farmland continues for many miles. A couple of miles to the north a stone bridge crosses the river. The bridge looks huge, even from this distance, and its three great arches span the Mitheithel with ease.
5770: To the south the remains of a rather large building that once stood two stories high can be found. An old sign in a rusty doorplate is still legible. Around the ruins, ancient oak trees that are several feet in diameter still grow, though one of them has been uprooted and is leaning against the remainder of a three feet tall wall. West from here is a smaller building that once served as a stable.
5771: The Inn at the Last Bridge

A large cockroach is crawling up the wall.
A large cockroach is crawling up the wall.

This was once the Last Inn. Now all that remains are the stone walls, a roof and a pile of rubble. In the centre of the old common room someone has cleared the area by removing the debris and has then used some of this waste to form a crude circular fireplace. Other than the remains of a recent fire, there are no signs of recent habitation at the inn.
5772:
The corpse of a vicious rat is lying here.
A small vicious black rat squeaks at you for disturbing it.
A small vicious black rat squeaks at you for disturbing it.

These stables were well made when originally constructed and have withstood the elements better than the main building. Though, time has taken its toll on this building but someone has recently done some maintenance to keep it standing and has fixed a section of the roof to allow for some protection in harsh weather.
5773: This building used to be a smithy, but a fire raged here some time ago and since then the building has remained a hollowed ruin for the stones in the walls crumbled and cracked under the intense heat of the fire. On the blackened floor there are some small puddles of metal left over from the days when this building was used by the blacksmith. A door which opens in the western wall leads out towards the small path.
5774: A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.

The water of the river Mitheithel swirls under the Last Bridge's three great arches. While the big rectangular stone blocks used to construct the bridge have been worn smooth by the river, they are still in surprisingly good condition. High above you, close to the top of the middle arch, some birds have been recently nesting.
5775: Just north of here is a large and impressive stone bridge known as the Last Bridge. For the bridge to have survived these many years, the men who built it, ages past, must have been master stone masons. The eastern shore of the river has eroded away forming a steep bank that is impossible to climb. The river makes a sharp turn here and, for many miles, flows westward.
5776: Below this slope and to the east the road is sweeping around the hills and finally connects to a large stone bridge that spans the river. The ground is strewn with sharp rocks and the passage down the slope, which leads to the bridge, is impassable. South of here the ground slopes more gently into the river. At the river bank only traces of the sparse vegetation can be found.
5777: A badger is here, exploring for food.

A bit north of here a large stone bridge spans the river Mitheithel. Next to the bridge on the east side, nested among some trees, the ruins of several stone buildings remain. South of here, a long time ago, crops were once grown and harvested but now the only thing that grows over there are some weeds and a few lonely strands of wheat.
5778: Edge of an Old Wheat Field

This used to be the edge of an old wheat field but no one has cultivated this land for many years. Nearby, to the north in a grove of large trees, lies the remains of a small number of stone buildings. While only rubbles can be seen from here, one of these buildings was once quite large and at least two stories high. To the south the old and abandoned farmland continues for many miles, though here and there it is broken up by old irrigation channels and crumbled stone walls.
5779: To the north and west the remains of some stone buildings are preceded by a thick grove of large trees, while the Old East Road north of here slowly winds its way around the grove and past the buildings. On the other side of the road a dark and sombre forest covers the hills and an even darker forest swallows up the old farmland to the south-east.
5780: This is the extreme edge of what was once a large cultivated area. North of here the Old East Road passes, and on its other side a dark and dense forest grows on top of steep hills. East and south another forest covers the level ground.
5781: A huge, black wolf is here, ready to devour.

Oaks, beeches, and some other broadleaf trees you cannot recognise run down the level slope to the Old East Road to the north. The unknown trees have dark-grey, almost black, boles and branches. Their dark-green leaves are somewhat like the oak leaves in shape - except where the edges of oak leaves are round smooth curves, the edges of these leaves are sharp zigzags, as if these were oak leaves which decided to grow claws.
