Short green and yellow grass grows here and contrasts the beautiful variety of plants and flowers that grow in this part of the meadow. The grass dies quickly to the north as the road passes through, but grows richly to the south and west.
6255: Close by the roadway, the grass grows short and looks rather yellow. But wildflowers proliferate nonetheless, littering the entire landscape with their bright colours, and stretching into the distance, to the east, west and south. Both flowers and grass seem to crowd around the trunks of the few scattered pines, as if seeking the shade of their dark-green tops.
6256: A few sturdy pine trees grow right up to the roadside here, their branches reaching out over the thoroughfare, as if willing to offer shelter to weary travellers passing by. Thick grass and tall bushes carpet the flat ground. However, a few of them creep beyond the trees and onto the rocky surface, as though jealous of the territory borrowed by the road, threatening to encroach upon it.
6257: Though the hill top does not stand all that high above the surrounding lands, it is nevertheless extremely exposed, and virtually no vegetation manages to cling to its stony crown. To the east and south a forest wraps around the foot of the hill. To the west lies only a vast open plain. In contrast, the northern face plummets down into a deep cutting, through which the Great East Road runs.
6258: A woodpecker is here, tapping on a tree.

Cedars abound in this raised area of the forest, as though they had migrated here over the years, perhaps trying to be as close as possible to the sun. On the north, the ground comes to a sudden end in the escarp face of a gully. But the trees crowd up to the very edge of the wall, and even further, as some of them hang precariously from the cliff top. To the east and south, the terrain descends to the encounter of the near Bruinen river.
6259: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Large pine saplings have managed to spring up amid the rocky soil here. Their tender boughs partially obscure the sky. To the north and west stand tall, thick-boled trees, growing so densely they prevent all light from penetrating their canopy. Many of the saplings have their lower limbs broken off, as though some large creature had forced its way through here recently. To the south, the Great East Road continues its endless way through Eriador.
6260: A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

From this narrow ledge, half-way down the rocky wall of the forested plateau, you can see the Old Road heading into a deep cutting, only one or two miles away to the east. Below the projecting perch, the rock face drops vertically, preventing any attempt to descend down to the road. But one can climb up to the top, or progress along the cliff, making use of the many footholds.
6261: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

A wide, rocky platform reaches out from atop this cliff of reddish stone, as if hanging on the air. No other spot nearby can offer such a view. At the foot of the rock face, many feet below, the Great East Road cuts its way through the narrow glen. But a bit further eastwards, it suddenly emerges out of the high, imprisoning walls, and after a steep descent, it finally reaches the ford in the river Bruinen, and then disappears into the foothills beyond.
6262: An Old Trail along the Riverbank

Even at the riverside, the terrain looks quite rugged. The Bruinen flows along the bottom of an abrupt dale, and the ground ascends steeply as it leaves the waters behind. Parallel to the course of the stream, a blurred track leads in a north-south direction, zigzagging through the projecting rocks and clumps of trees, to meet the Great East Road.
6263:
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Although the trees never lose all of their leaves, they renew them slowly every year, and the fallen ones gather in a thick layer, carpeting the ground like a colourful mantle. Dark green and dun shades abound the most, but also yellowish, ochre, and brown hues. It's not uncommon to hear the creak of the dead leaves beneath the feet of some small beast. And it mixes with the merry singing of the birds, especially in the sunny summer afternoons.
6264:
A low and wide-spread tree grows here.
On the tree's branches, there are three juicy plums.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

The soil must be extraordinarily fertile in this area, bathed by the clean, foamy waters of the Bruinen. The trees grow closely, but that doesn't seem to take any bit of their vitality away. Hundreds of pinecones, large and small, lie half-buried among the fallen leaves. The unmistakable sound of flowing water reaches your ears from the southeast, but there the wood comes to a sudden end in a high embankment that towers over the unapproachable stream.
6265: A long-tailed bird watches you from the vegetation.

You are now immersed in a gentle-looking, lively forest. On sunny days,a glimmering cascade of light filters in through the canopy. When the nights are clear, the bright starlight dyes the trees in silvery shades. Both the youngest saplings and the millennial, lofty trunks bear a wholesome look upon them, the tender buds dotting their branches with every new spring.
6266: This section of the grasslands is relatively protected from the harsh winds that blow from the mountains. It lies somewhat squeezed between the leafy forest that stands on the east and the sheer wall that ascends to a higher plateau southwards. Vegetation grows wild and flowers abound, perhaps swept from the stretching plains to the northwest, and dropped here.
6267: Although this is certainly an uneven region, dotted with prominent ridges, sharp bluffs, deep cuttings and rounded hillocks, this particular area seems to have been embedded into the landscape, for its lack of features and its dreary flatness. Somehow, the whole plain appears to have sunken as, a few miles further, the terrain ascends to the south and east.
6268: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Around you is a depression filled with many varieties of coloured grasses. Tall, brown stalks to the east give way to a plain of green grass that eventually turns to yellow needlelike leaves to the west. A wide clearing rises above you to the north, and a strange bed of dark green grass covers the western part of the depression.
6269: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Tall brown and yellow stalks of grass sway in the shifting breeze all around the meadow. The ground is firm and dry and few other plants grow in the meadow. A bed of green grass seems out of place in the eastern part of the meadow.
6270:
A snake slithers towards you.
A roe deer is standing here, watching the terrain while chewing the vegetation.
A roe deer is standing here, watching the terrain while chewing the vegetation.

The grass here is a consistent shade of green, dominating the horizon to the north and east. A small patch of grass grows strangely taller on the western part of the meadow. It is of a different colour than the rest of the meadow.
6271: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

The fields give way to a small circular clearing. Boulders lie in a circle around the remains of many campfires. The ground here seems strangely soft for being so far away from the stream. A field lies to the west here and a strange patch of ground can be seen to the east of the camp.
6272: Somehow the land here is touched by neither weeds nor tracks. Recently planted shrubs grow along the southern end of the field and enclose a rich diversity of other plants and trees. A plain lies to the west and the vegetation opens slightly to the east.
6273: An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.

Rising a little the land here opens to rows of weed dominated plants. Very few plants remain untouched by the weeds, those that survive only do so barely, growing low to the ground. The fields continue in all directions, though in the west a low valley can be seen in the distance.
6274:
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A restless rabbit bounces around.

The land here blends into the surrounding land making it hard to judge the distance travelled. A variety of green grass grows in abundance here, a perfect grazing field for horses, ponies, and cows. The meadow grows rich in the lands to the far east and north.
6275: Tall stalks of grass shift in the breeze around you like the whitecaps of a lake. The ground is soft and wet but this part of the meadow is less cultivated than the surrounding meadows in the west and south.
6276: Plants, grass, and weeds of a large variety grow in this part of the meadow. The colourful array of shapes and sizes draw your eyes away from the lands around you. The meadow continues to grow in the lands to the west and south.
6277: The ground becomes firm and brown, the grass parts, and a circular clearing forms. The ground is littered with remains of previous camps, and animal dens. Stones formed in circles for campfires litter the ground beneath you. The land is green and fertile to the north, and slopes down to the south.
6278: A grass-carpeted prairie extends all over this area. Wild flowers dot the ground here and there, adding a touch of colour to the green background. The wind howls throughout the open plain, the tall grass waving to and fro as in time with it. Standing in the middle of this wide expanse, everything would probably look smaller and less important, in comparison to the apparently boundless grasslands.
6279: A Small Clump of Pines in the Grasslands

A bunch of small, leafy, lively-looking pine trees grow together here, as if expelled from the wholesome woodland that stands only a couple of miles further to the east. All about the trees, countless needle-like leaves lie scattered among the lush grass, carried along by the wind all over the nearby plains. All in all, the tiny forest looks quite curious, the mixed undergrowth showing many different green shades.
6280: Tall evergreens thrive here on the lower reaches of a small hillside. But unlike the more famous and feared forests of this part of the world, this one stands open and inviting, its lofty canopy being thin enough to permit light and refreshing breezes to penetrate all the way to the forest floor. But it is during the sunny spring days that the forest blooms in all its splendour, when the leaves shine in their brightest green hues.
6281: The river continues to wind through these uneven dales. Here the stream bends from east to south, in the shadow of a tall embankment of worn rock, crowned by a dense forest. Some of the trees seem to stretch their limbs out towards the river, as if willing, though incapable, to touch the surface. It is not uncommon to hear the deep sound of a little branch dropping down into the waters, nor to find a pinecone or needle floating on them.
6282:
A trout swims here.
A fat carp swims here.

Slowly but steadily, the Bruinen - that the men call Loudwater - continues its sinuous course through these rugged lands. Many leagues downstream, to the southwest, it meets with another great river that flows down from the frozen northern vales. The elven people call that river Mitheithel, but its name is Hoarwell in the tongue of the men. And from there on it is known as Gwathlo, or Greyflood, and it cuts through all of Eriador until it meets with the Great Sea at Lond Daen.
6283: The current accelerates notably, and the depth of the river lessens, as it runs closer to a fordable area clearly visible only a couple miles southwards. A small eddy here and there hints about the presence of large, treacherous boulders underwater. The river flows confined between two hillocks with sheer hillsides, their wet, rocky faces plummeting down into the waters.
6284: A Meander in the Bruinen River

The descending stream bends once again sharply to the south. Here it seems to hasten shyly, almost imperceptibly, as if anticipating something. When the beasts are quiet and weather is mild, and silence reigns in the valley, one can hear the soft rippling of the flowing waters. And it sounds like a faint whisper, as though the murmuring river recalled tales of ancient battles waged in these lands in a long-forgotten past.
6285: Protruding rock and fallen trees mark the end of the dark, gloomy forest that lies to the north. A thick bed of brownish pine needles carpets the floor, but here and there moist rocks show up among the undergrowth, giving hint of the rocky ground that must lie underneath. The wood comes to an end to the south, where it meets a road leading in an east-west direction.
6286: A brutish forest troll is hunting here, looking for some tasty flesh.
The wide variety of trees in this part of the forest seem to grow out of one another, blocking passage in most directions. A large mound of animal remains lies on the ground at your feet.
6287: The tall cedar trees grow more densely around this part of the forest path, and a towering wall of pines looms above you at the southern extreme of the woodland. The only apparent exit from this area seems to be to the north.
6288: The path from the road begins to fade and the forest quickly engulfs you with its power. Tall trees of numerous varieties grow at first well apart, then seemingly on top of one another. What light that the south and west offer stops immediately at a group of fir trees to the north.
6289:
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.
*a Troll* is standing here.
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

Fir trees claim this part of the forest for their own, their needles cover the forest floor. Remains of animals sit piled in a small mound near a group of trees to the east. The Trollshaws begin to separate to the south and a hint of light can be seen there.
6290: A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

This dismal forest seems to have grown deliberately for the creatures for which it is named: the trolls. Not even the dimmest ray of light opens its way through the black canopy of the trees. Below them, only an emaciated, brown, sickly-looking undergrowth seems to sprout among huge stones projecting from the ground. A strong, piercing smell impregnates the air.
6291: A dreary growth of fir trees blocks the passage eastwards, though the other parts of the forest are clear enough to pass. A thick stench rises from the gathered heap of corpses, animal remains, and rotting bones that lie here.
6292: A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

As one steps into the deepest parts of the forest, it only becomes stranger and stranger. At times, you find lofty trees bent like aged men, as if trying to conceal with their leaves any small chink in the dark canopy. At other times, you encounter huge trunks lying on the ground, as though torn from the earth for some unknown purpose.
6293: A demon wolf lurks here, its dark form twisting and hiding its shape.

Rows of fir trees soon block any hope of going north through the forest. The ground here is hard, dried, and littered with dead or dying vines and leaves. The forest continues to loom over the ground to the east and south, and an intersection of trees can be seen to the west.
6294:
Some thick writhing vines whip all around you.
A brutish forest troll is hunting here, looking for some tasty flesh.

The enormous trees that grow here seem to tear the earth apart as they force their way skywards. They are so tall that their tops are entirely hidden from view amongst the deep shadows. The scrubby plant-life growing at the fringes of the forest quickly dies out as the gloom deepens. To the east, the forest appears to become lighter.
6295: Lofty and straight stand the trunks of the trees in this area of the forest, like carefully arranged living pillars. And in the heights, their dark tops, shrouded in black shadows, form an unreachable canopy of leaves. But down here pale ferns and prickly vines grow plunged into the darkness, springing out from the thick layer of needles and moss that carpets the stony ground.
6296: A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.

You are now in the corner of a high plateau. This is an abrupt area indeed, and any attempt to progress demands considerable effort. To the south, it is possible to climb down to a narrow perch that hangs above a deep hollow, but not further. Conversely, a gravelly embankment drops down along the east face, but a small ridge leans against the cliff, making the descent shorter and easier. Large heather grow among the rocks, and so do a few lonely trees wherever the boulders leave enough room for their roots.
6297: At the Foot of an Embankment

A small pinnacle of stone leans against the greyish wall that rises in the west, as if it had fallen during a fierce storm, or as though it had been pushed down by a giant among giants, and turned into a stair of stone. From atop the ridge it is possible to find a route to the summit of the cliff. Turning to the east the lands descend abruptly towards the river, partially seen behind the rocky crags.
6298: A sheer wall of bare, grey rock plummets down into the rocky and rather barren lands below. The slope is too steep to attempt any descent here. Nevertheless, the edge of the high plain stretches away to the north and south, and it may be possible to find a way down a bit further. Huge pine trees stand close to the west, on the fringes of a wide forest. However, they bear a somewhat awkward appearance.
6299: A cliff of cold, grey stone towers imposingly on the west, preventing any attempt to move in that direction. Only a few stunted, dried trees perch atop it, their boughs mostly devoid of leaves because of the wind. Nights come fast in the shadow of the great rock wall. But the rocky ground is often covered in hoarfrost when the first rays of light begin to shine over the summits of the Misty Mountains.
6300: A narrow track flanks the river, following its course. The path is merely a diffused line as a result of the pass of travellers and beasts, rather than a deliberately laid road. A group of trees with half-bare branches grow beside the path here and there, but the ground is mostly covered in thicket. To the north, the earth becomes more barren, vegetation is scarce, and the trail fades away.
6301:
A slender plant grows here, with clusters of tiny pink flowers atop its stem.
A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

This ample extension of land is surrounded by the calm stream that takes a gentle turn here from north to west. The bank looks certainly fertile, perhaps due to the fact that it is bathed by the pure waters of the Bruinen. Grass sprouts thick beside the water, but the further you move away from the flow, vegetation grows more and more scarcely. Even though, there are little pools littered about in the plains, maybe a sign that the river once had a different course through the flatland.
6302: A Bend in the River Bruinen

After the turbulent meeting of both forks, the river slowly recovers its quiet appearance, and goes on with its long course with redoubled strength. As the riverbed widens to accommodate the renewed stream, it also cuts its way deeper in the ground. The water looks quite clear again, and it runs down calmly, yet without a break, as if aware of the countless miles still awaiting ahead.
6303: The two branches of the river that for many leagues have come down separately from the mountains, finally merge at this spot into a single, mighty stream. As the two flows rush into each other, there is a lot of turbulence in the troubled waters, and eddies abound. The surface is no longer crystalline, but rather cloudy, and one can hardly catch glimpse of the rock-strewn bottom. To the west, the strengthened Bruinen continues its long way towards the sea.
6304: The stream narrows in this area, confined between steep banks with slippery, sharp stones. The rocks on both sides look scratched and full of fissures, with pointy edges and deep crevices. These chinks are marks of river floods, when the violent waters carry large boulders away, like dead leaves blown onwards in gusts of wind. A bit further downstream, the flow roars noisily as both branches of the river meet.
6305: A crayfish is here, snapping its claws at you.

A high, cliff-like wall of dark grey stone rises all along the eastern bank of the river, as it winds its way through the moors of this rugged land. The waters, though limpid, are shrouded in the thick shadows cast by the rocky wall, and thus show rather dark shades usually. Every now and then, a small rock flies off from the stony face, dropping noisily into the calm waters, and rising small ring-shaped waves that quickly fade.
6306: You have entered a crude and apparently recently made tunnel. It does not seem that the workers cared too much for the quality of their labour, for the walls, floor and ceiling are all quite uneven. Winding westward, the passageway enters what appears to be a larger, natural cavern.
6307: The ledge gets more and more dilapidated as you move along it, and to the south, the rubble looks so unstable that it would seem that digging in it might not be a wise idea. However, it is obvious that some recent work has taken place here, with large sections of the western wall brutally ripped away, leaving piles of boulders scattered about, and what looks like the start of a tunnel opening out before you.
6308: A brown bear is sleeping here.

You find yourself within a fairly large cave. Its walls and ceiling look quite natural, although in places they have apparently been worn rather smooth over the years. The floor is marked by numerous small scratches and scuff-marks, and a few old bones are scattered here and there. Toward the rear of the cave the floor drops off rapidly, and it looks like there might be a small tunnel which leads off in that direction. To the north, only a few small bushes block the way out.
6309:
The corpse of an earth troll is lying here.
The corpse of a large earth troll is lying here.
The corpse of a young troll is lying here.
Travel on this little stairway is difficult. Assorted rocks have been thrown together to make a rough stairway. The light of a torch to the south shows a small cavern.
6310: The foul stench of something which has remained too long unburied fill the entire tunnel. Somewhere to the east a small light can be seen, revealing a little stairway which curves downward, out of sight. To the south of here another tunnel opens out before you.
6311:
A half-rotten corpse is hanging here.
A rotten corpse is hanging here.
A half-rotten corpse is hanging here.
A rotten corpse is hanging here.
An ancient fungus smothers the boulders.
As you enter this room, the smell of decaying flesh hits you in the face. You see to the north and south what looks to be piles of dead bodies and stripped carcasses.
6312: A powerful young troll stares at you.

This narrow stone walkway perches high on a rock wall, overlooking a vast, and seemingly bottomless chasm. Westward the slender pathway continues, climbing steadily as it does so, and to the north it descends through a small fissure, entering an enclosed tunnel.
6313: The narrow walkway stretches downward to the east, but to the south it curves gently upward, where it reaches a broad fissure in the wall of the cavern. To the north lies only the cold stone wall, upon which this pathway perches so precariously.
6314: A powerful young troll stares at you.

This peculiar side passage seems to burrow indiscriminately through the thick dirt itself. Only creatures of massive strength could attempt such a feat, but the lack of any refinements indicates a lack for the finer points of construction. The smell of filth and loam fills the air.
6315: A powerful young troll stares at you.

Onwards, the tunnel continues, a gaping maw carved in the very ground of Arda. Roots stick out from all directions, as well as the blind eyes of very large earthworms. The thick rancid smell of troll pervades the tunnel, leaving no doubts as to who carved this path.
6316: Pieces of dirt and rock filter down from the ceiling, covering your head or helmet in its filth. This does nothing to assuage your fears about the stability of this tunnel, yet it seems to have gotten a lot of use. Large, splayed footprints lead both ways, and a rancid, metallic smell dominates your senses.
6317: This small and lonely hill rises above the height of the forests, which curve around its base to the north and to the west. Eastward the land slopes gently down into a narrow ribbon of low, rolling hills, which border the Old East Road. East and west, the road cuts like a scar across the land, just to the south of here, and this prominence offers you a commanding view of all who travel by this route.
6318: In a Dark and Gloomy Forest

Hemmed in, between a small hill to the south, and a sprawling stream to the north, this part of the forest is characterised by its muddy ground. But, though comparatively little undergrowth manages to survive in the soggy earth, the trees here are surprisingly tall and form a dense, almost impenetrable canopy overhead. Perhaps their roots, digging deeper into the ground than those of the smaller plants, are able to find less choking conditions.
6319: A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

A small stream makes its way through the woods just north of here, and its waters must often breach their low banks, for the land is quite muddy. Little undergrowth manages to survive in this swampy soil, but the trees loom high above you, forming a dense canopy overhead. Little or no natural light can ever reach this place, and because of this the area is pervaded by the smell of death and decay.
6320: Death and decay besmirch the air in this part of the forest. A small stream flows idly by, just to the northeast, and its lazy waters spread out across the shore, rotting any deadwood, and choking the undergrowth. only the trees seem able to survive, perhaps because their roots dig so much deeper. And with no competition from other plants, they have thrived, growing tall and dense, their boughs knotting together to form a dense canopy through which no natural light can pass.
6321:
A tall plant grows here, with grey-green leaves and grey flowers.
A tall plant grows here, with grey-green leaves and grey flowers.
A very large tree branch has been ripped from a tree.

The waters of the small stream which meanders past here to the north must often break their banks, for the land here is rather boggy. Deadwood from the trees has rotted badly upon the ground, and few bushes and weeds manage to grow. Yet the trees themselves are tall and dense, perhaps because their roots dig that much deeper. The result is that they have thrived, and their long limbs stretch out overhead, blotting out any view of the sky above.
6322: At the Eaves of a Dark Forest
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

Nestled against the side of a hill to the east, the forest seems to be rather dense here, yet ends abruptly just to the south. The dividing line seems quite unnaturally regular, as if someone had cleared the lands between here and the road. Little undergrowth is to be seen, and indeed it might be that someone has also cut that away. But the trees themselves grow tall and strong, their long limbs knitting close together, forming an dense canopy overhead, through which no natural light seems able to penetrate.
6323: A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

Though the stream flows continually through this area, its waters are quite choked with fallen boughs and other deadwood, which has partially rotted. This pollutes the air with the distinctive odour of decay, lending an unwholesome aspect to the waterway. Thick trees lean over the brook from both of its muddy banks, casting a pall on even the brightest of sunny days or moonlit nights.
6324: In a Dark and Brooding Woodland

A small patch of dark-green moss grows in the deepest shade.
A disgusting forest troll is searching for fresh meat here.

Tall trees, wide in girth and great in age stand all about you, their heavy boughs knitting together to form an impenetrable canopy, through which almost no natural light can filter. And because of this, and because of the muddy ground underfoot, almost no undergrowth is to be seen in this part of the forest. A few twisted weeds, and an occasional thin, spindly bush are all that grows at ground level, and much of this is tainted by rot and mould.
6325: The stream here has a very slight current and is crystal clear. The bank of the water is lined with small stones of diverse variety. The river continues its winding journey through the forest to the southeast.
6326: The bank of the water on all sides is rocky and steep, making it impossible to climb. The stream bends here heading south along base of the hills. Soon the turns come too often to see what the next one will bring.
6327:
A trout swims here.
A trout swims here.
The bank of the water to the west is lined with rocks, yet can be easily climbed to view the lush meadow that lies there. The stream continues its eastward trek to the Trollshaws in the east.
6328: The water here flows among many stones and broken trees, making ripples in the normally flat surface. The stream opens slightly in the east to a valley below the hills and continues south along the Trollshaws.
6329: The water here quickly becomes deeper and somehow darker. The forest slowly encroaches the edges of the waterway, and soon all that surrounds you is the forest known as the Trollshaws. The water continues east here, deeper into the darkness. The water flows from the north out of the hills above the forest.
6330: The forest around the stream is so dark that the water is barely visible below you. The trees slowly open to the east, and it is possible to climb the hill there that looms above the Trollshaws. The stream turns from west to south here.
6331: The hill here is quite barren of life except for the grass at your feet. The hill rises high like the hills to the west and gives a clear view to the land to the south and the stream that intersects the road in the east.
6332: The land steadily rises to a tall hill here giving a clear view of the Road. Small bushes and trees grow in abundance on this knoll, but it is hard to avoid gazing at the mountains of the north that claim the horizon for their own majesty.
6333: Grass grows in abundance along the twisting stream. There are few bushes or trees near, but soon the vegetation becomes more dense. A soft shoulder along the stream makes it easy to reach the crystal waters that flow here.
6334:
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

Turning here from north to east, the stream continues to meander through the dense woodland. Tall trees loom high above you, their branches leaning out part way across the water, casting a gloomy pall on the area, and allowing all manner of insects to thrive. Despite the gentle current of the waterway, the near-constant shadows have hastened decay, and a sickly odour of rotting wood seems to pervade the area.
6335: The stream ambles lazily between the trees which overshadow its banks. Turning here from the west to the south, it passes through some particularly gloomy parts of the forest, where the canopy is so dense as to eliminate any natural light. Thus, even the waterway is cast in gloom for most of the day.
6336: A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

High and dark the forest grows over, above and around you. The trunks of the trees seem almost black in the dim light, their branches seem to descend and grasp at and tangle with your head and body. The rustling of branches and leaves rises and falls though no wind can be felt under the canopy.
6337: A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

The land seems lower here, though the thick forest all around makes the gauging of direction or distance difficult. The trees crowd you, their low hanging branches knocking and scratching at heads. In all direction the dark forest continues, its dark canopy overshadowing the black earth.
6338: Long, slender pines let the light travel between their branches. The smell of an old forest fills your nostrils and relaxes you. There is a large hill some distance to the northeast.
6339:
A brown snake watches you.
A brown snake watches you.
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A restless rabbit bounces around.

The land around you begins to rise slowly to a stony hill above the forest. A few clumps of trees sprout out alongside the mound. The landscape is dominated by the mountains to the north, whereas a dark forest governs the region to the east.
6341: A slight path can be seen here, worn from travellers far and wide coming here to view the spectacular scenery. Ashes of long gone campfires remain in contrast to the greenery that surrounds them. The land begins to descend to the east here, whereas the hills remain high to the south and west.
6343: Rocks seem to be growing out of the earth all around you. A huge pile of large boulders dominates the northern end of the hill. The huge grey stones, placed in no particular order, seem awkward and dangerously close to falling over the edge into the valley below.
6344: A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

The ground here is soft from the flowing waters to the west. The descent down to the water is clear and easily made. A group of large, dark trees blocks the passage to the east, the Trollshaws have begun.
6345:
A statue of a troll is posed in a moment of flight yet forever frozen in stone.
Clusters of slender stems and tall leaves thrive in the mud and shallows.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.

The waters of the gentle stream spread wide here, making the ground to either side somewhat marshy. Sedges and bullrushes abound, and the area makes an ideal habitat for all manner of water-loving insects, since the tall trees of the surrounding woodland leave it in deep shade for much of the day.
6346: A Shallow Stream below the Weir

Clusters of slender stems and tall leaves thrive in the mud and shallows.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.

Water cascades lightly over the edge of a natural weir, which restricts the outflow of a small lake just north of here. Spreading around this shallow basin, the stream is quite shallow at this point, and its current is very gentle as it flows off to the east, its way south blocked here by a rising hillside.
6347: A small stone building once stood here. What remains now is mostly in ruins, but the innermost room is still partially intact. However, brief inspection appears to indicate a long period of abandonment, judging by the advanced state of decay. The floor is cracked in places, the walls have crumbled down, and no roof covers the structure.
6348: A small hill lies just north of here, and it must be from its crest that so many boulders and stones have toppled. Close inspection suggests that many, or perhaps most of these are in fact tooled, and it seems likely that they were once a part of the ruined structure which sits atop the hill. But wherever they came from, they have wreaked havoc on the plant life of this area. A few mighty tree trunks lie flat amid the rocks, and only a single living tree survives.
6349: At the Edge of the Woods

The forest comes to an abrupt ending just south of here, as if someone had deliberately razed the trees to the ground. And beyond a wide, open area lies the unmistakable expanse of a road, cutting its way from east to west across the land. To the north the woods peter out more gradually, as they enter upon a region of tumbled rocks and mighty boulders.
6350: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

A broad band of the forest has been razed to the ground, leaving a field of broken stumps, stretching south toward the road. Some of the trees have been felled by axe or saw, but others have been burned down along with the under- growth. It is apparent that this was done quite some time ago, for thin grass and a few small weeds are already peaking up through the ruined soil, and no ash and cinders are to be seen, even on the biggest of the burned out stumps.
6351: At the Edge of the Forest

Oaks and elms, ancient and hoary stand proud amid a proliferation of younger firs and pines. The trees grow close together, and beneath them thrives a dense undergrowth of bushes, wildflowers and weeds. The only strange thing about this forest is how abruptly it seems to end. Whilst the road to the south offers partial explanation, there is little to suggest why the foliage should not continue unabated to the east.
6352: It was no act of nature which caused the flourishing forest to the north to end so abruptly, and at such a distance from the road. Clearly the woodland was visited by an act of deliberate destruction. The undergrowth has been burned away completely, to leave not a single bush or shrub above about six inches in height. And every tree that was too large simply to burn down has been felled by axe or saw, then its timbers removed or destroyed, leaving behind only the ragged stumps.
6353: The Broken Remains of a Forest

Where once there stood oaks and elms, tall pines and firs, now remain only a host of charred and broken stumps. Even the undergrowth which must once have flourished here has been destroyed. But all of this destruction must have happened long ago, for now a few thin patches of grass, and some tiny clumps of weeds have begun to take hold, and the area is starting to return to life once more.
6354: At the Eaves of a Dense Forest

The forest stretches out to the north, to the east and to the west, but to the south it ends rather abruptly as if cut down by someone. Further to the north the woods are characterised by rather swampy terrain, which strangles all the undergrowth, but here the forest seems quite a natural and airy one, with a variety of bushes, shrubs and flowers thriving amid the tall trees.
6355: Rising sharply to the west, the land merges with a narrow ridge of hills. To the north it rises more gradually, where it draws close to a forest. South and east, a wide road passes by, travelling through a shallow dip in the countryside. Rocks and stones litter the ground here, and no small number of these must tumble regularly toward the thoroughfare.
6356: The land here forms what is almost a peak, dropping off gently in every direction. Westward it enters a broad gully, whilst to the south it slopes off toward a rocky incline, which marks the eastern end of a narrow ridge of hills. To the north and east the gradient is more gentle, and in these directions the woodland itself stretches out before you.
6357: Spruce and tall, rather spindly firs stand in scattered clusters, with wide areas comprised of little but brush and scrub growing between them. Each individual knot of trees seems to crowd together and the ground between them looks as though it might often have been beaten into rough trails, for even now there is a discernible break in the vegetation heading from the gully to the west, north toward another break in the forest.
6358: The rough trail comes to an abrupt end here, as it enters a wide clearing in the forest. The nearest trees describe an almost perfect circle about the place, and at the very centre of this circle a pit has been dug. In this pit lie the bones of many creatures, large and small, as well as the charred remains of logs and flesh. A pronounced stench of death and seared meat still pervades the air, and it seems that no breeze could fully cleanse the reek.
6359: The trees here are rather thin, and only some twisted shrubs and a few rank and sickly weeds serve for undergrowth. The entire area here appears to have been visited by frequent denuding, as if some large and uncaring creature chose on occasion to beat a path through this part of the forest. Not far to the west there is a complete break in the woodland, where a deep and rocky channel cuts from north to south.
6360: Pines and fir trees predominate in this part of the woodland, their heavy trunks reaching high into the sky. Bushes and shrubs proliferate, making a dense undergrowth, which is probably home to innumerable small creatures, but there is little sign of larger game. But just west of here is an abrupt break in the vegetation, where a deep gully cuts across the land.
6361: A horse of the Rohirrim (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Fed by the waters of the stream to the east, the ground here is rich, and supports a variety of bushes and small plants. Standing high enough above the level of the water, it is not at all marshy, but rather a thick, rich loam. Tall pines and firs, and a number of massive deciduous trees all thrive here, and a dense carpet of grass and weeds covers the ground.
6362: The steep slope to the west drops down into the woodland surrounding you. Pine trees grow across the foot of the slope together with many bushes and shrubs. To the north, somewhere out of sight, a stream can be heard splashing and gurgling its course. To the east and south the forest thickens.
6363: The swift running river from the north bends sharply around a large rock in its course, racing onward to the east with many a swirl and splash. The large rock may have tumbled down from the steep slope, rising sharply upward immediately to the west of the river. The brow of the slope frowns down upon you from several hundred feet above your head.
6364: Two small streams merge here, one flowing swiftly down from the north, the second tumbling into the flow from the west. Both streams run in valleys cut into the steep hillside to the north and west. Thick grass grows over the banks of the stream as it continues its rapid journey to the south. To the east, a forest begins several hundred yards distant.
6365: Rushing downhill from the west, a swiftly flowing stream tumbles into a small lake to the east. To then north and south, trees crowd over the stream, growing almost down to the waters edge. The stream has undercut banks several feet deep and grasses and roots hang out over the watercourse.
6366: A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.

A small lake spreads blackly out around you. To the east, many reeds and rushes can be seen growing in the still water of the lake. To the west a stream feeds the lake with fresh water, its splashing and tinkling can be heard echoing out over the lake surface. A dark stand of trees grows along the northerly edge of the lake whilst to the south, excess water from the lake appears to spill through a gap in the trees.
6367: A large pike is lurking in the mud by the bottom.

Many branches and twigs have been washed down into the lake to the north by the streams feeding it. These have become stuck at this outfall and over the years have gradually built up a weir over which the lake now empties its excess water. Trees grow down to the water's edge to the east and the west and it may well be their roots which have started the choke of debris from which you now gaze.
6368: All around, a thick stand of pine trees sprouts forth from the moist earth. The chirpings of woodland birds can be heard from the branches above. The ground underfoot is springy, the thick moss and tightly packed heather growing around the feet of the tree trunks.
6369: The ground is sodden underfoot. Water wells up around feet and hooves as they press down into the soggy vegetation. Many bushes grow thickly to a height of three or four feet. A few trees grow amid the brush but they seem stunted by the excess water. Many biting insects flourish in the damp conditions and once disturbed, follow your movements through the undergrowth.
6370: A small lake to the west ends underfoot here in a soggy morass of rushes, mud and weeds. Floundering through this marshland is hard going indeed as the mud sucks at feet and hooves making each step an effort. To the north, south and east woodland surrounds the marsh, indicating that firmer ground may lie in those directions.
6371: A huge black fungus is here, exuding a foul stench.

The forest floor is damp and sodden underfoot. With the trees sucking moisture from the ground, some water source must be present nearby to maintain the soil in this state. A moist brown odour rises from the forest floor, most likely dead vegetation rotting in the soggy conditions.
6372: Crooked, twisted trees shut out any light from above, lending the forest a dark and sombre atmosphere. No colours brighten the drab undergrowth and in all directions, dim grey trees stretch away. From somewhere to the south, running water can be heard, tinkling and splashing beyond sight.
6373: The forest rises dark and sombre all around. Nary a chink of light passes from above the black foliage of the closely packed boughs. The dark shadows play tricks upon your eyes, the dark branches seeming to writhe and twist toward you with their long fingers of crooked twigs. An evil presence hangs over these woods.
6374:
A small rat runs about, oblivious to your presence.
A swarm of midges is here, humming around you.

Dim, dark boughs hang around you. The forest of the trollshaws seems unkind toward strangers and it seems as if the trees almost jostle one another in their attempt to enclose you and impede progress. High above you the sky must gaze down, but the dark foliage blocks out even a glimpse of the sun or stars.
6375:
A large shrub covered with dark violet berries grows here.
On the shrub, there are three piles of violet berries.

The tree roots stick up from the damp earth underfoot. Their surfaces are slippy with moisture and footsteps on the earth between causes water to well up from the ground. The trees seem to thrive in these damp conditions and many varieties of deciduous and coniferous trees grow together in a mish-mash of shapes and sizes.
6376: Many trees grow on the south-east facing slope. The soil seems thick and fertile and the hill and cliffs to the north-west provide partial shelter from the bitter north winds. To the south and east the land drops away to the lower forests of the trollshaws.
6377: A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

The trees grow high up the sheltered southern face of the hillside. Through gaps in the forest, the trollshaws can be seen stretching out for miles to the south and the east. To the west the lands drops down into a steep-sided valley. To the north the trees peter out as the hillside climbs ever upward.
6378: The upper branches of the woodland grow together to form a green canopy over the forest floor. Here and there a chink in the foliage allows light to filter from above. The rich smell of moist earth and wood lingers in the still air of the forest. To the west, the ground seems to rise slightly.
6379: The thick foliage of the woodland cuts down any light from the skies above to a mere glimmer amid the permanent dusk. The choking of the light prevents the growth of underbrush and the forest floor is a uniform gray-brown carpet of decaying leaves and branches. The gloom extends around you in all directions, deepening to black as the trees close in.
6380: Dark fir trees grow tall from the moist black earth. Their aspect is singular and foreboding. The air of the forest seems heavy with suspense, though no immediate danger seems obvious. Only a few furtive rustles and cracks break the dead silence of the woods.
6381: The network of branches above your head thickens to the extent that little light can pass through its dark leafy canopy. The trees themselves are twisted and misshapen. The forest has a tainted aura which seems to have infected the flora and fauna with its insidious grasp. Unrecognisable harsh cries sounds out occasionally, breaking the ominous silence.
6382: In the Lee of a Hill

The bare northern face of this mound gazes out over the forest of the trollshaws. The land slopes down to the north, east and west where the trees begin nigh a hundred feet from your present position. To the south, you could scramble up the slope which looks to climb another few hundred feet to the low summit.
6383: An almost sheer vertical face of cliff looms over you to the west. To gaze upon its summit requires you to lean back and crane your neck as you gaze upward. The trees of the surrounding forest to the north, south and east grow almost to the foot of the cliff, with only piles of fallen rock and rubble separating the two.
6384: A wolf spider is here, among the trees.

High above you, a steep cliff peers down from the broad flank of the hillside to the west. Many rocks and boulders have fallen from the cliff, eroded from the living rock by the ravages of the wind, rain and ice. To the north, east and the south, forest grows on the lower slopes of the hillside.
6385: Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.

This is the highest point at the eastern end of the range of hills curving deep into the heart of the trollshaws. Several miles to the west, a higher peak can be spied, its lofty summit looking down even on this high peak. Immediately to the east, the hillside drops away down a dizzying cliff to the forest far below.
6386: Looking over the cliff edge to the east is a giddying experience. The ground drops away nigh vertically for hundreds of feet. Far below, the treetops of the forest sway in the breeze. To the south the hill climbs toward its summit and to the north you can travel down and out upon a long spur of high ground.
6387: A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.

Several yards to the west a stream races southward, swirling and splashing down over the rocks of the streambed. The tinkling, splashing sound of the water fills the air. At the sides of the stream, grass grows thickly in the moist fertile ground. To the west and north, high hillside rises upward from your vantage point. To the east, dark pines grow thick and black.
6388: A small stream tumbles southward down the hillside. The tinkling and gurgling of water splashing down over the rocks breaks the otherwise enveloping silence of the woods. Many clumps of green mosses and rushes grow in the moist earth beside the stream.
6389: At the Head of a Stream

A small brook wells up from the broken rock of the hillside and trickles down the slope to the south. Over the years the stream has cut into the hillside and clumps of moss and heather grow in the sheltered niche cut by the stream. The hillside rises to the south west and continues along the flank to the east.
6390:
A brown snake watches you.
A small brown snake is slithering around here.

The loose, friable rock of the slope makes progress across this terrain difficult. This exposed flank is bounded by a steep-sided gully to the west. From your present position, the bottom of the gully cannot be seen. To the east the land rises up a shallow ridge. Sparse woodland covers the lower slopes to the north.
6391: A few yards from you, a small waterfall tumbles down from the hillside to the west. The splashing of the water on the rocks of the streambed causes a mist of fine water droplets to hang in the air making exposed flesh and clothing damp. Several tiny fish dart around in the pools by the fall.
6392: This high knuckle of hillside stands sentinel over the low ground to the north and east. The hillside drops steeply down from your present location, downward into a river gouged valley to the north and east. To the south and west you can continue along the ridge of high ground.
6393: Nestled below the hill summit to the north-west, this small clump of trees flourishes in the natural protection from the harsh northerly winds. Here and there other shrubs or a small pine grows amidst the birch and larch trees which make most of the stand. The ground slopes downward to the south and the east.
6394: A small stream trickles forth from a cleft in the hillside. The stream dances and splashes away to the east, tumbling down the hillside as it races downhill. A valley cuts into the hillside to the east and spurs of hill encompass the cut to the north-east and south-east sides.
6395: Far below you the green forests of the trollshaws stretch away to the east. A small river can be seen cutting its way through the trees as it winds its way south-east. Any movements on the loose rock of this lofty perch cause small stones and rocks to clatter away down the slope, giving away your presence.
6396:
A large pile of boulders is sitting here, probably debris from a rockslide.
A mottled snake is sneaking here, ready to sink its fangs into flesh.
A mottled snake is sneaking here, ready to sink its fangs into flesh.

A sheer cliff of hard, grey stone looms above you to the north, marking the end of a vast ridge, which cuts across the forest from northwest to southeast. The land climbs away from here, both east and west, and this rocky gully makes a gentle descent to the south. Boulders and smaller rubble are strewn all about you, as if this gully were perhaps once a part of the ridge, blasted into small pieces by some unknown force. Loose rocks and scree make both walls unappealing prospects for exit, especially as they are almost vertical at this point.
6397: Climbing gently to the north, the gully stretches out before you, its bottom a barren sea of tumbled rocks and boulders. To the south the rocky debris gives way once more to the endless forest, which also rears above you to the east and west, beyond the walls of this wide, stony trench. Both sides of the chasm are very steep and covered in loose scree, but whilst the eastern one is almost vertical, the western one has a shallower grade, and it is probably possible to scramble out in that direction.
6398: Some ugly blow-flies are buzzing around here.

A wide trench cuts through the forest from north to south. For most of its length it is quite bare of vegetation, a bed of rocks and boulders, smaller stones and sharp scree. But here the woods have reclaimed part of the gully, and several small stands of pines and firs cling to life in the rocky ground.
6399: Some ugly blow-flies are buzzing around here.

Running almost due north to south, this deep gully cuts a long wound through the forest, with almost no vegetation clinging to life in its rocky bottom. No river bed, it is something of a mystery what could have carved this stony chasm into the land. Its walls here are quite gently sloped, and the trench floor itself rises to both the north and south.
6400: Some ugly blow-flies are buzzing around here.

Thick forests grow to either side of this long trench, which stretches off into the distance, to the north. But here there is no vegetation at all, the entire area being a barren sea of rocks and stones, in which not even a few tiny weeds can be seen. East and west the walls of the gully rise gently toward the woodland. To the south the land also climbs steadily, as it reaches the lower slopes of a ridge of hills.
6401: Toward the End of a Hilly Ridge

Already the hills have begun to descend toward the lower land to the east. A steeper southern slope leads down towards the Old East Road. To the north rather a steep grade offers access to a deep gully, which stretches due north for a considerable distance, cutting the forest in two.
6402: Covered in short furry grass like the back of a sheep, the hills carry on in the north and descend down to a north-south trail in the east. In the west the view is blocked by pines which form almost a natural wall on the hill.
6403: Ascending slowly from the lowlands, these widely sloping hills are blanketed with a lush carpet of grasses. Strewn in bunches are delicate clusters of tawny flowers raising their faces to the sky from among the grassbeds. From here you can descend the gradual slope the the trail below, climb up towards a particularly high and wide hill, or merely remain here a bit and enjoy this area's pastoral simplicity.
6404: Slithering through the hills, this small but well-defined trail offers a comfortable means of travel unlike the wilderness to either side. Bordering the trail are tufts of pale grass and struggling patches of heather and furze. You can follow the trail either to the east or south, or ascend into the nearby hills.
6405: The trail winds sinuously down from the hills to the north into scattered brush intermingled with stands of varied evergreens. The undergrowth borders close upon the trail in sparse tangled patches, but there are few trees to muddle the horizon. Looming to the east is a series of uplands, while the trail meanders to the north and west.
6406: A large expanse of heath borders the trail thickening into some woodlands to your east. The area is thickly grown with ling and broom and cornel, exuding a mild fresh scent. A few small knots of dwarf pines and blue-green firs are scattered about, more prominent as one nears the woodlands. To the south the earth rises so sharply as to deny all access via this route.
6407: The land rises suddenly into jagged ridges of rock to which cling spindly wind-battered pines. Hardy grasses and lichen also cover the fractured rocks and boulders. The land slopes downward to the west overlooking forests and beyond that the landscape rises into more hills.
6408: The land is less rough here, and slopes up to a large rocky hill that affords a good view of the Old East Road below you. The landscape is endowed with a thick blanket of underbrush from which rises a number of pines and spruce. The vegetation suddenly ends at a sheer dropoff of a sort that no sane man would dare to climb.
6410: Ringed on three sides by hills, this shady vale seems lusher and more wholesome than surrounding environs. A multitude of evergreens thrive in the fertile soil which also supports equally plentiful brush and smaller greenery.
6411: A sheer bluff dominates the north section of this area, even a skilled mountaineer could not ascend the steep limestone cliff. Pines, spruce, and birch cluster below the cliffside in round bundles, relieved occasionaly by patches of grass and heather. The dusty strip of the road can be spotted to the south, while the woods continue below the uplands.
6412: Bushy bundles of heather and briar cover the lightly sloping ground, interspersed with solitary pines or larches. The flora's dry brown semblance complements the dusky dun-coloured turf--even the trees here are dull and dessicated. The winding ribbon of the road lies to your southeast, in the opposite direction the land rears up into randomly rolling hills and cliffs.
6413: Your surroundings defy all attempts to categorise or define them; divergence, discordance, and mutation prevail here. The land rises and falls without pattern, sometimes covered in snarled tanglings of bramble or heath, in other places covered with tumblings of fractured rock with pale tufts of grass emerging from cracks and fissures. Various trees sprawl about, individually or in small stands, their limbs tangled and askew. While progess in any direction is difficult, the land becomes calmer and more even to the south and east.
6414: Trees cling precariously to scree-covered slopes or nestle in small niches in the rising rockfaces. It appears that with skill one could scale the jagged ridge of tumbled rock. All about you the land seems twisted and aimlessly constructed.
6415:
A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.
A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

Tumbles of rocks are piled upon each other in a random and haphazard fashion; trees sprout from them without form or regularity, their branches swept into odd directions and shapes by the relentless wind. The road and surrounding lands spread out to your south--you might descend the steep slope with care and skill.
6416: The land juts up into fractured peaks and promontories. Piles of broken rock lie scattered about, and rifts and fissures abound; it would be best to tread carefully here. A few trees grow in cracks and shelters, but they are far from abundant. To the south the land becomes even more precarious; the land above you rises high above all else, affording an excellent vista.
6417: Misty and gloomy, something about this area sends a uncomfortable prickling running along your spine. Certainly it is dark enough, the trees and brush are vague indistinguishable blobs even in the daytime.
6418: The uplands loom dim and near to the southeast, towering over the scattered line of trees that thickens to your south. The earth is soft and moist, supporting hearty patches of brush, and a few handfuls of variegated wildflowers quivering colourfully in the breeze. The woods open up to the west revealing a pathway, to the east there is a V-shaped indentation cleft into the steeply rising hills.
6419: This sandy mire supports little life, but on small mounds emerging from the muck, scraggled, twisted spruces raise sparsely-needled boughs toward the firmanent, doggedly persisting in this unforgiving soil. There is a distinct smell of ordure and rot--the water is darkly mottled with decaying vegetation and other organics. Southwards the land ascends slowly towards some ragged uplands jutting above the horizon.
6420: A green frog is here, hopping around.

The ground is wet, and in some places little ponds have formed to keep the water on surface. Small streams seem to slowly carry rest of it eastwards. The trees are mostly spruce, with occassional patches of short birches.
6421: Tall and straight pines surround you with their trunks and branches that float on the ground before diving deeper in the soil. Here the ground is still quite dry, but in the south-east it turns more wet.
6422: The trail makes its way north-east and south-west, changing the course to pass the few obstacles on the way. Here it seems to follow the edge of the forest in the east and in the south, until further north it disappears on a hill.
6423: The trail bends like a snake around the trees and bushes, looking for an easy way to get to the end, but no end can be seen as far as the view is clear. In the south it disappears behind trees, and in the east it does not get far before another turn north.
6424: An almost unnoticeable rise in the terrain from the north keeps the grass drier here, almost ideal for a little field. But of course no one lives here to farm it, and it shall remain as it is until overgrown by the great forest of which the huge trees in the west are a good example.
6425: This little valley seems to be where the pouring rain eventually ends up from the forest west of here and the hills in the east. It is not quite a swamp yet, but one could easily imagine in turning into one in the future, once the dry seasons are no longer enough for the grass to grow up.
6426: A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

The forest is getting less thick in the south, revealing a little trail rising up and down in the ravines. The branches of the trees, which mostly seem to be evergreen in this part, have been cut in the lower parts by force. Probably a sign of some animal marking its territory.
6427: The trail bends northeast where it continues until the hills seen far in the distance. On the west side of the bend, a row of about twenty trees have grown funnily in a direct north-south course. Another range of hills start nearby in the south, and the trail turns to progress around it.
6428: The trail climbs down in the south, where it continues to follow the edge of the hills, and on the east side it is bordered by a forest, mostly pine.
6429: A grey wolf is here, salivating profusely.

The sandy trail follows the edge of the green hills on their east side. The trail is separated by a small region of thornbushes from the spruce forest in the east, where the ground gets wet and in places a bit swampy.
6430:
The elongated shape of a stoat can be seen darting across the terrain.
A hungry warg (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A vaguely distinguishable trail meanders north-south through a wide expanse of pale sand flats, interrupted only rarely by various tufts of dark-green ribbon grass. The land slopes gradually upwards to lush grassy hills to your west and to the east descends into a sickly mire.
6431: A hungry warg (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

This slightly sandy trail veers west, avoiding the lightly forested regions to the south. Beyond the forest the land can be seen to rise into some craggy and desolate uplands to the east and south. Aside from a few wan flowers by the wayside, the area seems forlorn and abandoned.
6432: A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

You find yourself in an intermediate area of pine and cedar woodlands, fading slowly into brush and heath to the northwest, darkening into heavier forests to the southeast. The trees grow in compact stands, scattered patchwork amidst a rich variety of scrub, heath, and creeping bramble. As with its surroundings, this area is ominously quiet.
6433: Tall boughs interweave to form a dense canopy that blocks out most of the sunlight. The forest floor exudes a moist, fungal odor; scattered about are fiery-capped mushrooms, encrustations of brain-coral fungus, and creeping slime molds. Northwest the forest fades into mixed trees and heathland, while to the southeast tall uplands climb skyward. It appears that with skill and luck one could clamber up a nearby rockface.
6434: Wind-swept pines send their roots deep into to stony soil, their branches bent back by the prevailing wind. The land swells and dips in steep jagged hills and ridges, most notably to your east where the ground has been thrust upward without rhyme or reason.
6435: Despite the rocky, uneven terrain, tall pines grow strong and closely packed, darkening the forest floor. The dimness, coupled with the stony earth allows little growth underneath the canopy. Tiny rock-chips crackle underfoot and render travel a slow and slippery affair.
6436:
A sturdy billy goat stands here, proudly protecting his goats.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.

Twisted pines grow closely on rough scree-covered slopes, preventing most illumination from penetrating here. Indeed, the footing is precarious here, progress is limited to stumbling and sliding along talus and debris. Below you the road dips and curves along a wooded area.
6437: A Mingling of Deciduous and Cone-Bearing Trees

A large belt of larches prosper here, their tall branches straining skyward in open competition with the more predominant pines and firs. The undergrowth is lush and fecund, covering most of the earth with a carpet of greenery. Scattered amidst the green are bright clusters of purple rhododendrons, exuding a delicate perfume that rises and mingles with the sweet resinous odor wafted into the breeze by the proud larches. A single lonely bird pierces the silence with a melancholy tune.
6438: This road appears to have been not so much as built but instead blasted into existence by some strange power. The surface is black and smooth, with a glassy obsidian-like quality. Still the road gives sufficient traction to allow easy progress along its confines. The roadside is barren and still bears signs of whatever magics produced this trail--patches of blackened turf and skeletal tree-boles.
6439: The landscape here is desolate, unlike the heavily forested lands to your north. The dun-coloured soil still manages to support a few patches of heather and some withered trees stand morosely scattered by the roadside. The land is quiet and apparently devoid of fauna. Perhaps if a hungry traveller was in need of sustenance, they could hunt in the woods above the winding road.
6440: A cute, fluffy owlet pecks at some food on the ground.

At some recent juncture a fire swept through this area, leaving blackened stumps and contorted boles in its wake. The process of renewal has begun however; a fresh carpet of grass has sprung up in the enriched soil. Also thriving in the mineral-laden earth is a variety of culinary herbs; hooded morels lie in fresh rows ready for the picking. A thin crevasse sidles along to the northwest thwarting any progress in this direction. Southward the narrow ribbon of the Road can be faintly discerned.
6441:
A cute, fluffy owlet is waiting here for its mother to return with food.
A cute, fluffy owlet is waiting here for its mother to return with food.
A great horned owl looks cautiously around it.

Tall larches predominate here, their slender forms and sparse, feathery foliage of light green contrasting with the darker, stubbier pines hereabouts. Underneath the trees' delicate green tracery of needles and tall reddish brown trunks, small plants grow amidst a carpet of matted needles. The songs of birds echo lightly through the trees, and you espy a large nest in one of the nearby trees; evidently the tamaracks are a favourite nesting spot.
6442: The forest descends into a broadly sloping valley, well-favoured with alternating patches of pine, mountain ash, and small sweetly smelling meadows of wild rye grass sprinkled with variegated wildflowers. Some type of small subterranean-dwelling rodents have endeavoured to dig numerous burrows in the grass; occasionaly the head of one of these recluse creatures pops up to monitor you.
6443: The landscape is somewhat barren, with patches of scrub and grasses here and there with many bare spots inbetween. A fair number of conifers subsist in the unforgiving soil, their branches scraggly and sparsely-needled. The Road passes to the south.
6444: On the very edge of the road the woodland becomes quite thin, and the rocky ground seems to discourage the undergrowth which flourishes elsewhere in the forest. The trees here are mostly conifers, and no small number of these seem to be in decidedly ill health, their branches thin and weak.
6445: Climbing above the treeline, this narrow ridge stands above the forest, which sprawls out west and north of here. To the south it offers a commanding view of the Old East Road, which cuts its way across the land from east to west, travelling between the distant settlements of Bree and Rivendell.
6446: Atop a Narrow Ridge of Hills

Rising out of the forest to the north, and looming above the Old East Road to the south, this narrow ridge of hills stretches out both east and west from here. The cruel north winds must often flay this unprotected area, and only the barest covering of topsoil remains. It is therefore no surprise to see that only a few stunted patches of heather manage to cling to life here.
6447: A large eagle soars above you.

The land here slopes gently down toward a fold in the land not far to the east, but the gradient is no so steep as to have eroded the soil, and a rich variety of bushes, shrubs and wildflowers comprise the undergrowth. Massive pines and firs, and a few ancient birches and oak trees surround you.
6448: A roe deer is standing here, watching the terrain while chewing the vegetation.

The forest here is composed evenly of tall pine trees, and shorter, bushy fir trees. The ground is quite bare, with pine needles softening the sound of your tread. The forest seens to get darker to the east, while staying about the same to the north. To the west the woods seem lighter, whilst a ridge of hills rises to the south.
6449: To the south the forest seems fairly sparse, but here the trees grow close together, pines and firs mixing with a few deciduous species to form a rich, mixed forest. A variety of bushes and shrubs, mixed with weeds and a few tiny wildflowers make a dense undergrowth, which makes travel through this area rather more difficult, but at the same time adds to the wholesome air of this part of the woodland.
6450: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

This area transitions from some sparsely forested areas into a lowly rising meadow to the north. A few pines and firs populate the area, but they are neither prolific nor prosperous. Such scattered brush and herbs that prefer this limey soil manage fairly well here.
6451: Clusters of pines and firs with an occasional larch grow between small grassy meadows spotted with small flowers. All about are trees, not so thick as to block out the sky yet prevalent enough to dominate all fields of view.
6452: A narrow ravine winds alongside this freshly-scented zone of trees amid small patches of furze, heather, and bramble accentuated with tiny ground-clinging flowers. In every direction you see trees and more trees, although at some point across the ravine the trees become thin and feeble.
6453: Jutting from the cracked, lifeless earth is a tall ebony monolith that seems to reach up and pierce the sky. It looks as if it were not built so much as it was summoned from the bowels of the earth. The surface of the obelisk is covered with oddly formed runes that writhe and pulsate, emanating a sallow, unholy light. A small obsidian altar is beside it, square with a bowl-shaped indentation coated with some brownish-red powder.
6454: The glossy black trail suddenly winds to the east, where you espy a looming black monolith, limned by a sallow glow. Even from this distance, it is intuitively obvious that the obelisk is the source of ancient evil, embued with a malevolent power. Beyond the obelisk the land decays into a series of mud flats; a strange redolence reminiscent of rotten eggs eminates from that direction.
6455: A mass of dark green leaves clings to a wall.

The closely packed trees blanket a steeply rising slope. The ground is veritably cloaked with sedge, bramble, and ivy. Soft mutterings and occasional quiverings in the undergrowth imply the presence of some small animal life. A cliff rises almost vertically to the east and only at a slightly smaller gradient to the north.
6456: Fir trees grow profusely, exuding a deep, resinous odor that elicits twinges in your nostrils. Brush and brambles wind about the trees, slowing any travel. Close to the north a wide sawtooth ridge rises above the horizon.
6457: Constrained on either side by winding crevasses, the trail proceeds north and south. A palpable sense of evil radiates from the north, though the source or reason is unclear. Something tells you that you should be well prepared if you wish to return from there alive.
6458: Weaving its way along a precipice, a small goat-trail allows progress along the jagged ridge, rising eventually to a peak north of you, or descending rapidly downwards navigating the hillside in long cutbacks back and forth along the only available pathways downward. The rocky land is mainly barren, but as usual with this area, a few scraggly evergreens fight for life in any site with a modicum of shelter from the chill mountain winds.
6459: The jagged hills crest to a dizzying height here; indeed it seems as if one has reached the highest point of the Pennath Tar. The altitude affords a mighty vista overlooking the surrounding lands. To the south is a thin winding ribbon which must be the Old East Road curving and rising in unison with the rolling landscape. All about the hills the lands are blanketed in rich forests; on and on and on without visible end. A strange odour of rotting eggs wafts along the breeze, evidently from the immediate east. Peering downward you notice an expanse of seething mud flats, beyond which rises an odd black monolith.
6460: The land slowly slopes, equally divided between murky fens and small tree covered mounds rising from the waters. The terrain begins to rise steeply to the south and east; tall crags and ridges dominate the skyline. A large cleft to your south looks intriguing, and perhaps might afford a safe place to scale the ridge.
6461: The ground gets more wet going to the east, and in some places impossible to put ones feet upon. Around the trees there is some drier terrain, which makes it possible to carefully jump from one to another and proceed that way.
6462: This is the last patch of pine before the land becomes too wet for it to grow further in the east and south. Actually it looks like no trees whatsoever can exist in the thick mist that fills the air in the valley to the east.
6463: A group of birches have found a good place in the fertile soil, and they have grown tall and healthy to form this nice little grove. In the east the terrain carefully descents to a misty valley, that does not look all that nice anymore.
6464: An attempt has been made to block the trail to the north with branches, but it does not really take much effort to remove the blockage. After that the trail climbs up to a hill where it carries on. A small hill blocks the view in the east as well.
6465: Little bushes have been ripped off from the side of the road and thrown on the trail. Looks like some little animals have been feeding on the branches, they are covered with toothprints. The trail slopes gently down in the south, where it slightly bends westwards and disappears into the forest, but in the north it follows the outline of the hills as long as you can see. East of here the plain hills carry on endlessly.
6466: The hills seem to go on and on, without end. They are covered with little and large rocks and the terrain is hard to walk on. Sharp shadows dance on the close rock shapes as the wind sings in the cracks and valleys.
6467: The terrain climbs up and down, making travelling rather difficult. As far as one can see between the trunks, there seems to be some hills both in the west and in the south.
6468: The trees in this part of the forest are not very old and the wood is rather healthy. Maybe there was a fire that burned down the old forest and let a new one grow on a good soil. There is a steep rise in the terrain to the east, and a more gentle one to the south.
6469: This gently forested hill gives a perfect view on the path in the north and over the woods behind it. Far in the west you can see another trail running north-south, and a huge tower near the crossroads of the two.
6470: A huge grizzly bear is here, roaming the wild.

A steep slope rises to the west, filled with big lichen-covered rocks. One has to watch his steps very carefully here to avoid slipping on the mossy ground. Toward the east the wood changes slowly from spruce to a mix of deciduous trees.
6473: A dun-coloured grouse is sitting still in the heather.

Far and wide to the north the woodland stretches across the land. The treeline lies only a few hundred yards below you, snaking its way along the flank of the hill. Above the trees only a few hardy grasses and clumps of moss and heather cling to the stony ground.
6474: The hillside is covered with bushes and heather which thins out as the slope rises to the south and west. Down the slope to the north, thick pines grow on the side of the hill. To the east a spur of forest climbs higher up the hill, coming almost level with your present vantage point. Many tiny flies burst from any disturbed heather and cluster in the air around you.
6475: A fat rabbit sits here, chewing on some grass.

The trees struggle to cling to the ever increasing slope to the south. Here and there a pine tree lies fallen downhill, its roots torn out from their tenacious grasp by the ravages of the wind and rain. The lack of thick tree cover allows many bushes and heather to flourish on the coarse sandy soil of the hillside.
