The Hollin Plains flank the river Sirannon, as it bends from west to north. To the south and east the grass extend, dotted by berry laden holly bushes. Far to the east, the mysterious Misty Mountains can be seen, with three menacing snow-covered peaks towering above the rest.
13195: This mound over the riverbed, although lower than the surrounding hills, gives you a good view of the region. The hills are lush green and dotted red from berries ripening on the holly bushes. You can hear the nearby river Sirannon and to the west can gain access to the river. While the Sirannon is a small river, once, many years ago, it was much larger. Now, it looks like a mere trickle in the wide riverbed.
13196: The landscape of the low Hollin hills is one which incites peace and reflection. This is one of the most fruitful regions of Middle-earth, and was for a while the granary of the northern Numenorean kingdoms. Several plants growing here are indeed cereals which returned to the wild after the last peasants left the place.
13197: This land is a land of plains and of low and fertile green hills on which are scattered saplings, young walnut trees and fruit trees. A line of dry grass and hostile bushes grows over the remains of an enclosing wall. These hints, along with a few blocks of stones worked by a capable hand, are enough to prove that on this place a settling had been built.
13198: From here, hills can be seen all around, dotted red by berries on the plentiful holly bushes which pervade the area. Far to the east, you can see the crags of the Misty Mountains as they reach towards the sky. Closer to hand, you can see two rivers: One lies to the east and flows north to join the Sirannon as it wends its way towards the west where it will join the Glanduin, many leagues away.
13199:
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A large mother hawk is here looking for prey to feed her young.

The holly bushes which dominate the countryside also dominate the colour of this region, imposing their red berries and lush green leaves on the country- side. The hills stretch for many miles in all directions. No end to the hills is readily at sight, but you can see far in the east three rocky crowns of the Misty Mountains.
13200:
A bright green holly bush is growing here.
Partly covered by the bush's green leaves, there are two piles of hollyberries.
A porcupine is waddling around here, its tail full of sharp quills.

The pink-red hills spread all around you, covered in holly bushes which seem to have established a dominance in the area. Rolling hills stretch for miles in all directions. To the north-west, the hills are punctuated by the river Sirannon flowing softly between them and the Hollin Road which follows the path of the river. Apart from the river, the horizon is entirely dominated by the hills, except for the east, where the Misty Mountains reach towards the sky.
13201: From the trail to the west, a gentle slope climbs the green side of the hill. The low grass is slowly overcome by the holly-bushes which spread all around you. The trail leads to a ford north-west of here and continues through a forest far to the south, flanked by hills. To the north, you can easily make out the forlorn Sirannon, a shadow of its former might, and beyond it, the Hollin Road. The hills roll continuously to the east for many miles, and far, far beyond the hills, the Misty Mountains can be seen, dominating the horizon.
13202: A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

A small forest is here and continues to the south and west. To the north and east, the land rises to form a range of hills, covered with holly bushes. Small animals dart away at your coming and you can see other evidence of these animals in the multitude of small tracks which criss-cross the forest.
13203:
A large mother hawk is here looking for a prey to feed her young.
A porcupine is waddling around here, its tail full of sharp quills.

The holly bushes cling to the hillside here as they do to the north and east. To the west lies a small forest which continues to the south-west. A worn trail can be seen to the south as it winds its way to a stockaded village farther to the south.
13204:
A bright green holly bush is growing here.
Partly covered by the bush's green leaves, there are two piles of hollyberries.
A porcupine is waddling around here, its tail full of sharp quills.
An elk cow gazes coldly at you, chewing on a small branch.

The hills continue in all directions save south of here, outlined by the red berries of the predominant flora, holly bushes. To the south, a faint trail peters out, but continues to travel east. Beyond this trail, a village can be seen just beyond some farmland.
13205:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

The hills begin to flatten out as they merge into the Plains of Hollin to south. To the north and west, however, the hills continue for many miles. Far in the distant north, you can barely make out the Sirannon as it flows to the west, skirted by the remnants of the Hollin Road. To the south-west, you can see the faint outline of a small village which is on the outskirts of the nearby forest.
13206:
A tall, stately, dome-topped tree grows here.
On the plant, there are two green spiny capsules.

The lush grass that grows around your feet is criss-crossed by many small trails. On examining these trails you see that narrow trails don't always mean small creatures as there are some rather large footprints in the mud. The trails are partially covered by short, bushy vegetation, somewhat blending them with the surroundings and making them hard to spot from a distance. To the west and north the Hollin hills can be easily reached.
13207: A natural culvert begins here, channeling the water draining from the slight ridges to the east and south and forming a clear river flowing off to the north. To the south and west some peculiar-looking hills can be seen rising from the plains of Dunland, while far off on the eastern horizon the Misty Mountains thrust up their awe-inspiring peaks to the sky.
13208: Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

A mixture of grasses, both course and fine, grows underfoot, interspersed here and there with wildflowers of varying colours. The occasional stalk of wheat thrusting from the ground could indicate that this area was once cultivated, but there are no other signs of recent habitation except for a faint wisp of smoke to the southeast. Far off to the east the first peaks of the Misty Mountains raise their grey shoulders to the sky.
13209: Growing among the high grasses are several different types of wild wheats, indicating that this plain was once cultivated, in the faroff past. It would appear that only animals live here, except for the smoke coming from the south. The ground is hard to see, due to the unchecked vegetation growth.
13210: Animal tracks stretch in the high grasses, winding through the hills. To the north, the hills are dotted red by berries of the predominate flora, holly bushes. To the south, the hills are greener, as the bushes give way to grass.
13211: There are two handfuls of clover here.

The sound of the local wildlife fills your ears and you stroll lazily along this everlasting grassy plain, and you feel lost in a see of high grasses. To the north, hills covered by holly bushes stretch for miles. To the south, you can venture into what appears to be farmland and beyond it to a stockaded village. Far to the east, the snow covered peaks of the Misty Mountains can be seen.
13212: The plains are marked by the red berries of holly bushes which characterise the region. These plains look similar to the nearby hills, with the main difference being that they are level. The plains continue east and south and a small village can be seen in the distant west. Northwards, a faint trail, formed by the animals of this region, is barely visible as it cuts through the hills.
13213:
A small cluster of clover grows here.
A thin, crippled deer looks around timidly.
A thin, crippled deer looks around timidly.

These hills are covered with a blanket of thin grass that clings tenaciously to the earth as an effort to resist the strongs winds that scour this region. To the east, the hills lessen and some plains extend for a distant. Far beyond the plains, the grey peaks of the Misty Mountains can be discerned.
13214: Far to the east, the first peaks of the Misty Mountains stand like a grey stain on the horizon. These plains continue unabated to the east until the foothills are finally reached. At times, the terrain becomes less flat, and the rounded hills are dotted by the holly that is characteristic of the area.
13215: This land of grassy plains and rolling hills continues unabated until the foothills of the Misty Mountains are reached miles to the east. Somewhere among the plains to the south, the river Glanduin flows, while somewhere else in the distant north, the Sirannon follows the path of the old Hollin Road.
13216: A buck runs swiftly from place to place, looking about warily as it grazes.

In all directions, this land of low and grassy hills continues. The terrain is somewhat flatter to the west, while the hills appear to get slightly more pronounced to the north. In places, there is evidence that herd animals occasionally graze here - perhaps a group of Dunlendings have crossed the river Glanduin to make their home near.
13217: These low grass-covered hills roll unabated for miles in all directions. Somewhere beyond the hills, to the south, flows the River Glanduin, and beyond the river lies the Dunland. To the east, the grassy growth becomes dotted with small patches of vivid green holly bushes. To the north, the hills are a bit more rugged.
13218: The hills have flattened out into an endless plain. To the west and north the rolling hills paint the landscape with their curves, while somewhere, in the distant south, flows the River Glanduin. To the east the grass thickens, and none of the holly bushes so commonly seen to the north are visible.
13219: This area, the middle of an indistinguishable plain, is covered with a low coarse grass with a weed or small bush embedded from spot to spot among the grass. In all directions the land presents few distinct landmarks, making it difficult to get your bearings, though a small burned hut does lie to the south.
13220: To the far east, a rolling hill forms at the edge of the horizon as a precursor to the first peaks of the Misty Mountains. South of here, beyond sight, the river Glanduin flows and not so far to the north, some ten miles from here, the river Sirannon can be found as it winds around an ancient road. While at times the terrain becomes less flat, much of the surrounding, as is this area, is covered with short grass and a few holly bushes that become sprinkled with red berries during the warm months of spring and summer.
13221: The grassy hill forms a lazy upward slant towards the south where it meets a plateau some three miles away. To the west the remains of a burned out hut can be seen and five miles beyond it a water hole. To the north after many miles of plains the river Sirannon can be found and beyond it the old Hollin Road.
13222: The remains of a small hut are still visible. From the placement and age of this hut, some seven miles from the main village, it appears to have housed an outcast. While it is not obvious if the fire that destroyed this hut was set intentionally or accidentally, or if it was the cause of the occupant's death, it does appear from the various well placed trinkets that the dead occupant was honored.
13223: While the land is flat and indiscrete a number of nearby landmarks makes it easy to keep your bearings. To the west, well before the rolling hills, is a water hole, while to the east the remains of a burned out hut are visible. To the south a tall tree stands in defiance upon the plains while to the north the land is undistinguishable.
13226:
A brown fur is here lying on the ground.
A small and well-kept fire lights and warms the room.
An old man is sleeping here.

The inside of the hut is quite small and cramped. A strong stench comes from the walls, which are made of large branches packed with dried mud, where some wild animal has urinated. In the centre of the room, a fire blazes away and around the fire some animal skins have been left to dry.
13227:
A large dog curls his lips back and snarls.
A large dog curls his lips back and snarls.
A half wolf is here, loyally protecting his master.

This filthy cage, which smells of decaying flesh and excrement, is used by the settlement to keep a supply of war-dogs. It is a small cramp room, with no windows, and a grate as the east wall. The walls are scratched all around, probably made by the anxious dogs, lusting for freedom.
13228:
A large dog curls his lips back and snarls.
A swarthy Dunlending warrior is here, guarding his village against intruders.
A half wolf is here, loyally protecting his master.
A swarthy Dunlending warrior is here, guarding his village against intruders.
A swarthy Dunlending warrior is here, guarding his village against intruders.
A swarthy Dunlending warrior is here, guarding his village against intruders.

This is the entrance to the camps of some Dunlendings. Looking south, several crudely made huts can be seen spread out here and there; all facing the Village Circle, where meetings and general gathering take place. The Dun- lendings are a simple primitive people. They do not trust outsiders and are quick to resort to violence against intruders. It is often best to steer clear of them.
13229:
A small child is here playing happily.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.
A stocky mountain mule is here, waiting to serve.
A mother eagle flies high above looking for prey.
A mother eagle flies high above looking for prey.
A hungry warg (Rood) is standing here.

Leather skins line the walls on all sides of the small hut, keeping out drafts and other elements of bad weather. Through the thin cracks which formed between the outter plank lining of the hut, a small amount of light is able to penetrate the inside of the hut. Several beds made of leather padding and furs are crowded together, taking up most of the room.
13230:
The corpse of a Dunlending warrior is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending warrior is lying here.
The corpse of a half wolf is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending warrior is lying here.
A circular stone well has been built here.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.
Staub the Dwarf (SS), wielding a mighty dwarven axe, is standing here.
A great dark-grey horse stamps restively.
A horse of the Rohirrim (ulo) is standing here.

A small clearing in the camp serves as a meeting place for the Dunlendings. In the centre is a large fur lined chair raised on a small platform. This is the chieftain's private throne and from here he oversees the village meetings. Several worn-out leather mats fan out on both sides of the platform, completing a circle and providing seats to favourite soldiers of the chieftain.
13231: Leather skins line the walls on all sides inside the small hut, keeping out drafts and other elements of bad weather. Through thin cracks, formed between the outer plank lining of the hut, a small amount of daylight is allowed to penetrate the inside. Several beds, made of leather padding and furs, are crowded together taking up most of the room.
13232:
A huge, smoking campfire is burning here.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.

A large circular fireplace made of stones stands here in the open. Several pots are littered around the fireplace with remains of rabbit soup and roasted deer meat still inside. Large pieces of logs and slabs of dried cow dung are piled up near, ready to be fed into the hearth.
13233:
A large dog curls his lips back and snarls.
A chieftain of the Dunlendings stares at you with haughty contempt.
A small child is here playing happily.
A swarthy Dunlending warrior is here, guarding his village against intruders.
A swarthy Dunlending warrior is here, guarding his village against intruders.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.

The Chieftain's quarter is more elaborately decorated and spacious compared to the rest of the Dunlending camp. A large bed lined with rare white furs and soft leather sits at the far end of the room. Hung on the walls of the hut are personal trophies of the chieftain. The most noticeable trophy is a necklace made of brownish mountain-lion teeth in which each tooth represents proof of the renowned hunting abilities the chieftain possesses.
13234: A wooden chest stands in the corner.

This dark smelly room is crowded with weapons and tools of all shapes and sizes. Stacks of sharp flint tipped spears rest along the western wall. Slings made of soft leather hang in great bundles on nails hammered into the walls. Bows of different thicknesses lie against heaps of sharpened arrows with small stone tips. The flint-worker has been hard at work keeping this room well stocked with weapons.
13235:
A saddle lies here on the ground.
A great dark-grey horse stamps restively.

This good sized stall is the home of the most prized possesion of the Chieftain. It is large enough to almost provide running room for the beautiful steed that occupies it. The chieftain could not stand to have his favorite pet housed with the common horses of the clan, so he ordered this stall ... many sizes bigger than his own hut in fact ... to be built. Two double locked gates to the East and West allow entrance to this cleanly scrubbed stall.
13236:
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A brown donkey watches the surroundings, perhaps looking for a chance to graze.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

This medium sized enclosure serves as a stable for several horses. Each horse has its own individual stall, with a fresh water trough standing in front. Stacks of hay are line along northern wall of the pen, reaching almost all the way to the plank covered roof. A small double locked gate stands at the east wall. From here there is no way see what lies beyond the locked gate.
13237:
A cute, fluffy owlet pecks at some food on the ground.
A cute, fluffy owlet pecks at some food on the ground.
A large owl with small sharp horns looks cautiously around it.

This shallow cave seems to be the nesting place for some very large birds. A large nest takes up most of the space at the back of the cave, while bits of wood and twigs litter the front part, presumably extra nesting material if it is needed. The cave looks out over the valley through which the river Glanduin runs.
13238:
A tarnished arrowhead lies discarded on the ground.
A mass of vines entangles all who cross its path.

The fall of the northern wall has left what few pieces of this rampart that remain in a tenuous position. There is nothing other than the rubble of the wall to support this elevated ledge; it is apparent that a single misstep could bring what is here crashing down. At one time this rampart continued on to the east. That portion, however, appears to be completely destroyed. The only advantage to this position is its prime placement for viewing the Hollin Road which lies below, yet unreachable, to the north.
13239: A mass of vines entangles all who cross its path.

With the wall below destroyed, this narrow rampart is more of a badly decayed bridge than a sturdy passageway of this ancient city. The floor is cracked and in some places there are holes wide enough for a careless traveller to fall through. Loose stones from parts of the wall both above and below lay, untouched for centuries, covered in moss. Vines that start below have scaled their way up through the floor and attached themselves to both stone and other vines.
13240: Northwest Corner of a Broken Rampart

The rampart is rather sturdy here. It is snuggled into the wall corners and seems to have survived the brute force of whatever attack demolished the city. However, age has significantly worn the stones and moss grows heavily here along with vines.
13241:
A large black bat flitters near you.
A large black bat flitters near you.
A large black bat flitters near you.

This vaulted tower once held an enormous silver bell. A few strands of the ropes used to ring the bell still dangle overhead from the only remaining rafter. It runs from the northeast corner of where the roof once began to the southern edge of the eastern wall. Only the eastern wall is entirely intact. The northern and western walls are only half as high as they once were and the exposed edges continue to crumble. The southern wall is gone entirely giving an unobstructed view of the now overgrown city.
13246:
A small campfire burns here, its low flames giving off only a little light.
A tall, dark-haired elf is standing here (glowing).

Twisted metal rods that are bent and battered lie across the path. They appear to be part of a railing which cautioned travellers that down from this scenic walk way was the southern cliff and the rivers that lay beneath it. Now they serve little use. In fact, they only hinder passage on this overgrown path cut deep into the river bluff.
13247: A large, venomous-looking green snake is coiled up here.

Crumbling and overrun by bushes and shrubs, which have grown taller than some young trees, is the front facade of a single structure. Openings in this brick walling, most likely doors, indicate this building may have housed several families. What is left of the foundation slopes southward. The southern end of the slab is far more decayed that the northern. Below here is a meandering footpath and to the east a long abandoned walkway.
13248:
The corpse of a slithering snake is lying here.
A sly mongoose keeps an eye out for danger.

The two walls of a single structure is all that is left standing of what appears to have been a small development of homes. Less than six foundations in all, these homes seem to have been larger than those to the west judging by the distance between piles of stone rubble. Grasses that may once have been well kept lawns grow wild around and on top of the remains of this civilisation.
13249:
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.

Some venerable trees grow here in rows, equidistant from one another as they descend the hillside toward the south. Mounds of bricks, in piles numerous enough to each represent the fall of a small home, accompany each tree. The trees that look to have been planted by the homeowners now overwhelmingly surpass the ruinous foundations in both height and longevity.
13250: Greater parts of a broken weapon are lying on the ground.

This granite slab, more than a foot thick, is all that remains of this structure. The shape of the foundation shows it to be divided into four sections, most likely rooms. At the edge of one such section some writings are carved into the slab; the rest of the foundation is smooth. The walls appear to have been sliced off, in contrast to the structures to the west which have crumbed overtime. So little debris from the structure is left it seems as if this place was swept clean before being left to be overrun by vegetation. One can only imagine what type of weaponry could strip this structure away so completely. An overwhelming sweet smell emanates from several of the nearby flowering plants.
13251:
A shield, blackened by fire, lies on the ground.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

A stone hearth, and part of the wall that surrounds it, stands here almost completely obscured by large bushes and shrubs. Once part of a quaint elven home it now sits upon a shattered foundation. The roots of a large tree, that began as a tiny sprout growing between the cracks, have over time broken apart more of this home's foundation.
13252: This is the foundation of a small structure, only the arched framework of the entrance remains. Two modest cylindrical columns hold up a single rectangular granite block. A creeping ivy has grown up one of the columns, spread across and down the other. The entryway to this place is of very little consequence however, considering the walls of this structure are long gone; not a single granite brick remains. Amidst the plants that cover much of the foundation are a few shards of metal. Upon closer examination they appear to be bits and pieces of a silver sword. The blade is splintered beyond repair and only the hilt remains.
13253: This portion of the narrow footpath leads north to a large granite slab, from its size most likely the foundation of a small structure. In the shadow of the hillside above, the path looks dark as night with the exception of flakes of pulverised granite. Most likely the flakes are what is left of the granite bricks that would have formed the walls of the structure. Even through the sporadic grass, the way the granite flakes glisten in the moonlight preserves a certain amount of majestic nobility that was long ago vanquished. The path continues on to the east.
13254:
A small boar with big yellow tusks looks eager to fight.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

Running east to west this narrow avenue seems to be a means of passage through what appears to have been the garden district of this city. The path bends just briefly to the north before a large granite slab. Flakes of what looks to be the same type of granite are mixed into the dirt of this path giving it a marbleised or speckled appearance.
13255: Mixed in with the dirt and under the scramble of wild weeds tiny specks of granite chips can be seen embedded in a long ago well-travelled path. The flakes cover much of the ground even outside the bounds of the path but are more heavily concentrated to the north near the remains of a small home. The flakes seem to have been pieces of the granite bricks that once made up this humble abode.
13256: This narrow walkway carved into the side of the bluff seems to have been built on an angle just right for viewing the River Estelin to the south. The rushing waters sometimes weave a cool mist that in summer cool the air along the walkway. A few bars of iron are all that is left of what appears to be a guard rail that stopped onlookers from getting too close to the dangerous cliff. Centuries ago this would have been an easy stroll. Tough weeds have grown into large bushes that obstruct much of the path which leads westward.
13257: A small campfire burns here, its low flames giving off only a little light.

What twisted metal is left of a once dark wrought iron railing warns travellers of the steep drop to the south. Below in that direction lies the River Sirannon. The railing follows the length of this street until it ends most abruptly, like the land to the north, by falling piece by piece, and in this case cobblestone by cobblestone, into the river below. In places where the stones are all gone and the underlying dirt rinsed away by wind and rain one can see the cracks in the granite plate. The cracks seem to grow wider further to the north.
13258: Just like the land to the north, here too the remains of the city and the land on which it stood are falling over time into the River Sirannon which lies below to the east. Bushes and trees alike make futile attempts to dig their roots into the decaying soil of the bluff. Many trees have already met their demise falling into the fast flowing river along with crumbling blocks of granite that lay scattered in piles of four and five. Moss and fungus that thrive in such wet conditions have made the ground nearest the edge extremely slippery. Without warning the soil could shift under the feet of those peering over to catch a glimpse of the water below.
13259: At the Source of the Crack

Nothing is left standing at this point on the bluff, not the city wall nor the trees that grew years later in its place. Now even the small bushes of holly are falling into the river below to the east. All that survives is a thick covering of moss. At one time this area must have been more stable. Where all the dirt has washed away one can see deep cracks in the granite plate that lies under this entire area. Clearly this was not caused by a force of nature as the crack begins several yards in from the edge and spreads outward rather than cracking at the edge of the bluff where the land would have been naturally weaker. One could assume such a force intended the cracks to splinter further pulling everything that stood here for miles around slowly into the river.
13260:
The remains of a smothering mass of vines lie here in a heap of rotting compost.
The remains of a smothering mass of vines lie here in a heap of rotting compost.

The gargantuan vines that cover this area, making it almost impassable, seem to emanate from the west. Their widths range in diameter from the size of a wizards staff to that of the trunk of an ancient tree. They cling to dead trees no doubt strangled by the weight of these enormous tentacles. Using the trees as leverage they stretch up from the ground some thirty feet into the air. Some of the lower vines are marred with scratches that appear to have been made by a swift animal as it managed to negotiate the spaces between them. The scratches seem to have had a negligible effect on the rampant vines. The cuts are covered with a clear liquid, most likely sap from the healthy vines, creating a natural bandage over the exposed portions.
13261:
The remains of a smothering mass of vines lie here in a heap of rotting compost.
The remains of a smothering mass of vines lie here in a heap of rotting compost.

A few pieces of glass that look to be many centuries old lie on the ground outside a mostly obscured iron framework. The thick metal rods are twisted horribly out of shape but the frame is intact. The cause of this distortion is easily apparent; vines with some stems wider then the base of a well have sprouted out from inside what appears to have been a structure made completely of iron and glass. From the arrangement of the ruins and the variety of plant life, this must have been a place of cultivation, an arboretum of sorts. At one time it can be assumed these vines, along with other choice vegetation, were kept tame, pruned by their caretaker. Since their abandonment they must have first grown to the size of the structure and then over the ages as they gathered strength pushed outward expanding their habitat a great distance.
13262:
A mass of vines entangles all who cross its path.
A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.
A snake slithers towards you.

This area is entirely engulfed by a large system of vines. They grow thicker in the east and thin out slightly, in number and size, as they reach westward. So consuming are these monstrous vines that they have choked the life out of the trees; their heavy tentacles cover the branches in a serpentine manner, crushing any budding leaves before they can unfold. Nothing seems a hindrance to their rampant growth, not even the deep cuts in the portions that lay low to the ground. Most likely caused by the claws of a small swift animal able to sneak between the strands, sap quickly covers the cuts sealing the exposed area like a bandage.
13263:
The remains of a smothering mass of vines lie here in a heap of rotting compost.
The remains of a smothering mass of vines lie here in a heap of rotting compost.
A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

A wall, created by some enormous vines woven around and in between several dead trees, makes passage northward extremely difficult. Clearly the vines were the cause of the trees demise. So tightly wound around them are the tendrils of these vines that any new buds of life were quickly strangled leaving the tree with no leaves to gather what the trees needed from the sun. It is quite possible, as the vines continue to grow upward, that at some future point they will pull what remains of these trees to the ground. A few granite bricks can be seen buried deep under the vines covering the ground. Watchers with a quick eye might see the head or tail of some swift animals small enough to dart through these vines without becoming entangled. Their sharp claw marks are apparent on some of the larger vines.
13264: A sleek silver ferret darts from place to place.

It must have taken the weaponry of a great army to smash through this great city wall with such force as to push the bricks several yards across the city grounds. Not only did the wall separate at the spaces between the bricks but also shattered individual bricks at the point of impact. Much of the plant life that was once kept out of the city by the wall has breached the gap and now this place is more a continuance of the forest region than a city suburb. Creeping vines from the south have crawled over the widespread rubble.
13266: The sounds of the fast flowing River Sirannon seem to call the dirt from this bluff down into its depths. What destabilised this land is unknown, but it appears to have happened long ago, perhaps during the great war of Sauron and the Elves. Trees along the eastern edge, that have not yet fallen into the water, lean this same direction. Their roots desperately cling to the remaining soil. Moss and other fungi have flourished in this moist environment. A few scattered granite blocks remind visitors that there was once a great wall around this place. The crumbled remains of the wall along with what seems to be another structure blocks passage northward.
13267:
A holly bush with dark green leaves is growing here.
Partly covered by the bush's green leaves, there are a few inkberries.
A sly mongoose keeps an eye out for danger.
A snake slithers towards you.

Large thick bushes dominate this small square. In the centre is a large granite block which looks to have been the pedestal of a statue; only the feet of the figure remain. The knee-high base seems to have some writing etched into it. Outward from the statue, under the weeds and grass, are granite stepping stone paths leading outward in all four directions. Tall trees sporadically line the paths - some appear to be as old as Arda itself judging by their trunk size.
13268: Eight granite columns, as tall as some of the younger trees in this area, form a circle around this place. Several are chipped in many places but none of the pillars are broken or missing. Inside the circle formed by these towering granite spires are large stone steps descending down many feet to a central flat circular stone. The cascade of steps must have at one time surrounded the centre stone in all directions. Now, the eastern side is little more than a mix of dirt, weeds, and crumbled stone. On the northern side an entire section has been destroyed by a large fallen tree; it shattered each of the stone steps it landed upon from the highest down to just above the lowest. The southwestern part of this amphitheatre remains for the most part intact. A traveller with a passion for ancient history might consider sitting here upon the steps and imagining the great performances that once took place.
13269: A large dangerous looking green snake is coiled up here.

The variety and sheer number of plants, even in their unkempt and vastly overgrown condition, gives evidence that this may have once been a park. The roots of each seem equidistant from each other, contributing to the notion that they were planted and left to run rampant. Large horizontal stone blocks, both shattered and crumbling, frame this gathering area. The faint sound of rushing water can be heard emanating from the south.
13270: A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

A perfect vantage point from which to see down the sloping hillside to the south, the citizens of this city may have sat here watching the boats that at one time sailed along the river. Now, all that can be seen is the crumbling foundations where homes must have once stood and the overgrown footpaths not travelled for centuries. Some crystalline lattice work appears on the ground, a mix of glass and some unknown element. From the criss-cross design and the pattern of its destruction it is conceivable this was a large gazebo. A powerful sweet smell emanates from a large grouping of flowering plants that may have once been planted around this area. These now grow wild and cover much of the ground here.
13271:
A holly bush with dark green leaves is growing here.
Partly covered by the bush's green leaves, there are a few inkberries.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.
A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

A vast number of berry bushes cover this parcel of land. They seem to have grown unrestrained for centuries. Most are more than a story tall. The bushes mingled with wild grasses and vines form a small jungle nestled here within the ruins of the old city. A few bits of broken stone lie under all this greenery, hidden waiting to trip up weary travellers.
13272: Enormous pine, fir, and cedar trees arch in lush profusion over a scarcely recognisable trail winding in an east-west fashion from courtyard to gate. All save a few towering trees are draped in moss. Wildflowers and foliage blanket the ground in all directions. Just off the trail lies a slender stone beam broken in several places, perhaps the remains of a park bench.
13273:
A holly bush with dark green leaves is growing here.
A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.

Flowering plants that cover the entire spectrum of colours fill this forgotten place. The number of different varieties leads one to believe many of these plants are not native to this area. Probably imported for their beauty, left to run rampant some of the heartier bushes have clearly dominated this park setting making this area a small jungle of sorts. Through the jumble of greenery one can see the remains of a structure to the northwest. The grounds in that direction look more manageable.
13274: A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

Pieces of what seem to be an old stone marker are strewn among a variety of bushes and wild flowering weeds. Other slabs of stone, now crumbled to what appears to be a quarter of their original size, are arranged in two rows on either side of the markers' resting place. Moss covers much of the exposed stone and several stones are worn down to just a few inches above the ground. Perhaps these were benches upon which the residents of this city sat to reflect upon their days. Being located in a central spot of the eastern portion of the city this area gets a great deal of light except in the afternoons when, as the sun descends, it is blocked by the remains of a great tower to the west.
13276: A little stone lies on the ground.

Nestled under what looks to have been a rampart attached to the city wall all four walls of this building remain standing, although the roof is gone and the walls do not stand to their full height. The tops of each are crumbling from exposure to the elements not the ravages of war that destroyed the rampart above. The stone slabs here seem to been head and foot boards of beds stacked one upon the other. They were four beds high and there are almost twenty rows. None of the bedding remains and one might assume the slats on which the bedding had lain were made of a material that decayed over the ages. Judging from the narrow width and the elongated space from head to foot these clearly were the very modest resting places of the city guards.
13277: Large bricks, that once formed the walls of this tower, litter the ground. Only the north wall remains intact though badly eroded by the elements. Rubble piled almost as high as the walls that originally formed this tower are all that remains of the toppled walls to the south and east. Though badly damaged a stone stairway leading to the top of the tower remains; perhaps the fact that it was attached to the one surviving wall helped to preserve it. A large silver bell is on the floor, one side completely shattered. It looks to have fallen the great distance from the belfry above.
13278:
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

Mangled wrought iron, as black as the night sky, is all that is left of the fence that once stood between the cobblestone street to the west and what appears to have been a great eastern lawn dividing the city's two halves. It stood as a marker between the part of the city used as commerce and that part in which the citizens spent their leisure time. Now mostly obscured by vegetation it still serves as a means of division. The broken fence has an abundance of sharp edges that seem to catch anything passing by on the wind. Small shreds of clothing that appear to have been torn from the attire of present day travellers caution passage here might be painful.
13280:
A bright red mushroom is growing here.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

A dotting of trees and weeds growing waist high obscure the sharp spokes of wrought iron. This was once part of a great fence that divided the old city in two halves. Even against the dark colour of the metal shards one can see the stains of dried blood, pieces of cloth ripped from the clothes of latter day travellers, and animal fur. Passage over this tangle of iron and greenery might prove painful even to the most careful of beings. To the east, one can see nothing but wild weeds and moss covered trees and stone. The fencing seems to have ended here to the south. A pile of what appears to be wood lies here under a mass of mildew and fungus, home to a variety of mushrooms.
13281:
A tall, dark-haired elf is standing here (glowing).
A black raven flies in the sky searching for flesh to prey upon.

The cobblestone street to the north gives way to this winding walkway leading down and along the river bluff. Several stones from the street, over time, have found their way here to rest alongside the wild weeds and grasses. Whether this path ever contained similar stones is unknown. It is more likely that it was dirt or perhaps even gravel. It seems to have been designed more for aesthetics then usefulness. To the west or following the river walk downward one might get a better look at the confluence of rivers that border this high place.
13282: A tall, dark-haired elf is standing here (glowing).

Worn smooth with age and overgrown to the point of decay, this granite walkway travels up and down along the western rim of a large hillside basin. A mangled wrought iron fence, bent and twisted to the point of barbs, still prevents the careless passer-by from falling over the edge into the fast flowing river below.
13283: With the structures intact, this footpath was too small to traverse any way but single file. Whether it was planned or just good fortune, this served as an advantage slowing the attack of the encroaching army, perhaps long enough for some of the residents to escape. Overgrown with weeds, the path's dirt foundation contains a sprinkling of granite chips that might once have been part of the blocks that formed the hillside estates. It is quite likely that the forces that lay siege to this city for several years tired of negotiating this passageway and in turn decided to demolish the structures making passage easier. This would explain the fact that not even a single complete brick of granite can be found.
13284:
A crumbling fountain is in the middle of the place.
A holly bush with dark green leaves is growing here.
A mouse sniffs around, searching for a morsel of food.

This entire surrounding area resembles a shallow bowl. This parcel in the centre portion is rather flat. The base of what may have been an old fountain lies amidst a mass of flowering bushes. Trees ranging in age from before the cities founding to sapling just sprouting dot the landscape. A small area is sectioned off by a wrought iron gate. The gate now traps some small weeds grown into shrubs, however at one time it may have provided a safe play area for children keeping them far away from the rushing river not too far to the south.
13285: The granite flakes that create this paths speckled appearance lessen toward the south as it meets a weaving walk along the river bluff. Left abandoned and rarely travelled, trees have sprouted up where the residents once strolled. Wild weeds grow unrestrained yet this path survives even under the vegetation.
13286: Carved into the river bluff this sloping portion of the path does not offer quite as grand a view of the rivers as further down the walk to the south. In the mornings the abundance of water helps to weave a mist obscuring the wrought iron railing designed to keep travellers from getting too close to the edge. While the rail is broken and many sections are missing is still serves a cautionary purpose.
13287: The spectacle that is the confluence of the rushing rivers to the south and east can be best viewed here by standing close to a twisted iron railing. The white foam created by the meeting of the turbulent waters looks almost like a sea of clouds resting upon the waters. Much of the rail hangs down over the edge, teasing the swirling confluence of rivers below.
13288: This narrow walk travels along the outer rim of the sunken hillside. Carved high into the granite bluff here it meets a small footpath leading north. A mangled wrought iron railing coloured so dark it cannot be seen at night lines the southern edge of the walk. Perhaps the residents of this city did not walk this path after sunset or perhaps they had walked so many times admiring the rivers beauty they needed no rail to warn them of the bluff's edge.
13289: Specks of dirt and granite flakes, from the path to the north, have drifted down the hillside and cover the northern side of this narrow walkway. A large tree has fallen diagonally across the walkway and continues on to hang over the cliff to the south. Tangled in the branches are the remains of a wrought iron railing that once warned weary travellers of the abrupt edge. From its size the tree appears to be at least a thousand years old. An odd place for a tree to have grown so close, this one obviously took root and died all in the interim of time passed since this city's downfall.
13290: A wrought iron railing to the southwest and this once smooth walkway is the only evidence that this land was ever inhabited. This part of the walk is badly overgrown. The wild bushes block most of the walk and have entangled themselves in and around the railing obscuring it. The walkway continues up some overgrown and mildewed stone steps to the north and continues on eastward perhaps to better preserved areas of this kingdom.
13291:
A rotten corpse is hanging here.
A newborn spider is here.
A newborn spider is here.
A newborn spider is here.
A grey spider is stalking here, preparing to drain you of life.

Various fungi and spores flourish here covering every inch of the decaying foundation. Metal spools indicate that this might once have been a ropeworks. Being so close to the river it is quite possible this was a place to purchase and repair fishing nets. Perhaps the algae on nets that long ago dissolved into nothingness is what gave birth to the rampant mould.
13293: Perhaps this was once a beautiful, low-arched granite causeway which spanned the northern edge of the harbour down below. Through the ages, however, time has erased all of the grandeur it once held. Several thick stone support beams jut out irregularly to the side causing the bridge to lean precariously sideways, reminding the cautious traveller that too much weight here would not be prudent.
13294: Carved into the riverside bluff, this narrow path is bordered on the north by hillside and south by the rushing river. Even after centuries of abandonment, the path is still visible through the mass of weeds and clumps of dirt that have fallen from higher ground. From this point one cannot help but hear the rumbling river flow.
13295: Metal rods welded together to form the frame of a boat lay here, untouched for ages on the exposed foundation of this structure. Perhaps long ago a shipwright carefully built this boat here in his shop. He may have sat carefully fitting pieces of wood into the frame forming the curved base of a small sailing vessel. Wound on a metal stand are several lengths of chain accompanied by several anchors of varying sizes. Most of the metal chain has turned a bright, rusted amber colour.
13300: Southeast Corner of the Cobblestone Street

An entire section of stones is gone from this cobblestone street. The missing stones lie in a dishevelled pile along the eastern edge. This section of what appears to have been the city's main thoroughfare is one of the most badly damaged. Although most of the cobblestones remain in their places, they lie there shattered. The gaps left between them have allowed numerous sprouts of grasses and large weeds. The street carries on to the west to what looks to have been the centre of commerce for this city.
13301: This fragile precipice is only half intact. The eastern side has long ago fallen into the river below. A broken railing, made of black wrought iron, dangles off the edge reaching down several feet. Gazing over the edge to the west one can see water gushing from a chute in the bluff. The water must pass under this spot before cascading out in a great waterfall. The ground here vibrates from the pressure of the water's flow.
13302: Many of the cobblestones in this portion of the street are loose, allowing grass and extraneous flowering weeds to sprout between them. Moss grows rampant as well, flourishing in the moisture that has now been allowed to escape from below the once tightly aligned stones. In some places one must look straight down to even see the cobblestone street hidden under the greenery. In other spots there are piles of stones that have been pushed aside by the weeds, which have over time grown into large shrubs. The stones serve as a marker of the care that must have been taken to lay this mosaic-like street. Toward the south is an overlook that serves as a vantage point from which one can view the rushing water that can be heard from here.
13303: A colony of red ants is here. The ants seem to ignore you.

It is clear to see by the arrangement of the dirt coloured stones that whomever made up this street was a meticulous person. Even after thousands of years one can still see that the natural stones were carefully sorted by size before being placed in almost perfect rows. Many of the stones are chipped by what could have been the careless marching of an army through this street. Whatever chipped these stones no one remained behind to repair or replace them.
13304:
A tarnished arrowhead lies discarded on the ground.
A sly mongoose keeps an eye out for danger.

Only a very small portion of these chipped stairs are climbable. Most are so badly crumbled that any weight would cause them to practically disintegrate. Looking carefully a route can be plotted, skipping a step here and there, to take someone from this point at the base to the level above. Trying to picture their original state, one can see that these steps served a decorative purpose. The elongated widths and gentle slope create a notion of grandeur rather than expedience of use or simple functionality. Ending at the first step is the cobblestone street that encircles what is left of this part of the city. Looking down one might be mesmerised by the lack of change in the pattern of stones making up this street. While it makes some rather sharp turns continuing on in three directions, it is difficult to discern where the stones turn so that the rows of stones on each street all go the same direction.
13305: This piece of the cobblestone street must have seen a lot of traffic before this city's tragic end. Along the passageway between the city gate and the steps leading to the cultural centre of the city the stones bear the marks of horses hooves as well as age. Several stones are missing, perhaps shattered and their remains blown away. In the holes that remain wild weeds and grasses have shot up in their place.
13306: Cobblestone Street beside an Iron Railing

There is a wrought iron railing that closely follows along the southern section of the carefully laid cobblestone street. Twisted and broken in places, it still serves its purpose of warning travellers that a river lies several feet below. The sound of rushing water breaks the monotonous silence of this now dead city. Stepping close to the rail one can see a rising mist and feel the occasional spray of water. To the north appears to be an entrance to the lower portion of the ruined city.
13307:
An ancient fungus smothers the boulders.
An ancient fungus smothers the boulders.

Totally encompassed in mould and mildew, and left to fester over centuries, this entire room gives off a putrid smell. Even the fiercest of creatures would be humbled by this abominable muck. A long stone countertop that may have once lain atop a wooden counter now lies in pieces on the floor. One can only guess this may have been a grocery of some sort. The door to the south opens up on to the city's cobblestone street. A stairway leading up may have been a means of supplying produce to the restaurant above.
13308: The cobblestone street carries on both to the east and west. This section has withstood the centuries well; only a few stones are chipped. In one place several granite blocks, apparently once part of the structure to the north, have fallen with such great force through the cobblestones that they have imbedded themselves deeply into the granite plate below. There is the sound of rushing water from the confluence of the rivers Estulin and Sir Lontalaith, it breaks the deafening silence that echoes through this city which was long ago vanquished.
13309: The city street extends like a shelf over the edge of the bluff. Looking over the mangled wrought iron rail to the east one can see a thick spray of water gushing from a chute some thirty feet below. So fast does the water flow out from the bluff that its spray can be felt even here. It crashes into the water below creating a rising mass of foam. Below and to the south and west are equally fast flowing rivers.
13310: Southwest Corner of the Cobblestone Street

This quiet corner of cobblestone street is bordered on the west side by what is left of the old city wall. It stretches at least two stories high and protects this area from the forest on the other side. The branches of some very tall trees can be seen peering their way over the crumbling wall. In several places lower tree limbs have pushed through the wall knocking out blocks that were already weak with age. To the south is a mangled portion of wrought iron railing. The railing is too weak to hold anyone back from falling into the water below, but still serves as a warning sign of the steep drop.
13311: In the morning the light of the sun against what is left of the tower above to the east looks as if it would cast a dark shadow over this piece of street. The city wall to the west is completely destroyed. The blocks of granite have crumbled one upon another the weight of each serving to further crush one another. Once two stories high, in its current ruinous state it still serves to protect the city from the outside world. Only a few spaces just large enough for small animals to negotiate break the isolation.
13312:
A wild dog bares his yellow fangs at you.
A wild dog bares his yellow fangs at you.
A wild dog bares his yellow fangs at you.
A wild dog bares his yellow fangs at you.
A wild dog bares his yellow fangs at you.

Weeds have forced their way past the stones that form this street. Long abandoned, no one remained to pull the green sprouts as they first emerged. The tight arrangement of the stones by the street's builder, however, has kept the weeds small. Rather than overtaking the street they are limited to the spaces between the stones that have formed throughout years of neglect.
13313: A large owl with small sharp horns looks cautiously around it.

There is a large piece of soot covered granite wall that protrudes through the ceiling of this room. Narrow stone shelves that once lined the walls now lay broken on the ground, knocked lose by a sharp impact. The entire western wall has been pushed into this room leaving the exit west completely exposed. Dirt from the street has collected against the eastern wall. Some worn stone steps lean upward.
13314: A piece of the wall that surrounded this city stands three stories above the old cobblestone street. In most places the wall is just rubble, though still high enough to protect what is left of this place. Here one can see the granite bricks arranged one on top of the other in a clover design with one central brick and four of a similar shade of granite on each of its sides.
13315: Northwest Corner of the Cobblestone Street
A colony of red ants is here. The ants seem to ignore you.

This is the northwest corner of the once great city of Ost-in-Edhil. The tall city wall that ran along the north and down the western boundary has fallen inward here blocking half the street. The piles of granite blocks though no longer neatly arranged one on top of the other still serve to protect the city from the surrounding forest land. A small portion of wall still standing shows the meticulous care its builders took in the perfect arrangement of light and dark stones. Where the granite blocks have fallen the cobblestones are completely shattered.
13316: The cobblestones that make up this street are each about the length and width of an elven hand. They must have been carefully laid stone by stone over the course of many months. The dirt coloured stones lie one hundred across, setting the width of the ancient street. So close are they placed together that even after all these centuries very few sprouts of grass have pushed there way between the stones. To the south beside the remains of one of the city structures is a stone cart. Too heavy itself to have been used for carrying things from place to place it was most likely just for show.
13317: A small centipede is here scurrying about.

Rubble from both the old city wall and large pieces of granite which have fallen from the structures above combine and almost completely block this portion of street. Passage is possible only by walking close to the south along the ruins of an old shop as the rubble concentrates to the northern portion of the street. Though the arched doorway is partly obstructed, entrance to the shop looks possible. Hinges attached to the stone give evidence of perhaps a wooden door that has long ago decayed into nothingness. Above the door etched into the stone is some writing.
13318:
A rusty pickaxe with a broken handle lies discarded here.
A swarm of hornets is coming out of its nest.

A mess of pulverised stone along with battered and broken pieces of metal block off half this room. Behind the rubble, out of reach, is a large blackened anvil accompanied by the heads of several hammers. The wooden handles must have decayed long ago. Large brass hooks embedded into the crumbling walls look strong enough to have held shields and pieces of armour. What is here now, for the most part, is completely useless.
13319: Several rows of cobblestones have fallen down into what seems to be a large crater. Stretching out of this hole is a large granite spire stabbing deep into the ground like an ancient sword piercing the earth. Its base is cracked and crumbling while the spire itself remains smooth, narrowing in width as it enters the ground. Looking skyward one can see this was once the crowning jewel of the tower that stands at the centre of these ruins. From the blunt nature of the cracks in the granite, it is apparent that this decapitation was not the result of the towers age but rather caused by a deliberate act of aggression.
13320:
Little parts of a broken weapon are lying on the ground.
A brown snake watches you.

The shimmering copper gates that once both welcomed and forbade entry into this ancient city have turned green, corroded over time. The carved hinges from which they once must have swung open with ease now barely support the small piece of the gate that still hangs upon them. The rest of the gate lies on the ground in splintered fragments as if knocked down by a great force. Beginning here and carrying on westwards is a cobblestone street possibly leading to the barely visible remains of the city.
13321: As you step off the edge of the tower ruins you feel a momentary euphoria comparable to flying before you plummet downward.
13322:
A tarnished arrowhead lies discarded on the ground.
A nest is here.
A mother eagle flies high above, looking for prey.
A small, helpless eaglet screams for more food.
A small, helpless eaglet screams for more food.

Not only has the roof been sheared off the top of this tower, but two of this upper chamber's walls are completely gone as well. The remaining walls, south and west, are not much more than piles of cracked and crumbling granite bricks. Even after centuries of decay scoring on the bricks is a monument to the weapons of destruction launched against this once fair city. One can imagine the high elves standing before the now severed rectangular windows observing the day to day activities all over the city.
13323: As you step off the edge of the tower ruins you feel a momentary euphoria comparable to flying before you plummet downward.
13324: A large oval-shaped table made of granite has fallen off two of its four legs and splintered a portion of the floor. Piles of dust surrounding the table look to be the remnants of many wooden chairs broken down by the elements. Two large silver hooks are embedded into the northern wall, much like the sets of smaller hooks above windows throughout this tower. However here no windows exist. It is quite possible these hooks once held up a grand tapestry.
13325: Worse to the west than in other directions, the plaza tiles are badly damaged. While age has clearly taken its toll on these exposed slabs of granite most of this damage seems to be the ravages of war. The facade of the shop to the west has been breached in several places as if the small shop took the more of the attackers energy than the rest of this area.
13326: In the Shadow of the Citadel
A mouse sniffs around, searching for a morsel of food.

Even in its ruinous condition the once four-story citadel casts a wide shadow over the plaza below. Only in the very early hours of the morning does sunlight shine on this eastern side of the great tower unobstructed. By noon the lack of light hides the vast damage to the two-tone granite tiles that make up the plaza grounds. To the west is a great doorway made wider by what must have been some uninvited guests using powerful weaponry.
13327: A mouse sniffs around, searching for a morsel of food.

Thick granite tiles, a mix of light and dark, lying shattered on the ground were once a part of this plaza ground. So severely damaged are the once smooth polished tiles that they are now little more than flakes of rock holding tenuously on to their position as part of a grand checkerboard design. The patterned tiles end at the doorways of several crumbling structures. Bricks made of a similar granite, fallen over centuries from the citadel above, lay scattered about.
13328: Iron rods twisted into floral designs form at least twenty tables and numerous chairs that are scattered all over this enclosure. It is clear they were carefully constructed for outdoor use. There is no sign they were ever adorned by fabric or upholstery yet they look to have been quite comfortable. Part of what seems to have been an outdoor cafe, these ancient furnishings have withstood the centuries. A wall half as high as the ones that form this room obscure what is left of a stone stairway leading downward.
13329:
A small metal shield is on the ground.
A mouse sniffs around, searching for a morsel of food.

Almost two stories high, this single room must have once welcomed many honoured guests to this centre of elven culture, and some very unwelcome ones. The meticulously etched silver doors lie far against the western wall, severely battered. The doors were hit so hard that several feet of the surrounding wall was knocked in with them. A chandelier of hand blown glass has long ago fallen from its high perch and shattered in a million tiny shards all over the floor. A winding stair attached to the southern wall leads up toward this structure's crest.
13330: A single stone counter lays cracked here upon the floor amidst layer upon layer of the dusty remains of wood and shattered glass cases. A variety of small ornate stone boxes together with the shattered glass showcases give evidence that this was a jewellery shop. This place seems to have been violently torn apart. Every brick making up the walls has been punctured or cracked in the middle, as if someone was looking for a hidden compartment or chamber. Even the bricks in the floor have been searched. With the amount of force used to break these stones it's amazing that the floor has not collapsed. The walls have not withstood the destruction and ages so well; to the north and south they only stand half their original height.
13331: A crack in the ground emanating from the east ends here in a sunken crater several feet wide. Many of the alternating dark and light coloured granite tiles that make up this plaza's surface have over the centuries fallen into this hole. Scoring on the surrounding stone and along the crack gives evidence of a great impact of a deliberate nature.
13332: Resting Place of the Toppled Tower
Several shards of broken glass lie scattered about the ground.

What looks to be the top of the citadel above has found a new home after crashing through the ceiling of this small shop. Only two walls of the shop remain even partially intact. This portion of stone tower that fell from the sky was so heavy that not only did it destroy everything left inside here but it also pierced the floor leading to the room below. There is no way to discern what type of wares this place once sold. Judging by the amount of shattered glass that litters the ground, whatever it was must have been in liquid form.
13333: Covered in the debris of falling bricks from the citadel above one can barely discern the alternating light and dark granite tile design that cover this ancient plaza. Whole sections of the tower above in the form of crumbling stone fell upon this area with such great force they are embedded a foot into the ground. Tiny flakes of granite float up in the air on the occasional gusts of wind.
13334: Three vertical bookcases containing a vast amount of both horizontal and vertical storage areas stand here, looking as sturdy as the granite walls that form this room. Etched out of granite themselves, with decorative accents around each section, they were designed to showcase, store and protect the manuscripts, tomes, and sketches that described the art of the elven smiths. Whereas at one time each leaf of paper must have been carefully filed, its proper place annotated by small letters carved into the bookcase, now all is a shambles. Shreds of paper line the floor and not a single book or scroll remains on the ornate shelves.
13335: This hallway's etched columns, like the arched entranceway to this wing, showcases the grandeur and elegance of this place crafted by its elven inhabitants. More artful than functional, this large hall's only purpose is to provide entry to the northern vault and the library to the south. Every detail from the carved mouldings that line the floor to the stone picture frames carved into the walls shows how important it was for the Gwaith-i-Mirdain to spare no effort and settle for nothing less than perfection in their crafts.
13336: A black spider crawls here, a shiny red spot visible on its belly.

Steel shelves of varying depths protrude from the north and east walls. The west wall is lined with hooks of adequate size to hold metal shields. Looking closer at the shelves one can see threads of material, seeming to have been torn from silken cloths. Under foot are the bashed and battered remains of what might have once been considered an impenetrable metal cabinet's doors. Some great force seems to have sent them sprawling giving the intruders access to the many small sections of this vault. They stole whatever was contained ripping the silken cloths that covered the smaller swords and ornaments.
13337: A sleek silver ferret darts from place to place.

A meticulously carved granite arch forms the entrance to this wing of the underground halls. Higher than could be reached by two elves, one standing on the other's shoulders, it has remained undisturbed since its construction. This arch is supported by the same squared granite spires that support the domed ceiling. It must have taken careful work to carve such a ceiling out of the solid granite bluff while preserving the strength needed for the bluff to support the city above. Everything about this place is a work of art. Those that built these halls must have taken great pride in each detail.
13338: An obsessed man searches the surroundings (hidden).

Inside an arched granite frame sit two formidable tall bronze doors. Left unpolished for centuries the metal is discoloured in a few places. While the deep carvings that accent these doors draw some attention, far more noticeable here is the lack of a door handle of any sort. In the place of a handle, on the right door, seems to be an oval shaped recess with some elven runes carved into the door around the opening. Turning away from the doors one can see the large columns that run the course of this great hall and hear the rush of water from the water wall to the northwest.
13339: In the Presence of the Eldar

An arrow lies on the ground.
An arrow lies on the ground.
An arrow lies on the ground.
An arrow lies on the ground.

Along the smooth granite wall to the south are three large statues of Noldor elves. Equally spaced from one another they are all similar in size and none is given more importance than the others are. The carefully carved features showcase the work of a master sculptor. Each figure is carved in full attire with sheathed sword and crested shield lying at their feet. The writings etched in pedestals, apparently the names of these three, read Finwe, Ingwe and Elwe. Some smaller writing appears on the eastern wall.
13340: Slight splashes of water from the harnessed geyser to the west have moistened the floor. The cascade of white water rises with great force, hitting the domed ceiling above and falling back down upon its source. It forms a wall of water that is quite a marvel to behold. The elves through a feat of engineering have manage to harness this underground water source as it shot up toward the surface and redirected it so it not only could not continue its ascent but also was aesthetically pleasing to them.
13341: Like its counterpart corner to the west, this partial granite column fills the gap where the north and east walls would meet. Its smooth round surface seems to have been polished to a flawless shine. The column portion rests upon an etched pedestal that along with the walls supports its weight. About eye level up the column is a floral etching that when examined closely appears to in fact be some elven runes written in a way as to conceal themselves. A light mist of water fills this area, emanating from the fountain water wall nearby.
13342: The granite tile floor, once polished to a perfect reflective surface so that not a single pore remained to collect the water here, is not well preserved. Looking up one can see a small crack in the dome above used to channel the water downward. So precise is this water design that the small crack has misguided the flow and allowed some of the water to fall on the floor here wearing it down over centuries of abandonment and neglect.
13343: A tremendous thrust of water current propels you up into the domed granite ceiling with such force that it shatters every bone in your body.
13344: One quarter of a carved column sticks out in place of what would be the sharp edge of two walls meeting. A meticulously etched pedestal at the base of the platform along with its position in the corner space supports the solid granite column's weight. Some markings carved at eye level seem to be runes but the etchings are so fanciful these could easily be mistaken for decorative flourishes.
13345: A light spray of water from the wall of water to the east keeps this narrow ledge moist. The vertical stream shoots up from a forceful geyser below, crashes into the domed roof above and cascades back down upon its source. Other than the misty spray, the precise curvature of the roof keeps the surrounding areas dry. Looking downward over the edge of this shelf, one can see nothing but foamy white water.
13346:
An arrow lies on the ground.
An arrow lies on the ground.
An arrow lies on the ground.

Two tall stately silvery doors sit inside an arched frame in the western wall. A bit tarnished with age, the base of the doors shows some rust from the moisture in the air and a lack of polishing. Even more noticeable than the carvings in the thick doors is the fact they are missing any semblance of handles. In the place of a handle, on the left door, seems to be an oval shaped recess with some elven runes carved into the door around the opening. Turning away from the doors one can see the large columns that run the course of this great hall and hear the rush of water from the water wall to the northeast.
13347: A sleek silver ferret darts from place to place.

The sight to the north dominates this entire room. What appears to be a wall made of water blocks passage northward. Looking down you see the water shoots up through the floor and with an enormous thrust hits the domed ceiling above. The curvature of the ceiling then forces the water back downward in a mass of cascading waterfalls. Some water has escaped this feat of elven engineering and lays still upon the floor.
13348: This is the entrance point into the grand underground hall. The hall itself is as extraordinarily ornate as it is enormous. Columns more than three elves tall and about half as wide give support to the ceiling. They form two horizontal rows dividing this vast hall into several sections. Where the arched ceiling meets the smooth granite columns are elaborate etchings, some with carefully applied gold leaf laid so thin it cannot be scraped off. Each column is adorned with a decorative vine pattern in a serpentine arrangement from top to base. The hall, complete with its own large mural size etched patterns, stretches out in all directions.
13349: In the Presence of the Valar

The eight greatest of the Valar are represented here in statue, four along the southern wall and three along the western and one in the corner. In order stand Manwe, Varda, Ulmo, Yavanna, Aule, Mandos, Nienna and Orome. Though Manwe was held to be the High King of Arda his statue is no larger than that of the others, showing all eight were held in equal reverence. However, the statue of Aule stands at an angle in the corner with stone benches at either side. Perhaps this was done because Aule is the Vala concerned with the substance of Arda, rocks, metals, and minerals, endearing him to the elven smiths.
13350: Threshold to the House of Mirdain

An arrow lies on the ground.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Starting with a single narrow step, this stairway increases in width as it sweeps down gently northward to the hall below. Above the top step, engraved in the granite archway, are some elven runes etched so smooth each letter appears to flow into the next. The steps, so well constructed they still look polished, have well stood the ages. This place is, however, not without its scars. Sharp cuts in the steps and slices in the walls give evidence a great duel was fought. No doubt these had to have been mythical swords to be able to penetrate the stone in such a fashion. The fine silver banister, running the length of the stairs on both sides, is misshapen in a way that suggests a mighty warrior may have fallen upon it.
13351: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Several broken stone bookcases lie on their sides having been knocked down against the west wall. Elven words carved in some rounded stone posts that once stood at the end of each bookshelf seem to denote an ancient filing system. Lying on the floor are the remains of several stone boxes about the size of a large journal. It would have taken a rather strong person to have lifted these heavy stone containers high enough to have cracked them open against the floor exposing the manuscripts inside. Brown flaky dust covers the floor along with some small brass fasteners, apparently all that is left of this library's contents, eroded into nothingness over the course of centuries.
13352:
A black spider crawls here, a shiny red spot visible on its belly.
A mouse sniffs around, searching for a morsel of food.

Broad black smears cross the barren walls of this once great vaulted chamber of antiquities. When the sun or moon is aglow, bars of light cast through rents in the walls making motes of dust glitter throughout. Scorch-marks mar the walls, the floor, the ceiling. Shattered display cases of iron and glass litter the hall. It appears that whatever great heirlooms may have been housed here were looted long ago. A formidable stone staircase angles both upwards to the room above and twists downward to the room below.
13353: This hall with its high ceiling and ornate granite arches serves little function other than allowing entrance into the chamber to the west. A small granite bench, perhaps long enough to seat two elves, is pushed against the eastern wall. One could assume that those having business with or being called before the Gwaith-i-Mirdain were often kept waiting in this place. To the east are two extremely tall silver doors. Large murals cover the north and south walls.
13354: This square chamber lies between two sets of grand doors at the north and south. The granite walls stand like curtains between sets of large carved columns. The wall is constructed so it appears to be dividing the columns so only half of each can be seen within this room. The high domed ceiling carved out of the bluff above contains a beautiful painted mural that even time and the condensation of this moist underground has not damaged.
13355: Five large, elegant chairs of stone adorned with silver and gold are arranged in a semi-circle along the northern wall. Large hand blown glass chandeliers hang down in two long columns running north to south along the granite ceiling. The luminescence, though dimmed with age, is still rather brilliant leading one to believe they burn with a magical fire. A royal blue carpet runs the length of the chamber, from the entrance all the way up to the throne chairs.
