14356: This clearing is on a small rise, surrounded by wetlands to the east and a line of alder trees to the north. There is a small smoke pit built here, with signs of recent use, and a wooden shanty to the west. Apparently, someone has made a permanent camp here.
14357:
A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.
A duck is here, quacking happily.

The ground here is soaked, almost as a swamp in parts. Large pools of water lie everywhere, with tall reeds sprouting like pointing fingers. Dry land is still the majority, but even there the water squelches out of every footprint. The pools do not appear to be deep at least, and should not impede any traveller other than wetting their ankles. West the land rises and dries out, while east the pools of water become more abundant.
14358: A small oaken table has been set here.

This tiny shack was built in a hurry, with pieces of wood in different stages of decay. There are several holes in the wall, where the wood does not line up. The floor is made of dirt, and there is only a small table with trash piled upon it. In one corner there is some musty hay, which must be the bed. At least the roof is sound, since the floor is mostly dry.
14359: A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.

Large pools of water have overtaken the land here. There are hardly any dry patches left. Tall reeds abound, bordering the pools and restricting your view. The water is more like a shallow lake than dry land in parts, complete with the splashing of fish and the croaking of frogs.
14360:
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

Dry land is scarce here, although even there the earth is muddy and saturated with water. Tall, green reeds of grass with brown tips grow in large clumps along the edges of the shallow water, limiting your view. The water itself is stagnant, unmoving except in the wake of some small animal swimming.
14361:
An arrow lies on the ground.
A pigeon is strutting around here.
A duck is here, quacking happily.

Here the earth is largely below water, with only the tops of the grass and cattails sticking up out of a constant foot of water. The tips of the grass seem to make little islands in the water, but it is an illusion - there is no dry land here. North some giant thick brush mingles with the reeds to form an impenetrably tangled barrier, while east the water runs into a small pond in the plains.
14362: A slender plant grows here, with clusters of tiny pink flowers atop its stem.

The ground here is covered in shallow pools of stagnant, murky brown water. The muddy ground in-between sinks slightly, trying to swallow those who treads upon it. Clumps of reeds appear here and there, creating secluded nesting places for wildlife. North there is an abandoned way-station atop a small hill, which once housed a guard post and an inn for travellers on the Great South Road. To the south water trickles out of these wetlands and on through the plains in a small stream.
14363:
A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.
A swallow flies high above the ground.

Little more than a streamlet dribbling through the dustlands, this tiny line of water is one of many tributaries to the Isen, which it feeds into far south of here. It draws its waters from the wetlands around the Old South Road and, skirting around the edges of the hill, carries on through the plains. The water looks unclear, a little coloured by the soil maybe, but perfectly drinkable.
14364: Born from the wetlands a few miles north of here, this little stream is one of many tributaries to the mighty Isen a long way distant. Somehow it trickles and dribbles its way that far through the seemingly flat plains, pushed onwards by the constant flow of rainwater. It has some practical uses too, as a source of water for the Dunlending camp atop the hill just north of here. Every morning large amounts of water are collected onto a wheeled contraption, then hauled up the extremely steep southwestern hillside with a long rope and many horses.
14365: Miles of gently undulating plains are the norm in southern Enedwaith, and here is no exception. The nearest break in that pattern is a low flat hill several miles northwards. Even more distantly lie the White Mountains, on the horizon to the southeast, so named for their snow-capped peaks. Even at this distance their size is obvious; up close they must be truly towering. Just east of here a small trail picks its way through the terrain without trouble, one of the multitude of Dunlending paths that criss-cross these lands.
14366: These long plains are part of the huge upland of Enedwaith, which stretches between the great rivers of Greyflood on the borders of Eregion, and the Isen, still a long way south of here. Mostly they are uninhabited, with an occasional smattering of isolated Dunlending towns here and there. One of those towns can be seen a few miles north of here, atop a low flat hill. A path runs south from there, passing by just east of you, and continuing south until it passes out of your eyesight.
14367: The land is flat all around, for almost as far as the eye can see. The only exception is the faint impression left on the southern horizon by the White Mountains. Just east of here a small path runs north to south, but it too is subsumed into the plains, disappearing over both horizons. Quite possibly it is as much of a landmark as a path, as it would seem to be rather easy to get lost amongst the immensity of flat land, without any other landmark as a guide.
14368: A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Like a dotted line, infrequently marked by little white stones, this path makes its way across the flatlands. It appears to have no obvious end either to the north or south, stretching to both horizons and beyond. Underfoot it is merely well-trodden earth, with the ruts of wheelmarks and hooves visible. Far away to the southeast lie the White Mountains, the only feature on the landscape. All else is merely the plains of Enedwaith, stretching out endlessly.
14369: Like a smooth lawn the plains stretch out here, the grass little more than a tiny coverlet underfoot. The occasional sign of wildlife can be seen, with the burrows of small creatures and the droppings of larger ones. Eastwards the land becomes slightly less smooth as it approaches the downs, while west a path runs south to north. South the plains continue as far as you can see, without end it would seem.
14370: Not much of a feature these downs, but in comparison with the flat plains they do stick out. Covered with knee-high bushes, and a few clumps of trees, they are home to most of the wildlife in this part of the lands . It is probably not surprising to find that the locals hunt here, and indeed the Dunlendings of the nearby towns can be found here most months of the year. Some hunting paths wind over and around the downs, obviously frequently used.
14371: A swallow flies high above the ground.

Straddling a wide upturn of terrain between two deep fissures, the downs find themselves in a strange position. North and south the land is steadily eroding away, as the rainwater gathering in pools at the bottom eats away at the rocky cliffsides. Still, there is a large swathe of downs left, half a mile wide, and seems to be thriving. The ground it is based on must be quite fertile, as it is covered in lush grass and countless varieties of small bush.
14372: A brown furry gopher is here, ready to dive back underground.

The land rises up here slightly, then collapses into a yawning fissure to the south. Far too steep to descend down into, it is rather out of place in these normally flat plains. Across the fissure the grasslands continue as before, rolling onwards to the base of the White Mountains. Some distance to the east of here a path can be glimpsed, going north to south. It isn't the largest trail to be found though, and you cannot see where it might be going.
14373: A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.

Long ago, when it was the link between Arnor and Gondor, the South Road was frequented by countless merchants, soldiers and many other travellers. The watering holes every few dozen miles were essential for the long trek through Enedwaith, where dozens of miles can go between natural sources of water. This one has lost most of the brickwork, but it is still easy to see the form. It is a circular well, ten feet across, made from huge cubes of stone. Somehow the engineers of old managed to determine where the water was most likely to flow underground, an art long lost.
14374: Cracked stones pave the road, crumbled away in places to expose the smaller foundation stones below. Still, the skill of the makers can be seen, as the raised camber of the road allows rain to run off in parts. A small path leads away south from the road, leading to a ruined well in the plains, built long ago to quench the thirst of travellers. Endless plains stretch away from the road, away northeast to the snow-capped peaks of the Misty Mountains, and south to the foothills of the White Mountains.
14375: Crumbling Remains of the South Road

The remains of the Great South Road lie here, little more than a line of strewn stones running through the plains. Occasionally a larger uncracked flagstone can be seen amongst the rubble, smooth as the day it was laid. Mostly however the remains are a hindrance rather than an aid to travel, and quicker passage through the lands could be made by travelling through the plains either side of the road. Not far northwest of here the road crosses the wetlands on a raised causeway, or what remains of it.
14376: An Elevated Point in the Plains

Not quite a hill, this small rise offers a good view of the land nearby. It is covered in wild wheat and hay, about waist-height, with the sounds of various animals rustling about in the growth. To the north there is a great deal of farmland in the fertile plains, while south-west a town is visible atop a low, flat hill. Along the south and west of this rise run the remains of an old road.
14377: Not long ago these fields must have been a good source of wheat but now they have been abandoned and grow grass and hay, with a few small bushes giving some variety to the terrain. The ground slopes upwards south to a small rise in the plains, the ancient road skirting by to the south-west.
14378:
A black-haired farmhand is here.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

There are several fields here, all different grazing areas. This is to ensure the various farm animals don't wander into a field which is off rotation. Along the fences there are troughs, where the animals get fresh water. In some of the fields there are patches of wildflowers, but mostly they have been trampled. To the west beyond the gate is a paddock, on the south side of the farm.
14379:
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.

This paddock is enclosed by a small wooden fence, built to stop the animals from wandering. The ground is covered with short grass, recently grazed. There are several fields within the fence, some closed off so that the vegetation can regrow. Some troughs line the barn wall, filled with water. Outside the fenced area are fields that are no longer planted.
14380: Close to the north there is a wooden fence, and beyond it a small farm. Here the ground is covered with hay and small flower beds. Sometimes the hay moves rapidly as if there were something big moving amongst the grain, but it is an illusion of the wind. In the sky, several birds can be seen surveying the land below for prey, as it is abundant with wildlife. Directly south of here runs an old road, a barely surviving line of stones.
14381: A hungry warg (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

The road here was made with great attention to detail. One can see that the builders placed each of the flagstones next to each other with precision, even though time has taken its toll. Their workmanship can still be seen though, in the straight line of its route, and the little dikes that drain water. The land to the north of this great road is mainly gentle rolling plains before the main mountain range far to the north.
14382: A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.

Once this road ran all the way from Osgiliath in the south, to Annuminas in the north, passing through countless lands. All along its length it was paved, and constructed level and true for swift travel. This wonder of engineering was built by the Numenoreans to link the two kingdoms, and saw much traffic in its heyday. Since the destruction of Arnor near on a millennium ago, its use has dropped to nothing, and unmaintained it has fallen into disrepair. Nowadays most travellers will spurn the crumbled causeways upon which the road mounts to the northwest, preferring to skirt around the edges of the wetlands.
14383:
A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.
A black and white skunk is scuttling about here, searching for food.

Like the land of Rohan to the east, the plains of Enedwaith have little more than gentle undulations. This particular area is slightly wetter than the norm though, with frequent pools of stagnant rainwater to be seen all around. Just north of here the Old South Road was built half an age ago, raised up slightly on a causeway to protect it on the rainier days. The only other noticeable landmark nearer than the distant mountains is a Dunlending town atop a long flat hill, several miles to the northwest.
14384: A faint shift in the terrain is apparent here, almost like a borderland. South the plains roll by in irregular waves, whereas north the grasslands are as flat as a still pond. Threading through the heather are infrequent hunting paths, often faint and easy to lose. Mostly the only one through is to trample over the soft two foot heather. Although easy on the feet, it's a wearying way to travel.
14385: Like ocean waves the grassy downs roll over the land, covered in parts with great swathes of soft heather. Here and there the small hunting trails of the Dunlendings can be seen, used as frequently by those on four legs as those on two. Occasionally you come across a small camp, well hidden by the undulating landscape - obviously well used, someone must live off this land. Far to the east the downs give way to grey barren plains, where broken stone protrudes through the earth.
14386: This is just another small camp, like many the Dunlendings have built in these lands. The hunting is excellent around here, with small rabbits, voles and foxes in the heathery downs east of here, and much larger game - deer and some elks - to be found in the open plains. Around the campfire here the Dunlendings can be found most nights, boasting of their exploits and slugging down their coarse beer.
14387:
An arrow lies on the ground.
An arrow lies on the ground.
A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Straight north to south across the wide plain goes this path, from the large Dunlending town of Wulfston to the crossing points on the Isen far south. Here it passes by a small camp on the eastern side, where the Dunlendings stop by on their long hunting trips. The path itself is little more than a track worn by feet and hooves, marked occasionally by white stones but completely unpaved.
14388:
An arrow lies on the ground.
A swallow flies high above the ground.
A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Through these flat plains a path is not truly necessary, and indeed this one is just used to mark the swiftest route between two points. Northwards it leads to a Dunlending town, and many miles south to a boating point on the swift river Isen. It is unpaved, although with a white stone every hundred yards marking its side. Just north of here a small stream can be seen, bending away to the west.
14389: Spotted here and there with streaks of whins, these plains are nevertheless fairly easy to cross. Small hunting paths criss-cross the land, occasionally passing through recently used camps. The Dunlendings who frequent them live most of the year on these plains, hunting rabbits and boar. Some distance to the west a larger path can be made out, travelling north-south. It disappears over both horizons, and out of your sight.
14390: Firmer underfoot than some of the wetlands north of here, these plains are rather featureless. The occasional thicket of trees and wiry bushes breaks the skyline in parts, but generally there is little in the way of cover. Not far west of here a path can be seen going south towards the horizon, and north to the base of a Dunlending hill-town. A commanding position for a fort or town, it must be the home of a mighty overlord of these lands.
14391: A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Worn into the plains rather than built, this path takes a route straight north and south from here. Little in the terrain obstructs it, other than infrequent hollows. It serves as a supply and trading route for the large Dunlending fort north of here, sited on the crown of a low flat hillock. The trail runs to the eastern base of that hill, and then splits. One fork winds up the hillside to the only gates, while the other continues north to the remains of the Great South Road.
14392: Two rough trails meet here, at the eastern end of a long low hill. One heads a short length northwards to the Old South Road, and straight south through the plains. The other slowly ascends the hillside to the west, winding to lessen the climb. It is the only road up to the Dunlending fortress-camp, surrounded by earthen embankments along the crown of the hill. From here you can just pick out where it enters the town, passing through gates in the wooden ring.
14393: The lands of the Gap are wide, and differ greatly from place to place. Here the earth is usually somewhat wet, full of small pools and damp grass, as the light topsoil fails to absorb much of the rains that sweep across the flat lands of Enedwaith. Realising this, the engineers of Numenor built their great road on a causeway, the remains of which still survive to the northeast. West of here a small hill overlooks the surrounding plains, with a well defended town atop it.
14394: A black and white skunk is scuttling about here, searching for food.

Light moss covers the remaining paving stones here, although most have long since crumbled into gravel. This was once a great road, linking Arnor and Gondor over countless hundreds of miles. Now it is utterly decrepit, nothing more than a line of stones through the grasslands.
14395: Muddy Remains of an Old Road

The road has succumbed to the erosion of the water to the west, and now is only a muddy mix of gravel and small pools. The few remains of the once giant paving stones are covered in mud and slimy algae. Some stones have become so dislodged that their edges stick up out of the mud to trip up any unwary traveller. The road continues up away from the wetlands to the north, and travels through the plains to the east.
14396: The causeway which carries this road for many miles to the north-west begins here, near a deserted hilltop settlement to the west. East the lands are gentle rolling plains of well-kept farmlands, while west beyond the hills are mostly flat wetlands. These rains have made the soil in this land very fertile, but in parts the land floods when the water cannot drain away. Southwards the old road crumbles in a sunken muddy mess.
14397: The Tattered Remains of a Road

The worn remains of the Great South Road run around the base of a hillock here, where the ruins of a small settlement can be seen. The buildings are destitute and no people can be seen living there anymore. The road continues west on its causeway through the wetlands in a dreadful condition, pockmarked with holes and jagged slabs. South it lowers to the level of the plains.
14398: Probably not long ago abandoned, these fields now grow wild wheat in places and plain hay in others. Here and there the ground is so wet that nothing can grow, probably why they were abandoned. Just east of here there is a small wooden fence, enclosing some grazing areas. North of it are the farm buildings.
14399: A black and white skunk is scuttling about here, searching for food.

The grass is fairly short here, and in places there are piles of rocks and stones on the ground. There could have been buildings here some time long ago, but now nothing remains of them. From the number and locations of these piles one can count two, maybe three separate buildings. Over the road to the west there are a couple of buildings still standing atop a small hillside.
14400: This courtyard was once a fairly busy place, bustling with travellers and the guards posted here to watch the road. Since the road is now all but forgotten, the way station has long been abandoned. All that remains now is a small and overgrown gravel path leading to the centre of the courtyard, and two of the stone buildings. West was the stable yard, while north was the old inn. Nothing remains of the barracks to the north-west except scattered piles of stones. The courtyard slopes away downward to the south to a small muddy pond, and eastward down the hillside onto the great road.
14401: Here, pools of murky green water gather, reflecting the grass underneath. Along the edges of these pools of water grow tall reeds of grass and cattails. These tufts of vegetation make excellent nesting grounds, making the plains almost like the side of a lake. South, the reeds grow into thick brush, and become utterly impassable. East is the western side of a hillock, a steep bluff with no route up.
14402: A duck is here, quacking happily.

There are few patches of dry area in this land, almost completely flooded with water. Even the ground that appears dry seeps with water if any pressure is applied to it. The vegetation is sparse and tough, mostly near-dead brown grass and rustling ferns. Much small wildlife can be heard rustling about, but always out of sight. The wetlands continue in all directions, although receding to the north-west.
14403: A pigeon is strutting around here.

The large pools of water are not so predominant here as in the terrain to the east and south. There are tall reeds bordering the pools, excellent nesting places for several species of bird. Still, there is enough dry ground to follow a trail of sorts through here. To the south and east the pools grow in size, number and depth, and there is far less dry land around.
14404: A large mother hawk is here looking for a prey to feed her young.

These trees border the wetlands to the south and east, buffering them from the encroaching water. The trees are spread sparsely, which allows plenty of light during the day through their canopy of sinuous branches and leaves. Underfoot the ground is covered with light short grass and occasional puddles of water, submersing the roots of some of the trees.
14405: Here the land is flat and is covered with rich, green grass that is knee deep in spots. There is evidence of grazing in some areas where the grass has been chewed down to the ground. In the south, there is a line of alder trees. The trees continues to the east, while to the north the fields begin to gently rise up on the side of a bluff.
14406: Small to mid-size pools of water pepper the ground here. Being a slight bit higher than the surrounding land it is not as wet as south or north of here, where the land is completely saturated. Looking around it seems as if these wetlands are stagnant, the water unable to drain away. What little vegetation that grows here is brown and barely clinging to life, unable to draw much life from the poor soil.
14407: The ground in this area is too saturated to take in any more water. If even the gentlest pressure is applied the water beneath the grass seeps up and tries to cover the object displacing it. To the north and east an old earthen causeway carries a road through the wetlands. Its sides are slippery, the many small stones eroded from its banks making footing uncertain.
14408: The Tattered Remains of a Road

This road is near impassable, pitted with eroded marks. In parts the old paving stones give way to tip up the unwary traveller. What used to be the Great South Road turns slightly eastward here to pass around a hillock. The Numenoreans built a way-station there long ago, to provide food and shelter for travellers between Arnor and Gondor. The buildings are ruined now, with only the walls remaining. The road continues north-west, where it rises on an causeway to cut through the wetlands, and south-east towards the Gap of Rohan.
14409: Broken glass and crude wooden furniture are scattered about the floor here. The Dunlendings that hunt in these lands sometimes use this old building as shelter from the elements. Several centuries ago this was the inn where travellers on the Great South Road stayed overnight, but it has been abandoned a long while now, like the road. The bar is still standing at the far end of the room, where a clerk probably sold the guest rooms and general supplies. There is a set of stone stairs on the western wall, leading to the roofless upper level.
14410:
A swallow flies high above the ground.
A swallow flies high above the ground.

These rooms of the upper level are open to the elements now, the roof having fallen away long ago. It is hard to imagine this was once an inn where guests would relax during their journey on the Great South Road. The window frames are empty, giving views over the wetlands to the west and the road north and east. The stone floor is covered in all sorts of muck, from bird droppings to rubbish thrown away by travellers.
14411: Twenty feet above the already elevated hilltop town, there is an excellent view of the surrounding plains to be had here. The tower consists of a flat wooden top, with waist-high handrails on all sides but the west, where a rope ladder dangles down to the earthworks below. The tower itself appears in very poor condition, and creaks alarmingly most of the time. In the frequent high winds that streak across the Dunland plains it must seem positively perilous to be on watch duty.
14412: Small Trail by the Fortress Walls
The corpse of a Dunlending thief is lying here.

Between a large barn-like structure and the natural line of the earth walls, the track bends westward here. This is the dingiest part of the village, with litter everywhere and frequent street robbery. Small tents, mostly homes, lie on both sides of the track. The Dunlendings have never shaken off their hillman past, even though these ones have long since moved from those lands. Some way to the south lies the main gates, while to the west a few small buildings are scattered about, mainly shops.
14413: Moving between the huge number of tents, barns and small buildings, the track here follows the side of a long flat building. Most of it is taken up by the pub to the west, with a small tailor's shop built onto its eastern end. Through the open doors can be seen countless furs and leather clothing, of all shapes and sizes. The track continues to the west, bending around yet another large tent. North are the imposing earthen walls, topped with sharpened stakes.
14414: More a muddy trail than anything else, it is dank and gloomy here, overhung by the fortifications to the north. Little sunlight gets at the ground, and it has become filthy with litter, creating a stinking corner of the village where none but the poorest choose to live. Periodically the Dunlendings lay down wooden planks to traverse the muddy pools, but most of the year the only way through is to walk knee deep into them. The cheapest pub around lies to the south, partially sinking into the permanently wet earth.
14415: Wulfston is known for its countless tents, and nowhere is this more apparent than here. Tents lie to both sides of the track as far as the eye can see, the homes of the common townsfolk. Not far to the north are the walls, earthworks of some height with tall wooden stakes topping them. A walkway runs along their crest, but there is no way up from here. Turning along the base of the walls, the track enters a muddy and smelly part of the village. A seedy pub lies off the track along there, a wood and canvas building of dubious construction.
14416: Covered in small stones, this is one of the gathering areas for celebrations and the like. It is surrounded to the west by the earthworks that are the camp's defences, and to the east by the fighing pits. North leads to a dingy trail, and south a large open air tent. Mostly this place is busy round the clock with markets, fighting, story-telling or sometimes even just as a storage area.
14417:
Traces of fierce white tones form the aura of this place.
The corpse of Broghha's bodyguard is lying here.
The corpse of Broghha's bodyguard is lying here.
The corpse of Broghha's bodyguard is lying here.
The corpse of Broghha's bodyguard is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending Captain is lying here.
A Dunlending animist is lying here, incapacitated.
The shadow of Broghha's bodyguard is floating here.
Broghha the enormously fat Dunlending chieftain is here.

A huge tent, made out of animal hides stitched together, protects the square from the elements. It is fixed at each corner by a stone block, and hung from a thick tree trunk in the centre. Around this central support is the seat of the chieftain, surrounded by countless thick animal furs and some well-crafted wooden chairs. The vast sagging tent overhead covers a large enough area for many sporting events, when the weather does not allow them to be held outside.
14418:
A small child is here playing happily.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.

This wooden platform slightly overhangs the steep hillside having been built on countless ramshackle wooden branches. The platform is filled with coils of rope that are attached to a few large barrels. Most of the fort's water is supplied this way, hauled up from the stream below by overworked oxen. Northwards lies the town square, covered over by a large open air tent.
14419: These metalworks are contained in a spacious room, dominated by a primitive furnace on its southern wall. Much wood is stacked near to it, along with the other tools of the smith - bellows, tongs, hammers, and many shapes of moulds and anvils. The secret of metalworking is rather new to the Dunlendings, and the resulting products are not of the highest quality. Many broken or failed attempts at weapons and hauberks are strewn about the earthen floor, discarded in disgust by the novice smiths. However a few exceptions hanging on wall-pegs draw the eye. Broken in battle, but still showing signs of fine workmanship, most of the shields and chain-mail bear the designs of the horse-lords.
14420:
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

There are only half a dozen stalls here, made of roughly cut wooden logs and covered over by a hanging cow-hide roof. The Dunlendings, being by nature a hillman people, have never really adapted to the horseback form of fighting, unlike their Rohirrim enemies. Still, on occasion visitors come by horseback, usually the few outside merchants trusted enough to trade with. They may be allowed to keep their mounts here, but the care taken of them is questionable to say the least. Judging by the filthy stalls and the uncaring attitude of the stable-man, it might be foolhardy to stable any horse here.
14421: Most of the south-east corner of the town is a large field of trampled earth, with the occasional patch of grass. In the wild ungoverned lands of Enedwaith there are many threats, from rival Dunlendings to Rohirrim, and even marauding orcs from the north. These grounds are used to hone their skills against such enemies, and for some basic military manoeuvres. West of here are the stables, little more than a few tented stalls, and east the barracks. South are the high earthen defences, with no way up onto the ramparts from here.
14422:
A Dunlending Captain is here, overseeing his men.
A soldier dressed in polished equipment eyes you warily.
A soldier dressed in polished equipment eyes you warily.

Lines of beds fill this long flat tent, one of the biggest in the fort. It is home to the village guards, mostly mercenaries brought in from afar who will not challenge the village's leaders. Most of the barracks is untidy and fairly dirty, with clothes and possessions strewn all around. Dunlendings do not cope well with living inside, used as they are to the nomadic hillman life.
14423:
The corpse of a black-haired soldier is lying here.
The corpse of a black-haired soldier is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending Captain is lying here.
The corpse of a black-haired soldier is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending Captain is lying here.
The corpse of a black-haired soldier is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending gateguard is lying here.
The corpse of a black-haired soldier is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending Captain is lying here.
The corpse of a black-haired soldier is lying here.
The corpse of a Dunlending gateguard is lying here.
The corpse of the Dunlending gatekeeper is lying here.
The shadow of a Dunlending Captain is floating here.

Passing through a gap in the steeply piled earth surrounding the village, the area between the two gates is the first line of defence for its inhabitants. In here any attacking force would be caught in a hail of spears and arrows cast down from the wooden ramparts, assuming they were not first overpowered by the gate-guards. The main outside gates, each a dozen huge wooden poles tied with ropes of vines, are usually only closed at night, while the inside ones are only ever used in a siege. On the south side is a little covered area, where the guards try to escape the bitter eastern winds that sweep across from Rohan.
14424: You are underneath a watchtower, built on four thick beams above the camp's defensive earthworks. The wood itself looks heavily weather-beaten and is in terrible shape, rotten and flaking away in parts. Those unlucky enough to be chosen for watch duty are often exposed to driving wind and rain on the exposed tower, and can only hope the creaking platform doesn't collapse below them. The only way up is via a twenty foot rope ladder, swinging in the wind above you.
14425: Winding Track through the Canvas-Roofed Buildings

Most of the north of the camp is a sprawling expanse of wooden buildings and tented lodgings, built wherever there is a spare plot of land. Just west of here is a small inn, a rough building with a thatched roof. East leads up the earthworks to a wooden watchtower overlooking the surrounding flatlands, a high and often creaking platform. The beams look more than a little unstable, due to the bad workmanship and wet rot.
14426: An old tailor is sitting here, working with a piece of fabric.

This shop consists of one long tented room, with the tailor's wares hung on pegs on the supports. Looking closer all types of clothing can be seen - from leather trousers to long capes, from sandals to fur-lined boots. The old man who owns the shop is a prolific clothes-maker, and must take in quite a lot of money from the Dunlendings. He has no fears of robbery or assault also, as he is under the protection of Wulfston's fearsome leader, who values good clothes.
14427: Large blocks of uneven stone were laid here near the monument, many centuries ago. Mostly the paving stones have cracked or worn, and many now lie broken and splintered, leaving frequent hazardous potholes. To the west the paving gives way to a large square covered by a cavernous open-air tent. North, at the very centre of the village, are the fighting pits, where captured beasts and men are thrown to fight for the amusement of the Dunlendings.
14428: Standing somewhat incongruously amongst the countless tents are many ancient pillars, originally arranged in a large arc. Most have fallen into ruin, but the four largest on the western side still stand undiminished. They are built of a dull black rock that weather and time leave no mark on. Running in-between these monuments from another age is a trail, leading west towards an enormous open-air tent, and east to the gates.
14429: Most of the day these streets are bustling with merchants and traders, and the wagons carrying their goods. This is the only Dunlending settlement to accept contact, even stretching to outside trade, because of its leader's liking for foreign-made luxuries. The main path heads west from here, while a smaller side street full of dingy shops and tented homes leads north. Just to the east are the gates - sturdy constructions made of many long wooden poles.
14430:
A black and white skunk is scuttling about here, searching for food.
A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

You are by the gates of a Dunlending camp, which lies atop a low flat hill in the plains. This is the fortress of Wulfston, named after the Dunlending chief who ransacked Rohan nearly a century ago. It has survived to this day; besieged occasionally, but never captured due to the natural defences. The main gate is just to the west of you, through a gap in the earthworks. That fortification wall circles the crown of the hill, topped by sharp ten foot wooden stakes. It is clear to see that this fortress would take some power to storm.
14431: The corpse of a grimy publican is lying here.

So named after some obscure and long forgotten Dunlending legend, this place is a fairly cosy pub. Built of red clay and roofed with thatch over low wooden beams, it is probably the most popular drinking spot in the village. The choice of drink is limited though, with only a few different barrels available behind the bar. A small hallway leads out to a few bedrooms, where guests can stay for the night. The place is rather less than clean though, and anyone staying in those rooms might find they wake up with fleas or lice.
14432: This large tent is one of the few shops in the settlement, selling anything from basic outdoors items like rope and lanterns, to food. Some of this he bakes himself, but mostly he just buys meat straight from the hunters who live nearby. His produce is mostly lain out on dirty tables all around the tent, with the salted cuts of meat hanging from hooks on the tent poles. The only way out is the door flap on the southern side of the tent.
14433:
The corpse of a Dunlending thief is lying here.
A small child is here playing happily.
A small child is here playing happily.
A Dunlending woman is here tending to her children.

Few buildings of the Dunlendings are kept clean, but the interior of this pub is utterly filthy. Obviously no attempt at cleaning has been made in a long time. The pub itself consists of a central room with plain tables and benches for the common folk, and private rooms for those held in higher esteem. This place is in the worst part of the village, frequented by the small underworld population. Many of the drunken patrons have their purses stolen by some nimble fingered pickpocket every night, with the bar staff turning a blind eye.
14434: A circular depression creates a natural arena here, allowing many bloodthirsty Dunlendings to view the pits at one time. Anyone captured in battle, sometimes even travellers passing by on the old South Road, might find themselves thrown into the muddy enclosure to fight fierce creatures. Usually these are nothing more than a large boar or bull, but on days of celebration larger creatures may be found for the crowd's pleasure. On some occasions even hill trolls and orcs have been captured, and made to fight until death.
14435: A small and tough weed grows here.

This east-west ridge rises sharply from the plains to the north, but stays fairly level to the east and west. The highest point is about twenty-five feet higher than the surrounding land. Small rocks can be seen poking out of the ankle-length grass here and there. The Glanduin flows gently on to the south, following the curves of the land
14436: A bright green holly bush is growing here.

This short and grassy hill rises gently from the east, creating a much wider and taller ridge as the land travels to the west. The slope northwards is still gentle, but less so. While a constant layer of grass covers the entire hill, some portions of the southern slope have been claimed by patches of brush, sheltered in part from the wind.
14437: The grass grows long underfoot, even though it is sparse in rockier areas. Small, budding flowers are scattered throughout the area, thriving in the more fertile areas of this gentle landscape. Scattered patches of exposed rock create isolated brown islands in the vegetation. The land gradually slopes up to the west, creating a hill in this otherwise flat land.
14438: A constant layer of hardy grasses lie on the ground, making a carpet of green. The land is mostly flat, with only occasional gentle slopes to be seen. While there are small shrubs dotting the landscape, they do little to add colour to the area, or give shelter for travellers. Brownish rocks litter the ground at the bottom of the slopes, creating little problems negotiating the area.
14439: The land is flat, having no variation to its pitch or elevation. The only growth that can be seen is a constant layer of grass, covering the land with a layer of green. Small stones dot the ground, occasionally stacked into small piles by some unknown entity. The air here is fresh, carrying the pure scent of the open plains.
14440: The ground here is rarely level, with mild slopes intersecting one another constantly. The ground has a mixture of thick grasses and wild grains, creating an ideal area for grazing. Many bushes line the creases created by two or more slopes, often making it easier to walk around rather than through. Some fist- sized rocks litter the ground, almost hidden by the surrounding vegetation.
14441: Holes about a foot in diameter dot this area, littering the ground with small depressions that are impossible to see without the observer being right beside them. A traveller on foot would not have much trouble, but riders might find their mounts stumbling. The grass is over a foot long, giving good grazing to wild animals in the area.
14442: Dips and rises in the surrounding plains make it easy to see for long distances, but it can be difficult to determine exactly what will be on the other side of an individual rise. Wild grasses and patches of flowers grow abundantly on every available patch of ground. Not a stone or rock can be seen to mar the almost total swath of vegetation.
14443: While mostly flat, small dips and rises can be seen in the surrounding landscape. A healthy layer of grass covers everything, as if reluctant to let other types of vegetation grow in the fertile soil. The bright blooms of flowers make patches of colour against the otherwise green ground. The air is fresh here, free from the confusing mixture of smells that herald civilization.
14444:
Some delicious wild strawberries grow on the ground.
Some delicious wild strawberries grow on the ground.
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

Lush grass grows here, tall enough to cover a man's ankles. The land has a small amount of tilt and curve to it, gradually rising as it travels to the south. There are numerous small tracks and paths created mazelike in the grass, caused by many rodent scurrying about their business. An odd flower has risen out of the grass, creating a splash of colour to the green landscape.
14445: The ground here has a sporadic covering of vegetation. At times patches of grass appear to be growing healthy and well, but in places only the toughest of weeds will grow. The layer of earth covering this portion of plains appears to change consistency often, leaving no vegetation in spots and a thriving mass in others. Despite all of this, there is evidence that animals make their home here.
14446: The land here is alive, though apparently not overly fertile. A fairly constant covering of grass lies on the ground, neither thick nor overly tall. Many small and hardy bushes eke out a living, clustered together in areas that the grass does not grow in. Other portions of the plains would most likely offer more in the way of hunting opportunities.
14447: This area has little to see. A skimpy layer of earth allows only the hardiest weeds and shrubs to grow, creating a landscape that is more brown than green. Very few signs of animals life are apparent, mostly consisting of an old skeleton lying on top of the ground. Its previous owner may have been a deer.
14448: A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

The ground underfoot is covered with a sparse layer of grasses, alive yet not thriving on the open plains. The topsoil appears to be thin here, not allowing the normal amount of plant life to flourish. Some long patches of flat rock stick out of the earth, creating lifeless areas. Few animals seem to live here, most likely preferring healthier portions of the plains.
14449: The ground here has a barely discernable slope, which rises upwards over half of a mile to a small hill. Despite all of that, the hill is probably no more than thirty feet above the surrounding plains. At its top sits a small cairn, worn by age and the elements. Were it not for the otherwise featureless landscape, this three-foot tall obstacle may have been difficult to spot.
14450: The small amount of rise and fall the ground has here makes for a complacent view, when mixed with the grass blowing in the wind. Thick and verdant grass covers every inch of available soil, with wild flowers poking through in small patches.
14451: A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

The land is made up of a series of small, grassy rises spaced unevenly apart. None of those rises are large enough to be considered to be a hill, but make it impossible to see for any distance unless the observer is standing atop one. Grasses dominate the tops of the rises, with patches of flowers taking shelter along the gentle slopes. The small valleys created have small shrubs in them which are too small to impede any traveller's progress.
14452: A goat is here, grazing in the hills.

Long slopes and valleys, none of which are more than the height of a man, stretch on for miles in every direction. The ground is covered with a thick layer of grass, which is soft and springy to tread on. No flowers or shrubs grow here, as there is little protection from the elements. Small holes dot the area, perhaps the homes of foxes or woodchucks.
14453: The ground is mostly flat here, making it possible to see for miles in every direction. Wild grasses are plentiful, covering every inch of landscape with a thick carpet of green. Bushes grow sparsely, with little to shield them from the wind in this wide open area.
14454: The ground is flat and covered in grass. In some places, the vegetation has been trampled flat by many feet. There may be herds which use this area for pasture. Many piles of dung lie in the trampled area, left by previous four- legged visitors. Most of the tracks appear to come from and leave to the west, making a broad path. There might be something of interest to a herd in that direction.
14455: A goat is here, grazing in the hills.

The main focus of the land in this area seems to be a large pond which has most likely seen cleaner days. Hoofprints have torn up all of the grass around it, and manure covers much of the area. Despite all of that, the water appears to be drinkable. The grass for hundreds of yards around the water has been stripped to the ground, eaten by the animals which come to water here.
14456: A young colt is frolicking playfully.

A healthy carpet of grass covers the ground, eaten short in spots by herbivores. A rough animal track winds from the north to the east, making a round-about turn. Away from the track, several small clusters of wild flowers grow. Dotting the landscape are low-lying shrubs, vying for the sun in the wide open space.
14457: A constant layer of grasses and tall weeds covers the ground for miles in every direction. The land has little slope to it, being almost completely flat. A few low-lying bushes can be seen, huddled close to the earth. The openness of this area makes it ideal to see for miles in any direction, but offers little in the way to see.
14458: While generally flat, there are several long and gentle slopes, never steep enough to cause dangerous footing. Healthy grass covers the ground for miles in every direction. One or two small patches of flowers do little to add a splash of colour to the environment, or rid the area of an air of monotony.
14459: The ground here is flat and notable landmarks are few and far between. While a constant layer of grass covers the ground, it does not appear to flourish like it does in the surrounding portions of the plains. Few splashes of colour mark the landscape, making the whole area an almost uniform shade.
14460: Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

Small swells in the plains create a series of minute hills. The view from the top of a swell lets a traveller see for over a mile in every direction, although the dips often hide what they contain. A lush layer of grass thrives here, flourishing in the fertile soil. Many wild flowers bloom alone or in small patches, giving bright splashes of colour to the area.
14461: The plains here are mostly flat, with small swells preventing a viewer from seeing for miles in every direction. The wild grasses here grow several feet tall, well fed by the fertile soil. Many aimless paths have been plowed through the vegetation, most likely by the animals who come here to graze.
14462:
A shade is here, shrouded in an inky blackness.
A shade is here, shrouded in an inky blackness.

This small room gives the impression of being eternally dark, the dark dirt walls completely absorb light rather than reflecting it. The room is nothing more than a rough seven-foot cube hollowed out from the surrounding earth. The area is dry and the trapdoor above looks like it keeps out the rain well. The remains of two long wooden boxes are the sole items of interest here.
14463: The ground here is mostly flat, with a slope rising upwards to the north. Wild grasses grow in abundance, fed well by the fertile topsoil of these plains. Small patches of clover litter the countryside, blowing gently in even the faintest of breezes.
14464: Grass covers most of the ground on this section of the ridge, giving good footing. Small bare patches of rock dot the area to the north, where the ridge takes a steep turn downwards. A careful person would be able to scale that slope without risking life or limb.
14465: The ridges to the north and east converge at this spot, creating a wide area some thirty feet above the plains. The slopes to the west and south are generally moderate, while there is an almost vertical drop to the north-east. Scant amounts of topsoil allow for only hardy weeds to grow on the rocky ground.
14466: Wild grasses cover every portion of the level ground, not showing any hint of dirt or rock. Where the ground slopes up to the north, tougher weeds and bushes abound, being more suited to that environment. The slope eventually rises to become a high ridge, several times the height of a man.
14467: Thick and healthy grass grows in profusion, covering the land from horizon to horizon with a solid carpet of green. Some portions of the land look as if they have seen grazing in the recent past, with short-cropped grass and animal droppings. Many of the patches of sheared grass are in the south, giving an indication that something of interest to a herd may lie in that direction.
14468: A thick, green layer of grass covers the ground as far as the eye can see. Some patches of wild flowers bloom, creating a colourful display. An animal track winds its way generally north-south, making for an unseen destination. While it would be marginally easier to follow the track, much more direct routes in either direction would be to cut straight across the plains.
14469: The ground is flat and covered with a constant swath of healthy grass. Some portions of the vegetation have been eaten short by herbivores, but most are still growing wild and untamed. The occasional patch of flowers does little to change the overall appearance of the place. It is a vast open area with little cover and less variety.
14470: The garden snake slithers harmlessly here.

The land here is composed of a series of slopes and the ground is covered with a healthy layer of grass. There seems to be a thin but good layer of topsoil for the grass is flourishing thick and green upon the hard ground. The lack of bushes and flowers in this area make it somewhat dull and monotonous.
14471: A series of swells in the ground form a large number of minuscule hills. The ground is covered in a lush and healthy layer of vegetation. Foot-high grass makes up the majority of the greenery, while many different forms of grains rise up in patches much too small to be harvested. The swells seem to grow in number to the east, and become longer and more gentle to the north.
14472: The ground here is almost perfectly flat, with rare swells and dips which do little to change elevation or impede vision. A rich and healthy layer of grass covers the ground, adding a spring to the step. Small shrubs can be seen clustered together, making low windbreaks. There are signs that animals often come to this area to graze or eat berries off of the shrubs.
14473: Long grasses rise out of this mostly flat landscape, with patches of hay and other wild grains vying for the sun. Animals have made many paths in the long grass, seeming to go nowhere in particular. There is a low and grassy hill to the north that breaks up the seeming monotony of this landscape.
14474:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
The garden snake slithers harmlessly here.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

The land here ascends to a long, thin hill which runs from the east to the west. Its entire length is covered in a thick and rich layer of grass, with several small patches of flowers providing some colour and scent. The hill descends steeply to the north and south, but has a gentle slope which gradually merges into the plains to the east.
14475:
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

While the vegetation covering the ground here is over a foot tall, it's made up of weeds and grass rather than any domesticated sort of grain. The ground has some slope to it, which seems to rise as it travels to the west, and descend to the east. There is little colour to the scenery, with few flowers able to push up past the grass towards the sun.
14476:
A small cluster of clover grows here.
A restless rabbit bounces around.

The ground here appears to be fashioned in the shape of a very wide and fairly shallow bowl. The mostly flat sides of the incline make for easy surveying, but since the viewer is standing in the middle of an approximately ten-foot depression, the line-of-sight is limited. The ground vegetation is predominately a constant layer of grass, intermixed with patches of clover and small wildflowers.
14477:
A small child is here playing happily.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A restless rabbit bounces around.

A layer of grass covers the ground, sparse in places. Stones and bare earth create a series of brown patches, overshadowed by many small shrubs which lie close to the ground. Piles of dung litter the area, mostly clustered around patches of grass which have been eaten close to the ground. There are many small and aimless animal tracks in the area, but one particularly well-trodden appears to lead to the east.
14478: A temporary camp has been pitched here. A twenty-foot diameter area of ground has been roughly stamped flat with a small fire pit in its centre. Litter and refuse lie in piles beyond the inhabited areas, some of it obviously pitched from the sleeping area. Outside of the camp, the plains are generally flat and covered with a half-eaten layer of vegetation.
14479:
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

The ground is generally flat, covered in a constant layer of grass which has been eaten close to the ground. The animals have made crude paths which zig-zag through the area, mostly going from one grazing patch to another. As would be expected, large amounts of dung litter the ground, creating a fertile environment for the grass to regrow.
14480:
The garden snake slithers harmlessly here.
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

The ground here is almost perfectly flat, allowing any observer to see for miles. A constant and healthy, if not overly thick, layer of grass covers the ground as far as the eye can see. The soil here does not seem to be overly deep and rich, the probable cause for the lack of flowers and such vegetation. A tall ridge rises up some thirty feet in the east, providing a good view of the surroundings.
14481: In the Corner of Two Small Ridges
A small cluster of clover grows here.

Beds of clover thrive in this sheltered corner, protected from the elements by ridges to the south and west. The land is mostly flat, with small rises which could not possibly be considered hills. An almost sheer cliff to the west makes progress in that direction impossible. A steep and rocky slope to the south should make a vigorous but not overly difficult climb.
14482: A tall ridge is easily the most noticeable feature in the immediate area. The majority of it is covered with scattered bushes and tough weeds, growing out of cracks in the rock. One of the flatter sections of stone has crude paintings drawn on it, faded with age. The slope to the east is sharp and would require an agile climber, but the western descent is much less dangerous.
14483: A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

Patches of bare rock show through the grass in places, unusual in these healthy plains of Hollin. Some stones can be found lying on top of the ground, from fist-sized to weighing several hundred pounds. It does not appear that very many animals make their homes here, prefering the more verdant parts of the plains. A ridge rises high in the east, with a steep bank which offers many places for a climber to find purchase.
14484: Small piles of stones have been made at irregular intervals. No obvious markings can be seen on them, so they may not have any sort of religious significance. A healthy but short layer of grass lies on the ground, obviously eaten short by grazing animals. There may have been flowers in the area at one time, but they have all been eaten or trampled.
14485: The ground has been trampled by many, many feet. The grass, while once green, has been beaten into the ground by a constant traffic of herds moving about the area. Many patches of earth have been torn up by cloven hooves, creating a brown rather than green landscape. Some rocks have been inadvertently dug up, lying on top of the soil.
14486:
A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

Slight tilts to the land cause a series of intersecting hills with gentle slopes. A layer of thick and lush grass causes steps to bounce with extra energy. Many patches of flowers make the plains seem less than drab, despite the effect of continuing on for miles in every direction.
14487: An almost perfectly level and green land has some bright colours added by many patches of thriving flowers. The varied types of vegatation compete to reach the sun, with grasses and flowers growing over a foot tall, and grains higher still. Many small trails in the vegetation attest that this area is home to a large number of animals.
14488: The land here has little slope to it, creating an almost perfectly level area several miles square. The ground is mostly covered with a mixed layer of grass and wild grains. The grains stand about three feet high, and grow in uneven clusters. While the area has rocks and stones, the majority of them appear to have been piled together long ago.
14489: The plains here have small dips and rises, creating an uneven series of miniature hills. Most of the ground is covered by a healthy layer of grass, but some areas have clusters of hay growing several feet tall. Areas have seen heavy grazing, with the vegetation cropped short. While there are stones in the area, they seem to have been cleared from the portions which the hay grows in.
14490: Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.

While the ground is mostly flat, it is difficult to see any particular thing on the ground from a distance away. A tall layer of hay and wild grains grow several feet tall, and obscure what may lie on the ground. The whole landscape seems to move as breezes cause wave-like swells through the taller grains.
14491:
A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.
A cluster of white star-shaped forget-me-nots flourish here in reminiscence.

The ground is mostly flat, covered in a rich and healthy layer of grass. A small and sheltered hollow contains a small pond, a precious commodity in times of little rain. Many patches of flowers grow around the pond, watered well. There are many signs of animals frequenting this area.
14492: The garden snake slithers harmlessly here.

The ground here is mostly flat, with the occasional swell to break up the monotony of the otherwise flat plains. A rich and fertile layer of vegetation covers the ground, comprising a mixture of grasses, weeds, and wild grains. A clump of bushes rests in a shallow hollow, marginally sheltered from the elements.
14493: A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

A perfectly healthy and fertile section of plains can be found here. Healthy green grass covers the ground, interspersed with patches of multi-coloured flowers. There is little slope to the land, creating no shelter against the elements. The land to the east has seen heavy grazing, with piles of dung and the grass sheared short.
14494: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

A short layer of wild grasses covers the flat plains, creating a layer of green that stretches from horizon to horizon. Almost every foot of the greenery has been eaten to within a couple of inches high. Many piles of animal dung indicate that herds visit this area regularly. While animal tracks abound, they are so numerous that it is impossible to tell which track came from which animal.
14495: Small undulations of the ground cause a regular pattern of dips and rises, but none of them rise to the height of a moderately-sized hill. A constant layer of grass covers the ground, with patches of clover thriving in places. Both short grass and scattered dung attest that this area has seen grazing recently.
14496: The ground takes a dip below the surrounding countryside, creating a wide bowl about fifteen feet deep. The slopes of the bowl are covered in a variety of wildflowers, which make a colourful display on the lush grass. This depression is made to look more severe than it is by the ridge to the east, which rises well above the surrounding plains.
14497: This small hill is some twenty feet above the flat plains, allowing a fair view of the surroundings. Grass grows in profusion, creating a deep carpet over its entire surface. The slope to the south descends slowly, but rises again to form a ridge higher and much steeper than this.
14498: The ground here is soft and green, covered in a thick carpet of healthy grass. The ridge to the west has a steep slope which would be difficult but not impossible to scale. Some stones have fallen down at its base, creating a small pile of rubble.
14499: Healthy, green grass grows in abundance on this flat stretch of land, seemingly at odds with the mountains looming far to the east. Small patches of bright flowers liven up the landscape. In the distance to the north and south, small hills can be seen rising above the surroundings.
14500: A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

The ground here is level with most of the plains, but the presence of an almost vertical slope to the north and a hill to the south give the illusion of being in a depression. Rocks dot the area, and have most likely fallen from the ridge to the north. The tough grasses growing here look slightly withered, as if they are not receiving enough sunlight.
14501:
A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.
A very large lion with a dark mane watches you lazily.
A powerful lioness is barely visible in the grass.
A lion cub is here hunting grasshoppers.
A powerful lioness is barely visible in the grass.
A lion cub is here hunting grasshoppers.

The plains here are mostly flat, with a slight rolling to the gait of the land. No rises are more than a couple of feet high, with gentle slopes down all sides. A thick and healthy layer of grass covers the entire landscape, suggesting that this area would be ideal for agriculture. To the east, a ridge with a moderate slope rises above the plains.
14502: This land is mostly flat. It rises and falls seldom, creating good vantage points few and far between. A constant layer of grass covers the ground, eaten short by many animals. Bushes and shrubs grow clustered together, sheltering each other from the wind. Old animal droppings can be seen at a glance. A herd of some sort must frequent this area often.
14503: A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

The ground here is composed of gentle slopes, creating a series of small rises in the plains. A healthy layer of grass hugs the ground, giving an extra spring to a traveller's step. Some patches of grass have been cropped short where a herd has stopped to graze. The air is fresh and clean, blowing across the plains for many miles without encountering the taint of civilization.
14504: The land to the north is rocky and has little animal or plant life on it. The land gets progressively more fertile as it travels to the south, causing much more healthy vegetation to grow. Small changes in elevation begin in the east, creating a series of grass-covered rises. Sections of grass have seen grazing recently, probably from a roaming herd.
14505: A large wild horse is here, protecting his herd.

A constant layer of growing grass covers this generally flat area, creating ideal condition for animals to graze. Some sections of the vegetation have been eaten close to the ground, attesting that herds occasionally visit this region. Some patches of weeds and grains grow here, rising up to two feet higher than the surrounding vegetation.
14506:
Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

This mostly flat area is covered with a healthy layer of grass and other forms of vegetation. There are sections of land which have had the stones cleared off and piled together. Patches of grains still grow there, even though it appears as if this region hasn't had someone to tend it in quite a while.
14507:
Some cereals that look like wheat are lying here.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

The land in this area is flat and unassuming, with little colour from any source. Tall fields of hay rise three feet high and sway constantly in the breeze. Signs that herd animals come here to feed are abundant, from small wandering paths to many piles of dung. A tall ridge begins sloping upwards to the north.
14508: On a Ridge in the Plains

A small and tough weed grows here.
A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

This is the corner of a bent ridge, continuing on to the north and east. The ground remains at a constant level as the ridge travels north, but rises slightly in the east. A sparse covering of brush can be found, thinning out to the south. Many patches of tall and tough weeds grow between the taller bushes and from nooks and crannies formed by rocks.
14509: On a Ridge in the Plains

A holly bush with dark green leaves is growing here.
Partly covered by the bush's green leaves, there are two piles of inkberries.
A large marmot is here, scurrying in between the rocks.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

This ridge rises well above the surrounding plains, perhaps thirty feet in places. The ground is a mixture of grass and stones, while an almost constant layer of bushes grow on top of that. The slopes down in all directions are mild, allowing mounted riders to easily access this area. The ridge continues on to the west, becoming slightly lower.
14510: The ground rises slightly here, forming a large raised area. All around you the ground slopes slightly downhill away from this spot, creating an ideal view of the immediate surroundings. The ground is covered with a constant green layer of grass for miles in every direction, making the few vibrantly coloured flowers stand out against the background.
14511: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

The ground here is rocky and hard, providing little in the way of thriving vegetation. While sturdy grasses grow in areas with more topsoil, tough bushes create most of the greenery. Some evidence of animals is apparent, though they probably use this area to travel to a more fertile portion of the plains.
14512: The corpse of a kid is lying here.

Patches of shrubs and bushes grow together, clustered in the more sheltered areas. Some grass grows where the bushes do not, yet much of the ground is bare earth and stone. Rocks litter the ground, scattered around the area. There is some slope to the ground, creating long stretches of gentle inclines.
14513: The ground is mostly flat, with small dips and rises which have slopes too gentle to be considered hills. The ground is covered with a short layer of grass, much of it sheared close to the ground by grazing animals. Small piles of stones are placed widely apart, clearing the majority of the ground for prime grazing land.
14514: The ground is mostly flat here, covered with a thick layer of grass. Some areas look like they have seen grazing recently, the vegetation is unnaturally short in those spots. Rocks and stones dot the area to the east, leading up to a gentle incline.
14515:
A Dunlending herdsman, in ragged leather stands here watching over his herd.
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

This ridge dominates the surrounding landscape, easily rising higher than any other feature for miles around. At its southern tip it is almost thirty feet high, ending abruptly in an almost vertical drop. The slope to the east and west is less severe but will require careful navigation. The ground is bare of vegetation in spots making footing uneven.
14516: The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

This large flat area lies in a depression. The slopes of the ridge to the west are covered with a mixture of wild flowers and sturdy grasses. A ditch created by water runoff from one of the steeper parts of the western ridge fans out at the base with sand which was carried down.
14517: There are many types of short shrubs growing here, clinging to the ridge. Many small paths have been made in the surrounding brush as well, created by animals forced to walk in single file. The vegetation thins out as the land progresses southwards, giving way to grasses and tall weeds. The ridge has a steep but constant incline to the north-east, allowing access in that direction.
14519: There is a primarily flat landscape here, with few curves which amount to small rises. While there is a generally healthy layer of grass, many small paths wind through the area, creating long tracks with no vegetation. Many small bushes dot the area, apparently faring better than the weeds, which have been eaten close to the ground.
14520:
Klaees (thedon), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Drazud (freshmeat), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.

The land here is generally flat, covered with an uneven layer of grass. Some portions of the area have been heavily trodden by human and animal feet, making many small paths which wind through the plains. Grazing has shortened most of the remaining grass close to the ground, letting as much brown earth as green grass show. Many small stones litter the ground, dug up by the passing traffic.
14521: Some portions of the ground have been worn away to bare earth, due to many feet travelling over the same path. The land is flat, stretching as far as the eye can see in every direction. The grass here has been eaten to different lengths, most likely sheared close to the ground and allowed to regrow before the animals come back for more.
14522: Short-cropped grass covers most of the ground in this flat section of the Hollin plains. Piles of dung litter the area, left over from a domesticated herd of some sort. Holly bushes grow in the southern area, trampled back from the more travelled land to the north.
14523: The ground here is covered with short-cropped grass, eaten by herd animals of some sort. There are many tracks of hoofed animals, making it difficult to determine the path of any individual. Though worn bare in spots, this is obviously prime grazing land for a domesticated herd.
14524: This appears to be the corner of a ridge, running to the south and east. The ground is covered with a hardy layer of grass, with tough weeds growing in the rockier areas. The top of the ridge sits over twenty feet above the surrounding plains, but would cause no great difficulty to climb.
14525: On Top of the Small Rise

The top of this small hill sits over twenty feet higher than the surrounding countryside. A ridge running east-west intersects with the hill some ten feet lower than the crown, which is covered in a thick layer of grass. The sides of the hill slope down at a moderate angle to the north and south, making for an easy climb.
14526:
A large thorny branched shrub is growing here.
A brown snake watches you.

Looking about you, you can find absolutely no evidence that this was once one of the more populated regions of Arda, home of both Elf and Dwarf, who together brought more glories to this land than it has ever seen, or is ever likely to see again. Indeed it is not hard to believe, looking at the beauty of these parts, it's just that there is no sign of civilization anywhere.
14527: The landscape begins to change a little here, as you see forested land to the west of here, and the mountains begin to flatten out a bit to the north. Despite the change in terrain, the colour stays fairly constant, with several different shades and hues of green everywhere, with other colours mixed in. There are even a few birds here and there to accompany the lovely sight with their songs.
14528:
A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.
A woodpecker is here, tapping on a tree.

A cheerful atmosphere brightens the journey in this lush forest, making your footfalls light and you thoughts equally so. The trees here are not yet full grown, as this area joins the forest with the hills to the east. As a result, the sky is clearly visible, the trees not having aged enough to form the vibrant canopy they exhibit to the west. A small stream flows north.
14529: A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

Here the forest continues on, as lovely as ever, with the large trees spreading their leaves above, and the large, leafy bushes and ferns that cover the ground. There is a feeling of gaity in the air, perhaps created by the playful melodies of the songbirds in the trees and the many animal cubs around, making mischief and hiding from their mothers.
14530:
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.
Klaees (thedon), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Drazud (freshmeat), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

Vibrant colour strikes your eye from all angles as you walk through this gorgeous forested area. It is easy to see why both Elf and Dwarf chose to live in these parts so many years ago, certainly unrivaled in beauty and perfection. You are completely surrounded by forest here, with no choice but to continue wandering through it, to see what other splendours it has in store for you.
14531: You stand in the lush greenery of Hollin Forest. Dew glistens off the leaves above as well as ferns growing close to the ground. Birds chirp happily and small animals are often seen scampering around. There are some odd tracks here and there, but you can detect no feel of evil hanging anywhere in the air. To the west, you can proceed up a small incline to a wooded ridge. From there, you ought to be able to get a good view of the surrounding land.
14532: Above Hollin Forest the ridge ascends, fairly gently, but steeply enough that there seems to be only one path by which you might climb it. You stand high enough that your eyes can behold all the splendours of Eregion, from the lush hills and forest that surround you, to the imposing Misty Mountains which lie far to the east. You may follow the tree-lined ridge to the west, or descend into the vibrantly foliated forest.
14533: The ridge continues here, still giving an excellent view of Nan-Eregdos and its gorgeous landscape. Trees and bushes dot the ridge and its slopes, although not as thickly as in the forest below, some distance to the east. It is only possible to walk east here or try to scale the steep slope which would probably prove a tough challenge.
14534: It was really a bad idea to take that last step, you think to yourself after falling to the bottom of the cliff. At first you think you must be pretty lucky, since you seem to be unhurt after falling all the way down and landing on your back. Then however you discover that there is no ground beneath you, and you finally see the long, sharp rock exiting your body through your chest.
14535:
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A cute rabbit is here.

The hills here run above the once-mighty River Sirannon. They are high enough, in fact, as to not be able to enter it from here without a short climb down to it. To the west, the riverbed runs its course towards the sea, becoming smaller and smaller until it is just a ribbon running into the horizon. The terrain far to the east is dominated by Caradhras, Celebdil, and Fanuidhol, the ominous mountains of Moria.
14536: The hills here are fairly grassy, perhaps not as foliated as they might have been in days of old. Still, there is a reasonably generous amount of vegetation to be seen around you, despite the fact that the soil seems to be not terribly The terrain to the north of the river looks much more lush from here, even in the shadow of the mountains of Moria.
14537: Overlooking the Sirannon here, is a rocky ledge jutting out from the rugged terrain and over the river, the work of years of erosion and weathering. Those who possess a fear of heights are very uneasy here, as it is a long way down to the base of this cliff of sorts. Still, the view is quite nice indeed, if you can avoid looking down behind you.
14538: The tiny stream bends here, continuing to the east and north, winding its sparkling ribbon through the Hollin countryside.
