16252: A sheer granite incline stands westwards preventing any lateral movement along the ridge, but a rectangular cut in the rock allows a limited access onto the precarious rock spire above. Eastwards the Redhorn pass crosses the ridge and makes a descent into the Dale below.
16253: Standing amidst the austere mountains of Moria, this narrow spire allows a wide and sweeping view of the surrounding areas. Northwards can be seen the Redhorn Pass as it creeps around Caradhras and climbs into the Dimrill Dale in the south. Far to the south, Moria's eastern gate can be seen emerging from the rock face.
16254: Shards of scree and broken rock cover this precarious ascent. Occasionally, small rocks will fall lazily down the slope gathering at the bottom. A sheer cliff looming over the slope prevents any further travel to the west but it is possible to move laterally along the ridge by going north.
16255: The bottom of this steep-sided rocky hollow has become filled by masses of jagged stones of all sizes. Even a few boulders have tumbled here from the craggy mountain-sides above. With near vertical ascents to the east and west, the only ways out of this hollow are to scale its rather gentler northern slope, or to continue south, in the hope of finding an alternative egress.
16256:
A pool with many big pieces of ice floating in it is here.
Calarion the Elf, wielding a broadsword, is standing here.
A large warhorse is standing here, clad in mail.

The cross-section of the cave is like a squashed circle. The floor is fairly flat, whilst the walls and roof describe a low, sweeping curve. The cold, hard stone is scarred by numerous tiny cracks and fissures, and through these quite a considerable quantity of water seeps, and it is at this end of the cave that it has pooled, running down the very slight incline of the ground.
16257:
A grizzly cub is here, snarling loudly.
A grizzly cub is here, fighting Calarion.
A grizzly bear is here, fighting Calarion.
Calarion the Elf, wielding a broadsword, is here, fighting a grizzly cub.
A large warhorse is standing here, clad in mail.

The cave is at its widest here, narrowing to little more than a tunnel at either extremity. The roof, however, remains fairly low above your head. Tiny rivulets of water seep though innumerable narrow cracks in the walls. The water then gathers, tricking across the slightly sloped floor of the cave to form a pool at one end.
16258:
A large pile of boulders is sitting here, probably debris from a rockslide.
Radikas the Dwarf (rd), wielding the Hammer of Belegost, is standing here.
Dan the Half-Elf, wielding a bejewelled oak staff, is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

A wide, round hole punctures the low roof of the cave, and immediately beneath this stands a large pile of rocks, boulders and rubble, which must have fallen into the cavern to make the aperture. The stone of the walls and of the ceiling offers a clue as to how the hole was made, for they are almost covered in a network of cracks and fissues, suggesting an inherent instability in the groundrock of this immediate area.
16259:
Radikas the Dwarf (rd), wielding the Hammer of Belegost, is standing here.
Dan the Half-Elf, wielding a bejewelled oak staff, is standing here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Ringed about by steep cliffs and mountain peaks is a small, secluded meadow. The land rises steeply from its centre toward the rock faces, leaving only a comparatively small area which is flat enough to support vegetation, but this area is surprisingly rich. Tiny wildflowers spring up amid thin grass, and even a few small bushes and shrubs grow here. Not far from one of the walls of the basin a large round hole lets down into a cavern below.
16260: Golden, brown alpine grass and purple flowered heather grow amidst dolemite protrusions as the rocky soil prohibits any more plant life. Westwards, the ground slopes down toward a scree slope, whilst to the north the ridge continues its ascent across the flanks of Celebdil. To the south the slope falls abruptly into a shadowy valley far below.
16261: Giant slabs of talus litter the ground making footing uneasy. A mild slope runs westward up onto the scree sides of Celebdil. The scent of rich earth and wildflowers drifts from the east, where a low ridge rises, dropping sharply to the south into a shadowy dale.
16262: Weatherworn, lichen-coated slabs of talus lie scattered on the banks of this dale. Running down from the diminishing western ridge, this slope comes to an end as it gently meanders to the bottom of the valley. A few wildflowers grow here in the cracks filled with soil.
16263: A large marmot is here, scurrying in between the rocks.

The wide, multi-coloured rocks lay scattered on the ground, the product of a recent slide off of Celebdil. Glimpses of brown, dead grass can be seen under the stone revealing that this was once a grassy field. Several large clawed footprints are amidst, all seemingly gathered near a particularly large stone.
16264: A big cavebear is padding around here.

The thick scent of damp earth and decay is overwhelming. Scattered bones lie across the floor, stripped of their meat and bleached with age. Large, clawed footprints design the muddy floor and reveal this to be the dwelling of some large animal.
16265: The footing upon this narrow ridge is decidedly unsteady. Wind and rain, ice and snow have all taken their toll on the rocks, and repeated seasons of freezing and thawing have led to immense cracks, with massive slabs of stone shearing off the ridge and smaller debris creating extensive scree fields in the area. To the northwest the ridge becomes completely impassable, but to the south it appears rather safe.
16266: A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.

Low and rocky, this saddle point in the ridgeline nevertheless supports some stunted shubs and a few wildflowers, perhaps due to its sheltered location between several higher areas. A trail once passed along this ridge, climbing from the north, but it peters out as the land rises east of here.
16267: At the End of the Strange Trail

You find yourself upon a strange old trail, which travels a winding path through the mountain crags, climbing steadily toward the south. It is in a terrible state, with cracks leading from the ground up the surrounding walls, and the floor itself is littered with rocks and stones.
16268:
A large shrub grows here, its branches loosely spreading.
A porcupine is waddling around here, its tail full of sharp quills.

Rows of sunflower plants cover almost a mile of this area. When in bloom, the bright orange and gold flowers are almost the twice the length of a hobbit's foot. They provide shade for the small animals that graze on their stalks. Some small stones dot the ground but, for the most part the soil is soft and rich in nutrients. If this basin was not kept secret by the mountainous surroundings, some farmer would have surely claimed it for crops.
16269: This is the northernmost of a trio of mountains reaching far in to the sky. From here looking directly south or at an angle to the southeast one can see straight across to the other two, however, the clouds obscure the very top of these triple peaks. The air is thin yet moist from the cloudy fog that seems to cling to the peaks.
16270: A large eagle soars above you.

As sharp as the cuts in these cliffs are, it is surprising they are home to so much greenery. The blue-green grasses give these cliffs an almost royal cloak. Some large rocks could be mistaken for thrones on which one could sit or stand tall shouting hollow proclamations into the valley below to the east.
16271: A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

Nestled in between two large groups of mountains, this plateau is far above sea-level. Bordered to the south and east by mountainside and to the west by cliffs, this area appears to be safe from anything except that which would drop from the sky. The low vine-like grass from the spread from the north covers the ground. It grows a bit higher here and often catches the footsteps of travellers only long enough for the thin roots to snap.
16272: Tall fir trees cover the top of this mountain. Their prickly evergreen leaves cut the strong northern winds that often blow soil and stray branches or sometimes even small trees to the south. Sparser than those trees to the north, a traveller through these parts could look and see the sky.
16273: A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

Trees almost thick enough to be a forest grow here in natural lines. They stretch up tall into the sky adding to the mountain's height. Evergreen, they have long trunks with few branches. The branches that do grow get shorter the farther up the tree they grow. The ground beneath must have soil cover enough to house the roots of these trees, as none poke out through the ground.
16274: A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.

The tall evergreen trees obscure the view of the surrounding mountains. If not for the thinner air and the occasional fog from a low lying cloud one might think this place is a lowland forest rather than a high mountain peak. The sound of water rushing over rock can be heard coming from the north.
16275: The flow of the shallow water is so constant that it almost looks calm. A falling leaf into the stream quickly shows otherwise. The current is quick and its facade of serenity most deceiving. Travellers should take care not to let their valuables fall into the stream lest they be swept away.
16276: Rocks of various sizes piled one on top of another make up the ground. High winds blowing down from the towering peaks to the west, over time, have sent tons of rock, dirt and whole cliffs crashing down to these lower bluffs. Small animals have tunnelled through the spaces between these materials. They build homes that are often destroyed as quickly as it takes another rock to fall.
16277: Clumps of dirt cling to rocks embedded in the ground. Small animals are able to weave between the narrow gaps between the stones. Tufts of fur and the occasional mark of dried blood and torn skin serve as a reminder that travel here can be perilous if not taken slowly. A few scattered shrubs grow in the shaded shelter of some of the larger rocks. Some flowering weeds give the ground a touch of a colour other than brown dirt and the grey of the stone.
16278: The ground here appears somewhat level, forming a small eroding plateau which crumbles at the southeast edge. From this low rocky rise one can look up at the higher peaks to the northwest or down onto a rushing stream of water to the southeast. Some wheat grasses have taken seed and grown close to a foot tall. This secluded plateau seems to be a haven compared to the otherwise rocky and treacherous terrain.
16279: The ground slopes upward and eastward. The air thins the higher one travels. There are some scattered weeds growing in the shelter of some large rocks, however very little grass survives in this rocky terrain. Dirt and shards of rock crumble under the footsteps of travellers.
16280: Shade trees grow here in the shadow of the western mountain range. Tall elm trees with their large branches rise above smaller red maple and weeping willow trees. Among the branches are the nests of birds, some in use, others left abandoned for seasons. A soft thin layer of grass covers the ground.
16281: Rushing out of a narrow gully to the west, Nimrodel now enters a wider and less rocky channel. The line of cliffs which has marked the southern bounds of the watercourse are now descending rapidly, and a second stream can be seen in the distance, flowing toward a confluence with this brook. To the north the valley is quite open, and the immediate area offers a gently sloping, grassy shoreline.
16282: In a Valley along a Stream

Sloping down gently towards a stream, which sweeps here from the west to the north, the land is beginning to gain a fertility which is absent further up the valley. Though the topsoil is thin, it is well-watered, and a variety of tiny wildflowers nestle among a thin carpet of grass. Rocks and stones have tumbled here and there, but there are fewer here than there are closer to the cliffs and ridges of the region.
16283: The land climbs steadily to the west, as it advances toward the mountains. Immediately to the north a long ridgeline rises above you, a steep cliff face offering the most direct route from here to its spine. The land here bears blemishes from these slopes, being littered with sharp stones, the debris of many past rockslides.
16284: In a Valley along a Stream

Jutting out into the path of the stream to the south, the valley floor here is comprised of a broad table of solid granite. Tilted like the rest of the surrounding land, it too slopes upward to the west and the north, following the general contour of the vale in which it stands. The vast flat plate of stone, with only the sparest covering of topsoil means that very few plants manage to grow here.
16285: Flowing through a narrow gully, defined by the cliffs to the south, and a large, protruding table of rock, which juts into the channel from the north, Nimrodel is deep and very fast-flowing here. The presence of many large, sharp-sided boulders beneath the rushing waters makes negotiating the area quite troublesome. Many others break the surface, leading to a profusion of foamy white caps.
16287: The road begins a steep descent into the dale below. Broken rock and pavement litter the path, making travel precarious. To the east are many sparkling cascades flowing into a dark mere. The northern direction reveals only the endless sky of mountains, occasionally peaked with a glittering glacier. The thick scent of earth becomes prominent as the road breaks down into a muddy, rocky path to the south.
16288: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

This ancient, once paved road has turned into a steep muddy path from years of negligence. Water seeping down from the Dimrill Stair and Naragul destroyed this particular section. Westwards begins a rocky ascent onto the side of Celebdil. To the south is a rich, grassy field littered with wildflowers and rocks. The trail makes a bend here to the east, then runs parallel to long tarn.
16289: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

Sharp rock fragments lie scattered across the road. Purple flowered heather lines the roadside, the only thing growing in this stony turf. Eastwards lies a deep, long, tarn. Its midnight waters reflect the shining peak of Celebdil to the west. The path follows the tarn to the south or continues northwards onto a muddy trail.
16290: Stunted birches and scraggy pines attempt to grow in between the rocks along the roadside. This broken road reveals that is was once a well-travelled path by the scattered slabs of pavement and its wide nature. It continues into the mountains to the north, and through the dale to the south.
16291: A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

Dwarven works of stone lay ruined along the roadside. Moss and lichen flourish on these decaying statues. The path continues up into the mountains north, and runs out of the dale to the south. To the east you can see a dark mere.
16292: Here the track which borders the smooth, dark lake to the northeast is met by a stone road descending from the south. There is ruined dwarven stone-work all around. Dark, sad pines border the track. Westwards, the grassy field meets the base of Celebdil.
16293: A Path by a Standing Stone

A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

Tracing a path not far from the long, oval lake, the narrow trail makes an westward bend here, drawing closer to the water. Not far from the roadside, at the bottom of a long, grassy slope, a tall standing stone can be seen, just by the shore of the Mirrormere.
16294: The Trail out of the Valley

Climbing downward, between the arms of the dale, the path now makes its way past the end of the Mirrormere, and bends to the east, away from Silvertine, and round the base of Cloudyhead. Some distance to the east you can make out the bright sound of a lively stream.
16305: A Trail through the Jade Trees

A forest spider is here crawling around.
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.
A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

A canopy of high branches covers this portion of the trail. While the trees are younger than others of this region it would still take three elves, standing with their feet on each other's shoulders, to touch the mossy green branches or deep green leaves. During the day, the rays of sun, managing to seep through the veil of green, create emerald streams of light that illuminate the trail.
16306: A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

Through years of use and the constant pounding of footsteps, the hoofs of horses and the erosion of time, this trail has been carved into the landscape. So beaten down is the soil that it has solidified into a thick unmoldable clay. Bordering the roadway, large trees stretch up towards the heavens.
16307: The ground of the trail lies lower than the forested land on either side as if the trail was carved out by some hand from the heavens. The long jagged scratches that run its length are deep and the ground is so hard it would take insurmountable weight to flatten them back out.
16308: A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

Not a single blade of grass pokes through the hard soil that makes up this trail. The dark brown soil is more like molded clay than dirt. It has the consistency of mud that has been petrified. With a sharp sword one might be able to scrape away at the trail. From the looks of it, however, the sword might be dented in the process. On the eastern side of the trail, a grove of ancient knotted trees yawn eerily overhead.
16309: Set about a foot lower than the surrounding land this trail seems to have been carved out long before the trees that grow along its sides were even saplings. Now the tall tree roots are all that burst through the trail's hard clay. The trail carries on to the north and to the west.
16310: A stone mason carving a block of granite might have tools that could carve a deep trail such as this. A foot into the surrounding land this trail is made of hard clay. Long ago the ground must have been softer and more easily molded as deep scars have been cut into the length of the trail. The ground is now hard and unyielding.
16311: Towering cliffs surround the trail here to the east and the west. Try as one might it would be impossible to scale them and reach the lands above. The crumbled rock and soil eroded from the cliffs above litter the ground here giving it a speckled appearance. Some larger pieces of cliff have also fallen and are wedged deep into the ground.
16312: Much narrower than the trail to the south, this part of the trail is tucked between tall cliffs to the east and west. Rocks, having fallen from above, litter the trail. While many things have been known to fall from the lands above, reaching those lands above from this part of the trail would be impossible even for the greatest climber.
16313: This old trail seems to have been carved out of the ground. It sits a few feet into the surrounding land. It is plausible to think that this hard clay lies below all the surrounding pastures. This might explain the lack of vegetation that would grow deeper than a few inches into the soil. To the north, the trail narrows as it leads into the mountains.
16314: This far stretching trail seems to lead in one direction toward the mountains to the north. In the other, it winds through the hills and meadowlands. Etched into the ground at least two feet not a stray seed can break the surface to take root. The hard clay trail is almost impossible to mar.
16315: The wild grasses in the meadow to the south barely encroach upon this deeply cut trail. Strewn seedlings that are blown on the wind merely sit upon the trail's hard surface unable to penetrate what once was dirt but over centuries has hardened to become clay the density of rock.
16316: This hardened trail is much rougher on the hoofs of horses than the surrounding lands. The lack of vegetation however makes it more easily passable than cutting through the meadowlands. So hard is the ground it may be mistaken for rock. Continuing east and west it is clearly well used and fit for travelling.
16317: From here the trail continues miles to the east and just as far southward. It appears to be carved a few feet into the ground. Deep scratches indicate a great force etched it into the ground, removing the fertile soil and leaving this hard, clay layer exposed.
16318: The ground of the trail is a little more malleable in these parts than it is farther to the east. Depressions in the thick clay sometimes reveal hoof prints and the heel prints of some travellers on foot. Those choosing to tread lightly could easily avoid leaving any impressions. The trail appears to end here however, fading into the western prairie.
16319: The tall wheat grass, that grows undisturbed elsewhere, seems to have a fierce enemy in those that travel here. Wanderers off a westerly trail have trampled the grains and cleared large portions when hastily making camp. Ashes of campfires litter the ground. These scattered barren spots where fires were lit long ago are starting to show some little signs of being reclaimed by the sea of grain.
16320:
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.
A woodchuck is watching for enemies here.

Grains the colour of the burning sun stretch for miles. Their tall stems sway with the wind as it blows. They bow and bend as even the smallest of insects land upon their single stalks. The ground, three feet below their golden tips, is littered with the remnants of the previous seasons' growth.
16321: A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

Scattered rocks and clumps of dirt lie in these mountain foothills. A few sturdy plants have managed to grow in the uneven and ever-shifting terrain. Fresh layers of rock and dirt that fall from the higher peaks, often strike dry dirt, kicking it up into the air.
16322: This thin ledge can be followed up and down the western side of the mountain. A few hundred feet wide, it allows travellers an easier way to traverse the steep mountainside. Rocks, clumps of dirt and vegetation have fallen from the upper cliffs and lie here embedded deep into the ground.
16323: Jagged and sharp are the best words to describe the rocks jutting out from this mountain slope. A fallen tree has impaled itself on one of the larger shards of rock. One can imagine the force at which it must have fallen. Its trunk is now split in two, with the sharp point of the rock still exposed.
16324: This mountain is the perfect companion of its mate to the northeast. Both are the perfect places to gaze at the work of Tintalle the Kindler, the creator of the stars. Her husband Manwe, master of air and weather, must think this a good place to honour her as well because the weather here is milder than in the surrounding areas and rarely does a cloud block the view of his beloved's artistry.
16325: This shelf is so narrow that travellers must pass here in single file. Battle here would be very treacherous, as there is no place to hide and only two ways to run, and the choice between the high summit to the north or the dangerous cliffs to the east would fill those in a panic with equal dismay. There are a few crevices in the mountain wall that might provide one with a place to hide but for the briefest period of time.
16326: This flat parcel of land is nestled between a mountain summit and a steep drop downward. The ground is dark brown dirt and in some places is flecked with bits of grey materials that look like ashes. There are some sporadic patches of grass and a few stray bushes.
16327: At the apex of this western mountain, one can look straight across to the lower peaks in the east. On a clear day even a glimpse of the far off meadowlands can be gleamed. The air here is thin and clean with a scent that can only be described as resembling the air after a fresh spring rain.
16328:
A small flower grows here, with a purple bloom and wide leaves.
A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

Nestled within the protection of the mountains, this fertile basin is home to a plentiful variety of plants and animals. Shaded from the sun at all times but noon the air here is cool and crisp. Because of its secluded location, this basin has barely been touched. Had it been seen by many, surely some farmer would wish to cultivate this place.
16329: For miles westward, the only way to travel is upward. The land makes a quick shift from rolling hills to steep rising mountains that hinder travellers' passage. Shards of rock, broken off the high cliffs, lie here, embedded deep in the ground by the force of their fall.
16330: A few small rocks are trapped in the clay that forms the trail. At some point this hardened ground must have been soft enough for the rocks to penetrate the surface. Now, not even the heaviest rider on the largest steed would make any imprint in this hard surface.
16331: As if it was a carved moat, dug two feet deep in the ground, this sunken clay trail serves to divide these fertile grasslands. Ridges of the hard clay line either side of the trail here about ankle high. These ridges and the lack of nutrients in the clay to nurture plant life keeps the vegetation from encroaching upon the trail.
16332: When this volcano erupted, a pool of lava filled the inner cavern to the west. It gathered there, pushing out in all directions. Some of the rock on the western edge of this area gave way, sending lava crashing eastward and creating this corridor. Since then, the weight of the mountain above has born down on this point, causing much of the area to be filled with charred and broken rock.
16333:
A sturdy rope has been tied here and descends to the east.
A mother eagle is sleeping here.
Alexia the Half-Elf, wielding a double edged eket, is standing here.

A cloudy haze engulfs this summit. Oblivious to the changing of the seasons, snowflakes lie upon the ground. Towards the centre of the summit a long jagged ridge comes to halt in the form of a great crack in the ground. More than large enough for a man to enter, this opening in the earth seems to delve down into this mountain's secrets.
16334:
A pair of rigid leather boots are on the ground.
A sturdy leather backpack has been left here.
There is a water skin lying on the ground.
A coil of rope is lying here.

Only a little light passes through the entrance to this small crack in the mountainside. The remnants of fires that were probably made by those who found this quiet place to rest from their arduous climb, cover the ground. Several sketches have been carved into the stone mountain wall.
16335: Flowing through small cracks and fissures in the rock of the cliff faces, numerous tiny rivulets gather here, to form the beginnings of a mountain stream. The main channel, which flows in from the northwest, does so along a most narrow and steeply sloped notch between the cliffs, which is quite impassable for any person.
16336: At the Top of a Precipice

A narrow strip of sloping land runs down from a high mesa towards the top of a soaring cliff. As crisp and sharp as a knife edge, the margin of these highlands stretches off to the west, and sweeps round to the northeast, but the terrain quickly becomes broken and uneven, and undoubtedly quite unsafe for travel.
16337: A long, narrow plateau stretches out to the east, like a vast table-top. Far above the floor of the valley below, it is an area of some seclusion, and the higher mountain peaks and ridges hereabouts make it quite well hidden. To the south the land falls off quite rapidly, as it approaches the top of a mighty cliff.
16338: A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.

You find yourself upon a long, narrow plateau, which rises high above the surrounding lands. Hidden as it is, at a high elevation, and sheltered from view by so many mountain peaks and ridges, it is a comparitively quiet and undisturbed area. As flat as a table-top, it stretches away to the west, and near its centre a small body of water nourishes its soils.
16339: The strange route has broken off from the path to the north and runs north-east here, winding among the rocks and the boulders. It is not marked in any way and rather hard to follow, and it seems that any rockslide could make it disappear altogether.
16340: A small concealed path cuts through the mountain range, enshrouded by the high rockfaces and completely hidden from view. A small rocky ledge sprouts to the north. South lies an area which you really can't seem to make out. A trail begins just to the east, and part of this path is to the west.
16341: A small rocky ledge juts out from the path, curving alongside the mountain and providing a narrow walking space for the curious. The ledge continues to the north, and you can also go back to the path which lies just to the south.
16342: The trail continues onwards stretching from east to west. There is not much to see except the small stones and pebbles that line the floor. Your vision is completely blocked by the rock walls that surround the trail. A crisp and fresh scent is carried on the air by the mountain wind.
16343: The ledge here has been broken in many places. Great pieces of rock are missing at various points of the walkway making it a treacherous climb. With great care and difficulty the ledge can still be compromised but its condition is far from safe. One must tread with care!
16344: This is a deep ravine, and as you peer from side to side only tall steep slopes meet your gaze. As you plod on along the bottom the sounds of footsteps are echoed through the ravine. You can follow it to the north or to the east.
16345: A huge stone giant is here, glaring at you.
A deep and winding ravine is here in the mountains. Both sides of the ravine are extremely steep and unclimable. The only roadworthy route is along the bottom of the ravine, it goes north and south.
16346: Steep walls overshadow you to the south, the east and the west, whilst to the north this scree-filled hollow stretches out before you. The ground beneath your feet is extremely treacherous, since the rocks and stones seem to shift and slide with your every movement. Yet even here there is a little vegetation. Tiny weeds poke their heads tenaciously through the rocky floor, a mute testament to the faceless will of life to find a way to survive.
16347: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Bright pansies and purple flowered gentians provide variation to the wide, grassy field. Westwards, the terrain becomes rockier as a talus slide has covered the ground. A rough path, littered with broken pavement, runs north and south at the far side of the meadow, beside the shore of the lake.
16348: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

Various fragrances of wild flowers, and the rich scent of the black soil in which they flourish, dominates the air. Carmine orchids and bright, purple gentians dot the flowing meadow as it continues to the south and west. Not far to the east a path marks the route through the valley, and just beyond it lie the shores of the Mirrormere.
16350: Moria's eastern gate stands proudly at the top of this aged, marble stair. Emerging from the jagged rock face its fine sculpture and strong columns hint at the former Dwarven kingdom's majesty. The gleaming glacier capped mountains of Celebdil, Fanuidhol, and Caradhras dominate the sky line. Northwards, cradled between two jagged ridges, lies a shadowy dale. At its northern point can be seen a dark, oval mere. To the east the mountains level out into a rolling forest.
16351: On the Slopes of a Rising Ridge

A lofty peak looms high above you to the south, quite unscalable from this point. However, by following the land as it rises to the west you can attain the top of a long ridgeline, which cuts across the countryside from northwest to southeast, and which appears to climb toward summit. By descending the more gentle slope to the east you would find yourself at the southern end of the Mirrormere.
16352: Though not one of the highest peaks in the Misty Mountains, this mountaintop nevertheless affords a spectacular view of the surrounding lands. To the north- west stand mighty Celebdil and Caradhras and to the northeast Fanuidhol is the dominant feature. Due east, and far below you, lies the vast expanse of the Golden Wood, spanning the Silverlode, and reaching far into the distance.
16353: Near vertical in places, this section of the ridgeline is extremely steep and treacherous. Although eastward the terrain becomes easier to travel, to the north it becomes steeper still, demanding that anyone who wishes to journey from here to the mountain peak resort to climbing.
16354:
A huge, poisonous spider is here.
A huge, poisonous spider is here.
A huge, poisonous spider is here.

Cracks and fissures criss-cross the walls and floor of this cavern, making a pattern that looks like nothing so much as giant spider webs. But the webs which are strung across the chamber itself are no illusion. A noisome smell pervades the place, and the remains of many creatures, some small, and others not so small, litter the ground.
16355: A natural fault line in the rock of the cliffs has been eroded and enlarged by centuries of dripping water. The walls of the resulting tunnel meet at a point quite far above your head, but even at floor level the passage is not wide, so that anyone particularly tall would find their shoulders brushing against the cold, hard stone. Whilst to the south the channel gets no wider, to the north it begins to open out into a larger cavern.
16356: At the Head of the Valley

Nestled between two commanding cliff-faces, which meet in an almost perfect vee at the western end of the valley, a narrow mountain vale opens out before you. Eastward it rolls down from the mountains, toward the lowlands of the Great River and the mighty forest of Lothlorien. But here, amid the rocks and boulders of this craggy land, only a little vegetation manages to survive.
16357: Some sort of a natural cataclysm must have visited this section of the ridge, for the sharp saddle has been reduced to a wider, flatter table, rimmed by steep, crumbling walls. The ground is a little lower here than it is further east along the ridge, and progress further westward, as well as climbing down from the ridge either to the north or to the south, has been rendered quite impossible by the highly unstable, crumbling walls of this small basin.
16358: Sheer drop-offs to either side make progress along this steep ridge rather perilous. However, the elevation of the lands below you to the south is rather greater than that of the valley lying north, and it might be possible to make the southerly descent in safety. Westward the path becomes steeper, and the ground appears to be more scarred by cracks and fissures.
16359: The valley becomes ever more narrow as it climbs west into the arms of the mountains. Sheer walls, quite unclimable due to their weak, crumbling stone, rear up before you to the south, whilst to the east the landscape opens out as it loses altitude. The ground about you is littered with rocks and stones, which stand out like an archipelago, amid a sea of thin grass.
16360: Steep walls sweep around you to the north and west, confining the valley. The ground here is rather poor, with numerous rocks and boulders littering the valley floor, but to the south and especially to the west, where the valley opens out and loses altitude, the land seems to be at least a little richer and less rocky.
16361: A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.

Climbing higher here than it did further to the east, the ridgeline also describes a curve to the northwest, reaching steadily toward a mountain peak. Far below you, at the bottom of a vertical cliff, you can see a narrow valley, which makes a steady ascent into the mountains to the west. And east of here the ridge stretches out before you.
16362: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

From the southeast to the northwest the craggy ridge makes its way steadily towards a lofty pinnacle. Far below you lie the southern reaches of the Dimrill Dale, and in the distance the shimmering waters of the Mirrormere dominate the view. From here you can trek down the ridgeline to the south, or you can climb higher along it to the west.
16363: High above you the mountain slopes climb toward the summit. Although this is not one of the tallest of the Misty Mountains, it is nevertheless a formidable peak. Its sides are sheer in many places, and the crown cannot be reached by a direct assault from here, but only by traversing one of the prominent ridges, which cut across the land from the northwest to the southeast.
16364: A large marmot is here, scurrying in between the rocks.

The terrain here is fairly steep, and travelling across it is not made any easier by the fact that loose rocks and stones are scattered all around, making your footing decidedly uncertain. West and south the land climbs up toward the mountains, but to the east and north you can make your way into the southern end of a long valley.
16365: The ground climbs briskly to the west, as it reaches into the mountains, but eastward it falls away toward a vale. Between valley and peaks lies a land littered by innumerable stones, and a few larger boulders, the products of rockslides from above. But all around this debris green grass and myriad tiny wildflowers flourish, despite the sloping ground.
16366: Rocks and stone litter the ground all about you, but between them a thin carpet of short, green grass grows. Here and there tiny wildflowers peep up through the green stalks, lending new colours to the tapestry of green and grey. Descending eastward from the mountains, this wide expanse is bordered by a rocky trail, which itself traces its route from the path of a lively little stream.
16367: Standing north of a pleasant little valley, this ridge cuts a swath across the land from east to west. Further north the land falls away gently toward the southern end of the Dimrill Dale, and in the distance the landscape is dominated by a large oval lake, which nestles in the valley floor, between the arms of Celebdil and Fanuidhol.
16368: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

Bordered to the north and south by the sprawling arms of two mountain ridges, this narrow valley offers a refuge for all manner of wildlife. Wildflowers and a few small shrubs grow on the sloping ground, and the short-cropped grasses attest to the existence here of a variety of animals.
16369:
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

Narrow and sloping, confined to the north and south by craggy ridges, the valley floor rises steadily to the west, where it climbs to the base of one of the Misty Mountains. Though not the tallest peak by far, this lofty eminence nevertheless casts long shadows across the entire vale for much of the day, and sunset must come early to this land.
16370: Crumbling and rocky, this narrow ridge makes its rather precarious way from east to west, where it ascends into the mountains. The terrain has something of the look of a path, but either it is one which has long since fallen into disuse, or perhaps it is nothing more than a game trail. Whichever is true, the fact remains that this is no longer an easy route to travel.
16371: Stretching from east to west, a long ridge runs like a scar across the land just north of here. Southward the ground slopes gently down toward the banks of a lively stream, whose waters enable even such poor and rocky terrain as this to support a variety of vegetation. Although in this immediate area it is largely restricted to grasses and wildflowers, further to the east some bushes and shrubs begin to take hold, marking the very outskirts of a forest.
16372: Fed by the waters of a southern tributary, Nimrodel has gained in stature when compared to her earlier reaches. But she remains a rather small and very shallow waterway, which could easily be forded at most points. Here the stream travels through an area of fairly craggy land, and this has made her channel quite rocky, but the waters roll gently past the obstructions, since the current is quite sedate.
16373: At a Confluence of Two Streams

A major tributary flows into Nimrodel from the south here, their waters merging into a lively, but still rather shallow stream. Sweeping from east to north, the beck curves gracefully past the outskirts of a forest, which stand on slightly higher ground, then the stream travels on northwestward, toward an eventual confluence with the far mightier Celebrant.
16374:
A hairy black spider wraps up a silken package with her hind legs.
A hairy black spider wraps up a silken package with her hind legs.
A hairy black spider wraps up a silken package with her hind legs.

The fast, steady flow of the water cleanses away the dust and dirt from the banks. Some such materials gather here. Travellers should be wary not to be tripped up by the swift current as they cross into the trees to the east, gazing into what treasures may have been carried to this shimmering rock bed.
16375: Tranquil in appearance, these waters are anything but still. The quick current flows amazingly steady hence the deception. The silver rocks that line the riverbed do not move in the current. They merely stick firm into the clay below and let the water wear them down. The stream stretches on to the north and west.
16376: Water, as crystal clear as fine blown glass, flows here at a very constant pace. At first glance the water looks still and calm, yet it truly does flow as quick as blood through veins. Should it not flow so swiftly, leaves and dirt would gather in such masses that this water would not be fit to drink.
16377: Not fields of gold, nor forests of green, compare in brilliance to the silver shine of this rivulet. In day, the sun highlights its wonder. At night, the moon's light gives the rocky stream such a glow it almost lights the surrounding area. Travellers might see a magical quality in this water, but alas it is only nature's beauty. The rivulet continues on to the east and south.
16378: Glistening grey rocks seem to line the ground under this shallow stream. Water, barely two feet deep, does nothing to diminish the shimmering tone. A few rocks that have been tossed out of the stream by whatever means, show these stones to me no more than ordinary. Water spilled outside the riverbed does not glisten with the same brilliance. Only together do these two elements form such a beautiful silvery illusion.
16379:
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.

The stream makes a turn to the north here. While the change in direction is subtle, it is enough to kick up some of the silvery rocks that line the riverbed. They lie like fish out of water, craving the rare splashes of water that might keep them from drying out and losing their luminescence.
16380: High above the much used trail to the east, this is a good place to survey the surrounding lands. Towards the eastern edge the land is badly eroded and jagged edges have formed from pieces of this ground falling down the cliff to the trail below. An adventurous traveller could travel down the same way but returning to this surface would be impossible.
16381: Shadowed in the afternoons by the tall mountains in the west, this high place itself shadows the narrow trail below to the east. The ground is smooth, having been worn away by wind. The eastern edge is frayed from wind shear and pieces of this precipice have fallen to the ground below.
16382: Within sight of the etched trail that runs to the east and south, this area is a stark contrast to the grasslands on the trail's opposing side. The ground is uneven and rocky, having collected the droppings of rock, dirt and other debris from the mountains above.
16383: A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.

Tufts of black fur are stuck to low portions of the trees. The coarse black fur seems to have been left by creatures merely wanting to scratch their backs against the rough bark. The tree-lined mountaintops stretch on to the north and south.
16384: Rocks, dirt and hay have collected to form this ground, either blown off the mountain peaks or across the trail to the south. Some rocks have been pressed deep into the soil from the speed at which they fell from high cliffs.
16385: A small cluster of clover grows here.

While still touching the lower clouds, this mountain is far lower than the three to the west. It looks almost like a child in comparison to them. Not nearly as impressive, it does boast a burgeoning plant life. A few areas of clover provide a soft green cover to the ground. Some wild daisies grow adding their white and gold brilliance to the scene.
16386: These foothills run from farther north and continue southwest. They appear to be the last resting spot for travellers from the east. A few shrubs are the only plant life, a stark contrast to the fertile fields to the east. The sunlight disappears right after noon, when the sun shifts to the western horizon and is blocked by the towering mountainside.
16387: Rocks that have fallen from high peaks and the imposing shadow of the mountains, seek to dissuade travellers from continuing westward. Deep cuts into the soft dirt between the rocks show evidence that this land is passable. A few small plants, barely more than seedlings with a few days growth, are the only vegetation.
16388: From here, the base of the mountains, it is impossible to see at the height to which these mountains rise. When looking up and to the west, the colossal mounds block even the sky. In the afternoon, no sunlight touches these foothills. Only a few bushes, adapted to the shade, manage to grow.
16389: A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

In the shadows of the mountains, these foothills see little unfiltered sunlight. The ground is strewn with rocks and dirt that the wind has swept from the high peaks. A few stray grasses and shrubs have managed to grow here despite the inconsistent terrain.
16390: High in the clouds, the air surrounding this mountain peak is thin but not clear. The clouds, that hang about this summit, create a light fog. If not for the fog, from this high place one could see the entire mountain range and perhaps even into the meadows and prairie lands below. Breaking through the misty haze are the tops of trees that disappear once more when covered by higher clouds. This appears to be one of several peaks atop a large mountain base.
16391: A large shrub grows here, its branches loosely spreading.

Teeming with life, this hidden basin seems to be a well kept secret from those who might want to clear away the beautiful wild flowers and grasses to plant crops. The fertile land lies practically untouched. Only a few wanderers through the mountains might stumble upon this place accidentally.
16392:
A large thorny branched shrub is growing here.
An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Flowers of violet and crimson fill this part of the basin. Their vibrant colour dominates over the pale green grasses. Some birch trees stand tall in groups of two or three. The white colour of their peeling bark accents the light airy feel of this plentiful place. Several berry bushes add to the scene and provide food for some native animals.
16393: The dark brown dirt on the ground is mixed with light grey ashes giving it a speckled look. Some unusual small plants grow barely a boot tip high off the ground. Their tiny leaves almost resemble clover and they cover the ground much in the same way. Some of the ash has separated from the dirt and lies upon the plant cover.
16394: A large eagle soars above you.

A painter would be hard pressed to capture the perfect blend of blue and green that makes up the colour of this thick grass. The shade is one that would have been saved only for use on portraits commissioned by great lords of the land. It covers the jagged cliffs here in defiance of any caste system showing its beauty to all that pass through this place.
16395: Between the slopes of two of the taller western mountain peaks, this pass does little else but provide a resting place for those weary of climbing. At first glance it often appears to weave through the mountains providing an easier route than to climb. However, following the pass westward only leads to a steep mountainside that must be climbed.
16396: Tintalle the Kindler, the creator of the stars, best known as Elbereth Gilthoniel, might consider this mountain a good place to pay tribute to her greatness. Each night, from atop this celestial peak one can gaze at the splendour of her creations. The calm night air at this lofty height allows humbled stargazers the freedom to meditate on the tales told by the constellations.
16397: This narrow ledge is kinder on travellers than other parts of the mountainside, since the slope is not as steep. Unfortunately, this ridge meanders so much that it is difficult to tell how much distance, if any, is gained until reaching the end of the ledge. From then on the climb is arduous at best. To the east, the land slopes downward through heavy brush.
16398: The little beck begins to grow fairly rapidly as it flows eastward through the vale, gathering to itself numerous tiny runnels of water as it flows on downward. But, although it is confined to a narrow and rocky channel, it still remains very shallow, and many of the larger boulders sit clear above its sparkling and foaming surface.
16399: Near the Head of the Valley

Not far to the west the canyon walls draw so close together as to appear to meet, though the stream below you does proceed just a little further in that direction. The ground slopes upward both north and west, making it difficult to walk along the valley. Southward it falls rapidly down to the stream. Only a few tiny mountain plants can cling to life here, their roots seeking tiny fissures in the rocky slope.
16400: So steep are the walls of this narrow vale that there is virtually no flat ground upon which to travel. The cliffs loom high above you, both to the north and to the south, beyond a modest brook. Westward they draw ever closer together, as the valley climbs into the mountain heights. Little grows upon this sloping ground, since no top-soil remains to support plant life.
16401: To the north the valley opens out somewhat, but to the south the creek is flanked by steep cliffs, which rise high above it. This, however provides an extra source of waters for the stream, which is widening with every mile it travels from the western mountains. Though it remains quite shallow, the steep grade of the valley floor causes it to flow along quite briskly, and as it buffets protruding rocks and boulders, its surface is covered by white caps.
16402: Thick bushes and wild weeds that have grown as large as shrubs line this part of the narrow ridge. The large plants reduce the space in which travellers may pass through, making the abrupt ridge seem even more narrow.
16403: The rough terrain shows signs of its age. The wind has worn away much of the top soil and lashed at the mountainside. Some grasses grow scattered in the shelter of large boulders. A few flowering weeds add a bit of colour to this otherwise two-tone setting of dusty rock and weak green grass.
16404:
An apple tree with bright green leaves grows here.
On the tree's branches are three apples.
A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.
A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.
A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.

Underneath the jagged cliffs lies this hidden valley. It sits perhaps even lower in elevation than the meadowlands on the eastern side of this mountain range. Several apple trees grow here providing nourishment for some small animals. Some bushes laden with unrecognisable purple berries complement the low trees and the thin green grass.
16405: A small campfire burns here, its low flames giving off only a little light.

Thick blades of blue-green grass cover these cliffs like the thick fur of a bear. Each strand of grass is resilient to the wind and the pressures that may fall upon them. So thick is the grass, even with the rise and fall of the cliffs almost no bare soil can be seen. The deep rich colouring of these grasses gives this whole area a luxurious look.
16406:
A nest is here.
A small, helpless eaglet screams for more food.

The uneven ground is covered in wild blue-green grasses. The thick carpet is undisturbed by the rises and falls of the mountainous terrain. A sharp drop to the east descends to the lowlands. To the south the soft grass cover continues. Toward the east the constantly changing slopes of this land seem to reach a plateau.
16407: This sky-scraping peak, together with the one to the north and the one to the east, is the most recognisable facet of this mountain range. For miles to the east, the three peaks dominate the western horizon. The three towering behemoths point far into the clouds. Only on rare clear days is it possible to spot which is the tallest of these peaks that seem to share a common mountain base.
16408: About half as high as the mountains to the east, this plateau looks down upon a canyon to the north and faces steep cliffs to the west. Blades of grass attached by thin vine-like roots spread for miles. Some saplings that pushed through the tangle of grass roots have grown into fine young trees. None of the trees are tall enough to provide any shade.
16409: This odd shaped canyon connects the low land to the north with the high plateau to the south. Linear cuts in the canyon walls allow travellers to walk down into or up out of this place fairly easily. The ground and walls are made of light coloured solid rock that look as if they could support some weight.
16410:
There are two piles of wild strawberries here.
A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.
A partridge attempts to hide in the undergrowth.

In the spring, the scent of strawberries fills the air. They grow wild in clusters of ten to twelve plants, attracting many small animals hungry for the sweet fruit. The tall mountain cliffs shadow this place, making it an ideal picnic spot for rodents and travellers alike. Looking up from here one can only see about half the way up the mountainside.
16411: Descending more gently than its neighbouring slopes this terrain increases in greenery as it leads southward. Scant grasses grow thicker in that direction along with some berry laden bushes. The lands to the east and west are far more barren.
16412: A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.

This portion of mountainside resembles giant steps made from mud. Some of these natural steps are as tall as an elf, others are the height of a hobbit. They span widths between five and fifty feet between drops. The vertical portions are host to a variety of wild grasses and some hardy bushes.
16413: Hugging a steep cliff-face to the south, the brook makes its way along its rocky channel, located at the bottom of a long valley. Running from west to east, the gorge loses altitude steadily, and so the burn flows along rapidly. Its lively waters send up a constant fine spray, which hangs in the air like a very fine mist.
16414: The lie of the land is quite steep, as the valley climbs into the arms of the westerly mountains. Sloping also to the north, the ground climbs toward the base of a mighty cliff face, which rears vertically, far above your head. Not far below you, to the south, a small stream makes its way from the west to the east, flowing out of the heights.
16415: A gaping tunnel leads into the side of the mountain to the north, whilst to the south all that faces you is the edge of the cliffs, with a sheer drop-off to the valley below. This fairly narrow ledge slopes gently upward to the west, whilst to the east it ends abruptly.
16416: This is a tunnel which runs underneath the mountain, it is very dark and you can see lithe shadows dancing on the wall. The tunnel spreads north, and to the south you can exit the mountain. Above you is a huge crack which leads back outside.
16417: This is a tunnel which runs underneath the mountain. It is very dark and you can see lithe shadows dancing on the wall. The tunnel leads into a large empty space to the east, and to the south you can follow it into the depths of the mountain.
16418: The trail continues onwards stretching from east to west. There is nothing much to see except the small stones and pebbles that line the floor. Your vision is completely blocked by the rock walls that surround the trail. A crisp and fresh scent is carried on the air by the mountain wind.
16419: A trail winds its way through the mountain enclosure, hidden from all external view. One can only wonder how it came to be. The space is narrow and the rockfaces stretch high above your head. The wind is whistling a strange and eerie tune, probably due to the way it blows through this rock formation.
16420: You move on the little path which has broken away from the main trail. The path promptly comes to an end at your feet. Your options are to continue west, back along the path, or to crawl through the narrow crack which leads downwards to an empty darkness.
16421: You are on a fairly narrow ledge, high up on a mountain side. A few small patches of thin grass grow here, as well as a few tiny mountain flowers, but there seems to be no other sign of life nearby. Higher up, and to the west, stands a large plateau.
16422:
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.

During spring's thaw, snow turns into small rills, cascading down the mountains north and south of here forming this fast flowing rivulet. Natural springs welling up from the ground give life to this swift moving waterway throughout the rest of the year. The cool clear water amplifies the brilliance of the silver stones that line this stream's bed. The stones, which once had jagged edges, are now worn smooth by the steady, even flow of the water. Over time, these rocks will be nothing but pebbles in the bottom of the stream.
16423: One might expect this mountain's peak to point to the heavens, if it had a pointed peak. Instead what is here is ground so flat, it is as if the mountain's summit was knocked off with a hammer and chisel. The level ground is covered in wild weeds and a few young trees that someday will give this apex its pointed top.
16424: Plants cover this portion of the mountainside. Large bushes keep the soil from sliding down the slope. Wild flowers grow in clusters farther down the mountain to the south and west.
16425: These cliffs are rather devoid of plant life. The odd shrub grows in the arid soil. A few grassy patches grow on bits of level ground. The land here is too dry and rocky to support much else. Deposits of dirt and mud run down the slope of the mountainside pile here sometimes two to three feet high.
16426: At the Top of a Waterfall

The waters of the stream swirl and roil here, as they gather in a small pool at the edge of an almost vertical drop-off. For whilst the lands to the north make a fairly steady ascent from east to west, the channel through which the brook makes its way is stepped here. At the rim of the pool, the water flows over a flat slab of stone, then tumbles down to another pool below.
16427: Hemmed in to both north and south by tall mountain ridges which draw closer toward one another as they venture westward, the valley grows more narrow as it climbs in that direction. At its lowest point, not far to the south of here, a small stream races along the rocky floor.
16428: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

A ceiling of solid rock hangs heavily, not too far above your head. Beneath your feet the stony ground has been worn smooth in places, and the cold, stone walls bear signs of tooling. It is impossible to tell what type of design was once etched there, and as to whose hand did this work, you can only guess.
16429: Some orange-red blossoms grow amid grey-green foliage.

The cliff face turns east and south here, and a fairly spacious rocky ledge protrudes from this angle. The surface of the stone is extremely uneven and is pitted with tiny cracks and fissures. Sloping off quite rapidly in both directions, it seems hardly to be a safe place to linger.
16430: You are within a massive chamber of such cavernous dimensions that it might easily hold more than two hundred men. Its immense proportions mean that it is almost impossible to see one end from the other, but careful exploration shows that there are but three exits from this enormous space. To the west is a wide tunnel through which cool, fresh air flows. Set in the floor to the south is access to a lower series of tunnels, and in the eastern wall is a narrow opening, which appears to lead upwards.
16431: The trail continues onwards stretching from east to west. There is not much to see except the small stones and pebbles that line the rocky floor. Your vision is completely blocked by the rock walls that surround the trail. A crisp and fresh scent is carried on the air by the mountain wind.
16432: This is the beggining of a long and deep ravine. It branches away from the trail to the north, and carries on westwards. The base of the ravine has a glazed look, due to constant weathering by the elements. The ground is completely bare and naked, apart from some stones scattered to the north.
16433: This is just another bend in the trail which you have been following. The trail continues north and east. To your south there is a difference in the rock. You are unable to see clearly just what lies in that direction from such a distance.
16434: A collection of scree and moraine make this once grassy field lifeless and choppy. The vertical base of Celebdil standing westwards is responsible for the debris, as rock slides are very common in this region. To the north and east, the ground becomes softer and the soil black, as is particular to this dale.
16435: On the Slopes of a Rising Ridge

A jagged mountain ridge rises before you, its saw-toothed profile sweeping across the land from northwest to southeast. The ground underfoot here is treacherous with loose rocks and debris, making the ascent to the top of the ridge that much harder. And to the north the rocky terrain continues, though the land flattens out markedly in this direction, as it enters the floor of the valley.
16436:
A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.
A lone hawk soars high above you.

Though steep, this broad section of the ridgeline is fairly easily travelled. To the southeast it climbs steadily toward a lofty mountain peak, and west of here it descends into a saddle. To the east the land slopes off towards the valley floor at a fairly gentle gradient.
16437: This narrow ridge rises steeply, yet steadily, from the northwest, climbing toward a lofty mountain peak. High above the valley floor, this place offers a grand view of the southeastern reaches of the Dimrill Dale, and in the distance you can see the glimmering waters of a large, dark, oval lake.
16438: Here the trail continues, bending west and south at the feet of the mountain slopes. The sky seems to hang low above the mountain tops, and the ground seems to possess some uncanny quality you cannot define - something unnatural either about its colour and texture, or about the shadows that fall on it.
16439: The strange trail runs north-south here, following the feet of the mountains. At this point it runs so straight and seems so long, as if it had no beginning or end anywhere. Nothing catches your eyes on or off the trail; everything seems barren, dull and dead.
16440: Here the trail bends, and you can follow it either northwards or westwards. The surroundings of the trail remain pretty much the same, desolate, empty and bland, with no signs of animal life or vegetation.
16441: Climbing steeply from the cavern to the west, this narrow, but high-roofed tunnel meanders up through the interior of the mountain. In places it appears as if the floor has been carved into very crude stairs, but it is hard to tell if these are truly artifacts, or if some trick of nature has accidentally made the passage look this way. Whichever is the case, they are an invaluable aid in traversing this precipitous shaft.
16442: Above the Floor of the Valley

Hugging the face of the cliff, the land here has climbed more rapidly than has the valley floor below, creating a rocky shelf which is several feet wide, and at some distance above the surrounding countryside. In places the ground has been worn quite smooth, but rocks and stones are scattered all around. Some of these are fairly large, and it seems that perhaps they are not the result of natural landslides, for many appear to be arranged in rows, as if forming the foundation of some dwelling, long since ruined.
16443: The valley here is somewhat stepped, with three distinct levels. Above you, to the north, a ledge nestles against the face of a tall cliff. To the south, and below the level of the stream bank lies a dark pool, fed by a merry little waterfall. Climbing to the west, the sloping floor of the valley draws level with the upper reaches of the fast-flowing mountain stream.
16444: A deep pool stands at the bottom of the waterfall. Although the drop is not especially high, the falls nevertheless send up a constant light spray of cool water. As she flows on eastward from here, following a channel along the base of the cliffs to the south, Nimrodel is forced into a narrow gully, which causes some of the water to swirl backward, making the surface here quite choppy for such a small stream.
16445: Trees line the eastern side of one of the great mountains in this range. They grow out of soil at a sharp angle, often with their roots exposed. Only plants with roots that dig in deep could even hope to survive in this area's loose soil. The few shrubs and wild plants that give the mountainside a bit of green cover grow densely along a few flat ledges along the slope. Northward, a waterfall can be seen in the distance.
16446: Pieces of granite protrude from the earth breaking up the otherwise uninterrupted carpet of short green grass. Down the slope to the east is an old track which winds around the southern tip of the cold, deep Mirrormere.
16447: Bright, fragrant wildflowers dot this grassy slope into the dale. The terrain is soft and yielding from the tiny rivulets of water, which flow down the sloping ground, from the mountain peaks and ridges above, to join the Dimrill Stair in its progress toward the large oval lake below.
16448: The sound of rushing water from the east is all that can be heard in this barren land. Northwards stands proud Caradhras, whose towering peak ranks tallest among these mountains. Beside him, to the east, glitters the summit of Fanuidhol, and to the west is Celebdil. From the turning point of this ridge, a lush dale can be seen below.
16449:
A mountain ibex is jumping from rock to rock.
A mountain ibex is jumping from rock to rock.
A mountain ibex is jumping from rock to rock.
A mountain ibex is jumping from rock to rock.

The trail bends, making an unexpected turn. To the east your eye spies a faint glimmer, something shiny in the distance. The Redhorn Pass continues to the south and west, remaining as it was throughout the dark ages. This dangerous route has stood through and survived the evil which had ravaged the land, and as you tread upon it, memories of the past can be felt lingering in the cold, crisp and frosty air.
16450: The small stream follows the mountain line. It travels a fairly straight path and joins a bigger river in the east. The stream is quite strong here and seems to be inhabited by many fish. The surface of the water flashes tinges of silver, but perhaps it is nothing more than light playing tricks on your weary eyes.
16451: Travelling just north of a small, but lively stream, not too far below, the narrow ridge undulates gently up and down as it marches steadily from east to west. But the general trend is for the altitude to drop as you progress eastward, toward the Dimrill Stair.
16452:
A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.
A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.
A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.

The ground here is covered with blotches of weedy and unkempt grass. The blades are short, unable to grow fully due to the harsh conditions in this region. The earth seems quite worn, as this is probably the only place where the local wildlife can feed.
16453: An immensely large tundra-like plain is buried in the heart of the mountain range. Small patches of dead grass litter the ground around you, making the the area seem unkempt. Little other vegetation grows here, and your eye can behold little of beauty. The tundra stretches onward to the west, growing ever more bleak, whilst to the south there is a precipitous drop-off to the waters of a fast-flowing mountain stream, which sweeps past to the east of here.
16454: This is the source of the river Naragul. Here it collects the droplets of water from the snow-capped peaks and the glaciers of the Misty Mountains. It begins very slow and narrow, but peering southwards you can see that it picks up both speed and a wider form. The scent of grass is lingering in the air upon this area and to the west you detect a wide plain.
16455: A large, vicious and jagged chunk of rock extends out from the mountain. This stone feature is sharp like a knife's edge, giving the impression that knife-like spears are actually protruding from the mountain, spears created to fend off the unwanted and guard the secrets which Caradhras holds.
16456: A large, vicious and jagged chunk of rock extends out from the mountain. This stone feature is sharp like a knife's edge, giving the impression that knife-like spears are actually protruding from the mountain, spears created to fend off the unwanted and guard the secrets which Caradhras holds.
16457: A large, vicious and jagged chunk of rock extends out from the mountain. This stone feature is sharp like a knife's edge, giving the impression that knife-like spears are actually protruding from the mountain, spears created to fend off the unwanted and guard the secrets which Caradhras holds. At this point of the outcropping a rocky steppe looms above your head, providing some shelter.
16458: A grey-skinned mountain troll stands here.

This north-facing ledge is overshadowed by a rocky shelf which effectively hides it from direct sunlight. From here, to the northwest, can be seen the great south face of Caradhras, and beyond it the lesser peaks of the Misty Mountains extending to the north. Due north of here the land is a clutter of stony spires and crags.
16459: This stone shelf offers a sweeping view of the golden wood of Lorien which stretches many leagues to the east. To the southwest the mighty Silverlode can be seen cutting through the forest, gaining momentum from the many mountain streams and rivers feeding into it.
16460: A strong scent of vanilla drifts through the air, emitted from one of the many types of wildflowers this dale hosts. The black soil is soft and yielding, allowing this meadow to flourish, but to the west the ground becomes rocky as it nears the base of the mountains.
16461: A worm is here slithering around.

Bright pansies and white, drooping lilies dot the otherwise uninterrupted carpet of tall grass. The meadow is bordered by the lively waters of the Dimrill Stair to the west, and to the south lies a long, oval lake. The field rolls on to the north, but to the east travel is rapidly blocked by the encroaching mountains.
16462: The tarn's midnight waters reflect the icy summits of Celebdil, Caradhras, and Fanuidhol, the mountains of Moria. The mere emits a severe cold from its seemingly bottomless depths. To the east lies a hilly forest, whose tall evergreens run right up onto the banks of these waters.
16463: The tarn's midnight waters reflect the icy summits of Celebdil, Caradhras, and Fanuidhol, the mountains of Moria. The mere emits a severe cold from its seemingly bottomless depths. The water hosts no fish or plant life, and lies undisturbed by the foliage from the deep forest running eastwards.
16464: The tarn's midnight waters reflect the icy summits of Celebdil, Caradhras, and Fanuidhol, the mountains of Moria. The mere emits a severe cold from its seemingly bottomless depths. To the southeast, a tall pillar stands on a grassy slope.
16465: The tarn's midnight waters reflect the icy summits of Celebdil, Caradhras, and Fanuidhol, the mountains of Moria. The mere emits a severe cold from its seemingly bottomless depths. To the west, a rocky path travels north - south through the dale.
16466: There is some snow on the ground.

The tarn's midnight waters reflect the icy summits of Celebdil, Caradhras, and Fanuidhol, the mountains of Moria. The mere emits a severe cold from its seemingly bottomless depths. Northwards the lake narrows, reaching between mountain on the east and rocky shore to the west.
16467: There is some snow on the ground.

The tarn's midnight waters reflect the icy summits of Celebdil, Caradhras, and Fanuidhol, the mountains of Moria. The mere emits a severe cold from its seemingly bottomless depths. Northwards the gleaming Dimrill Stair falls into the dale. Forming a small pool at its bottom, it leaks under a pile of moraine, slowly feeding into Mirrormere.
16468: Small effervescent waterfalls decorate this narrow path into the dale. The smooth, rounded mineral rocks that bed its rapid flow, keep the stream clear. A fine mist hangs in the air from the constant splash. Rich smells of earth emerge from the hilly forest to the east. Westwards lies a larger fall resulting in an icy pool. Below, the stair continues merging with a dark mere.
16469: This tremendous dolomite protrusion offers a sweeping view of a rich and shadowy dale. Cradled between the arms of Caradhras and Fanuidhol, it runs southwards out of the mountains of Moria. At the head of the dale begins an oval mere, whose dark waters reflect the rocky ridges and icy peaks of her surroundings. Westwards can be heard the noisy Naragul as it spills into a series of small waterfalls.
16470: A large, vicious and jagged chunk of rock extends out from the mountain. This stone feature is sharp like a knife's edge, giving the impression that knife-like spears are actually protruding from the mountain, spears created to fend off the unwanted and guard the secrets which Caradhras holds.
16471: A large, vicious and jagged chunk of rock extends out from the mountain. This stone feature is sharp like a knife's edge, giving the impression that knife-like spears are actually protruding from the mountain, spears created to fend off the unwanted and guard the secrets which Caradhras holds.
16472: This small body of water is running its course through the fortress of peaks which surround it. The water is chilly having kept most of the frigid nature of the glaciers which it has sprung from. It has inherited the attributes of the surrounding lands of which it is housed. It is cold and unfeeling, no warmth or love runs through it. Much like a river of silver.
16473: This small body of water is running its course through the fortress of peaks which surround it. The water is chilly having kept most of the frigid nature of the glaciers which it has sprung from. The riverbank is small and muddy, making it extremely hard and uncomfortable to move on.
16474: This is the meeting point of two streams, where the Naragul which originates from small glacial pockets in the mountains absorbs the smaller stream which flows from the west. The Naragul then continues flowing southwards where it will eventually meet the Mirrormere. These waters which you are standing in are flowing with quite some velocity but yet are crossable by foot.
16475: This is the stream Naragul which has its roots from the great glacial peak of the deadly Caradhras. It flows both quick and swift providing a strong current. On the western bank you spy a trail which remains hidden by the mountains. To the north lies a fork of the stream and southwards the Naragul flows on.
16476: This raging torrent smashes against its jagged banks throwing up a fine mist. The crashing of worn rocks resisting the river's barrage dominates the air. Small eddies twirl violently above submerged rocks threatening any who might come within their reach. To the west can be seen Celebdil, whose icy peak feeds this brook. Southwards the Naragul begins a steep series of falls carrying into the dale below.
16477: The roar of the Naragul making its first drop is deafening. Falling into a small moraine dammed pool, it flows more calmly to the east. Large rocks near the pool are covered with a thick carpet of moss from the constant exposure to water. To the south can be seen an aged, once paved road making a steep descent and switchback into the dale below.
16478: On the Slopes of a Ridgeline
A high ridgeline rises to the west of you, and a lower mountain ridge crosses the land to the south. To the east the land gradually flattens out, as it approaches a region of tundra.
16479: The serpentine ridgeline continues writhing and curving through the mountains. The path is treacherous as no foothold is safe, and if you trust your eyes, what appears to be firm may send you plunging down to your death.
16480: The sheer slope climbs to the top of a reptilian-like ridge, the very backbone of Caradhras itself. Looking up, you can see the jagged edge of the ridgeline silhouetted sharply across the sky. Far below you, a snow-filled valley glimmers white in a gap between two mountains.
16482: A burly giant is here, covered with thick fur and snow.

A steep rockface extends from the mountain peak towards the stream which runs on slightly lower ground. The ground is dead and barren and life is unapparent on this mountain. Perhaps this emptiness is due to the harsh and unpleasant frost which leeches itself to this area, or perhaps it is due to some other reason which you cannot possibly comprehend.
16483: The corpse of a huge white bear is lying here.

This is the highest point of the mountain ridge - from here the dark forests of Mirkwood can be seen near the eastern horizon, just beyond the great river Anduin. The area surrounding the summit is extremely rough and mostly impassable. In every direction the peaks of Hithaeglir rise, reaching towards the sky with rocky fingers.
16484: This is a horribly steep and treacherous ridgeline. Its sides are very tall and plunge into the depths. Above you is the mountain summit, to the east the ridgeline continues.
16485: You find yourself precariously situated on the steep southern face of the tall stone mountain looming high overhead.
