16716: Small bushes and short grass are the dominating forms of vegetation in this area. A few lonely trees stand amidst the plains, proudly reaching for the sky. The ground beneath the grassy cover is soft and in places muddy. A large fogbank can be spotted on the western horizon. In all other directions the plains continue.
16717: The grass grows thick and tall in these plains. No source of water can be seen, yet the soil is moist and even muddy in some spots. Some large footprints can be seen caked into some dry mud, and there is a distinct animal smell coming from somewhere nearby. The terrain to the north seems to be covered in a grey dust.
16718: One living thing is dominant here: a great mallorn. With its smooth silvery-grey bark and its magnificent crown it stands, proudly reaching for the sky, lonely and obviously a wild seed from a mallorn of Lorien. Around it grass grows vigorously, while the mallorn stands like a guardian, spreading its branches like wings. To the north the air appears to be dark grey, and no sounds of wildlife come from that direction.
16719:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

A small pond is here, almost hidden in grass and vegetation. The water seems clear and refreshing, and the growth around the pond is rich and vigorous, which also can be said about the wildlife here. Plains can be seen stretching to the horizon in all directions except to the northwest where a heavy grey dust seems to cover the land. The wildlife seems to avoid that area.
16720: The soil in this part of the plains is dry and barren, with many cracks crossing its parched crust. The grass is rather yellowish and dead-looking, and there are spots where even this grass refuses to grow. Occasional trees and shrubs look as lifeless as the grass. A few small hills mark the landscape to the south, while the terrain in other directions looks more flat and vigorous.
16721: The smooth, dry grasslands continue onwards, never making a sudden rise or descent. The years seem to have worn off the edges of this land; whatever hills were once present now lie smooth, bland and desolated, a tribute to the never-ending power of wind and rain.
16722: A swallow flies high above the ground.

This, a higher point in the landscape, is less protected from the strong winds, which make progress sometimes quite difficult. The air is the only thing in motion here, sweeping over the hills and through the valleys. Only grass can be seen for several miles in all directions, swaying slowly in the wind.
16723: A small hill has formed here, slightly elevated from the rest of the surrounding landscape but not high enough to provide much of a view. The ground slopes downward to the east. To the west the land becomes much more barren, while grasslands can be seen to the south.
16724: The ground slopes steeply westwards here, but the climb is fairly easy. The ground is firm and bare due to the constant winds which have blown away most of the loose soil. The hill in the west seems the highest point in the landscape, but doesn't seem high enough to provide much of a view.
16725: The ground is hard and cracked in places, and even though life seems completely impossible in such a desolation, some persistent grasses can be seen pushing through the soil. The even ground rises towards a high hill which stands west from here. At this point travelling is quite comfortable as the slope is not very steep yet.
16726: This arid plateau slopes descending to the east towards a valley. A dry streambed can be seen to the east, running north-south, like a large snake traversing the land. Here the landscape is desert-like, the sandy soil growing only some sparse tufts of dry yellow grass.
16727: The ground descends towards the valley in the northeast. The slope is barren and dry, and only short grass thrives in the unfertile soil. Here and there patches of bare brown soil dot the carpet of yellowy grass. Below, in the north, an ancient mill can be seen by the long-dried stream.
16728: Running north and south the dry riverbed crosses the plains. On the banks grow tufts of dry grass, and in places the channel has crumbled and the slides make it easy to cross. Once, long ago, it had perhaps been a swift river, but now it is little but a shallow track in the middle of these endless plains.
16729: Small tufts of grass are the predominant flora over these bleak, silent plains, interrupted only occasionally by some higher grass or a small shrub or two. Little wildlife can be heard; this lands only faithful visitor is the wind. To the southeast some large rocks can be seen in the distance. The plains continue in all directions.
16730: A low shrub with bright green, oblong leaves is growing here.

Large boulders lie scattered around here and the landscape is barren and bleak. Some grass grows here in clumps, but mostly the terrain is dominated by big stony formations. While the surrounding landscape is fairly level, the ground here is rough and passage more difficult. Southwards the rocky plains seem to continue, but in other directions the grasslands reign.
16731: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

A half dozen leafless trees here do little to shelter you from the winds blowing across the plains. Yet from this shallow basin you are unable to see much of the surrounding terrain other than hills to the south. The earth is soft, wet, smells of peat and is perhaps not firm enough to support your weight. With your every movement water fills in the footprints. Glancing at these little pools, you see they are teeming with small water insects.
16732: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The brown and gold of the bracken on these slight slopes contrasts with the greens and lighter browns of the grasslands to the north and the darker shades of the heath to the south. This vegetation crunches under foot, sounding unnaturally loud in the silence. The horizon to the north and west is filled with the light grey shadow of a forest.
16733: A faint trail crosses the rolling plains in the north, winds through boulder-strewn fields and climbs into the low hills in the south. Short grasses cover the ground; here and there tufts of longer grass or thistles wave in the breeze. A few small cool streams cross the trail and run away to the southeast. The grassland flattens to the northwest and undulating plains stretch out to the east.
16734:
A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

In the vast fields of tall grass stand a half dozen forms made of hard stone, defying the elements. The sand carried by the winds has worn away the softer stone in this outcropping. Small cracks in the stone have trapped some soil and water that nurtures a few flowering mountain plants. The ground rises to the south; to the west you are able to make out a fine north-south trail. The blue-grey shadow of a forest looms on the horizon to the northeast.
16735: An ancient burial mound sits here, looking somewhat out of place in the otherwise featureless grass-covered moorlands. The ash-coloured sides of the mound are devoid of vegetation and look unnatural. On one of the sides a few rocks have been arranged into a strange pattern. From the top of the mound in good light one can make out the odd ruined building or cairn which catches the sun. An outcrop of rocks rises to the west. In all other directions the grasslands roll away from you.
16736: Due to unstable soil and the shifting rock strata, a giant sinkhole has formed in the ground here. Small bushes and trees cling to its steep sides which shelter them from the winds. Some large rocks are haphazardly arranged at the bottom. The shape of the sinkhole causes the wind to swirl around it; over many years, the wind and the water have eroded many cracks in the rocks below. A faint track leads directly down at an alarming angle.
16737: The grasslands extend in all directions as far as the eye can see. In the north the monotony is broken by the silhouette of a small mound and the dark shadow of a forest on the horizon beyond the mound. Here and there small streams cross the land in knee-deep cuts. The dark water of the streams seems to have been stained by the local soils.
16738: The undulating fields are covered by thick green grass. Looking westwards, this featureless land gives you little sense of distance to measure your progress. The general lie of the land appears to fall to the southeast. Close to the east there is a large wood, the edge of which curves round to the north.
16739: Two tall trees stand like a pair of great pillars in this clearing near the eaves of the forest. They are heavily charred, having been struck by lightning which seems to have ended their ancient reign. To the west you glimpse rolling grasslands through the thin belt of trees. The area around the pair of trees seems to have been used for a camp, perhaps for a large host, but not since the last rain.
16740: The forest here has petered out into a mixture of scrub and brushland. This vegetation gives some cover from prying eyes. A gentle slope to the west rolls into the grasslands which stretch endlessly into the distance. Judging by the many burrows among the tree roots, a host of small animals have made this area their home. Bright marsh flowers grow here and there, thriving in the moist soil. A few tiny streams run eastward.
16741: A tall silvery plant grows here, surrounded by mist.

Thin wiry bushes cover this gentle slope that leads into the forest in the north and east. The clay ground holds a lot of water making passage a little tricky. A small hillock rises to the west; on its top you can just make out a small pile of stones. The ground falls to the south and east where marsh flowers and small bushes grow among the grasses with flat leaves.
16742: A cluster of white star-shaped forget-me-nots flourish here in reminiscence.

A small pile of stones stands on the top of a low hillock as the sole marker of a forlorn grave of a deceased warrior or traveller. A solitary dead tree is visible at some distance to the north. Beyond it, the darker wall of the forest looms on the horizon. The ground slopes down gently to the southeast where it gradually becomes softer. A few flowering plants and small shrubs dot the even grassland; these seem to grow more frequent to the east.
16743: A small cluster of clover grows here.

These fields of long grass are fairly unremarkable, with no distinct landmarks save the odd stripe of greener grass covering long unused thoroughfares and the curtain of the forest rising to the north. Many small insects jump around in the grass or climb the tall stems. The ground slopes down gently to the south and then rises again in the distance before rolling away in a series of glacial folds.
16744:
The remains of a black fungus lie here in a heap of rotting compost.
The remains of a black fungus lie here in a heap of rotting compost.

This is the very edge of a large forest. The trees thin out toward the south. There appears to be a change in soil conditions to the south, accounting for different vegetation. The ground holds more water there and in places becomes marshy. Low marsh plants and wiry bushes gradually replace the trees, most of which are dead and rotting.
16745: The bank skirts the bend of the river that flows to the northeast. Trees overhang the water, seemingly pleased with being able to catch more light. The trees are mostly grey and bear few leaves in spite of all the sunlight they get. Farther from the riverbank the forest floor is carpeted with small dense shrubs. A fallen tree at the water's edge has provided a place for beavers to create a little pool of water by building a small dam. A few leaves and insects on the water show a gentle back-eddy. Here and there you spot the tracks of a small bird or animal.
16746: Thick Woods at the Edge of the River

The closely standing trees and the thick undergrowth form a dense barrier between the river and the large expanse of forest to the west. The clay bank is high and slippery but is held together by a tangle of roots and boulders. There is no suitable place to land a boat. The water below the bank foams as it rushes through channels formed by large rocks, in places creating a spray of white water.
16747: The trees here are old and carry an air of nobility. Although they show clear signs of age, they seem well preserved as if by some magic; yet perhaps now is the eve of their life. The sound of a river rushing through the rapids can be heard in the east. To the north you can see a dilapidated wooden structure. To the south the vegetation between the trees grows thicker.
16748: A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

The collapsed remains of a large boathouse are perched on the bank above a bend in the river. The walls of the structure are wooden, but the slipway is constructed of neat stone blocks. The slipway is now covered with debris but could still be serviceable. Moss, lichen and fungi grow on the wooden parts of the ruined building. Golden crowns of the mellyrn light up the woodland to the west, but the forest to the south is bleak and silent.
16749: The river here is slightly wider and slower than it is both upstream and downstream as it flows between two bends on a gentle gradient. To the north the bank is a sheer cliff. Slightly above the water level a narrow ledge juts out from the northern bank. The whispers of the woodlands to the south are complemented by the rumbling sound of distant rapids.
16750: The river turns from the west to the south here. The water is white in places where it crashes against large rocks. These rocks must have been carried down the river during times of high flooding, caused by the melting of ice and snow during the short summers seen high in the Misty Mountains. The green woods to the north of the river stand on top of a sheer bank, but to the east the bank is not so steep and the trees climb down to the very edge of the water.
16751: Here the River Anduin is strong and swift. The banks grow steeper from the north to the south. A rumbling sound of rapids comes from the south. Thick woods stand on the high banks, forming an avenue where the passage of the river could easily be watched. There are a few spots on the west bank where one might be able to scramble ashore.
16752: Jammed by steep banks on both sides, the river here is in turmoil. Large rocks in the middle of the river create dangerous rapids. There seems to be no way of leaving the river here and the strength of the water prevents you from going upstream. Forests stand on the high banks making this stretch of water cool and sunless.
16753: The river turns from the north to the east here. Skirting the woodlands to the west and south, it hurries forward on its quest to find the sea. The water is white in places where great rocks channel it into short rapids. Several small streams tumble down to the river from the forest above.
16754: A stocky mountain mule is here, waiting to serve.

Old, grey trees grow on the very edge of the river that makes a bend to the north. The bank is high and steep, with many overhangs where river creatures could lurk. In a few spots forest streams cut through the bank, washing their way through the sand and clay. At these openings the trees dip their roots into the river below, creating natural jetties. Water swirls through them, creating back currents that could be dangerous for a careless swimmer.
16755:
A wolf cub happily plays here.
A wolf cub happily plays here.
A wolf cub happily plays here.
The mother wolf stands here, protecting her young cubs.

This forest between the river to the northeast and the plain to the southwest is a mixture of oak, elm and ash. The trees nearer the river look unhealthy; many of them are dead and rotting, apparently due to the flooding caused by several severe winters. To the north the trees grow thicker.
16756: A mass of dark green leaves clings to a wall.

A ruined stone building stands here. The forest has largely overgrown it and there is little left of the roof or the top portion of the walls. From the top of the ruins one can see beyond the low bushes to the south. The view in that direction is that of grassy rolling plains with a small hillock. A small pile of stones sits on the top of the hillock; it is the only distinctive feature in the otherwise bleak scene.
16757:
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A forest spider is here crawling around.

The forest here is so dense that virtually no light penetrates the canopy of branches. Many beards of moss hang from the trees, blocking the light. Large masses of mud and branches in the crowns of the trees are also visible in the gloom. The vegetation on the ground is scrappy and leafless, but there are many thorny bushes that appear to thrive in the dark.
16758: A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

The trees here are closely packed. Most of them are tall, thin and bear few leaves. Thorny bushes and fallen branches make passage through the forest slow and painful. You hear the occasional crack of a dry branch and the sounds of small animals or birds picking their way through the brambles.
16759:
A wolf spider is here, among the trees.
A wolf spider is here, among the trees.

The forest here is still, silent and airless. The trees are grey and bear few leaves. Dry leaves, rotten branches and large sheets of bark litter the ground. On the tree-boles there are many bare patches covered in a pepper of white fungus. Many large spider webs are strung between the branches; in some of them you spot cocooned corpses of small animals. In all directions except to the south the forest seems to grow lighter, but to the south it gets even duller and darker.
16760: The trees here are young, healthy and bright with many blossoms; here and there you can spot the golden crowns of the mellyrn. On one of the wooded lawns a lone dead mallorn attracts the eye. The chattering of birds and other woodland creatures seems to have stopped around it. To the south the trees darken, but in the west they grow lighter although the forest does not seem to grow less dense. To the north the ground slopes down to the river as it does to the east, where one can see the remains of a wooden building.
16761: The river turns from the north to the east, widening a little before continuing east. The water is white with foam in the spots where it meets small rocks or sharp rock edges but calms as the river turns. The northeast bank is high and rises sharply. The woods to the south and west are bright; some of the trees are in blossom and have a distinct feel of springtime.
16762: Several blooms of snow-white and palest green cover the ground.

A river runs through the forest to the east. The trees by the riverbank are bright with golden leaves, silvery bark and occasional blossoms; their branches bend like those of the weeping willows. The trees at the water's edge dip the tips of their branches into the water. A carpet of golden leaves lines the natural avenues formed by the rows of trees. The forest to the south darkens a bit.
16763: The trees here are young and bright. Many are in blossom and perhaps one in five is a golden mallorn. A light, refreshing breeze moves the tree branches. From the northeast you hear many odd noises similar to the sounds made by water birds and frogs. Small white mushrooms grow on the grass lawns between the trees.
16764: A dense carpet of blue flowers dip their heads in the breeze.

The mixed trees here are mature and well spaced as if they had been planted this way on purpose. They exhibit a tapestry of colours - several shades of green, brown, orange and gold, with white pink and yellow blossoms. A small path leads north; as your eye follows it you catch a glimpse of a golden mallorn-tree gleaming in the soft light. The trees to the south grow dense and darken a little.
16765: An ancient oak tree lies here. From its condition it is apparent that it was brought down by high winds and lightning. Many of the top branches have been trimmed with neat axe strokes. The wood is still green and the only growth on the trunk is the moss on what was the southern face. Several of the surrounding trees appear to have been damaged by the fall.
16766: The ancient oaks stand well apart and there is little vegetation between them, which allows light to trickle down through the leaves all the way to the ground. The leaves of the oaks rustle as if squirrels were scampering among the branches. Birds chatter in the trees-tops; now and then, the woods are disturbed by a howl of a wolf.
16767: The tall oak trees here are old and strong. Between the trees, many stumps are rotting in the ground. Judging by the axe marks on the stumps, these trees were probably felled for timber. The remains of a small camp are visible amid the grass; the campsite looks several weeks old. A few barely discernible cart tracks lead south, disappearing in the featureless grasslands.
16768: The grasses on these south-facing slopes are interspersed with small flowing plants and thistles. From the shape of the land it appears that this area might have once been farmed. There are various tracks on the ground; most have been made by mounts, but several deep cuts in the earth seem to have been caused by the dragging of heavy objects.
16769: The mixed trees thin out rapidly to the south and west. Many have been felled, leaving rotting stumps and branches strewn carelessly on the forest floor. You can clearly see the marks where the trunks have been dragged away. Other remains, including small circles of ashes from campfires, show that it has been a few weeks since the last activity in this area.
16770: The trees here are tall and thin, bearing almost no leaves on their long branches. The occasional leaves and bark are covered with a fine dusting of parasitic growth. Large slugs and snails cluster in the root lattices; tracks of their sticky residue leave a silvery film, further contributing to the lack of colour in the area. The forest continues in all directions.
16771: The majority of trees here are old and gnarled. Great fronds of fungal flesh cling to them. While none of the trees appear to be dead, there seems to be a continuous struggle as if the forest was touched by evil. To the north and east the trees thicken, their bright green leaves indicating the healthier parts of the forest. The trees to the south are dark and grey with few leaves on their branches. You hear the occasional cautious call of a lone bird. To the west the trees thin out.
16772: The forest here seems to exhibit the signs of all the seasons simultaneously. Some trees are showing new leaves, some are in blossom, others are bearing fruit and a few are shedding leaves. You hear the gentle trickle of a spring to the east, the singing of birds and the chatter of small tree-dwelling animals. The ground between the trees is covered by a golden carpet of leaves.
16773: Delicate golden blooms adorn the ground like a cascade of stars.

Here the trees are widely spaced, creating natural avenues. Single mallorn trees stand in islands of light. Your eye is drawn to their silvery-grey bark and golden crowns. Many of the other trees are in blossom or have bright green leaves of spring growth. The ground is covered with lawns of soft grass and carpets of golden leaves. Here and there small white flowers grow in patches like a light sprinkling of snow.
16774: A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

A patchwork of greens, browns and golds greets your eyes in this part of the forest. The frequency of mellyrn increases to the north and east. A small stream runs east-west, and alongside it a small track winds its way among the roots. The forest continues in all directions. Just to the west the ground rises steeply.
16777:
An ancient fungus smothers the boulders.
An ancient fungus smothers the boulders.

A small grove of ancient elm trees marks the edge of the forest that continues to the east and north. The trees stand well apart; between them are tracts of bright green grass and a few weathered boulders. The ancient trees appear to be home to a variety of large fungi. These saprophytes look nearly as old as the trees, and seem to do them no harm. The soil is soft and dark and pocked by the feet of many grazing animals. The air smells damp and is unusually still. Now and then you hear the odd snort of an ox or cow.
16778: The ground here is sodden and sports only a few tufts of grass amid the pools of stagnant water. Trees surround the swampy area on three sides with grasslands stretching out to the west. The position of any traveller in this terrain would be strategically weak, as it is impossible to move quickly and one could easily be surprised by any would be attackers from the forest a bow's shot away.
16779: This small group of trees stands about a hundred paces from the large forest to the east. The ground around is soft and wet, which accounts for the absence of trees immediately to the east and to the north. In the branches of one of the trees someone has strung up a few ropes that form what appears to be a makeshift bed. There are no other signs of inhabitance.
16780: A large potato is growing here.

This south-facing field is dark and furrowed. It steams, gently releasing the heat it has absorbed during the day. While you can see the great hoof-prints of a large workhorse, there is no other sign of a farmer. The smell of the earth is pleasant, as no manure has been used. Trees to the north and east could easily conceal onlookers, but you hear nothing but a gentle breeze in branches.
16781: The ground dips slightly, forming a small depression in which thick grass grows over three feet high. Animal droppings, bones and tracks indicate that this area conceals a variety of small animals and perhaps larger predators. To the west you can see a strip of shorter grass of a lighter colour; this might be an animal track. Beyond that strip, there is little to break up the rolling grasslands. You are unable to see much of the terrain in other directions due to the elevation and the amount of vegetation, but you can detect the scent of the forest carried on the north-easterly breeze.
16782: The trail here is marked only by different length and pattern of grass. It cannot have seen much heavy use recently. Tall grass covers the plains to the east and west. The trail to the north bends westwards. To the south the land begins to rise.
16783: Here an ill-defined trail through the wild grasses turns west and south. The forest threatens to invade the trail in places, striking from the northeast. To the east between the trail and the trees lies a ploughed field. The ground to the north is riddled with mole hills and rabbit holes showing the russet-coloured soil. You hear the occasional chatter of birds.
16796: On the Fringes of the Forest
Delicate golden blooms adorn the ground like a cascade of stars.

At the border of the forest in the north the faint scent of the plants of the Golden Wood can be sensed. Here the smell of woods hangs in the air and the forest consists mostly of various broadleaf trees, but farther in the woods one can catch a glimpse of the silvery trunks of the mellyrn.
16798:
A shrub with maple-like leaves is growing here.
On the shrub, there are three handfuls of blackcurrant berries.

Thinning southwards the forest is a mixture of both mellyrn and other plants of the Golden Wood and ordinary, though healthy and beautiful, vegetation. Even here the Elven plants seem to radiate a faint, special glow but the effect is more noticeable in the north. In all other directions the forest ends and level grasslands take place.
16799: The mellyrn grow thicker here than in the surrounding area. The trees lean to each other, their many branches reaching for the sunlight, intertwining and forming a solid canopy of leaves. At the dim forest floor some plants seem to reflect a faint, golden light revealing the rich and varying undergrowth of many plants, grasses and moss. To the north a forest clearing can be seen.
16800: A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

On the outskirts of this forest, the vegetation grows lighter and the ground becomes less moist. Under the trees low shrubbery covers the ground. The undergrowth is easy to walk in, but becomes heavier in the north. Southwards, an expanse of grasslands extends into the distance.
16801: The trees here grow more sparsely than to the north, yet their stature is still breathtaking. A few mellyrn are scattered among the other trees. The golden trees appear to be the source of a faint radiance which grows stronger in the north. The forest continues to the north, east and west, while to the south it opens up into the plains.
16802: Here mellyrn and other trees seem to blend perfectly. The light golden glow of the mellyrn and the fragrant smell of pines pervade the senses. The forest border is evident to the south, as almost no animal tracks lead in that direction. The forest continues to the north, east and west.
16803: Draughts of air move quietly through the forest, circling around the still branches of the massive trees overhead. A peaceful, serene atmosphere reigns here, disturbed only by the footfalls of the occasional traveller, passing by on the way to a faraway destination. At the foot of a large tree on the south side, tall grass seems to conceal something. The forest continues to the north, east and west, while rocks and trees make southern passage impossible.
16804: Delicate golden blooms adorn the ground like a cascade of stars.

Tall golden mellyrn tower above the ground. Mixing with them are other kinds of trees: firs, pines and a few rowans bearing clusters of red berries. Many shrubs and bushes grow by the base of the trees, providing a source of nourishment for the local wildlife.
16805: In this part of the forest mellyrn mingle with the ordinary trees. Although the golden trees are fairer than the others, all of the trees here are astonishing, seemingly beyond the trees of any other forest in beauty and stature. It is possible to continue to the north, south and east, but to the west the forest grows too dense, making passage impossible.
16806:
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.
A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

A path can be seen running through the forest to the north. On the sides of the path tall mellyrn raise their branches to the sky. To the south the golden-crowned trees of Lothlorien seem to dwindle, giving way to trees with crowns of green. The fresh, sharp smell of pine needles is in the air. The dense forest makes passage to the east impossible.
16807: The small forest path winds its way through the dense forest. Judging by the animal tracks by the sides of the path wildlife flourishes here. The path continues to the west, winding through the mixed forest, and to the north where it heads towards a tall stand of mellyrn. To the south, more tall trees can be seen.
16808: The forest stretches out all around. Its great trees tower majestically above the ground. A small clearing can be seen to the west, where a low slope rises gently into the distance. To the north, a few fallen logs can be seen scattered across the forest floor. Beyond them, the glimmer of mellyrn rises into the sky like a drop of the morning sun. A small forest path leads east.
16809:
A cute rabbit is here.
A snake slithers towards you.

Lying on a small hill, this clearing offers a good view of the surrounding forest. To the north the crowns of the mellyrn dot the horizon like sparks of golden light. A small forest path runs down the slope of the hill to the east. A heady scent of flowers is in the air.
16810: A light wind whispers softly in the branches of the trees. A sweet, fresh smell of foliage permeates the air. The scent seems to fade to the east where a small clearing in the forest can be seen upon a low hill. Judging by the occasional animal sounds and the tracks on the ground, there is a lot of animal activity in this part of the great forest.
16811: The trees in this part of the forest are mostly slender, grey-barked mellyrn. Thriving in the moist, fertile ground, the grass under the trees is plentiful and thick. High-pitched insect sounds can be heard, although no insects are visible. To the north the forest grows more dense. To the south the grassy fields seem to continue forever.
16812: A squirrel scampers around here, looking for nuts from the trees.

The ground is soft and fertile supporting many trees and a variety of grasses. The tree-branches spread out in all directions, blocking much of the view of the sky above. To both the north and west the forest gets thicker. To the far south a small hill rises above the plains.
16813: A few trees can be seen growing in the soft soil, marking the edge of a dense forest which extends to the north and west. Most of the trees growing here are quite young; they are the offspring of the older trees found in the forest. Slowly but constantly the forest sows its seeds, in an attempt to extend its borders in all possible directions.
16814: The forest here is very dense. Trees grow side by side with little free space between them. The canopy formed by the branches of the trees is so dense that the space below is devoid of all sunlight. Due to the lack of sunlight, almost no undergrowth has managed to grow in this area. A few bushes can be seen, most of them short and sickly-looking.
16815: This dense forest appears to be as ancient as recorded history. Many of the trees are older than the oldest dwarf. Their trunks, though twisted and scarred, are as solid now as they were a hundred years ago. Some of the trees are thicker than a man at his widest girth and a few are over eighty feet in height. A barely noticeable track, most likely formed by the passage of deer and other animals, runs east-west through the forest. The little space that did exist between the trees has been filled by a few small bushes that struggle in the shadows.
16816: The ground here is a little lower than the surrounding area and forms the edge of a perfectly shaped circular valley full of trees and bushes. The centre of the bowl contains a small natural clearing. In that clearing there is an old fire pit, which appears to have been unused for many years. The fire pit is surrounded by a few old trunks which were most likely set there by a previous user of the camp.
16817: Several blooms of snow-white and palest green cover the ground.

The ground here slants slightly inwards from all directions. A pool of water has collected in this depression and around it the ground is wet and spongy. This has caused the land to be less hospitable for the trees of the golden forest. Still this area proves difficult for travellers to traverse, for where the trees were unable to grow, bushes quickly took root and reduced vision to a few feet.
16818: Damp from the waters of the clear blue river to the north this land is densely packed with trees. Many of the trees are ancient and quite large, though not overly tall. The trees have many branches, some very low and some high. Those trees that grow to the north, next to the river, have their lowest branches upon the surface of the river and often below the surface when the river floods.
16819:
A trout swims here.
A bass swims here.

After flowing straight east several miles into the forest of Lothlorien, the river bends northward. At the bend the water flows gently, its surface smooth and reflective like a mirror. The reflection of the forest upon the water is so sharp and bright that it is nearly impossible to distinguish it from the real forest which surrounds the river.
16820: The water here is deep blue and very clear, allowing you to see the rocky bottom with little difficulty. A few small fish playfully swim around the rocks and gravel as they search for food. The river is surrounded on both sides by tall slender trees, some of which bend across it forming a series of natural archways. A few leaves float gently upon the water as they drift eastwards.
16822: The steep bank to the north does not seem hostile, yet there seems to be no way to reach the roots and undergrowth that would help to climb out of the water. The golden forest to the south, rich in wildlife, offers a pleasant rest spot for a traveller. The river flows east from here.
16823:
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.

Here the waters lose some of the speed that they gained from the western rapids and quietly flow east. The fry dash back and forth at the reeds decorating the riverbank to the south. The muddy northern bank is too slippery to climb; even the tree roots, which have tangled into a natural ladder, are too far for anyone to reach.
16824: In ages past, a small waterfall enthroned this area, to the pride and joy of many elves. But as all things must come to an end, the falling waters eroded the solid riverbed inch by inch, leading to the collapse of the top of the waterfall. Now rapids, high rising riverbanks, and descending waters are the only reminders of days gone past.
16825:
A salmon swims here.
A bass swims here.
A salmon swims here.

The water flows east, as it must have done from days beyond reckoning. The somewhat mountainous riverbanks to north and south have witnessed the struggle this river has gone through, carving its way through earth and rock. Once a stream, now it is the beautiful Celebrant.
16826:
A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.
A bass swims here.
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.

This part of the river is teeming with small fish. Apparently, depending on the season, these creatures either simply pass their daily lives here or swim upstream to lay spawn in order to continue their breed, somehow managing to find strength to work their way against the strong current. The riverbank to the north is very steep and offers no safe landing. The waters flow eastwards, but to the south can be seen a natural pier extending into the water, an ideal spot for fishing.
16827: A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.

The river flows straight east here, emerging in the west from under a natural arch formed by two trees on either shore. The northern bank is not too steep, but it is impossible to reach the roots of the trees that would help you to climb out of the water. The southern bank is low and level, the forest turf beginning at the very edge of the water.
16828:
A salmon swims here.
A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.

The river flows from the west to the east. Massive tree-trunks on either shore prevent you from climbing out of the water. The tree-crowns meet at the top, forming a graceful arch over the river. As far as the eye can see until the river bends and is hidden out of sight, this appears to be the only bridge to the secretive northern shore of the Celebrant.
16829:
A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.
A brook trout is here, swimming in the current.
A bass swims here.
A salmon swims here.

The river flows from the west to the east. The bank to the north is quite steep and there appears to be no way to reach the roots and the undergrowth that would help a swimmer climb out of the water. The golden forest to the south, on the other hand, seems to offer a pleasant resting spot for the weary.
16830: The river makes a sharp turn and flows east as far as the eye can see rushing straight and swift like the flight of an eagle. The trees to the west and south grow gloriously golden and seem to offer a weary traveller a place to rest and listen to their age-old time-chant.
16831: The sound of pounding and rushing water can be heard clearly here as the river rushes by to the north. The forested shore has eroded slightly after taking such a beating for many years. Plant life thrives here, fed by the fresh water. The trees here are mostly mellyrn, and their fallen golden leaves can be seen on the ground.
16832: A light breeze picks its way through the forest, slightly stirring the leaves on the branches and the ground. Pine and oak trees are easy to spot amongst the golden crowns and slender branches of the mellyrn. Moss completely covers the base of some of the trees. Small insects can be seen feeding off the moss.
16833: A nightingale is here, chirping a sweet melody.

Mellyrn and birches mingle here, the white boles of the birches mixing with the silvery-grey boles of the golden trees. Some fallen leaves can be seen on the ground, but they bear no sign of rot or decay. Except for the singing of birds and the rustling of dry leaves, the forest is quiet, the great mellyrn standing solemn and motionless like guardians keeping watch.
16834: An arrow made from a grey wood lies here.

Ancient trees, mellyrn and birches, grow here side by side with small saplings. The green and golden tree-crowns merge, almost completely hiding the sky which is visible only when the wind moves the branches apart. Though the forest appears peaceful, there is a feeling of watchfulness, as if some unseen eyes were looking down from the tree-tops.
16835:
There are two ash arrows here.
A small mushroom grows nearby.

A few mellyrn brighten the forest here with their golden crowns and silvery boles, but the rest of the trees are mostly dark pines which seem even darker by comparison. The ground below the trees is cluttered by fallen branches, leaves and pine-needles in which small insects can be seen scurrying. Fungi and moss are plentiful here, as the soil is moist and not much sunlight reaches the ground.
16836: A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

Little outside light reaches the forest ground where darkened shadows fool the eye into seeing things. Leaves of the bushes rustle quietly as some unseen animal stalks through the forest. The trees themselves are enormous, their great trunks rising into the roof of leaves and disappearing out of sight. An occasional cry of a bird can be heard from above, but mostly the forest is quiet.
16837: Trees of all kinds grow here, clustered all together. Pine, oak, and maple thrive in this forest. Pine-needles, leaves, and branches cover the ground but in some places small saplings pop through the cover as they fight for survival. Thick bushes and other undergrowth cover the ground.
16838: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

This part of the forest is so quiet that the light rustling of the tree-leaves in the wind can be heard distinctly. The forest consists mostly of elms, but here and there you can spot an occasional clump of the golden mellyrn. There is little undergrowth and the ground under the trees is mostly bare, covered only by a carpet of fallen leaves.
16839: Trees grow densely here amidst the other forms of vegetation. Some red and blue forest flowers grow on the ground among shrubs and bushes. Green moss covers the trunks of some trees, and small fungi grow around the base of the others.
16840: A few trees that once stood proud and tall now lie here, fallen to the earth. This has created an opportunity for small saplings and other vegetation to rise where they once stood. The ground below the trees is covered by dead leaves and fallen branches which shelter many small forest insects.
16841: The forest is dense, and the trees are thick and tall. Many different species grow together, broad-leaf trees mixing with the conifers. The wind gently caresses the leaves, making them stir slightly, and their whisper carries through the forest.
16842: A giant, mean looking earth beetle is standing here.

Mellyrn can be spotted easily among the other trees as they stand out with their silvery boles and golden crowns. Fallen leaves lie on the ground, mixed with an occasional golden blossom; the leaves are quite dry and crumble whenever anyone steps upon them. As the wind gently stirs the tree-branches, glimpses of the sky can be seen. Calls of birds and various animal noises echo loudly from the depths of the forest.
16843: A soft wind scatters the leaves that have fallen on the ground and gently sways the leaves on the tree-branches. Small insects scurry about as their cover is blown away. A few fallen trees lie here, creating a perfect environment for many different kinds of fungi to grow.
16844: Fallen leaves and branches cover the moist, rich earth in which many kinds of bushes and shrubs and a few tree-saplings thrive, reaching to the light. Animal tracks can be seen among the undergrowth, a few of them apparently made by rather large animals.
16845: A few bird nests can be seen in the tree-branches, half-hidden by the thick canopy. The moist, soft soil is covered by fallen leaves and is apparently a perfect place for many plants to grow. Short bushes and various forest flowers are quite common here and seem to grow everywhere, the bright colours of their blooms enlivening the forest.
16846: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

A few small rocks stick out of the ground here, half-hidden by the vegetation. Moss and fungi grow all around, covering the bark of many trees and the surface of the rocks. A few mushrooms can be seen on the forest floor, peeking out from under the fallen leaves.
16847: The trees grow very closely together here, forming a dense canopy overhead. This canopy partially blocks out the sky, while making a perfect nesting spot for many birds. Roots of some trees have popped out from under the earth, making travel difficult.
16848: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Mellyrn grow sparsely here as the Golden Wood to the north gives way to an ordinary forest, but their golden crowns are still visible amongst the other trees. Small bushes grow around that surely produce berries and other fruit. Broken branches and fallen leaves blanket the earth.
16849: The mellyrn have become sparse, as the golden forest gives way to a beautiful river that rushes north of here. Although the peaceful waters, the chirping of birds and the softness of the turf would seem to make anyone want to linger here, there is a strange yet enchanting sensation of tranquility emanating from the other shore.
16850: A long-tailed bird watches you from the vegetation.

Here the southern shore of the River Celebrant displays signs of recent activity. The grass is unevenly cut short and the riverbank is rather trodden. This appears to be a spot where animals of all varieties come and drink from the waters' edge. On the other, steeper, bank grow golden trees of the same kind as the trees on this bank. To the east you can see a graceful tree arching above the river.
16851: A woodpecker is here, tapping on a tree.

A large tree arches gracefully over the swift river to the north, providing a natural bridge to the other side of the river. Another tree can be seen on the opposite shore, completing the path. Climbing over the branched bridge would require steady footing.
16852: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Horse stables take up the greater part of this barn. There is a smell of hay and horse manure in the air. Many farmer utensils including pitchforks and shovels are stacked up against the northern wall. A ramp is against one wall, leading up to the roof of this building. A lot of campfire ashes can be seen on the ground, apparently left here by many people seeking shelter from the forces of nature.
16853: Short bushes and small trees hide a small path that leads to a wooden barn in the west. The forest looks as if it had been thinned by loggers as there are many dead trees and decaying stumps. There is a lot of undergrowth here since the trees are not so thick, and the sunlight is able to reach the ground. Some of the grass looks as if it had been grazed.
16854: Some thick writhing vines whip all around you (red aura).

The thick trees rise up hundreds of feet. Little shrubs or bushes grow here, as very little sunlight reaches the ground, making it hard for them to survive. In the spot where an old tree had fallen, creating an opening in the canopy, many young trees fight over a place under the opening that would allow them to catch some sunlight.
16855: The thick green canopy formed by the foliage of the tall trees blocks out the life-giving sun. Thus most vegetation that usually grows in forests seems to avoid this place. There is little grass, bushes and flowers. Instead the ground is covered by fallen leaves and branches which slowly decay away.
16856: This part of the forest is quite dark, and there is little vegetation besides trees. A few bushes grow by the side of the tree-trunks, but their branches seem too thin and their leaves appear too pale. The trees are the dominating force here, growing so close together that their foliage forms an uninterrupted canopy which blocks out the sky. Occasional bird calls echo down from the tree-branches.
16857: A giant, mean looking earth beetle is standing here.

Trees here grow slightly apart, and the ground below them is covered by grass. Most of the trees aren't nearly as tall as those one can see to the north. To the south endless plains stretch as far as the eye can see. The soft green grass seems to be everywhere, covering every inch of the ground.
16858: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

The forest ends to the south as the land opens into a wide grassy plain. Nearing the edge of the forest, the trees appear to decrease in size as well as in number. Occasional animal sounds can be heard from the north where the trees stand closer and the undergrowth is more dense. Many small bushes grow here, some of them bearing small berries.
16859: Many different kinds of trees grow here, together with other kinds of vegetation. Bushes, flowers, and many different kinds of grass are everywhere. The colourful flowers form a dense carpet, surrounded by thick grass. In some spots the grass has been trampled by many animals and is turning brown.
16860: The size of the trees decreases to the south and so does their number as they are replaced by many small bushes and flowers. Green grass is everywhere and in some places it has been trampled, as if many animals have wandered around here. Even farther to the south, the trees disappear as the forest gives way to grasslands.
16861:
A tall plant grows here, with grey-green leaves and grey flowers.
A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

Birches and mellyrn rise like the masts of sunken ships from a green and uneven sea of ferns, hinting at the presence of water nearby. This impression is affirmed by slurping muddy noises that emerge from under the tall plants when anyone moves past. Here and there can be seen a number of fallen trees and rocks covered with thick moss, untouched by nature's trimming hand.
16862: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

A light wind gently moves the grass as it makes its way through the plains. Clusters of various flowers and bushes are scattered all around. Some of the bushes have black fruit growing on them. An occasional tree can be seen, but they aren't clustered together like in a forest. The forest of Lorien can be seen in the north, but passage in that direction is blocked by a wall of a wooden building.
16863: A giant, mean looking earth beetle is standing here.

To the south the trees start to give way to grass and other undergrowth, mostly flowers and bushes, but here the forest is quite dense. The tree-branches block out parts of the sky, but in places large patches of the sky can be seen. Fallen leaves blanket the thin layer of grass that grows on the ground. Thick knots of bushes create barriers in some spots, making passage difficult.
16864:
Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.
A colony of red ants is here. The ants seem to ignore you.
A giant, mean looking earth beetle is standing here.

Leaves and fallen tree-trunks cover the ground. Here and there rocks peep out from underneath the cover. The rocks are covered with green moss and small insects that feed on this moss. Large trees grow everywhere, making it impossible to see the sky, as their canopies combine to form together one gigantic canopy.
16865: The ground here is completely covered by debris, mostly fallen leaves and branches. The trees that grow here are of many different varieties and sizes, yet they all grow mixed together. In a spot where the sunlight can shine down through the canopy, a circle of blue flowers grows amid the grass.
16866:
A dense carpet of blue flowers dip their heads in the breeze.
A small mushroom grows nearby.
A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.
A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

The forest here consists mostly of birches, ashes and rowans and is quite light and airy. The ground is covered with green grass on which many dry tree-leaves are scattered, rustling with every movement of the air. To the south the trees recede as the forest opens up into a wide grassy plain.
16867: Light golden grass grows wildly here. Many bushes grow together, and on a few of them one can see some kind of fruit. Flowers of all varieties and colours, blue, red, orange, white and purple, dot the landscape. The plains extend south as far as the eye can see.
16868: A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

Light golden grass covers the area, waving back and forth from the lightest breeze. Underneath the grass lies fertile earth that sits there untouched by a hand of a farmer. Traces left by many animals can be seen clearly by the way the grass has been bent and torn.
16869: To the south the plains stretch out seemingly to the very horizon. The land is populated by many animals, as indicated by the many small burrows that can be found here. The fertile earth is suitable for almost any kind of vegetation. Stunted trees intermingle with bushes and flowers of many different colours.
16870: A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

The forest to the north seems to grow slowly in this direction, crawling across the land. No bare earth can be seen as a variety of grasses completely blankets the fertile ground. Thick knots of bushes and shrubs mix together, growing by the base of the trees. To the south, the trees disappear completely, leading to barren plains.
16871: A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

Sturdier conifers that have no objection to drier and sandier soil mix here with birches, tenants of marshland forests. The ground gets considerably drier to the south where mostly pines grow. To the north can be spotted an occasional fern, suggesting that the descending forest is turning to marsh in that direction. Among the pines and the birches are a few strange trees, native to no other forest on Arda. Their crowns and boles glisten with varying shades of gold and silver.
16872:
A colony of red ants is here. The ants seem to ignore you.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Birches and tall pines surround the immediate area. Nearby, fallen needles of conifers have been carefully piled to construct a small anthill. Ants can be seen scurrying along, fulfilling numerous tasks. A spine of some unwary reptile can be seen bleaching in the anthill, trophy left by a reckless intruder. The ground turns to marshland farther north, while becoming drier to the south.
16873:
A low shrub with bright green, oblong leaves is growing here.
A long-tailed bird watches you from the vegetation.
A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

Tall pines and birches surround this small clearing where grass has been trampled by countless hoofed feet of the tenants of this forest. Many animals seem to choose this clearing as their favourite grazing spot. A few bushes grow at the edge of the clearing, yielding berries that might fill the stomach of other, more sentient, beings.
16874: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Many different grasses thrive here, fed by the constant rain and warmed by the rays of the sun. Swaying gently in the wind that crosses the plains, the tall grass rustles slightly. Small crickets can be heard constantly chirping.
16875: The hillsides and the land between the hills is a mix of grassland and forest. A lot of trees grow to the north, but the more south you look, the less trees you see and the more grass. The size of the trees appears to decrease with their number. To the south the land grows more even and less forested and the wind picks up speed, as there aren't many trees to interfere with its movement.
16876:
A large beautiful rose bush is blooming here.
Deep inside the bush, there are two red roses with leaves and thorny stems.

The forest here is thinner than to the north, as trees have given way to the undergrowth of thick bushes, shrubs and flowers. As the undergrowth grows more lush, the trees seem to shrink and grow stunted. Yet farther to the south the undergrowth disperses as well as the land stretches out into an endless grassy plain.
16877: A mass of wriggling vines drops on you from the trees.

To the north the forest grows thicker and darker, but to the south the gaps between the trees grow wider until eventually the trees disappear and the terrain opens up into a wide plain that stretches all the way to the horizon. The forest ground is soft and moist, and the undergrowth consists mostly of small shrubs and bright forest flowers.
16878: A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

The air here is fresh and clear, allowing to see for a great distance. A forest seems to start in the north, but looking southward you can see nothing except a vast expanse of plains and low hills. There is little vegetation except for the ever-present grass. Trees cling to the hillsides, but for a few copses of tall pines, they are dwarf-trees, barely distinguishable from bushes.
16879: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

The light golden grass brightens the plains by day, and even at night is still easy to see. Bending ever so gently in the wind, it is everywhere. There is no other vegetation except for a few large bushes that grow here almost to the height of stunted trees. These bushes all bear some kind of black fruit.
16880: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Rising and falling, the land changes slightly, but everywhere it is covered by grass. A few stringy bushes with pale-green leaves grow here next to a couple of bent trees that look more dead than alive. Very rarely one can see an occasional flower lift its head out of the deep grass.
16881: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

The grass here is wilted and brown. Few animal tracks can be seen here, but many small insects can be found hiding underneath rocks that protect them from the environment. Most of the vegetation has been swept away by the wind along with much of the topsoil.
16882:
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.
A large eagle soars above you.

There is very little cover protecting these lands from the harsh sunlight; the landscape here is barren and deserted. The grass is brown and wilted. Whatever bushes and trees once grew here appear to have dried up and died, and the same probably happened to all the flowers.
16883: The forest ends in a steep sandy slope. Except for the pines, little other vegetation can be seen. Pine needles and cones carpet the ground. The wildlife here is scarce compared to that of the northern forest, where the ground is more fertile. The few animals that occasionally come here are witnesses to the never-ending struggle between vibrant nature and scorched barrenness.
16884: This appears to be the southern end of the sandy forest. Pines and a few stunted bushes are all that grow in the sandy soil and intrusive barrenness. To the north the forest becomes thicker and more lively. The ground climbs slowly upwards to the south, forming a rather steep sandy slope. Except for the most agile climbers, anyone trying to scale the slope would probably slide back into the forest.
16885: This seems to be one of the shadiest corners of the forest. It is impossible to penetrate the tangled bushes to the east. To the south the ground rises and forms a steep sandy slope, along which only the best of climbers might be able to ascend to the fields above. Most plants have abandoned the fight to subsist in this part of the forest. Sturdy pines are the sole survivors in this struggle for survival, which would have ended long ago, if not for the mystical breath of strength emanating from the forest to the north.
16886: At the Edge of the Forest

Mighty pines and birches block your way north and west, where sandy and unyielding fields have become fertile soil on which these trees tower. It could be that this forest has secrets to hide and secrets to share, but in any case one would have to find another way to enter it. One could also travel to the southern plains, although these seem quite barren and hostile to all forms of life. An eye-catching mound lies to the southeast.
16887: Grass grows bountifully here as the plains continue on. Short grass, tall grass, golden grass and green grass all mix together to form a thick blanket over the earth. Occasional trees can be spotted among the plains, some of them growing alone and some in circles around a few earthen mounds. Small insects jump around in the grass.
16888:
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

The grass here is quite dry, and with your every movement its slight rustling makes small insects jump away. There is little traffic through these plains, and broken and bent grass-stems make any tracks easy to see. The few bushes that can be seen here are huge and grow together in clumps. The rolling plains continue in all directions except to the north where the land becomes more hilly.
16889: A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

To the north the edge of a forest can be seen, but in all other directions seemingly endless plains extend as far as the eye can see. Stunted trees grow along the sides of the few low hills that can be seen among the plains. A deep carpet of grass covers the ground. Animal tracks have worn a few paths in the grass, making it easier to travel through the area.
16890:
A large thorny branched shrub is growing here.
On the shrub, there are two piles of blackberries.

The grass here is tall, and occasional breezes send it rippling like a wave on the sea, the smooth passage of the grassy wave unbroken except where it runs into a small mound. A cluster of bushes grows against the mound, their short branches bearing dark, almost black, fruit. Every time the wind passes across the plains, many different kinds of flowers send their seeds out and the wind gently blows them away.
16891: A tall pine tree grows here.

A small copse of young pine trees grows around a small hill that rises above the thick carpet of grass. The hill is just a few yards in diameter and its sides are covered with pine-needles and pine-cones. Many pine-cones are broken or crushed, as if some animals had fed upon them.
16892:
A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

The waters of a clear spring that bursts from under the ground here keep this area lively and vibrant. Many bushes grow around the spring and even a few trees have found a home here, growing almost as high as they might in a forest. Tracks of animals cover the ground all around the spring, as this is apparently their favourite watering spot.
16893: The terrain undulates softly. Barely noticeable hills and valleys between them make the landscape somewhat less boring than it might appear from a distance and also somewhat harder to traverse. There is not enough grass to cover the ground completely, but there are many small bushes growing all around.
16894: A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

Dead trees cover the landscape, indicative of a water shortage here. The wind gusts, blowing dust and soil around. There is little vegetation here, other than stubborn tufts of yellow-brown grass. However, there are signs of sparse animal habitation.
16895: A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

The wind is very strong here, blowing dirt and dust all over. The grass and weeds do little to protect the topsoil and fail to prevent it from being eaten at by the strong gusts. The result is a very barren landscape, as only the strongest grasses can survive here.
16896: Sandy Fields at the Forest's Edge
A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The ground begins to slope downward to the north where, all of a sudden, it disappears. Where one would expect to see more dunes, mighty trees spiral towards the sky. This surprising and drastic change in scenery suggests that some unearthly powers have put an end to the sandstorms that long claimed the fertile lands under a reign of barrenness.
16897: Sandy Fields at the Forest's Edge
A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.

Endless waves of sand extend all around you, except to the north, where the land drops and an unexpected green forest starts below the level of the sandy fields. As the slope is rather steep, a step in that direction might result in a swift trip to the forest floor. These lifeless plains are in sharp contrast with the tall trees, forming a picture that might appear unnatural to mortal eyes.
16898: Sandy Fields at the Forest's Edge
A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.

Visible in the shapes of the trees and lines of the terrain, there appears to be a link between a coppice far to the south and the outskirts of the northern forest. So drastic is the change in scenery from the barren landscape to the lush forest, it suggests some unearthly power put a stop to the moving sand preventing it from encroaching upon the tree-covered land.
16899: These sandy fields lie between many different forms of terrain. The few patches of grass here are dried and withered, in stark contrast to the mighty forest that lies northward, and in these level plains one would not quite expect to find a high mound emerging from the ground to the southeast. To the southwest lies a coppice of trees that is probably better at supporting life than the southwestern barrenness.
16900: Footpath between the Mound and the Forest

Scenery on both sides of the path is somewhat bleak. Infrequent tussocks and plants extend from the dry sandy soil, providing little solace for weary travellers. The faint path is lined with small white rocks gathered from the nearby fields, but except for this, no other sign of life or activity can be seen. The path continues north and east. At some distance north one can see a green forest, and to the south the ground rises and forms a small mound.
16901:
A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

A hill with a flat top rises amid the vast expanse of plains that continues in every direction. A small spring bubbles on the top of the hill, as a steady stream of water flows down the southern hillside. Animal tracks are everywhere as the animals come here to drink.
16902: A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

Golden and green, the grass sways as the wind constantly pounds it, bending its stems back and forth. Small bushes lose their leaves as the powerful wind beats upon them. A great old tree stands here, creaking dangerously as the wind hurls itself upon its branches.
16903: The plains continue in all directions. There are no trees around, but there are many stringy-looking bushes with brownish leaves and knotted roots which stick out of the ground. The grass that grows here has thin green stems with closely fitting leaves and sometimes a tiny white flower on the top.
16904: A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The grass here is so thick that in places its strands tangle together forming knots and thickets. Some of these knots appear flattened and pressed to the ground, as if somebody had stepped upon them or an animal had slept there at night. A couple of pine trees flank a small patch of bare ground where the grass appears to have been burnt out, apparently the site of some traveller's campfire.
16905:
Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.
A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The land here is level and treeless, but below the dense carpet of grass there appear to be many tree-roots in the ground. Some properties of the climate or of the soil of these plains must have allowed these roots to stay hidden, intact and undecayed long after the trees themselves were gone until winds, rains or roots of plants eroded the top layer of the ground, exposing the ancient tree-roots.
16906:
A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.
A fallow deer is grazing peacefully here.

Winds blow through the plains incessantly, their strong gusts bending and tearing the gentle grass and making every tree sway and creak as the trunk refuses to move together with the branches. Even the shortest bushes are almost pulled out of the ground by the powerful winds.
16907: Winds that blow constantly through these plains have carried away most of the top layer of the soil, exposing sand and clay that lay below. Clumps of grass and rare clusters of bushes cling to the barren ground. While occasional tree-roots in the ground indicate that this area was once home to many trees, the few trees that do grow here now appear skinny and fragile, their thin branches barely supporting brownish leaves.
16908: Little vegetation grows in this dry, sparsely populated area. Few animals dare roam here, as there is nary a drop of water to be found, and food is very scarce. Years of erosion have taken their toll on the soil, reducing it to blowing sand and small, dry patches of sickly-looking dirt.
16909: A giant earth beetle is standing here.

The sparse vegetation that grows here looks almost dead. Trees that normally would stand straight and tall have become dwarfed, stooping over so that a tall human might reach greater heights than their tops. Winds whip up the topsoil and dust from the earth as it erodes.
16910: The dunes continue north and south. Any traveller through this barren terrain will soon face the onslaught of fatigue, as tiredness fetters the feet and dry air makes the throat yearn for cold and refreshing water. Faraway trees lie to the north, and the landscape slopes upwards to the south - both directions offering livelier scenery than this desolate place.
16911:
A mass of dark green leaves clings to a wall.
A circular stone well has been built here.
A nightingale is here, chirping a sweet melody.

This narrow bar of grassland between the wall of a decrepit building and the eastern barren fields appears to be a rare outpost of greenery in this area. The small well located here must have been dug deep with hard and tedious work in order to reach fresh clean waters. A pelt, taut on sidelong poles, would provide shade from sun and rain if not for signs of wear and small holes scattered across the surface.
16912: What once was a yielding and fertile field of various crops has now turned into a cracked and dry plain of sandy soil. The wind has fretted the regular furrows into faint signs of a regardful hand that had probably grown tired of fighting the relentless weather years ago. The planks that once formed a fence to keep various beasts out have been trampled down and left to rot.
16913: Plains along the Side of the Mound

No trees or bushes grow here, and even grass has trouble taking root in this hard soil, leaving these plains barren and easy to traverse. To the east the ground rises steadily and forms a noticeble mound. In some places the earthen blanket has slid away revealing a hard surface, on which stripes mark different strata that have eventually formed this rise. To the southwest you spot a coppice where, unlike in these barren fields, one might be able to find signs of wildlife.
16914: A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

Turning from the east to the south, the faint path meanders up a gentle slope. There is no grass or plant life and no shade of green catches the eye, except the distant forest far to the north and a few trees on the top of the mound to the southeast.
16915: The surrounding scenery is somewhat bleak and barren, providing little solace for a weary traveller. The path circles a number of trees that form a small wall to the south, then continues west where it climbs toward the very same mound that makes going south impossible, then follows the slope of the mound south only to turn east closer to the top. The fields around the path are extremely poor in plants and trees, but there is little doubt that more could be found in the forest that can be seen to the north.
16916: Snakes and other creatures that find little solace in mighty trees and lush grasses of more fruitful lands seem to be the few tenants of these fields. The ground is regularly covered with small white stones that will probably soon erode into featureless sand. In some places, however, someone has gathered the stones, leaving noticeable empty spots. To the southwest a strange mound catches the eye.
16917: The landscape here is considerably more barren than the outskirts of the forest to the north. It is no wonder there are no animals to be seen for miles around. The plants are stunted and the sparse grass is withered. The contrast between this desolation and the viable northern forest might seem unfathomable, yet here it is.
16918: A large eagle soars above you.

Sparsely growing trees and bushes make travelling through such terrain easy, but the fact that almost no grass grows in the sandy soil is probably a sign of scarcity of water in this area. A cautious traveller would probably head north, where nature seems to strengthen, and an adventurous one might travel south where nature seems to provide little support for life.
16919: Scanty slender plants and occasional patches of dried grass fail to remedy the overall impression of desolation. These plains differ in no way from the vast fields all around. Any traveller would have a hard time navigating here, if not for the dark stripe on the northern horizon that marks the start of a forest.
16920: Little plant life has managed to grow in the hard clay ground. The land to the north is more fertile and a number of trees can be seen growing there. A long and deep crevice lies to the east and on the farther side an old hut is faintly visible. Regardless of the crevice's origin, it creates an impassable boundary making it impossible to reach the hut from here.
16921: A fairly large hut, a lone structure in this border area between forest and plains, stands to the west. From a distance the hut looks somewhat run-down. Upon closer inspection it appears that not only is the hut frequently occupied but also well maintained. The hut is built from a light timber stained for protection from the elements and guarded by a sturdy wooden door. To the east a well-trampled path forms a route through the trees and into the vast plains that spread south of the forest of Lorien.
16922: Shaped by the passage of many travellers across the terrain, a path of hard dirt packed tightly together leads through the plains. While the rains fail to dent its surface, the soft ground to the side of the path shows the tracks of many small critters that pass this way as they skirt around the path. A number of tall trees grow just off the path, keeping it narrow and neat. Through the trees to the north a low mound of earth is visible, while to the west the path leads towards a hut.
16923: Tall, majestic trees line both sides of this well-worn path as it winds its way west and east across the fields. The way east is towards the Lorien plains where the path is clearly visible, while to the west it winds through a dense patch of trees and then vanishes.
16924: A rough and narrow path runs east-west through the plains. The path is damp and muddy, and while any footprints that were older than a day or two have washed away, new ones have already formed. Many trees, tall and straight, line the edges of the path. The trees continue to mark the path for many miles to the west, but to the east they vanish a few miles from here as the trail dissipates upon the open plains of Lorien.
16925: A thin stream of water slowly winds its way southwards. The ground around the stream is moist and fertile allowing a variety of grasses to grow long and thick stems. A small path traces the brook and another appears to crisscross it as it leads westwards through the trees. To the east the wide open plains of Lorien dominate the landscape.
16926: Being very moist and fertile, the soil of these plains supports a lush carpet of tall thick grasses. The grasses stand a good three feet tall and are dense enough to impede the most agile of travellers. To the west a small brook can be seen flowing softly across the plains.
16927: The grass which covers this area is tall, broad and prickly. The sounds of small animals can be heard as they move through the tall grass. To the south, east and west the grass remains abundant, but to the north the ground becomes more rocky and slopes downwards.
16928: A small cluster of clover grows here.

Several clumps of flowers, such as daisies, can be seen poking out among the long blades of the thick grass. The soil is moist and fertile, as needed to support the rich vegetation. The landscape is dotted by just enough bushes with prickly thorns to hinder smooth travel. Far to the north a steep hill is visible, while a single tall tree stands in the east.
16929: This area is covered by rich grasses that surround a single, extremely tall, tree. The tree, which rises majestically above the plains, is covered by a thick bark that has many knots on the surface. Many of the lower branches of the tree can be seen strutting out and are probably capable of supporting the weight of a heavy troll.
16930: The flat plains are covered in tall grass. The lush grass conceals soft and muddy ground below. A small brook can be spotted running through the plains, its clear waters flowing from the south and turning east towards the plains covered in a grey mist. A single large tree can be seen to the west and some hills are visible in the north, but the grassy plains dominate the view.
16931: A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.

The ground here is soft and muddy, covered by puddles of water that grow in size to the southeast. A traveller on foot would find it nearly impossible to walk through this terrain without stepping into the dark water. A dim fogbank starts here and continues to the east and south through the swampy lands. Drier fields and plains stretch out to the west and north.
16932: Water dominates the area, the soft ground about one foot below its surface. In some places small bushes and other vegetation grow on drier elevations, but since the area is covered in fog, it is hard to see where these spots are. The fog seems to clear to the north and west while it gets denser to the south. There is little wildlife, but occasional movement can be seen or felt in the dirty water.
16933: This part of the plains is dominated by water and grass. The ground is soft and muddy. Small bushes grow here, but there is no larger growth.
