Several crushed skeletons lie on the bottom of this dried up well. The well has become a mass grave for the previous citizens of this destroyed village. A few stones of the well ring have fallen down into here and crushed the pitiful corpses further. The walls of the well are rather rugged making it possible to climb out.
17932:
An orc sentry of the Ohurk-uai is here on patrol.
An orc sentry of the Ohurk-uai is here on patrol.

This small, well hidden trail leads through the bushes to the tower, which rises above the thorns. The large bushes create an impenetrable wall around you, almost like a tunnel of green and brown into which the sun only partly reaches.
17933: There is a water skin lying on the ground.

This wooden hut must once have been clean and well cared for, but now has fallen into a state of decay. A window in the western wall must have long ago provided this home's owner with a nice view. A wood burning stove sits in the middle of the room. In another part of the floor lies a door to the cellar.
17934: A tiny spider is here, eating a tiny bug.

Cobwebs fill this long deserted cellar. It seems to have been designed for storing beer. The walls are stone that were covered with wood. The wood shows advanced signs of rot. The northern wall is in such disrepair it's hard to imagine its previous state.
17935: Several silver coins lie scattered about here.

The room is empty, but for a table at its centre and a chest pushed against the eastern wall. The table is covered with a thick layer of dust, under which there are some playing cards. There are some rat holes in the walls and other evidence of the rodents in the form of scratches on the floor.
17939: This must be the uppermost level of the castle. You can clearly see that the many years of abandonment have taken their toll on this place. Three large, round windows, facing north, south and west, are now empty of their glazing, and a cold wind blows through the chamber. But they do afford a spectacular view of the forest, which surrounds the castle.
17943: A narrow corridor leading south, partially lit by the doorkeep. The only choices are heading back down to Imladris, or exploring the prayer room ahead. A small draft also blows through this small hallway.
17944: Here, spiritual growth, above all else, is practiced. This is a room usually shrouded in silence. The only noises are those of the northern grumblings, and the barely audible sounds of turning pages from the south.
17945: An Elven steward stands here, watching over the household.
This was at one time a library full of texts and lores of the ages. Now it is a place of study and rest for the weary Priest. A steward is posted here to keep the place tidy.
17950:
A small white fountain is here.
An Elven steward stands here, watching over the household.

Several large windows open up this room to the stars and the sun, letting the splendour and light of the West fill and caress the features of the room. The light is reflected in a myriad of colours from crystals inlaid in carvings and statues. Pillars of marble lift the dome-shaped ceiling shaped as to create a feeling of space and freedom and two small trees grow in the centre of the room act as a constant reminder of the lost Trees, Telperion and Laurelin and thus the light of the Silmarilli, the great gems that Maglor fought so many battles for.
17951: This medium-sized room looks like a mixture between a library, a laboratory and a geographer's workshop. Heavy tomes are aligned on many shelves fixed to the walls; some other ancient-looking books lie in glass boxes, to preserve them from exposure. A wooden desk lies in front of the windows, to the east; some more texts are piled in a corner, while great part of the desk is taken by a spread map of the Misty Mountains east of Rivendell. Many quill pens and vials of ink rest in an open drawer, always ready for use. Other maps hang from the walls, showing places both near and far. In the northwestern corner there is another table, this time made of marble; strangely coloured patches mar its otherwise perfect surface. Doorways lead both south, to the living room, and west, to Galawon's bedroom.
17952: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

This bedroom's windows, as opposed to the ones in the rest of the house, face west, towards the house of Elrond, and north. A comfortable bed lies in the southwestern corner; a finely carved oak nightstand is beside it. A few well-thumbed books rest on the nightstand, probably Galawon uses them to read before sleeping. Shown on display on the walls you can see Galawon's most treasured trophies, a dented two-handed sword and a shredded fragment of black cloth, together with fine oil paintings of various landscapes of Arda. The only door is east, to Galawon's study.
17982: A Rocky Hill in the Wild Forest

A small hill rises up in the forest here, blocked off in all directions except back to the east. There is little vegetation on this hill, as it is covered mainly in rocks and pebbles. There are a number of bones scattered about the hill.
17983: The numbing stench of dead and rotting carcases permeates the air in this cramped, and sloping tunnel. Bending from north to west, the passageway makes a precipitous descent. Northward it opens out somewhat, entering quite a large cave.
17984:
An old, strong cave troll is standing here.
A large earth troll is digging here, looking for some tasty morsels.
A small, mean earth troll is standing here, thinking of something hideous.
A small, mean earth troll is standing here, thinking of something hideous.

A light breeze blows up from a large crevice on the entire western side of this narrow ledge. The little outcropping seems a little unstable as you walk across it. You can't even imagine how far you would fall if this section of rock were to give way to your weight.
17985:
The corpse of a young troll is lying here.
A pool of darkish water has formed in a depression of the stone.

You can go no further along the ledge, for here it comes to an abrupt end at a massive rockfall. Even the floor underfoot appears to be unstable, and chilly water seeps through the roof, and through broad cracks in the walls. It would seem wise to return the way you came, as soon as possible.
17986: Rocks of every shape and size can be seen scattered along the path to the top of the hill. No grass grows here, just stones and hard brown dirt cover the ground. A small circle of stones sits atop the hill surrounded by boulders to sit on. Remains of camps are scattered among the rocks.
17987: The cave is a mere scoop in the cliff and provides almost no protection from wind, rain and snow. Neither does it protect you from the sounds that seem to come from all directions at once - wind in the chinks of rock, water dripping, a crack, the sudden rattling fall of a loose stone.
17988: A lurg-leader with cat-like eyes wields a wicked spear.

You descend the spiral stairs from the hall above into a long hallway whose name is all too appropriate. The length of this arrased corridor is lit by a variety of lamps fixed to the north wall which illuminate a dozen large woven pictures. The tapestries depict the history of the grandson of Radorac. The first hanging in the eastern hall shows the isle of Numenor in its last days, Armenelos wreathed in black smoke whilst a great fleet of ships are armed in the havens of Romenna. Further tapestries show the sailing of the great Armada towards Valinor, Radorac II standing on the flagship Alcarondas. Towards the east end of the hall is shown the landings of Ar-Pharazon and his small party on Tuna, and their entombment in the Caves of the Forgotten at the changing of the world. In the final weaves in the western hall, by Manwe's decree the tomb is opened and Pharazon, Radorac II and Septumar are forced to sail to Endor to atone for their crimes. The eastern hall ends at an arched portal above which a plaque stands. A similar plaque marks the western door of iron. In front of this door a valet stands guard awaiting his master.
18046: Hidden in a desolate valley surrounded by almost impassable shrubs, this house might have evaded attention for centuries. Lately someone has begun the refurnishment of the exterior by patching the roof and covering the walls with black sticky tar in hope that the wooden planks can withstand another decade. The interior appears to consist of three fairly large rooms, with this one being the largest. A few plush armchairs and sofas provide comfort; while a large dark table, which is surrounded by oaken chairs, probably serves equally as dining table and meeting table judging by the number of notes and diagrams spread across it.
18047: Right Wing of a Dunadan Mansion

The walls and windows of this room are covered completely with red and black sheets. Several shields and stuffed animal heads protrude in the places the sheets join with each other. A steel lamp, constructed as a spiral, is hanging from the ceiling and focuses its beam on the centre of the room where a strange book is attached with iron bolts to a heavy dark oak pedestal.
18051: The river rushes quickly, speeding away from its roots in the western forest. Some leaves and twigs float in the water, little pieces of the forest it carries with it like mementos of its origin. All this river has collected is swiftly carried away from here, as the river continues on to some destination in the east. Most of these seeds of the forest will be left along the shores of the river before reaching the river's end.
18052:
A large sign is posted upon the wall for you to read.
A large bulletin board, entitled "Board of the Free Peoples", is mounted here.
A fine marble chessboard with ivory and ebony pieces is set here.
A steward of the Valar stands here, ready to assist you into a room.

Built on the western shores of Aman, facing only the Encircling Sea and the Wall of the Night stand the vast Halls of Mandos. In this small and remote corner of the Halls of Awaiting you tarry in a time of recollection, perhaps listening to echoes of times long gone by, or perhaps dreaming dreams of your own and wondering when the time will come that you are able to return once more to roam freely upon Middle-earth.
18053: A mailbox stands here stuffed full of messages.

Vast and strong are the Halls of Awaiting, tall are the Pelori, called also the Mountains of Defence, and long and mysterious is the Straight Way to the True West, and yet still sometimes rumour reaches this place of the deeds and words of those who still dwell upon Middle-earth.
18054: A large bulletin board, entitled "Tales", is mounted here.

Half-substance, half-shadow, high walls rise to the distant roof of the Halls. Far above, just below the roof, many narrow windows have been cut in the shadowy fabric. Through these windows golden and silvery light enters the Halls and strange scents and whispers drift in. Some of these whispers speak of strange lands and things; others are in no language of Middle-earth that you can recognise.
18055: A large bulletin board, entitled "Free Peoples' Chronicles", is mounted here.

In this corner of the Halls of Awaiting you might hear echoes and rumours of things long gone by, or catch a glimpse of more recent events on Middle-earth. For though you are far removed here from the events in the mortal realm, still like reflections and dreams their tales sometimes reach you here.
18057: This broad tunnel delves slowly down into the great Blue Mountains. It ends to the east at the base of a wide staircase, leading to the upper, public areas of the caverns. The corridor is broad and tall and brightly lit by many lanterns along the walls.
18058: This broad staircase connects the lower levels of these halls with the topmost level opening on the outside world. Dwarves ascend and descend these steps, buying provisions at the stores above, and venturing out into the forests and meadows of these mountain vales, or returning from abroad to their homes. The risers are inscribed at the edges with intricately detailed abstract patterns.
18059: This is a great circular pit carved in the native stone of the mountains. A great staircase, wide enough for twenty dwarves to walk abreast, rises gradually upward, turning counter-clockwise as it goes. Its risers are paved with marble, and black onyx sconces on the wall hold lamps which are continually filled from an unseen source and kept burning.
18060:
An elven guard is standing here at his post.
An elven guard is standing here at his post.

Several guards are stationed here at all times. You are currently standing in their living quarters. There are several bunks and a large table where you assume they eat and probably play cards. You can only exit back to the west.
18061: A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

An old birch marks the beginning of what seems to be a long line of trees continuing as far east as eye can see. The lowest branches of the tree are too high to reach, and the trunk is simply too big to scale without any support.
18062: A large stone fireplace with a roaring fire warms the room.
A large table resides in the centre of the room. Fine dinnerware is set about it and comfortable wooden chairs await any guests. A window on the wall allows you to view the scenic countryside.
18063: Otho Sackville looks at you with obvious distaste.

This room is very clean and neat. On the shelves you can see dishes and other household utensils. A table with some chairs around it occupy the centre of the room. An old stove in good condition is ready to cook a meal. The room has the faint smell of hot tea.
18064:
A small oaken table has been set here.
On the table, there are three seed-cakes, a piece of smoked, cured meat, a bowl of salad, a loaf of bread, and two pork-pies.
A small barrel made of aged oak and strong iron hoops stands here.
A beer barrel has been left here.
Lobelia Sackville wants you out of HER house.
Otho Sackville looks at you with obvious distaste.

Within the pantry here resides a wide variety of foodstuffs, and it becomes apparent that Mr. Baggins puts a high priority on food. Breads, cakes, meats, and vegetables are organized neatly along shelves. In the corner of the room sit some caskets, most likely filled with beer and wine.
18065: You are in a spacious, comfortable room. A large sofa, by hobbit proportions, lies in the corner of the room. An ornate bookstand rests next to it, with an open book and an empty tea cup on top. A doorway leads into the bedroom.
18066: Entering the room you realise that this is the ideal place to rest after a long day's work. A huge bed looks really cosy and comfortable. A small bookstand rests next to the bed.
18067: As comfortable as the master bedroom, this bedroom is used primarily by guests. This bed is quite larger than the one in the master bedroom, but still seems a tad small to allow a human a comfortable rest. This room looks like it hasn't been used recently though, maybe due to the new owners.
18068: This hilltop is the highest point for leagues in any direction. Below you, to the south, the little village of Hobbiton lies in the lush, tree-lined valley of the stream called only The Water. Further south, a road can be dimly seen, running east and west. The sides of the Hill are terraced and covered with vines, fruit trees, and vegetable gardens.
18069:
A tall and strong guard is here.
A tall and strong guard is here.

After leaving the forest of pine, the area opens up to a large clearing. In the centre of this clearing, stands a white gazebo, with forest green trim. Standing next to the gazebo in a very guardian-like manner, off to the east, is a huge statue erected on honour of the Hobbit-Ainu, Lorena. This statue is about eight feet tall in height, and made of marble. Lorena is depicted as standing very astute, with one hand in her pocket, and the other one giving a high-five. Within the gazebo are many small chairs. Four noticeably large, adorned chairs sit in the middle of the room, facing outwards to the other smaller chairs. On the back of these chairs are the names: Shatter, Larkspur, Hawthorn, and Feather. Hanging outside of the gazebo are pictures of what you discern to be family members, and close friends of the Underhills.
18070: The Housekeeper looks fed up with her job. She scowls at you unhappily.

You have found the Guild of Mystics. This is quite a large room, with shadows filling the nooks and crannies of the room. At a glance about the room, you see that it is filled with strange fluids in various beakers, scrying pools, caged lab rats, and various other indescribable apparatus. The smell from chemical vapors drift up from some vials, and fills your nose, making you cringe. Vials sit on the shelves, full of strange body parts from different animals. Shatter, the Guildmaster of Mystics, has apparently been dabbling in some advanced magic, by the look of the room, but those results remain to be seen. On one wall hang the scalps of Orcs, Trolls, and Black Numenoreans that Shatter has vanquished. Shatter's housekeeper is here, cleaning the room, while Shatter is about saving Arda from Sauron's clutches.
18071: A tall and strong guard is here.

Many flower beds and various bushy growths create a nice mosaic of plant life in this garden. A large hill forms the natural centre of the garden. A small round door and some small windows are dug into the side of the hill. A gravel path leads from the door in the hill to the large roadway just south of this garden.
18072: The Housekeeper looks fed up with her job. She scowls at you unhappily.

This room is cluttered by wooden furniture. The earthen walls are hidden by sturdy closets and cabinets. The south wall has a small, round door flanked with two small windows while a large red curtain on the north wall conceals what lies beyond. A fireplace has been inserted into the west wall.
18073: A large bed takes up most of this room. A small wooden table is on the right hand side of the bed and a silver lamp on the table provides a flickering light. The earthen walls are covered with several gobelins, many of which picture everyday life in the Shire. Some of the gobelins, however, give evidence that the inhabitant of this home might not be an average hobbit.
18074: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

After a long day of patrolling the shire, making sure everything is in check, Torque retires to this small, but exquisite, room. The green curtains are pulled together allowing only a small amount of light to enter the room. Seeing the bed, you can be sure that it is worthy of the finest make in the area. It looks amazingly soft, but it needs to be, Torque must relax his tired muscles. Along side the bed, there is a table made from a tree stump. Sitting on the table, there is a portrait in a small wooden frame.
18093: A tiny spider is here, eating a tiny bug.

Through a narrow fissure runs a route used by the dwarves in times of war. Should the dwarven stronghold fall, this is where the last retreat would be made. Little work has been put into the forging of the route, and judging by the rough and natural walls full of long cracks and deep holes, the dwarven pickaxes rarely pay this tunnel a visit. The fissure takes a sudden plunge upwards, but cracks and holes provide a good foothold even for a heavy and clumsy dwarf to proceed. A distinct draught of cold air indicates that an exit must be near.
18094: A multitude of sharp rocks and cracked splinters lines the floor in the narrow passageway under the mountain. Gleaming fragments of ore in the otherwise pitch-black walls reveal the richness of the underground that lies beneath the Blue Mountains. The cracked ceiling with its long razor-sharp protrusions nearly touches the rubble floor in places, making the passage through the escape route somewhat difficult. It would appear that the dwarves have not yet completed construction in this tunnel.
18095: Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.

In the depths of the mountain several cave systems take root, often extending all the way to the open lands outside. This tunnel seems to be a part of one such system, with a sudden breeze indicating that some form of exit may lie nearby. Although the walls of this tunnel show some indications of widening to allow easier passage, in general it appears to be one of those natural tunnels which has been discovered during mining operations and further utilised because it just happens to be heading in the right direction.
18096: A smooth ceiling curving gently up towards the centre of the cavern makes an impressive display of the astonishing skill of tunneling and carving that is so commonly found among dwarves. Around the cavern the walls rise towards the ceiling in a harmony of blue colours that seem to originate from the mountain itself. To the north a heavy door is set, and a faint draught of fresh air comes from that direction; yet there is no light to be seen.
18097:
A dwarven miner is here, digging the hard rock with his pick.
A dwarven miner is here, digging the hard rock with his pick.

You entered one of the many small mines that the Dwarves are operating here in the Blue Mountains. The tunnels around you are very small and twisty, as they follow the poor ore veins of the Blue Mountains. The timbers look very strong and safe: this mine is a good demonstration of the great construction skills of the Dwarves. From here, you can climb a metal ladder on the wall of the main shaft and exit the mine.
18106:
A small hobbit bartender is here, bragging about the beer.
A hobbit is here walking around.

You are in the common room of the River Inn. The merry Hobbits of Rushey come and go, laughing, singing, and drinking mugs of beer. Against the far wall, there is a bar where you can order a beer for yourself. A stairway leads upstairs where you can rent a room for a night or two.
18107:
A heavy desk, made of solid oak, stands here.
A well-fed hobbit has set up an inn here, renting out rooms.
A domesticated pony, beast of burden to many, stands here.

You have found the innkeeper of the River Inn. As you step into the room, your feet throw up a cloud of dust. You start to wonder if this innkeeper ever sweeps the floor. As you are wondering this, you notice a trail in the dust next to the desk.
18108: You manage to squeeze through the opening behind the desk. There are no windows or doors, except for the opening you just came through. Judging by the secrecy of this room, you think that the innkeeper must keep some very valuable things in here.
18109: There are many different types of tall bushes and small trees growing in this area. Tiny twisting paths among the shrubs show that children from the village in the south must quite often use this little forest as their playground.
18110: An old hobbit, wrinkled with age and a bit pudgy, leans on a walking-stick.

A wagon trail comes from the north and turns east, entering a small village. This must be how the crops from the fields in the northwest are transported to the hobbits living in the central villages. There are a few smials among the fields, built on the sides of small hills.
18111:
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.

Several bushes of various size grow all over this field. The short grass and signs in the ground suggest that this is common feeding ground for sheep or other farm animals. The bushes grow thicker, yet not impassable, to the east.
18112:
A white-painted bench is here.
A hobbit farmer, wielding a sickle, is sitting here.

Fields of wheat and corn surround this little hut which has a small, round door, suggesting that a hobbit lives here. Outside the hut there is a bench where the weary farmer can rest after a day's work and watch the sun set across his crops.
18113: A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.

The path coming from the forest in the west continues through farmed fields and leads toward a small hut in the east. The fields seem to be carefully planned, even a small irrigation system has been built and connected to a nearby spring.
18114: These fields have been recently harvested, although there is still some live crop growing. There are carrots, lettuce and radishes planted on both sides of a wide but shallow ditch that runs south to the river. According to the tracks on the ground this is the favourite place of all the local rabbit population.
18115: The fields around here are prospering due to careful farming by their owners. Full of a variety of crops, it is obvious almost anything could be grown in this fertile soil. A small ditch runs south through the fields where a few wooden planks form a bridge across it. The bridge is clearly well travelled judging by the tracks in the ground which show it to be often crossed with a carriage.
18116:
A fat rabbit sits here, chewing on some grass.
A fat rabbit sits here, chewing on some grass.

There are lot of sounds here that indicate presence of wildlife, but even the sharpest eye would not catch all that hide behind the dense foliage of the underbrush. An east-west path traverses through this small island of forest.
18117: Some vegetables and wild corn grow here and there, but otherwise there is no sign of organized farming nearby. There is no obvious explanation to why the fields have been abandoned even though the river in the south would provide all the moisture for succesfull farming. A few ditches have been dug in the ground long ago, but they are now overgrown as well.
18118: Hay grows all over this field, and much of it has already been piled below a small shelter in the centre of the field. Tracks of a pony and a carriage form an often used trail from the shelter, leading southeast. The field extends far to the north, where it turns into bushes.
18119: A large beautiful rose bush is blooming here.

A lack of trees in the area has allowed taller bushes to take root. Many of them blossom in the summer, their peace only disturbed by random travellers on the small footpath going west and east through the opening.
18120:
A large stone fireplace with a roaring fire warms the room.
A large bookshelf sits against the wall.
On the bookshelf, there are two piles of pipe-weed and a wooden pipe.

The simple yet carefully maintained furniture that fills this hut, tells a story of a hobbit, who besides working hard, for a hobbit in the fields, also does lot of work indoors. A fine collection of pipes and weed is stacked on a bookshelf on the back wall, while two small windows with curtains on each side give a view of the yard.
18121: Many small rocks have been neatly set in the riverbank to serve as stairs leading down to the river. Above, the riverside has been found to be perfect spot for a lonely smial, which by the look of the yard houses some very active hobbit children.
18122: A low shrub with bright green, oblong leaves is growing here.

The forest gets darker and gloomier here, the underbrush becoming thick with shrubs and small vegetation. The bushes create excellent hiding places for many small animals that have left their markings along the path that runs east-west.
18123: The river to the south has eroded its way deep into the ground, forming a steep bank here. The ground slopes slighly upwards in the north and as it slowly turns into forest. Some kind of wooden rail has been built on the slope, possibly this is used to send logs down to the river.
18124: The forest grows denser to the north, while here it is pretty light and colourful thriving in the vast amount of sunlight that reaches the ground. A small footpath traverses up from the bog in the west and continues east through the forest, circling around trees like a snake.
18125:
A hollow length of stout reed lies here.
A hollow length of stout reed lies here.

As the ground slopes slightly toward east it becomes drier. There are still numerous small pools and patches of reeds in the vicinity. A couple of long planks have been set upon the ground, making it possible to walk between dry patches without wetting ones' toes.
18126:
A hollow length of stout reed lies here.
A hollow length of stout reed lies here.
A hollow length of stout reed lies here.

There is very little solid ground here, and even the few patches are covered with reeds. The water is rather shallow however, allowing some hobbits to manage exploring this area when the water level is low.
18127: A hollow length of stout reed lies here.

Only a small ridge of solid ground reaches to the bog from the east, making a way through many small pools of water. While the water flows freely in the river south of here, in the west and north the surface is hidden by endless stretches of reed.
18128: The soil gets more swampy as it descends into a slight bog in the east. Slowly it becomes more difficult, yet not overly dangerous, to travel through. The ground is quite uneven, allowing for small pools of water to collect upon the ground.
18129: The fields on this side of the river would be good for farming if not for the fact it looks like the water seems to often flood this area. The soil is not quite as swampy as it seems to be on the south side of the river. Still, efficient farming would require more work against the flooding than the hobbits probably consider worthwhile.
18130:
A war-weary wight-warrior is standing here.
A war-weary wight-warrior is standing here.

Walls of stone surround you completely, except for the staircase going up. There are no ornaments, no altars, no colours and no coffins, just bare, grey stonewalls. The room is about five yards by five and ten feet high.
18141: The balcony here connects the guest rooms that lie both west and east. To the north is a wooden door, leading to similar guest quarters. Overlooking the Bruinen, the balcony offers an expansive view southward. Some vines spiral their way around the posts supporting the balcony's edge, almost as if trying to mimic the elven carvings that cover other parts of the posts.
18142: The balcony continues east and west, giving easy access to several doors that line its northern side. The paved white stones underfoot form a simple and graceful pattern. Opposite the doorway that lies to the north, the southern side of the balcony opens up giving a wide view over the River Bruinen, its water glistening.
18143: Off the doorway at the north, the balcony continues in an east-westerly manner. At some places its southern supporting posts are covered with entwining vines, their green leaves trying to overwhelm the white stone. The sound of rushing water draws attention to the south, where the River Bruinen can be seen flowing below.
18144: The waters of the Bruinen softly flow below the southern side of the balcony as the white stone-laid walkway continues on its way to east and west. Its simple yet elegant design does not include many complex decorations, the carvings on the balcony posts and the lively vines seem to create an almost artistic harmony.
18145: The white stone balcony comes to a small corner as it turns both to the west and north. Westwards one can catch a glimpse of the many doorways that line the inner edge of the balcony, while to the north the balcony continues, leading passers-by towards the library. Down below flows the River Bruinen, the bubbly murmur of its waters are well heard even here.
18146: An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

The stone-laid white balcony follows the doorways that lead to several guest rooms. Southwards the balcony forms a corner overlooking the river, with the vines that circle the posts, hanging over the rim. To the west lies a doorway, its surface lit up during each dawn as the sun peaks its first rays over the eastern horizon.
18147: The stone balcony ends here, as further on westwards lies the library of Rivendell. Looking towards south, one can still clearly see the doors that line the balcony, leading into the guest rooms. The faint sound of rushing water can be heard from the same direction, as it travels up to the walkway from the River Bruinen which lies beneath.
18150: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

The dark blue walls and the skyblue ceiling of this room are merging together. The floor is made of dark oaken wood and it is painted black. A fireplace has been set in the centre of the room. A cosy single bed has been placed alongside the wall opposite the oakdoor. An enchanted painting of Domy adorns the wall above the bed. The painting glows faintly and makes the room to glitter.
18151:
A small white fountain is here.
The Housekeeper looks fed up with her job. She scowls at you unhappily.

The floor is made of pine boards, that have been treated with various natural oils, to make it white. Two five-foot high windows let in fresh air and the colours of Rivendell. The light walls and floor create a contrast with the furniture that has been carved of ebony.
18154: A sturdy target for arrows, made out of thatch, stands here.

The ceiling in this large natural cavern is filled with stalactites, while the ground has somehow been levelled to a rough but even area. The walls are lined with skeletons, chains and broken shields. A few decaying bodies full of arrows lie scattered in groups. The tunnel to the east is partly blocked with rubble and large stones, narrowing the exit considerably. The air is filled with the rancid stench of rotted flesh mixed with clouds of flies.
18155:
The Housekeeper looks fed up with her job. She scowls at you unhappily.
An elf is here walking around.

A large pavilion has been hastily but efficiently erected here in a clearing for the shelter of elves who have vacated their homes in the wilderness. The walls are silken cloth; the area is roofed with withes cemented with clay. Comfortable pallets are arranged here; bundles and crates are stacked nearby, containing the possessions of the refugees.
18156: The waters of this deep underground stream flow so slowly as to be almost a stagnant pool. Rich in minerals, the chilly liquid has a sharp metallic tang.
18157: In the Depths of the Underground Waterway

A deep cleft has been cut through the cold, hard rock of the hills, creating a cramped waterway. But whilst the waters must once have flowed freely through here, now they stand, almost stagnant. To the north the gully opens out into a broad tunnel mouth, whilst to the south bits and pieces of debris are piled against the wall of the chamber, almost obscuring the wide cracks and fissures which can be seen in the rock.
18158: In the Depths of an Underground Waterway
A grey snake slides along the water.
To the south the tunnel walls converge, but to the north the way opens out somewhat, and both the floor and roof climb higher. It should be possible to swim to the surface in that direction.
18159: The cavern is large and lofty, though the roof falls sharply to the floor at the southern end, and the floor slopes upward to the east, so that at that end there is dry land. The rest of the chamber is filled with cold, dark and almost stagnant water, which has a sharp metallic tang. A sluggish inflow seeps through a heavy pile of rocks and boulders, which lies against the northern wall, and if this were once a lively underground stream, it is clear that this obstruction played at least some part in bringing its waters to an almost complete standstill. But why they did not simply drain away cannot be told from here.
18160: A giant, strange looking green fungus is here, ready to devour you in seconds.

This cavern appears to be a natural one, its walls, floor and even its roof worn quite smooth by the action of water. Sloping downward to the south and to the west, one end of the cave is covered by the chilly water of a near- stagnant underground waterway.
18161: The murky waters of the pool surround you, chilling you to the very core. Filling a narrow gulf, this dirty pond would not be, but for a crude dam to the south, whilst to the north its waters are very slowly replenished by a sluggish inflow, via a number of wide crasks and fissures in the rocky wall.
18162: A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A rugged trail heads north to south here, through successive regions of scrub and tall grasses. The ground is softer on the foot and the vegetation springs back as one passes, leaving little sign by which to see tracks, but there are markings of small animals leading to and from the bushes.
18163: A poorly marked mud trail heads off through the waving grasses towards the south, weaving back and forth across the seemingly endless greensward. The grasses range from two to three feet in height and seem to be even taller in the distance.
18164: Bend in the Great South Road

The road sweeps in a great curve towards the north and the east. It is in poor shape, mostly broken and crumbled, except for the occasional flagstone which remains whole and undamaged. They serve as the only lasting reminder of the glorious past of the road's skilled builders.
18165: Overgrown and damaged through centuries of neglect, the Great South Road winds its way through the open plains. The low, scrub bushes and brambles reach up between cracked flagstones. Splintered and shattered by twisting roots, the surface of the road is uneven and difficult to traverse.
18166:
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.
A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.

The land is parched, and the plant life has adjusted to the harshness of the exposed plain. The ground is covered by short, spiny-leaved grasses of a yellowish-brown colour. Wherever there is a a hint of moisture upon the splintered sandstone rock the grasses are tufted together, poking tenuously forth from the sandy soil. The rocks are a bit larger towards the road further south.
18167: A recently used trail passes through this area full of mixed scrubs and grassland. There are stunted trees that show the marks of stripping by metal tools. Also, there are many saplings that are scattered about the grassland. The occasional bushel of eorna appears as though it was nurtured by a helping hand. The plant itself resembles a form of barley and seems to be vibrant and in good health, possibly cultivated.
18168:
A brown cow is here, contemplating a higher reality whilst chewing slowly.
A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.

A trodden path heads north and south through a seemingly poor, but well-used pasture. The taller grasses to the north appear cropped and cut short by local herd animals. Their presence is evidenced by the telltale signs of noticeable quantities of fresh manure scattered about the ground.
18169: A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

An obviously well tended field of eorna barley encompasses the landscape here. It appears to be crudely irrigated and free of invasive scrubs. Southeast from here lies a raised and sturdy wooden palisade wall that looms imposingly; ready to keep out all but the most determined intruder.
18170: A Dunlending hold, constructed of stone and packed earth, looms menacingly to the east. It is complete with a large wooden palisade. A great, bronze gate is there to deny entrance to intruders. The dwellings within, as far as one can see, are squat, windowless structures with wood framed roofs, covered in stretched hides.
18171:
A golden, firm onion is here.
A large potato is growing here.
A round turnip is growing here.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

This field of cultivated potatoes, onions and turnips looks well cared for. The irrigation channels have been cleverly dug to make the best use of the rain, as well as making the hard job of keeping the crops healthy a little easier. The wooden walls of a palisade loom to the northeast and a beaten path bends away from the hold northward.
18172:
Some ugly blow-flies are buzzing around here.
A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A sturdy, sharp-pointed, timber wall rises up to the north, atop an earthen, ramped base. The slope that is at the foot of the wall here, appears to have been at some time, used as the tipping point for refuse from the other side. The odour that is wafting from that direction seems to have attracted clouds of flies. To the west, a mud trail passes through some irrigated fields, on its way around the wood walled settlement to the north.
18173:
A pig is here, covered in mud.
A blue dragonfly is circling around.

This shallow, watering hole seems to have been used quite a lot recently. The water bed has been disturbed, kicking up mud and turning the water a mucky brown colour. Animal tracks are in evidence all around it. A worn trail heads north towards a wooden walled settlement.
18174: A blue dragonfly is circling around.

The fortified settlement to the west seems to be surrounded by a wooden, palisade wall with sharpened tips. A heavily built, postern gate provides a possible entrance, but it seems as though it was built to keep out any visitors that were not welcomed. A trail leads from the gate to a muddy, watering hole that is nearby to the south.
18175: A trail traverses through long-stemmed grasses here, which show faint signs of having been cut back, not too long ago. To the southwest, a very high-walled, wooden palisade stands atop an earth embankment. The palisade appears to be surrounding a small, but seemingly active settlement.
18176:
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.
A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A large, wooden palisade wall, towering to the south, stands atop an embankment of packed mud. The tips of the wall's timbers, have been sharpened to a point and charred to withstand the elements. The timbers themselves seem to have been coated with a muddy clay, to lessen the chance of them being set afire.
18177:
The starving cow stands here looking for a patch of grass.
The starving cow stands here looking for a patch of grass.

The grass here has been nibbled on, almost to death. Nowhere is it any longer than a finger or two in height, and in many places, the ground is bare earth. Wild, grazing animals have ravaged the grasses and uprooted the few remaining fungi and the roots of the fresh vegetation.
18178: Tall grass grows here, ranging three or four feet in some places. The strong, springy shoots have stretched upwards trying to outreach its neighbour in search of the sun. At this areas eastern edge, however, there are signs of some recent grazing and the grass is considerably shorter.
18179: A trained horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

The tall grasses here have been blown into an eerie pattern of perfect circles, most likely some peculiar trick of nature and the elements. The circles vary in size from several feet, to several hundred feet and seem to all have been here for some time. What their purpose is, or who may have laid them, seems to be a mystery.
18180: A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.

This verdant sward of grassland, just south of the Great South Road, has considerably more vegetation than the poor, stony soil to the north. The multitude of grasses are heavily interspersed with brambles and some low bushes, providing a perfect habitat for insects and the smaller rodents.
18181: This road was once a major thoroughfare, connecting the realms of Gondor and Arnor. Now the passage of traffic has been reduced and the road has fallen into a state of disrepair. In recent years, it has served as an age-old reminder of the path that ancient travellers took. The easiest path along the road now is the grass by its side rather than the road itself. Along the southern edge of the road, an old drainage system is dug, preventing easy access to the lush grasslands.
18182: The vast, monotonous stretch of prairie is interrupted to the south by what remains of the Great South Road. The grass is generally of a medium length, except for where it seems to have been eaten short by animals. A soft rustling of the grass in the wind invites the weary traveller to rest here.
18183: A tufted carpet of short grasses envelopes this region, interspersed with the occasional low, scrub bush and invasion of heather. This blanket rolls along at a gradual slope for miles around. The ground underfoot here is very hard and compact, carrying even faint noises a fair distance.
18184:
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A wild mare is watching you warily.

A field of hardy grain grows abundantly, unchecked on this wide level plain. Resembling barley, the eorna plant has spread over a wide area and seems to be uncontrolled by irrigation or fences. The fine grains of the barley emanate a strong scent, undoubtedly attracting any nearby horses.
18185: The stripped, barren land prevalent in this area gives way further to the north to a final, craggy outcrop of the Misty Mountains far off in the distance. An intrusion of granite stands prominently forth amidst the more numerous masses of limestone boulders. There are signs of some ancient quarrying that are still visible.
18186: The ground is littered with rocks and pebbles of various sizes, making travel on foot treacherous. The risk of a twisted or broken ankle seems high and the going is slow. All around, the scenery here is barren and desolate, seemingly devoid of all life.
18187: The land is barren and practically devoid of any form of plant life. With little to hold the soil together, much of the upper layers have been blown away, leaving stony, hard ground behind. Cracked, aged bones peek out from beneath the remaining soil, bearing the only evidence the life that has inhabited this land.
18188: The grass grows short and comparatively sparse here in contrast with the moist, fertile soil further to the east. The soil is dry and infertile, making it to be possible for only the heartiest grasses to survive. Moisture from the River Isen does not reach the soil here. Further to the west, the land is even more barren and unproductive.
18189: An ample supply of short, tufted grasses are sprinkled with rabbit pellets and shallow burrows, along with numerous holes in the soft soil. There are soft, light tufts of thrift and small shrubs, such as hounds-tongue, that have poked up here and there, where the rabbits have left them to grow.
18190: A carelessly placed foot can damage a blade of grass permanently, often killing it. Haphazardly running over a field of grass will crush many blades of the green vegetation. A whole herd of rampant animals, romping across a flat plain, will usually crush and destroy all the tender blades of grass. That is what has happened here it would seem.
18191: This vast flatland is covered in thick grass, standing about five feet high, that stretches for miles in all directions. The soil here is very rich and fertile, with the potential for new life. However, the fierce winds that sweep across this meadow, make it impossible for most of the plant life to flourish.
18192: Prickly, white-stemmed plants, with blue flower heads grow in abundance.

The vast, verdant green plains stretch out for many miles in every direction. Occasionally, the living jade carpet underfoot is marred by the deep tracks of many hoofed animals. The tracks lead away towards the southeast. Beyond the beaten earth, the bright, snow-capped peaks of Ered Nimrais rise above the horizon.
18193:
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

These vast plains spread far to the south and east, where plenty of the wild creatures can feed off many forms of vegetation, which grow in this fertile land. The grass is shorter here than in other areas, only reaching a foot in height. The plains continue all around, ending only at the mountains that rise up on the northern and southern horizons.
18194: The Gap of Rohan stretches out in every direction, framed in the north and the south by massive mountain ranges. Thick, vibrant jade grasses cover the plains with barely a tree or bush in sight. If the slightest breeze blows, the blades of grass bend in waves. Far in the east, an errant flicker of light can often be seen in the mornings, possibly a reflection of water.
18195:
A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

A dense carpet of grey-green grasses covers the gently undulating landscape. Few distractions obstruct the view of the open land save a clearing in the east. A medium-sized road in that direction leads north and appears to have seen recent use. The road, however, lies several miles away.
18196: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

A well-kept dirt road breaks softly rolling plains to the east. The road bends around this patch of green grass as it runs from the south, turns east, and then continues north. On the other side of the road, the river Isen flows down from the north and runs towards the distant peaks of Erid Nimrais.
18197: This is a remarkably well kept dirt trail. No grass, weed or stone litter the earth within the boundaries of this path. The earth is so tightly packed by the repeated footfalls of man and beast, that even the harshest storms do not appear to have an adverse effect. As the trail leads farther north, the dark peaks of the Misty Mountains rise above the horizon. In the south, the path follows the Isen towards the ford.
18198: The river slowly beings to gain speed, as it flows directly south for many miles. The water is clear and constantly cold no matter the season. The riverbed lies many feet beneath the surface, but is perfectly visible. Small bleached rocks line the riverbed, and are occasionally hidden by the large fish that swim by. Atop the steep western bank, a dirt road follows the river's course.
18199: The waters flow fast and cold, even as the Isen bends to the west. As the river flows farther south, the water cuts steeper and steeper banks along the river's edge. The rocky bed lies many feet beneath the surface of the water, but can be seen as easily as if it were mere inches away. There are places in the riverbed where large ruts have formed, particularly near the edges. It appears that someone has dug up large areas of the rock and sand mix.
18200: Gently undulating plains are abruptly halted by the swift waters of the Isen, flowing just beyond its eastern bank here. For eons, the water has cut tall, steep banks into the earth. Thick grass covers the slope, and remains wet both day and night. Moving down those slopes is nearly impossible. Along the top of the bank, repeated footfalls of both man and beast have worn down the grass to almost nothing. This worn-down area follows the top of the riverbank very closely.
18201:
You see two piles of wild strawberries on the ground.
A sly cat prepares to pounce from its grassy hiding place.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

Vast, treeless plains gently roll to the east for more miles than mortal eyes can see. Green waves slowly flow over the wide meads in even the gentlest of winds. Tall blades of grass grow high enough to tickle the underbellies of the mighty horses that wander these plains. In the warmer months, tiny purple flowers can often be seen flourishing between the stalks of grass. In the winter, all that remains are the grey-green stalks between the still thick carpets of grass.
18202:
Prickly, white-stemmed plants, with blue flower heads grow in abundance.
Prickly, white-stemmed plants, with blue flower heads grow in abundance.

Gently rolling plains stretch out to the east and south for uncounted miles. Green stalks of grass grow as high as a man's legs, and move in the gentle breeze. In the distant west, the swiftly moving waters of the Isen sing a babbling melody day and night. Framing the plains to the north and south, two majestic mountain ranges rise above the horizon, dark in the north, and in the south, white as the driven snow.
18203: Upon the horizon, far to the north, the Misty Mountains climb into sight. The land stretches in plains in several directions, except for immediately to the north, where a ridge rises above the flat lands. Golden wheat seems to grow in small patches here, being a sure sign that a traveller is entering further into the plains of Rohan.
18204: A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Wild wheat grass grows atop the rich Rohan soil. To the west lie additional clusters of yellow wheat while to the north the grass becomes shorter and thinner. Mixed among the short grass to the north live several small bundles of sagebrush. A ramshackle collection of wooden structures can barely be seen on the horizon to the east.
18205: The plains are covered with a verdant grass, growing close to the ground. Many, large stones and treacherous holes mark the ground, making travel through these parts difficult. To the west and south, the grass grows taller in richer soil, while springy and green it grows abundantly to the north.
18206: Some waist-high grass has covered the plains all around, a break from the broken plains nearby. The nourishment of the river Isen is the reason, which is winding its way through the flatlands just west of here, in a stony bed of rocks below. It is marking the western borders of the Rohirrim, although, few currently live in this part of their land.
18207: The waters of the Isen swirl around here, narrowing down from the north through several small outcrops of rock. The current of the river does not change much though, still a sedate meandering through the flat lands of the Gap. Its banks are noticeably different in terrain, with the west side being comprised mostly of rolling folds of land, while the east is mainly broken, with stony plains which rise up out of this stony bed of rocks.
18208: Plains between Isen and the Road

The two most significant features of the landscape here are the river Isen, flowing south in this section of Rohan, and the road that follows its path to the west. Underfoot, the going is easy, with the soft turf making for an easy ride or walk. These plains are mostly uninhabited, due to the frequent raids of Dunlendings and orcs.
18209: The ancient highway continues on its path here, following roughly the line of the Isen a few miles east. Northward, it makes a route towards a deeply cut valley between the two ends of the Misty Mountains, and south it appears to travel across the central plains of the Gap of Rohan. Underfoot, there is no paving, but the road is wide and well-kept, with the hard-packed earth making for easy travel.
18210: Last Remnants of the Northern Ridge

A cute, fluffy owlet is waiting here for its mother to return with food.
A cute, fluffy owlet is waiting here for its mother to return with food.
A great horned owl looks cautiously around it.
A Dunlending herdsman in ragged leather stands here, watching over his herd.
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

The ridge runs for miles north of here, slowly dissipating into a little more than a grassy slope. The road runs at its base to the east, a wide and well maintained trail. The land underfoot is as soft and easy on the traveller as most of the grasslands here, terrain much suited to the liking of horses.
18211: The wide, open land continues in every direction, with the flatlands comprising the Gap of Rohan it would appear. Bound to the north and south by some of the vast mountain ranges, it acts as a large, natural wind tunnel. Nevertheless, it is a fertile country with short, verdant grass that serves as a springy carpet for miles around.
18212: A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

The land dips here, into a bowl-shaped depression. The vegetation has flourished in this sheltered area, becoming thicker to the north where the depression increases and blocks further passage. Little can be seen of the plains that surround it, but the towering Misty Mountains to the north still raise their peaks above the horizon.
18213: A rotting wagon lies on its side in the midst of these rolling plains. The rear axle of it is obviously broken and its wheels are missing. All of the metal fittings appear to have been stripped or rusted, leaving no signs of who or what may have left it here.
18214: A nightingale is here, chirping a sweet melody.

The plains are broken by several low hillocks, covered in coarse grass and easy to climb. Dandelions and buttercups cover much of the slopes, wherever the grasses are short, breaking up the solid green with patches of yellow. Towards the north, the grasses give way to coarser shrubs and nettles.
18215: As the hillocks to the west come to an end, this area of raised ground provides a perfect place to look out over the surrounding land. Southward, the River Isen can be seen three to four miles distant. Beyond the broad river, some of the foothills of the White Mountains begin their building ascent towards the triple-crowned Thrihyrne. To the north and east there are grassy plains that seem to stretch as far as the eye can see.
18216: Rough meadow grasses, interspersed with dandelions, cover the majority of this area of plains, dotting the green bedding with yellow. To the south, the River Isen appears to begin to bend away to the southeast. Following its banks, one can see the diverse vegetation that lines its passage.
18217: A green cloak of rich grasses lies open, spangled with varying colours of wild meadow flowers. In the distant past, this area must have been a managed flood plain of grassland, harvested for hay by whomever lived here. To the south, the cold waters of the Isen flow swiftly by.
18218: A blue dragonfly is circling around.

Quiet plains, untouched by human interference, lie covered here in the wild grasses and meadow of flowers. To the south, the River Isen can be seen winding its way roughly westward. The plants lining the riverbanks are all quite tall and more vibrant than elsewhere, a reflection of the abundant water.
18219: A huge, carved limestone monolith thrusts upwards from a tufted grass hillock amidst these desolate, ruined plains. The carvings upon the tall slab of this stone appear intricate and expertly carved, though it would appear to have no discernible significance. To the east and the south, the banks of the River Isen bar any easy travel.
18220: The river runs clear, clean and swift. It seems to pick up speed as it turns around a bend. This is an unusual occurrence for any river, as most tend to slow where they bend. The only explanation is a change in water depth - the water is fairly shallow here. As the river continues southward, the steep, sandy banks turn into rocky cliffs.
18221: Clear, ice blue waters quickly flow around this bend and continue westward. The riverbed, consisting mainly of a few small rocks and sand, is clearly visible, as the waters are clean, yet deep. Fish dart by under the surface, most following the current. The steep banks are alive with thick, green grass that makes the slopes difficult to navigate.
18222: A well-travelled dirt trail follows the Isen's path as it flows southwest through Rohan. The road is riddled with deep depressions. The trail is free of weed or grass, a clear sign of its repeated use. The trail runs dangerously close to the sharply sloping riverbank but appears stable enough to support heavy weights.
18223: A well-travelled dirt trail follows the Isen's path through Rohan. The road is covered with small holes and slight depressions - tell-tale signs of nature's battle with man-made creations. Although the trail isn't very well tended, it is still free of weed or grass, a clear sign of its repeated use. In the north, the path runs towards the ford, while in the south, it heads towards to snow-capped peaks of the White Mountains.
18224: A tiny firefly flits around the foliage.

Deep horse tracks are imprinted upon the path, an effect of long-term, repeated use. There is not a sprig of greenery on the trail. No plant life could survive the constant and harsh treatment this road receives. As the trail follows the river's course, it sometimes runs very close the steep eastern bank. One misstep could have very wet results.
18225: Deep, lush green grasses quickly spring up between two very different roads in the east and west. To the east, an ancient stone roadway winds its way deeper into the heart of Rohan. In the west, a worn dirt trail follows the Isen in its trek towards the sea. Between these roads, a characteristic feature of Rohan takes hold of the land once more: thick grey-green grasses.
18226:
A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

As two roads diverge in the south, a wide wedge of green opens between them. Knee-deep grasses cover the gently rolling plains as they stretch out towards the wooded foothills of the White Mountains in the south. When the light is waning at sunset, reflections off the distant waters of Sir Angren dance on the western horizon. When the winds gently blow, the blades of grass move like waves on a grey-green sea.
18227: Rengold the Bard of the Rohirric people stands here proudly.

An ancient and weathered cobblestone roadway runs a direct path from the strongholds of Rohan, to the beginning of Rohan territory at the Fords of Isen. The widest stones of the pavement have been broken by the force of nature, and repaired by the hands of man. Large, jagged rocks have been placed crudely, but effectively, to repair the roadway and keep it functional. Those who restored this road were not concerned about appearances however, as the repaired areas are easily spotted, hasty patchwork as they are.
18228: A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.

The earth underfoot begins to rise slowly as one moves farther south. The foothills of the White Mountains soon take hold of the land as the plains give way to the mountains. Verdant grasses still cover the earth, only thinning as they approach the white peaks of Erid Nimrais. Directly west, a wide, ancient road makes its way towards the hills.
18229: A cow stands here, chewing her cud.

Old wooden fences, in urgent need of mending, box in a small piece of land that connects to a ramshackle village in the north. Inside the fences, the earth has been worn barren by over-grazing of herd animals. Occasionally a small horse or cow will wander near the fence, hoping to snag a mouthful of green grass just beyond its reach. Beyond the fence, a mix of golden grains fights with the lush grey-green grasses for dominion of this area. The wheat stalks hold their ground for less than a mile, before surrendering to the sea of green.
18230: In the east stands a small farming village, barely more than a few houses surrounding a young tree and a well. Flanking the village to the north and south are small, cultivated fields of wheat, which are adjacent to livestock corrals for horses and smaller pens for farm animals. A few miles west of the village entrance, the Great South Road bends and winds its way to the White Mountains in the south.
18231: Grey-green plains give way to cultivated fields of amber grains and small horse corrals, as the outskirts of a small village encroach upon the open land. Less than a mile to the south, the heart of that small village can be seen through the small wisps of smoke from chimneys. In the northeast, the verdant grasses of Rohan lay claim to the land for miles, until they reach the forested base of the Mountains of Mist.
18232:
The corpse of a Rohir marksman is lying here.
The corpse of a Rohir archer is lying here.
The corpse of a Rohir soldier is lying here.
On the ground, there are four soft leather helmets.
On the ground, there are three sturdy, soft leather helmets.
On the ground, there are two sturdy, rigid leather helmets.

The corpse of a Rohir archer is lying here.
The corpse of a Rohir marksman is lying here.
The corpse of a Rohir soldier is lying here.
The shadow of a Rohir commander is floating here.

Vast green plains stretch out in every direction. To the east, the gently undulating grasslands seem to flow into eternity while in the west a wide, stone roadway abruptly halts them. Though several miles away, the condition and make of the road are easily determined. It is an ancient piece of work, as evidenced by its uneven and weathered edges. Also, in stark contrast to the green surrounding it, the road is a dingy white, perhaps the effect of years of exposure to the sun.
18233: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

Muted green plains flow for miles in every direction. In the southwest, a large stone road cuts a wide scar through the gently rolling plains. From this distant vantage, the road appears to be worn by both weather and time, but its appearance could be an illusion - a trick played by the light.
18234: A sly cat prepares to pounce from its grassy hiding place.

The grass is slightly shorter here than in the surrounding plains. It still grows just as thick, but appears to have been cut down by repeated grazing. Small purple flowers grow here in abundance, particularly in areas where the grass has been eaten down to the bare soil.
18235:
You see two prickly plants with blue flower heads on the ground.
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

As the plains of Rohan gently roll in every direction, light and darkness frame the aptly named gap. Two mountain ranges, opposite in every way, block in the plains to the north and south. The dark peaks of the Misty Mountains in the north are shrouded and hidden in permanent clouds and mist. In the south the white, jagged peaks of Erid Nimrais stand stark and open against the sky.
18236: This well-worn footpath is expertly hidden by the thick, green grass. Though heavily travelled, this path is extremely narrow and winding, making it very difficult to navigate in these massive and seemingly unending plains. The repeated footfalls of both man and beast keep the path clear and easy to follow as long as one stays on the barren earth.
18237: The grey-green plains extend past the distant eastern horizon. A dense carpet of grass covers the land so completely, that no tree or bush obstructs the view for miles. Occasionally, a small herd of wild horses can be spotted grazing upon the fertile grasses, but little else breaks up the monotony of the sea of green.
18238: Wide green meads flow for miles around. Slightly undulating plains stretch as far as mortal eyes can see, forming a gap between the dark Misty Mountains in the north, and the snow-capped White Mountains in the south. If the light is favourable, Sir Angren can be seen, several miles west, cutting its wide scar through the Gap of Rohan before turning to meet the sea. Directly south, a small dirt trail winds a northeast to southwest path through the grassy lands.
18239: A tiny firefly flits around the foliage.

A small but heavily travelled dirt trail winds through the grassy plains of Rohan. This path is riddled with deep horse tracks that cross back and forth over each other, until the tracks become unreadable. Tall grass grows up on each side of the trail, forming miniature walls of green that constantly threaten to close in if the path is ever left unused. The trail continues south and east before becoming lost from vision, hidden by the grass.
18240: A narrow earthen path snakes a path though the plains of the Riddermark. The path is only visible for a few miles in the west and north before the thick grass swallows it from view. The trail itself is heavily used and barren of foliage. Heavy, deep hoof prints cover the ground. The tracks cross back and forth so many times that reading them becomes nearly impossible. On either side of the trail, the verdant grass so common on these plains takes possession of the land once more.
18241: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

The grassy plains of Rohan gently rise and fall as they stretch towards the horizon. Tall grey-green blades gently sway in even the gentlest breezes, giving the land the appearance of a green sea of waves. To the west and north, a small dirt trail cuts a windy path through the verdant grasses. In the east, the plains seem to continue on without end. Farther south, the grasses appear charred and trampled, but recovering from the abuse.
18242:
A sly cat prepares to pounce from its grassy hiding place.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

This land has been trampled and injured by some ancient battle. The thick grasses so common in Rohan grow sporadically here. Large patches of barren earth appear to be slowly shrinking though as the grasses begin to retake this area. Occasionally, the broken hilt of a sword or shaft of an arrow can be seen protruding from the ground. Whatever battle occurred here obviously loosed some terrible evil upon the earth, as the fertile soil is only now beginning to recover.
18243: The grey-green blades of grass seem to spread out as far as to the horizon. The land is nearly flat for miles in every direction, only slightly rising and falling, as the untilled earth tends to do. The skyline is unbroken by trees or structures for many miles. Where the earth and sky do meet, massive mountain ranges stretch their tall peaks into the air. In the north, the dark peaks of the Misty Mountains are almost always shrouded in a thick veil. In stark contrast, the snow-capped peaks of the White Mountains in the distant south climb up into the clouds.
18244: The green grass grows tall and thick underfoot, carpeting the land in a sea of waving green. The green seems to continue forever in every direction save the west. There, a large, cobblestone road runs a southerly path into the heart of Rohan. The road appears to be very old as many of the white stones used as pavement have broken and scattered over a wide area. Some of the stones have even been scattered miles away from their original placement.
18245: The plains stretch for miles around before being cornered near the entrance of a small village to the east and a large road to the west. This land remains uncultivated, despite the presence of Rohan settlers. The grass is lush and green, mixed with patches of clover and a few wild flowers. Near the edge of the road, a few bushes have taken root, possibly the result of some overly eager farmer.
18246: A tiny firefly flits around the foliage.

The main Rohan thoroughfare runs a southeast to northwestern path from the heart of Edoras, to the fords of the Isen. Ancient rocks form a pavement underfoot that allows for swift travel, despite the less than perfect placement of the cobblestones. The road continues to the north and south, before it bends again. The eastern plains gently roll off towards the horizon - a sea of green waving in the breeze.
18247: Flat, white, wide cobblestones line a southwestern path to the heart of Rohan. Time and weather have been harsh, as the pavement shows wear. Some of the larger stones have broken, and blades of grass spring up in the cracks. Despite time and nature, the road does not lie in disrepair. Someone has quickly repositioned the rocks near their original placement, giving the road a worn but traversable feel.
18248: A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.

The green colour of the plains meets the dull white of a once great roadway a short distance to the south and west. Lush blades of grass grow so thick, that when they meet the cobblestones of the West Road, a small green wall is formed that stands almost two feet tall. Under this deep carpet of green, insects buzz about, and small animals scurry to and fro, making small waves in the plains.
18249:
Some delicious wild strawberries grow on the ground.
Some delicious wild strawberries grow on the ground.
A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.

Grey-green grassy plains stretch out for miles to the southeast. The deep grass is thick and springy, cushioning each footfall. To the north, a small dirt trail leads to the northeast - farther into the Gap of Rohan. In the far south, the cobblestone West Road winds a white, rocky path deeper into the heart of Rohan.
18250: A wide footpath bends to the west and north here as it cuts a brown path in the verdant green grass. The plains of Calenardhon are covered with an uncommonly strong and resilient grass. In order to wear down the grass to the bare earth, nearly consistent traffic would have to walk this path. Upon the ground, numerous tracks of men and horses cross back and forth over each other until they become almost unintelligible.
18251: A small dirt trail runs a windy course through the gently rolling plains of the Riddermark. The earth underfoot is riddled with hoof prints that criss- cross each other so many times that it is almost impossible to discern how many have travelled this way. The path is only wide enough for perhaps two horses to walk side by side. The edges of the trail are lined with small wildflowers that bloom in vibrant purples and yellows in the summer.
18252: The usually tall and vibrant fields of grass have been stunted and scorched in large patches. In some places the grass grows almost as tall as two feet, but in other spots the earth is barren and stained with blood. Charred areas run for a few feet and then stop abruptly. The grass is trampled in a few large areas and nearly untouched in others. These kinds of battle scars mark areas of unrest in Rohan.
18253: An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.

The grass-covered earth gently rolls throughout the Gap of Rohan, undulating like timid waves on a calm sea. Between the dark peaks of the Misty Mountains and the snow-capped ridges of Erid Nimrais, the grey-green plains open like a long gulf between the opposing ranges. Only occasionally is the green interrupted by small patches of purple heather or yellow buttercups.
18254: A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Lush green grasses spread out in every direction, save east, where the Isen flows quickly by. Far to the north, the dark peaks of the Misty Mountains rise above the horizon, creating a jagged tear between the land and the sky. Mirroring the dark peaks in the north, the snow-capped peaks of the White Mountains pierce the sky in the distant south. Between these opposites, grey-green grass flows for hundreds of miles.
18255: A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

Near the banks of the Isen, patches of reeds as tall as a man spring up from the earth, nearly blocking the view of the river to the west. Among the deep thicket, small birds can be heard chirping, but are rarely seen. At the base of the patches of reeds, thick verdant grass takes possession of the land again, and spreads out for miles to the north, east and south.
18256: The rolling plains of Calenardhon are hemmed in by various features of the landscape on the west, south and east. Mighty and swift, Sir Angren flows in the west, blocking all travel in that direction with its steep, unconquerable banks. To the east and south, a dirt trail bends and winds its way though the plains, as it leads to a large camp farther south. In the ground, repeated horse tracks lead off to the north, and back again south. Also, deep scars can occasionally be seen in the grass, marking spots where earth was displaced for some reason.
18257: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

This trail sees heavy use by both horses and men. The constant trampling of the dirt has packed it so tightly, that even weeds cannot flourish. The path has not suffered the use well however. Deep ruts, potholes and grooves await travellers at every turn. Also, there are places where the earth has been stained a deep reddish-brown - the colour of dried blood.
18258:
A sturdy target for arrows, made out of thatch, stands here.
A weapons rack stands against the wall.
An archer of the Mark is here.
A Rohir marksman surveys the landscape, targeting would-be adversaries.
A foot-soldier of Rohan is here.
A stout Rohir lieutenant is here.

A large Rohan encampment has been settled here. Numerous tents and campfires are scattered across the plains. Repeated footfalls have worn dirt paths to and from various tents. Several flags and markers enclose a long and narrow archery range. A huge hole at the southern end of camp has the largest path leading to and from it. It also emits a pungent odour of trash and decay. The West Road runs along the camp's western edge and just beyond lies the Ford of Isen.
18259: A large cobblestone road cuts a winding path though the plains of the Riddermark. This road is an ancient pathway connecting the western and eastern ends of Rohan. Time and nature have been unkind to this passage, as its pavement is broken and scattered over a wide area. Swift repairs keep the road in working order, even if it is not as smooth as it once was to ride or walk upon.
18260: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

Large, sun-bleached cobblestones wind away towards southern Rohan. This road is wide enough to accommodate several horses riding side by side, or a large caravan. The pavement has been repaired hastily with small round pebbles that do not match the original stonework. The road is not as smooth as it once was, but it is functional and easy to walk upon.
18261: A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Rolling plains cover the Westfold Vale with a deep and springy grey-green blanket. Here at the northwestern end of Rohan however, two travelled roads meet near the banks of the river Isen. To the west, a narrow dirt trail follows the path of the river, as the river flows to the southwest. To the east, a large, white cobblestone road runs an opposite diagonal course, towards the heart of Rohan in the southeast. Between those two roads, a wedge of grassland grows wider and wider to the south.
18262: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

As this dirt path leads away from the cobblestone road in the east, it follows the river's bank to the west. The trail winds dangerously close to the edge of the steep eastern bank of the Isen, making travel along it difficult. If the deep tracks in the dirt are any indication, this trail is heavily travelled by both man and beast.
18263: A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

This narrow dirt trail splits off from the road north of here. Hoofprints dot the main part of the muddy path, clear evidence of recent use by many horses. The trail itself follows the path of the Isen further into the West-Fold. Gazing westwards, the Isen can be viewed as it flows quickly by, whereas on the east side on the trail, the West Road makes its way through the landscape.
18264: The occupants of this land have recently repaired the once broken cobblestone road. Stones, bleached white by the sun, have been obviously rearranged from their original positions in order to fill in old gaps in the pavement. Blades of green grass poke up from in between the stones, but none are very tall. The road continues southeast into Rohan.
18265: Just east of the Fords of Isen, the West Road lies along the edge of a military encampment. The road is composed of broken white cobblestones, weathered and worn by time. Someone maintains this road however, as the broken pieces have been uprooted and rearranged to cut down the amount of potholes and ruts. The troops camped east of here must use this road often. Numerous tracks of both human and horse litter the earth.
