18266: As the river turns west, its raging waters smash against the insurmountable eastern bank. Large eddies and whirlpools have formed at the bend and suck down most of the debris in the water. As small brush, weeds and even fish get sucked into the vortex; they only stay under the surface for a few seconds, before being catapulted back into the air. Atop the eastern bank, a worn dirt trail can be seen skirting along the edge of the earth.
18267: The eastern banks rise even farther above the river's surface as the current runs southwards. The western back is still steep and difficult to traverse, but does not climb as high as the eastern bank. Leaving the cold, clear water by way of those grassy slopes would be near impossible. In the south, the river bends towards two very large dirt mounds that appear to have been erected in the middle of the river.
18268: The river flows swiftly between two steep, slippery slopes. The clear blue water speeds to the south, and approaches two mounds of earth several miles away. Deep beneath the rippling water's surface, schools of fish swim sometimes with, sometimes against the current. Aquating plants wave in the undercurrent, fed by the sun's light even down on the riverbed.
18269: Clear azure waters speed their way south to the Great Sea. Between the water's rippling surface and the smooth rocks of the riverbed, a world of creatures swim by. Small forests of plant life spurt up from the sandy, rocky mix at the bottom of the Isen. Along the riverbanks, deep green bushes rise above grey- green grasses, as more life flourishes in the saturated earth. A clearly defined road sits atop the western bank.
18270: The trail bends to the north and west in its course through the Gap of Rohan. Sounds of quickly moving water can be heard in the east as the Isen picks up speed in its southerly course. Directly south, a small patch of land, only a few miles long has been trapped between the trail and the river as the road veers west and then south again. Just beyond that stretch of green, massive mounds of earth rise above the plains, blocking the view.
18271: A lush variety of small bushes and shrubs grow along the western bank of the Isen. The riverbank is extremely steep, an effect of the quickly flowing current coming down from the mountains. Small, twisted roots are visible, as the earth is pulled away from the banks little by little. To the west, a distinct dirt road runs north and south.
18272: The vast verdant plains of Rohan come to an abrupt halt. The Isen runs directly east of here and then bends towards the southwest. The thick grass underfoot is deep and lush, but it can not hide the huge ruts and holes that litter the land. Some distance south, someone has dug up huge amounts of dirt, and built it back up into a small fort on the river's edge. In the west, two very different roads converge, and head towards the earthen fort in the south.
18273: The cold, clear waters slow as the riverbanks bend to the west and the north. The riverbed lies somewhere far beneath the river's surface, but can be seen as clearly as if it were at one's fingertips. The banks are covered in thick, grey-green grasses that remain permanently water-soaked. The greenery, combined with the steep slopes of the banks, makes it nearly impossible to climb. But just a bit south, a large eyot sits in the river, allowing land travellers to ford the river and boaters or swimmers an escape route from the water.
18274: An ancient white cobblestone road dives directly into the waters of Sir Angren, forming one of two large fords. Smooth, pale stones have been piled here to allow safe passage across the swiftly moving waters. Wide enough for a small army to cross, this ford connects to a small island in the middle of the Isen. Standing tall upon that eyot are two massive earthen forts with a wide road running between them.
18275: After the fords, the river picks up a more common pace, as it speeds through the Gap of Rohan. The farther one moves south, the deeper the water gets, and the steeper the banks become. It would be extremely difficult to traverse those grassy, slick slopes. As the water continues its southerly flow, fish life becomes far more abundant, particularly near the river's edge. It is easy to note the variety of life swimming along in the Isen, as the waters are crystal clear.
18276: The river picks up both speed and depth as it flows around a bend. The banks begin to squeeze the river as they draw nearer to each other, which, despite the bend, have caused an increase in water speed. As the banks close in, plant- life on them springs up everywhere. It is difficult to discern even one small bit of barren earth from those saturated embankments. Thick grasses grow so tall, that their tops bend over and appear to drink from the water.
18277: A sly cat prepares to pounce from its grassy hiding place.

The small but well used dirt trail runs along the Isen as it journeys south. The earth is very packed, but ill cared for. Potholes await the careless traveller with every step. Some holes have merged into large ruts that run the entire breadth of the trail. The path originates a few miles northeast, where it can be seen splitting off the Great South Road.
18278: As the river flows west, it picks up small debris from its banks and carries them downstream. The cold, clear water swiftly pushes anything in its path farther west and towards the sea. The river bed lies many feet beneath the waters surface, but can be seen perfectly, as can the multitude of fish and river life passing long with the current.
18279: Clear blue water rushes swiftly around a nearby bend in the river. The swift current has cut deeply into the earth and formed very steep, slick banks. Climbing up those banks would be extremely difficult, as they are nearly vertical and covered with moist, thick grass. The water itself is cold and deep. Even in the hottest summer months, the Isen is strangely cold. In the winter the water's temperature becomes unbearable as the river continues to flow despite the freezing cold.
18280:
An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.
A badger is here, exploring for food.

A grassy field is blocked in on the north, east and south sides. In the north, the lush, green grass is gradually stamped out by the multitude of white stones from the Great South Road. In the south and east, the river Isen swiftly flows down from the Misty Mountains and heads towards the sea. This close to the water, the western bank of the river is easily seen and traversed, but across the swift and wide current, the east bank steeply rises - seemingly impossible to climb.
18281: The Great South Road bends to meet the Fords of Isen in the east. The edges of this wide cobblestone road spread as they near the bank, expanding the width of the road by more than double. The road clearly continues across the river by way of two large fords and a small island. White, smooth stones lead to the water's edge and then continue, forming an easy path across Sir Angren. Another way across the water cannot be seen either up or down stream.
18282: This broken cobblestone road looks ancient when compared to the well-maintained dirt road that splits off to the north. The ground directly underfoot is littered with small white broken stones that resemble an extremely wide roadway. Years of use, weather and nature have not been kind and the pavement has been shattered and scattered over the grasslands. Despite the sad condition of the stones, it is still fairly easy to determine the direction the road was built to follow. To the southeast, the road meets the fords of Isen. In the northwest, the Great South Road disappears into the tall grasses of Rohan.
18283: A dirt trail, or perhaps a very narrow road, splits from the Great South Road directly south. The once large but now broken cobblestones litter the earth for miles, but this trail has been cleared of them. Small piles of white pebbles collect on both sides of this dirt road. Long lines in the earth have been left by the rocks as they were raked to the sides of the cleared dirt. To the southeast, the Isen bends to flow around two massive earth mounds.
18284: The trail begins to widen, as it leads farther south and narrows to the north. Well travelled, this near road has no signs of weed or grass encroaching on its borders. Repeated footfalls of two and four legged creatures have packed the dirt so tightly that even the harshest rains have not caused damage. Also, someone undoubtedly tends to the condition of this trail. Along its western edge, small white pebbles litter the grass, but there are none on the ground here. At the trails edges, small piles of pebbles appear to have been raked out of the path by a very wide stick, or perhaps a large boot.
18285: The road that leads to and from Isengard is a well-maintained dirt passageway. Heavy traffic to and from the stronghold has packed the earth well, giving the trail the ability to withstand even the harshest weather. The path of the roadway bends here, turning east and south. Past the edge of the eastern bend, the Isen can be seen, swiftly passing in its journey down from the Misty Mountains, and towards the Great Sea. In the south, a wide patch of white rocks can be spotted in the vibrant green grass.
18286:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.
A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.

Deep green fields flow out in every direction. The nearly treeless landscape offers few guides for the inexperienced traveller to follow. In the east however, someone has seen fit to clear a large swath in the grass. A well-worn road leads northwards, towards the dark peaks of the Misty Mountains. In the south, the road intersects with a larger road in a horrid state of disrepair.
18287: Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

Near the corner of a wide intersection, lush emerald grasses butt up to the edge of two very different roads. In the east, a clear, well-kept dirt road leads in a nearly straight northwards line. To the south, an ancient, broken cobblestone road winds its way through the grasslands of Rohan. Hoofed animals have beaten the grass down here; as many tracks can be seem in the earth. Small white pebbles, once a part of the Great South Road, have been scattered far from the road by the same hooves that trampled the grass.
18288: The dilapidated roadway underfoot is only a shadow of its former self. It is clear that in the distant past, this was a wide and well-travelled road. Even now, the cobblestones that remain are still lain wide enough to accommodate three horses and their riders side by side. The edges of the bleached white road are hard to discern, as years of weather and use have broken and scattered the pavement. Weeds have grown up from between the rocks and pushed even the largest stones aside. The broken highway cuts a northwest to southeast path through the Gap of Rohan.
18289: A sly cat prepares to pounce from its grassy hiding place.

As the Great South Road approaches Sir Angren to the southeast, small repaired areas are noticeable in the cobblestone pavement. The original roadway was paved in large white cobblestones but the hasty patchwork has been done in packed earth, giving the roadway a mottled appearance. A few miles southeast, the road leads towards two large earthen mounds that rise above the grassy green plains.
18290: The open plains so common in Rohan are boxed in here on the north, east and distant south. To the north, the Great South Road cuts a white, rocky scar through the Gap of Rohan as is turns to meet the Isen, which blocks the plains to the east. Where the road and the river meet, massive mounds of earth rise above the plains, obviously man-made. The Isen runs south for several miles before bending to the west, blocking off the plains in the south. In a land characterized by vast, open, unending plains, this uncharacteristic configuration of landmarks may draw more attention than other areas of Rohan.
18291: Gently undulating grasslands stretch out to the west for many miles. In every other direction the plains are boxed in by road or water. Sir Angren blocks all south and easterly passage. The Great South Road must be crossed if one wishes to travel north. This area sees heavy traffic from the local animal life as evidenced by the numerous tracks in the earth leading towards the riverbanks. All the tracks double back and cross over themselves dozens of times, indicating repeated visits to this water source.
18292:
An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

The grey-green grasses of the Rohan plains thicken as they reach the fertile banks of the Isen. The river flows quickly as it travels southwest. The swift stream has cut steep banks into the earth and the slopes quickly drop off, like a miniature cliff. The banks continue to the west before turning south to follow the river's course south.
18293: Water runs cold and fast between the twists and turns of the river's banks. The water is clear, blue and deep, making it easy to see the riverbed but impossible to stay still long enough to discern many details. The occasional errant twig or uprooted plant travels swiftly with the speeding current.
18294: As the river flows southwards, it gains momentum, splashing loudly against a few large rocks that have popped up above the rippled surface. It is possible to see the riverbed here as the waters run fairly clear, only marred by the occasional twig or errant leaf. The waters seem to increase in speed as they approach a small bend in the south.
18295: Some delicious wild strawberries grow on the ground.

The fertile earth near the banks of the Isen overflow with lush green grass, creating a slippery slope leading into the waters of the river. Even in the driest seasons, the verdant grass grows so thick that the embankment becomes extremely difficult to traverse. No bushes or trees offer any handholds on this particular section of the river's edge.
18296:
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.
A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.

The earth slopes gently downwards and becomes slightly waterlogged towards the south. The change in soil has caused a dramatic change in what was once the greenery. Hundreds of wild flowers have taken root in the saturated dirt and choked out the grass that is so prevalent in these plains. Multi-hued flower heads sway in even the gentlest of breezes and grow several feet tall. The wild flowers only last for about a mile before the grass reclaims its hold over the land, but the change is dramatic enough to make this spot a small landmark on the otherwise endless plains.
18297: Vast grassy plains stretch out for miles. The earth is covered in a deep sea of green that waves in a strong breeze. Many miles south, reflections of light play on the choppy surface of a mighty river. In the distant east, a wide road creates an off-white path through the grass as it winds towards far off mountain ranges in the north and south.
18298:
A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.
A tiny firefly flits around the foliage.

Small pebbles hidden in the almost impossibly tall grass threaten to undo any sure-footed passer-by. The small stones have somehow been flung away from the large cobblestone roadway in the north and east. The scattered stones could have been moved by the hooves of wandering animals, as several horse tracks can be seen in the dirt. If one were to take note of the surroundings anywhere but underfoot, thick, green grass flows to the south for as far as the eye can see. On a clear day, a slight glimmer can be seen, far in the southeast, as light reflects off some water source.
18299: A cobblestone roadway lies in ruins. Large, white, flat stones that once were set close enough to stifle the verdant grass have been broken and worn into very small, scattered pebbles. From where the rocks lie, it is safe to assume that this road would have accommodated large caravans easily. However, the lush green grass has now uprooted the pavement and scattered it over a larger area. Unless one stands in the centre of the road, its direction is difficult to ascertain, but from mid-road, it is clear that the road leads southeast and northwest.
18300:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.
A tiny firefly flits around the foliage.

The verdant grass abates to the south and is littered by small, white pebbles. The cause of this change in the scenery is a wide, cobblestone road in a state of remarkable disrepair that lies directly south. Where the rocks have snuffed out the grass, small veracious weeds have sprung up, colouring the land with touches of yellow, lavender and blue. As the road runs to the southeast, it intersects with a small trail leading northward.
18301: Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

Huge mountains in the north and south border these plains, forming a large gap in the landscape. This gap is covered with a thick, green carpet of lush grass, unmarred by tree or rock for many miles. Small imperfections underfoot can be seen through the grass. Rabbit holes litter the earth here, the result of a family's nest. This makes mounted travel difficult, but not impossible.
18302: A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.

Green, vibrant plains gently roll in the sporadic breeze. When the light reflects off the grass just right, the land sparkles in rich golden tones that seem to warm the earth. In the distant east, the odd sparkle of light shines off the river Isen. Framing the grasslands to the north and south, vast mountain ranges rise above the horizons.
18303: Erratic rocks litter the land, interrupting the green grass with small, flat patches of white. Farther south, the small stones on the ground become more prevalent. The source of this change in scenery is an ill cared for cobblestone road directly south. It is difficult to make out the direction the road takes at this point, but it appears to be heading towards two small hills in the southeast. Along what may have been the edge of the path, small colourful flowers grow in abundance.
18304: A once great road lies beneath your feet. Paved with cobblestones, this road, when maintained, could easily have accommodated several riders on horseback. Time has not been kind to this highway, and the flagstones that were once laid in neat rows have been scattered over the land. From directly above the road, it is still possible to discern the direction the pathway takes. Although it bends as it leads away, the road clearly runs towards two small mounds of earth in the southeast.
18305: Thick vegetation extends southwards from the edge of a broken, paved roadway. Several varieties of plant life have intertwined here to create a formidable thicket. While not impenetrable, the brush does slow down any progress towards the south. Northwards, the cobblestone road looks easier to traverse. A few miles east, the road can be seen bending towards a raised area much farther to the southeast.
18306: Nestled between mighty mountain ranges in the north and south, these plains make up an area referred to as the Gap of Rohan. The snow-covered peaks of the White Mountains lie far to the south, while in the north, the dark range of the Misty Mountains tear jagged edges into the smooth horizon. This area, and the surrounding plains, are characteristically covered in verdant, green grass. Sometimes the grass could grow tall enough to tickle the underbelly of a pony, whereas other times the grass is unnaturally short, as if grazed upon.
18307: Jade green grasses cover the land in every direction. Colourful wildflowers poke their heads through the thick grassy carpet, breaking up the monotony. Hoof prints can be seen spread throughout the grass, often near patches of grazed down, barren earth. The tracks do not appear to be part of a very large herd, but the general direction of all the tracks leads south and southeast.
18308: Vibrant, lush grass-covered lands roll on for miles. Several miles in the southeast, a large river throws off sparkles of light during the day and a muted glow at night. As the plains approach the river, the earth falls away towards the riverbank, and the grasses abate. Beyond the river, tall mountain peaks tower many miles away.
18309: The river Isen, running slow and steady, has cut a small ridge into the plains. This has led to the creation of a steep sandy bank. The grass so common in the Gap abates and gets choked by sand, as it grows closer to its life-giving water source. Where dirt and sand still mix, a clear footpath has been worn into the land. Repeated use of this bank as a trail along the river has formed a path even the most naive tracker could follow.
18310:
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.

In times long past, the River Isen must have swept through this land, sweeping its way southwards, ultimately towards the sea. Over the ages, however, the course of the river has altered and a bend in the river has silted over, which now leaves an isolated lake that still retains some water and life, only does this occasionally refill when the river floods.
18311: The river Isen formed the ancient, hay meadow in the distant past. It was once flooded every year, but now the river seems to have calmed quite a bit, leaving the earth drier. The hay grows in short stalks. The rocky soil underneath causes any rain water that does fall here to be absorbed quickly by the ground underneath.
18312: Short, yellow to a greenish-blue coloured grassland, devoid of trees and with only the occasional, low scrub bush that extends across this landscape. The soil here is very dry and rocky. The general slope of this land moves from flat to gently undulating as it moves further south. To the east, the ground slopes very gently into the Gap of Rohan.
18313:
A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

A small hill seems to have grown up out of the centre of the green grass that is covering the ground. All around this tiny knoll, brightly coloured flowers can be noticed rising up out of the verdant turf. From this vantage, one can see the land sloping gently to the east, leading into the Gap of Rohan.
18314: A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

The grassland here seems to be an area of regrowth, having recovered from the many travellers that spilled over from the road in ages past. There are some natural flora of the area that has taken root once again, as rough scrub and young saplings have begun to colonise the landscape.
18315: When the Kingdoms of Gondor and Arnor thrived, this road must have bustled with traffic and activity. With the fall of Arnor and the decline of Gondor, the road has been neglected and seldom travelled. Originally, this road was built upon a small embankment, rising to five feet above the surrounding plains. Over time, however, these embankments have crumbled, leaving the road pockmarked and uneven.
18316: The vast, grassy plains roll seemingly endlessly here. To the south lies the Great South Road that once connected the kingdoms of Gondor and Arnor. The short, dry grass indicates that the plains here do not receive very much precipitation. An occasional, dried blossom bears further testimony to this fact.
18317: A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

The flat steppes are covered with short grass. In some places, the hooves of the herds of wild horses that roam these lands, have trampled the grass. Only a few, randomly scattered bushes dare to brave the fierce winds. These plains seem to stretch north as far as the eye can see.
18318: A large surface of exposed rock rises up from the surface of the prevailing, flat grassland. The surface of the stone looks as though it was etched and marked by a sword or a knife. This is a site of some obvious, ancient religious significance. This is evidenced by images of large, carved warriors returning from a hunt, scored deeply into the exposed rock face, which is now covered with deep green moss.
18319: Dry rocks and pebbles, interrupted by patches of short tufted grasses and hardy bushes, lie strewn across the uneven land. In the plains here, the majority of the ground cover is bare earth, albeit with readily visible, scraped holes and burrows that are quite frequent in its surface. These plains stretch out in all directions, sloping very slightly up towards the west and broken by a roadway to the south. To the north, the plains appear to be interrupted.
18320: The Numenoreans that built this road provided it with a slight raised camber in the centre. Any falling rain would flow to the sides of the road and wash down the embankments to the surrounding plains. The surface of the road is now broken and damaged. What remains of the road cuts a true path running east to west, dissecting the plains surrounding it.
18321: A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.

A recently disturbed mound of earth, topped by a ring of twelve, broken spears lies nearby the road toward the south. Nestled amidst the long grasses of the plains, the mound is largely covered by flat heavy stones, obviously they were taken from the road to the north. The spears look like they have barely been tarnished or corroded by the elements.
18322: The burnt and blackened skeletal remains of a human are here.

The grasses and earth are churned, trampled down and littered with some broken weapons and shattered pieces of armour. Some hoof prints mill back and forth amongst booted footprints and spilt blood has stained the earth black, leading one to believe a bloody battle took place here recently.
18323:
A brown cow is here, contemplating a higher reality whilst chewing slowly.
A brown cow is here, contemplating a higher reality whilst chewing slowly.

Meadow grasses and flowers have dried here through poor drainage and a lack of water. What is left, is a natural hay field, which seems to have become quite a favoured eating place for a variety of plant-eating grazers. Dung from the many overfed animals appears to be everywhere, in various stages of moistness and fragrance.
18324: The smooth, meadow grass and yellow dandelions grow a little more than several boot-lengths in height and are well grazed. Dry, but fertile soil, accompanied by a ready supply of fresh manure, has led to a rich variety of wildflower growth, as well as the buzzing of various insects through the meadow.
18325: Closely, cropped grasses cover this area. Barely an inch or two in height, they carpet the gently undulating ground. Horse and cow droppings are common to find amongst this landscape. There are a few, straggly bushes of gorse and smaller shrubs that look distinctly nibbled upon.
18326:
A low, many-branched shrub covers the ground here.
A colony of red ants is here. The ants seem to ignore you.

Much of this area of lowland grasses are covered with strange, low mounds of dirt, covered in short grass and small trailing plants such as rockrose and wild thyme. The ground seems alive with small movements, as several hundreds of tiny ants go about their work.
18327: Dusty, parched stems of long grasses move gently around on the wind, brittle and tinder dry, in this area of stony, drained soil. Dried out bracken and heathers await a spark or flame to cleanse the land and even the occasional small animal that passes through seems to sense the tension.
18328: There is almost no life here in the soil or on the ground. What does remain is wilted, dried out for lack of moisture. The hardier strains of plants exist further out on the fronds of land, forming a jagged oval of dead land. There are no great signs of battle or any evidence of inhabitants.
18329: An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.

The tall grasses that are rising around this place, conceal a rich variety of plants, other than those in plain view. Dandelions and daisies, rye grass and thistle are all found here in quantity. In more secluded patches of growth, purple and spotted orchids are poking forth.
18330: The wild grasses of these plains have a distinctly flattened look, as if many people spent time around here or camped on this spot for a long time. Grass here, is more yellow then the rest and in several places, showing wear. Other signs suggest the presence of old campfires.
18331: Broken stones and the occasional pothole make travel on this portion of road hereafter treacherous. The embankment to the south of the road is crumbling and falling apart. A portion of the road on that side has collapsed into it. A small, rocky incline borders the road to the north. Falling rocks and some stones from the slope, lie in a pile of debris by the edge of the road.
18332: The plains that stretch out to the north are put asunder here by a small ramp as the land falls by about fifteen feet. At the bottom of the incline lies the Great South Road. There is almost no grass growing on the slope, leaving the surface loose and crumbly and making the footing uncertain.
18333: Downy and meadow oat grass predominantly covers these limestone-soiled plains. These are interspersed with the occasional hawkweed patch, primarily in areas where the soil is especially suited. The ground is soft and springy underfoot, causing to travel through on foot a bit easier.
18334: The land here undulates gently, covered in all directions with low grasses and sedges. Small flowers can be seen dotting the surface of this green sea. The ground seems to be soft underfoot, and appears to be a fine place to rest and escape the cares of travelling. Towards the south, the ground slopes slowly upwards, a slight break to the otherwise, flat terrain.
18335: The largely flattened landscape, typical of this region, is interrupted here by a small rise almost like a dune, arguably a hill. From its peak, a little more than thirty feet above the surrounding terrain, the course of the Great South Road can be clearly seen. It curves southward to avoid the rise that runs along the eastern edge.
18336: The road skirts around a small rise in the land towards the north. The flagstones that originally constituted this road's surface are chapped and crumbling from centuries of neglect. Flat plains stretch out to the south, while the view to the north is obstructed by a small hill.
18337: Long grasses that have spread away from the paved road to the north, stretch out to the south in a haze of mixed yellows and greens. Travelling through the waist high grasses seems strangely unreal, almost as if they are guiding those who travel here across a tranquil sea, creating the illusion of the land drifting idly by on a current of grass.
18338: Long, bending grasses rise well above waist height, creating a vista of yellow and green. In certain places, they rise even more, almost to a height of being over ones head. Occasionally, a thicket of thistles makes travel a bit more difficult. For the most part, however, the going is easy, for one with a good sense of direction.
18339: Scorched, bare earth, barely colonized by a variety of small shoots of some type of plant life, stretch for a mile or so in the midst of the grassland. The earth looks dry and baked, with grasses at the edges of this blackened zone to look as if they could burst into flames with the smallest spark.
18340:
A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.
A wild bull seems ready to charge you.

Tall grasses and invading heather battle for control of this area of the landscape. Other plants and wild flowers such as ling, bedstraw and old man's beard watch the battle for supremacy from their unobtrusive hiding places amongst the stronger weeds, awaiting the outcome.
18341: This ancient grassland, undisturbed by the plough or hoe, is growing here in abundance. The slender grasses reach no higher than the toe of a boot or a shoe. Harebell and cowslips grow amongst the grasses as well. There are also the telltale signs of ant colonies, tufts of miniature hillocks of moss and matted grasses.
18342: Grass for animal herds and yellow, oat grass dominates your view, with only the occasional buttercup or other flower visible amongst the tall vegetation. To the north, an invasion of heather and gorses looks to be imminent, but for now, the grassland dominates the view, with some scrubs far to the north.
18343:
A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.
A wild bull seems ready to charge you.

Heather, purple moor grass and bracken dominate this darkened area of heath, although all the plants here look like seedlings. The soil is covered in old ash, with some bleached and blackened bones peaking out from under the new growths. It looks as though a ferocious inferno must have burnt here, quit some time ago.
18344: A dried-up pond, now filled only with dust and dying plant life, lies in a low dip amidst the wilting grasses. The pond seems to have no obvious source of refilling, leading to the assumption that it may only fill through some heavy rainfall. Whatever the cause, there is little here to sustain life.
18345: The stones underfoot bear a strong resemblance to the foundation of a stables complex, with room for several horses and possibly even a hay wagon or two, or what remains of them. The occasional beam marks out where the stalls once stood. Everywhere, invading plant life is reclaiming the land. A large, stone water trough is lining the outside wall.
18346: A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A very decayed, yet once sturdy waystation, built in the classic Dunadan style lies here, ruined with its interior exposed to the elements. The house seems to have been unoccupied for many years and its surrounding wall and hedge are in a state of disrepair and chaos. A rusty gate leads to the road just north, while the crumbled remains of the station wall keep the ancient garden separate from the great plains of the Dunlands. This waystation probably housed many visitors when the Great South Road was first built.
18347: Bend in the Great South Road

A thick layer of leached soil covers much of the road, as it continues on to the east and the north. Buried amongst the scrub vegetation that grows wildly here, is a broken wheel from some long gone wagon or carriage. It lies abandoned and rotting, a sign of a bygone age, reminding travellers this road was once a major route of commerce between two mighty and prosperous kingdoms. Along the southern road-side an old hedge-row grows, blocking all passage, except for an opening to the south, guarded by a rusty old iron gate.
18348: A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

The road curves from west to south here, avoiding a small hill directly to the east. Completely overgrown with brush and scrubs, some portions of the road's stonework are only occasionally visible, broken and posing more of a hazard than an aid to those wishing to travel over. The better used section of road along the northern edge testifies to the more popular route.
18349: The absence of water has made the ground a little more than dry and sun-cracked. All but the most hardy of plant life has perished, leaving in the remaining desolation none but the more waxy, spiny plants that have adapted to such arid conditions. This lack of water extends further to the north, where the land is all but dead.
18350: The ground dips here, forming a slight depression that is no more than thirty feet across and perhaps five feet deep. Its slopes are lined with arrow grass and other damp-loving plant life. All the water to be found, is in the centre of this area, in the form of a small puddle, muddy and choked with a lot of pondweeds. To the west there is a strange rock, barely visible off in the distance.
18351: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

The remains of the Great South Road lie here, marking an east-west trail as the great road once did. In places, the road is in remarkable condition, especially since it hasn't been maintained for a long time. The short, stubble grass on either side of the road offers an inviting place to rest. The terrain is flat and the road stretches towards the horizon in both directions.
18352:
A drone bee flies around here, angrily buzzing.
The bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.
The bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.
The bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.

Cudweed and knotgrass appear to grow abundantly amongst forget-me-nots, poppies and speedwells. Nearby, a great road bends to the north and east but all passage to and from it is blocked by an ancient hedge-row. As one gets further from the road, the grasses grow taller and overtake the smaller, but less competitive plants. To the south, there seems to be a small opening in the tall grass.
18353:
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

A carefully, paved path passes east to west from the ruins of an extremely old looking house, to what seems to be the remnants of a once beautiful garden. The path is difficult to see until stumbled upon, as grasses and a few, tall, scraggly bushes provide almost total seclusion.
18354: Wild primroses and cowslips grow plentifully amongst the undisturbed, wild grasses. The soil is damp and the vegetation is lush and vibrant. There is a tiny spring trickling up from the earth, but is quickly absorbed by the surrounding soil, making it unusable as a water source.
18355: A combination of rather unpromising soil conditions and the lack of wind breaking the vegetation, has led to the development of heath land here. Heather and gorse dominate the plant life, choking down the tall grasses that are present elsewhere in the region.
18356: The rolling grassland gives way to an area of heath here, showing signs of fire consuming it not too long ago, possibly to make way for farming. New shoots of grass are peaking out from the ashes of the previous, flora-look green and vibrant. The grass in many places obviously seemed a tasty treat for some animals.
18357:
A sprawling green bush of stinging nettle grows here.
A dun-coloured grouse is sitting still in the heather.

This area is full of wild nettles that are interspersed with the rolling grasses that rise above waist height. Ground-nesting birds and a few other small animals are visible in the brush. The ground is soft and damp to touch, hinting at an underground water source, tantalizingly out of reach.
18358: A goat is here, grazing in the hills.

An area of hawthorn scrubs have forced its way in amongst the tall grasses, thriving on the dry, well-drained soil that is prevalent in these plains. The ground under and around the hawthorn bushes is carpeted in dog rose and brambles. Perhaps, in several years from now, taller trees will start to develop.
18359:
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.
A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A dry, hard mud trail wends its way through the long, surrounding grasses. The ground seems well-drained and generally dry. Purple fescue grasses grow along the edges of the trail. Here and there, signs of grazing by livestock and horses are visible. The trail continues west and north.
18360: A pack horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

A faint trail either begins, or perhaps come to an end here, leading to the south through medium to tall grasses and shrubs. The path is very faint and it is hard to tell whether the trail is caused by people, or perhaps being the work of animals. The sides of it are covered by tall shrubs and some scraggly plants.
18361: The rolling, grassy plains around this region have recently been disturbed, as evidenced by a number of freshly excavated holes and patches of newly turned earth. The cause of this disruption is not immediately evident, as there are no signs of any man-made cause.
18362:
A woody evergreen plant grows here, with many stems reaching upward.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

An overgrown garden, full of barley, oats and buckwheat has been left here, but barely visible amongst the tall grasses that have invaded its boundaries from without. There are no signs remaining here of any dwelling that may have once accompanied the garden. Within a few more years perhaps the remaining signs of the garden itself will also be erased.
18363: A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

Thistle, cornflower and poppies stand out amongst the one to two feet tall, wild grasses that populate this area. The grass is teeming with some small wildlife and is rarely silent, constantly disturbed by the movement of the wind through the stalks and leaves, along with the chattering of the hidden animals and insects.
18364: The stone used to build this road was hauled here from quarries long distances away. Running in an east-west direction here, the remains of the Great South Road cut through the vast plains that constitute the Gap of Rohan. There are short grasses that cover much of the road and the surrounding plains. To the north there is a large rock that is barely visible. South of the road, an old hedge-row grows, making passage into the open meadows quite hard, if not impossible.
18365: A huge, black boulder rests partially embedded into the ground, some fifteen feet high and nearly thirty feet across. It is surrounded by many, smaller rocks, all strewn about with no apparent meaning to their arrangement. The rocks give a refreshing break from the monotony of the flat landscape that is surrounding them.
18366: The grass that once grew here has dried from lack of water. In some places, what remained of the grass has been eaten or trampled by animals. South of here lies the ancient road that once ran between the Kingdoms of Gondor and Arnor. Far away to the north the Misty Mountains are visible, climbing imposingly out of the prairie.
18367: Buried underneath the dust and weeds, one can discern the remains of what was once a mighty road. On either sides of the road lie vast, windswept plains. Hampered by the flagstones concealed underneath, the path of the road is largely devoid of any thick vegetation and presents a fairly negotiable path to travellers. South of the road, an old and deep drainage dike is replaced by a hedge-row further to the east, blocking passage into the open southern plains.
18368:
A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

From deep green to an almost blue, a sea of grass seems to swell and ebb all about like the tide of an ocean. The variety of different grasses all blend together to form an endless pattern in all directions. To the north, on the other side of an ancient, drainage canal are the remains of the Great South Road that runs east and west continuing its ancient journey across the Dunlands.
18369: Several varieties of sweet smelling shrubs, combine with verdant grasses, to create a heady scent that is overpowering this grassy plain. A vast variety of rich plant life, overflows with only the occasional cropped spot, due to obvious grazing. The shrubs grow denser towards the east.
18370: A furry, striped raccoon is here, nosing around for some berries or roots.

The grassland forms a dense turf, much shorter than in the surrounding lands. The soil is well drained and dry. The grass is replaced here and there, with mosses and a variety of fungi. Stands of various types seem to be widespread and a number of other types of plants appear to grow hardily from old horse dung, which is plentiful here.
18371: A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Medium length grasses, interspersed with buttercups and cowslips, cover much of this area. Many of the plants look well nibbled upon. Much of the grass has been well grazed, often down to the base and many plants have made use of the rich soil provided through an abundance of horse dung.
18372: A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

A slightly worn path appears out of the plains here and continues to the north, where it intersects with other trails. The signs of disuse are clearly visible by the number of weeds growing on the edge of the trampled ground. When the local inhabitants ceased using it, the verdant green grasses quickly reclaimed the plains.
18373: A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

Several small, worn trails criss-cross here, although south and east they appear to be less used. To the north, one can barely see a ridge in the plains, while to the west lies the southern skirt of the Misty Mountains. The only signs of life are the countless hoof-marks that pepper the mud of the trail. It would appear that recently a great number of beasts were driven or ridden along it.
18374: A long-bodied animal with thick brown fur bounds through the trees.

Cutting its way across the plains, this trail is but one of many created by the movements of beasts and hunters. Hoof marks are easily visible in the soft turf, often clumped together in areas near the track. To the north are the burnt remnants of a village below a rising ridgeline, and beyond it on the horizon are the southernmost foothills of the Misty Mountains, Dol Baran.
18375: The high grass nearby gives way to a clearing, burnt by fire that appears to have been fairly recent. A few remnants of wooden buildings still remain, scorched and blackened. It is impossible to tell who lived here, but with the constant wars between Rohirrim, Dunlendings and orcs in this area, such raids are commonplace. A ridge rises above the plains to the north and east, while to the south the flatlands continue as far as the eye can see.
18376: Atop a Ridge in the Plains

A ridge runs for miles along the plains, a little more than a small scree here. Plants and shrubs of many different varieties grow atop it, giving way to short lush turf elsewhere. The ridge continues southeast across the plains, becoming steeper in the distance. To the east, grasses and scraggly bushes grow densely.
18377: A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

Tall stalks of brown grass shift unsteadily from the constant breeze that blows through the Gap of Rohan. The sea of green and brown seems without end, the same turf covering the plains for miles around. To the north it fades slightly away into a richly-coloured valley, cleaving into the mountains.
18378:
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Brown and green grasses dominate the surrounding view to the south. Much of the same vegetation can be seen continuing to the west and east. Mountains begin to dominate the horizon further north, a drastic end to the flat plains that make up the Gap of Rohan. A valley, immediately north, opens up between the mountains.
18379: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

The ground becomes hard and rocky here, making travel difficult. The mountains appear to grow right out of the plains, a vivid contrast between the green plains and the grey rock of the mountains. The route above becomes a difficult climb, while the valley to south continues on in the distance.
18380: There are some small plants growing on the outer edge of the cliff, brave enough to battle the harsh environment of the mountains. The ground is solid and there is enough room to walk side by side. The mountains that are to the west, grow even steeper as the peaks rise higher and higher.
18381: A mix of clay and mud, the earthen walls of this cave seem to have once been smooth and unscarred. Now, in many places, they are marred with scratches of sharp claws. Upon the ground, which is clearly made of the very same material as the walls, one can see more scratches coupled with the occasional small feather pressed deep into the earth. The hollow itself is no more than twelve feet wide and from roof to ground no more than ten feet.
18382: Atop a broad plateau, this section of the plains is somewhat barren. There are towering mountains, which rise up to the north and west, while the land drops away gradually to the south and east. With the run-off of water from above and the winds that sweep across the land at this altitude, this is not the kind of terrain where plant life can flourish easily.
18383: The rocky soil is the host to a variety of bushes and densely growing vines, slowing travel somewhat. To the north, the plains slope upwards and are fairly steep, before giving way to the majestic Misty Mountains. The foothills, or roots of these mountains, extend all the way to this section of Rohan, some twenty miles south of Isengard itself.
18384: A short evergreen plant, with slightly bluish needles, grows here.

The southern end of the Misty Mountains are blocking the view to the north, like a giant wall across the horizon for dozens of miles. To the northeast, the line breaks, allowing an entrance to Nan Curunir, the valley of the wizards. The sea of green grass continues to both the south and west, while just head-on to the north, the slopes form an entrance to a cave, with many, heavy footprints that lead in that direction.
18385: The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

The Misty Mountains that block the way to the north are a formidable array of peaks. There appears to be no way past those heights. Further eastwards, they lower into a series of hills, which are the entrance to the valley of Isengard. Here, the land is quite rocky, although interspersed with clumps of growth. As the land lowers to the south, the greenery there appears to become more prevalent.
18387: At the Foot of Dol Baran

At the foot of a spur of hills, it is impossible to advance to the north, west or east, because flat rocks reach into the sky and form a nearly vertical rock wall. Far above to the east, the heather-covered crown of Dol Baran, like an imperious throne, watches the land. And even further to the east, lies the impassable Misty Mountains that appear to tower into the clouds; while to the south the rocky area ends, dropping away into the grassy flatlands of the Gap of Rohan.
18389:
There are two handfuls of clover here.
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

Wildlife flourishes here, quickly fleeing into tall grass at the first sign of any movement. Birds can often be seen calling out to each other, as they fly far overhead with some hidden purpose. The plains roll on to the south and the west, but to the north, they are abruptly halted by the southern end of the Misty Mountains.
18390:
Prickly, white-stemmed plants, with blue flower heads grow in abundance.
A dun-coloured grouse is sitting still in the heather.
A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.

There are many varieties of plant life, laying on the border lands between the plains and the mountains here. The colour of the field has made it a perfect hiding spot for small birds and other creatures that live in the low grasses and brush. The vast plains continue to the south and west. To the east, the vegetation becomes too thick to pass.
18391: The orderly nature of the plains ceases here, and a dense green thicket of undergrowth sprouts up in a sudden depression. The dark vegetation is a harsh contrast to the otherwise light shades of plains to the west. Water from the densely vegetated thorns, which stretch out just east and north, must drain to here, for the base of the depression is slightly boggy in parts.
18392: The grass in this area is little more than a browned coverlet, partly due to the sun and the stony soil. North, the plains resume their normal covering of springy turf, whilst south the ridge falls fairly steep down, offering a climb of about a dozen yards.
18393:
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Underneath a large, rocky protrusion in the plains, this area has been well sheltered from the winds which sweep across the Gap of Rohan. The grass has responded well to this respite, growing to the height of a man's waist in parts. Dense growth makes it hard to see, and countless boulders that have fallen from the ridge above, make it hard to progress beyond this place.
18394: This small path leads to the rotten remains of a farmstead just south of here, now being little used, since its owners are long gone. In places the trail all but disappears, only to pop up again a few dozen yards away. There is a large ridge that cuts across the plains to the northeast, blocking passage due to its stony sides.
18395:
A golden, firm onion is here.
A round turnip is growing here.
A starving cow stands here, looking for a patch of grass.
A starving cow stands here, looking for a patch of grass.
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

The natural grass and plant life has taken over what was once an orderly row of vegetables and grains. A few parts of the former crop grow here, but now very sparse among the lush plains of grass. There is no sign of a farm house, but parts of broken farm implements lie upon the ground, abandoned some time ago. Beyond the farm remains, lies a thicket growing out of a depression in the earth, which blocks further travel southward.
18396:
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Leaning back into the hillside of Dol Baran above, this open dale is protected from much of the winds that sweep through the Gap of Rohan. Its steep sides are covered in lichen, and the lower banks by several, thick, thorny bushes. Occasional trees and tall hawthorns rise from the soft, springy turf that populate the glen, while above on the horizon, rise first the bare hills and then the snow-capped Misty Mountains.
18397: Broad and hard, the ancient highway was laid down, and it has been well maintained. Towards the north, it approaches the entrance to the valley of Isengard, where the road and river pass into the cleft at the end of the Misty Mountains. The arms of the mountains wrap around it like pincers, leaving only a narrow gap of a few miles. Below, to the west, is the steep side of a dale, open only to the south. A trail leads towards the riverside to the east.
18398: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

This hilly range is the western spur guarding the entrance to the valley of Isengard. Dol Baran is the last of that range with its round, imperious and heather-covered crown. Once there was an outpost of some sort here, but it has long since been abandoned, leaving nothing but the lichen-covered stone foundations. Around the hill's eastern feet runs a wide highway, roughly following the line of the river, while a steep slope of flat large rocks descends to the west.
18399: The brown shoulder of the road to the east slowly gives way to a sea of green grass that is about one foot in height. A few shrubs and plants are growing along the edge of the road, well nourished by the nearby waters of the Isen. To the north, a secluded glen that opens up on the side of a large round hill, which is but a spur from the vast heights of the Misty Mountains that lies to the northwest.
18400: This well-maintained road runs north to south, and although it seems to be used relatively frequently, it is still in good order. Someone has taken great care to keep it in excellent condition for the fast transport of people and beasts. To the west, the plains stretch for miles upon miles of sweet upland turf. To the east, the grass is interrupted in the distance by the line of the river Isen.
18401: Bend in the Road to Isengard

The road bends here along with the river, on a raised embankment that is above any chance of flooding. Running swiftly on its stony bed, the Isen marks the western border of Rohan. Southwards, the road and the river enter a long, but wide valley. Northwards though, they each head towards the entrance of a large valley.
18402: The river here is broad and slow, not to regain its mountain swiftness while in the flat lands of the Gap. The broken plains on the eastern bank are the only view of the land of Rohan, while to the north the giant presence of the Misty Mountains dominate the horizon. The river downstream enters a broad valley, its eastern bank beginning to grow steep.
18403: Many, small boulders and underwater rock formations would have made this a dangerous part of the river, but the current is not quick enough here to pose any hazard. The water ramps over and around the smooth-sided rocks in many places, forming many whirls and small side currents. On its west bank runs a road at the base of a steep ridge, while to the east the riverbank slopes steeply towards broken plains.
18404: A low shoulder of rock allows passage to the west bank, where the road bends away from the river to avoid flooding. The Isen is wide and slow here, with a steep slope of half a dozen yards on its eastern side. To the south, the valley through which it runs opens up into the flat lands of the Gap, where miles upon miles of soft turf stretch out in the distance.
18405:
A bass swims here.
A trout swims here.
A bass swims here.

The river begins to run calm here, as it widens during its flow southward. The water becomes shallow near the banks, with the smooth algae-covered bed that is clearly visible a few feet down. A tall shoulder of steep rock prevents any passage to the eastern bank, while on the western side there are rolling folds that are so typical in the Gap of Rohan. A small, water channel runs through them, and empties its trickle of water into the river.
18406: The river is wider here than at any other visible point, flooding out into the reedy banks to the west. The eastern bank is steeper, although it has eroded into a muddy and slippery slope. The water below is still deep though, easily deep enough to prevent any chance of fording even at its lowest level. The stony river bed is only visible near the banks, while in the central channel the only thing noticeable underwater is the occasional darting fish.
18407:
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

Waist high grass, coloured somewhere between green and brown, almost covers these riverside fields completely. Travel is somewhat slow because of this. It gets even worse to the east, where the land grows very soggy as it nears the waters of the Isen. Westwards, the road to Isengard runs by on slightly higher ground, avoiding any chance of flooding.
18408:
Clusters of slender stems and tall leaves thrive in the mud and shallows.
A restless rabbit bounces around.

Rolling down in gentle folds of land from the road to the west, these plains are simply miles of soft, upland turf. An occasional clump of reeds or low bushes lies nearer to the river, but the grass dominates. Flowing down from the road is a small line of water, in an almost perfectly straight channel. This connects to the gutters of the old highway, and keeps it free of any flooding even during heavy rains.
18409: Curve in the Road to Isengard
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

Unpaved, but flat and smooth, this broad highway was cut by the men of Numenor in ages past, linking the fortress of Isengard to the Fords of Isen. It is still maintained today, so that armies can sweep down to quickly block the Gap of Rohan. It follows the line of the Isen for the most part. Further south, it diverges by a few miles, taking a more direct route.
18410: The ancient roadway runs its course north to south on a narrow strip of land between the steep, valley slopes and the river. It is a wide road, made for swift passage, so travel is easy and unimpeded. South, the valley opens up into the plains of the Gap of Rohan, while to the north the road and river head towards the mouth of Nan Curunir. The valley lies in a cleft at the end of the Misty Mountains with its countless vast peaks rising on either side.
18411: This part of the road passes under a pebbled slope on its western side, which grows to a ridge further south. The highway itself is in order, and has seen much work of late. Near the riverside, large wooden props now support the edge of the roadway, which was being eroded by the waters.
18412: This otherwise ancient road appears to be well maintained. It continues its smooth passage to the east and south, along the river banks of the Isen. The plains that lie on the western side of the road seem to go on forever into the horizon, interrupted only by the snow-capped peaks of the Misty Mountains on their northern side.
18413: Flat for miles around, the plains are only split to the south, where there is a ridge that rises above the road, running just east of here. The grass sways constantly in the breezes that swirl up the valley of the Isen, creating some ocean-like waves in the short grass.
18414:
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

The ridgeline diminishes from its mighty height south-west to a mere slope here over the road. Slightly treacherous because of the loose stones, it nevertheless seems to be an easy route down. Underfoot the turf is soft and springy, as it is for miles around to the west and north. The only interruption to the plains are the peaks of the Misty Mountains, which rise into the clouds not many miles north of here.
18415: Overlooking the Valley of the Isen

The steep, western slopes of the valley runs across the plains westwards from here, a great ridgeline blocking travel for many miles. It would be possible to climb down eastwards, although not without risk, while to the south, the slope is too steep to descend. Below, the road to Isengard bends around the feet of the ridge, and continues on in a north-south direction. The river Isen itself lies about two miles east, a wide waterway marking the western borders of Rohan.
18416: Bend in the Road to Isengard

Coming up against the steep slopes of the valley, the road bends away east, nearer to the river Isen. Underfoot, it is a wide highway, being unpaved but smooth and hard-packed. It was built so that a large army could ride swiftly down from Isengard to block the Fords of Isen, and for that purpose it is still kept in good order. Westwards, a long running ridge overshadows a fertile valley, thriving in its shelter, while south the road continues along the western side of the valley.
18417: The road travels under the shadow of a ridge on the western edge, which reaches its highest point nearby. Between it and the road, there is a small line of water that runs down a gutter, cutting under the road in a narrow, man-made tunnel and heads towards the river. Such water channels were built long ago by the Numenoreans to prevent flooding of vital military highways, and have been maintained by the Rohirrim and the guardians of Isengard ever since.
18418: Tracks of men and horses are scattered on the road, which runs north to south in the valley of the Isen here. The Isen River runs only a few miles to the east, its sparkling mountain waters are easily visible. To the west lies the pebbled, western slope leading up to a ridge, where a scree of stones appears to be treacherous underfoot. It would be easier to ascend south of here, where the slope is less steep.
18419:
A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

The ridge here is a little more than a grassy scree of countless small stones, often rolling down to the base of the wide road below. To the west, the grass wins its battle with the pebbles, and stretches for many miles into the turf of southern Dunland. East, the River Isen lies just a mile or so beyond the road, marking the western border of Rohan.
18420: A small ridge forms here, overlooking the road and the River Isen below. To the west, the plains continue as rolling grasslands through the Gap of Rohan, while to the north the land dips below another ridge into a lush valley. That would probably prove the easiest route to the road below, as the slope here would need careful climbing to descend.
18421: Overshadowed by the ridge to the north, the grasslands here have become lush in their sheltered valley. Once a mostly deserted land due to the wars of orcs and men, now wildlife flourishes from the rich earth. All around, the valley plants and shrubs sprout from the ground, well nourished by the nearby waters of the Isen. Just before the river to the east lies a wide road, following the line of the water north and south.
18422: A lone hawk soars high above you.

The ridge continues on, running east to west, cutting across the plains below. The ground is somewhat solid, but rocky in parts as the exposed ridge pokes through the soil. The ridgeline diminishes a little to the east as it edges towards the valley of the Isen, while to the west there is a narrow and very knife-like outcrop that thrusts out from the rock.
18423: Rolling sedately along, the grasslands reach a peak here and begin to fall away gently to the south and east. Eventually the land there drops down a ridge, a line that splits the plains for miles. Beyond that the plains continues north up to the mountains as miles, upon miles, of soft, springy turf.
18424: A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

Tall stalks of yellow-brown grass sway in the wind, growing over two feet high in places. The dense clumps of green grass to the west, mask a rocky fall into a valley, too steep to descend. The earth appears to be soft and springy below the verdant growth. It is well watered by underground sources from the nearby mountains.
18426: Walls of thorns and shrubs seem to grow thickly all around here, in particular to the south, where the tangle of vegetation is extremely dense. All of the surrounding greenery turns dismally dark to the north, where a valley of dark green grass cowers below a ridge.
18427: The plains here are spread across a large ridge, which dips down noticeably to the south. This part is the highest for miles around, which exposes it to the winds that whistle through the Gap of Rohan. However, the grass that is underfoot, does not seem to have suffered. It is lush and soft everywhere.
18428:
A young colt is frolicking playfully.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

Thrusting outward from the ridge that splits the plains, this outcrop is a thin knife-like sliver of land. On all sides, the descent is treacherous, as the eroded rock is not very stable. To the north, the plains appear to rise somewhat. Noticeable beyond the plains there, the southern end of the Misty Mountains rises forcefully.
18429: In the Shadow of a Ridge

The wild ox seems ready to charge you.
The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

The ridge to the north is a knife-like outcrop, appearing to be near impossible to climb and seemingly in danger of sudden collapse. Here, under its height, lies a large, fertile valley. It runs through various shades of green as it stretches out away from the ridge. To the west, some sort of trail is barely visible in the distance.
18430: The field is covered in grass about one foot high, with some small shrubs growing on the outlying area of the ridge to the north. Small rodents and game birds thrive here, quickly scurrying to take cover at the scent of any large animal or other threatening disturbances.
18431: This section of the well-kept road connects the valley of Isengard to the outside world. The tracks of wheeled carts and many hoof prints are an obvious sign of the heavy use it is put to. On the riverbank to the east, there is a small watchtower atop a brick building, almost giving a full view over the entrance to the valley.
18432: The River Isen flows on, widening and slowing down as it leaves the valley of Isengard and its mountain enclosure. However, at this point, the water still flows quite swiftly. There are a lot of debris that has fallen into the river from the rocky outcrops on its eastern side, making the water choppy. On the western bank lies a wooden watchtower, built to survey any approach to the valley.
18433: The ground is particularly rough and stony, with small rocky outcroppings that thrust out into the river. Only patches of short grasses are able to grow in the soil. To the west, the River Isen flows strongly southwards. Entry into the river is possible, although it would require climbing down from the rocks. To the north, the rocky river bank continues with large outcroppings further away.
18434: Littered with boulder-like protrusions, these plains are rather unhelpful to travellers, but this is the only visible passage on this side of the river. The Isen flows by in a narrow channel below here, with the bank on this side being a sheer drop of a half-dozen yards or more. The outskirts of the Misty Mountains are barely visible to the north.
18435: The rough, rocky ground here dominates the landscape for miles on this side of the river, making travel tiresome and slow. The terrain on the other bank is less hostile, and indeed a road is visible not far from the water. Both the river and the road alongside it, seem to originate in the mouth of a large mountain valley a few miles to the north.
18436: An opossum stands here, sniffing around the ground.

The landscape here is scarred and scattered, with countless, loose rocks and boulders. In its stony riverbed to the west the river Isen flows, the edges are lined with sharp rocks. The rocky terrain rises up to the south, at this point little more than a simple slope. However, it does becomes steeper even further south, continuing through the plains for many miles.
18437: Beginnings of a Ridge through the Plains

The ridge here is at its lowest point and steadily rises further as its run in a south-west direction. It is not as rocky or uneven, as the lands just below, or the terrain further up the ridge to the south. The waters of the Isen flow by to the west, issuing from the mouth of a mountain valley a few miles to the north.
18438: Rocks, boulders and holes in the earth scar the plains. Travel by mount would be impossible due to the inconsistent terrain. The land appears to continue roughly to the north, where it slopes away down to the river. South of here the plains continue, seemingly less marred with rough terrain. Far to the north, the caps of the Misty Mountains are barely visible in the clouds.
18439: The landscape here is rough and marred by rocks and holes. Some lush, green grass spreads in patches, interspersed between the stony outcrops. To the west, the land can be seen falling away into a valley, while away to the far north, the peaks of the Misty Mountains can be discerned. To the south, the ground slopes downwards into a depression.
18440: The land dips into a large and shallow bowl-shaped pit. Small fissures are leading away from the steep eastern side, too narrow to enter, while on the other sides the slopes are more gradual. The base of the depression is covered in tough, grey-green grass, occasionally dotted with rocks and pebbles.
18441: Ridge through the Plains of Rohan

A large, rough ridge climbs slowly above the plains here, growing steadily as it goes. The ground is hard and lined with stones and sudden pits. It sports little vegetation except for a short covering of hardy grass. To the north, the land dips again, towards a depression in the plains. Below to the west, bright green plains roll southward.
18442: A lone hawk soars high above you.

Covered in relentlessly waving beds of grass, this sheltered area lies in the angle of a bending ridge. To the north it is steep overhead, perhaps half a dozen yards or so, while to the east the ridge is merely a grassy slope that appears to be inaccessible from this side. Directly above, it seems possible to climb up out of this area.
18443: This high ridge rises slowly from the green plains and runs for several miles north of here. Below, the river Isen runs by in its valley, with what appears to be a road barely visible on the far bank. The vegetation on this ridge is poor, in many places nothing but a light, mossy covering for the rough stone beneath. To the south, the plains continues, just below the ridge. To the east, the ridge slopes downwards.
18444: The stony soil here can support little more than the sparse vegetation, which grows between the countless, rocky outcrops that dot this ridgeline. Near the edge of the ridge, the ground is not very stable and appears that it would be easy to trip on a crumbling chunk of rock. A steep slope leads down to the riverside to the west, which is nothing more than a small chunk of broken plains before the water itself.
18445: This elevated ridge, runs in a giant curve through the plains, enclosing the valley of the Isen on its western side. This side of the river is mostly a broken land, with the crumbled potholes common in the stony soil that cause any mounted travel nearly impossible. Below and to the west, are some rocky plains that expand over a few hundred yards. Even further away the Isen can be noticed as well.
18446: The wild ox seems ready to charge you.

The ridge above is steep for a dozen yards or so, with a small and shallow valley forming at its base. The ground here is rich and damp, with small, low bushes covering much of it. The River Isen flows by to the northwest of here, bending away from the far bank. The ridge to the east is a rocky and sheer outcrop, although climbing straight up seems possible.
18447: The river Isen bends slightly west here, cutting around the stony outcrops on its eastern bank. The water is chilly, although the fish, which are frequently visible below the surface, do not seem to mind. The shallower water near the eastern bank is full of sharp rocks and slippery stones, and is probably not the best place to leave the river.
18448: The water is still chilly, flowing directly in swift descent from the towering Misty Mountains that lies north of here. The river loses most of its force in the flatter lands of the Gap, but it will take many miles before it looses its icy touch. To the north, the river narrows into a steep-sided channel, with a watchtower visible far off in the distance, while downstreams it bends to the west.
18449: The river flows considerably faster here, becoming very narrow as it is squeezed between the sheer rock of the eastern bank and the steep western side. However, it still moves at a comparatively sedate pace, compared to its mountain origins further upstream. The current is gentle, but persuasive and moving everything downstream unless one swims with force against it.
18450: The trail leads from the road to a short distance to the west, where there is a watchtower standing. The base is a simple, brick building, built without much grace. A large, wooden tower that rises thirty or so feet above the brick building at its base, provides a good view over the entrance to Nan Curunir. The valley lies just to the north of here, opening up beyond the arms of the mountains that enclose the entrance.
18451: To the south and east, the river Isen is visible, flowing slowly through the flat lands. One can see patches of bushes and even occasional small trees growing here and there, but mostly the land is nothing but short, springy turf. West lies the road that leads north into the valley of Isengard, and south through Rohan towards Dunland.
18452: Although this place lies dozens of miles away from the Misty Mountains where the Isen is born, the water still carries the cold of its icy origins. It has long since lost the swift mountain current though, broadening and slowing down in these flat lands. On the western bank is a wide road, which seems to follow the line of the river.
18453: A hairy black spider wraps up a silken package with her hind legs.

The river continues its flow north and west here, through the flatlands. There is a well-kept road that runs parallel to the river on its western side, elevated slightly by the earthen embankments. On the eastern bank, there are broken plains, scattered with fissures and cracks in the ground. Far to the northeast, the peaks of the Misty Mountains are visible in the distance as is the Forest of Fangorn.
18454: The rough ground here is hard to travel, with many rocks and stones kicking up underfoot. Large holes can also be seen all around the plains, all appearing to be deep and seemingly impossible to climb back up from. A few miles to the east, lies the eastern walls of the valley, too steep to climb though. Below, a slippery slope leads down to the river Isen.
18455: Narrow Strip of Land by the River

These stony plains are stuck between the high, eastern, valley walls and the river Isen to the west. A steep slope leads into the water, while the climb up to the high ridge that is to the east, looks impossible. The landscape is very uneven and hard to travel due to large rocks, boulders and some deep holes. It seems to get even worse to the north.
18456: This large, rolling ridge that lies just east of the rivern Isen, has blocked any passage west. The plains here are similar to the lands southwards, flat and green with a few rocks scattered on the ground. The land to the north seems less hospitable and harder to travel through.
18457:
A wild bull seems ready to charge you.
A wild bull seems ready to charge you.

The River Isen provides a small variety to the otherwise unending plains. While the usual vegetation of plains consists of grass only, closer to the river are bushes that brave the harsh, stony soil and thrive off all the nourishment that the river water provides. Hoof prints can be seen in the dusty earth, some of them quite fresh.
18458:
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The rocky wasteland is littered with stony debris and lined with fine cracks that tear down beneath the parched surface of the plains. The dusty landscape continues in all directions, except to the south where a spur of hills rises higher than the surrounding plains.
18459: The sun-scarred surface of the rocky plateau is covered with a fine mosaic of greys and browns, split finely by the myriad of dark cracks diving under the stony surface. Sparse tufts of dry, brown grass whistle in the blowing wind and gritty dust stirs up with every step. A low ridge cuts of the otherwise flat landscape to the south, too steep to be climbed. Misshapen piles of broken granite and weatherworn sandstone heaps dots the ground in all other directions.
18460: The tinder dry earth of the rocky plateau is littered with larger rocks and drifting, stinging sand. Dry, pale lichen splayed out upon the cracked earth crunches under feet and the wind whistles sharply through the wiry, brown tufts of grass. West and south, the land slopes steeply upwards into the mountain arms that enclose this valley.
18461: A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

The steep incline of this mountainside is solid and only low plants have found footing and nourishment to grow here. Even the hardy plains grass seems to have difficulty pushing their roots into the thin layer of rocky soil. Evidence of old landslides caused by the lashing force of the harsh elements can be seen in the wide gullies overhead. To the west, the sheer face of the mountainside bars any thought of travel in that direction.
