18462: The parched plain is cracked and littered with wind-carved sandstone formations and loose stones. The only thing that manages to survive here is the hardy plains grass, shoving up from the hard-packed earth in small, tufted clumps. A dry wind sears across the plains, whipping the tufts and stirring up eddies of choking dust. To the south and near west loom the steep and barren cliffs of the Misty Mountains, enclosing the valley in their arms.
18463: The rock-strewn slope draws up sharply to the southwest, naked to the harsher elements of wind and rain except for the minimal shelter provided by the sparse collection of small, dry shrubs that line the lower flanks of the mountains. Thin, spidery lichen splays out across the uneven ground, giving a pale yellow tone to the stony landscape.
18464: The broad plateau is flat and barren, littered with tortured rock formations and loose scree. A handful of small, twisted thornbushes dot the landscape and a myriad of web-like cracks fracture the hard ground into a mosaic of clay-hued grey and dusty earth-tones. To the southwest, you see a formidable wall of rising mountains, marching away along the horizon.
18465: The steep slope of this mountainside is covered with loose rock and scant vegetation. The coarse grass and dry lichen have a tenuous footing in the thin layer of rocky soil and the overall landscape appears bleak and barren. The mighty arms of the southernmost Misty Mountains tower high above you into the endless sky, sheer and magnificent in their stark beauty.
18466: The uneven, hard packed earth is covered here with loose gravel and sparse, brown grass. The mountains rise steeply westwards, blocking any thought of ground passage in that direction. To the east, the valley broadens, spilling into the open plains of Nan Curunir.
18467: The steep slope of the mountainside climbs vertically to the northwest, with sheer cliff walls. Not even the lichen and grasses that are so plentiful in the hillsides around have found stable footing on the sheer rockface.
18468: The rocky terrain is barren and unforgiving here, littered with arrays of granite boulders and strange sandstone formations. The sheer face of a dark cliff rises sharply to the north, while the stony landscape continues uninterrupted in all other directions. Cold winds push and pull at the loose shrubs and bushes frequently, lifting up sand and litter migrating across the plain.
18469: The rocky plateau is flat and barren, covered with the dried husks of pale lichen and littered with broken heaps of slag and sandstone. Nothing seems to thrive in this desolate landscape and the hard-packed, stony earth is lined with deep cracks that seem to grow wider to the east. On the horizon, both north and south, east and west, the towering Misty Mountains stand prominently.
18470: A rock lizard is here, motionless as it observes you.

The rocky plains that stretch away to the northeast come to an abrupt end here, bordered by a deep crevice in the dry earth. In the darkness far below the outlines of boulders are visible, along with faint white lines rather like bones. To the northwest the steep slopes of the mountains are visible, their massive heights dominating the horizon. A hard wind lashes at anything that ventures in this harsh terrain, stirring up clouds of dust all about you.
18471: A dark chasm falls away before your feet, plunging deep into the cracked, stony earth. The rift tears its way north and southwards through the barren plain, the other side a dozen yards or more away to the east. Nothing much lives on the rocky plains here, except the rare tufts of dry, brown grass. A few miles to the west, the towering walls of the Misty Mountains dominate the land.
18472: The rocky plains are sharply severed here as a narrow rift delves deep below the surface of the plateau at your feet. The climb down does not seem so difficult, but ascending would be tiring. Across the crevice to the east the barren plains marches off to the horizon, with only the occasional mound of crumbled rock or small, withered bush to interrupt the emptiness.
18473: The rocky plateau is flat and barren, dotted with scattered rocks and piles of boulders. No larger plant life remains here, only the hardy plains grass manages to thrive, in windswept clumps. The terrain is lined with a tortured mosaic of fine cracks that dive sharply down into the rocky earth.
18474: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The desolate valley plateau stretches onwards in all directions, the monotony broken by the intricate arrangement of fine cracks decorating the dusty surface of this forsaken land. Loose piles of broken rock gathered by the wind and small tufts of brown grass are scattered on the ground.
18475: The dry wasteland stretches out in every direction from here; the forces of nature having stripped all of the lush growth from the once fertile plain. The only plant life that manages to remain, are the few tufts of wiry, brown grass that rustles in the dry wind. Far upon the eastern horizon, the faint line of a distant road can be made out.
18476: The dry wind stirs up eddies of grey dust and gritty sand here, obscuring the view of the surrounding landscape. Few plants have survived the harsh climate and weather on this plain; only brown tufts of grass is seen on the ground. A large outcropping of dark rock can be discerned to the northeast; the granite formation appears to have been deposited here ages ago by some vast ice slide or perhaps hurled from afar from some volcanic source long since quieted.
18477: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The gritty mantle of dust and gravel lies uneasily upon the parched plain at your feet. The elements have stripped all life from this tortured landscape, leaving gaping cracks in the dry and rocky soil. To the southeast, a large granite outcropping stands like a rotund monolith on the horizon.
18478:
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A snake slithers towards you.

The barren plain continues onward, decorated sparsely with dusty boulders and piles of crumbled rock. Even the hardy plains grass has given up on survival here; deep cracks in the parched earth are evidence of the hardships that this once great land has suffered. High mountains loom on the distant horizons to the east and west.
18479: What was once a green and fertile plain lies now in dust; the stony ground is littered with crumbled sandstone and brown clumps of dried grass that whip about stiffly in the wind. The plain is divided sharply by a system of fine cracks in the earth that seem to grow larger westwards. Elsewhere, the flat land continues until the mountains that surround this valley.
18480: A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

The dry earth is covered with cracks. The cracks vary in width from a few inches to a foot, and most of them are parallel, going from the north to the south. Westwards a larger crevice blocks movement, its dark depths not visible from here. Barely surviving in the poor earth are a few scraggly bushes, their withered branches showing little vigour or life.
18481:
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The cracked land breaks up to the west in a wide crevice, a dozen yards in width. It narrows north and south into a thin fissure, and then disappears altogether. The area around is fairly flat, with little growth and no larger plants at all. The dirt is dry and filled with small cracks from the influence of the sun. The valley continues in all directions, framed by the Misty Mountains on all sides.
18482: At the Edge of a Fissure

Covered in a thin haze of dust that swirls in the wind, the ground here is cut by tiny fissures as if it had been without water for decades. A large crack opens up the ground west of here, too wide to cross. The near side is too steep to descend, overhanging the base of the crevice below. The far side looks to be less of a challenge, and could be climbed with care.
18483: This barren and rocky plain is lined with thousands of fine, dark cracks that extend along the surface of the ground. Heaps of broken rock and small boulders decorate the tortured landscape and only small clumps of wiry, brown grasses have survived the drought that has plighted the lands. A dry wind throws a small cloud of dust and gritty sand into the air.
18484: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The flat surface of this rocky wasteland is dotted with a loose collection of short, withered bushes. The twisted branches splay out across the dusty terrain and jerk stiffly in the dry wind that whips now and then across the heath. About you, the rocky plains continue in all directions, though the ground to the west seems more barren and lined with dark cracks.
18485: A ridge of the mountains, coming from the west, breaks the flat plateau. Where the ridge ends, a large dike begins, leading eastwards, across the valley. The dike is deep and wide, preventing travel to the northernmost parts of the valley. The ground is dry and rocky from the apparent drought and the harsh climate; only a few clumps of dry, brown grass grows here.
18486:
A diamond-back rattlesnake is coiled here, ready to strike.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The stark terrain is harsh; the only plant life that seems to survive are the occasional tufts of brown grass. The hard-packed earth elsewhere is covered in gritty debris and larger rock formations. Beneath the drifting carpet of dun-hued dust, you see an intricate network of narrow cracks, growing into a large yawning chasm to the south. The ground opens up to the north, into a deep dike preventing access northwards. The bases of the cracks and the dike, far below, are littered with cracked boulders and often sun-bleached bones.
18487: A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

The rocky ground is littered with piles of crumbling boulders and loose gravel that grates sharply under foot or hoof. The bones of a small animal, a mule or pony perhaps, stand out starkly against the brown earth. All around you, except to the north, the valley plains march on, rising slightly towards the mountains that surround them. The plains northwards are blocked by a deep dike, preventing any access.
18488: The rocky table of this barren plateau is dotted with countless rocks and piles of broken boulders. A fair distance to the northeast, the shadow of a giant tree breaks the flat lands, against the background of the stark vastness of the Misty Mountains.
18490: A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

The rough terrain dwindles and ends to the east, where it meets the paved roadway that leads to Isengard. Far to the north, you can see the towering pinnacle of Orthanc, rising sharply before the mountain peaks. The surrounding terrain is littered with small stones and boulders, and a few rib-cages of slain animals.
18491: This wide and well-maintained roadway leads from north to south, while the surrounding lands rise steadily northwards as they approach the mountains encircling the ring of Isengard. A lonely pinnacle rising in its centre, the towering Orthanc, can be seen against the mountain background. The swift flowing waters of the Isen lies directly east of the road, a short distance down a soft bank.
18492: The water is crystal clear and deep, the stony riverbed can be seen clearly below. The western riverbank inclines faintly to the west, at the top of which you can see a road following the edge. The swift flow of the river runs southwards, moving along any loose debris. High mountain walls form the eastern bank of the river.
18493: The wide river Isen flows past at the eastern end of the valley. The water is a bit murky here, as silt and sand deposited along its bed are turned up by the deeper currents. A small amount of greenery clings to the low banks of the river. The water flows on southwards, deep and strong.
18494: The river floats by, wide and deep, in a straight line from north to south. The sandy riverbed along the bottom can be seen, through the deep and strongly flowing water. Small ferns and young striplings have taken root here along the riverbank, cherishing the cold water.
18495: The water is crystal clear and chill to the touch. Several stone slabs line the sandy river bottom deep below the surface of Isen. The water flows wide and deep here, at a gentle speed but an unforgiving force. A massive line of mountains lies along the eastern bank, offering little foothold for both plants and travellers.
18496: The Isen continues on southwards, the fast flowing water from the north slows down as it approaches a great bend in the route. Rippling a soft murmur, the fresh mountain water pass out of the valley of Isengard not far to the south. The arms of the Misty Mountains nearly meet further south, the gap being the only exit from Nan Curunir.
18497: A worm is here slithering around.

The stony ground from the south ends abruptly in an outcrop of rock. The jagged edge of the outcrop overhangs the river Isen. The river flows from the north, past this outcrop and continues south, just west of here. Along the far bank the paved roadway to Isengard lies, leading north alongside the river. The climb down to the water is tricky from here; the rocks look wet and slippery. The horizon is filled with mountain peaks, in all directions except due south.
18498: Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

Largely brown and thinning, the grass gradually gives way to stones that form a sharp hillside to the east. Small patches of buttercups provide the only bright colours as far as the eye can see. The sharp and rocky banks of the River Isen make travel to the west treacherous while to the southeast lie flat, grassy plains.
18499:
A salmon swims here.
A trout swims here.

The water moves swiftly along the river Isen, on its way south, out of the valley. A paved road at its western shore and steep mountain walls not far from the eastern shore, other than that, the plains stretch away across the valley, unhindered. The river has a fresh, wholesome appearance, and the relentless force of the water makes a loud noise. The shallow western bank is easily accessible from the water, but to ascend the eastern bank would mean scrambling up the wet slippery rocks.
18500: The river Isen continues along slowly here, forming the eastern border of the rocky plains and the road to Isengard. At this point, the river makes a soft turn in its course from east to south. The water is cold and clear, seeming to home a great variety of fish.
18501: Soft Bend in the Road to Isengard

The Numenorean designed military road appears to be in excellent condition. Wide and paved, the roadway follows the course of the Isen on its western bank, turning slightly here as the river bends. Not far to the south the road and river pass through the arms of the mountains and leave the valley.
18502:
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

The well-travelled and well-tended road to Isengard, follows the swift flow of the Isen, on its west bank. The military road is wide and paved with great stones, having been laid with careful design by the Numenorean crafters of old. Here, the roadway leads from north to south, where it passes through the arms of the mountains and leaves the valley.
18503: The wide, flat surface of the Numenorean-built roadway is in excellent condition, having been maintained over the centuries by the troops garrisoned inside the fortress of Isengard. The road runs in a straight line from north to south, the cold flow of the river Isen on its eastern side.
18504: A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

A thin layer of gravel and small stones cover the parched plain like a grey mantle. Larger rocks lie scattered about, a constant annoyance to an inattentive traveller, with their sharp edges and uneven surfaces. To the east, the dry landscape intersects with the paved roadway that runs from Isengard to the Gap of Rohan.
18505: The chaotic arrangement of broken boulders and gravel continues in all directions along the parched plain. Far away on the horizon, the outline of the jagged Misty Mountains can be seen. Two arms from the main range to the north split away, surrounding the valley on its eastern and western sides. A dry wind stirs up eddies of dust and stinging, gritty sand in the air.
18506:
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The flat terrain beneath the grey mantle of gritty sand and rock appears to consist of a table of solid rock. To the southwest, a huge outcropping of granite can be seen in the middle of the wasteland. To the southeast, you can just make out the dark line of a road - the road to Isengard.
18507: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The rocky terrain, barren and dry, seems to come to an end in the east, as it intersects with the paved road to Isengard. The ground here is littered with loose gravel and small rocks, and you can barely make out the tracks of men and horses that have deviated from the roadway.
18508: The Numenorean designed roadway seems to have shouldered the centuries well. Wide and paved with great stones, the road leads from the northeast to the south, following the flow of the river Isen that lies just to the east. The valley here is surrounded on all sides but south with the vastness of the mountains, looming on the near horizon.
18509: The rocky mantle of this parched plateau seems to dwindle to the east as it approaches the road to Isengard. Not far to the northwest, you see a huge grey block of stone, apparently rammed into the ground by an incalculable force. The terrain here is littered with loose gravel and broken boulders.
18510: A thin, grey layer of stones and gravel would make this terrain a fair path to travel, even in wet weather, although larger piles of fragmented boulders could easily trip the inattentive traveller. To the southeast, the brutal landscape collides with the paved roadway to Isengard.
18511: This great roadway was laid down many years ago, by the great craftsmen of Gondor. The paving stones that form it seem to have been recently reset in parts, and it appears to be none the worse for its great age. Between the spaces lining the great stones you see what appears to be fragments of bone, having changed from grey to brown with time.
18512:
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.
A snake slithers towards you.

The rocky riverbank to the east of the roadway is close, as the road to Isengard lies next to the waters of the Isen. Large, flat slabs of rock rise sharply from the rippling surface. The road bends slightly away from the Isen southwards, making its way around a brick watch-tower.
18513: A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

The road makes a soft turn from south to east, following the course of the Isen, which flows swiftly, just east of the pavestones. The mighty Numenorean architectural design remains in excellent condition; the road is wide and paved, allowing for swift movement of legions from Isengard in times of war.
18514: The wide and paved roadway marches directly north and south here, its stony surface worn by time but remaining in excellent condition. Afar in the north a ring of encircling walls running from an outcrop of rock can be seen, and the black pinnacle of Orthanc standing starkly against the sky in its centre. Just to the east, down a sharp bank, flows the course of the Isen, its far bank steep and unclimbable.
18515: Bend in the Road to Isengard

The wide roadway remains in excellent condition, its Numenorean design having been maintained over the centuries. It follows the curve of the flowing Isen, running for many miles to the valley opening far to the south. The road ends west of here, at the gates of Isengard. A fortress whose outer defence can be seen not far away to the northwest: a giant ring thrust out from the mountains themselves, with a central tower like a black spike.
18516: The wide, paved road runs through the gates of Isengard from the north, leading away through the valley to the southeast. Immediately south of the gates it bends away slightly to the east, passing through a gap in the ancient dike spanning across the valley. The Numenorean-designed road appears to have been maintained over the years, still well paved with not a blade of grass visible between the stones.
18517: A small black cricket is here, chirping loudly.

The high hills are covered with serrated, black basalt rock formations, making travel much more difficult and dangerous. From the east, you can hear the faint sound of falling water. To the west lie the stone walls of Isengard, a defensive ring over a mile from edge to edge. At the ring's centre the tower of Orthanc can be seen, a tower made of four giant peaks of stone.
18518: The clear water cascades over a fall of stones into this azure pool, throwing pearls of spray into the air and singing a soft murmuring song. The water is quite cold and quite shallow, the bottom can be seen just beneath beneath the surface, with ripples widening out from the cascade.
18519: A wide river runs through the valle, from the mountains further north. Water rushes down in a great fury of spray and foam in a deep hollow. The cold water is clear, but often obscured by the turbulent flow. The river calms downstream, southwards. The west bank is rather steep and would require some effort to scale, while the eastern mountain wall is utterly impossible to climb.
18520:
A salmon swims here.
A salmon swims here.

The river flows steadily southwards, gently along the mountainside and the road to Isengard, on each side of the water. The water is cold to the touch, and fishes can be seen through the clear water. The western riverbank, up to the road, is quite steep and the sand offers no grip.
18521: The small platform slopes very steeply to the east, and the footing consists of slippery and wet moss, growing on a layer of small pebbles. High above you see a mountain peak rising sharply into the sky. It is but one of a giant line of heights that stretches north for countless hundreds of miles.
18522: A short evergreen plant, with slightly bluish needles, grows here.

A sparkling spring, seemingly one of the few sources of water in this barren and stony highland, drops down a series of small falls from the north and through this small creek. South it flows through a series of large fallen boulders and then falls over the lip of a short waterfall.
18523: The highest peak overlooking the valley, this is but a mere doorstop compared to the mountains you can see further north. Falling away beneath your feet in a vast semi-circle are steep cliffs and sheer overhangs. Far below you, the valley of Nan Curunir spreads out. The Road to Isengard, only a faint and dark ribbon on the plain, stretches on away further to the south.
18524:
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

The rocky terrain is littered with small rocks and broken boulders. A deep dike lies to the north, worn by wind and weather. On the far side of the old defensive line lies the ring wall of Isengard, and behind them the tower of Orthanc, hundreds of feet high. To the east, the paved roadway along the river Isen lies, while the western horizon is parted in two by a looming, ancient, dead tree.
18525: Low, jagged rock formations jut sharply from the flat surface of the withered valley. Scattered amongst the piles of broken boulders, black thickets of tangled thorn-bushes fight for survival in the harsh elements of this once lush valley. To the north the land gains altitude swiftly, sweeping far up above the stony plateau in mountainous heights. On the outcrop from one such height lies the ring of Isengard, a vast fortress. A small house of stone stands against the wall. To the south the land falls away into an ancient dike, crumbled but still an obstacle to movement.
18526: The rocky valley base is scattered with a random arrangement of small, twisted bushes, the dry wind whistling through their thorny, bare branches. The dusty earth is littered with countless dark rocks and drifting swathes of gritty, grey dust. The land gently rises to the north, before being broken by a line of mountains. South is the remnants of a wall and dike, which once ran for miles west-east, signifying the outer border of Isengard's control.
18527: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The rocky plateau is dry and cracked, littered with the strange formations of wind-carved sandstone and piles of granite boulders. One such nearby pile has tumbled, or been forced over, spilling across the earth. Mountains dominate the entire horizon, rising sheer and encircling the valley in their arms.
18528: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The dry plain continues in all directions, dotted with loose rocks and the rare twisted shrub or wiry clump of browned grass. At the base of a large granite rock, a jumbled collection of sun-bleached bones lie, humanoid in shape, but whether from man, elf or orc no one can tell. Far to the west a wall of mountains rising sharply up from the rocky valley can be seen.
18529: The land is higher here, compared to the plains in the east. Bushes and smaller trees grow in the dry earth between the rocks and boulders. A house built of stone stands firmly down beyond the mild slope to the north while the trees grow more abundantly west of here.
18530: A huge and lonely oak tree once grew here but now is only a black and dried shadow of its former glory - appearing as a strange and horrific pillar rising from the stony plain. The ground here is littered with clay-hued boulders dug up from the old dike to the north. The land appears utterly parched as if from long periods of drought, although rain must fall here from the mountains frequently.
18531: The rocky plateau is cracked and barren, littered with the debris from broken granite boulders and the husks of dead grasses. Two dark figures loom on the horizon; to the east stands the black shadow of a huge tree, while far to the northeast you can see the high, spiked peaks of the tower of Orthanc, the centre of the sheer-walled ring of Isengard. Just north, the crumbled remnants of a once lengthy dike lie, now little of an obstruction to movement.
18532: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The barren wasteland marches on in every direction, only broken by a deep and wide dike dug across the valley just south of here. Sand and gritty brown earth cling to every available surface and loose stones and gravel lies in heaps everywhere. Mountains surround the valley completely, ridges and peaks growing upwards in the distance.
18533: Some Trees on the Barren Flats

Near the edge of the barren, rocky valley, a couple of small, black-barked trees jut sharply from the hard-packed earth. A dry wind whistle through their twisted, barren branches. Strangely formed sandstone outcroppings dot the landscape, and a dense mass of trees occupy the slopes rising towards the mountains in the west.
18534:
A heavy desk, made of solid oak, stands here.
A large bookshelf sits against the wall.
On the bookshelf, there are two pieces of paper.
An old sage, clad in white, is standing here.
An Isengard guard is standing here, alert for trouble-makers.
An Isengard guard is standing here, alert for trouble-makers.
An Isengard guard is standing here, alert for trouble-makers.
An Isengard guard is standing here, alert for trouble-makers.

The entrance of the guardpost consists of a square room, with doors in two of its four walls. The front door, to the south, is a thick wooden door, as is the door in the north wall. The house is built of stone and lies directly to the large wall surrounding Isengard, with the ring wall as the room's eastern wall. A desk and a bookcase stand towards the eastern wall, while a passage in the opposite wall leads into another room.
18536: A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

The rocky plateau continues, littered with sandstone rock formations and crumbling boulders. The landscape appears much like the bottom of some vast ocean, long since drained, leaving only the rocky residue that collects on the floor. Rising up to the north and west, and slightly further to the east, the mountain walls towers above.
18537: An old weathered scarecrow is planted firmly in the ground here.

In contrast to the barren areas nearby, this part of the valley is rich with nourished plant life. A large field of wheat and grains grows here, in neat rows and plenty of water. Sharp sounds of insects can be heard from somewhere within the field. Boxed in by steep mountain walls, the field continues westwards, while rocks and bushes occupy the plains to the south.
18538:
A bale of wheat is lying here.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

An abundant field of wheat grows at the foot of the mountain. The healthy grain sways in the chilly wind, like a yellow sea. A flat, featureless mountain wall stops the field from growing northwards, while neat, dug ditches irrigates the crop from the southwest. The field continues in all other directions.
18539:
Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.
A hungry warg stands here, sniffing around for flesh.
A black crow flies low to the ground here, looking for carrion to eat.

Piles of rocks and stones lie scattered on the plain, methodically picked up and removed. Several ditches has been dug, in square formations, to irrigate the field that will grow here in the coming season. The chilly wind reminds of the harsh environment and the high mountain peaks tower in the horizon.
18540:
An old weathered scarecrow is planted firmly in the ground here.
A cow stands here, chewing her cud.
A tall muscular farmer stands here, working hard.

Cornered by towering mountains, wheat grows in neat rows in the large field. The field's healthy grains sway in the cold wind, catching the eye. Small bugs can be seen in the rich growth between the yellow stalks. A house is built by the western mountainside, with a pair of large barn-doors facing the field in this direction.
18541:
A wooden, two-wheeled cart stands here.
A cow stands here, chewing her cud.
A cow stands here, chewing her cud.

A small barn stands erected at the foot of the mountainside. Three of the walls are built out of stone, while the west-most wall is the mountain itself. The ceiling is low and made of thatch. The air is dry and stale, smelling of livestock. Two large wooden barn doors are built in the eastern wall, and a small door in the south leads further into the house. Most of the space is used for storing and drying hay and wheat, but a couple of stalls for cows or horses are built near the larger doors.
18542: A simple house, made out of the most abundant building material nearby; stone. The room is dark; its thatched roof blocks out any light and the windows are small. Few things occupy the room, a table, benches, and various cupboards. A small door in the northern wall, an open doorway to the west, leading further into the house, and a small window livens up the monotonous walls.
18543:
A stove stands against one wall here.
A small loyal cat is here.
The farmer's wife is bustling busily around.

This is a dark room with stone walls and a thatched roof. The floor is laid with flat rocks of various sizes. A large stove lights up and occupies the entire northern wall and a large, sturdy table fills most of the room. The walls are hung with pots and pans, whisks and utensils.
18544: The mountain walls rise straight up to the northwest and the land slopes quite steeply eastwards. The woods are sparse and show little new growth in the dry earth. The harsh climate of sun and wind, rain and snow, clouds and thunder draws away all nurture from the soil. The standing trees are old, with no or little greenery.
18545: Rocky Plain in Front of a Small House
A circular stone well has been built here.

The plateau continues from the southeast and meets the irrigated fields in the north. Framed in by steep mountain walls a farm stands against the western rockface. Tracks of carts and horses show in the dirt and dust, leading to and from the houses. The farm's main building lies directly to the west.
18546:
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

The ground slopes quite steeply here, from the mountains in the west, down to the plateau to the east. A high mountain ridge makes passage to the south impossible. Trees grow thinly spaced out, savouring the water of a small rivulet flowing down the slope. The soil looks poor, dry and full of sharp rocks and large boulders.
18547:
A sturdy peg for hanging armour from is on the wall.
A weapons rack stands against the wall.
An Isengard guard is standing here, alert for trouble-makers.
An Isengard guard is standing here, alert for trouble-makers.

The square room is filled with beds, in straight rows. The beds are neatly made, ready for inspection. The bare stone walls appears clean and smooth. A rack for weapons and several pegs for hanging armour stand near the door in the east wall. The floor is minutely swept and not a single piece of dust or spider web can be seen.
18548:
Put the Mountain Troll is standing here watching Nan Curunir.
Taara the Mountain Troll (TT) is standing here.
Glacius the Black Numenorean (GG), wielding a steel-tipped spear, is standing here.

Set in stone, with large window frames in all direction, this watchtower has been built on top of the guardhouse. The panoramic view from here is impressive, but somewhat limited by the mountains. The floor is made of wood, and a ladder connects to the bottom floor, through an open hatch.
18549:
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.
A mountain goat is here, jumping from cliff to cliff.

The slope up from the plain rises steeply, meeting the mountain wall. Water pours and drips down along the cliff face, into the ground. The water gathers into a small rivulet and continues down the slope. Several large and robust trees grow here, protected from the winds and harsh climate by the high mountains.
18550:
A high and strong tree, scarred by axes, stands here.
A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.

In lee of the towering mountain wall, deep in a crevice, a small spring sets forth. Water is gently flowing from below, clear and cold. Onwards, downwards and northwards, between rocks and roots, through moss and lichen, below fern and tree, it flows. The vegetation drinks from the pure water, sheltered by the mountains, blessed with sun. The place almost shines with purity.
18551: At the mountain offshoot, the most narrow point of the valley, a deep dike has been dug. With walls too steep to scale, the bottom deeper than the tallest of trolls, wider than any horse can jump, it effectively divides the plains into two parts: north of it and south of it. Westwards, where the dike meets the mountain, the wall is less steep, allowing passage to the south.
18552: Debris at the Bottom of a Dike

The dike continues to the east and west, deep down below the plains. The walls are high, steep and effectively hinder any passage to the north or south. Several large boulders lie on the dike's floor, together with heaps of gravel, stones, broken bits of metal and remains of dead animals. The high walls hide most of the sky, but parts of it can be seen straight up.
18553: A diamond-back rattlesnake is coiled here, ready to strike.

A dike dug deep through the plains passes through the brown dirt while bending slightly, going from west and continuing to the northeast. The sharp edges of the plain above create long and deep dark shadows. Together with the large number of boulders, the area is filled with potholes and crevices. The wall to the east is firm and steep while the southern wall is slanting slightly, with several hand and footholds.
18554: Dug deep, below the plains, a dike spans the Nan Curunir from west to east. Grey rocks and stones can be seen among the otherwise brown earth and dirt along the walls of the dike. The northern wall is merely slanting, with several hand and footholds it forms a convenient way in or out of the dike, while the western and the south-eastern are sufficiently steep to prevent all scaling attempts.
18555: The dike continues along the latitude, with bare smooth walls on both sides. With walls too high and unstructured to scale, a gap too wide for even horses to jump, it is a formidable obstruction for any would-be invaders of the valley. The ground of the dike is dry, with several uneven boulders lying around, unwanted in the fields above.
18557: The dike is deep with smooth earth walls. Several rocks stick out through the surface, but none large enough to use as foothold. The ground between the walls is strewn with debris, making it hard to walk around unencumbered. The passage continues westwards. The south wall is less steep than the others, permitting an easy climb in and out of the trench.
18558:
The corpse of a Man lies in the dust.
A small flask has been left here on the ground.
A shortbow has been left here.
A quiver lies on the ground.
A plain hood lies on the ground.
There is a water skin lying on the ground.
A small hunting knife lies on the ground.
A plain shirt is on the ground.
A pair of thin leather gloves are lying here.
A bear cub is here, looking around for something to play with.
A bear cub is here, looking around for something to play with.

The rocky ceiling of the cavern has collapsed in places, leaving large heaps of broken granite and sandstone. The cold floor beneath your feet is littered with stony debris, sand, and bones from various creatures. The only apparent exit lies back towards the south, where the cavern seems to widen out, allowing more passage of air.
18559: A big cavebear is padding around here.

The steep walls of the narrow crevice rise up close upon either side, obscuring the sky overhead from view. To the north the crack comes to a swift and stony end, while the cliffs gently separate to the south, allowing more light and fresh air into the dark crevice. Large rocky formations and loose scree sliding underfoot hinders your movement here. Lying amidst the boulders is a collection of bare and broken bones.
18560: A brass lantern has been set on the ground.

The crevice cuts a deep, dark wound through the rocky plains. Widest at this point, the crack narrows both north and south. Movement is difficult across the stony floor of the crevice, as loose stones slide underfoot and fallen boulders lie strewn about. The sandstone cliffs climb high on either side, sheltering both your passage and any clear view of the surrounding terrain.
18561: Earth movements eons ago opened up a large crack in the plains. The edges are worn and the bottom is sloping slightly downwards to the north. Loose sand and gravel lies between boulders and rocky outcroppings. The crack grows wider and delves deeper below the surface of the rocky plains to the north. To the south, the crevice comes to a quick and shallow halt.
18562: Stunted stalks of brown grass impede progress throughout the area. A small stand of ash-leaved maple trees provides little shelter from the elements. To the south, a barely discernible trail meanders across the lowlands while to the east the greenish-brown prairies stretch for miles.
18563: A small cluster of clover grows here.

Copious clover coats the plains alongside a small trail jutting to the south and west. Several long-discarded cairns standing inches off the ground dot the landscape alongside the road. The mighty River Isen provides the only break to the widespread grassland dominating the area.
18564: Stretching several leagues to the north and east, the trail lies sprinkled with rubble from unremitting use and ill-care. Beside the road lie diminutive collections of pebbles washed aside by downpours over time. The road slopes gently to the south and northeast where it meets the verdant plains.
18565: Rough grass coats the floor of this minor dale formed by a rugged road to the north and east as well as the beginning of a lengthy ridge to the west. A few blackberry bushes grow interspersed among the coarse grass. The harsh grassland continues to the south.
18566: Thriving grass coats the floor of the valley. Mixed in the midst of the grass are tiny plants with round, smooth stems and a woody root. To the west lie weedy grasslands with thinning grass littered by rocks. In contrast, lush grass with abundant shrubbery sits atop the prairie to the north. The pleasant grassland ends abruptly to the south, becoming stony terrain.
18567: Stiff and rugged bluebunch wheatgrass underfoot slows any traveler throughout this area. However, the bristly grass and other tough weeds present easier terrain than the harsh, craggy rocks to the west. Pleasant grassland to the east provides a stark contrast to the rough terrain in the north and west.
18568: Short, rough crabgrass coats the floor of the vale here. In numerous places, bedrock pushes its way through the grass. The ground slopes sharply to the west down to a rocky dip on the plains. In the south, several bunches of three-foot high bushes stand atop a luscious green grass while in the east the green grass dominates the landscape as far as the eye can see.
18569: The various thick leaves of several wild plants give this area a sweet smell. Small insects buzz quietly, lured by sugary nectar secreted by the vegetation. Beneath the variety of plants, rough grass lines the slope descending from a ridge to the west. In the south, small clumps of wheat grass lie huddled together while to the east sit more gently rolling, flat grasslands.
18570:
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.
A cute rabbit is here.
A cute rabbit is here.

The fertile soil allows the growth of dense meadows. The thick, green grass provides a cushion for one's feet and excellent nourishment for herbivores that inhabit the surrounding grasslands. To the south, the grassland ends suddenly in a wall of impassable thickets. A small village, seemingly abandoned, is scarcely visible to the east.
18571:
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.
A cute rabbit is here.
A cute rabbit is here.

Beautiful grass coupled with a large quantity of wild flowers smother the floor of the prairie. A small incline to the west leads up to more grassland while the prairie leads gently down a slope to the north to more lush grass and flora. Impenetrable brush blocks the way southward. Similarly, the prairie ends abruptly to the east as a small village, seemingly deserted, begins.
18572:
A mass of dark green leaves clings to a wall.
A circular stone well has been built here.

The remains of a once-flourishing village lie apparently abandoned here. A stone well, its sides worn smooth over time, stands in the centre of the village, the only functioning component of the forsaken village. The buildings provide a clear sign of the vacant nature of the settlement as entire boards are missing from the walls of the most structures and only a handful of glass panes remain in windows. In some places, plants grow on the wooden walls while in other places holes puncture the buildings.
18573: Ubiquitous weeds sprout from the compacted earth here. At one time, this courtyard served as the hub of activity for the farmstead. Beyond the doorway to the north, stalls remain visible while to the south a small entrance leads to a utility building. The courtyard extends westward where a small well sits in the centre of the square. Finally, the land to the east served as grazing lands for the animals housed in the small barn to the north.
18574:
A large shrub grows here, its branches loosely spreading.
On the shrub, there are two piles of cherries.

Thick shrubs of all shapes and sizes dominate the countryside. So dense is the vegetation that it is quite possible not a single inch of the ground beneath ever feels the touch of sunlight. To the south the coverage is so complete that it would make it impossible for any new seedlings to sprout through. Northeast of here a a brown trail provides a sharp contrast to this sea of green and a very faint footpath seems to in one direction lead north from here and then turn east towards that trail, and in the other head towards a village seen to the west.
18575:
A large thorny branched shrub is growing here.
On the shrub, there are a number of blackberries.

Countless shrubs lie amalgamated among the rolling meads of grass. The branching, oval stems of one shrub eventually give way to notched, heart-shaped leaves covered with grey hair. Another bush with large elliptical leaves on branched stems possesses yellow, succulent berries. To the south the underbrush thickens to a point making passage in that direction impossible.
18576: Thriving grasses dominate the landscape. In some places, the grass hinders passage due to its height and density. A minor bridge crossing a gully dominates the northern horizon. The land slopes down gently to a shrub-filled glen in the west and leads upwards to a trail passing in the east.
18577: A large number of stones and clumps of weeds litter the remnants of what was once the surface of a road. A steep, rocky cliff forces the abrupt end of the trail to the south. The remains of a small camp show the possible destination of the trail. A collection of rocks covered by moss and other weeds form a small circle at the end of the trail, suggesting the location of a campfire in the past.
18578: A large mother hawk is here looking for a prey to feed her young.

The grasses of the rolling meadow stand several feet tall in most places. An occasional part in the high grass reveals a location where some creature passed. Similarly flourishing grasslands surround the area, with the exception of a large yellow patch of grass in the north. A small trail to the west ends when it meets a steep precipice in the south.
18579: Tall shoots of grass surrounded by thick patches of weed cover the flat ground. The only barren areas of the grass-covered land are some ancient flats of rock pushing from the ground. Remains of a long since abandoned campfire can be seen nearby on one of the rocky flats. Far in the east the level grasslands turn into rows of low hills.
18580:
A man's-waist high evergreen shrub grows here, with bright green branches.
A snake slithers towards you.
A snake slithers towards you.
A black snake, with red markings, is lying here.

The rolling golden-green lands grow verdant with tall and coarse grass. Some slender trees grow nearby swaying back and forth as if they were unsure of their place in the grassy landscape. Small bushes and shrubs dot the hilly grass-covered land. The grasslands become more level to the west and continue in steady waves in other directions.
18581: Tall and coarse grass covers the rolling lands. Far to the northeast the lands turn into bleak marshy plains. A serpentine stream can be seen cutting across the plains in the east. A particularly lush tract of land, overgrown with grasses and shrubs, lies before the stream. The rolling grasslands span far to the west and north.
18582: Tall and coarse grass, sometimes as high as three feet, covers the moist ground of this tract of land. Some flowers, mostly blue and violet, grow amidst the grasses. A stream slowly makes its way across the lands in the east. The part of the stream in the east looks shallow and fordable. To the north the lands become marshy and covered with mist while to the west the grassy rolling plains continue far to the horizon.
18583:
A bass swims here.
A sparrow is flapping around on the ground.
A snake slithers towards you.

Here the stream running from the north becomes shallow and weak as if it was tired from its passage through the marsh. To the west, the land is overgrown with grasses and low-lying bushes while to the east level, grassy plains stretch themselves as far as one can see. To the south the stream quickly becomes deeper and swifter again as it continues its way into the plains of Rohan.
18584: In the west, the waters of the stream running from the north have become shallow and the stream can be forded. To the south, the stream quickly becomes deeper and swifter again as it runs towards the grassy plains of Rohan. A mist-covered marshland lies to the north while in the east the ground gently slopes into verdant, grassy lowlands.
18585: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

The verdant lowlands, covered with a carpet of tall grass, expand to the north, where they gradually rise to the plains above. A long and gentle treeless slope, dotted with red flowers, rises in the east. The air down in the vale is moist and rich with the fragrance of the grasslands. Glimmering spots of blue shine through the grasses, where puddles of water have formed.
18586: From the verdant lowlands in the west the land climbs up to the wind-beaten plains in the east, a gentle treeless slope, furrowed with folds and gullies. Some white and purple flowers dot the grassy slope. A gust of wind sweeping across the plains carries the faint scent of the grassy meadows. The grassy plains of the Rohirrim stretch away to the horizon.
18587:
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.
A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

The empty wind-beaten lands grow scarce with grass, the short turf breaking away in some places, exposing the barren, heavily textured soil. The wide grey-green plains stretch far to the southerly lands of the realm of Rohan. To the north and west the ground slopes down to the plains below, gradually turning into verdant grasslands.
18588: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Sparse grasses, short and needle-like, grow in patches scattered across the windy plains. The short turf has withdrawn in places to reveal the coarse soil underneath. The wind-beaten lands spread out to the southerly lands of the realm of Rohan while to the north the lands become more verdant with green slopes and waves of grass.
18589: Nothing but the short needle-like grass grows on this long wind-beaten slope. The ground steadily climbs upwards from the grassy expanse in the north to the windy plains in the south. Far to the north the eaves of the great forest can be seen, a distant shadow at the feet of the Misty Mountains.
18590: Tufts of tall yellow-green grass sprout from the short turf between strips of barren land that reveal the coarse soil underneath. Some white poppies grow amidst the patches of grass. The grasslands expand to the north towards the distant forest while to the south the land gradually climbs towards the wind-beaten plains.
18591:
A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.
A restless rabbit bounces around.

The grassy land has been bruised in a great circle. Many heavy feet have beaten the land and turf has been torn and grass been trampled. At the centre of the ring lie charred remains of a tree torn from the ground. Tracks lead out from the ring north-westwards, towards the mountains that lies ten or more leagues away. To the south, the level grasslands reach far to the horizon.
18592: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Patches of short needle-like grass grow on the barren dusty ground of the wide plains. Tufts of taller grass sprout between the patches scattered across the plains. In spots, the grass has withdrawn to expose the barren textured soil. To the north some overgrown ruins sit amidst the grasses. The wide plains spread out in every direction.
18593: A pile of stones and rotting planks, overgrown with grasses, sit at the centre of a dusty clearing, all that is left of a building that once stood here. The house must have been burned down, judging by the blackened stones and few charred remains of wood. A barely noticeable path, overgrown by weeds, leads northwards to a wide field of golden-yellow hay. The grasslands stretch away to the south and west.
18594: A worm is here slithering around.

Wide rows of hay stand tall in a field of pale gold, swaying to and fro when a gust of wind blows from the plains. The thick fragrance of hay mingles with the scent of the surrounding grasslands. Barely noticeable amidst the tall hay, remains of a wooden barn lie in a decaying pile, overgrown with grasses and weeds. The field of hay expands to the north.
18595: Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.

Countless wildflowers grow amidst the flowing rows of tall grass. Flowers of every imaginable colour can be seen dotting the moist meadows. These colourful fields seem to stretch on for miles to the east, while to the south the lands get more plain again. The land slopes slightly in the east to a verdant flower filled valley.
18679:
A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.
A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The verdant green valley floor is painted in a variety of colours with countless flowers. Some bushes grow scattered on the steep hillsides. A small pond of sparkling clear water has formed at the far end of the valley, providing refreshing water to the wildlife and the occasional traveller. Some boulders near the pond provide a good resting place for the weary.
18680:
A black snake, with red markings, is lying here.
A snake slithers towards you.
A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.

As the moist flower-clad meadows grow lush in a line of downs ahead, the grassy lands continue in endless waves of green. In the west the land slopes steeply to a verdant, colourful valley. Down in the valley a glimmering pond can be seen. To the east the lands turn into marshy, bleak plains. A stream can be seen cutting across the country.
18681: The miry lands are predominated by sedges and cattails. Where the cover of the mist floating above the marsh breaks away, the wet, soft and treacherous ground can be seen. The yielding land makes travelling slow and often precarious. A serpentine stream cuts through the marsh in the east while to the west the marsh gradually turns into verdant meadows and rolling grasslands.
18682: A rabbit is here eyeing your presence warily.

In places where the veil of mist breaks away, the treacherous mire underneath can be seen. Numerous cattails with their brown furry heads sway silently above the cover of the mist. The progress through the marsh is precarious and soon becomes tiresome. To the west the mist gradually thins out and the marsh turns into rolling grasslands.
18683: In the east the grasslands slowly descend to marshy plains where a silvery stream can be seen cutting across the country. The treeless golden-green slopes and downs continue in other directions in sinuous waves of grass. Far to the southwest a particularly verdant and flourishing valley can be seen; the glimmering waters of a pond at the nearest end of the valley attracting animals and wanderers alike.
18684: Tall coarse grass grows in every direction on undulating hills and valleys. Only an occasional bush or a solitary tree break the monotony of the seemingly never ending waves of grass. Far to the west and north the landscape slowly turns into level plains while the eastern and southern horizons are predominated by the hilly landscape. In the south the land abruptly slopes down into a verdant flower-clad valley.
18685: A nightingale is here, chirping a sweet melody.

The broad expanse of grassland continues in all directions as far as the eye can see. The treeless monotony of the grasslands is broken by a rising hillock to the north. Far beyond it glimmers the white head of Methedras, the last peak of the Misty Mountains. Some fresh animal droppings speak of the presence of wildlife in these plains. Far to the east the level lands turn into undulating hills and valleys.
18686: Although not incredibly high, this small, grassy mound offers the best view of the surrounding countryside. Rolling plains predominate the landscape to the east, south, and west. Far to the east, a wide river cuts north to south across the undulating meads. A small trail traverses across the southwestern horizon. To the north sits a small, tree-covered hillock providing a safe habitat for songbirds and small animals.
18687:
The corpse of a powerful lioness is lying here.
The corpse of a powerful lioness is lying here.
The corpse of a dark-maned lion is lying here.
The corpse of a fuzzy little lion cub is lying here.
The corpse of a fuzzy little lion cub is lying here.
The corpse of a fuzzy little lion cub is lying here.
A fuzzy little lion cub is sleeping here.
A fuzzy little lion cub is sleeping here.
A powerful lioness is sleeping here.
A powerful lioness is sleeping here.
A dark-maned lion is sleeping here.
A snake slithers towards you.

Steep, rocky walls surround the area to the east and west. Large boulders and loose rocks that crumbled in the north complete the formation of an unusual gorge on the grassland floor. The gradient of the ravine makes passage to the east, west, or south somewhat difficult. Padded earth lined with fur coats one corner of the enclosure. Fresh air seems to sneak through holes in the fallen rock to the north.
18688: A large beautiful rose bush is blooming here.

Atop the green grasses of the prairie stand several luxurious bushes of wild roses. When in bloom, the red roses provide a sharp contrast to the green so ubiquitous throughout the area. Far to the northeast and east, rolling fields of grass dominate the landscape while a small trail cuts across the western horizon. Immediately east is a sharp drop into a small, but steep ravine.
18689: A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

Sloping downward slightly as it approaches from the west, the trail becomes rougher as it stretches southward. The trail narrows slightly in order to bend around a small cluster of oak trees. Beyond a group of bushes to the east, the green plains stretch as far as the eye can see. More grassland dominates the landscape to the southwest.
18690: Ruts and stones are commonplace atop the surface of the roadway. The condition of the road seems comparable to the east while in the north it improves at the intersection of several pathways. Beside the trail stand several large bushes. The pointed shrubs, standing over three feet tall, possess leafy, smooth stems and fuzzy, green leaves.
18691: With the exception of a few lone maple trees standing atop the prairie, the plains here are dominated by soft, dense grass. Gentle on the feet, the grass provides ample nourishment for the numerous animals that live in these parts. Bordered on the north and east by a small trail, the rich grassland continues on to the south and west.
18692: Loose gravel, accumulated over years, covers the ground and makes footing shaky here. Pebbles treacherously litter a small slope leading down from the road to the north. The prairie to the south and west appears far less dangerous and contains an abundance of magnificent, green grass.
18693: In addition to bountiful grass, a single type of shrub marks the ground of the prairie here. With dark-green leaves paired in groups of two to six, the tubular flowers possess thick stems that are hairy near the base. To the south, the plains end abruptly as they dip sharply to an austere countryside while to the north the fields are topped by a group of alder trees.
18694: Undersized, lightly serrated leaves scratch at anything near the ground here. Growing from small bushes of a light-coloured, rod-like plant, the leaves are more of a nuisance than an impediment. In addition to their abrasive leaves, the plants fill the area with a pleasant aroma. Similar scrub brush and pleasant grass surround the immediate area.
18695: A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The lobed, prickly-edged leaves of the milk thistle dominate the area. Streaked with conspicuous white veins, the leaves present a stark contrast to the green grass on which they grow. In the distance to the north runs a small road. Further beyond the road lies more grassland and some small foothills on the northern horizon.
18696: A colossal tree, its trunk as wide as a small cottage, stands here.

An isolated group of trees sits atop the yellow-green grass of the prairie, offering a meager amount of shade during the day. Diminutive tracks in the soil reveal that tiny animals occasionally gather here. Beautiful grassland surrounds this small group of trees on all sides with a road cutting through the prairie to the north.
18697: Bending northwards and eastward, the trail cuts diagonally across the plains. Although not in perfect condition, the road appears well maintained and well travelled. Beside the road lies an assortment of tiny wildflowers. Amethyst- purple sego lilies and the tube-like petals of a wild orange flower provide a splash of colour to the dull brown and green hues that dominate this area.
18698: Traversing the land between rolling plains, the trail can easily be followed as it runs east to west. Other than an occasional rut or hollow, probably caused by a small animal, the pathway remains relatively flat and straight. In the distance in both the east and west, the trail appears to bend north and south, respectively. To the north lies a field of clover while to the south lies gentle, wavy grass.
18699: A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

Tracks of hooves and other beasts suggest the route here is well travelled. The road splits in three directions as the trails heading north and south merge with a road approaching from the west. To the east lies fertile, golden-green grass. Similar grassland can be seen bordering the roads to the south and north.
18700: With the exception of green fields to the east, a collection of roads meets in the west and forms a border in all directions. The ground slopes down slightly from the trail in the south, west, and north, leaving this area littered with small stones that were washed down the inclines over time by rain and snow. Amidst the collection of rocks, clumps of grass poke their heads up reaching for the sky.
18701:
A small mushroom grows nearby.
A small mushroom grows nearby.

Among the thinning grass lay an assortment of wild mushrooms. The cream-colour stems of the mushrooms slowly give way to a tinged pale pinkish top. Sticky to touch, the mushroom tops possess a mild odour barely noticeable to passersby. On the distant horizon in the north, west, and south, a rough trail cuts across the grassy prairie.
18702: Copious grass conceals the earthen floor of the vale. Similar to the grasslands in the north, small plants blend among the grass. A patch of auburn mushrooms spots the prairie in the west while the grass to the east runs up to a small knoll topped by a ring of trees. To the south, loose rocks form a stony outcropping atop the prairie.
18703: Small Coppice on a Low Knoll

About a dozen maple trees stand clustered closely atop a small knoll. The boughs of the trees interlace and provide cover from the sky. On the outskirts of the trees, small plants with thick, coarse-toothed leaves predominate and provide ample food resources for the number of animals that make the small copse their home. To the south lies a treeless, grassy knoll while to the west lie more flat grasslands.
18704:
A brown furry gopher is here, ready to dive back underground.
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.
A buck runs swiftly from place to place, looking about warily as it grazes.

The most prominent feature here is a rising hillock standing only slightly higher than the surrounding grasslands. The grass effectively hides any dips and burrows in the hill. A sturdy tree stands firmly on one side of the grassy mound, casting a gentle shadow over a patch of white poppies. The grass-covered fields dominate the view for miles all around the hill.
18705: A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.

The plains of grass continue in all directions, the level fields turning into rolling lands in the east and south. Some bushes flourish nearby, their red flowers giving off a rich scent to the air. A small burrow can be made out under their branches. Tracks of some animals can be seen on the moist ground near the bushes.
18706: A small campfire burns here, its low flames giving off only a little light.

The rolling grass-covered hills decline gradually to more level plains in the north. Long treeless slopes and grassy hills stand in line after line for many miles in other directions. Far in the east the land gradually slopes down to a marshy plain where a stream can be seen cutting across the horizon from north to south.
18707:
Clusters of slender stems and tall leaves thrive in the mud and shallows.
A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.
A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

Sedges and cattails predominate the marsh, eerily swaying back and forth in a veil of mist that softly caresses the wet ground underfoot. The precarious lands make the progress tedious. A serpentine stream snakes through the marshland in the east. To the west the miry land turns into rolling plains of grass.
18708:
A worm is here slithering around.
A field lark stands here, focused on finding food.
A badger is here, exploring for food.

A thin cover of mist floats above the sodden ground that yields underfoot. Tall grasses and tufted marsh plants grow in patches all around. The miry lands stretch far to the south while in the west the marsh turns into green, verdant plains. A stream flowing southwards runs across the plains and passes east of here.
18709: The broad and level golden-green expanse of grass continues for many miles to the western horizon whereas to the east the lands abruptly turn into a marshy plain. Rolling hills dominate the southerly lands. Tall coarse grass effectively hides all possible landmarks making it difficult to orientate. Not a single tree can be seen for miles around.
18710: A broad treeless expanse of grasslands can be seen in all directions. The fertile soil of the plains is covered with tall coarse grasses that silently sway when the wind blows. Droppings on the ground near some low-lying shrubbery speak of the animals that live on the plains. Some distance to the north a farm can be seen, apparently abandoned.
18711: Far to the north and east all that is visible is grass, shrubs, and spots of water where the thick grass fails to cover the land. Flowers of all colours spring up here and there throughout the fields, sparkling among the rows of grass and weed. The air here is thick and fragrant. The grass becomes slightly thinner to the west while a small hill can be seen south of here.
18712: A large thorny branched shrub is growing here.

The grass thins noticeably as the tips of granite bedrock become conspicuous. The coarse crabgrass presents a stark contrast to the thick, tall grass prevalent in all other directions. A few tangled blackberry brambles have managed to take root among the outcroppings. To the south, a small cluster of maple trees tops a knoll.
18713: The light, dry soil provides an extremely fertile environment for varied foliage. One plant, standing erect with a many-branched, cylindrical stem, possesses light, feathery leaves. The verdant plains dominate the view in every direction with a single road traversing the northwestern horizon serving as the only break in the sea of green.
18714: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

Narrow, long blades of grass with tapering points coat the floor of the vale. Mixed with the longer grass is a shorter variety possessing elongated, barbed awns with a sparse coating of hair along their veins. Large fields of brown and cream-coloured mushrooms are visible to the south.
18715: Bending west and north, the trail cuts diagonally across the green plains. Clumps of scattered brush line the sides of the path. Although not a large road, tracks upon its surface indicate that something occasionally utilizes it. Beyond the brush that borders the road, grassy plains are visible upon the northwestern and southeastern horizons.
18716: A finch flies low above the ground.

Sloping gently from the east, the narrow, worn trail continues to the south up an even smaller incline. Handfuls of tiny flowers grow beside the roadway in several places. To the south, the trail meets a barely discernible path coming from the west. Fields of green are visible beyond the boulder-strewn grass to the north.
18717: A small cluster of clover grows here.

Massive clusters of clover intermingle with the thick grass that is prevalent underfoot. The bulky clover measures up to several inches across in width and stands more than a foot high in some dense patches. To the west and south, a small trail zigzags across the plains. In the north and east, vibrant fields of green grass cover the earth comprising the plains.
18718: The roadway marches roughly south and west as in several places, craggy outcroppings force the road to diverge from a straight path. The surface of the road could use some repair but remains largely intact. To the north small holes and bushes provide the only interruption to the endless grassland. Far to the west, the road appears to split and head back to the north as well as the south.
18719: Wild berry plants covered with sharp thorns and wind-blown leaves partially cover the roadway. A small coppice to the south assuredly provided the foliage atop the roadway. To the north lie rolling prairies as far as the eye can see. The road becomes more visible to the west and east as no undergrowth or leaves obscure the roadway.
18720: Intermittent blades of grass thrust through the cobbled roadway, revealing the often barren nature of the pathway. Stretching both north and east, the trail provides one of the few visible breaks to the otherwise prevailing plains. The only other anomaly, the River Isen, cuts a path through the flatlands several miles to the west.
18721: A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Wobbly cobblestones lie atop the surface of the trail. Fertile steppes border the road to the north and east, sprinkled by small groups of trees and assorted flora. The road runs west and south through the plains for several miles, interrupted only by irregular, erosion-induced blemishes.
18722: Lengthy, luxuriant grass covers a thick, springy soil throughout the surrounding locale. Underneath the thick grass, the rich earth provides an extremely fertile area for a wide range of flora to prosper. A long, treeless slope to the north rises above the gently sloping lands while to the southwest an unadorned trail juts across the flat grasslands.
18723: A gigantic weasel glares at you.

Short stalks of green grass shift underfoot throughout the area. Aside from a few rocky crags and the occasional animal hole, the soft grassland allows for easy travel. With the exception of a trail to the south, golden-green grass covers the plains as far as the eye can see in all directions.
18724: A brown furry gopher is here, ready to dive back underground.

Beautiful, lush grass abounds as far as the eye can see. Amalgamated among the grass stands waist high plants with lance-shaped, hairy leaves and pink, tubular flowers measuring a few inches in length. A scarcely distinguishable trail mars the grassland to the southwest while an effervescent meadow of clover sits atop the land to the south.
18725:
Some small rocks have been piled into a mound here.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

Numerous rocks poke their heads out of the short and rough grass ubiquitous throughout this area. Some of the boulders appear bunched together in small piles. Long, thin blades of grass grow between the clusters of rocks. Beautiful grasslands surround most of the area. In the south and east, bumpy trails made of dirt cut across the grassland heading in opposite directions.
18726: Cutting east and south, the dirt trail stands out atop the green grass of the prairie. Small holes caused by dislodged rocks mark the earthen surface of the roadway and make travel tricky. Small rocks have collected beside the trail, probably a result of getting washed aside by rain. Past the trail in the northwest and southeast sits bountiful green grassland.
18727: Characterized by long, deep ruts and small, crusty holes, the trail roughly runs a north to west path across the rolling meads. Portions of the road remain firmly compacted, showing that at one time the road was a popular thoroughfare. Green countryside stretches before one's eyes for miles in both the southeast and northwest.
18728: Profuse hordes of shrubs of all sizes top the grass-covered countryside. Many of the low-growing, evergreen shrubs posses leaves with a leathery feel, oval in shape with tapering ends. Some taller plants with serrated, yellowish leaves have an unforgettable scent and lucid veins. Various types of foliage, primarily shrubs and grasses, cover the surrounding countryside. The only noticeable exception is a trail on the northwestern horizon.
18729: Thick brush makes travel difficult. Many of the plants stand several feet taller than the profuse grass. The toothed spines of one plant cut at any weak surface. The bright rose-coloured flowers clustered at the top of another thick-stemmed plant release an extremely powerful scent. To the south, the vegetation thins considerably as rocky tips peek through the grass.
18730: A buck runs swiftly from place to place, looking about warily as it grazes.

Thick and tall grasses, coloured in shades of green, cover the plains. The grass grows here at different heights making these plains look uneven. The ground is moist and fertile with occasional puddles of water forming in small dips and furrows. The verdant grasslands stretch away, all the way to the feet of the Misty Mountains rising in the northwest.
18731: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

A large untended patch of crops has survived the nature and grows here wildly, golden rows of wheat rustling in the occasional breezes. Remains of a fallen fence lie rotting on the ground beside the field. There are no remains of tools or signs of recent farming. Apparently, the farm has been abandoned long ago. A barely distinguishable path makes its way northwards. To the east lies a farmyard.
18732: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

From this higher tract of land the stream below can be seen, making its way steadily southwards. The stream is forced to take a slight turn to the east where it meets the wide grassy mound. In the west stands a farm, judging by its decayed state it is apparently abandoned. A ramshackle wooden structure stands just to the west. The grassy plains continue far to the southern horizon.
18733: The stream flowing in from the north narrows here considerably, bending east where it continues its meandering way across the grassy plains southwards towards the marshes that lie ahead. A thin veil of mist floats above the sodden fields to the south. A grassy hillock overlooks the stream in the west. The climb up should not be too difficult.
18734: The relatively swiftly flowing stream coming from the west cleaves deeply into the grassy plains which stretch themselves for many miles around. The stream makes a sharp turn southwards towards the marshlands that loom still far ahead. The banks of the stream are bare of any vegetation and should be easy to climb.
18735: The stream here is stronger and swifter and its banks deep cloven. The waters rushing in from the north create enough turbulence to bring up the basic sediment making the stream muddy and filled with clods. A thick row of bushes grow on the western bank, making passage there impossible. The stream continues its way east.
18736: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

A small brook with brownish water carefully makes its way east where it joins another stream. The ground is wet and muddy near the brook. A large patch of thorny bushes grow huddled together near the stream in the east. They are low grown but dense and with their combined width they make the passage east difficult. A barely distinguishable path leads south towards an apparently abandoned farm.
18737: A finch flies low above the ground.

Only few small trees and bushes reach their branches above the tall green grass. The ground slopes slightly downwards in the west where the grasslands turn more marshy. In all other directions, the grass-covered plains expand as far as the eye can see. Far to the north lies the great forest and to the northwest are the skirts of the Misty Mountains.
18738: A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

Lower than most of the surrounding countryside, the ground appears as though it collects a lot of rain water making this area feel quite humid. Numerous cattails grow around the edges of the more water-filled ground, evidence of just how flooded this area can become. A dense, brown furry spike tops the tall stems and light green, flat leaves of the cattails. A small trail snakes across the plains to the north while thick brush dominates the landscape to the south.
18739: The trail crosses the thick grassland, heading north and west across the plains. Pockets of vegetation grow in areas where the surface of the road has weakened. Beside the road to the east and south stand shrubs of many sizes and varieties mixed among the endless fields of grass. To the north, the road continues to cut a path across the undulating prairie.
18740: Zigzagging slowly across the prairie, the trail continues a roughly southwest to northeast jaunt. An occasional small bush and even a short tree can be sporadically seen on both sides of the trail. Scorched terrain to the north presents a vivid difference to the flowing, grassy fields in the southwest.
18741: Tall milkweed plants spring up among the thick grass. Strong, thick stems allow the long, rough-textured seed pods of the milkweed to hover above the tips of the yellow and green blades of grass. The height of the milkweed becomes even more impressive when considering the short, rough grassland to the north and the flat trail in the south.
18742: Flourishing grasses predominantly coat the plains here. The grass appears very similar to the north and east but in the north it is interspersed by masses of wild flowers. On the southeastern horizon, a trail slices a diagonal path across the plains.
18743: Standing nearly two feet high in some areas, tall stalks of yellow-green grass occasionally sway gently. The earth beneath this grass seems more fertile than the surrounding countryside but what could have caused this is unknown. The grassland continues on in every direction except the east where bountiful quantities of exquisite wildflowers dominate the landscape.
