Descending from the murky surface the water becomes cold and the visibility extends only a few yards away in the muddy lake. The pool is surprisingly deep, and close to the mossy bottom no sunlight can reach from the marsh above.
104071: The water in the marshy lake is dark and cold. Mud and mossy debris fills every inch of the pool, and no sunlight reaches from the surface above. Along the bottom moss and lichen resides, preventing deeper venturing, but the moss itself must reach even further down into the ground.
104072:
The burnt and blackened skeletal remains of a human are here.
A weapons rack stands against the wall.

At some point in history, this structure housed the protectors of this village. That must have happened long ago though, as is clear from the present state of things. Nothing here has been left intact. The broken walls barely provide enough support for the collapsing roof, and the beds are in no better condition than the walls they stand next to. The floor is cluttered with pieces of torn mattresses and the fragments of what used to be a small table. Against the western wall there is a weapons rack, now smashed apart and unable to hold any weapons. Perhaps looters caused this destruction after the village was abandoned, but from the look of it the village was abandoned because of this great destruction.
104073:
A large cabinet capable of storing goods is here.
An elven scout stands here, blending in with the background.

This cave, dug into the side of the hill, may have been an hobbit hole a long time ago. The stone walls that surround it appear to form a rectangular shape with rounded corners, broken to the north by a wooden door, while the earthen ceiling is supported by large beams. There are a few, very simple pieces of furniture, made of oak, firmly standing on the ground.
104096:
A white-painted bench is here.
A small oaken table has been set here.
A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

This small house was built from some white-grey stone, with thick oaken beams supporting the roof. A large window to the south opens up towards the Bruinen valley and an inspiring vista. The house is sparsely decorated with simple and sturdy furniture and few decorative items, with a large tapestry hanging on the eastern wall, depicting some ancient battle by the elves; seemingly, this is the only item of any larger value.
104097: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

This is where Gelmir returns to rest after his forays into Arda. The walls are made of a light brown wood, and many fine rugs of blue and silver lie on the floor. Instead of furniture, squashy cushions made of shimmering fabric dot the domed and relatively high room. Even though this room lies within a vineyard, the air in this round chamber smells of fresh winds near the sea.
104098: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

The entrance leads a bit down and all around are thick branches and heavy, green leaves. All walls and the roof here seem to be one single, thick bush. A bed indicates this room gets used for sleeping and even when the roof, consisting of a thick layer of interwoven branches and leaves, seems waterproof, this room is quite moist and warm. The result is a thick, white fog that reaches over the knee of an elf and that completely hides the floor. Rarely something strange, like a magic fizzle or spark, seems to be felt.
104099:
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

This little hut is made entirely out of wood, the floor from simple wooden planks and the walls from oaken beams. A large window is carved out of the southern wall, giving a nice view over the Bruinen valley. A wooden table and chairs stand in front of the window, making it a good place to rest and philosophise over life. A small and dirty bed stands in the north-west corner, covered by dirty robes and pointy hats. A wide shelf covers the eastern wall, filled with old scrolls, strange brews, and books of magic and wizardry.
104122: This terrace was made from white stones. The views are partly obscured by the tips of the large, green bushes and slender trees that grow next to the Last Homely Home. The low balustrade is made of the same white stone and shows many different, very detailed patterns that resemble deliquesce branches and leaves. A narrow stair leads down towards a wide ledge above the Bruinen, while a wider one in the east leads a bit upwards to the Balcony of the Sunset.
104123: This is the western end of the stone-laid balcony. The precisely laid stones that form the walkway come to an end in the north, at the beginning of a stone stairway. The edge of the balcony is made of white stone bearing etchings of leaves that circle its supporting posts. In the west, a wide but rather short stair leads a bit down to a white terrace.
104131: This corner of the balcony stands above the River Bruinen and the bridge that crosses it. When looking down over the white stone edge of the balcony, one can often catch a glimpse of the glimmering waters, running on their course under the ornately arched bridge. To the east the balcony continues, leading past many doorways on its way.
104152: The Bruinen rushes a bit to the south and below through the Valley. North and above, the graceful Last Homely Home can be seen, with all its terraces and white arches; with all its graceful trees and its surrounding green, lively vegetation. The path here was paved with smooth stones and all around are beds of flowers and lower bushes of all kinds. Here and there, smaller paths paved with white stones lead through the beds.
104154: All around grow and prosper large, seemingly wild bushes that are interwoven with thick tangles and ancient vines. Smaller, snaking paths have carefully been cut through the vegetation while, in a few places, the glimpse of overgrown marble can be spotted through the leaves; if those stones are part of old buildings or forgotten statues can only be guessed. The murmur of the Bruinen can be heard just to the south, while somewhat above and north, sections of the Last Homely Home are visible.
104155: The path leads along the steep ledge. Behind the low, white wall and below, the Bruinen flows through the wide river bed. Occasional archs of bright stone, partly overgrown, partly decorated with fine carvings, span over the path. Everywhere along and on the small wall stand massive pots in which all kinds of well-tended plants grow, quite many of these plants are herbs, probably used as spices by the kitchen. A makeshift path twists to the south, leading to the bank of a small offshoot of the Bruinen.
104156: Near the end of the path stands a white, mostly overgrown pavilion that is known as the Last Pavilion or the Pavilion of the Bruinen. Not that far below lies the river and the Pier of the Bruinen, while the part of the Last Homely Home that is visible just to the north and a bit above, is covered with dense vines.
104157: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

Once you stepped into this room, suddenly warm presence surrounds your body. The circular room is large and beautiful. There is no furniture but a round table and four chairs in the centre of the room. The solid walls of soft, polished oak are without windows. The light in this room comes from a mysterious, shimmering bowl of stone on the table. The blue glow is very bright and fills the room like a clear, transparent cloud.
104163: The Great Hedge blocks access to the Old East Road which runs on the other side just to the north. This trail is seldom-used as there are very few breaks in the hedge to allow access. Where the grass is still worn away along the trail, the tracks of many sheep are evident.
104164:
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.
A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

This seldom-used trail mirrors the Old East Road that runs alongside the opposite side of the Great Hedge to the north. In many places, the trail is almost lost due to the encroachment of the rich grass that covers the gentle hills of the South Downs, which continue to the southern horizon.
104165: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

The Great Hedge bends from west to south here, and the trail is forced to bend with it. This portion of the trail is becoming overgrown with the grasses common on the downs to the south, and sometimes it is lost for a bit under the carpet of grass.
104166: The gentle hills of the downs to the south become a little steeper to the southeast. To the north, the Great Hedge blocks the Old East Road from sight, though it might be possible to glimpse it from the large hill to the southeast. The trail continues north and east in the shadow of the hedge, following the line layed out by the Old East Road.
104167: Gently rolling hills extend to the south all the way to the horizon. Some of the hills are dotted by stands of small trees, stunted and twisted by the wind, but by and large the thick green grass holds sway here.
104168: The landscape is very monotonous, as in every direction only rolling treeless hills can be seen. The hills are green with thick grass -- in places cropped by sheep -- and large clover patches. There is little shelter from the wind that blows almost constantly, and this may account for the lack of trees.
104169: A hungry warg (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Throughout this area, the hillsides are formed of many flat and grassy terraces. Each of the shelves lies approximately ten feet over the one below, and it is unclear whether or not these steps are of natural origin. The ground is covered with thick, spongy grass that resiliently springs back after being trodden upon, along with patches of clover and dandelions.
104170: The ground is carpeted here by a tough grass that resiliently springs back upright after each footstep. In some places, the grass has been closely cropped -- probably by sheep -- while elsewhere it flourishes up to three feet in height. To the south, the rolling hills become more pronounced, while to the north the ground slopes gently downward until it is lost in the hazy distance.
104171: Winds whip across this hilly landscape, unobstructed by any obstacles. The low and rounded hills are carpeted with thick grass, and the hissing of the wind through the grass provides an almost constant background noise. From the tops of the hills, the dark line of the Great Hedge can be spied to the north -- beyond which lie the Old East Road and the Midgewater Marshes.
104172: The thick grassy carpet covering the hills has been closely cropped by grazing animals. Sometimes the tops of the hills have bare patches, and the chalky soil is revealed. To the south the hills become rockier and crowd together, forcing anyone travelling that direction to enter a narrow, winding canyon.
104173: This ridge is higher than most of the surrounding hills, and to the north it terminates in a high rounded knob. The grass resembles that of a well-kept lawn in a peaceful town, as it has been cropped closely by some type of grazing animal -- probably sheep judging by the shortness of the remaining grass.
104174:
A shepherd is standing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.

To the west, the hills rise up and form a low ridge that runs north and south. In every other direction, the green slopes rise and fall until lost from sight. The grass is soft and spongy, and judging from the numerous spoor, it provides an ideal haven for a number of small animals.
104175: Among these lonely and windswept hills, the only sounds, save for the constant rustling of the plush grass, are the sporadic calls of birds and the distant bleating of sheep. In every direction the hills continue, like waves on the ocean.
104176: A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.

A deep and placid pond of clear water nestles here among the lush grassland. A few small trees have taken root nearby, providing comfortable shade from the sun during the day. In every direction, the rolling hills of the South Downs stretch, becoming drier and more brown to the east.
104177: The grass-covered hills of the South Downs rise on all sides in lonely splendour. Patches of coloured wildflowers dot the green carpet of the lush grass, giving the landscape an air of serenity. East and west, small ponds in low places among the hills can be seen, providing fresh water for the thirsty traveller.
104185: The hedge grows close to the side of a large hill to the south, and the trail passes closely between the two. The hedge is not quite as dense here as at other places, as the plants have not flourished on the rocky soil. It quickly recovers its normal thickness both east and west though.
104186: The gentle hills of the South Downs roll away toward the southern horizon in a panoramic vista. To the north and east, the Great Hedge and the trail that runs on its southern flank wends its way between Bree and Weathertop. The grass is very lush, and often is mingled with large patches of small yellow flowers or clover.
104187: The hillsides here are terraced, with each of the grassy shelves sitting about ten feet over the one below it. It is unclear whether this is a natural phenomenum, or whether it is due to some artificial construction. The grass is thick and spongy, seeming to promise bliss to those who will remove their shoes and run carefree through it.
104188: This small mound is very symmetrical and crowned by a few stones that may have been quarried and carried here. Whatever once stood here has long been claimed by time and erosion. Directly to the east, a high hill at the north end of a grassy ridge rises. It should be possible to see much of the land from that vantage point.
104189: The crown of this hill is several hundred feet higher than the surrounding rolling grasslands. From this vantage point, the Old East Road can be clearly espied as it passes some four or five miles to the north, beyond the dark green line of the hedge. Farther north -- beyond the road -- a low white mist hangs over the trackless Midgewater marshes.
104190: To the west, a high hill rises proudly over the others. It lies at the northern edge of a ridge that runs to the south. Just to the north, the seldom-used trail along the southern edge of the Great Hedge can be made out. In the grass, there are numerous signs that rabbits, foxes, and other small animals have flourished among the lonely hills.
104191: Here among the lonely hills of the South Downs, rabbits and many other small animals have found an ideal home in the tall grass. In some places, the grass looks as if it has been clipped, so evidently some grazing is done here -- probably by sheep occasional led here by their shepherd.
104192: The grassy slopes of the South Downs undulate gently toward the horizon. To the south, there is a small depression filled with a pond. Northward, the dark green line of the Great Hedge can be made out, with the Old East Road presumably on the other side.
104193: A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

The rich grass is criss-crossed by trails left by scampering animals. There are signs that sheep graze here occasionally, as several of the hills have had their grassy covering shorn close to the ground. To the north, the dark green line of the Great Hedge can be made out, beyond which runs the Old East Road.
104194: The gentle hills wear a cover of thick grass interspersed with patches of clover. Where the soil is exposed, it is a rich black loam with sporadic outcroppings of chalky limestone. The wind rustling through the grass is the only sound heard for hours at a time, along with the rare calls of lonely birds and the bleating of distant sheep.
104195:
A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.
A bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.
A bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.
A bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.

This flat area is overgrown with a soft carpet of clover. The hills surround this place like the edges of a bowl, proving shelter from the strong winds. A small pond is nestled in one corner of the depression, and it is filled with clear spring water.
104196: This trail runs parallel to the Old East Road, separated from it by the Great Hedge. Eastward the land begins to climb gently upward, until finally the Weather Hills are reached. South of here, the grassy slopes of the South Downs lie, seemingly empty of all but grass.
104197: Running parallel to the Old East Road, but separated from it by the Great Hedge, this trail skirts the northern end of the South Downs. The hills to the south are carpeted with rich grass, and look to be an ideal environment for a great many small animals.
104198: This trail runs along the southern side of the Great Hedge, mirroring the Old East Road between Bree and Weathertop. To the south, the gentle hills of the South Downs begin, stretching like a green sea to the southern horizon.
104199: Directly to the north, the twisted vegetation of the Great Hedge blocks access to the Old East Road and to the Midgewater Marshes beyond. The trail here along the southern edge of the hedge is in places completely overgrown, as most travellers prefer to use the Old East Road. Southward, the grassy hills of the South Downs begin, and they extend in that direction as far as the eye can see.
104200: This almost-overgrown trail runs east and west along the southern edge of the Great Hedge. To the south, empty and grass-covered hills begin and continue until lost from vision. Beyond the hedge lies the Old East Road, presumably, but the vegetation is much too thick to see it.
104201: These palatious ruins show that before the fall of the kingdom of Arthedain Arnor Lane probably was one of the most noble areas in the city. Today, many of the old ruins have been removed, while the pavement has been renewed with white stone, possibly imported from the White Hills near Forlond. The coat-of-arms of the Eketta family, one of the seven major houses of Arthedain, has been inlaid into the pavement in coloured stones, faded over time.
104206: Before the Kingdom of Arthedain fell to the raid of the witch-kings, Arnor Lane was one of the noblest areas of Fornost. Here, a few great ruins are waiting to be rebuilt: their current shape still shows traces of their former glamour. The coat-of-arms of the Noirins-family is still visible in the old pavement. Many new houses have been built between the old ruins, ruins that appears to have been used as quarries.
104207: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Arnor Street ends in front of a magnificent ruin which might once have been a guild or court hall. Most of the other ruins have already been used as quarry to get new stones for all the newer buildings that can be seen around. The old hall seems to have become some sort of small park, as the roof has collapsed long ago and is overgrown with grasses and mosses by now. Other plants, even trees, were also able to take root. The coat-of-arms of the Tarma family, inlaid in the pavement of the road, is one of the few still intact leftovers of a time that is long gone.
104208:
A tall and strong guard is here.
A tall and strong guard is here.

This room is floored and lined with polished white marble, furrowed with black veins of sparkling ore. The ceiling is a great dome, decorated with frescoes of great battles and myths of Middle-earth's past, and the floor bears the mark of a giant elf-rune. The south wall is broken by a large window, framed with red curtains which can be flung back to let in the sunlight. An open archway leads north to what appears to be a sorcerous work-room, and a pair of great doors with lions carved into the woodwork lead east.
104209: A tall and strong guard is here.

Flasks and alembics cover a massive oak work table. On one side of the work table are clustered piles of books and scrolls. A cage with a small ferret inside hangs from the ceiling, and hung from the east wall is a great tapestry upon which has been painted a detailed map of Middle-earth.
104210:
A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.
A tall and strong guard is here.

A great canopy-bed hung with golden curtains dominates the room. To one side is a polished oak armoire, and beside a fancifully carved writing desk. On the opposite side of the room is a fireplace that burns without apparent need to be refueled. Hung on the walls are trophies of war: orc scimitars and shields.
104211: This large structure with a loft ceiling is the main meeting and dining area. Along the walls you see several paintings. To the north there is a passage to a kitchen and near the south wall you notice a small chapel. Oftentimes you can hear a minstrel, on a raised gallery overlooking the Great Hall, singing Pedrag's favourite songs about the mysteries of Arda.
104212: A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

A small fireplace gives this cosy room a warm glow. In the western corner you see a king-sized bed, covered in warm blankets. A small wardrobe, filled with Pedrag's clothes and weaponry, can be seen on the northern wall. Near the fireplace stand a comfortable chair and an elegant bookshelf stacked with Tales of Arda.
104228: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

A few ruins, reminiscent of great architecture, remain along this straight part of Arnor Lane; many of the old ruins have either been removed or changed to be used for housing. The colourful coat-of-arms of the Orros family, one of the seven major noble houses of the fallen Kingdom of Arthedain, has been inlaid into the white pavement.
104231: A hungry warg is standing here, ridden by Backdraft.

A sharp drop in the plain blocks all passage westwards, as a twenty feet high cliff wall plunges down onto the grassy plain beneath it. Along the ridge, a few scattered bushes are kept low in stature by the winds that must blow here most of the time. South of here one can notice the beginnings of a downward slope.
104233: This mud-covered slope quickly drops towards the west into what appears to be a mud pit. As the earth slides down the slope underfoot, it threatens to take anything standing on this hill with it. No trees or large plants grow here to offer handhold and no grass that would offer foothold could survive in this highly moist environment. Moving up the northern slope seems the easiest way out of this muddy mess.
104235:
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.
A large bullfrog croaks loudly.
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

Water high enough to soak even the highest boot covers the land, turning this basin into a swamp. Water reeds and lilies grow in abundance. Wading through is possible here but becomes more difficult in the north. The reeds eventually become so thick, they totally block all sight of the land northward. High levees have been constructed to the east and south of here to reign in the water and protect the roads and settlements just beyond.
104236:
A grey snake slides along the water.
A grey snake slides along the water.
A grey snake slides along the water.

Suddenly, the mud beneath you begins to sink, taking you down with it. Reeds and water plants tangle up your legs and arms, refusing to allow departure. In every direction, mud contains you, weighing down your limbs, making it extremely difficult to move quickly enough to free yourself from the reeds. And slowly, you sink further into the mud.
104237: The earth has become saturated here by an unseen water source. Grass still grows but dies quickly as the earth to the south and west rapidly turns to mud. To the north and east, hills rise out of this basin. To the south, the earth continues to slope downward very quickly. Thick water reeds obscure vision in that direction. Travel in that direction would be difficult indeed.
104238:
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

A muddy mix of brush, water plants and earth engulf any creature who travels here. Movement becomes tortuous as arms and legs are caked with heavy mud. The stagnant water sits here almost as deep as a hobbit is tall, but it is so thick with mud that wading through it is like trying to move through warm wax. The easiest way out of this tiring mess seems to be back north. A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
104239: A thick, gooey, muddy mess slows your descent into this basin. The stagnant water and the earth have merged into a thick, unyielding mud that threatens to swallow adventurous travellers whole. Strong water reeds, almost floating in the muddy earth, offer even more resistance to any who attempt to move through this area. They snag on clothes, in hair, or anything else and hang on so tightly it almost seems that they have a sense of purpose. The earth seems to slope downwards even more directly to the east.
104240:
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A green frog is here, hopping around.

Knee-high to a man, water floods these lands and is contained by the levees and hills to the south and east. Water lilies and reeds thrive in this watery basin, while the grass and earth under the water have become a muddy and difficult surface to walk upon. To the south, a mud-covered hill leads up to the Old Forest Road but is impassable from this depression, as the slope is moderately steep and too slick to find foothold.
104241:
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.
A green frog is here, hopping around.

All around are various water grasses and reeds, some as tall as a pony. The earth is so water-soaked in this area that a man would sink in to his knees standing here. Walking through this area is difficult enough but riding proves to be impossible. The earth seems a bit more solid to the north and east of here but venturing farther south could be more difficult.
104242:
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.
A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.
A green frog is here, hopping around.
A green frog is here, hopping around.
A large bullfrog croaks loudly.

It's difficult to tell whether the substance surrounding your feet is muddy water or watery mud. Movement through this area is less like walking and more like wading. Whatever water source supplies this depression must be very near. Rising above the water-covered land to the south, the Old Forest Road can be seen running east and west.
104243:
A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A large bullfrog croaks loudly.

An underground water source exits the earth in this depression, flooding the land for miles around. The water immediately mixes with the brown earth to form watery, messy paste that sticks to everything. To the west and south, steep muddy slopes keep the water contained and off the Old Forest Road. Coming down those slopes seems easy enough but travelling back up through the mud might not be possible.
104244: This burrow is most likely the old home of a badger but it has been widened to allow the passage of a humanoid. The entrance is concealed by the remains of a shrub. The burrow widens even more going south giving room for a door with its casing firmly embedded in the sides of the burrow. A lot of fresh footmarks on the ground suggests that this place is not abandoned.
104245:
A large, dusty alcove sits in a wall, smelling of soot.
A small oaken table has been set here.

A small room has been excavated at the end of the burrow giving room for a bed and a crude table. A wooden door is set in the north wall so it is possible to block the exit keeping out animals of the wilderness. Its massive wooden frame is embedded in the earthen sides of the burrow making it very secure. There is a small gap over the door making it possible for the smoke from the fireplace to leave the room.
104254: The ancient Dwarven passage known as Hwain's Way ascends, as usual, from the east to the west. The quantity of dust on the ground slowly increases as one travels towards West Door; this might have something to do with the presence of a very wide vertical chimney to the west. Eastwards the road proceeds in its course; it should soon reach the chambers of the Deeps.
104255: You are walking along an ancient corridor in the depths of Khazad-dum. The grey walls are full of small cracks, while the floor shows signs of heavy usage in the past. From time to time a droplet of water falls from the ceiling and lands with a faint 'plinck'.
104256: The old corridor known as Hwain's Way continues its slow descent towards what was once the heart of Khazad-dum: the Royal Chambers of the Seventh Deep. From the echoes you hear, coming from the east, you guess that you are not far from a large chamber. Before the coming of the Balrog, the sounds of hundreds of busy Dwarves would have met you here. This is not the case any more: now the faint echo of heavy footsteps and of some occasional drum roll makes one wonder what terrible, foul creatures are defacing the Dwarven halls.
104257:
A black uruk, armoured heavily, stands confidently here.
A black uruk, armoured heavily, stands confidently here.
A black uruk, armoured heavily, stands confidently here.
A black uruk, armoured heavily, stands confidently here.
A black uruk, armoured heavily, stands confidently here.
A huge troll, with skin as black as pitch, glowers at you.

You have reached the eastern end of Hwain's Way, a large and straight corridor connecting the Seventh Deep of Moria to the western entrance. To the east the cracked grey walls acquire a blue-greenish tinge, as the corridor ends in an enormous vaulted hall. To the west the road goes on and on, vanishing in the darkness ahead; your feet ache as you think of how long it would take to walk all the way from here to West Door.
104258: The great fault line twists from west to south, the roadway following its tracks from ledge to pillar and back again. In this part of the system of ledges and bridges there is railing to hold on to, making you feel a lot safer than when navigating the walkways without any kind of safety at all. Even though most of the roadways are quite broad and easy to travel on, the assurance of the railing does a lot for your self-confidence. You barely complete that thought before your hands find a loose section of the barrier between you and the depths below. You teeter on the rim of the stone bridge, luckily manage to catch your balance and watch the broken pieces of the railing plummet downwards into the dark depths. You breathe a sigh of relief and swallow hard; better not trust that railing after all...
104261: The immense road system runs north-south, the black depths broken by huge pillars of rock rearing up like so many teeth. The roadway continues onward too, using these pillars to hop across the yawning depths. Looking back the way you came you see the many bridges and walkways you have traversed behind you. From this distance they look precariously thin and fragile and you wonder how you ever managed to cross them. The ground below your feet seem solid enough though, and you know that these walkways could probably hold countless times your weight, and that it is just your imagination playing tricks on you. At least you try desperately to convince yourself of that...
104262: Standing on the seemingly solid walkway you are acutely aware of the monstrous depths below you. From the far west you seem to make out a deep rumbling sound, adding to the otherwise eerie silence. The roadway angles sharply from south to west as the echoing drop yawn blackly east and north. Seeking some point of focus for your vision, your gaze wanders upward to the dark ceiling. Huge stalactites are suspended high above, looking like they might plunge down to impale you at any instant. You hastily turn down your gaze to the somewhat more reassuring ground below your feet.
104264: The trees grow to about three yards height, their crowns becoming rather dense and creating a permanent dusk here. In the shadows of the trees several smaller birds and wild animals have their dens, well out of sight from any larger bird that might prey on them.
104289:
A holly bush with dark green leaves is growing here.
Partly covered by the bush's green leaves, there are two piles of inkberries.

Within the deep, thick brush thorny branches lie on the ground. The sharp thorns make any attempt to move very unpleasant and painful. North of here the Road of the Smiths continues east and west. A small stream passes by to the east.

These sharp thorns from all the bushes makes every move an unpleasant and painful experience. To the south east lies a small forest, with its young pine trees.

You are in a room so low, that even smaller orcs cannot enter here unbent. The acrid stench of urine and rotten meat fills your nostrils and makes your eyes itch. The ground is soiled and wet, covered by a layer of animal hair and a few hunks of half-eaten meat are lying around.

You can enter some plains to the north and west.

The river continues to the north and south, or you can leave up to the sturdy bridge you see above your head.

The river flows lazily here. Although this river is not known especially for it's strong current, but it's wide and deep enough to make travel across it uncomfortable. 104330: The river flows lazily south bound. Although this river is not known especially for it's strong current, but it's wide and deep enough to make travel across it uncomfortable. Birds nest here and chirp softly, but land mammals have a difficult time navigating the swift river currents.

Here the river narrows somewhat and the current increases a little bit. A small island rises out of the stream east of you, inviting you to a short rest. To the south the river continues its way through the landscape of Eriador.

To your west, a portion of the current flows over an impassible, shallow mud flat and continues southward on the far side of the bar. The bank north of here is too steep to climb.

Here a shallow mud bar, extending from the north bank of the river, has become overgrown with bushes and leafy shrubs. Colorful songbirds sing in the trees by day; by night, a chorus of deep-throated frogs can be heard from the shallows. Northwest of this island the river flows over an impassible mud bank, too treacherous to walk on and too shallow to paddle or swim.
104358: There is some snow on the ground.

You are slowly drifting away southwards towards the Grey Havens. As you look around you notice a small island to your direct west. On your eastern side you can see a trail slowly following the river northwards towards unknown destination.

The waters of a side channel of the River Lhun flow lazily southward here. To the east is a small island, actually part of a long bar of sand and mud that separates this backwater from the miles-wide expanse of the main channel. At times, however, when the river is in flood, its waters must overflow the bar and create a single vast raging torrent; this explains the steep, undercut bank which rises impassibly to the west of you, where earth and trees have been ripped away. To the north, where the water flows over the mud bar, it is too shallow to swim and the bed is too soft and treacherous to walk.
104360: There is some snow on the ground.

You are in the western channel of the River Lhun, which is separated from the river's eastern part by a miles-long bar of sand and mud. North and south of your location the bar is overgrown with foliage, but to the east of you the river's waters wash over the bar.
104361:
There is some snow on the ground.

The river passes just west of a large island. It flows lazily to the south from the north. You can hear a bird's song linger in the air.

The river passes just west of a large island. It flows lazily to the south, from the north. The water is not very deep here, and you can spot some fishes lurking around at the pebble covered bottom.

This side channel of the Lhun flows lazily southward; to the east is a long island which separates it from the vast main channel. South of here the waters rejoin. To the west is a high earthen bank, too steep to climb; at its top you can see great leafy trees whose roots are naked at the top of the bank, ready to be washed away when the next flood undercuts the bank a few feet more.
104364:

A large sturgeon swims slowly along the bottom.
A salmon swims here.

You are near the west bank of a mighty river. The water flows calmly here, but its power is great. To the south is a great hill, topped by tall pines among which you can see the grey stones of a ruined building. The river's waters have undercut the side of the hill, carving a great undercut cliff; in some future flood, trees, ruins, and all will collapse and be washed away, and eventually the river will proceed southward unobstructed as it wishes.
104365:
There is some snow on the ground.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
You are on the river between two islands, one north and one south of you. The water is calm in the lee of the northern island; perhaps there is a slight current from east to west.
104366: You are on a narrow island in the River Lhun whose long dimension is north and south. Lush bushes and trees have grown up on this muddy bar. The island seems to be visited seldom, if ever, and there are no signs of large animals here.

You are near the centre of a narrow island in the River Lhun, whose long dimension is north and south, parallel to the river's flow. To the east and west the water laps at the island's muddy shore. Tall oaks and great old gnarled maples rise up here from the lush undergrowth.

To the north tall broad-leafed trees rise up from the fertile, oft-flooded soil. To the south a stiffer breeze ruffles the broad surface of the Lhun, which looks more like a great lake or estuary than a mere stream.

The river's water swirls slowly but powerfully here, as the current from a side channel to the west merges with the vast main southward flow. To the southwest spume rises from a rocky point; you can barely see the eastward bank of the river, which has more the look of a lake or strait here. North of here you see some trees on a point of land.

You are floating on what seems to be the calmer part of the river. East of here is another part of the river that seems to border a trail. You can also continue south along the river.

The river is here floating from north to south at a pleasant speed. As you look east, you see a trail following the river. But west of here is a stronger part of the river. These waters seem quite safe, but not as safe as having the firm ground under your feet.
104372: There is a lot of snow on the ground.
The river is floating from north to south at a pleasant speed. You can see that the current to the west is somewhat stronger, but you sense that it is quite safe.

The river continues calmly along here, and you begin to relax your tightened muscles during your long and tabescent journey. To the distant east, you can make out a well-used path with some bushes behind it. You can continue along the river in all other directions.

This part of the river is calmer than the surrounding areas since the main currents flows closely to the western shore. Here and there sandbanks can be discerned in the muddy water, no doubt a peril for the fishing-boats and such vessels that traffic the river.

There is a smell of seaweeds and salt mixed with musty odors from the surrounding woods here.

To enter the shore to the east seems to be impossible due to the twisted weeds and rotting logs that litter the shore. It is possible to travel north on the river or south onto the gulf.

A salty breeze blows in steadily from the sea filling the air with the special smell that is prevalent in this area. Although the Lhun lies some distance to the north the water is muddy here. The waters here are known to be fair fishing-waters and the sails of the elven fishing-boats that here and there can be seen at the horizon indicates that the river now approaches the elven-lands around the Grey Havens.

It is possible to go north of here, against the current, but much easier is going with the current to the south.

The western shore of the river lies west of here but to enter the wood that line the horizon there seems impossible due to a steep cliff that effectively blocks the way. North, South and East of here the great Lhun runs on and on towards its ultimate goal: the great ocean.

The river flows quietly along here, and you feel at peace in the placid surroundings. You can keep flowing along the river south, or you can go to another part of the river east. Further east, you see the worn trail which leads to the humble lands of the Dwarves.

The river continues peacfully from the south to the north. This delta area of the Lhun meeting the Nan Duin makes huge masses of water here. The current is not very strong, and there is no problem for you to stay on the the same spot.

The river continues peacfully from the south to the north. The current is not very strong, and there is no problem for you to stay on the the same spot. To the west you see a quite large island, covered with trees.

The river grows real wide here, flowing slowly through the flat landscape. It continues west and south. East of here, you are able to spot a trail.

The river floats steadily along here, calming your fears about what might exist so far from the towns. You can continue onto the river going west, or you could go to the trail south. The river continues to the north too, enraged.

The eastern shore can be reached easily while open and more turbulent waters lie westward.

Directly to the east stands a wooden dock allowing large boats to be tied up to shelter safely from the sea. The water is quite calm here and the ocean opens up to the west, while coastal waters continue northeast. A hollow in the rocks to the south might provide a safe landing.

Here the tributary mixes its waters with the main river. Just above your head is a low bridge which you can climb up to without any difficulty. The tributary arrives from the west and quickly loses its identity when thrown together with the larger flow. Fish are mingling among the rocks, looking like they are hungry.

The river narrows to the north. To the east you can see a tributary meld with the river. The water is very clear here, and you can easily see the sandy bottom beneath you. Small fish dart in and out among rocks, and green aquatic plants sway in the current.

You have reached the end of Lhun Street. There are far fewer people here than further south on the street. Although you can see the north gate of Forlond ahead of you, it appears that it is used very rarely. To the west you can see some benches arranged in a circle. It appears to be a meeting place. Off to the east is a small building.

You are still on Lhun Street but you have moved away from the crowded part of the street near all the shops. The pace is much slower here and you can enjoy a leisurely walk. Up ahead you can see the north gate of Forlond and a park lies to your west. On the east is a building with a greal deal of noise coming from it, but there does not appear to be an entrance from this side.
104478: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

Certainly not as many elves bustle about this section of the street. You are allowed the luxury of walking softly and breathing in the warm sea air and gentle breeze. Those that are so inclined can stroll west along a beautiful shaded lane under the shelter of many trees. To the north past the northern gate lies Ered Luin, one of the few remaining dwarven strongholds. Several sailors and other rougher looking characters saunter east to a pleasant court filled with activity.
104479:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

You find yourself amid the busiest section of Lhun Street. At all times of the day, elves and visitors to this fair city swarm about, carrying hapless folk along in their wake. Perhaps its central location, between the armoury and tailor's shop plays some part in this. The guards and adventurers that require Gildor's fine merchandise spend much time here, and all elves need the quality clothes offered by the tailor. Also, those hardy folk that will venture northwards, to the Blue Mountains, must pass north to the gate. Southwards the sailors and travellers flow, towards the ships and quays.
104480: There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.

This section of Lhun Street is bordered by many small shops. A building to the west has many arcane symbols in relief around the doorway. It is hard to tell that the street is formed from sandstone blocks since they are all slowly wearing away. Many elves are roaming around here. Some appear to be wandering aimlessly while other obviously have a specific destination in mind.
104481:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
A seagull is soaring above you.

This wide street named after the Gulf of Lhun to the south is made of small sandstone blocks. Traffic on the street is quite high as many elves are out shopping. The quay lies to the south while the street heads off to the north. The city garrison lies to the west.
104482: An elven guard is wandering here, keeping the peace.

Though large, and apparently quite often frequented by the horses belonging to the elven guardsmen, this paved yard is kept completely clean. To the south a large wooden building dominates the area, and to the west a broad gateway opens onto Lhun Street beyond.
104483:
A dented pail has been carelessly left here.
A coil of rope is lying here.
A large torch lies here among the dust.
An elven youth is busy attending to the animals.

Rows of spacious loose-boxes line the back wall of the building, with fresh straw covering their floors, and a stout trough of fresh water at the rear of each one. At one end of the building stand massive bins for oats and bran, and nest to these are piles many buckets. Above them neat rows of pegs are affixed to the wall, where halters and ropes might be hung. A small sign, penned in a meticulous hand, is pinned next to the pegs.
104491: The corpse of a grizzly bear is lying here.

The wood here is a strange combination of birch and spruce. Birds can be heard singing their song up in the trees, where they probably are nesting. In the south-east all the trees disappear before a long ridge of brush-covered hills.
104493: The Old Forest Road comes to an abrupt end at this large wall of brush. During the day, it is obvious where the wall ends and the gates begin because the good-natured inhabitants of this town leave the gates open. But at night, when necessity demands more security and prudence, the gates are closed, and it becomes virtually impossible to discern the end of the wall from the start of the gates.
104494: A small grasshopper clings to a blade of grass, ready to spring.

At a meeting of the Old Forest Road and a wide footpath, a large, well-guarded Beorning settlement has prospered. Completely encased in a wall of trees and brush, the village gates open to the Old Forest Road. The road leaves the village heading west and bends northwards as it cuts a swath through the vale.
104495: Bend in the Old Forest Road
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

Although the road bends and runs to the north and east, the footfalls of many men and animals have worn the edges of the road away. What was a sharp bend in the Old Forest Road is now a gentle curve. In the east, the road leads to a small Beorning village. In the north, the road continues for a short time before turning back to the west.
104496: This patch of barren ground near a bend in the Old Forest Road has been trampled so often by travellers it appears to almost be part of the road. Those following the road from the north often cut through here shortening their journey a few miles before re-entering the road east of here. Often these travellers are in a hurry to reach the small settlement that causes an abrupt end to the eastward path of the Old Forest Road.
104497: A cockroach is scuttling across the floor carrying some debris.

Insects buzz about, oblivious to anyone or anything but their work. This close to the Old Forest Road, the grass that covers much of this land is noticeably absent. It apparently could not survive the heavy off-road foot traffic. In its place, weeds, as oblivious to travellers as the insects are, grow despite the footfalls of man and beast that crushed the life out of the grass.
104498: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

Bees and other insects hover around, gathering nectar from the variety of wildflowers that grow here. In opposition of the plant life that makes up a vast portion of the Anduin Vales, no grass grows in this area near the road. The only plants that can survive this close to a well-travelled road such as the Old Forest Road are weeds, and they grow here is abundance.
104499: A Field Covered with Weeds and Grass

A bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.
A bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.

This field is covered with wide expanses of weeds and flowers in the northern part and thick grass and low bushes in the southern part. Presence of living organisms shows itself by bees buzzing around in the weeds, and ants and beetles crawling around in the grass. The surrounding fields to the north and west are also covered with weeds, while to the south and east the flat plains are covered with thick high grasses and an occasional bush.
104500: Some delicious wild strawberries grow on the ground.

This field is covered in thick tufts of weeds with slender, sharp-edged leaves. Tiny, vine-like plants are creeping along the branches of the few young trees and berry bushes growing here. Also noticeable, are some patches of wild strawberries among the weeds. The grasslands seem to continue in all directions; a slope leads down to a small pond in the south, while in the north a small hill rising above the plains might offer a better view over the landscape.
104507: A cockroach is scuttling across the floor carrying some debris.

The open plains are covered with various grasses, some high and some low. Other annual vegetation raise slightly above the grass, thereby attracting insects to its sparse flowers. To the north the vegetation gets lower and instead of grass mostly weeds seem to cover the soil.
104511: The grasses here seem to be more thick and dense as compared to those to the west. Various flowers and other plants, standing out from the grass, can be seen scattered around the fields. Faint tracks lead to a small hole nearly hidden below the grass. Similar fields stretch on in all directions, though the ground appears to turn rockier and less fertile to the south.
104512: The northern part of these fields, which lie just south of a well-travelled road, are covered with weeds. Contrary to this, the uneven southern part is covered with dense grasses and an occasional sapling of cottonwood or willow. To the far south small fences surrounding cultivated fields can be spotted.
104513: Fields bordering the Old Forest Road

The largest part of this landscape is covered with grass and small saplings of trees. However, the bare soil, imprinted with tracks, is visible through the sparse weeds in the northeastern corner of these fields, as if travellers following the road cut a corner to shorten their journey. Far to the south, some farm buildings are barely visible above the horizon.
104514: Bend in the Old Forest Road

The Old Forest Road makes a deep curve from the north to the east, leaving the way west partly blocked by a steep earthen wall. The surface of the road consists mostly of dry mud with here and there small dots of yellowish green grass. Circular entrances of the nests of swallows are abundant in the steep earthen wall.
104515:
A light boat made of reeds has been left here.
A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.

A quiet pond lies here in the middle of an open field of grass. The sandy bottom of the pond is visible a few feet away from the bank, but then the water seems to suddenly get much deeper; no rushes or water lilies can be seen growing farther away from the shore. The carpet of grass is wet and sinking near the bank and it would be easy to get one's boots soaked there. A dry path leads away from the pond, starting at the southern bank, where someone has built a small jetty.
104516: This field is covered with varied species of grass. Some tussocks, with long stalks with white stripes running from top to bottom, are standing out between the otherwise dark green grasses. A partly burned tree, apparently struck by lightning, provides a viewing point for birds that prey on the small animals living in the grasslands.
104517: Some patches of wild wheat are fighting for space among the bushes and young trees in these overgrown fields. It seems like there was once a wide field of corn here, but now only one small patch in the south seems well-tended. A pile of boards that looks like the remains of a small barn lies hidden amidst a thorny shrubbery in the middle of the field. A narrow dirt path starting from the door of a farmhouse in the west leads down a grassy slope towards a pond far in the north.
104518: A Peaceful Meadow under the Elms

A large beautiful rose bush is blooming here.
Deep inside the bush, there is a red rose with leaves and thorny stem.

Two tall elms shade this smooth meadow with their reaching branches. The one with the thicker trunk is forked near the ground, making it easy to climb; there are also some markings on its bark. A thick rope, firmly attached from both ends to a branch several feet above the ground, sways gently back and forth. A circle of flowering shrubs surrounds the meadow completely; the sweet fragrance that is barely noticeable on their dry leaves must fill the air on warm summer nights.
104519:
A cluster of dark green, feathery fronds flourishes in the shade.
A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.
A large elk gazes coldly at you, chewing on a small branch.

A smooth layer of moss covers the soil and the large rocks sticking out of the ground here. The vegetation gets dense towards a shady depression in the south, while a field of hay extends to the west. No trees grow in this rocky area; only thick ferns and the woody stems of short perennial shrubs rise above the evergreen carpet of moss.
104520: A long-bodied animal with thick brown fur bounds through the trees.

The ground here is wet and the thick weeds that did not make it through the last winter are slowly rotting away, turning into yet another layer of peat. It seems like there once was a pond here; a cluster of rushes is withering on the bottom of a depression, where the carpet of moss makes a squelching sound as it sinks under anything heavier than a rabbit. Shrubs with leathery, oblong leaves are thriving in the fields surrounding the depression.
104521: The lonely birches and pines here are surrounded by a widespread growth of heather. On the ground, the tiny pink flowers fallen off the heathers have rolled into small piles and turned mostly brown. The dry needles and sticks rustle quietly around anything moving through these heathlands, and the knocking sounds of a woodpecker can be heard at times somewhere in the distance.
104525: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

The sandy ground is tightly packed up by the roots of various bushes and plants with woody stems growing here. The slope is steepest down in the north, where the heath seems to continue as far as the eye can see, but there are also some dangerous-looking spots on the rocky slope in the west. Stumps, mounds and other odd shapes lie amidst the tangled undergrowth; clear paths are scarce here.
104526: Harsh ground to the west slowly gives way to a more hospitable environment. Scattered shrubs grow in sporadic clusters, while traces of heather intermingle with other wild flowers. The ground itself is a mixture of sand and rich farming soil. Aside from a make-shift trail that serves no apparent purpose, the land seems mostly unaltered from its natural state. A faint path leads from a ruined building in the east to a cottage in the north.
104527: A woodpecker is here, tapping on a tree.

A small field of gravel has formed into this hollow, surrounded by tall pines at the edge of the heathlands. The source of the gravel seems to be at the hillside in the south, where the roots of the trees and bushes growing on the slope have failed to stop a landslide. Some dying trunks, brought down by the rolling gravel, are lying on the bottom of the hollow while drying up and dropping their last leaves one by one. A high hill rises above the heath in the south, but climbing that way might be even harder than it looks.
104535:
Some pine nuts lie scattered upon the ground.
A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

This is the highest point in this chain of hilltops stretching out to the east and west, yet there are no good places to see far into the heathlands below. Pine trees rise high above the ground here, and even their lowest branches seem unreachable, while younger saplings are sprouting out of the sandy ground among tussocks of grass. One must be careful while walking around here, for there are rolling pine nuts and burly roots above the ground everywhere. Despite the elevated location, even some flowering plants that normally do not thrive in windy locations can be found on the slopes among the trees.
104540: Rocky hills dominate the horizon, yet lower ground lies to the north and east of here. The curvature of this landscape seems to act as a natural wind tunnel, creating gustier conditions than one would expect. Scattered across the hills are various types of pine trees, creating homes for small birds and animals. Most low level foliage is scarce and sure footing is a rarity. To the west the slope moves upward as it reaches its unimpressive apex.
104541: Old and pitiful pine trees dot the area, reaching great heights but lacking many branches. The grass here seems especially weathered, perhaps a result of high winds coming from the south. Occasional shrubs grow between the grasses, though it is difficult to tell if they are dead or alive.
104542: At the centre of these lightly wooded surroundings stands a small cottage, which appears to have been abandoned some time ago. It is made completely of rough stone except for the primitive wooden door which barely sticks out through the thick overgrowth. Jutting up from the roof, a small chimney points to the sky. Five long, flat rocks create steps leading up to the humble abode.
104543: A spirit floats towards you and howls with an evil laughter.

The rough stones forming the walls of this cottage are covered with thick layers of moss. The front door, still sturdy despite the very damp air and deep dents carved by sharp blades, provides an effective closure to the outside world. Remains of furniture and household items are scattered on the floor, while in the far corner various bones, some probably humanoid of origin, lie partly covered between some ragged clothing.
104544: The ground is soft and squishy underfoot. Creeping fig has taken over the majority of this soft landscape, creating a beautiful dark green blanket of small round leaves. A few young cottonwoods struggle to break free from the foliage. To the south an old cottage can be spotted.
104545: This field is covered with wide expanses of grass and flowers without any obstructions for large animals or humanoids. Hoofprints of those animals visiting these abundant fields during wet days have been captured in the muddy soil. On the lower somewhat sheltered grounds leaves litter the ground, dwarfing tiny ants that carry them.
104546: The fields are covered with grass, weeds, and low bushes. A large willow has toppled over, creating a long barrier of thick boughs and thin branches to grow out from its top side. In the eastern part of the fields, a half-erect pile of wood, most likely a poorly constructed shelter barely able to stand, sits in the fields. To the west a pair of elms form a natural landmark.
104547:
A Beorning herder is standing here, watching around.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.
A young goat playfully charges and hops away.
A goat is here, grazing in the hills.

Numerous little holes fill the serene grasslands, it is most likely an underground tunnelling system of some indigenous rodents. The grasslands drop down steeply in the east, ending in a rocky slope leading to a crevice. The divide is shallow at first, allowing travelling down into it, but is already twice the height of a Beorning further to the east.
104555:
A woodchuck is watching for enemies here.
A large hawk-like bird is here overlooking its territory.

Leafless trees, signs of a flourishing past, mark these dry fields. Between the dusty soil small tussocks of grass and patches of low weed fight for the little water which is left underground. Apparently the ground water flow has been altered radically by the tectonic movement in the past, from which the result, a crevice stretching many miles south, is visible intersecting the fields.
104556: The ground here is rocky and hard. Running to the east for miles lies a long strip of ruptured earth. It appears the ground gave way to the emerging stone after some sort of tectonic shift under the surface. Though shallow and narrow enough to pose no obstruction to man nor beast here, it seems to have acted as a natural barrier to the local flora, separating different types of naturally growing plants and wild flowers. To the south the ground is split apart by a deep crevice.
104557: A large hawk-like bird is here overlooking its territory.

Fields from the north and south meet here at what appears to be a natural stone barrier, running for miles to the east and west. The stone is short and easily walked over, but it seems to have acted as a hindrance to the low-lying vines on its west side. It is likely the protruding stone originated from some subterranean shift or movement.
104558: A short, natural barricade of stone protrudes from the ground, rupturing the fields in an unbroken line. While it stretches for miles to the west, it seems to taper off slowly in height steadily towards the northeast. Some small patches of dead grass lie on top of the six feet wide protrusion. A few pine trees are scattered about, one of which apparently was toppled by the rock emerging from underneath its base.
104559:
A small mushroom grows nearby.
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

The field here is covered with grass and flowers, enriching the landscape with their colours. A small ridge, some ten feet long, creates a shady place where brown coloured mushrooms, some with teeth marks of small animals, are prospering. To the north a hollow road leading to some sort of forest is barely visible between the grasslands.
104560: A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

The northern border of the Old Forest Road is covered by huge trees. The grass to the south once was evenly abundant on the road, however today the road is only covered with small patches of dry grass in between large patches of mud. After a while the trees to the north become so dense that they form an impenetrable wall. High above, in one of the huge trees a small wooden platform has been built.
104561: Junction in the Old Forest Road

Between grassy plains the Old Forest Road, covered with tracks of heavy carts, runs from east to west. A muddy path, to which most fresh tracks lead, runs south into the open plains. To the northwest a settlement, protected by dense trees and a wooden wall, dominates the view. A stone, engraved with some markings, has been placed at the junction of the path and road.
104562: Due to centuries of travel the road has been worn out, now forming a hollow way between the plains. The road itself is partly overgrown, but some imprints of hoofs are still present. The steep banks bordering it are covered in weeds and small flowers, with here and there a small hole in them. Further away the flat plains are covered with grasses and small shrubs.
104563: The old hollow road runs through vast grasslands, and is itself partly overgrown with grasses and weeds. Stones, which used to border the road, are barely visible between tussocks of grass and piled up dirt. In the grasslands surrounding the road, some solitary trees and low bushes grow here and there.
104564: The grasslands are covered with a thick vegetation of typical grassland plants, like clover, white daisies, purple thistle and yellow dandelion. Some grey stones, mostly covered with yellow lichen, placed in a circular pattern form a relic of an ancient civilisation. To the north of those stones a depression splits the plains into two parts.
104565:
There are two mushrooms here.
A reddish fawn romps harmlessly among the tender grass shoots.

The grass grows high on the dark black soil, leaving no space for clover or any other weeds. A few large grey stones covered with lichen dot the grassland. In the shade of one of these stones small mushrooms grow on the fertile soil. To the north a road, lying lower than the surrounding plains, runs from east to west, while to the west a trail leads to the south.
104566: A clear spring babbles as cool water trickles out of the ground.

This trail, covered with fresh tracks of cartwheels, is bordered by some large willow trees and rotten logs of former trees. A small spring, dotted with animal tracks, makes the path muddy, but also provides water to the trees and the surrounding grassland. The trail splits off a larger road in the north and continues its way to the south.
104567: The grass in this grassland has grown to a height of a few feet, indicating a rich soil beneath it. At some places the long stalks have toppled due to the wind and rain. The quiet sounds of small animals rustling through the high grass and buzzing insects fill the air. To the north the grasslands are interrupted by a road and a small path intercepts them to the east.
104568: A red-furred doe wanders peacefully among the grass.

The ground is invisible because of the thick layer of vegetation. Grass covers most of the plains, except where young trees and low bushes have taken over its role. Some unnatural ditches divide the plains into regular sections. Water has collected into each of the even ditches giving reeds and other wetland plants a suitable habitat.
104569:
A swallow flies high above the ground.
A trained horse (Rood) is standing here, ridden by you.

Lush grass and large bushes cover the fertile ground of these plains. A few scattered trees dot the landscape, the shade from their leaves providing some protection from the elements to the creatures that live in the area. Signs of small fauna can be seen across the landscape, the most obvious being an animal trail leading south toward a copse of birch trees.
104570: Close to the path in the west the remains of a camp fire can be seen; a circle of grey stones surround a patch of burned earth. Around the stones the grasses covering the plains have been pressed down by something large. A few skeletons of deer, with knife marks all over them, lie scattered around those flattened spaces.
104571: The trail, consisting of bare soil with small pebbles, is replaced by rich grasslands to the east. In this area a dark patch, probably created by a fire, is visible. Just west of the trail a haystack with a long wooden pole in the middle has been made by the local people. Beyond the haystack cultivated fields dominate the view.
104572: A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

Dry grasses, cut from their roots close to the soil, cover the extent of this hayfield. Scattered among the yellowish grass pyramid-shaped constructions made of thin wooden stakes have been erected. On these wooden frames fluffy patches of grass have been spread out which are drying in the wind. To the east a haystack has been constructed next to a trail, while to the south a small ditch borders the same trail.
104573: A worm is here slithering around.

The landscape here has two quite different looks. To the west of a stone wall pasture fields dominate the view, while east of the wall the rich black soil, typical of this area, is revealed. On these recently ploughed fields birds look for easy meal consisting of worms and larvae.
104574:
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A grey bird with a bright orange-red belly sits here, singing a melodic tune.

A lush, verdant landscape is offset only by the slight smell of fresh manure. Short-cropped patches of grass dotted with daisies cover the nearby soil, while from some distance way the sound of mooing comes from the silhouettes of cattle. A single oak tree towers above and provides an almost unnaturally large canopy. In the distance to the north, a hand-crafted rock wall no more than four feet tall intersects the fields.
104575:
A bee flies around here, collecting nectar from the flowers.
A grey bird with a bright orange-red belly sits here, singing a melodic tune.

The surroundings depict a pasture full of local animal life. The grass grows tall and seems healthy. A hand-crafted rock wall runs down from the north of this place of solace to a crevice in the southwest where it is joined by a wooden fence, which keeps the herds at a safe distance from the steep edge.
104576:
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.
A worm is here slithering around.

At the centre of this field lies a giant depression, full of natural waste. It seems its caretakers are meticulous about its planning and upkeep, because no detritus is on the ground around it. It is impossible to tell how deep the pit goes, but its contents fill it to the point of staying flush with the ground. Surrounding the pit, grass and other vegetation seem especially healthy.
104577:
On the ground, there are two potatoes.
On the ground, there are three carrots.
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Starting from the farmstead which stands in the east, these fields show a variety of crops; carrots, potatoes and cabbage are all growing here. Among the fields you can see one that lies fallow revealing the rich, black soil characteristic of the farms found in this area. A wooden fence separates the most western fields from the edge of a ravine.
104578:
A large, loyal falcon is circling above.
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

The cultivated rye fields are separated by low earthen walls. The rye grows over a foot high, with the occasional blue flower popping up here and there. Some small tracks lead through the dense fields to a partly overgrown trail in the east. A wooden fence prevents careless animals or others from walking over the edge of the fields onto a pile of loose rocks leading into a deep crevice.
104579:
A pig is here, covered in mud.
A pig is here, covered in mud.

This small yard, with here and there a tussock of low grass, ends at a wooden barn to the north and a small house to the south. Near the barn, within an enclosure of wooden poles, some pigs enjoy the mud, while at the other end a large pile of wood, chopped into small blocks is placed against the wall of the small house. From the west the smell of decomposing plants enters the yard, while to the east the yard continues.
104580:
A circular stone well has been built here.
A sturdy pack horse is standing here.

The trail ends in an open space with a small house to the south. The space itself is covered in dust with here and there a tussock of grass or a lonely weed. A shallow water-well, covered with a reed thatched roof, has been erected in the southeastern corner of the yard. This well provides the local inhabitants, their domesticated animals and the seedbeds with young vegetables ready to be replanted in surrounding fields with water.
104581: The trail across the grassland is marked with tracks of carts and cattle and bordered with some moss covered grey stones. One of them appears to have some markings on it. Some flies hover above a fresh pile of droppings on the path. A partly overgrown track leading south diverges from the main path leading to some buildings.
104582: The trail curves from north to west through the rich fields before leading to a small village. Fresh tracks of carts and some droppings at the edge of the trail indicate recent humanoid use. At the edge of the trail the vestiges of a cart, wheels broken and the planks rotten, is partly hidden by the vegetation. At the southern border regular stacked willow branches form a few tall piles.
104587: A small animal, all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

Grasses and other vegetation grow abundantly on the rich soil. The local birds build their nests in the few solitary trees growing in this area, while animal tracks leading from small holes beneath the trunks of those trees. The plains extend to all directions except to the west where they are bordered by a trail.
104615:
A shallow pond is here, tinted green with algae.
A shrub with maple-like leaves is growing here.

A small copse of birch trees surrounds a waterhole that provides sustenance to fauna in the area; trails made by deer and small mammals converge to this place from the surrounding plains. This permanent source of water allows for a lush grass cover that provides smaller mammals with shelter. Several shrubs are scattered among the trees; laden with berries they make ideal food sources for birds and other small animals.
104616: On the ground the grass seems healthy; dry ears with spikelets consisting of some florets raise above the green level of the leaves. The purple flowers of thistles add colour to the surrounding landscape. Some animal tracks, marked by droppings in the flattened grass lead to the east where a few birch trees decorate the horizon.
104617:
A magpie is flying around looking for some food.
A nightingale is here, chirping a sweet melody.

The willow saplings have been planted close together in the fertile soil. Crowded in such a dense grove, the willows have grown straight and tall with few side branches at all. Some open spaces in this miniature forest and piles of neatly stacked branches north near a trail indicate recent harvesting of some of the year-old saplings. To the south the young trees are replaced by older knotted ones.
104618: A reddish fawn romps harmlessly among the tender grass shoots.

A trail worn by the passage of both humans and animals passes through the plains. Nevertheless, recent tracks are scarce and small shrubs and bushes grow in different spots along it. The trail runs along a gentle slope from the harvested fields to the west towards small copse of trees to the east.
104619: The trail, completely covered by long thick grass approximately three feet tall, bends from a northward to a westward direction, avoiding the marsh to the south. East of the trail young willow trees, with thin straight branches emerging from their knotted crowns, grow in unnaturally straight lines.
104620:
A nest is here.
A magpie is sitting here protecting her nest.
A nightingale is here, chirping a sweet melody.
A magpie is flying around looking for some food.

The trees in the southern marshy part of the willow fields are very old, while to the north on dryer ground the trees seem younger and healthier. Thick crowns, spanning several feet sit on top of the thick short trunks. From these crowns thin branches make the top of the trees look like giant hedgehogs. At the shade side of the willow trunks brown fungi decorate them. To the south and west wetlands border the forest.
104621:
A small boar with big yellow tusks looks eager to fight.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

Lush grasses cover these fertile fields which stretch south and east. While birds and small mammals seem to make up most of the animal life, hoof marks form the evidence of grazing by large mammal. Occasional ash and birch trees dot these plains, providing shelter for sparrows and other birds that can be seen flying about. To the west the grasses are replaced by fields of old willows.
104622: These rich grasslands stretch west and south, the tall grass carpet broken only by the occasional birch or elm tree. Shrubs and a small patch of willow trees surround a small depression filled with muddy water containing small larvae and bugs. Trails left by large animals feeding on the leaves of these shrubs are marked by dried droppings and grazed leaves. To the northeast the gloomy eaves of Mirkwood can be seen in the distance.
104623: Sparse brush covers the terrain here, providing shelter and maintenance to myriad smaller animals. An overgrown and seldom used trail is all that is left between the stones bordering once a wide path. Little evidence is left of anyone using this route at all, save for the remains of a small camp site. However, northwards and westwards cultivated fields are the sign of recent human activity in this area.
104624:
An erect shrub with green pinnate leaves is growing here.
Inside the shrub, there are some crimson raspberries.
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

The fields are covered with regular spaced stumps of agriculture products like corn and wheat, with deep tracks of wheels marking the places where carts stood to load the harvested crops. On the ground mice run around collecting and eating the leftovers, while in the sky birds spying for prey circle around. To the north a low earthen wall covered with shrubs blocks the passage.
104625:
A fine pelt lies here, soft and smooth.
A large stone fireplace with a roaring fire warms the room.

A small but well-maintained and well-furnished house features a big, warm fireplace with deer pelts around it. Dried leaves are used to decorate the windows. Around the room various baskets, at different stages of completion, lie about. A workbench with typical basket weaver tools is placed beneath one of the windows. A screen partially blocks the way to an area in the back of the house.
104626:
A plain shirt is on the ground.
A sturdy bed made from solid oak lies here, covered in warm blankets.
On the bed, there is a warm blanket.

This small room is separated from the main part of the house by a screen. A large, brown fur covers most of the floor and the walls were constructed using thick wooden beams. A small window shuttered by wooden planks provides the room with some daylight. A pile of old, dusty clothes has been piled up in the far corner of the room, and a sturdy bed is placed under the small window.
104627:
A stove stands against one wall here.
A wooden cupboard stands here.
A peaceful farmer is here, whistling merrily.
A cute little girl is here.
The farmer's wife is bustling busily around.

Small windows made in the thick wooden walls enable the sunlight to penetrate to the inside of the building.
