The edges of the road slope down to wide, shallow ditches that are overgrown with tall grasses and scrub bushes. This brush becomes more dense to the south and east, where taller bushes rise up in great thickets that block movement in those directions.
116835: A wide, paved road turns from south to east here. The road is raised slightly above the surrounding land, and it slopes down to shallow ditches on either side. It is paved with large, uniform stones that are relatively flat on top, creating a smooth surface for the passage of carts and carriages. There appear to have once been gravel paths on either side of the road, above the ditches; over time, however, these gravel surfaces have eroded into the ditches, leaving only a bump as the sides of the road slope downwards. To the north and west, beyond the ditches alongside the road, tall shrubs rise up, tangled and thorny enough to prevent passage in those directions.
116836: A road runs from south to north here, its wide roadbed raised above the fields that border it. The road is paved with wide stones, naturally shaped but flat enough on top to create a smooth and uniform surface. Here and there corners of these paving stones have crumbled or broken, leaving small gaps that risk a turned ankle for those walking along the road, but are not large enough to create a bumpy journey for carriages or carts that follow its passage. Off each side of the road, a short slope leads down to a wide ditch that is hard to see due to the brush and grasses that grow tall enough to appear level with the grasses in the fields beyond. To the east and west, beyond the ditches and fields, tall lines of tangled brush rise up, blocking movement.
116837: A wide road runs through the fields here. The road bed is raised, paved with flat, square stones that fit closely together. Here and there patches of some sort of cement fill the gaps between the paving stones, securing them in place and smoothing the road surface. The edges of the road slope down to a gravel walking path that runs along each side before continuing down into shallow ditches. The gravel paths look unused: tall herbaceous weeds poke through, and the gravel surface is eroding into the ditches. To the east and south the fields next to the road quickly give way to obstructive lines of brush, tangled and dense enough to block movement.
116838: A raised road, paved with large, flat stones runs from west to east here. The paving stones fit together closely, although in places there are wider gaps left from damage to the stones or a shifting of the stones over time. In these gaps the surface beneath can be glimpsed: a packed mix of fine gravel and rock dust, forming a stable base that allows for drainage. The edges of the road slope down to wide ditches before rising again into the fields on either side of the road. In these ditches grow different grasses than in the fields beyond, with larger, taller stems and a spreading rather than clump-forming habit.
116839: The north curb of the lane stretches out into a disused dirt track, while the main road continues east and west. In the cracks of the lane, wild oats grow stubbornly among the horse dung and gravel. On the either side of the road, a shallow ditch grows thick with rustling bulrush and reeds. To the south, rolling fields of barley grow well-tended before some rather rugged hills. To the north, fields of oats thrive in neat, flat parcels.
116840: A hilly arm of Chetwood presses into the path of the road from the southeast, forcing the road to press along a decrepit stone wall to the north and west. The gravel shoulder of the road completely disappears, a problem little aided by the derelict conditions of the main paving stones as it rounds the bend. Over the wall, fields of alfalfa grow green and hale, stretching to the vista.
116841: The western shoulder of the lane has been choked off by loose dirt and rocks that have tumbled down from a sloping field. A great view of the land stretches up, bunched with juniper scrub, gnarly blackthorn, and sparse grasses. A hilly arm of Chetwood jabs its way into the road from the east, forcing it to narrow as it bends around to the northeast.
116842: A swallow flies high above the ground.

A road of cracked paving stones is bordered by loose gravel on either side. In places, the cracks in the pavement are so severe that it is easier to pull a cart along the gravel than it is to traverse the ridges and fissures created by the cracks. Hills rise to either side: the Bree-land forest looming in the east, and a slick ascent to a barren ridge in the west.
116843: The raised lane is lined on each side by long, narrow ditches and leads exactly to the north and south. The road is paved with smooth, polished stones and is still in great condition. However, huge blocks of stone are beginning to move, most likely the passed ages finally start to take their tribute.
116844: The raised road runs in a straight line to the north and south and is in good condition. Huge trees with big trunks and hard bark line the road beside long, narrow ditches. In between the trees lie many large, white boulders. Smooth paving stones in the road are beginning to shift from the heavy daily traffic.
116845: Small grasses grow all over the nearly flat meadow. Spots of different coloured grasses are the only change in colour as far as the eye can see. To the north the grass gets lower and slightly darker. A well-paved and well-travelled road lines the eastern horizon.
116846: The raised road runs straight to the north and to the south, lying in a constant shade of ancient trees. The trees have bordered this road for countless years and their crowns rise high above, forming archways big enough even for giants. Long, narrow ditches are dug into the ground between the road and the trees.
116847: The bark of the ancient trees lining the road is smooth and very hard. The road itself seems to be in very good condition. It is raised slightly above the surrounding landscape, and paved with smooth stones. Long, narrow ditches are dug into the ground, running parallel to the road.
116848: Running to the north and to the south and being bordered by ancient, huge trees which form a giant archway over the road, the lane looks more like an avenue for kings from old and forgotten days; not as the path of travellers, adventurers, and merchants that it is today. The road is slightly raised above the surrounding land, and paved with smooth stones.
116850: A large paved road is here, worn down from many years of use. Countless travellers and wheels have left their marks on the surface of the road. Dust hovers over the ground from constant use, and its firm surface allows for easy travel.
116851: Many trees dot the plains here south of a thick wall of thorny bush. Light heath spreads out in all directions as far as can be seen, except for a low ridge of hills that rises to the south-west. In the distance to the south-east is a rocky crevice that dips steeply from the otherwise flat plains.
116852: The upward slope of the plains grant a commanding view in all directions. To the north the plains are covered in tall bushes, while to the west the plains stretch towards hills in the distance. Eastwards the ground drops steeply into a narrow valley, but the slope is so sharp that it is impossible to descend from this point.
116853:
A brown bear is sleeping here.
A brown bear is sleeping here.

This small cave in the hillside is thick with the musty scent of wild animal, who must have made this their home. Scraps of fur and a single, gnawed bone make this all the more clear. The only exit is via a small hole in the roof of the cave.
116854: Gorse bushes and a few shrubs are the only flora to be seen on these rugged plains. The rough terrain expands all around, except to the east where the ground drops sharply into a narrow valley which runs north-south through the uneven plains. The descending slope is covered with a scree of small stones such that descent could be extremely hazardous.
116855: Few plants grow atop this rocky ridge, except for some short thick grass that grows amongst the boulders. Westwards the land descends into a wide area of plains, while to the east it dips into a narrow valley before continuing to rise into a range of tall hills.
116856: This flat, grassy shelf of rock juts out above the river. Below, the river continues the process of eroding the riverbank. To the east, at the foot of a steep bank can be seen the end of a narrow valley while below to the west can be seen a rocky inlet. Southward a dense brush lies beyond the river and far in the distance a narrow tower rises against the horizon.
116857: The edge of the brush meets the edge of a cliff, with trees ending at a sheer and quite impassable drop to the south. The edge is a fine vantage point, giving a view of a long valley running far to the south. By contrast, the view is obscured to the north, where bushes grow denser. Rough plains stretch out to the west.
116859: At the edge of the brush to the north, the old trees and rough bushes of the brushland give way to more sparsely growing plains. The ground is covered with low undergrowth with the occasional clump of trees. Further to the south, the greenery gives way all together.
116860: The transition between the open plains to the south and the untamed brushland to the north is marked by a dense wall of old trees. The ground is dotted with trees and small bushes and the occasional large boulder. The trees here are much younger, however, than those that rise amidst the bushes to the north.
116861: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

The open plains to the south gradually give way to wiry underbrush here, and to the north the bushes thicken greatly at the edge of a dense scrubland. The Fornost-Bree road is not far away to the west, however, for those of a less adventurous nature.
116862: The wide plains continue unbroken, the only break from the monotony provided by the occasional tree or gorse bush. To the west, however, the land begins to rise gently into a range of rocky hills. Northwards, a line of trees on the horizon marks the border of what seems to be a thick brushland.
116863: A brown fox is here, looking for some rabbits to chew up.

Here the ground begins to rise up from the plains, into a range of hills that extend southward. The ground becomes increasingly rocky and the flora more sparse as the hills ascend. The occasional rocky outcrop provides a good place to pause and survey the surrounding landscape.
116864: This large tract of open land stretches away to the south and to the north in a wide sea of green grass. The road is not too far away to the west, the only visible symbol of civilisation. Far to the east stands a range of hills, among which one tall peak stands out alone.
116865: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

The land here is flat and open, with only the occasional tree or bush to break the monotony. The ground is covered with thick grass which seems to support a variety of small grazing animals. Far to the east can be seen a range of hills, but it is difficult to guess how long it would take to reach them.
116866: The land begins to rise gently up from the plains into a range of rocky hills running from the north to the south. The low, bushy ridge separates broad sections of fields to the west and flat, rocky ground to the east. The vantage point offered here shows numerous landmarks. A road stretches out in the west, with a large ruin beyond it.
116867: The land here is wide and open, but to the west it begins to rise gently towards a range of hills in the distance. To the south, the ground dips into a shallow depression. North and east the plains continue as far as the eye can see.
116868: The ground of this shallow depression is covered with thick grass and is marshy in places, where rain-water running down from above has collected in small pools and mires. From this low point it is not possible to discern much of the surrounding area, except for the faint sound of running water to the south and the top of a rocky ridge to the west.
116869:
A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.
A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

Rocks and boulders litter the ground here, as the land rises into the hills to the north. The occasional gorse bush is the only plant-life to be seen. Here and there little gullies have been formed by water running down the slopes after heavy rainfall. The abundance of small stones and pebbles makes it difficult to keep a sure footing.
116870: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

A wide area of plains stretches away to the north here. To the east the land dips briefly, before starting a gentle rise into a distant range of hills. To the south, the land remains flat but becomes more uneven being covered with rocks and boulders. The road from Bree to Fornost can be seen not far away to the west.
116871: A sharp-eyed hawk is here stalking some prey.

The ground here is flat though somewhat uneven, being covered with rocks and boulders, some of great size. The occasional rustling sound indicates the presence of some wildlife, though of what sort is unclear. The land to the north remains flat, while to the east a small hillock rises up. To the south, a wooded area can be seen, suggesting a water source in this otherwise desolate area.
116872:
A low and wide-spread tree grows here.
On the tree's branches, there is a juicy plum.
A river otter splashes playfully here.

This is the northern bank of a fast-flowing river. Many trees grow on the bank, though the undergrowth is not nearly as thick as on the other side of the river, where the edge of a dense brush can be seen. To the north, the trees give way to rocky plains and hills. Not far from here to the west lies the Fornost-Bree road.
116873: A heron is stalking the area, looking for fish.

The wooded riverbank is bounded to the south and east by a wide river. On the far side of the river a rising expanse of dense brushland can be seen, and only the occasional animal cry hints as to what lies inside. North of here the sparse trees give way to rocky hills, outriders of the North Downs which stretch all the way to Fornost and beyond.
116874: A small animal , all covered in spines, snuffles amongst the undergrowth.

The ground rises here to form the start of a small hillock, dotted with bushes and low shrubs. To the north, a sharp gradient leads up into a ridge of hills, while to the east the land flattens out to open, rocky plains. To the south the plains gradually give way to woody plains and wild brush beyond a rushing river.
116875: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

A natural dip in the surrounding hills and plains has formed into a little inlet which feeds the river to the south with run-off water. The steeply rising banks on three sides make this a secluded and tranquil spot, with only the sound of running water disturbing the silence.
116876: The narrow valley runs north-south, bounded by steep slopes. To the west climbs a steep yet traversable slope, while to the east a sheer cliff looms upwards for hundreds of feet. Erosion and continued rockfalls have covered the ground in small rocks and stones, but also made for a passable way up.
116877: A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

The valley comes to an abrupt end here at the base of an almost sheer cliff. Around the base of the cliff are large piles of rocks and boulders that have accumulated from rockfalls in the past. The sides of the valley are too steep to climb at this point, so the only choice is to leave via the south.
116878: The bottom of this dip in the downs runs north-south. Rocks and boulders litter the ground, some seeming to have fallen recently from above. To the east, the hillside rises sharply again, making progress in that direction impossible. The valley is strangely quiet, the only sound being the occasional pebble falling from above.
116879:
A reddish-brown shrub with purplish-pink flowers grows here.
Inside the shrub, there are two clusters of purplish-pink flowers.
A tall pine tree grows here.
A solitary hermit is sitting here, meditating with a serene expression.

The valley comes to an abrupt end here, with a steep drop to the river below. A small patch of ground has been cultivated to form a small, secluded garden in which grow various strange and unusual plants. A calm serenity fills this place, in part owing to the muted roar of a nearby waterfall.
116880:
A large wooden full shield is on the ground.
A cutlass is on the ground.
A shortsword is on the ground.

This mossy-walled cave appears to be a natural formation in the hillside. Water drips occasionally from the low ceiling, making the only sound in this otherwise silent place. Scraps of war-gear lie abandoned on the floor, much of it unusable, evidence perhaps of a deserter, or some warrior embracing a more peaceful life.
116881: The dense line of trees has been pushed back here, with scattered stumps showing how the field was cleared to create a flat, open plot of land. Evidence of a small camp site is still visible on the ground, a resting point off the long road to the east that has been repeatedly used and abandoned.
116882: Separated by a long, waterlogged ditch, the fields run up to the road to the east and off into the distance in all other directions. Patches of bindweed sprout from the damp soil, covering the old marks of what used to be a trail headed west. Rows of trees rise to the south, limiting the view of the fields that wind between them.
116883: What was once a broad plot of land is now a roiling sea of spiny brush and tall grasses, its rampant growth standing in contrast to the calmer fields to the east and west. The bushes join a dense copse of trees to the south, where crumbled walls peek over the horizon. The road, far to the east, is barely visible.
116884: This broad, square patch of fallow land is abandoned and empty of crops. Far from the safety of Fornost, the surrounding fields are much the same, left quiet and empty to be reclaimed by the wilderness. The road is some distance to the east, and more fields can be seen to the south.
116885: This field is covered in layers of weeds and other plants, growing wild despite the aged signs that it had once been cleared for farming. Halfway to being brush here, the farmlands vanish between dense bushes to the south but are easily traversed to the north and east.
116886: A shaggy-haired bull stands here, calmly looking around.

This corner of the field bears the mark of tilling, but time has worn away the work of Men. The edges of the farmland are defined by overgrown plots of trees, the artificial borders long decayed. The empty fields stretch to the south, with other routes barred by thickly-built fences.
116887: Trees loom all around, and thorny bushes grow in a whorl up towards the thick branches. The only traversable path is a narrow corridor that leads north- south, through the dense brush to the north and into more open plains to the south. The surrounding landscape is obscured, and further landmarks cannot be seen.
116888: An orchid of light violet petals blossoms nearby.

Hidden from sight by bushes to the north and tall rows of trees that conceal the surroundings, this field hosts hastily-arranged rows of unusual crops. A small wooden shed holds tools and various small barrels, evidence of organised activity in maintaining this curiously clandestine farm.
116889:
An apple tree with bright green leaves grows here.
On the tree's branches are two apples.

The fallow land has given rise to wild, brambly growth, stretching from the dense trees to the east into a broad thorny expanse to the west. The bountiful field is hidden beneath stabbing branches and prickly thorns, giving an air of aggression to the natural flora. The field clears out to the north and south.
116890: You see two handfuls of clover on the ground.

Bushes thickly blanket the old field, their stubborn thorns sticking to all in reach. Impassable to the west and dense to the south and east, the bushes recede to the north. Looming grimly in the distance to the south is a great, decaying ruin, visibly overgrown by the dense growth that surrounds it.
116891: On the ground, there are two handfuls of clover.

Dense thorny bushes grow tall here, sprawling across a field that is littered with crumbled rock. To the south stands a dark mossy wall, less a construction than an ordered pile of stones. The fields spread out to the east, with more overgrown brush to the north.
116892: Ringed by thick bushes and dense trees, this dry and barren plot of land lies empty of flora. A few scraggly shrubs dot the pale brown soil. Not far to the southwest a decaying ruin creeps over the horizon, giving an altogether deathly feel to this faded farmland. A rising hill blocks passage to the east.
116893: A shaggy-haired bull stands here, calmly looking around.

Lying at the base of an ancient stone wall, the field is filled with scattered stones, each weathered by time to various degrees. The decaying wall to the west and south stands more due to its own weight than any remaining integrity in its construction. Nearby, the sound of a river can be heard.
116894:
A large ram guards his flock of sheep.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.

This is a sloped patch of land ending above the northern back of a river. There is no safe way to access the river from this vantage point, but the clear view south shows a stone bridge to the southeast, and thick bushes reaching the old stone fortress to the southwest. The plains continue smoothly to both the east and west.
116895:
A large thorny branched shrub is growing here.
On the shrub, there are two piles of blackberries.
A large brown snake with black patches is coiled here.

Saplings and low bushes grow sporadically from the thick wall of trees to the east and south, slowly filling these plains with wild flora. The fields themselves are uneven, showing deep signs of erosion from what was once a gentle slope towards the plains to the east. The barely-visible road curves around to the east and south, but there is no way to reach it from here.
116896: Curving around a tall slope of trees growing into the side of a hill to the south-west, these plains are uneven and damp from runoff from the fields above. Erosion has worn empty, depressed patches into the soil filled with stagnant mud. More gentle elevation leads westwards, while thick bushes and a low stone wall create a sharp border to the east.
116897:
A large skin is lying here.
A fishing rod has been left here.
A small barrel made of aged oak and strong iron hoops stands here.
A sturdy crate made of nailed wooden planks sits on the floor.

This small shed is strewn with hastily-stored objects. The bare wooden floor is marked with scrapes and other marks of heavy objects being moved carelessly across it. What those objects are is quite clear, given the stack of heavy crates piled in a corner. The walls are well-constructed, insulating this place from the world outside, save for a small window.
116898: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

The plains stretch out broad and flat here, west of the road. Cut off from the farmland to the north, the open plains to the south and west leave this place with a sense of isolation. Distantly to the south is the shadow of a great construction, barely visible through spotty brushland and trees.
116899: Broad patches of trees form natural barriers to the north and south, bordering a grassy, overgrown field. The wind faintly howls as it is channeled through this natural corridor. The fields stretch east towards the distant road, and west deeper into the wilderness. No other landmarks are visible.
116900: The corpse of a dreadful snake is lying here.

Enclosed by thick trees and wooden fences, this patch of field has been isolated from the farmland barely visible around it. The soil is clear from any underbrush, but it has not been prepared for sowing and the only signs of growth are the slow reclamation of the surrounding wilderness.
116901: Heavy Brush near the Road to Fornost

The ground under the brush exists in eternal dimness, as very little light filters through the low, bushy canopy. The thick vegetation continues far to the east and north. Several small holes obscure dark underground passageways for animals and insects.
116902: The brush here is very dense, and is covered in a thick layer of vines and leaves. The ground is rooty and uneven, and small animal holes dot the ground. A precipitous gorge opens up to the south, preventing further travel in that direction. The heavy brush continues far to the north and east.
116903: Heavy brush continues for miles in all directions but south, where the ground drops away into a steep cliff. The ground here has a thick layer of decomposing leaves and moss, and this gives the brush a musty smell. No path can be gleaned through the undergrowth.
116904: Forested Brush near a Winding Trail
A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

A carpet of rotting leaves that covers the ground conceals damp, black soil. A small clump of massive oaks form a small forest in the centre of the brush here. Their thick canopy blots out all but a few sunbeams, even during the brightest of days.
116905: Scattered shrubs of various shapes and sizes dot the rocky ground here. Long growths of ivy provide a leafy covering to the bulbous flora. Several small holes provide home to small animals, and a hunting ground for snakes and honey badgers. The brush continues far to the east.
116906: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

This is an open area of grassy flatlands which stretch away to the south. The old Fornost-Bree road lies not far to the west while to the north lies a narrow ravine from where issues the sound of rushing water. To the east, the land rises into some rolling hills.
116907: In contrast to the bleak slopes further to the south, the hillside here is populated by a great many trees of various sizes and shapes - perhaps a result of the proximity of the river not far to the north. To the west the land dips into an area of grassy plains, while to the east the undergrowth thickens at the edge of a wild, untamed brush.
116908: Wild, chaotic brushland grows at the southern shore of the river. Thorny vines and broken branches cover the ground, lying amidst thin vegetation that seems to have difficulties growing here. With visibility limited by the thick growth, progression is difficult. Aside from the river to the north, a ridge of hills is visible through the bushes to the west.
116909: A fat rabbit is here, chewing on some grass.

The land here is wide, flat and grassy, with few landmarks to guide the way. Not far to the west lies the old Fornost-Bree road while to the east and south the land rises into a swathe of rolling hills. The open plains continue to the north.
116910: The rolling, low slopes of the North Downs continue to the north and south. The land to the west descends into an area of grassy flatlands, beyond which a broad road cuts across the land. Down a gentle slope to the east is the edge of a thick and brambly brush.
116911: The occasional decaying tree trunk is visible through a sea of winding branches in the midst of the dense brush. Wiry branches cover the ground, and the tall, dense bushes block out most of the view of the sky. Progress through the thorny terrain is extremely difficult.
116913:
There is an old street-lamp on the border of the street.
An old man is walking around, cleaning up.

There is a small archway set into the eastern side of the city wall, with a stony path leading out from it. Just over the wall, a few crumbling parapets are barely visible. The street continues to the south, while a large square stretches out west and north.
116914: A stone wall lining the path on either side provides shelter from all but the noon day sun. Vines and roots have covered the walls in a carpet of dense vegetation. The path itself is laid with stone, well worn by the tread of hoof and boot.
116915: The stony path gives way to a wooden bridge here. It is fairly small, but built solid, clearly strong enough for several men on horseback. A small river of crystal clear water runs silently under the bridge. An ancient castle can be seen to the north, while to the west the path continues through the walls of Fornost.
116916: Before the Gates of Minas Brethil

A huge gate towers up ahead, made of ancient beech wood. A sign is posted on one gate, with neat gold lettering upon dark wood. The castle itself is made of stone, and looks dark and fearsome, yet inviting. Dense vegetation abounds in the area, making the castle hard to see from a distance, although the walls stand about eighteen feet high. Towers dominate each corner of the castle, and movements can be seen on the battlements high above you.
116924: This small, wooden bridge seems very old. The planks are rotting and look ready to break into pieces at any moment. Despite this, the bridge has clearly stood for a long time. The elderly construction creaks faintly as it swings over a narrow but deep ravine.
116925: Thin undergrowth creeps across the land, covering the trail in a thin layer that does not completely hide it. To the east the path clears, showing a small bridge and the long, wide road in the distance. The west and north, however, are deeper into the brushland. The path snakes north, vanishing into the bushes.
116926: The faint path runs between an ancient wall to the west and a wild, overgrown hedge to the east. The trail runs straight, linking the thinning brush and road to the south to deeper bushes in the north, beyond which creep the walls of an eerie castle.
116927: Tall grass marks the border of this brushland, with the fields to the south giving way to thicker bushes here and to the north. The bushes spread out in a dense sea to the north and east, growing uncontrollably. Low stone ramparts can be seen far off to the north.
116928: This patch of dense vegetation is composed of small bushes, running between crumbled remains of stone walls. Sticking branches grasp aimlessly at any who pass by, drifting in a faint breeze. The wall to the west is impassable, though the bushes continue treacherously to the north and south.
116929: Curving from the east to the north, this winding path is almost completely obscured beneath the sharp, green thornbushes. The bushes continue into the southern wilderness, away from the creeping fortress along the path that dominates the landscape.
116930: The path underfoot bends here, bounded by a short, mossy stone wall to the north and thicker brushland to the east. Tall, waving branches limit visibility in this area, growing ever denser to the west. Despite its remoteness, the trail shows faint evidence of use.
116931:
An erect shrub with green pinnate leaves is growing here.
Inside the shrub, there are two piles of crimson raspberries.

Landmarks vanish behind dense bushes that grow taller than a Man here. Prodding branches threaten eyes and rough undergrowth is a constant tripping hazard. There is the hint of a path to the left, and that is all that can be perceived. To the south, the bushes somehow thicken.
116932:
A sprawling green bush of stinging nettle grows here.
A snake slithers towards you.

Savagely-thorned brush grows all around. So much like a natural hedge maze, the bushes have crawled over ancient rubble and low, weathered stone walls to enclose this bushy garden. The sky is still visible, though not much else is, save for the hint of a passable gap to the north.
116933: The far end of this path is hidden beneath a dense field of wild bushes, which abates along the trail to the south. The small path shows obvious signs of use by some unknown creatures, leading towards the dark, mouldering castle to the north.
116934: These are the remains of what must have once been a mighty drawbridge, spanning the ravine below where the fast river flows. Time and battles have done their work, however, and the mighty wooden beams are rotten and broken in many places. The sound of rushing water can be heard from below, while to the north looms the crumbling castle gate. A cold breeze whistles around the decaying stonework, but no sound of living creatures can be heard.
116935: Here stands the gate of a long-ruined stone fortress, its archway collapsed and walls ivy-clad. No gates bar this portal, the wood having long rotted away leaving only the rusted remains of huge metal hinges. Heaped earth and fallen stones are piled against the base of the walls, giving a once-proud fortification the grim face of a barrow.
116936: A sprawling green bush of stinging nettle grows here.

Arched trees and thick bushes have enclosed a small hollow in the brush, blocking sight and passage all around. A rushing stream can be heard nearby, and thin streams of light pierce through the canopy to the ground. The path is barely visible through the dense green thorns to the west.
116937: The thorny brushland dips sharply to form this ravine. The muddy base of the gully suggests that it was formed as run-off from the bushes above eroded the soil, year after year. A short distance above, a creaking wooden bridge hangs over the gap formed by the ravine, allowing travellers to avoid the obstruction altogether. The sloping ground is only traversable to the north.
116938: A spirit floats towards you and howls with an evil laughter.

What was once a proud fortification has been abandoned to time and war, its walls no longer constructions so much as heaps of crumbled stone that have yet to topple. Earthworks are the only decor, reinforcing old stone and grasping at the walls like great earthen claws. The dim barrow continues north, and exits south.
116939: The hallway widens slightly coming from the south, as more of the old castle's interior is sheltered from the utter ruin of its walls. The inside, however, is unusually cold and completely stripped of furnishings. Whatever purpose this place once served has been lost, now serving as a tomb for forgotten Men.
116940: Aeons have passed since this castle hosted the living. Now, the halls only contain hastily-built mounds of dirt and rubble, burying nameless Men from ages past. Unusably-rusted weapons are laid beside the graves, but all broken, as if the serviceable tools had long-since been taken. The barrow's halls lead in all directions.
116941: The northern edge of the central crypt is in worse condition than the other visible walls, damage from an old siege that was never repaired. Piles of crumbled rock around the base suggest that the only reason the wall still stands is that anything that could collapse already has. Hallways, like tunnels into the earth, lead west and east.
116942: A mound of stone has been raised here, forming an ancient grave.

Crude stone slabs, covered in dirt and dust, raise dozens of ancient corpses off the floor of the barrow. Even more lie buried in collapsed piles of rock, claimed by the continued deterioration of the castle. The cold, dry air bears no stench of the dead, their bodies having laid here for untold years.
116943:
A small mound rises from the disturbed ground.
A spirit floats towards you and howls with an evil laughter.

This enclosed section of the walls once would have had a specialized purpose, but now is no more than a musty cave amidst the collapsing ruin. Spaced evenly around the walls are ancient, dusty skeletons, heaped over partially with stone and rusted, warped scraps. The only exit leads eastwards.
116944: The toppled stairs are no longer usable, but fallen stones make for a crude imitations as the ruins pile upwards. The old and decrepit tower seems on the verge of collapse, its walls badly damaged by time and bearing faint evidence of heavy impacts.
116945: The heaping stone rubble ends at the remains of what must once have been some mighty fortification on top of the tower. The platform is still protected by low, eroded battlements, which once would have sheltered the castle's defenders. Despite the disrepair, this spot overlooks the surrounding countryside clearly. To the east lies the old Road to Fornost, beyond which plains stretch away to a line of hills in the far distance. To the southeast is the tangled Brushland of Fornost, while to the north stands the great city itself.
116946: A tall pile of rubble shows where an interior wall of the castle has completely collapsed under the weight of the decaying roof, blocking off this wing of the interior. Elements of metalwork are visible in the ruins, remnants of what once was a gate to the east. Some of the rocks were once apparently cleared away, perhaps for use elsewhere in the dolmen.
116947: A spirit floats towards you and howls with an evil laughter.

This room is in better condition than the rest of the ruin, showing no signs of having been turned into a tomb. The room's size and construction suggest it was of some importance, but there are no contents but the dust. Thin slits in the walls provide a defensible view of the outside, and offer a source of the cold breeze that eerily whistles through the castle's remains.
116948: A patch of moss grows here on a wet, flat stone.

Heaping rubble and dirt forms a narrow tunnel that runs to the east and ends here, leading up towards a heavy hatch in the ceiling. The walls and floor are built from large, heavy stone blocks, smoothed to form a hallway that now lies littered with old, crumbled rock. The air is stagnant and quiet.
116949: Dry, stale air hangs in this quiet stone hallway. The path is rubble-strewn and layered with dirt, and the ancient stonework is held together more by its own weight than its crumbled structural integrity. To the west and east is only darkness, as this ancient stone corridor continues.
116950: The roof of the tunnel has given way, collapsing to the east and permanently sealing it. The stone walls have crumbled, and water drips slowly from the rubble to the south. A curious explorer would have to leave to the west, where the tunnel disappears into the darkness.
116951: An ancient, crumbling skeleton lies under a broken pillar.

This ancient storage room, several dozen feet long and wide, contains little of interest. The only crates, lying toppled in a corner, are metal, with all wood presumably having rotted away. The room is cool and dry, insulated from the environment around it despite its poor condition. Perhaps it once held perishable goods for the castle's inhabitants.
116952: Water covers the floor of this concealed basement, less than a foot deep. The source of the water is not immediately clear, but the sounds of a river are audible through the cracks in the eastern wall. Long years of erosion have worn away the walls of this room, with the northern wall partially crumbled as the stonework gives way to time.
116953: A black catfish is here, lurking in the mud.

Here the river curves sharply south, narrowing as it passes into a cave opening. The current is too strong and treacherous for any person to continue safely in that direction, however. The rocky walls of the ravine are crumbled and cracked, worn away by centuries of erosion and tumbling rocks from the looming ruin on the cliffs above.
116954: A black catfish is here, lurking in the mud.

The path of the river bends sharply westward here, channeled by a rocky ridge to the north and east. To the north, tall stone wall forms an artificial cliff, reinforcing a shoreline that has been heavily eroded by runoff from the fields above. The fast-moving water makes travel eastward more and more difficult.
116955: A black catfish is here, lurking in the mud.

The river changes course once more from east to north at this point. The banks to the west and south have been severely eroded by the passing waters and are crumbling in many places. To the east, the river arrives through a narrow gap, over which a stone bridge has been built.
116956:
A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.
A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.

Marram Fields continue for miles toward the south. The soil is very dry and no trees can be spotted in the vicinity. The most prominent features of the landscape are the vast marram grass cereals. To the east a steep slope makes further travel impossible.
116957:
A small cluster of clover grows here.
A coloured game bird is visible in the vegetation, watching you warily.

A vast field of marram grass cereals continues to the north. The field is a gorgeous blanket of green sprinkled with wildflowers. Although the grass is thick, it is still possible to move through the field. The wildlife becomes more varied as you move south, and a steep slope to the east prevents further movement.
116958: A wild sheep with a short, greyish coat grazes here.

Wild weeds that are several feet tall and have sharp edges blanket the ground here, making it difficult to move about. The vibrant weeds are the aces of the fields, as if when dealt by nature's hand they belong there in a way the regimented rows of a garden can never do. The land is sparsely covered in low trees. Their crooked branches reach upward in an effort to touch the sky.
116959: A wild sheep with a short, greyish coat grazes here.

This field is covered by weeds in a perfect triangular form. They are several feet high and have slightly sharp edges. It is hard to travel here without gathering a few scratches. The terrain is descending toward the south leading into a secluded valley.
116960:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
A large mother hawk is here looking for prey to feed her young.

This small secluded valley is covered with dense vines and weeds making it seemingly impossible to continue further. To the east several large boulders cover the flank of the valley while the slope toward the north seems more feasible to travel.
116961: The foothills here roll along a deliberate march toward some high mountain peaks to the north and east. To the south, the hills can be seen receding in a spectacular vista that extends as far as the eye can see. Sparse vegetation grows among the rocky crags of the the hills between large boulders.
116962:
Klaees (thedon), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Bulg (pukespy), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.
Drazud (freshmeat), wielding a great warsword, is standing here.

Little more than a footpath, an old trail runs west from the roadway, and continues on under the protection of a high, curving cliff. This area might once have served as a campsite for travellers journeying through the pass. To the north and west, the cliff towers above the camp, but to the south the vista opens up.
116963: The old road here cuts through the mountains. It is very weathered and, given enough time, will eventually erode away into nothing. The path of the southerly road is straight and deliberate, as it extends out of sight. High mountains border the road to the east while some hills can be seen to the west.
116964: Turning eastward, the road from the south approaches a narrow pass through the mountains. To the south it stretches onward as far as the eye can see. Though cracked and pitted in a few places, the surface of the road is in surprisingly good condition, having been created simply by flattening the bedrock itself.
116965: The road continues east and west. Its journey takes it through a gorge that grows more narrow to the east. Westward the pass opens out somewhat, at the same time losing a little altitude, and more vegetation can be seen growing to either side of the road in that direction.
116966: A few low bushes sprout up protecting this narrow pass, but lacking sufficient topsoil to sustain their roots, none is thriving. The central part of the pass has been levelled to create a road through the mountains. The steep cliffs looming to either side offer the traveller little choice but to follow the pass onward through the mountains.
116967: Turning from north to west, the road is forced along the path dictated by the pass through which it travels. The road is in remarkably good shape, but countless boulders are littered across its somewhat cracked surface. Though it is still a good thoroughfare for travellers on foot or even horseback, it would no longer afford access to any large cart or wagon.
116968: The road runs from north to south here, constrained by the narrow pass through which it journeys. This is the narrowest section of the gorge, with tall cliffs looming above from both sides, and even at the height of noon, deep shadows exist here. Many large boulders lie all across the road, having fallen at some time from the cliffs above. A chill wind whistles by almost constantly.
116969: The road here is, for the most part, intact. The red stone that comprises its surface lies smooth, as if untouched by time. Traversing a narrow pass through a mountain spur, the road is somewhat protected from the elements. The narrow canyon walls serve to guide the road along its path at the foot of the looming peaks.
116970: The wreck of a wagon lies here on the road in the mountain pass.

Cresting a final rise, the road from the plains reaches the mouth of a mountain pass. Turning to the east, the ancient thoroughfare starts its journey between the towering peaks of the mountain spur that cuts from east to west across the land. In the comparative shelter of the pass, the roadway here is significantly less decayed than might be expected in a land that has so long been unoccupied.
116971: The road continues to climbs steadily from the plains below, up towards the mountain spur that cuts across the land just south of here. Turning from the north to the east, it makes its way relentlessly toward the mouth of a narrow pass that can be seen in the distance. The smooth red stones that paved the surface of this road have become pitted and cracked in the long years since they were laid down, and now this is little more than a mountain trail.
116972: The road sweeps back and forth across the land making several massive switchbacks. They climb from the plains below up to the altitude of a pass through the mountain spur that looms not far south of here. The red stone that was laid so long ago to provide a smooth surface for the road is now cracked and broken.
116973: This section of the road is largely intact, with most of its red stone surface free of any significant pits or cracks. Travelling in large arcs, the road snakes back and forth, following the contours of the land to gain the altitude it needs for its journey between the lower-lying plains and a mountain pass that lies to the southeast.
116974: The road twists and turns, snaking across the land from the low-lying plains, up towards a mountain pass that lies to the southeast of here. Though the road is in a poor state of repair, its red paving stones are largely intact, with only a few hardy weeds and shrubs making a brave attempt to encroach upon them. Here and there a thick, thorny bush sprouts up beside the road.
116975: Broken red stone litters the area, barely discernible under the large amount of grasses and silt that have settled here. The eastern and northern edges of the road are completely overgrown with thick thorny brush that seems to never end.
116976: The road turns here, picking up and following to the east the highest ground, so that it can make a steady ascent toward the mouth of a mountain pass visible a couple of leagues or so to the southeast. To the north it seems instead to seek the lower, more sheltered parts of the plains, though meagre is the protection offered from the elements in any part of this land. Large ruts and cracks bedevil the road. Where once there was a smooth surface of red stone to pave the way, now only shattered fragments remain, with grasses and weeds slowly taking over.
116977: The road starts an almost imperceptible ascent, as it travels from north to south across the plains, drawing slowly closer to a distant mountain spur. Here and there, it almost vanishes from sight, the flat red stones that once formed its smooth surface having become cracked and overgrown with weeds and coarse, yellow-brown grasses. Also, deposits of soft, silty soil further cover the paving.
116978: Little remains of what was a road, thinning to little more than a footpath here with silt and sand covering the red stone. Small bushes have grown over the road while grass covers the rest of the surrounding area. There is little evidence of any traffic that might utilise this path. The trail continues to the west and widens to the south.
116979: Thick brush from fields to the north and south encroach on this part of the road, making it nearly impassable. The red stones that once paved the route are now cracked and covered by soil and dirt. What remains of the surface is now little better than a rough trail. The road widens slightly, and its condition improves markedly further to the west, while it narrows more to the east.
116980: Many small rocks have been uprooted here, and have all but turned the road into a stony field. As if to help the transformation, weeds of all types have grown up between the rocks. To the south, a field grows out of the cobblestones, while what is left of the road continues to the north and east. To the west a large rock formation blocks the way, making it impossible to continue in that direction.
116981: The road continues to the north and south of here, meeting the brush to the east without clear transition as the road is overgrown with weeds and grasses of all types. The red chalky stone that originally composed this pavement is full of small juts and large cracks.
116982: The road here is overgrown with weeds and grasses, and large boulders jut out of what was once smooth paving. Cracks are evident everywhere in the rocks that were used in the road. A thick patch of brush grows to the north, clinging to the meagre shelter offered by a small plateau. The road continues to the east and south.
116983: Large rocks have been uprooted in the road here, making what was once smooth so long ago, a bumpy and unsteady road. The rocks themselves are worn with time and weather. There is only a slight transition between brush and broken road to the south and east, while the road continues to the west and north.
116984: A green frog is here, hopping around.

This narrow road appears to have fallen into disrepair from lack of use. The surface of the road is rough and grass has begun to creep over the sides of the road from the surrounding fields. A tableland lies to the west, and to the east there are grassy hills.
116985: The road makes a sharp bend at this point to avoid the tributary that runs directly to the north and east. Judging by the poor condition of the pavement, it would appear this roadway is no longer maintained. The banks of the river are too steep to descend safely. The road continues to the west and south.
116986:
The corpse of a rabid, grey wolf is lying here.
A green frog is here, hopping around.

This ancient road makes its way through the lands, twisting and turning around the tablelands and streams. The ford to the north allows easy passage across a tributary, and to the south a short slope rises to a tableland. Far into the distance to the southeast, the outline of the Misty Mountains is clearly defined against the horizon.
116987: Broad and level, the tableland rises higher than the surrounding lands. A soft grass thickly covers the top of the plateau and a few wildflowers can be found growing in the grass, raising their heads towards the sun. A faint road can be seen twisting its way through the plains, and beyond that green fields extend out next to a meandering stream.
116988: Flowing from east to northwest, the water level drops sufficiently to allow one to cross the tributary safely and easily. The height and depth of the bank indicates that the level of water was once much deeper at this point and the river bed itself is cluttered with various rocks and debris that became too large or heavy to be carried along with the current. The rough remains of an ancient roadway continue on to the south and north, winding their way through the plains.
116989:
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.
An uruk of the Morgundul tribe is here commanding his soldiers.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.

The tributary is shallow enough south of here to be easily crossed on foot or riding. The flow of the water is soft and smooth, swirling against the edges of the river bank and sending the occasional cloud of sand and dirt into the water. To the north, grassy plains slope upwards towards a plateau. The rough remains of this ancient road become more visible to the east.
116990: Bending past the large body of water flowing to the south, this small roadway heads to the north and west. A low point in the stream to the southwest offers an excellent place to cross the wide tributary and reach the lands beyond. Upon a small hill to the north stands some old ruins and tents that overlook the plains and this ancient, crumbling thoroughfare.
116991: The old and crumbling road runs along the field the north, where a camp has been built by the ruins. Continuing east and south, the road continues on its way through these barren lands. From the appearance of the roadway, it would seem this area is seldom frequented. The surface of the roadway is uneven and strewn with small rocks and stones. A grassy incline rises gently to the west.
116992: The small stream visible to the south forces the road to make a lazy turn and continue both north and west. It would be too difficult to cross the stream at this point without getting wet due to its steep banks and high water line, but it appears possible to ford the stream farther to the southwest.
116993:
A goblin raider shrieks as it searches for something to maim.
A goblin raider shrieks as it searches for something to maim.
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

The road runs straight by a fenced camp to the west, while to the north a landscape with lots of brushes is visible. Judging by the dilapidated condition of the road, it sees little traffic, and is maintained even less. On the other hand, the camp to the west seems to be in good repair, suggesting that perhaps the area is not completely deserted.
116994: The road continues straight on through the plains, heading from east to west. Short shrubs sprout up along an earthen bank to the north, their tangled and thorny branches making passage difficult. Beneath the shrubs, a vertical drop leads down to a depression, but it is too steep to climb. A small meadow lies to the south.
116995: A sharp bend turns the direction of the road to the west and north. The road is in poor condition with several bumps and rocks from lack of maintenance but is still an easier route to choose than travelling straight through the plains. In the south, a small stream flows happily by. To the east the, the plains seem to stretch out for many miles. Beyond that, some hills are visible.
116996: A grey wolf is here, salivating profusely.

Stretching out north and south, the road heads on through the grassy plains. The upright drop to the west would make travel in that direction impossible, but entering the brown fields, that border the road to the east, is quite possible.
116997:
An uruk of the Morgundul tribe is here commanding his soldiers.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.

Turning to avoid a depression in a field to the north, the road continues to the east and south. It is covered with potholes and broken stones, and the bushes growing on the bank to the west are beginning to spread out and creep over the roadway. Beyond the bushes to the west, the ground suddenly disappears exposing a depression in a field.
116998: Twisting and turning through the fields and plains, the road makes a wide arc and continues on to the north and west. There are small rocks and stones on the ground and a narrow ditch choked with weeds and grass borders the roadway on either side.
116999:
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.
A grey wolf is here, salivating profusely.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

This ancient road turns to bend around a depression to the west, continuing to the east and south. The surface of the road is cracked and crumbled in places, and the grass from the plains is beginning to creep onto the road as it lies unused in this desolate area. A thorny thicket blocks the way to the north.
117000: The narrow road winds its way through the countryside, bending to travel west and north. Apparently, this road is no longer used frequently as nature is beginning to reclaim the ground as its own. The roadway is bordered on both sides by a sea of tall weeds and there is a strip of grass straight down the middle of the road.
117001: Lack of use and care has caused the condition of this narrow road to degenerate but there is still a well-marked pathway visible through the plains that travels north and south in direction. Thorny thickets prevent the travel to the west. To the east, a ridge of loose gravel ascends too steeply to climb.
117002: The wide, once well-travelled road finds its way from the east to the south. A smaller, apparently less travelled trail leads westward away from the road and through the surrounding fields. A faint rock wall can be seen further to the west.
117003: This large, dusty road, running from the east to the west, is paved with badly worn bricks and stones reduced to mere pebbles, to allow large wagons to travel upon it. The road seems to have been well-used once upon a time. Dry, barren plains lie in all directions.
117004:
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.
An orc-guard of the Morgundul is on patrol here.

This wide road finds its way from north to west. Paved with stones and bricks, travel by large and heavy wagons would still be possible despite the obvious lack of maintenance. The road runs through sloping, barren fields that stretch out as far as the eye can see, save for the rock wall cliff that looms over the road to the northwest. The only forms of vegetation nearby are small patches of dry grass or the occasional thorn bush or small, misshapen tree.
117005:
The corpse of a goblin is lying here.
The wreck of a wagon lies here on the side of the road.

The ancient, broken road slowly curves its way from the north to the south. The road is paved with large bricks and broken stones, allowing large wagons to travel upon it. A steep, rock wall looms over the road to the north and the west. The road has been built slightly higher than the surrounding plains to the southeast, allowing excessive rainwater to flow away. The steep cliffs to the north and west do not allow passage.
117006: The road runs to the north and the west through barren fields that stretch out in all directions, save for the sharp spur that looms over the road to the northwest. The fields are covered with sparse patches of brown, dry grass, and the occasional small, prickly bush. The road, however, is built on soft sand, paved with large bricks and broken stones, allowing heavy wagons to travel. A few clusters of small flowers grow by the side of the road and expand to the south.
117007: Curving from north to south, this large and dusty road cuts through rock walls on the east and west sides. The cut that this road runs through does not allow travel to the east or west. Small patches of grass grow beside the road, whilst the road itself is paved with many bricks and stones, reinforcing it. Every here and there a small thicket of thorn bushes can be spotted, growing at the side of the road.
117008: Bend in the Ancient Broken Road

A wide and dusty road runs through a cut that runs from the south and opens to the east. The road is surfaced with stones and bricks, allowing the passage of heavy wagons. Small insects can be found crawling underneath the stones, serving as a meal for the many birds populating this area. Small patches of dried-out grass grow at the sides of the road.
117009: Small stones dot the bleakness of the dusty path as it cuts its way east and west through the valley. Small pieces of brush grow sporadically on the barren red slopes giving little to no shelter for any wildlife. The northern wall of the valley seems to be unclimbable, while to the south lie some passable hills.
117010: What was once a highly trafficked road is nothing more than a few odd pieces of flat stones heaved upward by the forces of nature on this trail. Long grass grows between the stones. The ground levels out into a plateau that extends far to the south. In the north a ridge rises up above the plains, making it quite impossible to travel in that direction. Hardly any traces of animal life can be seen here, save for the occasional bird, high aloft in the distance.
117011: Bend in the Ancient Broken Road

The broken stones and barren, dusty tracks that identify the course of the road point down to the north as well as to the west, following the contour of the valley. To the east are yet more plains, while to the south lie more of the semi-barren plains that make up this region.
117012: The faint outline of the trail bends to the south and east here, bordered by a swift roaring river to the north. The trail is composed of overgrown flat stones patched into a road. A tall ridge rises up to the west hindering all movement in that direction, and to the south, the plains continue almost unbroken for some miles.
117013: Bend in the Ancient Broken Road

The sound of rushing water can be heard to the north, where a wooden bridge spans a lively river, to the west the well-trodden path of the Ancient Broken Road continues. In the east, the river continues its meandering flow, while a trail continues south towards what appears to be a camp.
117014: A sturdy wooden bridge has been erected here, spanning the waters that rush swiftly by beneath. A cover has been added overhead, though seemingly as an afterthought, as the construction and workmanship does not seem to match the rest of the structure. Looking eastward over the wooden railing, one can see the waters of two streams pick up momentum as they collide, forming a swift river that continues far into the west.
117015: The soil of the path is springy and moist, being close to the crossing of the river to the southeast. On the east, the river flows past inaccessible banks, while to the south, a wooden bridge spans the width of the river as it passes underneath and continues west.
117016: The path of the road turns here to the south and east. Searching to the distant south, a long wooden bridge is visible. This is the low point of the valley with mostly plains and water marking its features. To the west however, a patch of densely packed trees rises up into the sky.
117017: The faint outline of the road bends to the west and north here, bordered on the south by the steadily flowing waters of a wide stream. To the east, an expanse of grassland opens out, initially soggy from the constant supply of water, but becoming drier further away. A shallow dike has been dug out to protect the road from the wetlands.
117018: A swallow flies high above the ground.

The road follows a north and south path, intersecting the downward slope of this valley. The occasional tracks of wildlife can be seen faintly in the dirt beside the road, leading eastward towards a small river that can barely be seen in the distance. To the west lie rocky fields which perhaps have the saving grace of changing the monotony of the landscape.
117019: Bend in the Ancient Broken Road

The worn path of the Ancient Broken Road makes a sharp bend here, although a small trail can be seen branching off to the west. A languid river runs its course through the landscape in the north, curving along the side of a wide plateau. To the east and south, the Ancient Broken Road continues for many miles.
117020: Bordered by a shallow river and its gently tumbling waters, the Ancient Broken Road continues its east-west direction. The road is mainly composed of large flat stones, although time has taken its toll and grass is quite a dominant feature in between the plates. Some leagues away to the east bumpy foothills give way for the towering Misty Mountains beyond. To the north, the river bank is impassable, while to the south dense, thick brush also blocks passage.
117021: Bend in the Ancient Broken Road
A ferocious warg is here, snarling angrily.

The road runs to the west and north here, blocked to the south by a natural barricade of rock and stone. The barricade itself is not very tall, but the drop on the far side would be a formidable challenge for even the most highly skilled climber. The land slopes off into a valley to the south and east, eventually meeting with a muddy waterway. To the northeast, another river can be seen softly flowing from the foothills of the Misty Mountains to the lowlands in the west.
117023: The land is sparsely covered with bushes and shrubs, but mostly comprised of a dry grass. It slopes gradually to the south and east, where a muddy stream can be seen. Another body of water can be seen to the north, cutting along the base of a steep plateau. To the south, the riverbank cuts harshly into the plains, preventing any travel in that direction.
117024:
*a Tarkhnarb Orc* (shiny), wielding an ornate, steel-shafted warhammer, is here, riding a hungry warg.
A large brown wolf stands here, its teeth partly bared.

Small patches of bare earth mix in with the occasional stone in these otherwise sparsely vegetated grasslands. A pile of mud covered branches seems to cover a hole in the ground. Piles of mashed skulls litter the ground, suggesting that some violent predators might live behind the branches. To the south lay a swamp, while the plains continue east and west.
117025: To the east the Misty Mountains tower up over this barren grassland. Sheer, rocky slopes lead up to the jagged, snow-clad peaks, gnawing on the horizon like sharp teeth. A narrow ridge lies to the north, while the sound of water can be heard from the muddy stream in the south.
117026: Aside from the sporadic patches of sod underfoot, not much seems to be living in these foothills of the Misty Mountains. The dirt is packed down here and is coloured dark brown with streaks of red. Some bushes dot the windy landscape.
117027: Flowing from east to west, the river cuts a wide path across the roadway here. At some time in the past great effort was made to make this ford an easy one to pass, by laying large, flat boulders in the bed to make the already shallow waters yet shallower. But through years of disrepair many have been jarred quite loose, and today the traveller should take care in making the crossing.
117028: Drawing close to a river the land becomes more fertile. A gentle incline climbs from the ford toward a flat expanse of higher ground to the north. To the south there are signs of periodic flooding by the river, bringing rich deposits of red-brown silt to nourish the grass and brush. The resulting jumble of grassy tussocks, weeds and brush thrives at the expense of the pavement, and so the road is almost completely lost to nature.
117029: A rough patchwork of broken pavers and tussocks of thin yellowing grass define the ancient roadway. Strangely, though this is such an exposed location, here it is that the road is in perhaps the best state of repair for many leagues. Here also the tufts of grass seem to be smaller and fewer, and perhaps herein lies the explanation for the condition of the pavement; the fierce, chill winds from the northern reaches of the Misty Mountains, and the thin layer of topsoil have less effect on the cold, hard stones than on the encroaching vegetation.
117030: Winding from south to east, the road meanders down a gentle slope. Little more here than a rough trail through the coarse grass, the road has certainly given in to the onslaught of wind and weather that has, through long years, conspired with the action of root and foot to assault its once well-kept surface. Just north of here, a small building nestles close by the rising plain.
117031: Road at the Foot of a Slope
A large rabbit looks peacefully at you, ready to dart away.

Turning here from its north to south course, the old road begins to make a gradual, slightly winding ascent toward a flat table of land above the plain, passing by a battered stone structure as it does so. The pavement here is, if anything, in an even worse state of repair than it is on the flat lands to the north. The broken remains of the pavers have succumbed to gravity and many of the pieces have tumbled down the gentle grade, to accumulate in a broad and tumbled pile here at the foot of the slope.
117032: Nestled by the foot of a rising escarpment, a stone building of modest size stands beside the roadway here. A small lean-to, perhaps to shelter fire wood, stands empty against the wall of the building. The windows are broken, and the roof shows signs of several developing holes. Yet the hard-packed earth in front of the doorway is virtually devoid of vegetation, suggesting that somebody's feet still tramp along the broken roadway and into the structure.
117033: Due north and south, the road stretches across a bleak and windy plain, running almost parallel to the far distant Misty Mountains. Massive paving stones lie shattered and broken among the coarse tufts of grass, but their ruined remains still show clearly that this was once a broad roadway, created to allow several people to travel abreast.
117034:
A demon wolf lurks here, its dark form twisting and hiding its shape.
A demon wolf lurks here, its dark form twisting and hiding its shape.

Tall, moss-covered trees loom above the road to the east, but westward it is flanked only by rotting and burned stumps, that nestle amid a sea of grass and rank weeds. The road itself is badly broken, its mighty pavers shattered over the years by the action of frost and vegetation.
117035: The road stretches south into the distance, as it journeys past a dark, twisted forest and onward across a blustery plain. The pavement from the road is so badly shattered that it has become quite obscured amongst the thick tufts of coarse grass. Beyond the road to the north a slight incline within the earth begins.
117036: Curve on the Ancient Broken Road

So few and scattered, and so broken are the great stones that once comprised this roadway, that its path is almost lost here. Looking up the slope to the north, the trail becomes plainer, but its route from this point southwards through the land can only be guessed at. A dark and twisted forest stands due south, but to the southwest the way seems clearer.
117037: The road continues onward to the south and north, bordered to the east by a tall, yet strangely twisted woodland. The road steadily descends to the south, as the land falls away toward a vast expanse of windswept plains. At one time this thoroughfare must have been an impressive sight. Even today it can be seen that the pavement could once accommodate several travellers riding abreast, but now most of the paving lies broken, and much of it is scattered, leaving only a shadow of how great this road must once have been.
117039: As it journeys past the woods that stand southeast of here, the road makes a gentle ascent toward the high point of a small, windswept plateau. It then turns south and begins its descent into the broad flatland below. The paving under foot has been invaded through the years by thick patches of yellowing grass, and today the stones lie scattered amidst the vegetation, so that the roadway is almost lost entirely.
117040: Drawing near to a dark forest, the road turns to the east, skirting beside the woodlands. The stonework that was once so carefully laid has been broken apart over long years of neglect by thick tufts of yellowing grass, and now for the most part appears more like stony grassland than a well-wrought thoroughfare.
117041: This broken stonework was once laid with great skill and care to ease the otherwise arduous journey through these wild lands. The pieces lie scattered and spread, a mere remnant of this road's rumoured greatness. Sturdy grasses have crept closer, slowly recovering the few yards of land that mankind borrowed over the years. The abandoned remains of the road continue both north and south from here, stretching towards the distant horizon in a thin straight line.
117044: Below your feet lie the broken remains of a once carefully laid road. Its broad stonework covers several yards in width, allowing a large number of horsemen to ride in formation. Now the stone-work is cracked and broken, the old road abandoned and the land slowly being reclaimed by the forces of the vast grassy plains that surround it.
117045: Running straight in a line north to south the old abandoned road lies bordered by vast and wild plains, stretching eternally towards the horizon in every direction. The road itself sits almost hidden beneath all the dirt and sturdy grasses that cling to the stones. A few larger stone markers stand to the side as a reminder of the great importance this now ruined road once held, as the main path to Khazad-dum.
117046: Broken stonework lies scattered across the grassy plains, as the once so proud and well-maintained road has fallen into oblivion. Large cracks scar the small remnants of almost unbroken road that still can be seen above the thick cover of dirt and grass.
117047: Hidden below a dense carpet of grass as well as a thick layer of soil, the remnants of this once important trade route to Khazad-dum can barely be seen. The broken slabs of stone, once so carefully transported and fitted to form this road, now lie cracked and broken below the triumphant grasses that have overwhelmed them.
117048: Covered by dust and weeds, the ground below you is most definitely the remains of an old road. Now it is forgotten and broken, but some signs that it was not always so can still be seen. Barely discernible beneath the soil are the huge slabs it was so skilfully paved with many centuries ago, cleaving a passage through the plains. Close to the north grow several dense thickets of thorns, amidst which rises a dark tower.
117049: Branching off the once so proud road, this small path was once well used and well tended. Now the surrounding plains are slowly reclaiming it, but the ground is still hard, cracked and dry. Opening up towards the northwest the vast plains roll on endlessly towards the horizon and just south of here there rises a bare cliff wall.
117050: This desolate crag marks the southwestern extreme of the plateau, and also its highest point. Scoured by the fierce winds that howl across this bleak part of the country, the land here has only the thinnest covering of soil over the underlying rock. A few hardy patches of coarse grass and scattered weeds cling to life, their roots struggling to find purchase in any small nook or cranny. Rolling gently downward to the east, the ground gradually becomes less exposed, the plants it supports healthier and less sparse.
117053: Paw and hoof prints from the occasional wolf or deer run along the loamy, northern edges of the Old East Road, sometimes crossing the wide throughway. Nearby and to the south, a large hedge separates this road from a smaller, fainter trail. Beyond the trail, gently rolling hillsides mark the horizon.
117054: A wooden sign hangs above the door of a building.

The road continues in its east-west orientation. A short path branches off the road and leads to what appears to be an inn to the south, situated between a thick thicket on the east and a large thicket on the west. The dense forest to the north makes travel impossible.
117055: The road divides the Chetwood forest into northern and southern halves, as a viridescent cloak girdled by a tan leather belt. A tangle of brushwood, unkempt hedge, and low buckthorn lie immediately to the south, while a curious rift in the greenery to the north beckons passage into the depths of the wood.
117056:
A low and wide-spread tree grows here.
On the tree's branches, there are two juicy plums.

Some of the trees covering the hillsides in this area are not found in other parts of the forest. There are still many pines, but here and there the occasional alder can be seen as well. In the denser portions of the wood, the ground is covered by a thick undergrowth of ferns.
117057: A suspicious innkeeper watches you carefully as you enter, wondering whether to give you a room.

The walls of this expansive inn are made of wood and decorated with hunting trophies of long-forgotten creatures. Three long tables and plenty of wooden chairs cover the floor. A huge lantern hanging from the ceiling throws a flickering light all around the room.
117058: The road travels east and west, connecting the village of Bree with the hidden valley of Rivendell, far beyond the eastern horizon. This section of the road has been well worn by the many travellers from distant lands who traverse it. To the north, a coppice scars the otherwise lush and verdant Chetwood. To the south, a faint trail leads into the wood.
117059:
The badly decayed head of John the man is spiked on a pole here.
A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.
John the Man is here, looking for some trees to chop down.

At the edges of this narrow path, the trees are quite large and grow in a moist, rich soil. The path leads north to the Old East Road, branches off into a smaller trail to the east, and opens up southwards to some grassy downs before curving towards the west.
117060: The road is worn away from vigorous use. Small bushes line the edges of the road with the Chetwood forest rising behind them. A small path leads toward a clearing in the distance to the north. To the south, some rolling downs are barely visible through the scattered trees.
117061: The Old East Road is wide and well-worn here. Frequent foot, hoof, and cart traffic has made the earth hard and smooth. A dense spinney to the north obscures any sightline into Chetwood forest. To the south, a broad break in the hedge leads into the southern part of the wood.
117062: The road runs east and west, separating the Chetwood forest to the north and south. The woods get increasingly dense to the south, limiting any access to the forest. Far to the west, the village of Bree, particularly its high hill, can be seen.
117063: The road continues its way east and west, dividing the Chetwood forest to the north and south as it goes. The forest has been thinned out to the north and small piles of brushwood border the road. To the south the trees rise up fairly high and a dense hedgerow blocks travel in that direction.
117064: The road keeps going east and west. A very sizable hill can be seen off in the west. To the south, the trees gradually give way to fields, and to the north, a thick hedgerow obstructs movement. The dirt on the road is smooth and firm from constant foot, hoof, and cart travel.
117065: The road turns gradually to the east and south. An approximately four hundred feet tall hill to the west obscures the view. A pasture with rich green grass is located at the foot of the hill to the west, while the hedgerow to the north blocks further movement in that direction.
117066: Bend in the Old East Road
A swallow flies high above the ground.
