It is a place of tranquillity where ladies and gents of an elitist circle come to get professional hair cuts and styling, manicures and pedicures, and often cosmetics, makeup and makeovers. Several tools such as scissors and combs or the famous heavy-duty toenail pliers are neatly organised on a table set against a wall with a big mirror. A comfortable hairdressers' chair sits in front of the table waiting for its next customer.
117717:
An ornate fountain made of polished granite stands here.
A humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.

Lush flowers and succulents populate this quaint courtyard. Small and cracked cobblestones lead in snaking paths throughout the courtyard. Dried grass grows among the cobblestones. Hanging vines grow along an arched entrance to the south. Three stone benches surround an ornate fountain in the centre of the courtyard.
117718: A long, varnished bar runs from the northern wall toward the south in this dimly lit tavern. Dark, stained wood lines the wall and the floor throughout this room. Four small, round tables sit next to the bar with three stools around each. Four stools sit under the long bar. Steel hooped oak barrels are stacked behind the bar with taps installed. There is a stairway going up just behind the opening behind the bar. There is an arched entrance to the east leading to the garden courtyard outside.
117719: In Front of the Riding Maiden's Inn

A comfortable-looking tavern stands at the edge of the park. It has been built with a respect to its surroundings, embracing the peaceful and calm athmosphere of the park. Flowers and herbs grow around the tavern while big, old trees stretch upwards warding this serene place. A warm light glints from the inn's round windows, welcoming everyone to drop by.
117720: A busy innkeeper hustles around, running his inn.

This wide, cosy tavern belongs to Temperance and is rumoured to serve the best beer in Bree! The brown- and gold-themed room is covered with broad floor planks and filled with oaken tables which come in two heights; customized to fit the needs of the big and little folk of Bree. The far end of the room is dominated by a long, smooth bar behind which stands a tall shelf, filled with bottles of all sorts and a healthy assortment of pipe weed. A few paintings, a roaring fireplace in the corner and the yellow thatched roof above complete the Inn's interior decoration.
117721: The distinctive rough red brick laid into the ground here spearates North Ridge Avenue from the old cobblestones of Westhill Way to the south. A few houses, also built from the same red brick, top the mounds of the hills lining the street.
117722: The street here is composed of a reddish dirt similar to clay. Wheel tracks are carved into the road by the countless wagons and carts that have crossed this path. The road here branches off to the east, west, and south, making this a fairly busy intersection.
117723: A cockroach is scuttling across the floor carrying some debris.

Low wooden fences surround the houses bordering the road. Large trees tower above the fences, curling over the street. The road here is lined with small pebbles, apparently an attempt by the local residents to improve the look of the ageing streets.
117724: Intersection of Bluff Street and Westhill Way

Here, Bluff Street and Westhill Way come to a crossing. The ground surrounding cobblestones streets is mostly dirt, with a few muddy spots. At the centre of the crossroads, a tall, iron, lampost stands like a beacon welcoming all who may come to this convergence.
117725: A guard of Bree stands here.

The street narrows here, almost like an alley that has been squeezed between houses. Snaking vines climb up the walls of the houses in their relentless pursuit of the sun. The walls of the houses, primarily made of stone, have been cracked from the tight embrace of the vines.
117726: A beggar is here, asking for a few coins.

The alley comes to an abrupt stop here. Tall houses constructed of mud-like bricks surround the street. The road itself used to be cobblestone but has been worn down to the point where it is now equal parts mud and pebbles.
117727: A low stone wall, crumbling and borken, wraps around some patchy lawns in front of the houses here. Covered in dead vines, the houses are built with shoddy laid stonework. The sloping roofs above are weather torn and appear to be barely holding on.
117728:
A tall, stately, dome-topped tree grows here.
A small loyal cat is here.

The ground is strewn with a white-grey gravel that crunches underfoot. In one corner of the square, some holes have been dug into the ground where a wide hitching post stands a few feet above the ground. The footprints of horses litter the ground.
117729: A neat row of grey stones lays along the sides of this pebble strewn road. The disparately sized pebbles are covered in mud and clay. A row of small, thorny, bushes lines the street on either side, making it perilous to crowd too closely in the road.
117730:
A large wooden sign is posted in the ground next to the pond.
A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.
A white-painted bench is here.
A fat carp swims here.

The grass stops abruptly and turns into mud as it approaches the pond. The water itself is relatively clear, though the muddy surface beneath gives it a brown tint. A shoddy wooden pier juts out into the water almost reaching the centre of the pond.
117731: While the brushwood has been removed some time ago it has started to grow back between the trees. The ground in this light forest is covered with soft moss and clusters of higher grass, with a noticeable, well-worn path cutting east and west. All around, small, fallen sticks and loppings can be spotted.
117732: Most of this area is lightly forested with low, wide trees whose canopy allows ample sunlight to reach the forest floor on clear days. A wide trail curves between the trees, heading westward. To the east, large piles of neatly stacked brushwood block any advance in that direction. In the southeastern distance, the trail continues, visible between the widely spaced tree trunks.
117733: A deep, hollow way has been carved into the landscape and bends north into the Chetwood forest from the village of Archet to the east. Tracks of horses and wagon wheels are engraved deep into the trail, which is muddy and rough. The smell of damp and rotten wood fills the air.
117734: A blue dragonfly is circling around.

A well-worn dirt road winds through a remote village nestled deep within the woods. Small clusters of various wildflowers and overgrown grasses line the road while flowering dogwoods provide ample shade. To the east, the path begins to fork much like a river of earth.
117735:
A mass of dark green leaves clings to a wall.
A blue dragonfly is circling around.

The remote settlement of Archet is made up of a number of stone houses and smials. The dirt roads that connect the buildings wind through the forest, eventually meeting at a meticulously crafted cobblestone street that serves as a makeshift town square near an overgrown barn. One bent and crooked poplar stands alone in the centre of the street.
117736:
A prominent wooden sign stands beside the fountain.
A small fountain made of polished rock is here.

A humble fountain constructed of polished river stone sits beneath a massive weeping willow. Countless bronze and silver coins shimmer at the bottom, a nameless grave for wishes long since forgotten. Ornate trellises latticed with wisteria vines form an arcing semi-circle around both the willow and well.
117737: The dirt road here bisects central Archet. A small tavern can be seen to the north, while an immaculate hedgerow blocks the way east. Trees, predominantly ash and elm, dominate the horizon. Deep cart tracks scar the earth, worn deep by the weight of the annual harvest.
117738: Little more than a dirt path now winds through an abandoned orchard. Dense cherry trees of unguessable age grow along the deepening forest and give little choice but to stay on the path. Severe rot and decay blight most of the cherry branches, starkly contrasting the surrounding luxuriant forest.
117739: Bordered by a forest clearing to the north and a deteriorating orchard to the west, several dense rows of hawthorn bushes grow rampant amongst the rolling hills of Archet. A modest footpath twists through the hawthorns, allowing passage through the relics of once pristine hedgerows. The shrubbery teems with countless species of wildlife.
117740: A shallow pond is here, tinted green with algae.

Hardly any sky can be seen overhead as thick undergrowth and crowded trees flourish all around. Chunky mosses and emerald-green ferns carpet the forest floor, while a humble earthen path provides the only means of escape from the encroaching woods. A diminutive vernal pond, edged by sedges and rushes, sits alongside the path and reflects the intertangled canopy above.
117741: A well-travelled trail connects the southern villages of Staddle and Combe with the more distant town of Archet, nestled deep in the Chetwood forest. The wheels of overladen wagons have carved deep ruts into the otherwise soft forest floor. Some footprints and wheel tracks lead north where the trail meanders deeper into the wood.
117742: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

Cleared of stray branches, leaf litter, and saplings, a rough trail winds its way through the forest. Occasionally, low bramble bushes impinge at the trail's edges and, in other places, planks of roughly hewn lumber have been laid across particularly damp stretches of the trail.
117743: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

The forest trail is not well-maintained in this area, and it is often obscured by ferns, bramble, and eager saplings. Fortunately, the trees are spaced apart widely enough that finding the trail again is simply a matter of looking a bit farther ahead.
117744: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

Oak, aspen, and giant fir trees span out in every direction, and the forest floor at the edges of the trail is crowded with ferns and brushwood. Off the trail, finding a way through the dense undergrowth would be a tiresome and tedious feat. No direct sunlight penetrates this place; instead, when the sun is directly overhead, an ambient, golden glow suffuses the dense forest.
117748: Birch trees cover the hillside, their leafy branches blotting out the sky. A lone hollow tree stands at the top in a grassy field. The trunk has been scarred with small holes, filled with nuts of all sorts. Rough stones of all shapes and sizes dot the ground.
117749: The ground slants ever so slightly downward to the east as it completes its descent from the western hilltop. Expansive oaks stretch their long branches high and wide overhead, shading much of the landscape. Underfoot, tiny caches of acorns are piled up on the leaf litter.
117750: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

The forest is crowded here, dominated by oaks above and alder buckthorn below. The trees clump together, blocking any path to the east or south. In the places where the great oaks have yet to claim their territory, dogwood trees take their humble stand, stretching their limbs low and wide.
117751: Mature trees grow in this area, but they are spaced far apart. Between them younger trees rise up, too small to cast significant shade, and the light reaching the ground has given rise to a dense brush cover that makes travel through the area difficult. The occasional fallen tree lies tangled within this brush, already covered by climbing vines, brambles, and tall, arching herbaceous weed stalks; these fallen trunks are largely hidden from view until stumbled upon. The easiest movement through this thin woodland is following the deer trails that wind between the trees, these narrow gaps through the brush still blocked in places by the stray branch reaching across.
117752:
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.

Tall, messy grasses dominate these fields, growing in clumps so close together that they provide continuous coverage of the soil. Many of the clumps are no longer standing straight up, their new green growth mixed with old, brown stems from past years that have bent and broken and pushed the entire clump to lean to one side or another. Here and there short scrubby pine trees have begun to grow, still small enough to be mostly hidden by the surrounding grass, and young gorse bushes face the same struggle to compete for light. To the east a tree line begins, the tangled brush and mature trunks forming an impassable barrier, while to the north a line of tangled shrubs mixed with briars prevents passage onto what appears to be a wide, paved road.
117753:
A fierce boar is here, making grunting noises.
A boar cub is playing here, and exploring the wide world.

Tall, messy clumps of grasses cover the ground here. Many of the clumps are topped with broken stems still bearing previous years' flower heads, the old brown growth contrasting with this year's green. Closer to the ground, more remnants of old growth are visible, loose curving brown blades and broken hollow stems collecting in a tangled mess that has yet to decay into the soil. Short bushes dot the fields at intervals, rising just far enough above the dense grasses to be able to compete for light. To the west hills rise up, low but steep enough to prevent movement. Their eastern face, visible from here, has eroded to expose bare rock. To the south is a light forest, and the border is a barrier of mature trees interspersed with tangled brush, dense enough to prevent movement in that direction.
117754: A swarm of hornets is coming out of its nest.

Tall, messy grasses dominate these fields, growing in clumps with a lower, finer-textured grass spreading in the spaces between. Dead stems and old flower heads are mixed in with the grass clumps, the growth of past years that has not yet broken down into the soil. Low bushes grow here in groups, with the outermost bushes of each group struggling to gain height over the dense grasses that grow through, next to and over them. To the west, hills rise up, not tall but steep enough to block movement. Erosion channels cut through these steep slopes, channelling water from rains down into the fields here; at the termination of each, the grasses extending beyond seem to grow taller and denser. To the north a wide, paved road can be seen.
117755: Rugged hills of rock and dirt protrude from the larger hills in the south. Reaching beyond the northwest corner of the forest, the hills jab into the road to Fornost as they curve between the forest and a stone wall. The elongated hills alternate between crude bumps and cutting valleys just wide enough to lose one's footing into. Near where the hills meet the road, on the northeastern side, they level out into a relatively even descent.
117756: Lightly wooded hills divide Chetwood in the east from the road to Fornost in the west. Not quite rising to the heights of the trees at the base of the hills, they offer little view other than a passing glimpse of those travelling the road directly to the west. Beyond the road, rising above the tree canopy, a barren ridge forms a straight line across the horizon.
117757:
A low and wide-spread tree grows here.
On the tree's branches, there are three juicy plums.

Some kind of animal, perhaps deer, seems to have nibbled on the barks of the trees in this light forest. These marks can be found on many trees at the height of maybe two to three feet from the ground. To the west a large pile of cut brushwood has been overgrown by grass.
117758:
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.

Many tracks left by heavy carts can be seen in the soft ground. In many places, stumps of fresh-cut brushwood stick out of the grass. Not long ago, the brushwood must have been removed. Since the light trees have not grown close together the eye can see a relatively long distance in this forest.
117759: Dust devils blow about the plains, obscuring the view with dust and debris. Patches of grass try to hold the ground together in patches. Where the vegetation is missing, the wind has eroded the ground and laid bare hard, red clay.
117760: Mature trees grow here, but they are spaced far enough from each other that plenty of light makes it to the ground below. Younger trees, mostly oak, are starting to grow in these gaps, rising up above the tall grasses and shrubs that dominate the understory. The ground underfoot is soft, with a layer of dead leaves from the previous season mixing with the grasses and crumbling into the soil. Some deer trails run through these light woods, winding around the mature trees and marked at intervals by piles of deer droppings.
117761: This mature forest is composed primarily of oak trees, with some rowan and birch mixed in. A few scraggly pine trees remain, although they appear to be dying out due to the lack of light beneath the canopy above: their lower branches are bare and broken, and only their tops still have green needles. The undergrowth on the forest floor is sparse here, due to the lack of light, limited to small herbaceous plants with large leaves and some short ferns that are confined to shallow depressions where the soil must retain water after a rain. To the north and east the forest thins out, the trees spaced far enough apart that light is able to reach through the canopy to the ground below.
117762:
A mass of wriggling vines drops on you from the trees.
A large bat is here, hanging in the darkness.

This mature deciduous forest is composed of oak and rowan trees, growing closely enough together to form a solid canopy overhead that blocks sunlight from reaching the ground below. Here and there the canopy thins slightly from where a tree has fallen in the past, but the surrounding trees have already filled in enough of the gap that no significant light makes it through. Old tree trunks lay on the forest floor, already starting to decompose, the bark sloughing off and lying in piles that are mixed with leaf debris from previous seasons. These trunks are drilled full of small holes, and lined with shelves of small, crinkly-edged fungi.
117763: A swift and agile forest cat moves silently through the vegetation.

The trees in this forest are spaced far enough apart that plenty of light makes it through to the understory. Many of the trees are pines, short and stubby and being overtaken by taller deciduous trees. Most of these pines are bare up to their tops, where a small green canopy of needles remains; only those that are far away from taller trees are still green all the way down. Small bushes and tall grasses grow between the trees, taking advantage of the light coming through the sparse canopy above. The forest grows more dense to the south, where the larger deciduous trees have taken over, growing closely enough together to form a solid canopy.
117764: At the edge of this forest, widely-spaced, short pine trees grow in abundance. They are interspersed with birch, and in some places clumps of birch are starting to rise over and shade out some of the pines. Plenty of light is able to reach the ground through this discontinuous canopy, allowing thick brush to grow between the trees. The brush is tall and tangled in some places, but mostly it grows low enough to allow easy movement. Gorse bushes are mixed with lower-growing heath and the occasional blueberry bush, many growing closely enough together that they will be competing for light in a few years' time. The forest grows more dense to the southeast, with the pines gradually replaced by taller deciduous trees.
117765:
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A forest spider is here crawling around.
A half wolf is here, loyally protecting his master.

The trees here at the edge of the forest are sparse, some growing in clumps but most spaced widely apart. They are mostly birch and pine, and rise up above tall, messy grasses that are choked with dead stems and old flower heads. Mixed with the grasses, and growing around the trees in the areas with the most light available, are tall gorse bushes, their branches tangled and scruffy. Briars are threaded through these with long, thorny stems, making travel through the brush hard, forcing travel to deer trails that wind around the trees.
117766: This area was once grassy, but shrubs are starting to overtake the grasses, shading and thinning them out. Gorse bushes mix with lower growing heath to form a shrubland of various heights, clumps merging into dense, wide thickets that extend to cover a significant amount of ground. Here and there flattened sections of brush show where deer have bed down, and clumps of deer droppings mark indistinct deer trails through the grassier areas of the brush. Some young pine and birch trees have begun to grow through the shorter areas of shrubs, branching after they have topped their neighbours, and beginning to shade out anything beneath.
117767: The trees at this forest edge are spaced fairly far apart, allowing light to filter through to the ground. Many of the trees are mature, but there are also a significant number of saplings and young trees beginning to grow in the gaps. Most of the trees here are pine and birch, although some younger oak trees appear to be getting established as well. The understory is brushy and dense, with briars and gorse bushes growing in the light filtering through the broken canopy above, and to the east and south this brush grows densely enough to block movement farther into the forest that lies in those directions.
117768: This area is covered with low-growing grasses, both a spreading type and one that has formed clumps topped with old, brown flower stems from the previous season's growth. Some small bushes grow through the thick grasses, heath and young gorse, individually and in clumps dense enough to outcompete the surrounding vegetation. There are a few small pine trees locked in a similar competition: they are all small and squat, their lowest, outer branches grown through with tall grass blades, and their tops poking above as sprays of green needles. The ground underfoot is uneven and rolling, dipping and rising with regularity until it joins the hills in the distance to the northeast.
117769: This area is covered by low vegetation, a mix of various low-growing grasses and short shrubs that reach no higher than knee-high on a man. In some areas the shrubs appear thin and spindly, with grasses growing right up through them, but in other spots the shrubs have formed dense clumps that have managed to outcompete the other vegetation. Here and there short, scrubby pine trees are just getting started, forming small mounds that peek above the dense grass. To the east and north the ground rises up and low hills begin, although long shelves of crumbling rock cut across the hills where the slopes become steeper, making passage too difficult and dangerous in those directions.
117770: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

Tall oat grass covers this area, although it is being outcompeted by shrubs, mostly gorse bushes. These are growing in clumps and groups, forming large and tall thickets of dense, tangled brush, with relatively open grassy areas between. Some short, spindly pine tree seedlings are starting to grow in the grassy areas, their tufts of long, soft needles just barely reaching above the tops of the grass clumps, but otherwise this area seems to be devoid of trees. To the north and west long thickets of gorse bushes merge into solid rows of shrubs that prevent passage.
117771: Low growing bent grass and heath are being displaced here by taller shrubs that grow in tangled, messy clumps. Briars and gorse bushes mix to create tall, wide thickets that cover a significant amount of ground, broken up by grassy spots full of old weed stalks. The ground underfoot is uneven, with large hummocks rising up before sinking into shallow depressions; many of these depressions are filled with shorter, greener grasses and sparse brush, suggesting that the soil stays waterlogged after a rain for longer than the rest of the vegetation in this area can tolerate. Here and there a small birch tree rises through a thicket, spreading its branches above as it reaches for the sky.
117772:
A rabid raccoon stands here, frothing at the mouth.
A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

Clumps of tall grasses are being displaced here by tall shrubs, mostly gorse bushes and brambles. These shrubs rise up to form tall, thorny thickets that are easier to move around than through. Lower-growing heath and broadleaf weeds grow in the areas between these thickets, competing for light and leaving behind the shaded, skeletal remains of the losers. The brush is thick enough here that the only direction not blocked by a maze of tangled thickets is east, where enough lower-growing areas connect to be followed as a trail.
117773:
A huge, black wolf is here, ready to devour.
A white wolf is here, prowling for something to eat.
A wolf cub happily plays here.
A wolf cub happily plays here.
A wolf cub happily plays here.
A wolf cub happily plays here.
The mother wolf stands here, protecting her young cubs.

This small cave has been hollowed out of the earth beneath a large hummock in the brushland. The ceiling seems to be held together by a dense mat of roots from the vegetation growing above, and in some places these roots trail down, adorned with small clods of dirt that dangle in mid-air. Clumps of fur gather in small piles in corners of this burrow, and the loose dirt floor is littered with small rocks and what appears to be the occasional bone of a small animal. At the entrance to the cave debris is piled up by the opening: dead leaves, plant stalks, and shreds of bark.
117774: This area is open and grassy, with the occasional mature tree that casts minimal shade. Low-growing grasses and the occasional heath or gorse bush cover the ground, which is uneven and rolling, with broad depressions and low hummocks. Here and there the vegetation thins out, the soil giving way to bare, exposed rock, which is tan and crumbling. To the north the ground becomes hilly, but near-vertical cuts along the sides of the steeper hills form enough of a barrier to prevent movement in that direction. To the south is a dense forest, its border overgrown with brush and impassable.
117775: An occasional mature tree rises above this grassland, but the vegetation here consists primarily of grasses and the occasional low bush. The ground is uneven, with many low hummocks and shallow depressions; on some of the hummocks rock peeks through the thin soil. To the south a forest rises above the plains, its edge dense with brush to the point of being impassable. To the north a series of crumbling, exposed rock ledges blocks the way to the hills that rise steeply above.
117776: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

A few mature trees dot these hills, but otherwise this area is open, the ground underfoot uneven and rolling. Low grasses cover the ground, mixed with heath and the occasional clump of gorse bushes. The grass in the low spots seems to be thicker and taller, suggesting that this area is low-lying, with water collecting in the depressions after a rain. To the south a dense forest can be seen, while to the north the ground rises sharply into a range of hills. Passage into the hills to the north is blocked by ledges of crumbling rock, too unstable to traverse or climb.
117777: An old, bent alder tree twists its gnarly frame against savage dogwood.

Brushy, red-twigged dogwood covers this morass with rampant, white-flowered branches. The shrubs only grow up to the waist of a man, but are so thick in the moist soil as to cause difficult travel. Grey, white-flecked alder trees fight for life in the wetter dips, their shiny green, leathery leaves set off against the red of the lower plants. Meandering through the brush is a seldom used trail, running roughly northeast to southwest.
117778:
A blooming water-lily floats on the surface of the water.
A water moccasin slithers out of sight just below the surface of the water.
A large bullfrog croaks loudly.

Luscious, yellow flowers clamber up between circular leaves that float in this black water. The lily pads are so abundant here, that the lands appears to be one, great, flat field. The water comes up to mid-thigh on a man, and the land that does rise up is so saturated as to provide sloppy footing. This footing does seem to lead through the land, and if followed is found to cross from southwest to northeast.
117779: Silver-leaved hawthorn shrubs grow tall on this spongy ground, interspersed under the wide canopies of crab apple trees. The ground is covered in mushy, leaf litter, and is shot through thick with new shoots of ever-growing brush, causing travel to be hindered and slow. Above, brown and white butterflies float among the crab apple flowers, landing on the trees for a rest. Hidden in the shade of the shrubs and trees is a meandering trail that runs from the southwest to the northeast.
117780: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

Patches of purple heather linger on this high moorland, the hills large and pitched. The rest of the ground is covered in a mat of starry flowers and black berries that hide between needle-like leaves. The ground is wet and peaty, springing back underfoot. Nary a sound is heard on these hills except for the trickling of water.
117781:
A powerful ram stands here, poised and alert.
A wild sheep with a short, greyish coat grazes here.
A wild sheep with a short, greyish coat grazes here.
A wild sheep with a short, greyish coat grazes here.

Bent, sparse, rock whitebeam trees cling to limestone overhangs on these hills. The rocky land concedes patches of grasses in the flatter areas, but otherwise is devoid of flora. Views from the hilltops allow a sight of the great marsh to the southeast where these hills dramatically slide into a watery morass, and to the north and west the hills drop off abruptly in staggering cliffs.
117782: This narrow trail still sees occasional use as the surrounding vegetation has not yet managed to cover it. To the east, a stand of willow trees rises out of the plains and marks the western edge of the Midgewater. To the west a lush grassland extends, providing a home to uncounted numbers of small animals. The trail continues along the edge of the marsh to both the north and south.
117783: This narrow trail bends sharply from south to east here, skirting a stand of hardwood trees that has flourished against the Midgewater Marshes. To the west and north extends a grass plain, seemingly teeming with small game.
117784: The trails converge here into a crude intersection. To the west, the land rises into some high moorlands, with a narrow, dusty trail heading in that direction. A large, slightly wider trail bends south and east. This one is packed more firm, evidence that it is well-travelled.
117785: Heaving green shrubs show their purple and yellow flowers on these high moorlands. The land stretches in long, waving views in all directions, eventually flattening to the east. To the south, the hills become sharp and impassable, and to the west, drop off in ragged cliffs. From the north and heading east is a lightly used dirt trail that is lost and found at many junctures by all but the most wisened travellers.
117786: High moorlands stretch out in all directions, hilly and covered in heath. The plants that grow here are hardy and thrive in the cold and wet environs. On steep dropoffs, limestone is exposed and small, twisted trees grow, fighting for life, able to escape the rampant shrubs. Running north and south through the land is a lightly worn trail.
117787: The narrow path bends as it makes its way through the bleak land, its path leading to the north and east. Some rocky hills prevent travel to the south while the rest of the ground is covered in heath. Few grasses, shrubs, and trees are able to take root here in the poor soil.
117788:
A grey wolf is here, salivating profusely.
A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

The narrow path continues straight north and south here, through the wild meadows to the east and west. A hill rises in the distance to the north. Otherwise, the land is flat and open, surrounded by waves of tall grasses and forbs flowing around islands of bushes.
117789: Stand of Trees on a Wild Plain

A small stand of tall, straight pines grows to the west, at the base of a tall ridge. A wild plain, filled with grazed grasses, stretches out in all other directions. Only the occasional tree or bush breaks the monotony of the landscape, with trees becoming more rare as the land moves south.
117790: A swarthy, little bandit advances forward.

A bleak land stretches out far into the distance before terminating at some rocky hills to the south. Some grasses do manage to take root here, but most of the ground is covered in heath. The occasional stunted tree and shrub can be seen taking root where the soil was rich enough.
117791: A valley of heath stretches here, nested between some rocky hills to the south, and a ridge topped with rowan trees to the north. A large number of shrubs grow in abundance here, finding pockets of soil rich enough to sustain them. Some meagre clumps of grass have also taken root along with an occasional tree.
117792: Ridge with a Cluster of Rowan Trees

A solid, but stunted, rowan tree has established itself here.
A black raven flies in the sky searching for flesh to prey upon.
A black raven flies in the sky searching for flesh to prey upon.
A black raven flies in the sky searching for flesh to prey upon.

A slight ridge inclines here out of the western fields, to a high point where a cluster of rowan trees has grown at its rocky top. They stand out among the surrounding fields, and a dried-out brook bed can be spotted towards the northwest. A valley stretches out towards the east, dotted with shrubs.
117793:
A white wolf is here, prowling for something to eat.
A thin, crippled deer looks around timidly.

Yellow and green gorse fight for life amid coarse brush in the hard packed dirt on this open field. As far as the eye can see are plains, and only the hazy outlines of hills are visible far to the east. The tips of a tall cliff can be seen, rising above the plain very far to the south.
117794:
Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.
An apple tree with bright green leaves grows here.
On the tree's branches are four apples.

Gorse, shrub, and buttercup scrounge for life on this wild plain. The ground is hard and often bare, exuding the smell of soil. The plain extends in all directions and only to the northeast is there any change of scenery: brown foothills rising slowly to the east.
117795: Hard shrubs cling on southerly sides of the larger stones that are scattered here. East of here, a bald scarp sharply rises, halting any travel in that direction. Otherwise the plain is unbroken in all directions. Vegetation grows thickly to the west, preventing travel in that direction.
117796: A long-stemmed plant that branches into many bright yellow flowers grows here.

This land transitions from a damp land to the west, gradually becoming drier to the east. Birch and brushwood grow thickly to the west, and a row of yellow buttercup grow next to them. Gradually the flora thins east where grasses and shrub give way to gorse.
117797:
A thin, crippled deer looks around timidly.
A white wolf is here, prowling for something to eat.

Northwest here, grasses overtake the birch and brushwood that dominate the western edge of this plain. The grass grows thick here, hiding insects and small animals beneath its depths. Some small shrubs sparsely decorate the land, bent and scraggly, and dirt swirls in the air.
117798: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

Dense thorny cover spreads over this field. The plant is called gorse in the common tongue, whereas rangers call it whin. Perpetually in bloom, its yellow flowers cover the land in all directions, and move as an ocean when the northern gales blow.
117799:
A small cluster of purplish-pink flowers lies here.
A roe deer is standing here, watching the terrain while chewing the vegetation.
A roe deer is standing here, watching the terrain while chewing the vegetation.

These small rolling hills are peaceful, the ground being covered in golden grasses that blow about mesmerizingly. The vista provides views in all directions, allowing little cover. To the west a sharp scarp impedes travel.
117800: This furrowed land gradually changes from a brush covered plain in the west to golden hills, thus beginning what the elves call Emyn Sul. The beginnings of these windswept hills are home to hardy herding animals and their predators. The land is wild and becomes more so to the east where far off hills are seen.
117801: These foothills furrow at abnormal angles, betraying some ancient disturbance, perhaps a battle. Otherwise, the land generally rises to the east ever so slightly, being covered in flora much undisturbed. The country is silent except for the ruffling of animals and insects.
117802: A small cluster of purplish-pink flowers lies here.

This land slopes up from the west in an impressive vista, giving a grand view of this high rolling plain. Hardy gorse grows in dense patches, filling in low spots, while grasses cover the rest. Leeward of the gorse provides refuge for insects and small animals.
117803: Foothills roll over land covered by golden grasses. No other plant seems to be able to withstand the dogged northern gales. To the south, the land drops sharply in a cliff where it overlooks a creek bed. Animal skeletons litter the land just before the eastern cliff, site of an animal feast. A path leads to the east.
117804: Rolling Hills above a Ruined Camp

A peak in the grassy, rolling hills stands high above tent roofs and the husks of aged buildings that appear between the undulating hills below. Scattered about the peak are small shrubs and stunted deciduous trees. A steep path winds down the hill to the east and south.
117805: A toppled monolith lies on the ground.

The land here lies lower than the surrounding hills to the north and west, and is surrounded on the east and south by brown leather tents. A tall, mossy pine lives south of the path, its branches providing a high perch for owls, squirrels, and snakes.
117806: A thin, crippled deer looks around timidly.

Yellow flowering gorse is prolific on this plain, growing wildly thick as it approaches the cliffs south and east. Deer or elk can be heard bleating to their young in the distance. North and west the plain continues unimpeded, the plant life there being more meagre.
117807: Grasses cover these foothills in a great golden landscape. The grasses stretch on and on, allowing an easterly view of hazy outlines of far off hills. To the west, a steep dropping scarp would stop any beast or man from travelling there.
117808: Large swaths of grasses are interrupted by an imposing brush-filled gully that runs from the southwest. The gully tapers to a traversable ditch northeast over this heath, splitting the land into two. An animal path is visible at the shallow end of the ditch, and the sour smell of musk pervades the furrow. To the east a formidable cliff seems untraversable.
117809: The western and northern edges of this plain drop dramatically, forming a long curving cliff. This is but the beginning of Emyn Sul, land of hardy shepherds and wolves who face the harsh northern wind with determination. The plains begin to roll, forming foothills that give a meagre life to grasses and shrubs.
117812: Two ancient pine trees bend like the earth's hands, blown over south by steady northerlies. Their bases are provided some cover by a small exposed dirt and rock cliff. The rest of this land is foothills low and sturdy covered in golden grass. East of here a large cliff rises, which continues to form a high plain.
117813: Hardy herd animals forage on the thick grasses here. Juniper holds on stubbornly in between rocky mounds that sit among the land. The land drops sharply far the west and south, preventing travel there. The hills undulate to the east and north.
117814: Stunted hills beget stunted trees and scraggly bushes. The land is sparse, mostly grasses and hardy bush, but leeward of hills, bent wych elm and black poplar huddle under cedar overhangs. A steep, rock-strewn scarp lies north. To the south the lands gives way to a steep cliff.
117815:
A grass-clogged creek lies at the base of two hills.
A water moccasin slithers out of sight just below the surface of the water.
A water moccasin slithers out of sight just below the surface of the water.
A swarm of midges is here, humming around you.

Blackthorn forms a thick meandering copse at the bottom of this hilly gap. The low lying land is obviously a creek bed, but its water depth is nearly impossible to tell, with all the brush choking the top. The bed runs south, heading into an even more jammed shrub-gully.
117816:
A shallow creek runs meekly at the base of the hill.
A swarm of midges is here, humming around you.

Tall cliff walls impose the land north and west, scrub pine cramming themselves on the rocky cliffs. Water stains indicate a few trickles which feed the brushy plants at the bottom of this gully. Running south is a creekbed, choked with lush blackthorn. Club moss covers any exposed rock, and the sounds of trickling water permeate the surroundings.
117817:
A grass-choked creek lies between a bend in the hills.
A noisy neekerbreeker is shrieking here.
A swarm of midges is here, humming around you.

Steep cliffs loom over both sides of this wild gully, blocking out all but midday light. Brambles grow thick and prickly in a clump on the southestern edge of the gully turn. A small pool can be seen shining just in front of the bend, choked with grass. Rocks intermix with mud and brush along the creekbed.
117818:
A soot-filled creek runs between the hills here.
A large leech is moving close to you, searching for blood.
A noisy neekerbreeker is shrieking here.

The ground here is rocky and steep, inclined north between the scarped walls of this gully. Little light gets here and the creekbed is well defined, as few plants are able to survive but clubmoss. The walls of the gully are cut of stone and are stained dark rust from water seeping down the sides.
117820: Brisk air blows from the north, bending what little plant life that exists to its will. The hills are low and strewn with prickly brush and bent pine. They continue northeast, gradually rising to form a larger range. Directly north of here the land ends in a steep scarped drop off.
117821: These foothills are thicketed with brambles and shrubs, intertwined with short grasses and large round stones. The landscape forms a natural maze, traversable by small animals with ease. A stiff northerly breeze is constantly sweeping overland, stirring up dirt and leaves in little dust devils.
117822:
A short evergreen plant, with slightly bluish needles, grows here.
On the plant, there are a cluster of hard, round, black berries.

This highland furrows in craggy knobs making travel arduous. Bent pine and juniper fight off thick brush in rough knots. The land descends sharply in all directions but north. A tall pine tree grows near the peak of the cliff, providing a home for birds and insects.
117823: A grassy path here is shaded by many branches of pines and elms. Roots from the trees crisscross the path, creating tiny hills and a home for insects and small animals. To the north the landscape rises to a peak, and the path continues southward. Exploration east and west is obstructed by tall rocky hills.
117824: Yellow flowers, with grey-green foliage, grow in clusters here.

Irregular sod gives way to packed earth, olive-coloured brush and spindly gorse. To the west and north, the land is much the same. To the east, a brush ridden cliff impedes travel. The land to the south rises sharply into a tall, rocky peak.
117825:
A brown bear is sleeping here.
A brown bear is sleeping here.

The ground drops down steeply here into a deep hollow. The air is permeated by a thick, damp mist, and an earthy smell of soggy leaves and toadstools is a constant presence here. The haphazard way in which this hollow was dug seems to indicate it was created by animals.
117828:
A dirty shovel is lying on the ground here.
A small black vicious rat squeaks at you for disturbing it.

A simple lean-to has been constructed along the back of this farmhouse, a continuation of the roof that slopes down at a lesser angle until it ends at support posts that have been driven deep into the bare dirt. A large wood pile has been stacked underneath the lean-to, near the back wall of the house but not against it, and a large stump with an axe sunk into it stands a short distance away. Various farm tools are hung on pegs on the back wall of the house by the wood pile, protected from the elements by the roof above. A simple wooden porch, no more than a few short planks laid together, leads to the back door of the house.
117829: These hills rise and fall gradually as they stretch in every direction except west and east, where they fall to blend into grassy fields. To the south passage is blocked by taller hills that rise up from steep, vertical rock faces; the rock is crumbling, and too unstable to climb. This area is marked by clumps of low-growing grasses of various heights, creating a three-dimensional patchwork mosaic. No mature trees grow here; some bare areas on the sides of the hills where bare rock has been exposed suggest that the dominance of low-growing vegetation is due to thin soil.
117830: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

These hills are low and rounded, rolling off into the distance in the east and south. A continuous line of vertical cuts in the hillsides to the north and west break this monotony, creating steep drops of crumbling stone that are too tall to traverse, and too unstable to climb. A great number of heath shrubs grow here, covering the hills in a low patchwork of vegetation. Gaps in this coverage are filled in by low, clump-forming grasses, creating a mix of tan and green that blends with distance. There are no mature trees here; some exposed, rocky outcroppings suggest that the soil is too thin.
117831: Heath-covered hills stretch in all directions, with exposed white rock showing through on the sharper angles. Closer inspection of the rock finds it to be crumbly and dry. In deeper cracks, leeward of the northern wind, scrub pines grow short and twisted. On the far northern and southern edges of these hills, cliffs drop off, high and treacherous.
117832: Coarse grasses roll on hills that heighten to the north and east, then drop off in sharp white cliffs. In low dips, the hills fill with spiky, green and yellow gorse, and rarely, a red-berried rowan grows bent and gnarly. South, the hills decline and the grass turns from rough, tan sedge into a green valley.
117833: Scabious and hay rattle fill this vast, low valley with periwinkle and yellow flowers as it pitches down from distant hills to the east. The air is filled with fresh, green scents, and long-tailed tits fly about in small flocks hunting for moths and butterflies.
117834:
A large elm tree spreads its branches over the surrounding land.
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.

This green valley gives a grand view of the land as it slopes up, east, slowly reaching far off hills. Grasses billow in gentle breezes, with yellow flowers dipping as small bees, wasps and flies hover towards their nectar. To the west, in the deepest part of the valley, great elm trees grow among thick gorse.
117835: Muted orange and tan grasses cover this low, shallow valley as it slopes down south and east. To the south, the land is rife with green and yellow shrubs, and to the east the valley stretches as far as the eye can see and is strewn with large, scattered pine trees. North and west, stunning white cliffs obtrude over the land.
117836: This shallow valley transitions from spiky, green shrubs in the west to purple, flowering grasses. The air is filled with bees and butterflies, and rarely an orange-breasted bird flies off. Overall, the land steadily rises to the east until it rolls into distant hills.
117837: This lush field is thick with sweet smells, rising up from meadowsweet that carpets the land. The ground is almost alive, bouncing back every step, and the air is riotous with insects and birds. To the east, the land rises slowly, and is interspersed with large elm trees. West, the land is pressed by a large, hanging cliff. South, the land turns from lush to boggy.
117838: There is a lot of snow on the ice.

This trail, running from the Chetwood north alongside the western edge of the Midgewater, here passes through a low area and consequently becomes very muddy. Several shallow ditches enter the marshes to the east, and there are no bridges along the trail. To the west of the trail, the land is much dryer and covered with thick grasses.
117839: There is a lot of snow on the ice.

This trail is pressed flush against the western border of the Midgewater Marshes. In many places, the reeds and sedges of the marsh actually intrude upon the trail. The ground is extremely muddy, and trail is often cut by stretches of shallow water (not suitable for drinking) over which there are no bridges.
117840:
A skeleton of some humanoid lies in the dust.
A reddish-brown shrub with purplish-pink flowers grows here.
A black raven flies in the sky searching for flesh to prey upon.
A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.
A black raven flies in the sky searching for flesh to prey upon.
A bear is here, covered with coarse black fur.

Rocky hills in the south transition to heath, relenting to hardy, purple and yellow flowered brush. The rocky ground is hard, grey limestone, whereas the heath covering is spongy, bouncing back any step. Winds blow cold and wet on the highlands, and except for the wind, all else is quiet. North, east and south, the hills drop off in formidable cliffs, allowing the only exit west.
117841:
A large elm tree spreads its branches over the surrounding land.
A tree-snake lies wrapped around one of the tree branches.

In this brushy valley, slick-barked buckthorn stick their thorny, black-berried branches up through green and yellow gorse in an ancient, verdant battle. In the deepest point of the valley, east, large elm trees grow, striking to the eye. Underfoot, skeletal shrubs, dead grasses and old weeds hinder travel.
117842: Small-leaved, yellow-flowered shrubs fill this low, wide valley as it rises up to the south. The shrubs form in close, and stick their spiky leaves out on club-like branches. The ground is uneven and rocky with hummocks and dips hidden in tangles of old, dense mats of grass. To the west, the shrubs grow wild and imposing, blocking travel that way.
117843: Rolling hills of various heights are visible to the north and west, although passage in those directions is blocked by nearly continuous cuts in the ground. These cuts mark sudden dropoffs, near-vertical hillsides of exposed rock that are steep and tall enough to prevent travel. Vegetation here is low-growing but plentiful; these hills are covered by grasses and short heath shrubs. In some areas the grass is very thin, the exposed soil giving way to bare rock that has been worn smooth by weather over many years.
117844: Source of a Stream in the Hills
A clear pool forms on the edge of a stream among large, round stones.

This valley is wide and flat, with the edges of the valley bowl rising up to the north and west in the form of rolling hills. A small stream twists through the valley, originating in an exposed cut of rock at the edge of the hills; the water flows even in dry weather, suggesting that a natural spring is the source. The stream bed is wide but shallow; the bottom is a mix of gravel and mud, and is easily stirred up to cloud the water with sediment. Tall brush grows along the edges of the stream, with an occasional tree rising above the tangle. Farther away from the stream bed the brush thins out to tall grasses, which mat down underfoot.
117845: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

Low, rolling hills rise above the plains to the west and a valley to the southeast. Steep cuts mar the hills in a number of places, including a long line of near-continuous cuts to the west and north that reveal steep, crumbling rock faces on the sides of the hills. These rock faces are tall enough to prevent movement in those directions, and unstable enough to make them too dangerous to climb. Low grasses grow in clumps of various heights here, with short heath growing above them in a patchwork pattern. Here and there rock has been exposed, suggesting that the soil is thin and poor.
117846: A beautiful and docile horse is standing here.

Hills rise up in all directions except east, where the valley descends as it continues. The hills appear at this distance to be covered with sparse vegetation, but in this low area the vegetation is lush and thick. Tall grasses grow in clumps, interspersed with some thickets of tall gorse bushes, and the occasional small tree rises above these. Some threads of greener grass cut through these fields, winding ribbons of brilliant colour in an otherwise muted landscape: closer inspection shows these to be drainage channels through the valley, and they likely stay wet long after a rain.
117847: These low, rolling hills are covered with short brush, both heath and young gorse bushes. These bushes hide narrow clefts and shallow depressions, hazards for those passing through here on foot as well as for those that are mounted. Some areas contain little to no vegetation, and on closer examination the soil appears to be extremely thin: bare rock is exposed in some of these areas, light-coloured and crumbling. North and south there are sudden, vertical cuts through the hills, steep and wide enough to block movement in those directions. To the west the low heath gives way to denser brush, and the tangled bushes, vines and thorns block the descent to the plains below.
117848: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

These rolling hills extend to the east, forming a border to the valley that slopes down to the north. South and west the hills are interrupted by abrupt cuts and sudden drops, with exposed, crumbling stone ledges that make travel impossible and climbing too dangerous to attempt. The vegetation here is low-growing, with no trees in sight: grass clumps of varying heights cover the ground, and small shrubs rise above the grasses, both heath and scraggly gorse. Bare rock is exposed on some of the slopes throughout these hills, suggesting that the soil here is thin.
117849: A tall stag is here, grazing peacefully.

These hills are steep, forming the edge of a wide, flat valley that extends to the north. To the south a continuous line of steep dropoffs prevents travel; the drop is not far, but the exposed, crumbling rock makes traversing to the plains below unsafe. Vegetation here is low-growing, consisting of clumps of grasses of various heights and a number of broadleaf forbs. No mature trees are visible among these hills; judging from the bare rock that is frequently exposed on the hillsides, a thin soil restricts the height of the vegetation. Drainage cuts and channels run in branching patterns through the hills towards the plains below, the gaps wide and deep.
117850: A large elk is standing here, chewing grass and leaves.

These hills are low and rolling, extending to the west and north. The low spots between the rises are brushy, full of tall grasses and dense vegetation. The ground in these low areas stays wet long after a rain, and some small stands of river birch have begun to rise up above the surrounding shrubs, thriving in the moist soil. Higher up on the hills rock is exposed, indicating the soil is thinner and drier; clumps of short grasses and the occasional low-growing shrub are the only things growing in these spots. To the south are steep dropoffs, the exposed rock crumbling and too unsafe to climb or traverse. To the east the hills descend quickly into a brushy marsh.
117851:
A grey snake slides along the water.
A grey snake slides along the water.
A grey snake slides along the water.
A grey snake slides along the water.

This overgrown fen is very wet, being low and collecting water from hills to the west. Rushes and reeds grow tall and hide sulphurous bogs and green pools. The land sinks in each step, drawing any land bound creature into the quagmire, slow and mucky. The land is so low that only to the west can one climb out, there being a gradual abatement of wetness.
117852: This valley is wide and flat, the edges rising up into hills to the south and east. Tall grasses dominate this area, their feathery seed heads bending with the slightest breeze. Dead stems and flower heads from previous years mix with the current green growth, creating a duller, lighter colour when viewed at a distance. Some shrubs are mixed in among the grasses, and here and there a young pine tree has established itself. Deer trails have worn the grass down to dirt and dead stems in places, revealing a rich, dark soil underfoot.
117853: Whortle-leaved shrubs hide in the dips of these low, rolling, heath-topped hills. Running through southeast, a small stream cuts deep into the ground, exposing bedrock and flows clear, showing its gravelly bottom. Where the stream sits at ground level, dark-leaved willows gather, small and stiff with papery-thin, bluish leaves.
117854: A mottled snake is sneaking here, ready to sink its fangs into flesh.

This cut under a rock ledge opens into a wider burrow, with rock overhead and a dirt floor. The burrow is not tall, and anyone except a hobbit would have to stoop to move around. There are some shallow depressions in the dirt floor, and many of them are filled with organic debris, mostly old grass stems and dead weed stalks. The rock at the back of the burrow has formed into a series of step-like ledges, with narrow but deep alcoves extending beyond each into the back wall of the cave. The air in here is damp, but there is little moisture visible other than some small beaded water droplets on the rock ceiling.
117855: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

This verdant meadow sweeps all about, the vetch and knapweed providing a green and purple, rippling view. A rich smell of life pervades the air, and insects buzz about, emboldened by their boundless numbers. Concealed in the grasses is a trail that runs generally north and south, muddy and narrow. To the west, grand oak trees peek over a wild, impenetrable bramble-wall.
117856: A purple-tinged meadow stretches about, the flowered grasses blowing gently in the breeze. White butterflies and small, yellow moths flutter lazily, dodging quick wagtails. The ground is spongy, and gets quite wet on the eastern side of this land. Running north and south through the meadow, a narrow, muddy trail meanders. To the west stands a striking forest, impassable with thorny bramble.
117857: A black wolf pads restlessly, looking for its next prey.

Horse-high goat willow grows rangy, dark-stemmed, and thick in this boggy land. Green, oval leaves grow in all directions as the shrubs close in on each other, vying for sunlight. A narrow trail snakes its way through the land, north and south, but is easily lost as the verdure grows quick to overtake the open space, creating a maze for all but the most vigilant. East, the willow shrubs grow so thick as to impede travel and give life to a colony of large, vivid, purple butterflies that fly about the shrub tops, flitting and wry.
117860: A fallen tree lies on the ground, its clump of roots pointing upwards.

This deciduous forest is mostly oak, but some birch and rowan trees are mixed throughout. Here and there the skeletal remains of a pine tree still stands, shaded into oblivion, branches bare and broken. Many of the living trees here look unhealthy, with dying and broken limbs that mirror those of the pines; some have succumbed to whatever is afflicting them. The bark on these is sloughing off in long strips, revealing a white threadlike fungus underneath. Piles of bark and dead, broken branches have collected beneath these trees, mixed with the leaf litter that covers the forest floor.
117861: This mature forest is populated with large trees, their trunks wide and devoid of branches until they spread out far overhead in a dense canopy that blocks the sky. Small saplings are trying to grow in this deep shade, scattered at random among the larger trunks. The occasional dead tree is still standing, but the canopy has already closed around the space its leafless branches left; others have fallen, either lying on the ground or wedged at an angle where they landed across the forked trunks of those still standing. Low-growing plants form clumps across the forest floor, which is otherwise devoid of brush.
117862: A wooden direction sign is here.

A small but well-defined trail extends westward into the wood. To the east, the trail becomes faint and harder to follow as it descends toward a deeply carved valley. Bird song dominates the aural atmosphere, interrupted occasionally by distant, guttural squeals likely originating from the infamous swineherd that wanders Chetwood.
117864: A small trail meanders through openings in the forest where fallen trees grow moss. The dense greenery does not hinder the birds above or the squirrels near the ground. Saplings and younger trees crowd the trail's edges until it opens as it approaches the settlement of Staddle to the south.
117865: Bordered on either side by low, wooden buildings, the village trail continues north and south. To the north, young oak trees appear at the edges of the trail, thickening into a deep wood on the horizon. To the south, fields of low, bushy, vibrantly green crops dominate the landscape, except for a large barn that appears beyond the curve of the trail.
117866: Deep ruts create a ridged pattern on the dirt trail, evidence of many carts travelling from the barn to the south, through and out of the village. A broken cart leans against the northern face of the barn and a damp earthy smell occasionally wafts from that direction.
117867:
A small oaken table has been set here.
On the table, there are two piles of pipe-weed.
A hobbit farmer is here, thinking about seeds and vegetables.
A skinny young man stands here, a blade of grass in his mouth.
A hobbit farmer is here, thinking about seeds and vegetables.

Immediately upon entering the barn, a distinct herbal and woody smell overpowers the senses. High overhead, stalks of pipeweed hang from the rafters of the ceiling. In the centre of the room are rows of wooden tables with benches at each end, on top of which dried flowers and leaves lay strewn about after having been clipped from their stalks.
117868: There are two bales of hay here.

Enormous round bales of hay sit perched atop the rolling hills of Archet while dense thickets of elderberry grow nestled in the valley troughs. A well-maintained fence built of fresh timber blocks the way north and east, bounding the fields from the neighbouring woodlands. A twin pair of birch trees, adorned with gleaming silver-grey bark, grow along the fence.
117869:
A placid pond is here, inviting you to take a refreshing drink.
A woolly sheep is grazing here.
A crayfish is here, snapping its claws at you.

A verdant green pasture has been cleared out from the heart of the woods for the purpose of farming, bordered by a well-maintained fence to the north. A small pond sits nestled between a group of stately oak trees that nourishes the local livestock. The surface of the water catches the reflection of the sky above, afforded by the large break in the forest canopy.
117870:
A large shrub grows here, its branches loosely spreading.
On the shrub, there are three piles of cherries.
A large shrub grows here, its branches loosely spreading.
On the shrub, there are some cherries.
A field mouse noses about hungrily, searching for food.

Dozens of mature, thick-trunked cherry trees have been meticulously planted in neat rows, making for a sizeable orchard. The sweet scent of cherry wood dominates the space and nary a noise can be heard in any direction. Several reed baskets in severe disrepair lie littered all around, casualties of long since forgotten harvests.
117871: A blue dragonfly is circling around.

Neatly cultivated hills of fertile soil dominate the landscape, nestled tightly between the Chetwood forest and fields of Bree. The remote village of Archet can be seen to the northeast, following a snaking dirt road in the distance. Large amounts of livestock wander about, unfettered by fence or chain, amongst the sea of tilled fields and emerald grasses.
117872:
There are two mushrooms here.
A patch of orange mushrooms springs from the ground here.

Lush, well-watered fields have been utilized for the prolific farming of mushrooms by the locals of Archet. Patches of golden chanterelles and russet bolete mushrooms grow along decaying elms and countless tufts of rye grass. Hills and forest begin to make way for an open valley to the south, while a green barn, overgrown with ivy, crowns a hill to the north.
117873: A narrow trail runs east and west, with a small scarp bordering it to the north. The trail runs along the base of the scarp. To the south lies an area of damp grassland, and beyond that the Midgewater Marshes. Sometimes the trail is damp and muddy when it passes through a low area, but mostly it is dry and made of packed earth.
117874: This trail of packed earth runs eastward along the base of the scarp marking the northern boundary of the Midgewater. To the south, it skirts the western edge of the marsh and eventually enters the Chetwood.
117878: Dense scrubs eke out a meagre existence on the hard earth. Brisk winds frequently sweep across the plains, often bringing a chill from the north. There is a small scarp immediately to the south, but travel in that direction is no real challenge.
117884: The land here is relatively flat, save for a slight elevation to the north that gradually ascends into some rolling foothills. To the east, the land is flat and covered in a thin, grassy carpet. There are few trees about, but the plains are dominated by scraggly brush and wiry thorn bushes.
117896: A gentle slope up from the southwest leads to the edge of this low bluff that overlooks the tangled vegetation of the Midgewater Marshes. Directly below, after a drop of about ten feet, the muddy pools and wet vegetation of the marsh hold sway, but this hill provides a dry respite for travellers.
117897: A noisy neekerbreeker is shrieking here.

Clouds of hungry insects are raised by each footstep, each seeking warm blood with a seemingly malevolent intelligence. The air is filled with the buzzing and chirping of insects, punctuated by the loud calls of frogs. The water is shallow for the most part, but there are occasional pockets of black mud that seem to have no bottom.
117898:
A brown toad is here, hunting flies.
A green frog is here, hopping around.
A robin is here, carrying small pieces of wood to its nest.

Marsh grasses and alders dot the landscape as the swampy soil of the northern marsh becomes firmer ground here at its southern edge. To the east and south, low hillocks rise out of the marshes, but a steep escarpment hinders southern travel. A light forest of oak and ash grows in the western distance.
117899: The ground is quite moist here and the small stones and brushwood underfoot are covered with a soft, yellowish green moss. Elm and alder trees grow all around and begin to crowd together as the western landscape transitions into dense forest. To the east, the reed-filled edge of the Midgewater Marshes is just visible, bordered on its southern edge by hillsides.
117900:
A huge, poisonous spider is here.
A huge, poisonous spider is here.

The low hills rise toward a small clearing surrounded by thick bushes and willows of many species. The firm, grass-covered ground gives way to soft patches of mud in certain places. To the north, a steep escarpment plunges toward a marsh, while the eastern and southern directions are blocked by impenetrable bushes and willow trees.
117901: The forest is lightly populated by oaks and yews. The thick, knobby trunks and reddish bark of the latter trees seem ominous, as if an ancient and inscrutable spirit lurks within. Distant sounds of foot and hoof traffic to the south occasionally break the eerie aura permeating this edge of the wood.
117902: Light Forest Bordering the Old East Road

Not too far to the north, the Chetwood becomes a dense and impenetrable tangle of brushwood, tall ferns, and old thick-trunked trees. In the immediate surroundings, however, only a few dozen oaks stand along the northern edge of the Old East Road. Charred grasses dot the space between trees, likely the remnants of recent camps made by travellers coming and going from Bree.
117903: A colossal tree dominates the landscape, its vast canopy towering above.

The surrounding forest is dominated by a single, massive yew tree. Smaller oaks and dogwoods appear scattered in the distance, their branches hanging low as if bending the knee to the kingly, ancient tree. The ground is littered with bright red arils that contrast starkly with the dull forest floor.
117904: A swarm of mosquitoes is here, humming around you.

A damp, decaying stench fills the air, accompanied by a cacophony of croaking from unseen marsh frogs. The ground underfoot is soft, waterlogged, and none too easy to wade through. In some areas, shallow brown puddles appear filled with low bur-reed and tall bulrush.
117905: The surrounding field explodes in colour as wildflowers of every hue and season reach toward the open sky. Toward the east, the flowers fade away as reeds spring stiffly from the soil. Piles of chopped wood and logs lie to the south, seemingly abandoned.
117906: A narrow field, full of wildflowers and tufts of grasses both short and tall, stretches between the eerily dark Chetwood forest to the west and the muggy Midgewater Marshes to the east. A cacophony of croaks and chirps echoes from the marshes and across the meadow.
117907: The ground is very wet here, almost swampy. Dense, small willows rise above the marshes to the north, east, and south, and there is an especially thick stand of reeds farther east. To the west, an open meadow stretches north and south and a dense tree line marks the western horizon.
117908: The frequent stretches of deep mud and black ponds make it impossible to travel in a given direction with any certainty. On all sides the marshes reign unchallenged, providing a home to ravenous hordes of biting and stinging insects, who in turn sustain a huge population of frogs and other less familiar predators.
117909: This field extends north and south, marking the boundary between the dense, Chetwood forest to the west and the Midgewater Marshes to the east. The trail bends away from the forest toward a narrow field in the north. Tall tufts of switchgrass line the trail, becoming thicker and more crowded nearer the marshes.
117910:
A brown toad is here, hunting flies.
A green frog is here, hopping around.

The solid ground of the western field has become squidgy underfoot, and every lifted footstep produces a soft squelching sound. Directly to the east lies a thick and impenetrable mound of brushwood. The marsh is totally overgrown here. The tendrils and thorns of the brushwood make any movement east inconceivable.
117911: A water moccasin slithers out of sight just below the surface of the water.

Sedges and bulrushes form walkable islands on the edge of a marsh. What ground exists is very muddy and gives to any step. Flat green plants cover the water's surface, while old stems stick through, dead and brown. To the west, where the land rises, tall, green shrubs grow in a thick, entangling wall, stopping travel in that direction.
117912:
A bent pine tree extends its scant branches in a modest attempt at survival.
A water moccasin slithers out of sight just below the surface of the water.
A large bullfrog croaks loudly.

Low rises form soggy islands that are overgrown with wide-leaved reedmace. The surrounding shallow water is thick with wet, fuzzy hornwort that sloshes onto any beast's foot that travels through. Sparingly, sickly, drowned pine trees grow on the higher ground, their trunks black and their needles yellow and drooping. The air is slightly sour and is abuzz with small, black bugs.
117913:
Clusters of slender stems and tall leaves thrive in the mud and shallows.
A water moccasin slithers out of sight just below the surface of the water.
A large bullfrog croaks loudly.

Insects create constant movement on the surface of the water that stagnates on the edge of a marsh. Dark pools surround low rises of narrow-bladed bulrushes, providing soggy footing for land bound travellers. In the water, choking plants vie for sunlight as the rushes droop over. The land is loud with the chirping sounds of frogs and crickets, and echoes sharply off the water.
117914:
There is some snow on the ice.
A buzzing dumbledor is here, flying around you in close circles.

The difficulties of navigating through this area are but a harbinger of the troubles that await those who dare explore deeper into the marsh. Frequently, treacherous pools of unknown depth are hidden beneath a cover of aquatic plants, and what land there is is far from solid.
117915: Clouds of insects clog the air, making it impossible to breathe with comfort. There is no way to travel in any one given direction with consistency, as the pools of muddy water and treacherous mudbanks seem to shift and conspire to prevent it.
117916: The marshes come to their end some distance to the west, as beyond the dense vegetation the dark wall of the trees of the Chetwood can sometimes be made out. Frogs and other small animals abound, flourishing on the veritable plague of small insects that give these marshes their name.
117917: A noisy neekerbreeker is shrieking here.

An old trail leading westward into the Chetwood is clearly marked, but it is soon lost in the eastward direction, swallowed by the marshes. The ground that lies above the level of the many dark pools in this area is very damp - giving slightly at each step.
117918: A small raised ridge of earth along the border of the marsh provides a home for a veritable tangle of young willow trees. To the south and east, the ground drops and then levels off into the untracked fens of the Midgewater, while to the north and west, a seldom-used trail runs.
117919: Water six inches deep covers the black earth, providing sustenance to unnumbered cattails. The ground beneath the water is a soupy organic sludge that sucks and pulls with each step. All around are hordes of insects - most of whom seem to bite or sing - that have taken advantage of the ideal environment provided by the marsh.
117920: The relatively flat ground of this area supports a great quantity of high grass that, judging from the spoor, in turn supports a large population of small mammals. To the south and east lies the Midgewater Marshes. To the west, the grass is dotted with small patches of hardwood.
117921: The water table is just below the surface here, and footprints quickly fill with water. Many varieties of sawgrass have flourished here on the northern edge of the Midgewater Marshes, and care must be taken to avoid being cut by their serrated blades. Circling this area along the northern edge, a small trail leads from east to west.
117922: Only twelve to fifteen feet wide, this small ledge forms a rocky path, yet seems quite safe to walk on. It leads along a dense wall of rock. Tiny bushes and wild grass grow out of cracks in the surface of the rock in the wall as well as on the path itself. Near the brink, the hard stone begins to crumble and break a sign of the passage of time and weather.
117923: Guard Post in Some Rolling Hills
A faded gaming table sits in the dirt.

Viewing holes cut into the black leather wall provide a limited view of hills to the west. Wooden chairs are placed in front of the holes, creating a primitive lookout spot in this guard post. The air inside the tent smells of stale beer and sweat.
117924:
A sturdy crate made of nailed wooden planks sits on the floor.
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

A turn in the hill here creates a natural windbreak, and a open-air storage tent has been constructed into it out of aged brown leather. Wooden provision crates are stacked neatly along the perimeter, and leather-wrapped poles prop up the sides. The ground here is a jumbled mix of pebbles, weeds, and patches of grass. To the north and east, a grassy path begins.
117925: East of an Open Storage Tent
A colourful butterfly is fluttering around here.

The hills to the north and south create a natural crease for a grassy path. The grass here has been kept short, and shows moderate use. To the west lies an open-aired storage tent, and the grassy pocket of a path continues eastward.
117926: The grassy path here is straddled on the north and south by tall hills. A broken, rocky, and nondescript stub of an ancient building lies on the southern hill. Within it a cluster of flower patches and shrubs have taken residence. The grassy path continues east and west.
117927: Tall green hills to the north and east guide the grassy path west and southward. A partially buried and cracked stone slab leans against a giant bay tree. Faint lines chiselled into it form a human warrior with an oversized shield and sword.
117928: The trampled, muddy, and rooty ground here shows signs of heavy use. To the east, a large brown leather tent is nestled within overgrown grass. A cracked skull is stitched into its skin using white leather strips, and its open doorway flutters in the breeze. To the north, a grassy path begins, and tall hills southward prevent further travel.
117929: Heavy use of this muddy path have exposed roots and subsurface rocks. The path forks here east-west and south. A mighty elm grows at the peak of the hill to the north. Thick green moss forms a patchy carpet on its bark, and twin vines dance up the tree.
117930: A thin veneer of grass winds its way east and west between decaying ruins to the north and south. Leaves, twigs and stones have collected at the bottom of a small depression here. Broken and twisted roots peek out from the sides of it. A tall and thorn-covered leather tent sits to the south. Two moneybags are crudely painted onto the side of it.
117931: The grass and vegetation here is sparse, indicating a well-trodden path. A towering, ancient oak provides shade and a home to a variety of fauna. A large, black leather tent is concealed within a decimated stone structure to the south. Two parallel swords are etched into its exterior with thin animal bones. To the east and west, the dirt path continues between the hills.
117932:
A beer barrel has been left here.
A small oaken table has been set here.
On the table, there are a bowl of gruel and a morsel of meat.
